{Merged research report built from twenty-four manuscripts (03, 04, 06--11 of one batch,\par

\begin{minipage}{0.9\textwidth}
\begin{abstract}
Write an omnific integer uniquely as $n+s$ with $n\in\Z$ and $s$ purely infinite, and let
$\ct(n+s)=n$. Every additive and multiplicative map from $\Oz$ to a set-sized ring, even
a noncommutative, nonreduced or nonunital one, has the form $x\mapsto\ct(x)e$ with $e$
idempotent; every set-sized $\Oz$-module is an abelian group with scalar action through
$\ct$. The same holds for $D+\Pi_K$ over any set field $K$ and unital $D\subseteq K$, for
the Gaussian ring $\Oz[i]$ (with $\Z[i]$), and, on the finite side, for standard part on
the finite surreal and surcomplex rings. Countable supports already force this
collapse while finite supports do not.

Over set-sized exponent groups the theorem becomes a detection threshold. For each of
five explicit set-sized rings (four integer parts inside $\Oz$, of sizes $\kappa^{\aleph_0}$,
$\kappa^{<\kappa}$, $\kappa$ and $\lambda$, and a lexicographic Hahn ring of size
$\kappa^{<\kappa}$), the least size of a ring
or module detecting any nonzero purely infinite element equals the size of the ring;
two of these values, and the exact thresholds of two examples in fixed exponent groups,
are new to this merge. The report also keeps the large-quotient side (a copy of $\No$ and
a Cantor algebra inside $\Oz/(1+\omega^a)$), the integral and complete integral closures
of $\Oz$, the arithmetic of integer-valued polynomials on $\Oz$, and a negative answer to a
posted question on natural ordinal arithmetic. Five later manuscripts add the ordinary
homological and tensor algebra of subrings of $\Oz$: for set-sized finite-support cores the
arithmetic quotient has flat dimension $d$ when the exponents form a coordinatewise cone of
rank $d$ and $1$ when they form a totally ordered cone, and coefficient-lattice ideals have
explicit tensor, Rees and duality algebra; and they add a fresh-scale image-gap theorem for
polynomial and rational maps. Three manuscripts of a third batch add exact relation counts and $\Tor$
groups of these ideals, a sharp bound on the ordinary outputs of integer-valued polynomials, and the
integral closure of $\Oz$ modulo the ideal generated by $\Pi$ as a Boolean power of the algebraic integers. A fourth
adds that the Boolean algebra of that power is atomless and a proper class, split uniformly over every set-sized subring,
with integrality local to the exponent group of an element. A fifth shows that for the coordinatewise cone of
rank $d$ the projective dimension of the arithmetic quotient is $d+1$. A sixth certifies rational functions of several
variables by finitely many values at one fresh scale, removes set-sized exceptional sets in every number of variables, and
transfers ordinary constant test sets exactly. A seventh shows that over one cyclic exponent group the extended ideal of
the integral closure is not radical, while the Boolean algebra of the reduced fibre is still atomless. Two manuscripts of an eighth batch
show, with global choice, that $1+\omega^a$ lies in characteristic-zero maximal class ideals of $\Oz$, modulo which exactly the monomials
$\omega^b$ with $b>na$ for every $n$ vanish and whose residue fields embed in $\SC$; and that a globally smooth semialgebraic map preserving
$\Oz^r$ is an integer-valued polynomial, while finitely smooth ones need not be even piecewise polynomial. Two more compute the flat
dimensions of radical monomial quotients of cone cores by the topology of their faces, and build set-sized omnific integer parts whose
henselization at the constant-term ideal has the maximal number of minimal primes although its completion is $\Q$. It is an AI-assisted
merge of unrefereed manuscripts; nothing in it is verified in Lean.
\end{abstract}
\end{minipage}

\section{Introduction}\label{osq:sec:intro}

\subsection{The question and the answer}\label{osq:sub:question}
The omnific integers $\Oz=\Z\oplus\Pi$ form a discretely ordered subring of $\No$ whose
fraction field is all of $\No$. Their purely infinite ideal $\Pi$ is a proper class; each of
its elements has a set-sized normal form, but below any positive exponent there is a proper
class of smaller exponent scales. The eight manuscripts of the first merge (03, 04, 06--11) ask
the same question: \emph{what can an ordinary, set-sized ring or module see of an omnific
integer?} All eight give the same answer, by different proofs, and two later manuscripts (13, 15)
reprove it independently: exactly its ordinary integer constant term. This
is much stronger than the observation that a proper-class field cannot embed in a set: the
source is a ring, its homomorphisms have large kernels, and the targets may have zero
divisors, nilpotents, noncommutative multiplication and any characteristic (06, 11). Nor is
it a consequence of divisibility of $\Pi$ by every integer, which only disposes of targets
of positive characteristic (04, 07).

The sources then go in different directions: exact cardinal thresholds for set-sized
integer parts (03, 06, 08, 09, 11), the finite side and the support threshold (04, 11), the
large quotients in which a purely infinite element becomes a unit (07), integral closure
(03), polynomial maps (10), and natural ordinal arithmetic (11). Three later manuscripts add
the ordinary homological and tensor algebra of subrings of $\Oz$ with finite supports or with
coefficient lattices (12, 14; \cref{osq:hd:sec:cores}), and fresh-scale arguments for polynomial and
rational maps (16; \cref{osq:fs:sub:gaps,osq:fs:sub:tests}). Three manuscripts of a third batch extend
three of these directions: relation modules, $\Tor$ groups and isomorphism classes of coefficient-lattice
ideals (17; \cref{osq:rel:sub:relations}), the ordinary-output loci of integer-valued polynomials (18;
\cref{osq:or:sub:outputs}), and the arithmetic fibre of the integral closure (19; \cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}). A manuscript
of a fourth batch determines how that fibre branches: its Boolean algebra of idempotents is atomless and a proper class,
and integrality is local to the exponent group of an element (20; \cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}).
A manuscript of a fifth batch determines the projective dimensions of the coordinate-cone cores, which 12 had bounded, and
computes the $\Tor$ algebra of lattice quotients, with arithmetic applications (21; \cref{osq:da:sub:derived}).
A manuscript of a sixth batch certifies rational functions of several variables by finitely many values at a single fresh scale,
removes set-sized exceptional sets in every number of variables and lifts ordinary constant test sets exactly; much of its
one-variable content re-derives 16's (22; \cref{osq:ft:sub:tests}).
A manuscript of a seventh batch decides the fixed-workspace questions on that fibre for cyclic exponent groups, with opposite
answers: the extended ideal is not radical, while the Boolean algebra of the reduced fibre is atomless, both by ramification over
the place $\omega^a=0$ of the rational functions in $\omega^a$ (23; \cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}).
Two manuscripts of an eighth batch go beyond set-sized targets and beyond polynomial maps. With global choice, every proper class ideal lies
in a maximal class ideal, so $1+\omega^a$ lies in characteristic-zero maximal ideals of $\Oz$ whose residue fields are proper-class fields embedded
in $\SC$, and the monomials vanishing there are exactly the $\omega^b$ with $b>na$ for every ordinary $n$ (24; \cref{osq:cr:sub:residues}).
Globally smooth semialgebraic maps preserving $\Oz^r$ are the integer-valued polynomials, while for every finite order of smoothness an
explicit bump, built at the same scale threshold, agrees with no finite family of polynomials on $\Oz$ (25; \cref{osq:sa:sub:semialgebraic}).
Two further manuscripts of that batch extend the cores and the fibre. Over an arbitrary rational polyhedral cone, the flat dimension of the quotient
keeping a face is the largest dimension of a face disjoint from it, so that the cone is simplicial exactly when every facet quotient has flat dimension one
(26; \cref{osq:pc:sub:polyhedral}). And a set-sized omnific integer part $\mathbb E\cap\Oz$ of any infinite cardinality $\kappa$ can have an idempotent
constant-term ideal whose local ring has completion $\Q$ but a henselization with $2^\kappa$ minimal primes, all with complex fraction field
(27; \cref{osq:hb:sub:henselian}).
This report prints the common spine once and keeps every result of every source.

\subsection{Main theorems}\label{osq:sub:main}

\begin{maintheorem}[Universal set-sized quotient]\label{osq:main:universal}
Let $K$ be a set field and $D\subseteq K$ a unital subring. Every additive multiplicative map
from $D+\Pi_K$ to a set-sized ring kills $\Pi_K$ and factors uniquely through $\ct$; unital
maps correspond bijectively to unital maps from $D$; every set-sized module is annihilated
by $\Pi_K$. For $\Oz$ the unique unital map to a set-sized ring $S$ is $x\mapsto\ct(x)1_S$, and
unital maps $\GOz\to S$ correspond to $j\in S$ with $j^2=-1$. The kernels admitting set-sized
quotients are exactly the $\ct^{-1}(\mathfrak a)$; for $\Oz$ they are $\Pi$ and $n\Oz$
($n\ge1$). (\Cref{osq:thm:universal,osq:cor:Oz,osq:cor:gaussian,osq:thm:quotients}; the eight
sources of the first merge, manuscripts 13 and 15, and manuscript 05 of the sibling report.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[The finite side and the support threshold]\label{osq:main:support}
Standard part is the universal set-sized quotient of the finite surreal and surcomplex rings,
and more generally of $D+\mm_k$ (04). For every infinite $\lambda$, the rings of normal forms
with supports of size at most $\lambda$ (full surreal exponents) already have universal
set-sized quotient $D$ on both sides, while the finite-support rings admit the augmentation
$\sum c_g\omega^g\mapsto\sum c_g$; a map on the finite-support ring extends to the countable-support
ring if and only if it factors through $\ct$ or $\st$ on the respective side (the failure for the augmentation is 04's and 11's,
the criterion is 11's). (\Cref{osq:thm:finite,osq:thm:support}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Detection threshold equals size]\label{osq:main:thresholds}
For each of five explicit set-sized rings $A$, namely four integer parts inside $\Oz$, of cardinality
$\kappa^{\aleph_0}$ ($\cf\kappa>\aleph_0$; 03), $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ ($\kappa$ regular
uncountable; 06), $\kappa$ (every infinite $\kappa$; 08) and $\lambda$ ($\lambda$ infinite, $\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$;
09), and 11's lexicographic Hahn ring of cardinality $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ (coefficient field with at
most $\max(\kappa,2^{\aleph_0})$ elements), the least cardinality of a ring target
or module detecting any nonzero purely infinite element is exactly $|A|$, in ZFC.
(\Cref{osq:thm:thresholds}.) The values for 06's and 11's rings are new here: 06 and 11 prove
exactness only under $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, and the unconditional value $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ follows
from 06's own collision lemma (\cref{osq:thm:model06,osq:prop:card11}). The same thresholds hold
for the first and second $\Ext$ groups of the homological package of 06, which extends to all five
rings (\cref{osq:thm:homological,osq:thm:extthreshold}).
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[The field bound in a fixed exponent group]\label{osq:main:fieldbound}
In a set-sized Hahn integer part, a ring or module detecting an element divisible by $X^{2c}$
has at least as many elements as the field $L_c(F)$ of elements of the ambient field $F$
supported in the scale subgroup $H_c$ (03, generalized through 06's lemma). This bound is exact in 04's example $\Q\oplus_{\mathrm{lex}}\Q$, where it
equals $2^{\aleph_0}$, and in an example with rational coefficients it exceeds by far all the
monomial and weighted counts of 04, 07 and 10, showing that 10's bound need not be attained.
(\Cref{osq:prop:fieldbound,osq:ex:lexQQ,osq:ex:countablecoeff}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Large internal fields]\label{osq:main:internal}
If a nonzero purely infinite element becomes a unit in a nonzero ring, the ring contains an
explicitly embedded copy of $\No$. The nonzero quotient $\Oz/(1+\omega^a)$, which has no
nonzero set-sized image, contains an algebraically closed field containing $\SC$, exact
cyclotomic algebras over it, and the Cantor algebra of locally constant functions on $\Z_2$
(07; one proposition of 06). With global choice, every proper class ideal of a commutative class ring lies in a maximal class
ideal, a principle equivalent to global choice; so $1+\omega^a$ lies in at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ maximal class ideals of $\Oz$, all of
characteristic $0$, modulo each of which $\omega^b$ ($b\ge0$) vanishes if $b>na$ for every ordinary $n$ and is a unit otherwise; these
residue fields embed in $\SC$, and the maps $\Oz\to\SC$ so obtained separate points, those vanishing on some $1+\omega^a$ without preserving
strong summability (24).
(\Cref{osq:if:thm:transfer,osq:if:thm:binomialkernel,osq:if:thm:cantor,osq:cr:thm:krull,osq:cr:thm:equivalence,osq:cr:thm:binomialmax,osq:cr:thm:cutoff,osq:cr:thm:cantor,osq:cr:thm:residually}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Closures and invisible equations]\label{osq:main:closure}
The complete integral closure of $\Oz$ is $\No$, while its integral closure is a proper,
fine-dense subring with zero conductor that no set generates; its constant slice is the real
algebraic integers, it has no finite quotients, and no nontrivial set-valued valuation of $\No$
contains $\Oz$ (03). For $\gamma>0$ and $m\ge2$ the equation $X^m=\omega^\gamma+1$ has no root in
$\GOz$, yet its image in every set-sized ring has the root $1$ (08). The extended ideal $\Pi\NN$ is
radical, $\NN/\Pi\NN$ is the finite-partition Boolean power $\overline\Z[\Idem]$ of the ring of all
complex algebraic integers, complexification doubles it integrally, and every set-sized domain image of
$\NN$ or $\NN_\C$ is $\overline\Z$ or $\Fpbar$ (19). Its Boolean algebra $\Idem(\NN/\Pi\NN)$ is atomless and a
proper class, one idempotent splits every nonzero element of any set-sized subring of $\NN/\Pi\NN$, and no set-indexed family
of maps to set-sized rings is jointly faithful on it; an element of $\NN$ supported in a set-sized group $G$ is integral over
the omnific integers supported in $G$ (20). In a cyclic workspace $\Z+\omega^a\R[\omega^a]$ the extended ideal of the
integral closure is not radical, its fibre having nilpotents of every index, while the Boolean algebra of the reduced fibre is atomless of
cardinality and order density $2^{\aleph_0}$, and the bounded-denominator Puiseux limit is reduced (23). For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$ a
real closed $\mathbb E\subseteq\No$ of cardinality $\kappa$ has an omnific integer part $\mathbb E\cap\Oz$ whose local ring at the constant-term ideal has
completion $\Q$, while its henselization has exactly $2^\kappa$ minimal primes, all with fraction field $\mathbb E[i]$ (27).
(\Cref{osq:hb:thm:main,osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:cor:atomless,osq:rm:thm:cardinality,osq:rm:thm:pui,osq:nm:thm:complete,osq:nm:thm:normalization,osq:nm:thm:valuation,osq:nm:thm:invisible,osq:nf:thm:radical,osq:nf:thm:boolean,osq:nf:thm:doubling,osq:nf:thm:domainimages,osq:bb:thm:descent,osq:bb:thm:uniform,osq:bb:thm:atoms,osq:bb:thm:noseparating}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Polynomial maps]\label{osq:main:polynomial}
The ring of finite-degree surreal polynomials preserving $\Oz^r$ is $\Pi[\mathbf X]\oplus\Int(\Z^r)$
with universal set-sized image $\Int(\Z^r)$; a Newton least-common-multiple condition decides
congruence preservation modulo every omnific integer; the $p$-adic completion is $C(\Z_p^r,\Z_p)$
and most of its characters are not evaluations; rational self-maps of $\Oz$ and $\GOz$ are
polynomial and the bijections are affine (10). For every unital $D\subseteq k\in\{\R,\C\}$ and every
polynomial $f$ of degree at least two with coefficients in a set-sized Hahn field $K_G$, a fresh
monomial $t$ has $f(D+\Pi_k)\cap(f(t)+K_G)=\{f(t)\}$, every root of $f(Y)=f(t)+c$ ($c\ne0$) having an
explicit forbidden block of negative exponents; rational self-maps of $D+\Pi_k$ are polynomials and the
surjective ones are the affine maps $uX+a$, $u\in D^\times$; $d+1$ points test degree $d$ and no fewer do,
while no set-sized sample tests all rational self-maps (16). A polynomial of degree $d\ge1$ preserving
$\Oz$ (or $\GOz$) sends at most $d$ inputs to $\Z$ (or $\Z[i]$) unless $f(X)=\ct_*(f)(X-\eta)$ for a
unique purely infinite $\eta$, which the two highest coefficients determine; in degree at least two at
most one coset $b+\Z$ (or $b+\Z[i]$) has more than $d$ preimages (18). For rational functions of $m$ variables with
coordinate degrees at most $d$, the values on an ordinary box and on $m$ grids with one coordinate at a single fresh monomial, at most
$(d+1)^m+m(2d^2+2d+1)^{m-1}$ of them, certify preservation of $\Oz$ (similarly of $\GOz$); set-sized exceptional sets are removable in
every number of variables; $\Num_m(\Oz)\cong\Oz\otimes_\Z\Int(\Z^m)$ and $\Num_m(\GOz)\cong\GOz\otimes_{\Z[i]}\Int(\Z[i]^m)$; and a
finite subset of $\Z^m$ (or $\Z[i]^m$) tests preservation of $\Oz$ (or $\GOz$) exactly when it tests $\Int(\Z^m)$ (or $\Int(\Z[i]^m)$) (22).
Over a real closed field with a cofinal discretely ordered subring $B$, a globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic map preserving $B^r$ has
coordinates in $\Num_r(B)$ ($C^{\mathsf D^2}$ suffices at graph degree $\mathsf D$), and every semialgebraic preserver of $B$ is polynomial on its two
tails; for every ordinary $\mathsf k$ a semialgebraic $C^{\mathsf k}$ map sends $\Oz$ into $\Pi$ and agrees with no finite family of polynomials on
$\Oz$, and no set of sample points tests preservation of $\Oz$ even for globally smooth quadratic algebraic branches (25).
(\Cref{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany,osq:sa:thm:tails,osq:sa:thm:bumps,osq:sa:thm:nosettests,osq:pm:thm:numreal,osq:pm:thm:cp,osq:pm:cor:completion,osq:pm:cor:bijections,osq:fs:thm:imagegap,osq:fs:thm:surjective,osq:fs:thm:lower,osq:fs:thm:nosmall,osq:or:thm:canonical,osq:or:thm:targets,osq:ft:thm:certificate,osq:ft:thm:exceptions,osq:ft:thm:basechange,osq:ft:thm:lifting}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Natural ordinal arithmetic]\label{osq:main:ordinal}
The Grothendieck ring of the ordinals under natural operations is not a quotient of $\Oz$; every
unital ring map from $\Oz$ to it has image $\Z$. This answers negatively the quotient question in
MathOverflow question 188430 of Jesse Elliott (11; independently 13). (\Cref{osq:thm:ordinal}.)
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}[Homological and tensor algebra of omnific cores]\label{osq:hd:main:cores}
Let $D\subseteq K$ be $\Z\subset\R$ or $\Z[i]\subset\C$. The set-sized subring
$A_d=D+\bigoplus_{0\ne\boldsymbol\alpha\in\Q_{\ge0}^d}KX^{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ of $\Oz$ (or $\GOz$), whose exponents form a
coordinatewise cone of rank $d$, has $\Tor^{A_d}_{>0}(D,D)=0$ but $\fd_{A_d}D=d$, with a complete multigraded
computation of $\Tor^{A_d}(D,A_d/(X_i:i\in F))$, and its finite quotients are those of $D$ (12). Enlarging the cone to
all positive exponents of the same ordered group is a nonflat extension over which $\fd D=1$ and $\pd D=2$, as for the
totally ordered cones of \cref{osq:sec:homological} (12, with the merge). Over $A_d$ itself $\pd_{A_d}D=d+1$, one more than the
flat dimension, with an explicit free telescope resolution and an embedding $D^{\N}/D^{(\N)}\hookrightarrow\Ext^{d+1}_{A_d}(D,A_d)$ (21).
For a coefficient lattice $M\subset K$ of rank
$r\ge2$, the module $L(M)=M+\Pi$ over $\Oz$ or $\GOz$ (or over the set-sized model $A_1$) has first syzygy $\Pi^{r-1}$,
tensor square $\Pi\oplus(M\otimes M)$ whose torsion is $\ker(M\otimes M\to M^2)$, nonlinear Rees equations exactly the
ordinary relations among the generators (the first one in degree $d$ for $(\omega,2^{1/d}\omega)$), isomorphism type
determined by $M$ up to a scalar, ideal classes realizing $\operatorname{Pic}$ of an order, and dual $\Pi$ (14).
Over $\Oz$ such a module has no presentation by a set of generators and a set of relations; over the
lexicographic model $R^{11}_{\Gamma_\kappa,<\kappa}\subset\Oz$ every finite free presentation of it needs exactly
$\kappa$ relations, for every uncountable regular $\kappa$ (17) and for $\kappa=\aleph_0$ (merge); there, for
$J=X^gL(M)$ and $J'=X^hL(N)$, $\Tor_1(J,A/J')\cong\Tor_2(A/J,A/J')\cong\mathcal T(M,N)=\ker(M\otimes_DN\to K)$,
and the ideals $(\omega,\alpha\omega)$,
$\alpha\notin\Frac(D)$, form $2^{\aleph_0}$ isomorphism classes, the orbits of $\mathrm{GL}_2(D)$ acting by
fractional linear maps (17). Over $A_d$ the projective dimensions of $L(M)$ and $A_d/J_g(M)$ are $d+1$ and $d+2$; over $T_\Q$ and
over the class ring read in two universes, the second $\Tor$ of the quotients by $J_g(\mathfrak o_1)$ and $J_h(\mathfrak o_2)$ for two orders
vanishes exactly when their fields are linearly disjoint, the self-$\Tor$ product is the antisymmetrized boundary tensor, and the
framed second $\Tor$ of an order recovers its multiplication (21). Over the core of any pointed rational polyhedral cone the quotient
keeping a face $F$ has flat dimension the largest dimension of a face disjoint from $F$; hence the cone is simplicial exactly when every facet quotient has
flat dimension one (26).
(\Cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti,osq:pc:thm:simplicial,osq:hd:thm:boolean,osq:hd:cor:fd,osq:hd:thm:collapse,osq:hd:thm:fdlattice,osq:tn:thm:syzygy,osq:tn:thm:tensor,osq:tn:thm:rees,osq:tn:thm:hom,osq:tn:thm:pic,osq:tn:thm:duals,osq:rel:thm:presentation,osq:rel:thm:kappa,osq:rel:thm:tor,osq:rel:thm:mobius,osq:da:cor:exactpd,osq:da:thm:lattice,osq:da:thm:disjoint,osq:da:thm:product,osq:da:thm:reconstruction}.)
\end{maintheorem}

Manuscript~05 of the same batch, \emph{Omnific Integers and Diophantine Rigidity}, is merged

(its ``set-target rigidity''), the clearing of set supports and common monomial divisors, and it

first three to 05 and 04 credits its finite-quotient background to manuscript~02 of the same
sibling report. Those credits are kept.

\paragraph{Where the merge chose.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Base.} 06 is the base: its coefficient-ring theorem over any set field (also
proved by 07 and 10) is the most general statement, and its scaled-field collision lemma (with
03's field bound, a special case) is the mechanism that yields the sharp cardinal bounds where
counting monomials does not suffice (03, 06, 11 and the fixed-group examples; 08 and 09 reach
their thresholds by counting monomials). The proof is written in 08's
choice-free Hartogs form, with 08's and 10's nonunital forms and 06's direct module argument.
04's explicit telescope, 09's and 10's direct division, 11's pairwise-difference families and 07's
weighted certificates are kept as second routes (\cref{osq:sub:universalthm}).
\item \emph{Support threshold.} Printed once, in 11's formulation (every infinite support bound,
with the extension criterion) together with 04's negative side (\cref{osq:thm:support}).
\item \emph{Thresholds.} Organized by one theorem (\cref{osq:thm:thresholds}) with the five
constructions of \cref{osq:sec:models}; generator counts are listed per construction and no
general law is stated.
\item \emph{Homological algebra.} 06's package is proved under three hypotheses that all five
constructions satisfy (\cref{osq:thm:homological}).
\item \emph{Foundations.} NBG with choice for sets; global choice, stated by 04, 06, 09 (and 05) and
by 17, 19 and 20, is used only for the class ultrafilters of 19 and 20, and the results depending on them say so
(\cref{osq:sub:foundations,osq:bb:rem:choice}). (Status (batch 34): 24 adds an essential use, maximal class ideals
(\cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}), whose unrestricted form is equivalent to global choice (\cref{osq:cr:thm:equivalence}); every result of
\cref{osq:cr:sub:residues} built on it states $\mathsf{GBC}$. 25 reads its class-sized support fields through set-sized ones and uses no global choice.)
\item \emph{Later manuscripts.} 13 and 15 reprove the universal theorem and its consequences; they are
credited where each result is printed, and only two one-line additions of 15 are printed
(\cref{osq:rep:cor:kernels,osq:rep:prop:projectivity}); 13's answer to Elliott's question is credited in
\cref{osq:sec:ordinal}. 12 and 14 form one new section (\cref{osq:hd:sec:cores}), placed after the homological
package it is to be compared with; the ring $A_0=A_1$ and the two-generator syzygy are printed once, the syzygy
in 14's rank generality over 12's rings. 16's results sit with 10's polynomial maps; where they overlap (rational
collapse, affine surjections, transfer, grids) the general-$D$ statement is printed once with 16's fresh-scale
proof and 10's statements keep their finite-difference and lattice proofs as a second route. 14's criterion for
unimodular projective directions and 13's fiber and norm theorems are printed in the Diophantine report
\cite{RepoOdg}, not here.
\item \emph{Third batch.} Each of 17--19 joins the section it extends, with its new results in one new
subsection. About half of 17 re-derives 14 (matrix kernels, lattice syzygy, Hom and isomorphism types, orders,
tensor torsion, power growth, flat dimensions) and 12 (the intersection $X^gA\cap cX^gA$); these are printed
once, under 14's and 12's labels with 17 added as a proving source, and 17's new statements are in
\cref{osq:rel:sub:relations}. 18's description of $\Num_r$, its tests, its rational collapse and its classification of
surjections repeat 10 and 16 and are credited there; its dichotomy package is \cref{osq:or:sub:outputs}. 19
re-derives 03's constant slices, the absence of finite quotients, the complexification defect (with a different
witness) and the universal theorem (with 04's telescope); these are credited, and its fibre theory is
\cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}. Genuinely different proofs are kept as short second routes.
\item \emph{Fourth batch.} 20 answers 19's question on the Boolean algebra and joins 19's section in one new subsection
(\cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}), placed after 19's. About a third of 20 re-derives 19 (contraction, radicality, saturation, the
residue $\mathsf v$, the coefficient copy, spectral idempotents and the Boolean power, doubling and $w_\pm$, factorization of
set-sized images, domain images, class ultrafilters and detection) with the same constructions; these are printed once, under
19's labels with 20 added as a proving source, and 20's proof of the universal theorem for $\Oz$ is credited at
\cref{osq:thm:universal}. 20's dominant-scale lemma is 16's Laurent-block theorem, which 20 could not see; it is printed as
16's with 20's surjectivity step added (\cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent}). 20's class-ultrafilter lemma, which starts from a set with
the finite intersection property, is printed beside 19's (\cref{osq:bb:lem:classultra}).
\item \emph{Fifth batch.} 21 answers the first clause of 12's and 14's question \cref{osq:hd:q:cores} and joins their section in one new
subsection (\cref{osq:da:sub:derived}), placed at the end of \cref{osq:hd:sec:cores} so that no earlier statement is renumbered; the
bounds it sharpens (\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}) carry pointers to it. Its second part re-derives 17's second-$\Tor$ identification with its rank,
the self-$\Tor$ rank, the pair $\Z[\sqrt2]$, $\Z[\sqrt3]$ and the $\Tor$ groups against modules killed by the tail, which 21 could not see;
these are printed once, under 17's labels with 21 added as a proving source (\cref{osq:rel:thm:tor,osq:rel:cor:selftor,osq:rel:thm:augmentation}),
and 21's extension of them to the class ring in a two-universe reading is stated in \cref{osq:da:sub:derived}. 21's flat face resolution,
flat dimensions and coefficient syzygy repeat 12's and 14's (\cref{osq:hd:thm:resolution,osq:hd:cor:fd,osq:hd:thm:fdlattice,osq:tn:thm:syzygy}),
as 21 says, and are cited, not reprinted. Its three questions are merged into \cref{osq:hd:q:cores,osq:tn:q:lattices,osq:rel:q:relations}.
\item \emph{Sixth batch.} 22 joins \cref{osq:sec:polynomial} in one new subsection (\cref{osq:ft:sub:tests}), placed after \cref{osq:pm:sub:scope} at the
end of the section so that no earlier statement is renumbered. About half of 22 re-derives 10's and 16's results, which were in this report at 22's pin
but which 22 did not read; these are printed once, under their labels with 22 added as a proving source
(\cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial,osq:pm:thm:grid,osq:pm:thm:numreal,osq:pm:thm:numgaussian,osq:fs:lem:fresh,osq:fs:thm:embedding,osq:fs:thm:lower,osq:fs:thm:nosmall}),
and its one-variable certificate, detector, multivariate collapse and one-variable removal of exceptions are credited at

(\cref{osq:ft:rem:probes}). Its question on Gaussian constant tests is merged into \cref{osq:fs:q:fresh}, and its other questions form

\paragraph{Results added in the merge.} Each carries the tag \merge\ and a complete proof:
the field bound for an arbitrary subfield of a fixed-group Hahn field
(\cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}); the exact thresholds $2^{\aleph_0}$ in 04's example and in the
rational-coefficient example (\cref{osq:ex:lexQQ,osq:ex:countablecoeff}), which answer 04's
question for its own example and show that 10's bound need not be attained; the criterion (b$'$) in \cref{osq:thm:criterion};
the exact value $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ of the sizes and thresholds of $A^{06}_\kappa$ and of 11's
example, in ZFC (\cref{osq:lem:card06,osq:thm:model06,osq:prop:card11}), which answers the first
half of 06's question on cardinal arithmetic (08 answers the second half); the organizing
theorem itself (\cref{osq:thm:thresholds}) and the reconciliation of the realized cardinals
(\cref{osq:rem:reconcile}); the homological package and the $\Ext$ thresholds for all five
constructions (\cref{osq:thm:homological,osq:thm:extthreshold}); the negative-side extension
criterion (\cref{osq:thm:support}(iv)); the embedding $\No\hookrightarrow\Frac(\Oz/P)$ for primes
not containing $\Pi$ (\cref{osq:if:rem:composition}); and the explicit elements of the
normalization provided by 08's equation (\cref{osq:nm:rem:rootinN}). From the later manuscripts:
the syzygy, noncoherence and nonflatness theorems in the common generality of 12's and 14's rings
(\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy,osq:tn:prop:nonflat}); the flat dimensions of lattice modules and cyclic quotients over
every core, which removes a superfluous hypothesis of 12 (\cref{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice}); exact projective dimensions
where 12 gives bounds, and $\pd D=2$ for every ring of \cref{osq:sec:homological} with countably generated tail
(\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}); and the comparison of the two kinds of flat-dimension statements
(\cref{osq:hd:rem:reconcile}). From the third batch: 17's relation count, flat dimensions and $\Tor$ formula for
$\kappa=\aleph_0$, with $\pd\Pi=1$ and $\pd L(M)=2$ there (\cref{osq:rel:rem:alephzero}); 17's $\Tor$ formula over 12's
cores and 14's $A_0$, which gives $\rk\Tor_2(A/H,A/H)=4-\rk(M^2)$ for 12's cyclic modules without the hypothesis $c^2\in D$
(\cref{osq:rel:thm:tor,osq:rel:cor:twelve}); the comparison of 18's and 16's Gaussian tests (\cref{osq:or:prop:gausstest}); and
the explicit candidates for idempotents of $\NN/\Pi\NN$ and the domain-image form of 08's invisible roots
(\cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates,osq:nf:rem:rootimages}). From the fourth batch: the descent
$\NN\cap F^{03}_\kappa=\NN_\kappa$ asked by 03, with its radical and Gaussian forms, from 20's support projection
(\cref{osq:bb:cor:descent03}); the splitting by 03's unit, which decides both candidates of \cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates}
(\cref{osq:bb:prop:candidates}); the observation that 20's splitting results need no global choice (\cref{osq:bb:rem:choice});
and the remark that $\mathsf B_\R$ is residually set-sized although no set of small targets is jointly faithful
(after \cref{osq:bb:thm:noseparating}). From the fifth batch: 21's projective dimensions of lattice modules over $A_d$ for every unital
$D\subseteq K$ (21 assumes a principal ideal domain only to have a basis; \cref{osq:da:thm:lattice}); and the observation that 21's cores
$A_d$ satisfy every hypothesis of \cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(v) except (H2) and have $\pd D=d+1$, so (H2) cannot be dropped there
(\cref{osq:da:rem:htwo}). From the sixth batch: the comparison of 22's single-scale certificate with 16's probe certificate
(\cref{osq:ft:rem:probes}); the conclusion of 16's no-set-test theorem for $\A_{D,k}$ with every unital $D\ne k$ (\cref{osq:ft:rem:otherD}); and the
observation that where 22's criterion gives no fresh exponent, 18's discrete-gap collapse still holds (after \cref{osq:ft:prop:relative}).
From the seventh batch: the comparison with the full class, that $\Pi\NN\cap K_{\Z a}$ is the radical of 23's extended ideal, so that the map of
the cyclic arithmetic fibre to $\NN/\Pi\NN$ kills exactly its nilradical and the radical in \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent} cannot be removed
(\cref{osq:rm:rem:fullclass}), with the explicit $\sqrt{\omega^{2a}+\omega^a}=\omega^{a/2}\sqrt{1+\omega^a}\in\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:rm:ex:sqrt}); the second
route to 23's Puiseux radicality through 19's finite-axiom theorem, with the Boolean-power form, doubling and absolute integral closedness of the
Puiseux fibre and the atomlessness of its Boolean algebra (\cref{osq:rm:rem:puiabstract}); the Boolean-power form of the cyclic reduced fibre, with
an atomless parameter of size and density $2^{\aleph_0}$, and for the real algebraic fragment the ring of locally constant $\overline\Z$-valued
functions on Cantor space (\cref{osq:rm:rem:booleanform}); and 19's $\upsilon_T$ as a witness inside the cyclic workspace (\cref{osq:rm:rem:nonreal}).
From the eighth batch: 19's and 20's class-ultrafilter lemmas as the Boolean-ring case of 24's maximal class extensions, for class families as well
as sets (\cref{osq:cr:rem:ultrafilters}); a second route to 24's monomial cutoff through 07's localization and the support description of
$\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$ (\cref{osq:cr:rem:cutofflocal}); a copy of $\SC$, not only an algebraically closed Hahn field, in every residue field above
$1+\omega^a$ (\cref{osq:cr:cor:properfield}); the identification of 24's first idempotents with 07's (\cref{osq:cr:rem:dyadic}); the extension of 07's
point evaluations on the Cantor subalgebra to homomorphisms of all of $\Qa_a$ onto fields containing $\EE_a$ (\cref{osq:cr:rem:evaluation}); the
observation that the embedded $\FF_a$ alone does not distinguish the maximal ideals above one binomial (status of \cref{osq:q:primes}); the
containment of \cref{osq:lem:Ha}(ii), \cref{osq:if:lem:gf} and 16's freshness in 25's absorption theorem (after \cref{osq:sa:thm:absorption}); the
equivalence of 24's and 25's thresholds with absorption of $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$ and with $\omega^b/(1+\omega^a)\in\Oz$
(\cref{osq:sa:rem:threshold}); $C^{\mathsf k}$ examples showing that 25's removal of exceptions needs global smoothness
(\cref{osq:sa:rem:exceptionsnecessary}); the isomorphism of a rational simplicial cone core with $A_d$, through which 26's simplicial face dimensions are
21's and the projective dimension of every simplicial face quotient is the upper endpoint of 26's interval (\cref{osq:pc:sub:polyhedral}); the flat
dimensions $d$ and $d+1$ of rank-at-least-two lattice modules and their quotients over every cone core, hence weak global dimension at least $d+1$ when $K\ne\Frac D$
(\cref{osq:pc:rem:lattice}); the identification of 27's $\sqrt{\Pi\NN}$ with $\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:hb:sub:henselian}); and the comparison of the branch
counts of 20, 23 and 27 (\cref{osq:hb:rem:counts}).
Each follows from lemmas of the sources; none is a new method.

\subsection{Relation to the repository}\label{osq:sub:repository}
The foundations report defines $\Oz=\Pi\oplus\Z$ (\nolinkurl{found:eq:omnific} in
\cite{RepoFound}), and omnific integers appear as kernels and integer parts in the trigonometry,
gamma--zeta, analysis and euclidean-three-space reports; the sibling report \cite{RepoOdg} treats
their Diophantine geometry. The euclidean-three-space report proves the group analogue of the
finite-side theorem for $\mathrm{SO}(3,\No)$ (\cref{osq:sec:finite}). The first-kappa report proves
closedness of bounded-support Hahn fields, which contains the closure step of 06's construction
(06 proves that step itself; \cref{osq:sub:model06}). Its Part~II (batch 32) treats the class fields of surreals
with fewer than $\kappa$ terms, whose omnific parts are the bounded rings of \cref{osq:thm:support}~(i) for $D=\Z$,
$k=\R$ and $\lambda=\kappa$; see the notes in and after the proof of that theorem. The
$\kappa$-bounded coefficient rings $\Z+K(\!(G^{<0})\!)_\kappa$ of L'Innocente--Mantova \cite{LM} are
the published precedent for the bounded-support rings of 06 and 11. The Hahn-evaluation report
\cite{RepoHahnEval}, cited by 12, separates finite polynomial evaluation at $\omega$ from evaluation of
unrestricted series; 12's embeddings use finite normal forms only. The repository now has actual
omnific and Gaussian omnific rings and shared support, degree, unit and ideal results;
their exact scope is mapped in \texttt{docs/FORMALIZATION.md}. The full-class universal
quotient theorem and the later cardinal classifications still need their own formal proofs.

\paragraph{Stale statements corrected.} Three sources report a repository code search for
``omnific'' with no hits (06, 08, 11; 09 reports an explicitly incomplete result). At their pins
the repository already defined $\Oz$ at \nolinkurl{found:eq:omnific} and used it in the reports
listed above; what it lacked was a report devoted to omnific arithmetic, and the collection now has
two (this one and \cite{RepoOdg}). 03's companion draft and 04's ``prior manuscript'' were not in the
repository at their pins; they are now manuscripts 05 and 02 of \cite{RepoOdg}. 07's description of
the staging directory (``Gamma--zeta ZIP archives'') was true at its pin and is a snapshot statement.
Of the later manuscripts, 13 and 15 (and 15's audit file) report that a repository search for ``omnific''
returned no matches; at their pin \texttt{71e9606} the foundations report already defined $\Oz$ at
\nolinkurl{found:eq:omnific}. 13 and 15 call the universal theorem a proposed, respectively candidate-original,
contribution, and 13 calls its answer to Elliott's question one; the same theorem and the same answer are in the
eight manuscripts of the first merge, dated a day earlier (\cref{osq:thm:universal,osq:thm:ordinal}), which 13 and 15
could not see, so both are independent re-derivations. 16 found no integer-valued-polynomial treatment in the
repository; at its pin that was accurate, and the collection now has 10's (\cref{osq:sec:polynomial}). 14's
``companion manuscripts'' are manuscripts 02 and 05 of the Diophantine report \cite{RepoOdg} and 03 of this one.
Of the third batch, 17 proposes as additions the constant-matrix descent criterion, the coefficient-lattice $\Hom$
and isomorphism classification and the multiplication-kernel computation of $\Tor$, with their consequences for
orders and ideal powers; at its pin \texttt{71e9606} none of these was in the repository, but the collection now
prints the descent criterion, the $\Hom$ classification, the multiplication kernel of the tensor square and the
power growth as 14's, and the intersection $(\omega^\gamma)\cap(\alpha\omega^\gamma)=\omega^\gamma\Pi$ as 12's
(\cref{osq:tn:thm:matrix,osq:tn:thm:hom,osq:tn:thm:tensor,osq:tn:cor:alldegrees,osq:tn:thm:syzygy}), so 17 is credited
there as an independent second source; its catalogue count of 49 main texts is a snapshot. 18 reports that targeted
repository searches for integer-valued polynomial and rational terminology returned no matches; at its pin
\texttt{befe739} manuscript~10 was present only as its check program \texttt{code/10-omnific-arithmetic-checks.py},
and the collection now prints 10's and 16's integer-valued polynomials, finite tests and rational self-maps
(\cref{osq:sec:polynomial}). 19 reports that the catalogue lists nine omnific manuscripts awaiting integration; that
was true at its pin, and the first batch has since been written into this report and its sibling; 19's ``repository
quotient manuscript'' was 06's text, now this report. 20 (pin \texttt{4cdeaec}) reports that the catalogue separates the
main reports from companions awaiting integration and cites this report under 06's title and date; both were true at its pin,
and 19, which 20 read only as a saved draft, has since been placed and written into this report
(\cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}). 20 proposes support-local descent, the dominant-scale branch construction, relative freeness, the
answers on atoms and size and the representation bounds as new; the identification of a fresh scale with Laurent blocks
over the old Hahn field is 16's (\cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding,osq:fs:cor:blocktest}), which was not in the repository at 20's pin, and
the reproved antecedents are 19's, as 20 says. 21 (pin \texttt{9693b28}) quotes \cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(iii) as $d\le\pd_{A_d}D\le d+1$
with the next paragraph leaving the value undetermined for $d\ge2$, and (iv) as bounds for lattice modules; both were accurate at its pin,
and 21 itself now settles them (\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd,osq:da:thm:lattice}). 21 lists as its contributions, beside the dimensions, a
uniform arbitrary-scale calculation of all $\Tor$ groups of two lattice quotients, the additive second-$\Tor$ identification (which it calls a
dimension-shift consequence of the report's tensor calculation), the self-$\Tor$ ranks, second $\Tor$ as a linear-disjointness test and
the $\Tor$ groups against constant-term modules. At its pin the report did not yet contain 17's \cref{osq:rel:sub:relations}, written in
\texttt{aae58bb} after 21's pin; the collection now prints the second-$\Tor$ identification with its rank, the self-$\Tor$ range, the pair
$\Z[\sqrt2]$, $\Z[\sqrt3]$ and the $\Tor$ groups against modules killed by the tail as 17's
(\cref{osq:rel:thm:tor,osq:rel:cor:selftor,osq:rel:thm:augmentation}), and 21 is credited there as a further source. The ``quadratic
self-$\Tor$ example'' that 21 finds in the report is 12's $\Tor_2(A/H,A/H)\cong D\oplus D$ (\cref{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice}). 22 (pin
\texttt{bcac55a}) states, in its introduction and in its audit (\texttt{22-finite-tests-SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}, its Section~4), that the precise statements
of its proposed package were not located in the selected repository material it inspected. That material did not include this report, which at 22's
pin already contained the Laurent-block detector at one fresh scale (\cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding,osq:fs:thm:onepoint}), workspace-uniform rational

files keep these statements verbatim; the README records the corrections.

\paragraph{Corrections to the sources.} 03's source lost a relation symbol and prints
``$C$ e $B[i]$'' for $C\ne B[i]$ (\cref{osq:nm:prop:complexdefect}). 09 attributes the separated-scale
division to Proposition~8.2.1 of \cite{LM}; the displayed separated-scale factorization is
Fact~8.0.1 (Gonshor's Theorem~8.6) with its example on p.~46, as 11 cites, while
Proposition~8.2.1 is the truncation criterion for divisibility cited by 08
(\cref{osq:sub:telescope}). For infinite $\lambda$, 09's hypothesis $\lambda\ge2^{\aleph_0}$ is implied by
$\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$ (\cref{osq:sub:model09}). 04's remark on its $\Q\oplus_{\mathrm{lex}}\Q$
example is true but misleading (\cref{osq:rem:04misleading}). 06's remark that
$|A^{06}_\kappa/xA^{06}_\kappa|\ge\kappa$ ``under the cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis'' needs no
hypothesis and in fact gives $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ (\cref{osq:sec:homological}). 06, 04 and 09 state
global choice, which is never used (\cref{osq:sub:foundations}). 12 assumes $c^2\in D$ for its flat dimensions
$d+1$ and $2$ of cyclic modules, but needs it only for its $\Tor_2$ formula (\cref{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice}), and gives
only bounds for projective dimensions that are exact in rank one (\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}; 21 has since determined them for every $d$,
\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd,osq:da:thm:lattice}). 14 credits the
Diophantine report's example $[1:\sqrt2]$ but not its rationality theorem for primitive directions, of which 14's
criterion is the Gaussian and principal-ideal extension (\cref{osq:tn:sub:hom}). 16's rational collapse has the
D-ring precedent that 16 itself credits (\cref{osq:fs:thm:collapse}). 17 assumes $\kappa$ uncountable for its exact
relation count, but the proof uses only regularity, so $\kappa=\aleph_0$ is allowed (\cref{osq:rel:rem:alephzero}). 19 did
not see 03's text and reproves four of its results without credit; they are credited here
(\cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}). The real analogue of 18's question on minimal tests with omnific nodes is answered by 16's
optimality theorem; the Gaussian question itself stays open (\cref{osq:or:q:outputs}). 20's dominant-scale lemma repeats 16's
Laurent blocks without credit (it could not see them); they are credited (\cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent}). 21 repeats 17's $\Tor$ results without
credit (it could not see them); they are credited (\cref{osq:da:sub:derived}); its proofs contain no error found in this merge. 22 repeats
10's and 16's results without credit (it did not read this report); they are credited (\cref{osq:ft:sub:tests}), and its proofs contain no error
found in this merge. 23 does not cite 20's continuum family or 19's finite-axiom theorem (see above; credited in
\cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}); its proofs contain no error found in this merge. 24 and 25 repeat 07's field core and 10's numerical polynomials
with credit, and 18's collapse, 16's and 22's sampling and exception theorems without precise citation (credited in
\cref{osq:cr:sub:residues,osq:sa:sub:semialgebraic}); no error was found in their proofs. 26 and 27 repeat 12's, 21's and 20's results with
general credit (\cref{osq:pc:sub:polyhedral,osq:hb:sub:henselian}); 27's statement that a repository search for ``hensel'' returned no match is
inaccurate at its pin, and no error was found in their proofs. No source contains a false theorem.

\section{Conventions, notation, and the constant-term retraction}
\label{osq:sec:conv}

\subsection{Foundations}\label{osq:sub:foundations}
We work in von Neumann--Bernays--G\"odel class theory (NBG) with the axiom of
choice for sets. Every surreal number, every normal-form support and every
coefficient field or target ring called \emph{set-sized} is a set; the carriers
$\No$, $\Oz$, $\SC$ and most rings of \cref{osq:sec:gaps,osq:sec:universal} are
proper classes. A homomorphism with a class source is a class function obeying
the usual identities, and its restriction to a set is a set.

The sources state different foundations. Manuscript~06 works in G\"odel--Bernays
set theory with global choice, 09 in GBC, and 04 in ``GBC, with ordinary choice
for sets'' (GBC already contains global choice); 07, 08 and 11 work in NBG with
choice for sets, 10 in NBG with choice, and 03 in NBG for the classes and ZFC for
its set-sized constructions; 07 remarks that global choice is unnecessary.
\emph{No argument of the first two batches uses global choice.} Of the third batch, 17 and 19 state
G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice; 17's uses of it (choosing preimages, a Schanuel
splitting) are avoided below, and 19's one essential use, a class ultrafilter on a Boolean algebra
that may be a proper class, is stated with its hypothesis (\cref{osq:nf:lem:classultra}); only the
results built on it (\cref{osq:nf:thm:kernel,osq:nf:cor:fieldtargets}) need global choice. 20 states the same foundation;
its splitting results need only choice for sets (\cref{osq:bb:rem:choice}), and its extension of branch maps
(\cref{osq:bb:thm:manymaps}) uses class ultrafilters as 19's detection does. 23 uses only set-sized rings and choice for sets. 24 works in
G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice and uses it essentially: its maximal class ideals (\cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}) come from a recursion with
set-valued stages along a global well-order, and for all class rings the principle is equivalent to global choice (\cref{osq:cr:thm:equivalence});
the results of \cref{osq:cr:sub:residues} that need it say so, while its monomial cutoff, truncation and support-prime classification do not. 25 reads
proper-class support fields pointwise, through set-sized divisible hulls, and uses no global choice. 26 uses only set-sized rings and modules, the full
class ring appearing only as the target of an embedding and of a finite relation; 27 uses set-sized fields, rings and spectra, set-length recursion and
choice for sets, with no class Zorn lemma. The collision step of the
universal theorem (\cref{osq:thm:universal}) is choice-free in the formulation of
08, which we adopt: for a set $S$, its Hartogs ordinal is an ordinal that does not
inject into $S$; it exists in ZF. The same device is used in the rotation-group
theorem \nolinkurl{e3:cut:thm:smallquotient} of \cite{RepoE3}. Choice for sets enters
only where it is visibly needed: maximal ideals of set-sized rings
(\cref{osq:sec:models}), cardinal arithmetic such as
$\kappa^{\aleph_0}=\max(2^{\aleph_0},|[\kappa]^{\le\aleph_0}|)$, and the
existence of residue fields.

\begin{definition}[Set-sized quotients and detection]\label{osq:def:setquotient}
A class ideal $J$ of a class ring $R$ \emph{admits a set-sized quotient} if there is a
surjective class ring homomorphism $R\to S$ onto a set-sized ring with kernel~$J$.
A ring homomorphism $\varphi$ \emph{detects} $x$ if $\varphi(x)\neq0$; a module $M$
detects $x$ if $xM\neq0$.
\end{definition}

This is the convention of 04 (``set-realizable quotient''), 08, 09 (``set-sized
realization''), 10 (``set-sized quotient presentation'') and 11. Manuscripts 06 and 07
alternatively represent a class quotient by Scott codes (the members of a coset of least
set-theoretic rank form a nonempty set); every quotient statement below may be read in
either way, and no set or class whose members are arbitrary proper classes is formed.
Notation such as $\Hom(\Oz,S)$ abbreviates a statement about individual class maps and
their factorizations; after the universal theorem these maps are coded by their
restrictions to a set-sized coefficient ring.

\paragraph{The universe-relative reading.} Manuscripts 04, 10 and 11 add an equivalent
reading: fix a lower universe containing the coefficient fields, targets and supports,
and place the surreal carrier in a higher universe; ``set-sized'' then means small in the
lower universe. The size restriction must be carried in the statement. A set-sized
fragment of surreal arithmetic viewed in a larger universe has its own identity map as a
set-sized target, so it does not satisfy the full-class theorem (11 insists that its main
theorem is relative to one fixed universe, not to fragments viewed in a larger one).

\subsection{Normal forms and the orientation of exponents}\label{osq:sub:orientation}
A nonzero surreal has a unique Conway normal form
$x=\sum_{\gamma\in S}r_\gamma\omega^\gamma$ with nonzero real coefficients and a
\emph{reverse well-ordered set} $S$ of exponents (every nonempty subset has a greatest
element) \cite{Conway,Gonshor,Berarducci}. We use \emph{large monomials}:
$\omega^\gamma$ is infinitely large when $\gamma>0$, and
$\omega^{\gamma+\delta}=\omega^\gamma\omega^\delta$ is Conway's monomial law, not an
exponential. For an abstract ordered abelian group $G$ we write formal monomials $X^g$
with the same orientation, and $\hahn kG$ for the Hahn series over a set field $k$ with
reverse well-ordered set supports in $G$ (for $G=\No$ a proper class of series). The
usual small-monomial notation is recovered by $t^g=X^{-g}$; sources that write $t$
with well-ordered supports reverse all signs. A family is strongly summable if the
union of its supports is reverse well ordered and each exponent receives finitely many
contributions; strong sums are coefficientwise and are \emph{not} limits of partial sums
in the fine order topology.

\emph{Purely infinite} refers to support, not to size or sign: $-\omega$ is purely
infinite, while $\omega-1$ is infinite but not purely infinite. This is the convention of
the foundations report, which defines $\Oz=\Pi\oplus\Z$ with $\Pi$ the purely infinite
normal forms (\nolinkurl{found:eq:omnific} in \cite{RepoFound}); the gamma--zeta report
uses the same symbol \cite{RepoGammaZeta}. The trigonometry report writes the same class
$\Pi$ as the normal forms supported at \emph{negative $t$-exponents}
(\nolinkurl{trigonometry:eq:split} in \cite{RepoTrig}), because it uses $t=\omega^{-1}$; the
two descriptions agree after the sign change $t^{g}=\omega^{-g}$.

\subsection{The rings}\label{osq:sub:rings}
Let $k$ be a set field, $G$ an ordered abelian group (a set, or the class $\No$), and
$D\subseteq k$ a unital subring. Put
\begin{align}
 \Pi_k(G)&=\{f\in\hahn kG:\supp f\subseteq G_{>0}\},&
 \mm_k(G)&=\{f\in\hahn kG:\supp f\subseteq G_{<0}\},\label{osq:eq:ideals}\\
 \A_{D,k}(G)&=D+\Pi_k(G),&
 \B_{D,k}(G)&=D+\mm_k(G).\label{osq:eq:rings}
\end{align}
Both sums are direct as additive groups, and the zero series belongs to both ideals.
We drop $(G)$ when $G=\No$ and write $\Pi=\Pi_\R$. For $k=\R$ and $k=\C$ the
identification $X^g\mapsto\omega^g$ gives $\hahn\R\No=\No$ and $\hahn\C\No=\SC$ (a
union of two reverse well-ordered supports is reverse well ordered, so complexification
is coefficientwise), and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:Ozdef}
 \Oz=\A_{\Z,\R}=\Z\oplus\Pi,\qquad
 \GOz=\Oz+i\Oz=\A_{\Z[i],\C}=\Z[i]\oplus\Pi_\C,\qquad \Pi_\C=\Pi+i\Pi .
\end{equation}
We call $\GOz$ the \emph{Gaussian omnific ring}; it is a subring of $\SC$, not the
surcomplex field, and not the integral closure of $\Z$ in $\SC$ (08, 09). The finite
surreal and surcomplex rings are $\OO_\R=\B_{\R,\R}$ and $\OO_\C=\B_{\C,\C}$, and
$\A_{\R,\R}=\R+\Pi$ is the nonnegative-support ring (03's $P_\R$). For a general set
field $k$ (06, 07, 10) the class field $\hahn k\No$ need not be realized inside the
surreals; nothing below requires such a realization.

\begin{lemma}[Constant term \src{03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16}]\label{osq:lem:ct}
The map $\ct:\A_{D,k}(G)\to D$ extracting the coefficient of $X^0$ is a surjective
unital ring homomorphism with kernel $\Pi_k(G)$, split by the inclusion of constants.
On $\B_{D,k}(G)$ the same coefficient is a split surjective ring homomorphism with kernel
$\mm_k(G)$; on $\OO_\R$ and $\OO_\C$ it is the standard part, written $\st$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The nonnegative support cone is closed under addition of exponents. Thus sums and
Hahn products of such series still have nonnegative support; cancellation only removes
exponents. A sum of two nonnegative exponents is zero only when both are zero, so the
constant coefficient of a product is the product of the constant coefficients and lies
in $D$. This also verifies that $\A_{D,k}(G)$ is a subring. Additivity, the kernel and
the section follow from the unique decomposition \eqref{osq:eq:rings}; surjectivity follows
because every $d\in D$ is a constant series. The same argument with nonpositive
exponents proves all assertions for $\B_{D,k}(G)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What $\ct$ is not]\label{osq:rem:ctnot}
The map $\ct$ is defined on a ring of generally infinite elements; it is not the standard
part, and coefficient extraction at $0$ is not multiplicative on $\No$:
$\omega\cdot\omega^{-1}=1$ although both factors have zero constant coefficient. This is
the warning recorded in \cite{RepoNotation} and \nolinkurl{diff:warn:ct} of
\cite{RepoDiffEq}. Nor is $\ct$ order preserving: $\omega-N>0$ but
$\ct(\omega-N)=-N$ for every ordinary $N\ge1$ (04, 08, 09, 11). On $\A_{D,k}$ the two
maps $\ct$ and $\st$ receive different names because they have different domains
(04), and \eqref{osq:eq:incompatible} below shows that they cannot be combined.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Degree and units \src{03, 04, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16}]\label{osq:lem:units}
For $x\neq0$ in $\hahn kG$ put $\degw(x)=\max\supp x$. Then
$\degw(xy)=\degw(x)+\degw(y)$ for $x,y\ne0$, so $\A_{D,k}(G)$ and $\B_{D,k}(G)$ are
domains, and
\[
 \A_{D,k}(G)^\times=D^\times,\qquad \Oz^\times=\{\pm1\},\qquad \GOz^\times=\{\pm1,\pm i\}.
\]
In particular every nonconstant element of $\A_{D,k}(G)$, such as $1+\omega^a$ or
$\omega^{\sqrt2}+\omega+1$, is a nonunit.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The leading coefficient of a product is the product of the leading coefficients, which is
nonzero because $k$ is a field; the degree identity follows. A nonzero element of
$\A_{D,k}(G)$ has nonnegative degree, so $xy=1$ forces both degrees to be $0$, i.e.\
both factors are constants in $D$ with $xy=1$ in $D$. The two unit lists are the units of
$\Z$ and $\Z[i]$.
\end{proof}

Here $\degw$ is the largest growth exponent (04); it is not the ordinal-valued degree of
the order type of a support used in parts of the factorization literature \cite{LM}.

\subsection{Notation and renamings}\label{osq:sub:notation}
The manuscripts use many symbols for the purely infinite ideal and several for the

Throughout, for $a>0$ in an ordered group $G$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:Ha}
 H_a(G)=\{h\in G: n|h|<a\text{ for every ordinary }n\ge1\},\qquad H_a=H_a(\No),
\end{equation}
and $h\ll a$ means $h>0$ and $h\in H_a(G)$. This is a comparison of \emph{exponents}:
$h\ll a$ does not say that $\omega^h$ is small (it is infinite whenever $h>0$). For a set
$S\subseteq G_{>0}$ we write $U_G(S)=\{a>0: na<s\text{ for all }s\in S,\ n\ge1\}$ (09's
$\operatorname{Tiny}(S)$, 10's $U(S)$). Letters $\kappa,\lambda,\mu,\theta$ denote
cardinals and are restated locally; $\mu=\cf\kappa$ and $\theta=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$ in
the construction of 03.

\section{Support gaps and the purely infinite ideal}\label{osq:sec:gaps}

This section collects the facts that use the full surreal exponent class. All eight
manuscripts of the first merge prove them, as do 13 and 15 and manuscript~05 of the sibling
report \cite{RepoOdg}, and 14 and 16 use them; of the third batch, 17 and 19 reprove the gaps, the
units and the common divisors, and 18 uses the constant term. They are background for the new results, not
claimed as new. Throughout, $k$ is a set
field and $D\subseteq k$ a unital subring.

\begin{lemma}[Gaps below and above a set \src{03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16}]\label{osq:lem:gap}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every set of surreal numbers has a strict upper and a strict lower bound in $\No$.
\item For every set $S\subseteq\No_{>0}$ there is $h>0$ with $nh<s$ for all $s\in S$
and all ordinary $n\ge1$; in particular $0<h<S$.
\item For such $S$ the class $U_{\No}(S)$ contains the interval $(0,h)$, which is not a
set, and for every ordinal $\Lambda$ the exponents
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:scales}
 a_\alpha=\frac{h}{\omega^{\alpha+1}}\qquad(\alpha<\Lambda)
\end{equation}
are distinct elements of $U_{\No}(S)$, each $\ll h$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a set $T$, the cuts $\{T\mid\varnothing\}$ and $\{\varnothing\mid T\}$ are set cuts
and give (i). For (ii), apply the set cut $\{0\mid T\}$ to the set
$T=\{s/n:s\in S,\ n\ge1\}$ of positive surreals; for $S=\varnothing$ take $h=1$. For
(iii), every $0<u<h$ satisfies $nu<nh<s$, so $(0,h)\subseteq U_{\No}(S)$.
If this interval were a set, (ii) would give a positive strict lower bound $\ell$;
since $h/2$ is in the interval, $0<\ell/2<h$, contradicting that lower bound.
The denominators $\omega^{\alpha+1}$ are the Conway monomials of the
ordinals $\alpha+1$ in the \emph{exponent} field; they strictly increase with $\alpha$ and
exceed every ordinary integer, so the $a_\alpha$ are distinct, positive and satisfy
$na_\alpha<h$.
\end{proof}

Only the existence of a separator is used, not its simplicity or birthday (08). The
sources use several equivalent families in place of \eqref{osq:eq:scales}:
$a/\omega^{\alpha+1}$ (04, 05, 06, 08, 09, 03), $a/(\omega+\alpha+1)$ with the
field sum of embedded ordinals (07), $\delta\omega^{-(\alpha+1)}$ (11),
$\epsilon\xi/\kappa$ (10), $\epsilon/(\bar\alpha+2)$ with $\bar\alpha$ the surreal ordinal (13), and
$g\omega^{-(\xi+1)}$ (15). Each is a set whenever $\alpha$ ranges over a set.

\begin{example}[Surreal gaps where real gaps fail \src{03, 06, 08, 10, 11}]\label{osq:ex:gap}
The series $f=\sum_{n\ge1}\omega^{1/n}$ lies in $\Pi$; its support has no positive
\emph{real} lower bound but has positive surreal lower bounds, for instance $1/\omega$.
With $a=2/\omega$ and $b=1/\omega$ one has $na<1/m$ for all ordinary $m,n$ (10). In the
fixed exponent group $\R$ the same series is purely infinite but is not divisible by any
$X^h$, $h>0$, inside the nonnegative-support ring (03); this is where the passage from
monomials to the whole ideal fails in a fixed group (\cref{osq:sec:fixed}).
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[Common monomial divisors \src{03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15}]\label{osq:prop:common}
Let $A=\A_{D,k}$ and $\Pi_k$ its purely infinite ideal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every set-sized family $\mathcal F\subseteq\Pi_k$ satisfies
$\mathcal F\subseteq X^a\Pi_k$ for some $a>0$.
\item Each $f\in\Pi_k$ is a single product of two elements of $\Pi_k$; hence
$\Pi_k^2=\Pi_k$, and $\Pi_k=\bigcup_{a>0}X^aA$ is a directed union of principal ideals.
\item $\Pi_k$ is not generated, as an ideal of $A$, by any set of its elements.
\item $d\Pi_k=\Pi_k$ for every $0\neq d\in D$; in particular $n\Pi_k=\Pi_k$ for every
ordinary integer $n$ whose image in $k$ is nonzero. In characteristic zero this includes
every nonzero ordinary integer.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(i) The union of the supports of the members of $\mathcal F$ is a set of positive surreals;
choose $0<a<$ that union by \cref{osq:lem:gap}; for an empty union take any $a>0$.
Translating each support by $-a$ leaves it
positive and reverse well ordered, so $X^{-a}f\in\Pi_k$.
(ii) Apply (i) to $\{f\}$: $f=X^a(X^{-a}f)$ with both factors in $\Pi_k$. If $0<b<a$ then
$X^aA\subseteq X^bA$. Each $X^aA$ is contained in $\Pi_k$, and (i) puts every member
of $\Pi_k$ in one of these ideals; choosing $b$ below any two positive indices proves
directedness. The ideal product $\Pi_k^2$ consists of finite sums of products;
the single-product factorization proves one inclusion, and the ideal property the other.
(iii) If a set generated $\Pi_k$, (i) would place the generated ideal inside $X^aA$; but
$X^{a/2}\in\Pi_k$ is not in $X^aA$, since its unique quotient by $X^a$ in the ambient field
is $X^{-a/2}$, which has a negative exponent.
(iv) Divide every coefficient by $d$, which is invertible in $k$; this preserves the
support. Multiplication by $d$ gives the reverse inclusion.
\end{proof}

The qualification on $n$ is essential when $k$ is not assumed to have characteristic
zero. If $k$ has characteristic $p>0$, then $p\Pi_k=0$, whereas $X^a\in\Pi_k$ is nonzero
for $a>0$. The unrestricted integer-divisibility clause in the earlier assembly was
therefore false in that generality; the coefficient statement $d\Pi_k=\Pi_k$ for
$d\ne0$ is unchanged.

Idempotence and divisibility do not by themselves prove the universal theorem: an
idempotent, rationally divisible ideal can act nontrivially on infinite set-sized
modules, and a homomorphism to an infinite characteristic-zero ring need not kill an
arbitrarily divisible additive subgroup (04, 06, 07, 08). When $k$ has characteristic zero
and the target has positive characteristic, the last item already suffices
(\cref{osq:rem:poschar}).

\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:nOz}
 n\Oz=n\Z+\Pi=\ct^{-1}(n\Z)\quad(n\ge1),\qquad
 d\,\GOz=d\Z[i]+\Pi_\C\quad(0\ne d\in\Z[i]).
\end{equation}
Indeed $n\Pi=\Pi$ and $d\Pi_\C=\Pi_\C$ by \cref{osq:prop:common}(iv). Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:intersection}
 \Pi=\bigcap_{n\ge1}n\Oz=\bigcap_{p\text{ prime}}p\Oz,\qquad
 \Pi_\C=\bigcap_{n\ge1}n\GOz,
\end{equation}
since a nonzero ordinary integer (or Gaussian integer) is not divisible by every $n$ or
every prime (08, 10, 11). For a general $D$ the intersection formula can fail: for $D=\Q$
every element of $\A_{\Q,\R}$ is divisible by every ordinary positive integer (11).

\begin{proposition}[Clearing and fraction fields \src{03, 04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 11, 14, 15, 16}]\label{osq:prop:fractions}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every set $E\subseteq\hahn k\No$ there is $h>0$ with $X^hE\subseteq\Pi_k$. For
$E\subseteq\No$ or $E\subseteq\SC$ this reads $\omega^hE\subseteq\Pi$, respectively
$\omega^hE\subseteq\Pi_\C$.
\item $\Frac(\A_{D,k})=\hahn k\No$; in particular $\Frac(\Oz)=\No$ and
$\Frac(\GOz)=\SC$.
\item Inverting the positive monomials gives the whole field: if
$\mathcal U=\{X^a:a>0\}\cup\{1\}$ then $\mathcal U^{-1}\A_{D,k}=\hahn k\No$.
\item Neither $\No$ nor $\SC$, nor any localization of $\A_{D,k}$ in which some nonzero
element of $\Pi_k$ becomes a unit, admits a unital homomorphism to a nonzero set-sized
ring or a nonzero set-sized unital module.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(i) The union of the supports of the members of $E$ is a set; by \cref{osq:lem:gap}(i)
choose $h>0$ larger than $-g$ for each exponent $g$ in it. Then every exponent of $X^hx$,
$x\in E$, is positive. (ii) and (iii) For $x\in\hahn k\No$ apply (i) to $\{x\}$:
$x=(X^hx)/X^h$ with numerator and denominator in $\A_{D,k}$; the reverse inclusions hold
because $\A_{D,k}$ is a subring of the field. (iv) is proved after the universal theorem
(\cref{osq:cor:nofield}).
\end{proof}

Part (i) is manuscript~05's ``Clearing supports'' theorem, now in the sibling report
\cite{RepoOdg}; 03 credits it to 05 and adds the algebra-wide formulation of
\cref{osq:sec:closure}. Clearing one element is weaker than clearing all powers of it
with one denominator, which \cref{osq:sec:closure} also supplies (03).

\section{The collision mechanism}\label{osq:sec:collision}

Every proof of the universal theorem combines two finite multiplicative identities with a
cardinal comparison. This section states the identities once, in the forms used by the
different sources. The first (\cref{osq:lem:collision}, from 06, and in a special form
from 03) gives a uniform proof of the sharp cardinal bounds of
\cref{osq:sec:fixed,osq:sec:models}, including those that counting monomials cannot reach;
the others are genuinely different routes and are kept as such.

\subsection{Scaled-field collision}\label{osq:sub:scaled}

\begin{lemma}[Scaled-field collision \src{06; 03}]\label{osq:lem:collision}
Let $A$ be a commutative subring of a field $F$, let $L\subseteq F$ be a subfield and let
$0\neq m\in F$ satisfy $mL\subseteq A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\varphi:A\to S$ is a ring homomorphism, $S$ any ring (not necessarily
commutative, unital or reduced), and $\varphi(m^2)\neq0$, then $x\mapsto\varphi(mx)$ is
injective on $L$.
\item If $M$ is a unital $A$-module, $v\in M$ and $m^2v\neq0$, then $x\mapsto(mx)v$ is
injective on $L$.
\end{enumerate}
For set-sized $L$ and targets, consequently, if $|L|>|S|$ then $\varphi(m^2)=0$, and
if $|L|>|M|$ then $m^2M=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $1\in L$, $m\in A$. For distinct $x,y\in L$ the element $m/(x-y)$ lies in
$mL\subseteq A$, and in $A$
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:collision}
 (mx-my)\cdot\frac{m}{x-y}=m^2 .
\end{equation}
If $\varphi(mx)=\varphi(my)$, applying $\varphi$ gives $\varphi(m^2)=0$; no cancellation
in $S$ is used. For the module, apply $m/(x-y)$ to $(mx)v=(my)v$; commutativity of $A$
turns the result into $m^2v=0$.
\end{proof}

The proof of (i) uses only that $A$ is closed under addition and multiplication and contains
$mL$; so it applies verbatim when $A$ is a nonunital subring such as $\Pi_K$, which is how it is
used in \cref{osq:thm:universal}(iii). The module version bounds $|M|$ itself. Deriving it through the ring $\End_\Z(M)$ would
only bound $|\End_\Z(M)|$, which can be much larger than $|M|$ (06, 03, 09); this matters
for every set-sized threshold below. In 03 the lemma appears as the identity
$\bigl(X^{h/2}(f-f')\bigr)\bigl(X^{h/2}/(f-f')\bigr)=X^h$ for $f\neq f'$ in a
smaller-scale field (03's ``smaller-scale field obstruction''), i.e.\ the case
$m=X^{h/2}$ of \eqref{osq:eq:collision}.

\begin{lemma}[The scale subgroup and its Hahn field \src{03, 06, 07}]\label{osq:lem:Ha}
Let $G$ be an ordered abelian group (a set or $\No$) and $a\in G_{>0}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $H_a(G)$ is a convex subgroup of $G$, divisible if $G$ is, and
$H_{c}(G)=H_{2c}(G)$ for every $c\in G_{>0}$.
\item $\hahn k{H_a(G)}$ is a subfield of $\hahn kG$, and $X^c\,\hahn k{H_a(G)}\subseteq
\Pi_k(G)$ for every $c\in G$ with $2c\ge a$; for instance $c=a$, or $c=a/2$ when
$a/2\in G$.
\item For $G=\No$ the field $\FF_a(k)=\hahn k{H_a}$ is a proper class: it contains the
distinct monomials $X^{a/\omega^{\alpha+1}}$ for every ordinal $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(i) If $h,h'\in H_a(G)$ then $2n|h|<a$ and $2n|h'|<a$ give $n|h+h'|<a$; negation and
convexity are immediate, and if $G$ is divisible then $h/m$ satisfies the same inequalities.
For every $c>0$, $n|h|<c$ for all $n$ is equivalent to $n|h|<2c$ for all $n$.
(ii) Supports of sums and products of series supported in a subgroup stay in it, and the
Hahn inverse of $f=cX^g(1+u)$, $\supp u<0$, is $c^{-1}X^{-g}\sum_{n\ge0}(-u)^n$, whose
support lies in the subgroup generated by $\supp f$. The geometric family is Hahn
summable by the Neumann support lemma; for a class exponent group this argument takes
place in the set-sized subgroup generated by the support of $f$.
If $2c\ge a$ and $h\in H_a(G)$ then
$2|h|<a\le 2c$, so $c+h>0$; hence $X^cf$ has positive support for
$f\in\hahn k{H_a(G)}$.
(iii) Put $a_\alpha=a/\omega^{\alpha+1}$. Each $a_\alpha\ll a$ lies in $H_a$, and
the exponents are distinct. If $\FF_a(k)$ were a set, restricting this family to its
Hartogs ordinal would give the forbidden injection into that set.
\end{proof}

The field $\FF_a=\FF_a(\R)$ is 07's $\mathscr F_a$ and 06's $L_a$ with $k=\R$; it is
real closed and contains a copy of all of $\No$ (\cref{osq:if:prop:closed,osq:if:thm:compression}).

\subsection{The geometric telescope}\label{osq:sub:telescope}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-exponent telescope \src{03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 15}]\label{osq:lem:telescope}
Let $G$ be an ordered abelian group, and let $0<b<a$ and $a\ll c$ in $G$. Put $d=a-b$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:telescope}
 q_{c;a,b}=\sum_{n\ge0}X^{c-a-nd}\ \in\ \Pi_k(G),
 \qquad (X^a-X^b)\,q_{c;a,b}=X^c .
\end{equation}
The support of $q_{c;a,b}$ is countable and strictly decreasing. For every ordinary
$N\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:finitetelescope}
 (X^a-X^b)\sum_{n=0}^{N}X^{c-a-nd}=X^c-X^{c-(N+1)d},
\end{equation}
and the remainder monomial $X^{c-(N+1)d}$ is still infinitely large.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each ordinary $n\ge0$, $a+nd\le(n+1)a<c$, so every exponent is positive; the
exponents strictly decrease with $n$, so every nonempty set of them has a largest element.
Multiplication by $X^a$ gives the exponents $c-nd$ and multiplication by $X^b$ gives
$c-(n+1)d$; at $c$ the coefficient is $1$ and at every $c-md$, $m\ge1$, it is $1-1=0$.
Each coefficient receives at most two contributions, so this is a Hahn identity. The finite
identity is the same computation truncated; its remainder exponent
$c-(N+1)d\ge c-(N+1)a>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No limit is taken and no sum is transported]\label{osq:rem:nolimit}
The remainders in \eqref{osq:eq:finitetelescope} are positive monomials; they do not tend
to $0$ in the order, valuation or fine topology, not even at the ordinary scale~$1$. The
infinite identity is a coefficient identity, not a limit of \eqref{osq:eq:finitetelescope}
(04, 06, 07, 08, 10, 03). A target homomorphism is never applied term by term to
$q_{c;a,b}$: the series is first a single element of the source ring, and only the finite
product identity is mapped (06, 08, 09, 11). This is why no continuity, valuation or
strong-additivity hypothesis on homomorphisms appears anywhere. It is also why a ring of
finite-support series behaves differently (\cref{osq:sec:support}): there
$q_{c;a,b}$ is absent and the nonzero remainder of \eqref{osq:eq:finitetelescope} cannot
be removed.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[A witness for $\omega$ \src{04, 10, 15}]\label{osq:ex:omegatelescope}
With $c=1$, $b=1/\omega$ and $a=2/\omega$,
$\bigl(\omega^{2/\omega}-\omega^{1/\omega}\bigr)\sum_{n\ge0}\omega^{1-(n+2)/\omega}=\omega$,
while the finite partial products leave the nonzero remainders
$\omega^{1-(N+1)/\omega}$ (04). In the lexicographic group $\Z\times\Z$ with $c=(1,0)$,
$a=(0,2)$, $b=(0,1)$ the quotient is $\sum_{n\ge0}X^{(1,-n-2)}$ and the $N$-th remainder is
$X^{(1,-N-1)}$ (10); under a compatible monomial realization each remainder is still
infinite. 15 uses the same series $q=\sum_{n\ge0}\omega^{1-(n+2)/\omega}$ to block the extension of the
finite-support augmentation (\cref{osq:sec:support}).
\end{example}

\paragraph{Precedents.} The countable geometric-series product with a monomial result is
already in L'Innocente--Mantova \cite[Remark~3.4.4]{LM}, used there to show that
$\deg\circ\operatorname{ot}$ is not multiplicative when the value group does not embed in
$\R$; 04 names it a direct precursor. The factorization of a series whose support meets two
distinct nonzero Archimedean classes is \cite[Fact~8.0.1]{LM} (Gonshor's
\cite[Thm.~8.6]{Gonshor}), with the geometric factorization displayed on p.~46 of the arXiv
version; 11 cites it as the precedent of the division below. Manuscript~09 credited
``Proposition~8.2.1 on separated-scale division''; that proposition is the truncation
criterion ($b$ divides $c$ if and only if $b$ divides a truncation $T_\Delta(c)$), whose
proof divides the higher-scale part of $c$ by $b$, and 08 cites it as the precedent for
higher-scale divisibility. We credit all three places; none of the sources claims the
geometric mechanism as new.

\begin{lemma}[Weighted certificate \src{07}]\label{osq:lem:weighted}
Let $K$ be a set field, $r,s\in K^\times$, $a>0$ and $\delta>\eta>0$ with $\delta\ll a$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:weighted}
 \frac{X^a}{rX^\delta-sX^\eta}
 =\frac1r\sum_{k\ge0}\Bigl(\frac sr\Bigr)^kX^{a-\delta-k(\delta-\eta)}\in\Pi_K ,
\end{equation}
If instead $\delta=\eta>0$, $\delta\ll a$ and $r\ne s$, the quotient is
$(r-s)^{-1}X^{a-\delta}\in\Pi_K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The exponents are those of \cref{osq:lem:telescope}; multiplying by $rX^\delta-sX^\eta$
gives, at exponent $a-k(\delta-\eta)$ with $k\ge1$, the two contributions
$r\cdot r^{-1}(s/r)^k$ and $-s\cdot r^{-1}(s/r)^{k-1}$, which cancel. At exponent $a$
only the initial term contributes, with coefficient $1$. The equal-exponent case
follows by factoring $(r-s)X^\delta$; its quotient exponent is positive because
$\delta<a$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Division of an arbitrary purely infinite element}\label{osq:sub:division}

The telescope divides a monomial. Manuscripts 09, 10 and 11 divide an arbitrary element
directly, which removes the separate reduction to monomials.

\begin{lemma}[Subordinate division \src{09, 10, 11, 13, 15}]\label{osq:lem:division}
Let $G$ be an ordered abelian group, $0\ne s=\sum_{g\in S}c_gX^g\in\Pi_k(G)$ and
$a>b>0$ in $U_G(S)$. Put $d=a-b$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:division}
 \frac{s}{X^a-X^b}=\sum_{g\in S}\sum_{n\ge0}c_g\,X^{g-a-nd}\ \in\ \Pi_k(G),
\end{equation}
so $s=(X^a-X^b)q$ with $q\in\Pi_k(G)$. The support of $q$ lies in
$\{g-a-nd:g\in S,\ n\in\N\}$, of cardinality at most $\max(|S|,\aleph_0)$; it is
countable when $S$ is.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the ambient Hahn field $(X^a-X^b)^{-1}=X^{-a}(1-X^{-d})^{-1}=X^{-a}\sum_{n\ge0}X^{-nd}$.
The product with $s$ is a Hahn product: the sum of two reverse well-ordered sets is reverse
well ordered and each exponent has finitely many representations (11 proves this two-support
lemma in full; it is the standard Neumann support lemma). Every exponent that can occur
satisfies $g-a-nd\ge g-(n+1)a>0$ because $(n+1)a<g$; cancellation cannot create new
exponents. Hence the quotient lies in $\Pi_k(G)$.
\end{proof}

The inverse of $X^a-X^b$ is not in the ring; only its product with the larger-scale $s$ is
(11).

\subsection{Separation principles}\label{osq:sub:separation}

\begin{lemma}[Separation \src{04, 09, 11; 03}]\label{osq:lem:separation}
Let $R$ be a ring (possibly a proper class), $e\in R$, and $(x_t)_{t\in T}$ a set-indexed
family with $e\in(x_s-x_t)R$ for all $s\ne t$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\varphi:R\to S$ is a ring homomorphism with $\varphi(e)\ne0$, then
$t\mapsto\varphi(x_t)$ is injective; hence $|T|\le|S|$ if $S$ is a set.
\item If $R$ is commutative, $M$ an $R$-module, $v\in M$ and $ev\ne0$, then
$t\mapsto x_tv$ is injective.
\item If for every cardinal $\lambda$ such a family with $|T|=\lambda$ exists, then every
homomorphism from $R$ to a set-sized ring kills $e$, and $e$ annihilates every set-sized
$R$-module.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $\varphi(x_s)=\varphi(x_t)$ with $e=(x_s-x_t)q$, then
$\varphi(e)=(\varphi(x_s)-\varphi(x_t))\varphi(q)=0$; neither commutativity of $S$ nor
preservation of $1$ is used. For (ii), commutativity lets us write
$ev=q(x_s-x_t)v=0$. For the ring assertion in (iii), choose a family whose index
set cannot inject into the target, and apply (i). For a module over a commutative
$R$, apply (ii) in the same way. For a possibly noncommutative $R$, use instead
the action homomorphism $R\to\End_\Z(M)$: the endomorphisms of the underlying
set-sized additive group form a set-sized ring, so the ring assertion makes the
action of $e$ zero. This last route proves annihilation but uses the size of
$\End_\Z(M)$, not the sharper bound by $|M|$ in (ii).
\end{proof}

Item (i) is 04's separation lemma, (ii) is 09's orbit separation and 03's exponent-family
obstruction, and (iii) is 11's collision--divisibility principle.

\begin{theorem}[Divisibility-separated families \src{11, 15}]\label{osq:thm:packing}
Let $\mathcal S\subseteq\Pi_k$ be a set and $\Lambda$ an ordinal. There are distinct
monomials $(u_\alpha)_{\alpha<\Lambda}$ in $\A_{D,k}$ with
\[
 s\in(u_\alpha-u_\beta)\Pi_k\qquad(s\in\mathcal S,\ \alpha\ne\beta).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\delta>0$ strictly below the union of the supports of the members of
$\mathcal S$ (\cref{osq:lem:gap}), put $a_\alpha=\delta\omega^{-(\alpha+1)}$ and
$u_\alpha=X^{a_\alpha}$. For $\alpha<\beta$, $0<a_\beta<a_\alpha\le\delta/\omega$, so
$na_\alpha<\delta$ for every $n$, and \cref{osq:lem:division} applies to each nonzero
$s$; for $s=0$ take quotient zero. Reversing the indices only changes the sign of the
quotient. The empty family $\mathcal S$ causes no restriction on the choice of $\delta$.
\end{proof}

The coefficients of the $u_\alpha$ are $1$; no independence of the coefficients of $s$ is
used, and cancellations inside $s$ or the quotient are harmless (11). 15 proves the same with the
family $u_\xi=\omega^{g\omega^{-(\xi+1)}}$, $\xi<\theta$, for every ordinal $\theta$, and simultaneously for a set
of elements $s$.

\section{The universal set-sized quotient}\label{osq:sec:universal}

\subsection{The theorem}\label{osq:sub:universalthm}

\begin{theorem}[Universal set-sized quotient \src{04, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 13, 15; 03, 05}]\label{osq:thm:universal}
Let $K$ be a set field, $D\subseteq K$ a unital subring, and $A=\A_{D,K}=D+\Pi_K$ with the
full surreal exponent class.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $S$ be a set-sized associative ring, not necessarily unital or commutative, and
let $\varphi:A\to S$ be an additive and multiplicative class map, not necessarily
preserving~$1$. Then $\varphi(\Pi_K)=0$, and $\varphi=\psi\circ\ct$ for a unique ring
homomorphism $\psi:D\to S$, namely $\psi=\varphi|_D$.
\item For every set-sized unital ring $S$, restriction to $D$ and composition with $\ct$
are mutually inverse bijections, natural in $S$,
\[
 \Homone(A,S)\ \longleftrightarrow\ \Homone(D,S).
\]
