\end{remark}

The finite-support augmentation appears independently in 03 (``two necessary warnings''),
04, 09, 11 and 15 (which blocks its extension with the single series of \cref{osq:ex:omegatelescope}),
and 12's cores carry it too (\cref{osq:hd:prop:finite}); 07 describes the same boundary in words (on a finite-support fragment the
certificate \eqref{osq:eq:telescope} need not exist, and a faithful interpretation in a
set-sized target can exist), and manuscript~05 of the sibling report \cite{RepoOdg}
observes that $\Z+\omega\R[\omega]$ has many real evaluation maps that do not extend to
$\Oz$. Proper-class size alone therefore does not prove the universal theorem: the
finite-support rings have a proper class of monomials and arbitrarily small positive
exponents, yet $E$ sees every monomial as $1$ (04). Neither size nor additive divisibility
alone suffices; the proof needs many subordinate scales together with enough support closure
for geometric division (11). For $D=\Z$, finite targets still kill the positive-support
ideal of $R_{\mathrm{fin}}$ ($f=n(f/n)$ in characteristic $n$), so its finite quotient theory is
ordinary congruence theory: for a finite unital target of characteristic $n\ge1$,
the equation $f=n(f/n)$ kills each positive finite-support element, and a
surjective map is determined by its ordinary integer scalars. Every kernel of
a finite quotient is therefore $n\Z+\Pi_{\mathrm{fin}}$, where
$\Pi_{\mathrm{fin}}=\Pi_k\cap R_{\mathrm{fin}}$, and every such kernel occurs.
Having profinite completion $\widehat\Z$ is thus weaker than having $\Z$
universal for all set-sized targets (09).

The quotient and module classifications extend to the bounded rings of (i), and so does the
derivation statement, because the monomial factorizations proving idempotence preserve support
cardinality (04). On the positive side the cofactor only translates the support;
on the finite side $\varepsilon=\omega^{-a/2}(\omega^{a/2}\varepsilon)$ does the
same, with the other factor a single monomial. For modules apply the bounded-ring
mapping property to the set-sized ring $\End_\Z(M)$; the resulting annihilation
and these factorizations then give the derivation correspondence. 04 does \emph{not} infer that these smaller rings have fraction field
$\hahn k\No$: arbitrary normal forms need not have the required support size. The result is
also different from completion or omitted-type questions for bounded-support series over a
\emph{fixed} set-sized exponent group (compare \cite{RepoFKC}): here the exponent class is
still large enough to supply a new separating family for every proposed target (04). The
fixed-group question is the subject of the next section.

(Status (batch 32): equal set-sized quotients do not make the bounded rings isomorphic. With $D=\Z$, $k=\R$, the
first-$\kappa$ report shows that the rings of (i) for $\lambda=\kappa$ and $\lambda=\kappa'$ are not isomorphic as
abstract rings when $\operatorname{cf}\kappa\ne\operatorname{cf}\kappa'$, since their fraction fields are not
(\nolinkurl{fkc:sb:cor:rings} in \cite{RepoFKC}); its Part~II also classifies the set-presented gaps and the
saturation of those fraction fields.)

\section{Fixed exponent groups: cardinal lower bounds and exact thresholds}\label{osq:sec:fixed}

Over a fixed set-sized exponent group the full-class theorem cannot hold verbatim: the ring
is itself a set, and its identity map is a set-sized target that retains every element
(03, 04, 07, 08, 10, 11). What survives is a lower bound on the size of a target that
detects a given element. This section compares the bounds proved by the sources, proves a
field bound that dominates them, and states the organizing theorem of the report: for each
of the set-sized constructions of \cref{osq:sec:models}, the exact detection threshold is
the size of the ring.

Throughout, $\Gamma$ is an ordered abelian set group, $k$ a set field, $D\subseteq k$ a
unital subring, $F\subseteq\hahn k\Gamma$ a subfield containing $k$ and every monomial
$X^g$, $\Pi(F)=\{f\in F:\supp f\subseteq\Gamma_{>0}\}$ and $A=D+\Pi(F)$. The case
$F=\hahn k\Gamma$ is the ring $\A_{D,k}(\Gamma)$ of \eqref{osq:eq:rings}; the constructions of
\cref{osq:sec:models} take $F$ to be a countable-support, a $<\kappa$-support, or a
controlled subfield.

\subsection{The bounds of the sources}\label{osq:sub:sourcebounds}

\begin{proposition}[Monomial-count bounds \src{03, 04, 07, 10, 13, 15}]\label{osq:prop:monomialbounds}
Let $A=\A_{D,k}(\Gamma)$ and $\varphi:A\to S$ a ring homomorphism.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\varphi(X^a)\ne0$ for some $a>0$, then $\gamma\mapsto\varphi(X^\gamma)$ is injective
on $H_a(\Gamma)_{>0}$ (04); more generally $r X^\delta\mapsto\varphi(rX^\delta)$ is injective on
$\{rX^\delta:r\in k^\times,\ 0<\delta\in H_a(\Gamma)\}$, and the same holds if $X^a$ divides
some $g$ with $\varphi(g)\ne0$ (07).
\item If $0\ne x\in\Pi_k(\Gamma)$ and $\varphi(x)\ne0$, then $a\mapsto\varphi(X^a)$ is injective on
$U_\Gamma(\supp x)$; this also holds for a nonunital map defined on $\Pi_k(\Gamma)$ alone (10; 15's
local criterion is this bound, and 13's criterion is the same injection on any set $T\subseteq\Gamma_{>0}$ with
$s>a+n(a-b)$ for $a>b$ in $T$, $s\in\supp x$).
\item On the negative side, if $0\ne\varepsilon\in\mm_k(\Gamma)$, $a=v(\varepsilon)$ and
$\varphi(\varepsilon)\ne0$ for a map $\varphi$ on $\B_{D,k}(\Gamma)$, then
$\gamma\mapsto\varphi(X^{-\gamma})$ is injective on $(0,a)_\Gamma$ (04).
\item For $h>0$, an $A$-module $M$ and $v\in M$ with $X^hv\ne0$, $a\mapsto X^av$ is injective on
$\{a\in\Gamma: a\ll h\}$ (03).
\end{enumerate}
No divisibility of $\Gamma$ is needed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For (i), subtract two distinct weighted monomials $rX^\delta$ and $sX^\eta$.
If $\delta\ne\eta$, order them and apply the weighted telescope; if they are
equal, then $r\ne s$ and use $(r-s)^{-1}X^{a-\delta}$. In both cases the
quotient multiplying the difference to $X^a$ has positive support. All exponents
are integer combinations of $a,\delta,\eta$, hence lie in $\Gamma$; the coefficients
lie in $k$. This proves the claimed injections by \cref{osq:lem:separation}(i).
If $g=X^aq$ is detected, then $X^a$ must be detected as well.

For (ii), the quotient in \cref{osq:lem:division} belongs to $\Pi_k(\Gamma)$,
so the same argument works even when the map is defined only on that nonunital
ring. For (iii), the valuation of
$\varepsilon/(X^{-\gamma}-X^{-\delta})$ is $a-\min(\gamma,\delta)>0$;
this is the proof of \cref{osq:lem:finitediff}, unchanged for any coefficient
field and ordered abelian group. The quotient belongs to $\mm_k(\Gamma)$.
For (iv), if $X^av=X^bv$ with distinct $a,b\ll h$, the telescope gives
$X^h=(X^a-X^b)q$ with $q\in A$. Acting by $q$ and using commutativity of $A$
contradicts $X^hv\ne0$. No step uses halves or division of an exponent by an
integer; this explains why divisibility of $\Gamma$ is unnecessary.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Where these bounds are vacuous \src{04, 08, 10, 13}]\label{osq:ex:archimedean}
If $\Gamma$ is Archimedean, $H_a(\Gamma)=\{0\}$ and the telescopes do not exist. For
$\Gamma=\Z$ a reverse well-ordered positive support is finite, $\A_{\Z,\R}(\Z)=\Z+X\R[X]$,
and evaluation at $X=1$ is a map to the set field $\R$ detecting $X$ (10). An arbitrary fixed
Hahn workspace cannot inherit the full theorem merely because its notation resembles $\No$
(08).
\end{example}

\subsection{The field bound}\label{osq:sub:fieldbound}

The monomial counts are far from optimal. The following bound is 03's ``smaller-scale field
obstruction'', obtained there for countable-support fields over divisible groups; the general
form below is a direct application of 06's scaled-field collision lemma and is recorded as a
merge statement.

\begin{proposition}[Field bound \src{03, 06} \merge]\label{osq:prop:fieldbound}
Let $c\in\Gamma_{>0}$ and $L_c(F)=F\cap\hahn k{H_c(\Gamma)}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L_c(F)$ is a subfield of $F$ and $X^cL_c(F)\subseteq\Pi(F)\subseteq A$.
\item If $\varphi:A\to S$ is a ring homomorphism with $\varphi(X^{2c})\neq0$, then
$f\mapsto\varphi(X^cf)$ is injective on $L_c(F)$; if $M$ is an $A$-module and
$X^{2c}v\ne0$, then $f\mapsto(X^cf)v$ is injective on $L_c(F)$.
\item Consequently, if $x\in X^{2c}A$ (for instance $x=X^{2c}$, or $0\ne x\in\Pi(F)$ with
$2c$ a strict lower bound of $\supp x$), every ring homomorphism and every module detecting
$x$ has cardinality at least $|L_c(F)|$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(i) $\hahn k{H_c(\Gamma)}$ is a subfield by \cref{osq:lem:Ha}(ii), so $L_c(F)$ is an
intersection of two subfields. For $h\in H_c(\Gamma)$, $|h|<c$, so $c+h>0$ and
$X^cf\in F$ has positive support. (ii) is \cref{osq:lem:collision} with $m=X^c$ and
$L=L_c(F)$, inside the field $\hahn k\Gamma$. More explicitly, for distinct
$f,g\in L_c(F)$ the multiplier $X^c/(f-g)$ belongs to $X^cL_c(F)\subseteq A$,
and
\[
 (X^cf-X^cg)\frac{X^c}{f-g}=X^{2c}.
\]
This gives both the ring injection and the module injection by acting on the
specified vector; it bounds the underlying set of $M$, not its endomorphism ring.
(iii) If $x=X^{2c}y$ with $y\in A$ and
$\varphi(x)\ne0$, then $\varphi(X^{2c})\ne0$; if $xv\ne0$ then $X^{2c}(yv)\ne0$. If $2c<\supp x$
then $X^{-2c}x\in F$ has positive support, so it lies in $\Pi(F)\subseteq A$.
This lower-bound condition is required for that example of (iii); arbitrary
positive support in a fixed group need not have a positive strict lower bound.
\end{proof}

For $F=\Hc{k}{\Gamma}$ and $c=h/2$ this is exactly 03's theorem ($H_{h/2}=H_h$). The bound
contains 04's and 10's monomial counts whenever those monomials lie in $H_c(\Gamma)$, and
07's weighted count, because $L_c(F)$ contains every $rX^\delta$ with $r\in k$ and
$\delta\in H_c(\Gamma)$; it also contains $k$ itself, so with real coefficients every target detecting an element as in (iii), in particular
a monomial $X^{2c}$, has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements (03). The following examples show that it can be
strictly and decisively larger.

\begin{example}[The exact threshold in 04's example \merge]\label{osq:ex:lexQQ}
Let $\Gamma=\Q\oplus_{\mathrm{lex}}\Q$ (first coordinate dominant), $k\in\{\R,\C\}$,
$A=\A_{D,k}(\Gamma)$ with full Hahn supports, and $a=(1,0)$. 04 computes the
positive part $H_a(\Gamma)_{>0}=\{(0,q):q\in\Q_{>0}\}$, so $H_a(\Gamma)=\{0\}\oplus\Q$, and notes that retaining $X^a$ requires only a countable family of
distinct images. With $c=(1/2,0)$, $H_c(\Gamma)=\{0\}\oplus\Q$ and
$L_c=\hahn k{\{0\}\oplus\Q}\cong k(\!(t^\Q)\!)$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$; and
$|A|\le|\hahn k\Gamma|\le 2^{\aleph_0}\cdot(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$, since
$\Gamma$ is countable. Hence the least cardinality of a ring target, and of a module, detecting
any nonzero $x\in X^{(1,0)}A$ is exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$, attained by the identity map and the regular
module. The same holds on the negative side: if $\varepsilon\in\mm_k(\Gamma)$ has
$v(\varepsilon)=(1,0)$, then with $c=(1/4,0)$ the element $X^{-2c}$ divides $\varepsilon$ in
$\B_{D,k}(\Gamma)$ (the cofactor $X^{2c}\varepsilon$ has largest exponent $(-1/2,0)<0$),
$X^{-c}L_c\subseteq\mm_k(\Gamma)$, and \cref{osq:lem:collision} gives the bound $2^{\aleph_0}$,
which is again attained by the identity of the negative-support ring and its
regular module: that ring also has at most continuum many elements.
\end{example}

In this example 07's weighted bound ($|k^\times|\cdot\aleph_0=2^{\aleph_0}$) is also attained,
while 04's and 10's monomial counts give only $\aleph_0$. With a countable coefficient field
all three source bounds fail:

\begin{example}[None of the monomial or weighted counts is attained \merge]\label{osq:ex:countablecoeff}
Let $k=D=\Q$, $\Gamma=\bigoplus_{n<\omega}\Q e_n$ with the least nonzero index dominant, and
$A=\A_{\Q,\Q}(\Gamma)$ with full Hahn supports. For $x=X^{e_0}$ and $c=e_0/2$,
$H_c(\Gamma)=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\Q e_n$, and $L_c$ contains the $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct series
$\sum_{n\in B}X^{e_n}$, $B\subseteq\omega\setminus\{0\}$ (the exponents $e_n$ decrease with $n$,
so each support is reverse well ordered). Since $\Gamma$ is countable,
$|A|\le2^{\aleph_0}\cdot\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$. So the exact detection threshold of
$X^{e_0}$ is $2^{\aleph_0}$, attained by the identity map and regular module of $A$, while 04's bound $|H_{e_0}(\Gamma)_{>0}|$, 07's bound
$|\Q^\times|\cdot|H_{e_0}(\Gamma)_{>0}|$ and 10's bound $|U_\Gamma(\{e_0\})|$ are all
$\aleph_0$. Indeed the group and coefficient field are countable, the positive
tail contains infinitely many $e_n$, and membership of $n$ in $B$ is recovered
from the coefficient of $X^{e_n}$. Thus the lower field bound really counts
continuum many distinct series; it is not just a count of monomials.
\end{example}

These examples settle the two example-level questions of the sources and leave the general
ones open: 04's question on optimal small targets in a fixed exponent group is answered for
its own example $\Q\oplus_{\mathrm{lex}}\Q$ (the answer is $2^{\aleph_0}$), and for 10's question
(when is the bound of \cref{osq:prop:monomialbounds}(ii) attained?)
\cref{osq:ex:countablecoeff} shows, in ZFC, that the bound need not be attained. The same phenomenon appears in 03's ring
$A^{03}_{\aleph_1}$ of \cref{osq:sec:model03}: there $|U_\Gamma(S)|\le\aleph_1$, while the
exact threshold is $2^{\aleph_0}$, so if the continuum hypothesis fails, 10's bound is not
attained there either. Remark~\ref{osq:rem:04misleading} records the corresponding correction
to a sentence of 04.

\begin{remark}[A correction to 04's commentary]\label{osq:rem:04misleading}
04 remarks that in $\Q\oplus_{\mathrm{lex}}\Q$ ``this is only a countable family'' which
``cannot contradict the existence of a sufficiently large infinite set target, such as the
ring itself''. The statement is true, but the ring itself has $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements and,
by \cref{osq:ex:lexQQ}, no smaller target detects $X^{(1,0)}$; the countable family is not the
obstruction that decides the answer.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Criteria that kill the whole ideal below a cardinal}\label{osq:sub:criteria}

To pass from monomials to the whole ideal one also needs a gap: every element must be
divisible by a positive monomial inside the ring. 03's example $\sum_{n\ge1}X^{1/n}$ over
$\Gamma=\R$ shows that this can fail (\cref{osq:ex:gap}), and 09's uncountable-support series
$f_*$ (\cref{osq:rem:fstar}) shows the same for full supports over a long group.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative criterion \src{08} \merge]\label{osq:thm:criterion}
Let $\Gamma$ be divisible, $\kappa$ an infinite cardinal, and suppose
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] every nonzero $f\in\Pi(F)$ has a positive exponent $\epsilon\in\Gamma$ strictly
below its support;
\item[(b)] for every $c>0$ in $\Gamma$, the set $\{a\in\Gamma:a\ll c\}$ has at least $\kappa$
elements.
\end{enumerate}
Then every ring homomorphism from $A$ to a ring of cardinality $<\kappa$ factors uniquely
through $\ct:A\to D$. \merge\ The same conclusion holds, with the same proof, if (b) is replaced
by (b$'$): $|L_c(F)|\ge\kappa$ for every $c>0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $c>0$. Under (b), for two distinct $a>b\ll c$ the series $q_{c;a,b}$ equals the rational
expression $X^c/(X^a-X^b)$ in $\hahn k\Gamma$, whose numerator and denominator lie in the field
$F$; so $q_{c;a,b}\in\Pi(F)\subseteq A$, and a nonzero image of $X^c$ would make the images of
$\kappa$ monomials distinct. Under (b$'$) use \cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(ii) with $c/2$ in
place of $c$. So every positive monomial is killed. For $f\in\Pi(F)$, (a) gives
$f=X^\epsilon g$ with $g=X^{-\epsilon}f\in F$ of positive support, so $f$ is killed.
Writing an arbitrary element as $d+f$ now gives the unique factor
$\varphi|_D$ through $\ct$; no unital hypothesis on $\varphi$ was used.
\end{proof}

Condition (a) is a gap property of the chosen field and (b) a supply of lower Archimedean
scales; neither says that homomorphisms preserve strongly summable families (08). 08 states
the theorem for a subfield $K\subseteq\R$ and constants $\Z$; the proof uses neither
restriction, and it is stated here in the setting of this section.

\begin{theorem}[Coinitiality criterion \src{11}]\label{osq:thm:coinitial}
Let $\Gamma$ be divisible, $\kappa$ uncountable, and $\coin(\Gamma_{>0})\ge\kappa$ (every set of
fewer than $\kappa$ positive elements has a positive strict lower bound). Put
$R_{\Gamma,<\kappa}=D+\{s\in\Pi_k(\Gamma):|\supp s|<\kappa\}$, a ring for every infinite $\kappa$.
Then every unital map $R_{\Gamma,<\kappa}\to S$ with $|S|<\kappa$ factors uniquely through
$\ct$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $s\ne0$ have $|\supp s|<\kappa$. Choose $\delta>0$ strictly below $\supp s$, and then a
positive strict lower bound $\eta$ of the countable set $\{\delta/n:n\ge1\}$ (possible since
$\kappa>\aleph_0$); every $a\in E=(0,\eta)$ satisfies $na<\delta$. The set $E$ has at least $\kappa$
elements: otherwise it would have a positive strict lower bound $b$, but then $b\in E$ (as
$b<\eta/2\in E$), which is absurd. For distinct $a,b\in E$, \cref{osq:lem:division} gives
$s\in(X^a-X^b)R_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ with a quotient of support size at most
$\max(|\supp s|,\aleph_0)<\kappa$. The inequality is valid without regularity,
since it is the maximum of two fixed cardinals below the uncountable $\kappa$.
All $X^a$ for $a\in E$ lie in the source. Since $|S|<\kappa\le|E|$, two images
collide, and applying the map to this finite product identity kills $s$.
The zero element needs no argument. Restriction to $D$ then supplies the unique
factorization of the map.
\end{proof}

This theorem concerns an ordinary set-sized source and cannot exclude its identity
representation; the target bound is indispensable. Regularity of $\kappa$ is not needed for the
theorem itself, only for the examples of \cref{osq:sub:model11} (11).

\begin{lemma}[Cyclic modules \src{08}]\label{osq:lem:cyclic}
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I$ an ideal and $\kappa$ a cardinal such that every ring
homomorphism from $A$ onto a ring of cardinality $<\kappa$ kills $I$. Then $IM=0$ for every
$A$-module $M$ with $|M|<\kappa$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $m\in M$, commutativity makes $\Ann(m)=\{a\in A:am=0\}$ a two-sided ideal.
The map $A/\Ann(m)\to Am$, $[a]\mapsto am$, is well defined and bijective:
equality of the two images is exactly $(a-b)m=0$. Thus its source has cardinality
$|Am|\le|M|<\kappa$. Apply the hypothesis to the surjective quotient ring map
$A\to A/\Ann(m)$ to obtain $I\subseteq\Ann(m)$. This holds for every $m$,
so $IM=0$. The set $Am$ is used only to count elements; it is not asserted to
be a subring of $M$.
\end{proof}

Applying the ring statement to $\End_\Z(M)$ would need an estimate of $|\End_\Z(M)|$, which may
exceed $\kappa$ even when $|M|<\kappa$; the lemma avoids that hidden cardinal-arithmetic
assumption (08). \Cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(ii) gives the module bound directly (06, 03, 09).

\subsection{The organizing theorem: the threshold is the size of the ring}\label{osq:sub:organizing}

The five constructions of \cref{osq:sec:models} are summarized here; their notation is tagged by
source because they are different rings. The first three rows use ordinary
integer constants, with the stated Gaussian variants for 03 and 06.
In the last two rows $D$ is a unital subring of the displayed coefficient
field. The last column records the least size of an ideal generating set,
not a support bound or the size of the ring.

\begin{center}\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lllllll@{}}
\toprule
ring & exponent group & supports & coefficients & hypotheses & size & gen.\ of $\Pi_A$\\
\midrule
$A^{03}_\kappa$ & $\bigoplus_{\kappa^{\mathrm{op}}+\kappa}\Q$, 2 arms & countable & $\R$ & $\cf\kappa>\aleph_0$ & $\kappa^{\aleph_0}$ & $\cf\kappa$\\
$A^{06}_\kappa$ & $\Span_\Q\{\omega^{\pm(\alpha+1)}\}$, 2 arms & $<\kappa$ & $\R$ & $\kappa$ reg.\ unctbl. & $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ & $\kappa$\\
$A^{08}_\kappa$ & $\bigoplus_{\xi<\kappa}\Q$, 1 arm & countable, controlled & $\R\cap\overline\Q$ & $\kappa$ infinite & $\kappa$ & $\cf\kappa$\\
$A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$ & $\bigoplus_{\omega_1\times\lambda}\Q$, 1 arm & countable & $k\in\{\R,\C\}$ & $\lambda\ge\aleph_0$, $\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$ & $\lambda$ & $\aleph_1$\\
$R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ & $\bigoplus_{\alpha<\kappa}\Q$, 1 arm & $<\kappa$ & $|K|\le\max(\kappa,2^{\aleph_0})$ & $\kappa$ reg.\ unctbl. & $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ & $\kappa$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

All are ZFC constructions. The sizes are proved in \cref{osq:sec:models}; for $A^{06}_\kappa$ and
$R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ the size $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ is a merge result (06 and 11 compute the size
only under $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$).

\begin{theorem}[Detection threshold equals size \src{03, 08, 09} \merge]\label{osq:thm:thresholds}
Let $A$ be any of the five rings of the table, with purely infinite ideal $\Pi_A$, and let
$0\ne x\in\Pi_A$. Then
\[
 \min\{|S|:\varphi:A\to S,\ \varphi(x)\ne0\}
 =\min\{|M|: M\text{ an }A\text{-module},\ xM\ne0\}=|A| .
\]
Every homomorphism from $A$ to a ring of cardinality $<|A|$ factors uniquely through $\ct$, every
$A$-module of cardinality $<|A|$ is annihilated by $\Pi_A$, and every quotient $A/J$ either is
$D/\ct(J)$ with $\Pi_A\subseteq J$ or has cardinality exactly $|A|$. The same holds for the
Gaussian versions of $A^{03}_\kappa$, $A^{06}_\kappa$ and $A^{09}_{\lambda,\Z[i]}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the ambient field $F$ and coefficient field of the chosen construction:
the countable-support field for 03 and 09, the $<\kappa$-support field
for 06 and 11, and the controlled field for 08. In each case
$A=D+\Pi(F)$, $F$ contains all its exponent-group monomials, and
$|F|=|A|$ by the size calculations in \cref{osq:sec:models}.
We first verify that every smaller-scale field has this same size:
\[
 |L_c(F)|=|A|\qquad(c>0).
\]
For 03 this is \cref{osq:lem:card03}; for 06 it is
\cref{osq:lem:card06}; and for 11 it is \cref{osq:prop:card11}
together with its ambient-field upper bound. For 08, the field $L_c(F)$
contains the $\kappa$ monomials $X^{e_\xi}$ with $\xi$ beyond the least
nonzero coordinate of $c$, by \cref{osq:lem:gammabounds}. They lie in
the controlled field and have exponents in $H_c$; the upper bound is
$|F|=\kappa$. For 09, apply \cref{osq:lem:tail} to $\{c\}$.
A single later row gives $\lambda$ distinct monomials in $L_c(F)$,
and $|F|=\lambda$ gives the upper bound. The real and Gaussian
coefficient choices use the same monomial families and their respective
field-size bounds.

Now fix $0\ne x\in\Pi(F)$. Each construction supplies a positive
strict lower bound $g$ of $\supp x$: use
\cref{osq:lem:smallcommon,osq:lem:kappagap,osq:lem:finitecoord,osq:lem:tail}
for 03, 06, 08 and 09, respectively, and
\cref{osq:prop:lex} with $|\supp x|<\kappa$ for 11.
Divisibility of the group gives $c=g/2>0$. Since $F$ is a field,
$b=X^{-2c}x\in F$; all its exponents are positive, so $b\in\Pi(F)$
and $x=X^{2c}b$. The field bound in
\cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(iii) now shows that every ring target or
module detecting $x$ has at least $|L_c(F)|=|A|$ elements. This proof
does not require a homomorphism to preserve $1$ or the target to be
commutative. For modules it counts the orbit of a vector directly.
The identity map and the regular module, with vector $1$, attain both
bounds. Thus both minima exist and equal $|A|$ for each such $x$.

A homomorphism into a smaller ring therefore kills all of $\Pi(F)$.
Writing $a=d+f$ shows that its factor through $\ct$ is exactly its
restriction to $D$, and the section $D\to A$ makes that factor unique.
The same decomposition supplies the unique induced $D$-action on every
smaller module. If $\Pi(F)\subseteq J$, the assignment
$a+J\mapsto\ct(a)+\ct(J)$ is a ring isomorphism
$A/J\to D/\ct(J)$. If this inclusion fails, the quotient map detects
some nonzero purely infinite element; hence
$|A|\le|A/J|\le|A|$. These alternatives are cases determined by
ideal containment, not necessarily disjoint lists of cardinalities.
The zero ring and, when $J=\Pi(F)$, the quotient $D$ are included.
\end{proof}

For $A^{03}_\kappa$, $A^{08}_\kappa$ and $A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$ the theorem is proved in the
sources (03 with the field bound; 08 and 09 by counting monomials, which suffices because there
the number of small monomials already equals $|A|$). For $A^{06}_\kappa$ 06 proves the lower
bound $\kappa$ and exactness under $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, and for $R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ 11
proves sharpness under $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$ and $|K|\le\kappa$; the unconditional exact value
$\kappa^{<\kappa}$ is new here (\cref{osq:thm:model06,osq:prop:card11}). The quotient alternative
is 08's and 09's for their rings and a one-line consequence for the others.

\begin{remark}[Reconciling the thresholds \merge]\label{osq:rem:reconcile}
\leavevmode
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Realized cardinals.} Since $(\kappa^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$, and
conversely an infinite cardinal $\theta$ with $\theta^{\aleph_0}=\theta$ has $\cf\theta>\aleph_0$ by
K\"onig's theorem (so $\kappa=\theta$ is allowed in 03), the thresholds realized by 03 are
exactly the infinite cardinals $\theta$ with $\theta^{\aleph_0}=\theta$; these are 09's cardinals
$\lambda$. The countable-cofinality obstruction is the diagonal argument
in \cref{osq:lem:cardinalfacts}: for infinite $\theta$ of countable
cofinality it gives $\theta^{\aleph_0}>\theta$.

06 and 11 realize $\theta=\kappa^{<\kappa}$ for regular uncountable
$\kappa$. These sizes also satisfy $\theta^{\aleph_0}=\theta$.
Indeed, realize $\theta$ as the cardinality of
$\bigcup_{\nu<\kappa}(\{\nu\}\times{}^\nu\kappa)$, where $\nu$
ranges over cardinals. A countable sequence of these functions has its
lengths bounded by some infinite $\rho<\kappa$, by regularity. For a
fixed $\rho$, there are at most $\kappa^{\rho\cdot\aleph_0}
=\kappa^\rho$ such sequences, including their length tags. Summing
over fewer than or equal to $\kappa$ choices of $\rho$ gives the upper
bound $\theta$; constant sequences give the lower bound.

Thus 08 is the only one of these five families reaching an infinite size
$\theta$ below $2^{\aleph_0}$ or with $\theta^{\aleph_0}>\theta$;
it reaches every infinite cardinal. The continuum obstruction has an
algebraic explanation in the real-coefficient models: if $rX^c$ lies
in the ring for every real $r$, every target detecting $X^{2c}$ has at
least $2^{\aleph_0}$ elements by \cref{osq:lem:collision} with $L=\R$.
08 instead uses real algebraic coefficients and a countable-stage closure.
The cardinal calculation above also covers 11's smaller coefficient
fields, where this particular real-coefficient argument is unavailable.
\item \emph{The same ring, different bounds.} $A^{06}_{\aleph_1}$ and $A^{03}_{\aleph_1}$ are
isomorphic: both are the countable-support real Hahn integer parts over the lexicographic sum
$\bigoplus_J\Q$ with $J$ of order type $\omega_1^{\mathrm{op}}+\omega_1$ (06's generators satisfy
$\epsilon_\beta\ll\epsilon_\alpha\ll h_\alpha\ll h_\beta$ for $\alpha<\beta$). 06 proves the
threshold is at least $\aleph_1$ and exactly $\aleph_1$ under CH; 03 proves it is exactly
$2^{\aleph_0}$ in ZFC; 06's own example already notes that without CH its ring need not have size
$\aleph_1$. These agree.
\item \emph{Generators.} The generator counts are $\cf\kappa$ (03, 08), $\kappa$ (06, and for
11's ring by the argument of (H3) in \cref{osq:sec:homological}) and $\aleph_1$ (09). In each case the proof exhibits a coinitial chain of monomials in the positive
cone of the exponent group of that length; the counts differ because the constructions differ,
and no general formula is asserted for other exponent groups or support restrictions.
For example, 08 at $\kappa=\aleph_0$ has threshold and generator count
$\aleph_0$, while 09 at $\lambda=2^{\aleph_0}$ has threshold
$2^{\aleph_0}$ and generator count $\aleph_1$; equality of the latter
two cardinals is precisely CH. The generator proof for 11 is given
directly after \cref{osq:prop:card11}.
\item \emph{Fraction fields.} $\Frac A=F$ is proved for 03 and 06, which use a second
(reversed) arm to clear negative exponents; 08 explicitly does not claim it for its one-armed
controlled field, and 09 and 11 do not address it.
\item \emph{Hypotheses.} Regularity in 06 and 11 bounds the union of
fewer than $\kappa$ supports, each of size less than $\kappa$. For 03,
$\mu=\cf\kappa>\aleph_0$ bounds the union of fewer than $\mu$
countable supports. In particular a single support has a gap in each
case. In 09 a countable union of finite coordinate supports has its first
coordinates bounded in $\omega_1$, without regularity of $\lambda$.
08 replaces these full-support bounds with its finite-coordinate
invariant, which confines each element to finitely many coordinates and
works even when $\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$. These are different reasons for
the gap property; a cardinal estimate alone does not supply it.
\end{itemize}
\end{remark}

\section{Set-sized rings with exact thresholds}\label{osq:sec:models}

Five constructions replace the proper-class supply of scales by a cardinal.
They are different rings and are tagged by source; all are ZFC
constructions of sets. The displayed real/integer models and the stated
Gaussian versions have embeddings into $\Oz$ and $\GOz$, respectively.
The general coefficient choices in 09 and 11 are kept as abstract Hahn
rings; no such embedding is asserted for every coefficient field.
For example, 11 permits $D=K=\F_p$, giving a ring of characteristic $p$,
which cannot embed unitally in either characteristic-zero omnific ring. For every one of them
\cref{osq:thm:thresholds} gives the exact detection threshold; this section supplies the
constructions and the size computations it uses. Manuscript 05 (sibling report
\cite{RepoOdg}) asked which set-sized exponent groups admit analogues of the common-divisor
and set-target theorems (its ``exact size boundary'' question); 03, 06, 08, 09 and 11 each
answer it with a sharp family, and none claims a classification of all exponent groups or
support restrictions.

\subsection{Countable supports over a two-armed group \texorpdfstring{\src{03}}{[03]}}\label{osq:sec:model03}

For an ordered abelian group $G$ and $k\in\{\R,\C\}$ let $\Hc kG$ be the Hahn series over $k$
with \emph{at most countable} reverse well-ordered support (any countable reverse order type is
allowed; the subscript means countable support, not order type $\omega$). It is the
$\aleph_1$-bounded Hahn field in the terminology of \cite{LM}.

\begin{lemma}[Countable-support Hahn fields \src{03}]\label{osq:lem:hcfield}
$\Hc kG$ is a field. If $G$ is divisible, $\Hc\R G$ is real closed, $\Hc\C G$ is algebraically
closed, and $\Hc\C G=\Hc\R G[i]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Given finitely many series, the subgroup $H\le G$ generated by the union of
their supports is countable: its elements are finite integer combinations
of a countable set. The series therefore lie in the full Hahn field
$\hahn kH$, and every series in that field still has countable support in
$G$. Sums, products, additive inverses and the inverse of each nonzero
series consequently remain in $\Hc kG$.

If $G$ is divisible, replace $H$ by its divisible hull inside $G$, namely
its rational span; this is still countable. The full Hahn field over this
divisible group is real closed for $k=\R$, and algebraically closed for
$k=\C$ \cite[Fact~2.1.1]{LM}. Thus every complex-coefficient nonconstant
polynomial has a root in a countable-support subfield. On the real side,
the same argument supplies a square root of each positive element and a
root of every odd-degree polynomial, proving real closedness in the
leading-term order. Finally, real and imaginary parts have supports
contained in the original countable support, and the union of two
countable supports is countable. This proves both inclusions in
$\Hc\C G=\Hc\R G[i]$.
\end{proof}

With $A(D,k,G)=D+\{f\in\Hc kG:\supp f\subseteq G_{>0}\}$, the constant term is a split surjection,
the units are $D^\times$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}), and for $(D,k)=(\Z,\R)$ the ring is a discretely
ordered integer part of $\Hc\R G$: write $x=P+r+\epsilon$ by positive, zero and negative exponents and
take $P+\lfloor r\rfloor$, except $P+r-1$ when $r\in\Z$ and $\epsilon<0$.
Indeed, $\epsilon$ is infinitesimal, so when $r\notin\Z$ it cannot cross
either endpoint of the interval $[\lfloor r\rfloor,\lfloor r\rfloor+1)$.
When $r\in\Z$, its sign decides between $P+r$ and $P+r-1$. Truncating
preserves countable support, so the chosen floor lies in the ring. Every
positive element of this ring is either a positive integer or has positive
leading exponent and hence exceeds every real constant; in particular
there is no element strictly between $0$ and $1$. Discarding all negative
exponents without the endpoint correction would send $-X^{-g}$ to $0$,
which is not its floor. The same rule gives the omnific integer part of
$\No$ (03, 06, 08; compare \cite{RepoTrig}).

\paragraph{The construction.} Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal with $\mu=\cf\kappa>\aleph_0$,
$\theta=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$, $J_\kappa=\kappa^{\mathrm{op}}+\kappa$ with indices $p_\alpha$ (reversed arm)
and $q_\alpha$ (forward arm), and
\[
 G_\kappa=\bigoplus_{j\in J_\kappa}\Q e_j,
\]
ordered lexicographically with the \emph{least} index of a nonzero vector deciding its sign; earlier
indices are larger scales ($ne_{j'}<e_j$ for $j<j'$). $\iota(e_{p_\alpha})=\omega^\alpha$,
$\iota(e_{q_\alpha})=\omega^{-(\alpha+1)}$ extends to an ordered additive embedding
$G_\kappa\hookrightarrow\No$, and $\sum a_gX^g\mapsto\sum a_g\omega^{\iota(g)}$ is an ordered field
embedding. Put
\[
 F^{03}_\kappa=\Hc\R{G_\kappa},\qquad A^{03}_\kappa=A(\Z,\R,G_\kappa)=F^{03}_\kappa\cap\Oz,\qquad
 \Pi^{03}_\kappa=\ker(\ct|_{A^{03}_\kappa}),
\]
and use the superscript $\C$ for the parallel construction over $\C$ and $\Z[i]$:
$F^{03,\C}_\kappa=F^{03}_\kappa[i]$, $A^{03,\C}_\kappa=A^{03}_\kappa[i]$,
$\Pi^{03,\C}_\kappa=\Pi^{03}_\kappa+i\Pi^{03}_\kappa$.

\begin{lemma}[Room on both sides \src{03}]\label{osq:lem:twosided}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every family of fewer than $\mu$ elements of $G_\kappa$ is bounded above and below in $G_\kappa$.
\item Every family of fewer than $\mu$ positive elements has a positive strict lower bound.
\item For every $h>0$, a final segment of the forward arm, of cardinality $\kappa$, consists of basis
vectors $e_{q_\alpha}\ll h$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $E$ be a family of fewer than $\mu$ vectors. Each vector has finite
coordinate support, so fewer than $\mu$ indices occur altogether. Since
$\mu=\cf\kappa$, their ordinal labels are bounded below $\kappa$ on each
arm. Choose $\beta<\kappa$ above all reversed-arm labels that occur. Then
$p_\beta$ precedes every occurring index, including every index of the
forward arm. Lexicographic comparison gives
$-e_{p_\beta}<v<e_{p_\beta}$ for every $v\in E$, proving (i).

For a family of positive vectors choose $\gamma<\kappa$ above all its
forward-arm labels. The index $q_\gamma$ follows every occurring index.
The first nonzero coordinate of each vector is positive and occurs before
$q_\gamma$, so each vector exceeds $ne_{q_\gamma}$ for every positive
integer $n$. In particular $e_{q_\gamma}$ is a positive strict lower bound,
proving (ii). Empty families impose no restriction on these choices.
For (iii), apply the same comparison to the single vector $h$: every
$\alpha$ beyond its finitely many forward-arm labels satisfies
$e_{q_\alpha}\ll h$. Such a final segment has cardinality $\kappa$, because
removing a bounded initial segment of the infinite cardinal $\kappa$
leaves $\kappa$ ordinals.
\end{proof}

The reversed arm supplies a denominator large enough to shift a countable support upward; the forward
arm supplies a positive divisor below a countable positive support and many indistinguishable smaller
scales (03).

\begin{lemma}[Small families have common divisors \src{03}]\label{osq:lem:smallcommon}
Every family of fewer than $\mu$ elements of $\Pi^{03}_\kappa$ (or $\Pi^{03,\C}_\kappa$) has a common
divisor $X^g$, $g>0$, with all quotients in the ideal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a family $E$ with $|E|<\mu$, the union
$T=\bigcup_{f\in E}\supp f$ has size at most
$|E|\cdot\aleph_0<\mu$ when $E$ is nonempty, because $\mu$ is regular
and uncountable. All members of $T$ are positive.
Choose $0<g<T$ by \cref{osq:lem:twosided}(ii). Then for every $f\in E$,
the series $X^{-g}f$ has positive, countable, reverse well-ordered support,
so it lies in the same purely infinite ideal. Translation neither changes
support cardinality nor the coefficient field. If $T$ is empty, every
member is zero and any positive $g$ works. The argument applies equally to
real and complex coefficients.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Every smaller-scale field has size $\theta$ \src{03}]\label{osq:lem:card03}
For either coefficient pair, the field, the ring, its purely infinite ideal and every
$L_h=\Hc k{H_h(G_\kappa)}$ ($h>0$) have cardinality $\theta=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $F$, $A$ and $\Pi_A$ for the field, ring and ideal of the chosen
coefficient pair. The finite-coordinate group $G_\kappa$ has cardinality $\kappa$. There are
at most $\kappa^{\aleph_0}$ countable supports in it, and each support
admits at most $(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}\le\theta$
coefficient functions, for either $k=\R$ or $k=\C$. This gives the common
upper bound $\theta$ for the field and all the indicated subsets.

For the lower bound choose a forward tail $T\subseteq\kappa$ of size
$\kappa$ with $e_{q_\alpha}\ll h$ for every $\alpha\in T$, using
\cref{osq:lem:twosided}(iii). Each countable $S\subseteq T$ determines
\[
 f_S=\sum_{\alpha\in S}X^{e_{q_\alpha}}\in L_h.
\]
Its support is reverse well ordered: a nonempty subset has a largest
exponent at its least ordinal index. Its coefficients recover $S$, so
these series are distinct. Also $L_h$ contains all constant series $k$.
Hence \cref{osq:lem:cardinalfacts} gives
$|L_h|\ge\max(|[\kappa]^{\le\aleph_0}|,2^{\aleph_0})=\theta$.
Finally $H_h(G_\kappa)=H_{h/2}(G_\kappa)$, and every exponent $u$ in
this subgroup satisfies $|u|<h/2$. Thus multiplication by $X^{h/2}$
is an injection $L_h\to\Pi_A$. Together with
$\Pi_A\subseteq A\subseteq F$, this proves all the claimed equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinal realization \src{03}]\label{osq:thm:model03}
Take $(A,F,D)=(A^{03}_\kappa,F^{03}_\kappa,\Z)$ or
$(A^{03,\C}_\kappa,F^{03,\C}_\kappa,\Z[i])$, with ideal $\Pi_A$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|F|=|A|=\theta$ and $\Frac(A)=F$;
\item every unital map $A\to R$ with $|R|<\theta$ factors uniquely through $\ct$ (for the Gaussian
ring the factorization through the Gaussian constant term is unique for a given map; different
square roots of $-1$ give different maps);
\item every $A$-module of cardinality $<\theta$ is annihilated by $\Pi_A$, and for every
$0\ne f\in\Pi_A$ the least cardinality of a ring target detecting $f$, and of a module on which $f$
acts nontrivially, is exactly $\theta$;
\item $\Pi_A$ needs exactly $\mu$ generators; it is flat with $\Pi_A^2=\Pi_A$, the module $D=A/\Pi_A$
is not flat, and $\Tor^A_n(D,N)=0$ for every $D$-module $N$ and $n>0$.
\end{enumerate}
No inaccessible cardinal, CH or other additional axiom is used.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) The sizes are \cref{osq:lem:card03}. For $x\in F$, apply
\cref{osq:lem:twosided}(i) to the countable set
$\{0\}\cup\{-g:g\in\supp x\}$. Its strict upper bound $h$ is positive
and satisfies $h+g>0$ for every exponent of $x$. Therefore
$X^h x\in\Pi_A$, $X^h\in\Pi_A\setminus\{0\}$ and
$x=(X^h x)/X^h$. Conversely $A\subseteq F$ and $F$ is a field, proving
the fraction-field assertion with the matching real or complex coefficients.

(ii)--(iii) We prove the lower bound directly, supplying this case of
\cref{osq:thm:thresholds}. For $0\ne f\in\Pi_A$,
\cref{osq:lem:smallcommon} gives $f=X^gb$ with $g>0$ and $b\in\Pi_A$.
Set $c=g/2$. By \cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(iii), a ring map detecting $f$
has a target of size at least $|L_c|=\theta$; a module with $fv\ne0$ has
the same bound, using the vector $bv$. The identity map and the regular
module $A$, with vector $1$, attain it. Thus a map to a smaller ring kills
every element of $\Pi_A$, and its unique factor is its restriction to
$D$: for $d\in D$ and $p\in\Pi_A$, $\varphi(d+p)=\varphi(d)$.
If $|M|<\theta$, no product $fv$ can be nonzero, so $\Pi_A M=0$.
The lower-bound argument also works for nonunital ring maps. In the unital
Gaussian case the restriction to $D=\Z[i]$ is fixed by the chosen map;
the theorem does not prescribe one square root of $-1$ for all maps.

(iv) Choose a strictly increasing cofinal sequence
$(\alpha_\xi)_{\xi<\mu}$ in $\kappa$ and put
$m_\xi=X^{e_{q_{\alpha_\xi}}}$. A countable positive support involves
only countably many coordinate indices; these are bounded on the forward
arm because $\cf\kappa>\aleph_0$. Consequently, for sufficiently large
$\xi$, $e_{q_{\alpha_\xi}}$ is strictly below every exponent of $f$, and
$f/m_\xi\in\Pi_A$. Moreover $m_\xi A\subsetneq m_\eta A$ when
$\xi<\eta$: the forward quotient is a positive monomial and the reverse
quotient has negative exponent. Thus
\[
 \Pi_A=\bigcup_{\xi<\mu}m_\xi A.
\]
This exhibits $\mu$ generators. Any family of fewer than $\mu$ elements
of $\Pi_A$ is contained in $X^hA$ for some $h>0$ by
\cref{osq:lem:smallcommon}. Its generated ideal is therefore contained
there too, whereas $X^{h/2}\in\Pi_A$ is missing: its unique quotient by
$X^h$ in $F$ is $X^{-h/2}\notin A$. Hence fewer generators cannot suffice.

Each $m_\xi A$ is free of rank one since $A$ is a domain, and the displayed
union is a directed colimit indexed by the set $\mu$. It is flat
\cite[Lemma~10.39.3]{StacksFlat}. The factorization $f=X^gb$ above has
both factors in $\Pi_A$, so $\Pi_A^2=\Pi_A$. If $N$ is a $D$-module
inflated along $\ct$, then $\Pi_A N=0$ and every elementary tensor
$f\otimes n=(X^gb)\otimes n=b\otimes X^g n$ vanishes. The flat
resolution $0\to\Pi_A\to A\to D\to0$ therefore gives
$\Tor^A_n(D,N)=0$ for every $n>0$. Nevertheless $D$ is not flat:
for $0\ne x\in\Pi_A$ the injection $xA\hookrightarrow A$, after
tensoring with $D$, becomes the zero map between two copies of the
nonzero module $D$. These are the parts of \cref{osq:thm:homological}
needed here; no assertion about the other four models is used.
\end{proof}

For $\kappa=\aleph_1$: $2^{\aleph_0}\le\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}\le(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$,
so $A^{03}_{\aleph_1}$ has the size of the continuum, every target of size below the continuum sees only
the constant term, whether or not CH holds, and the ideal needs $\aleph_1$ generators. For every
infinite $\rho$, $\kappa=2^\rho$ gives $\theta=2^\rho$ with $\cf(2^\rho)>\rho$; so arbitrarily large
thresholds are realized in ZFC. This is a realization theorem for this family, not a classification
of ordered exponent groups. The case $\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$ is excluded because countable supports can
then run cofinally through an arm (03).

\begin{lemma}[Cardinal facts \src{03}]\label{osq:lem:cardinalfacts}
For every infinite $\kappa$, $\kappa^{\aleph_0}=\max(2^{\aleph_0},|[\kappa]^{\le\aleph_0}|)$; for every
infinite $\rho$, $(2^\rho)^{\aleph_0}=2^\rho$ and $\cf(2^\rho)>\rho$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A sequence in $\kappa$ is determined by its nonempty countable range and
one of at most $\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$ sequences in that
range. This gives the upper bound by the stated maximum. Conversely,
binary sequences embed in $\kappa^\N$; and, by choice, select an
enumeration of each nonempty at-most-countable subset of $\kappa$,
repeating entries for finite subsets. Different ranges give different
sequences. Adjoining the empty subset does not change this infinite
cardinality. These two lower bounds prove the first formula.

For infinite $\rho$, cardinal exponentiation gives
$(2^\rho)^{\aleph_0}=2^{\rho\cdot\aleph_0}=2^\rho$.
For the cofinality claim, suppose the binary functions on $\rho$ were
covered by families $(E_\xi)_{\xi<\tau}$ with $0<\tau\le\rho$ and
$|E_\xi|<2^\rho$ for every $\xi$. Partition $\rho$ into $\tau$
disjoint blocks $B_\xi$, each of size $\rho$. There are $2^\rho$
binary patterns on $B_\xi$, but fewer than $2^\rho$ restrictions of
members of $E_\xi$, so choose a missing pattern on each block.
The assembled function differs from every member of $E_\xi$ on its
corresponding block, contradicting the cover. A cofinal sequence of
length at most $\rho$ in $2^\rho$ would give just such a cover by
smaller initial segments. Thus $\cf(2^\rho)>\rho$, the required
instance of K\"onig's theorem.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Supports of size \texorpdfstring{$<\kappa$}{< kappa} over a two-sided group \texorpdfstring{\src{06}}{[06]}}\label{osq:sub:model06}

Fix an uncountable regular cardinal $\kappa$. In the additive group of $\No$ put
\[
 h_\alpha=\omega^{\alpha+1},\qquad\epsilon_\alpha=\omega^{-(\alpha+1)}\quad(\alpha<\kappa),\qquad
 \Gamma^{06}_\kappa=\Span_\Q\{h_\alpha,\epsilon_\alpha:\alpha<\kappa\}
\]
(finite rational combinations of distinct Conway monomials, hence linearly independent). This is a
divisible ordered group of cardinality $\kappa$, and $\epsilon_\beta\ll\epsilon_\alpha\ll h_\alpha\ll
h_\beta$ for $\alpha<\beta$; here $\ll$ refers to the outer exponents.

\begin{lemma}[Simultaneous upper and lower scales \src{06}]\label{osq:lem:kappagap}
For every $T\subseteq\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$ with $|T|<\kappa$ there is $\beta<\kappa$ with
$\epsilon_\beta\ll|t|\ll h_\beta$ for all $t\in T\setminus\{0\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each member of $T$ uses finitely many of the generators. The union of
their index sets has cardinality less than $\kappa$, so regularity gives
$\beta<\kappa$ strictly above every index occurring. The empty union
allows any $\beta$. For a nonzero $t$, the largest Conway monomial in
its finite rational expression determines the Archimedean class of $|t|$;
its coefficient cannot cancel because the expression uses distinct monomials.
Both $h_\alpha$ and $\epsilon_\alpha$, for $\alpha<\beta$, have classes
strictly between those of $\epsilon_\beta$ and $h_\beta$. Thus for every
positive integer $n$, $n\epsilon_\beta<|t|$ and $n|t|<h_\beta$, as required.
\end{proof}

For $k\in\{\R,\C\}$ put $K^{06}_{\kappa,k}=\{f\in\hahn k{\Gamma^{06}_\kappa}:|\supp f|<\kappa\}$,
$K^{06}_\kappa=K^{06}_{\kappa,\R}$, $\Pi^{06}_\kappa=\{f\in K^{06}_\kappa:\supp f>0\}$ and
$A^{06}_\kappa=\Z+\Pi^{06}_\kappa$ (06's $R_\kappa$); $X^g\mapsto\omega^g$ makes them subsets of $\No$
and $\SC$.

\begin{proposition}[Field closure and integer part \src{06}]\label{osq:prop:fieldclosure}
$K^{06}_{\kappa,\R}$ is real closed, $K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}=K^{06}_{\kappa,\R}[i]$ is algebraically
closed, $A^{06}_\kappa=K^{06}_\kappa\cap\Oz$, $\Frac(A^{06}_\kappa)=K^{06}_\kappa$, and $A^{06}_\kappa$
is a discretely ordered integer part of $K^{06}_\kappa$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For finitely many series, let $S$ be the union of their supports and
$\Delta=\Span_\Q S\subseteq\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$. Then
\[
 |\Delta|\le\max(|S|,\aleph_0)<\kappa.
\]
All the chosen series lie in the full Hahn field $\hahn k\Delta$, and
every support in that field has size less than $\kappa$. This proves
closure under sums, products, negatives and nonzero inverses. Applied to
the finitely many coefficients of a polynomial over $K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}$,
the same argument places them in $\hahn\C\Delta$. This field is
algebraically closed because $\Delta$ is divisible
\cite[Corollary~4]{Poonen}; hence the polynomial splits within the support
bound. Splitting coefficients into real and imaginary parts preserves that
bound, and the union of two supports of size less than $\kappa$ still has
size less than $\kappa$. Therefore
$K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}=K^{06}_{\kappa,\R}[i]$. The real field is ordered by
its leading coefficient and has this algebraically closed quadratic
extension, so it is real closed. Only uncountability of $\kappa$, not
regularity, was used in this paragraph.

The embedding $X^g\mapsto\omega^g$ identifies $A^{06}_\kappa$ with
$K^{06}_\kappa\cap\Oz$: the normal-form characterization of $\Oz$
requires exactly nonnegative exponents and an integer coefficient at zero.
For $f\in K^{06}_\kappa$, apply \cref{osq:lem:kappagap} to $\supp f$.
Every $g$ in that support satisfies $h_\beta+g>0$, including $g=0$,
since $h_\beta>0$. Consequently $X^{h_\beta}f\in\Pi^{06}_\kappa$
and $X^{h_\beta}\in A^{06}_\kappa\setminus\{0\}$, giving
$f=(X^{h_\beta}f)/X^{h_\beta}$ and the fraction-field equality.

For the integer part, use the floor rule in \cref{osq:sec:model03}.
Its positive truncation and corrected integer constant retain support of
size less than $\kappa$, so the floor belongs to $A^{06}_\kappa$.
A positive element of this ring is either a positive integer or has
positive leading exponent and positive leading coefficient, in which case
it exceeds every real constant. Thus there is no ring element strictly
between $0$ and $1$. The sign condition is essential: $-X^g$ for $g>0$
also has positive leading exponent but is negative.
\end{proof}

Field closure uses only that $\kappa$ is uncountable; regularity is used for simultaneous gaps and
generation (06). The first-kappa report proves the closedness of $\{f\in k(\!(t^\Gamma)\!):|\supp f|<\kappa\}$
for every uncountable $\kappa$, possibly singular (\nolinkurl{fkc:thm:main} in \cite{RepoFKC}); 06's
closure argument is not a novelty claim, and singular support bounds may preserve field closure while
failing the simultaneous gap property used here. The two families $h_\alpha$ and $\epsilon_\alpha$ are
deliberate: the $\epsilon_\alpha$ provide smaller positive gaps and the $h_\alpha$ shift supports upward,
and a one-sided family would not automatically give the fraction-field assertion (06).

The failure of the gap property at a singular bound can be seen directly.
If the same formulas are used with an uncountable singular $\kappa$, choose
a strictly increasing cofinal sequence $(\alpha_\xi)_{\xi<\cf\kappa}$
in $\kappa$. The series
\[
 f=\sum_{\xi<\cf\kappa}X^{\epsilon_{\alpha_\xi}}
\]
has positive reverse well-ordered support of size $\cf\kappa<\kappa$.
Every $g>0$ in $\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$ has a finite coordinate expression,
so eventually $\epsilon_{\alpha_\xi}\ll g$. Thus $f/X^g$ has a negative
exponent and is not in the integer-part ring. This gives an element with
no positive monomial divisor there, although the support-bounded field
is still closed under field operations and algebraic roots. The regular
cardinal hypothesis is retained in the results below.

\begin{proposition}[A chain of principal ideals \src{06}]\label{osq:prop:kappachain}
$\Pi^{06}_\kappa=\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}X^{\epsilon_\alpha}A^{06}_\kappa$ is a strictly increasing union;
the ideal is idempotent and its least number of generators is $\kappa$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $A=A^{06}_\kappa$ and $I=\Pi^{06}_\kappa$. For $\alpha<\beta$,
\[
 X^{\epsilon_\alpha}
 =X^{\epsilon_\beta}X^{\epsilon_\alpha-\epsilon_\beta}
 \quad\text{with}\quad X^{\epsilon_\alpha-\epsilon_\beta}\in I.
\]
Hence $X^{\epsilon_\alpha}A\subseteq X^{\epsilon_\beta}A$. The inclusion
is strict: the only possible quotient of $X^{\epsilon_\beta}$ by
$X^{\epsilon_\alpha}$ in the ambient field has negative exponent, so
is not in $A$. For $f\in I$, \cref{osq:lem:kappagap} gives
$\epsilon_\alpha<g$ for every $g\in\supp f$, and therefore
$X^{-\epsilon_\alpha}f\in I$. This proves the union; it also factors
every $f$ as a product of two members of $I$, proving $I^2=I$.
Zero causes no exception, since its quotient is zero.

The displayed $\kappa$ monomials generate $I$. Conversely, if $E\subseteq I$
has cardinality less than $\kappa$, regularity gives
$|\bigcup_{f\in E}\supp f|<\kappa$. Apply the gap lemma to this union to
find a single $a=\epsilon_\beta>0$ with $E\subseteq X^aA$.
Every finite $A$-linear combination of members of $E$ still lies in $X^aA$.
But $X^{a/2}\in I$ does not: its unique quotient by $X^a$ is
$X^{-a/2}\notin A$. Thus $E$ cannot generate $I$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Size of the ring and of every smaller-scale field \merge]\label{osq:lem:card06}
For every $c>0$ in $\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$, the field $L_c=\{f\in K^{06}_\kappa:\supp f\subseteq
H_c(\Gamma^{06}_\kappa)\}$ has cardinality at least $\kappa^{<\kappa}$, and
\[
 |K^{06}_{\kappa,\R}|=|K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}|=|A^{06}_\kappa|=|\Pi^{06}_\kappa|=\kappa^{<\kappa}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First count the series from above. The exponent group has size $\kappa$.
A support of size $\nu<\kappa$, together with its real or complex
coefficient function, has at most
$\kappa^\nu(2^{\aleph_0})^\nu$ possible descriptions. For infinite
$\nu$, $(2^{\aleph_0})^\nu=2^\nu\le\kappa^\nu$, so this is at most
$\kappa^\nu$. Finite supports together contribute at most
$\kappa\cdot2^{\aleph_0}\le\kappa^{\aleph_0}\le\kappa^{<\kappa}$.
There are at most $\kappa$ possible cardinal sizes $\nu$, and
$\kappa^{<\kappa}\ge\kappa$, so summing these bounds gives
$|K^{06}_{\kappa,k}|\le\kappa^{<\kappa}$ for either coefficient field.

For the lower bound, all coordinates occurring in the finite expression
of $c$ have indices below some $\alpha_0<\kappa$. The final segment
$T=(\alpha_0,\kappa)$ has cardinality $\kappa$, and
$\epsilon_\alpha\ll c$ for every $\alpha\in T$. Each subset
$B\subseteq T$ of size less than $\kappa$ gives
\[
 f_B=\sum_{\alpha\in B}X^{\epsilon_\alpha}\in L_c.
\]
The support is reverse well ordered, since a nonempty subset has largest
exponent at its least ordinal index, and its cardinality is $|B|<\kappa$.
Its exponents lie in $H_c(\Gamma^{06}_\kappa)$. The coefficients recover
$B$, so the map $B\mapsto f_B$ is injective.

To justify the subset count, for any set $T$ of size $\kappa$ one has
$|[T]^{<\kappa}|=\kappa^{<\kappa}$. The upper bound follows by enumerating
each subset, giving at most $\sum_{\nu<\kappa}\kappa^\nu
=\kappa^{<\kappa}$ possibilities. For the reverse bound fix
$0<\nu<\kappa$ and a bijection $\nu\times T\to T$. The graph of each
function $\nu\to T$ becomes a distinct subset of $T$ of size
$\nu<\kappa$. Hence $|[T]^{<\kappa}|\ge\kappa^\nu$ for every such
$\nu$, and taking the supremum proves the claim.

Thus $|L_c|\ge\kappa^{<\kappa}$, and the upper bound already proved gives
equality. By \cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(i), multiplication by $X^c$ embeds
$L_c$ into $\Pi^{06}_\kappa$. The inclusions of the ideal in the ring,
the ring in the real field and the real field in its complexification
give all remaining equalities. The same lower-bound series have real
coefficients, so they also work in the complex smaller-scale field; its
upper bound is the one proved above.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The exact threshold of $A^{06}_\kappa$ \src{06} \merge]\label{osq:thm:model06}
Let $\kappa$ be uncountable and regular. Every homomorphism $A^{06}_\kappa\to S$ with
$|S|<\kappa^{<\kappa}$ factors through $\ct$, every $A^{06}_\kappa$-module $M$ with $|M|<\kappa^{<\kappa}$
satisfies $\Pi^{06}_\kappa M=0$, and for each $0\ne x\in\Pi^{06}_\kappa$ the least cardinality of a ring
target detecting $x$, and of a module on which $x$ acts nontrivially, is exactly $\kappa^{<\kappa}$. The
same holds for $A^{06}_\kappa[i]$ with $\Z[i]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $A=A^{06}_\kappa$, $I=\Pi^{06}_\kappa$ and
$\theta=\kappa^{<\kappa}=|A|$. For $0\ne x\in I$,
\cref{osq:lem:kappagap} supplies $\epsilon_\beta<\supp x$.
Put $c=\epsilon_\beta/2$ and $b=X^{-2c}x\in I$.
Then $x=X^{2c}b$, and \cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(iii), together with
\cref{osq:lem:card06}, bounds every ring or module detecting $x$
from below by $|L_c|=\theta$. In the module case, $xv\ne0$ implies
$X^{2c}(bv)\ne0$, so the injection is into the module itself.
The identity map of $A$ and the regular module with vector $1$ attain
this bound. This proves the exact threshold directly, and supplies the
present model's case of \cref{osq:thm:thresholds}.

Every map $\varphi$ into a smaller ring therefore kills $I$. Since
$A=\Z\oplus I$, it satisfies $\varphi=\varphi|_\Z\circ\ct$,
and this factor is unique by restricting to $\Z$. Every module of
size less than $\theta$ has $xv=0$ for all $x\in I$ and $v\in M$,
which is exactly $IM=0$. The ring argument uses only additivity and
multiplicativity, so includes nonunital maps.

For the Gaussian version, real and imaginary parts give
\[
 A[i]=\Z[i]+I_{\C},\qquad
 I_{\C}=I+iI
 =\{f\in K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}:\supp f>0\}.
\]
Finite unions of supports preserve the bound. Thus $|A[i]|=\theta$:
it contains $A$ and is contained in $K^{06}_{\kappa,\C}$, both of that
size. The gap lemma depends only on exponents, and the complex
smaller-scale fields also have size $\theta$ by the preceding proof.
The same collision and attainment arguments apply, with factorization
through $\Z[i]$ and annihilation by $I_{\C}$.
\end{proof}

06 proves the lower bound $\kappa$ (with the explicit telescope family of the $\kappa$ monomials
$X^{a+\epsilon_\alpha}$, each witness having countable support) and, under the extra hypothesis
$\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, that $|A^{06}_\kappa|=\kappa$ and the threshold is exactly $\kappa$; that is
the special case of the theorem where $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$. The lower bounds of 06 need no cardinal
arithmetic, and neither does the exact value $\kappa^{<\kappa}$, which comes from 06's own collision lemma
(compare 03's field bound). This answers the first half of 06's question ``Cardinal arithmetic without the
matching hypothesis'': the least size of a target detecting a fixed nonzero $x\in\Pi^{06}_\kappa$ is
$\kappa^{<\kappa}$ in ZFC. The second half (``a different integer-part construction of size exactly
$\kappa$ with the same lower-bound property under weaker hypotheses'') is answered by 08 in ZFC for every
infinite $\kappa$ (\cref{osq:thm:model08}), for a ring of size exactly $\kappa$ whose fraction field,
unlike $\Frac A^{06}_\kappa=K^{06}_\kappa$, is not claimed to be its ambient field.

\begin{example}[The first uncountable cardinal \src{06}]\label{osq:ex:CH}
Under CH, $\aleph_1^{<\aleph_1}=\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1$, so $A^{06}_{\aleph_1}$ has
size $\aleph_1$: every action on a countable abelian group is an ordinary integer action, while the regular
module of size $\aleph_1$ sees all purely infinite elements. Without CH the lower bound at $\aleph_1$ holds,
the ring has size $\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$, and by \cref{osq:thm:model06} the exact threshold is
$2^{\aleph_0}$; this ring is isomorphic to $A^{03}_{\aleph_1}$ (\cref{osq:rem:reconcile}).
\end{example}
\begin{proof}
Every cardinal below $\aleph_1$ is at most countable, so
$\aleph_1^{<\aleph_1}=\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}$. In ZFC,
\[
 2^{\aleph_0}\le\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}
 \le(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]
Apply \cref{osq:thm:model06}; CH only identifies this already computed
threshold with $\aleph_1$. A countable module is below the threshold
in either case and hence is acted on through $\ct$.

For the stated isomorphism, the assignments
$e_{p_\alpha}\mapsto h_\alpha$ and
$e_{q_\alpha}\mapsto\epsilon_\alpha$ extend to an ordered group
isomorphism $G_{\aleph_1}\to\Gamma^{06}_{\aleph_1}$: both groups have
these rational bases in the same two-arm order, with the first nonzero
coordinate determining the sign. Reindexing Hahn exponents by this map
preserves sums, products, support order and support cardinality. At
$\kappa=\aleph_1$ both fields allow exactly the at-most-countable
supports, so this gives a coefficient-preserving field isomorphism.
It restricts to $A^{03}_{\aleph_1}\cong A^{06}_{\aleph_1}$ and commutes
with $\ct$, because it preserves positivity and the zero exponent.
The same construction applies with complex coefficients and Gaussian
integer constants. This is a reindexing isomorphism; the two embedded
subrings of $\No$ need not be identified element by element.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A controlled field of size exactly \texorpdfstring{$\kappa$}{kappa} \texorpdfstring{\src{08}}{[08]}}\label{osq:sub:model08}

Let $\kappa$ be any infinite cardinal and $\Gamma^{08}_\kappa=\bigoplus_{\xi<\kappa}\Q e_\xi$, ordered
lexicographically with the least nonzero index deciding the sign, so $0<ne_\eta<e_\xi$ for $\xi<\eta$;
it is divisible of cardinality $\kappa$, and each nonzero element has a finite coordinate support.

\begin{lemma}[Scale and support bounds \src{08}]\label{osq:lem:gammabounds}
For every $c>0$ there are $\kappa$ positive $a\ll c$ (namely $e_\xi$ for $\xi$ beyond the least nonzero
index of $c$). If $S\subseteq(\Gamma^{08}_\kappa)_{>0}$ has fewer than $\cf\kappa$ elements, some
$\beta<\kappa$ has $e_\beta\ll s$ for all $s\in S$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\xi_0$ be the least nonzero coordinate of $c$. For every
$\xi>\xi_0$ and every positive integer $n$, the leading coordinate of
$c-ne_\xi$ is still the positive coordinate of $c$ at $\xi_0$.
Hence $e_\xi\ll c$. The final segment $(\xi_0,\kappa)$ has cardinality
$\kappa$, proving the first assertion.

For the second, each $s\in S$ has finite coordinate support. Their union
has size less than $\cf\kappa$ and is bounded below $\kappa$; this also
holds when $\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$, since then $S$ is finite. Choose
$\beta<\kappa$ strictly above every coordinate occurring. Each positive
$s$ has its first nonzero coordinate before $\beta$, so the same
comparison gives $e_\beta\ll s$. If $S$ is empty, any $\beta$ works.
\end{proof}

Let $K=\R\cap\overline\Q$ be the countable real closed field of real
algebraic numbers, $H=\hahn K{\Gamma^{08}_\kappa}$, and
$H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}\subseteq H$ the series with at most countable support.
This is a real closed subfield: finitely many series lie in $\hahn K\Delta$
for the countable divisible subgroup $\Delta$ generated by their supports.
The full Hahn field is real closed \cite[Fact~2.1.1]{LM} and all its
supports are countable. This supplies field operations, positive square
roots and odd-degree polynomial roots within $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$.

A \emph{truncation} restricts a series to an initial segment of its support
in decreasing order, including the empty and whole support. If the support
has countable reverse order type $\alpha$, there are $\alpha+1$ such
initial segments, hence at most countably many truncations. Arbitrary
subseries are not being adjoined.

For a subfield $E\subseteq H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$, its real closure here
means its relative algebraic closure: all elements of $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$
algebraic over $E$. This is a real closed subfield, since positive square
roots and odd-degree roots exist in $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$ and remain
algebraic over $E$. Let $F_0$ be this closure of the field generated by
$K$ and all $X^g$. Given $F_n$, adjoin all truncations of its elements
and take the same relative algebraic closure to obtain $F_{n+1}$.
These are increasing subfields; put $F=\bigcup_{n<\omega}F_n$.

\begin{lemma}[The controlled field \src{08}]\label{osq:lem:controlled}
$F$ is real closed and truncation-closed, has cardinality $\kappa$, consists of series with countable
support, and contains $K$ and every monomial.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The field generated by $K$ and all monomials has size $\kappa$: there
are $\kappa$ generators, every rational expression uses only finitely
many, and the distinct monomials already give the lower bound. An
algebraic extension of an infinite field of size $\kappa$ has size at
most $\kappa$, because there are $\kappa$ nonzero polynomials and each
has finitely many roots. Thus $|F_0|=\kappa$.

If $|F_n|=\kappa$, its elements together have at most
$\kappa\cdot\aleph_0=\kappa$ truncations. Adjoining these elements and
then taking an algebraic extension again gives size at most $\kappa$;
the monomials give equality. Induction proves $|F_n|=\kappa$ for all
$n$, and the countable union has size $\kappa$ as well. This calculation
uses neither regularity nor $\kappa^{\aleph_0}=\kappa$.

The union is a field because the stages increase, and it is real closed:
a positive element, or the finitely many coefficients of an odd-degree
polynomial, belongs to some real closed stage, which supplies the required
root. Every truncation of $f\in F_n$ belongs to $F_{n+1}$, proving
truncation closure of $F$. Finally every stage lies in
$H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$ and contains $K$ and the monomials, proving the
remaining assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-coordinate invariant \src{08}]\label{osq:lem:finitecoord}
Every $f\in F$ has $\supp f\subseteq\Gamma_E=\bigoplus_{\xi\in E}\Q e_\xi$ for some finite $E\subseteq\kappa$
(its support need not be finite).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For finite $E\subseteq\kappa$ put $H_E=\hahn K{\Gamma_E}$.
The group $\Gamma_E$ is countable and divisible, so $H_E$ is real
closed and lies in $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$. Also $H_E,H_{E'}\subseteq
H_{E\cup E'}$, giving a directed family. Its coefficients all belong
to the same field $K$; allowing infinitely many series terms does not
introduce additional basis coordinates.

Every element of the field generated by $K$ and the monomials is a
rational expression in finitely many monomials. The union of their finite
coordinate sets is finite, so the expression belongs to some $H_E$.
If $f\in F_0$, choose a nonzero polynomial witnessing its algebraicity
over that generated field. Its finitely many coefficients lie in one
$H_E$, so $f$ is algebraic over $H_E$. A real closed field has no
proper ordered algebraic extension; since $H_E(f)$ lies in the ordered
field $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$, it follows that $f\in H_E$.

Suppose the assertion holds for $F_n$. A truncation of an element of
$H_E$ still has all its exponents in $\Gamma_E$, and hence belongs
to $H_E$. Each rational expression in $F_n$ and the adjoined
truncations therefore belongs to some $H_E$, by taking the finite union
of the coordinate sets used by its inputs. For an element of $F_{n+1}$,
apply the preceding algebraicity argument to the finitely many
coefficients of a defining polynomial. This proves the invariant at
every stage, and thus throughout $F$.
\end{proof}

This invariant removes regularity: even at a singular $\kappa$ of countable cofinality, the coordinates in
one element are confined to a finite set. The proof uses countable supports to control the number of
truncations and finite coordinate sets to find smaller positive scales (08).
For example, $\sum_{n<\omega}X^{e_n}$ has a countable reverse well-ordered
support and lies in $H_{\mathrm{ctbl}}$, but it is not in $F$: its
exponents use infinitely many basis coordinates. Thus countable support
is a necessary condition on members of $F$, not a description of all its
members. This distinction allows the construction to have size $\kappa$
even when the full countable-support field is larger.

The map $\iota(\sum q_\xi e_\xi)=\sum q_\xi\omega^{-\xi}$ is an increasing additive embedding of
$\Gamma^{08}_\kappa$ into $\No$ (the least nonzero coordinate decides the sign on both sides), and
$\Phi(\sum a_gX^g)=\sum a_g\omega^{\iota(g)}$ is an ordered field embedding $H\hookrightarrow\No$
preserving truncations and constant terms. Put
\[
 F^{08}_\kappa=\Phi(F),\qquad
 A^{08}_\kappa=F^{08}_\kappa\cap\Oz
 =\Phi\bigl(\{f\in F:\supp f\ge0,\ \ct(f)\in\Z\}\bigr),
\]
and $\Pi^{08}_\kappa=\ker(\ct|_{A^{08}_\kappa})$. In calculations below
we identify a Hahn series with its image under $\Phi$; in particular
$X^{e_0}$ denotes the actual surreal $\omega$, since $\iota(e_0)=1$.
The ring has size $\kappa$: it is contained in $\Phi(F)$ of that size
and contains the $\kappa$ distinct positive monomials $X^{e_\xi}$.
It is a discretely ordered integer part of $F^{08}_\kappa$. Indeed,
for $x\in F$ its positive part $P$ is a truncation, hence lies in $F$,
and its constant coefficient $r$ belongs to $K\subseteq F$. Apply the
floor rule of \cref{osq:sec:model03} to $x=P+r+\epsilon$; the result
belongs to $F$ and has precisely the support and constant-term conditions
defining $A^{08}_\kappa$. Discreteness is inherited from $\Oz$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp models at every infinite cardinal \src{08}]\label{osq:thm:model08}
For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $F^{08}_\kappa$ is a truncation-closed real closed subfield of $\No$ with countable supports,
$|F^{08}_\kappa|=|A^{08}_\kappa|=\kappa$, and $A^{08}_\kappa$ is an integer part of it;
\item every homomorphism from $A^{08}_\kappa$ to a ring of cardinality $<\kappa$ factors through $\ct$;
\item every quotient ring of $A^{08}_\kappa$ is a quotient $\Z/n\Z$ ($n\ge0$) under $\ct$ or has cardinality
exactly $\kappa$;
\item $\Pi^{08}_\kappa$ needs exactly $\cf\kappa$ generators;
\item every unital $A^{08}_\kappa$-module of cardinality $<\kappa$ has action $f\cdot m=\ct(f)m$;
\item the positive-characteristic maximal residue fields are the $\F_p$, with maximal ideals $pA^{08}_\kappa$;
characteristic-zero maximal residue fields exist and all have cardinality exactly $\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}
No hypothesis such as CH, GCH, $\kappa^{\aleph_0}=\kappa$ or an
inaccessible cardinal is used.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $A=A^{08}_\kappa$ and $I=\Pi^{08}_\kappa$.
(i) follows from \cref{osq:lem:controlled} and the embedding and floor
argument above. In particular all ring quotients used below are sets.

(ii) Each $f\in I$ has support in some $\Gamma_E$ with $E$ finite,
by \cref{osq:lem:finitecoord}. Choose $\beta<\kappa$ strictly above
every member of $E$. Each nonzero exponent in this positive support
has its first nonzero coordinate in $E$, so exceeds $e_\beta$.
Also \cref{osq:lem:gammabounds} gives $\kappa$ scales below every
$c>0$. Apply \cref{osq:thm:criterion} to obtain annihilation of $I$.
The factor is the restriction to $\Z$, since
$\varphi(n+f)=\varphi(n)$ for $n\in\Z$, $f\in I$; it is unique.
The argument includes nonunital ring homomorphisms.

(iii) If $I\subseteq J$, the constant term identifies
$A/J\cong\Z/\ct(J)$, and every ideal of $\Z$ is $n\Z$ for a
unique $n\ge0$. If $I\not\subseteq J$, the quotient map detects
some element of $I$, so (ii) gives $|A/J|\ge\kappa$; the opposite
inequality follows from $|A|=\kappa$. The alternatives need not be
disjoint: for $\kappa=\aleph_0$, the quotient $A/I\cong\Z$ also
has size $\kappa$. The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ include $\Z$ and the
zero ring, respectively.

(iv) Choose a cofinal $C\subseteq\kappa$ of size $\cf\kappa$.
For $f\in I$, choose $\beta\in C$ beyond a finite coordinate set
for $f$. Then $X^{-e_\beta}f\in F$ has positive support, so lies in
$I$. Thus the monomials $X^{e_\beta}$, $\beta\in C$, generate $I$.
Conversely, a family of fewer than $\cf\kappa$ elements has its finite
coordinate sets bounded by some $\beta<\kappa$, even when
$\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$. All its members, and hence their generated
ideal, lie in $X^{e_\beta}A$. This ideal misses $X^{e_\beta/2}\in I$,
whose unique quotient by $X^{e_\beta}$ in the field is
$X^{-e_\beta/2}\notin A$. No smaller family can generate $I$.

(v) Apply \cref{osq:lem:cyclic} to (ii): for each $m\in M$, the
quotient ring $A/\Ann(m)$ is in bijection with $Am\subseteq M$,
so (ii) kills $I$ in that quotient. Thus $IM=0$. Since the action
is unital, the remaining action of $\Z$ is its ordinary additive
action, giving $f\cdot m=\ct(f)m$.

(vi) For every nonzero integer $n$, the constant $1/n$ belongs to
$K\subseteq F$, and multiplication by it preserves positive supports.
Thus $nI=I$ and $nA=n\Z+I$. This assertion is not used at $n=0$,
where $0I=0\ne I$. For a prime $p$, it gives $A/pA\cong\F_p$.
Any maximal ideal with residue characteristic $p$ contains $pA$,
and therefore equals it, since $pA$ is already maximal.

For characteristic zero, $u=1+X^{e_0}$ is a nonunit by
\cref{osq:lem:units}. Hence $uA$ is proper, and the ordinary maximal-ideal
theorem for the set-sized ring $A$ gives a maximal ideal $M\supseteq uA$.
If $0\ne n\in\Z$ belonged to $M$, the identity
$X^{e_0}=n(X^{e_0}/n)$, with $X^{e_0}/n\in I$, would put
$X^{e_0}$ and then $1=u-X^{e_0}$ in $M$, a contradiction.
So $A/M$ has characteristic zero. Finally, any characteristic-zero
maximal residue field of size less than $\kappa$ would, by (ii),
be a surjective image of $\Z$. Characteristic zero makes that map
injective, forcing the residue ring to be isomorphic to $\Z$, which
is not a field. Every such residue field therefore has size at least
$\kappa$, and exactly $\kappa$ because it is a quotient of $A$.
\end{proof}

For every $0\ne f\in\Pi^{08}_\kappa$, (ii) and (v) give the lower bound
$\kappa$ for a ring target detecting $f$ or a unital module on which $f$
acts nontrivially. The identity map and the regular module $A^{08}_\kappa$
with vector $1$ attain it, so the stated cardinal boundary is sharp for
each such element.

At $\kappa=\aleph_0$ the theorem restricts only finite targets, and the characteristic-zero residue fields are
countable and detect infinite monomials. For regular $\kappa$ the generator count is $\kappa$; at a singular
$\kappa$ it is smaller, so a countably generated ideal can be invisible to all ring targets below a much larger
singular $\kappa$ of countable cofinality. Two resources are separated: monomial generators coinitial in the
support scales ($\cf\kappa$) and pairwise collision witnesses below a fixed scale ($\kappa$) (08).

In the residue field of a maximal ideal containing $1+\omega$ the image of $\omega$ is $-1$, not $0$, and that
field has size $\kappa$; so for every infinite $\kappa$ the subring $A^{08}_\kappa\subseteq\Oz$ has a
characteristic-zero field quotient of cardinality $\kappa$ in which $\omega\mapsto-1$. This quotient map cannot
extend to $\Oz$, where every set-sized image sends $\omega$ to $0$: an explicit extension obstruction between a
set-sized integer part and the class ring (08). 08 does not identify $\Frac(A^{08}_\kappa)$ with
$F^{08}_\kappa$, imposes no initial-segment condition or birthday cutoff on the embedding, and designs the
construction for truncation, support control and cardinality, not for closure under a derivation or an
exponential; the isomorphism types of the residue fields are not classified.

\subsection{Countable supports over a long one-armed group \texorpdfstring{\src{09}}{[09]}}\label{osq:sub:model09}

Fix an infinite cardinal $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$.
Then $2^{\aleph_0}\le\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$, since $2\le\lambda$.
Thus 09's separate continuum lower bound is redundant under the stated
infinitude hypothesis. The qualification matters: $0$ and $1$ also satisfy
$\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$ and would not give this construction.
For example, $\lambda=2^\nu$ works for every infinite $\nu$, because
$(2^\nu)^{\aleph_0}=2^{\nu\cdot\aleph_0}=2^\nu$.
Neither regularity of $\lambda$ nor CH is assumed. Let
$L_\lambda=\omega_1\times\lambda$ with the lexicographic order and
$\Gamma^{09}_\lambda=\bigoplus_{\ell\in L_\lambda}\Q e_\ell$, the least nonzero index deciding the sign.

\begin{lemma}[A large small-exponent tail \src{09}]\label{osq:lem:tail}
For every countable $S\subseteq(\Gamma^{09}_\lambda)_{>0}$ there is $\alpha_0<\omega_1$ with
$e_{(\alpha,\beta)}\in U_{\Gamma}(S)$ for all $\alpha_0\le\alpha<\omega_1$ and $\beta<\lambda$; in particular
$U_\Gamma(S)$ contains $\lambda$ elements, and every countable positive set has a positive strict lower bound.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be the set of first coordinates appearing in the finite index
supports of elements of $S$. It is countable. Set
$\alpha_0=\sup\{\alpha+1:\alpha\in C\}<\omega_1$, with supremum $0$
if $C$ is empty. For $s\in S$, its least nonzero coordinate precedes every
$(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha\ge\alpha_0$, and its coefficient there is
positive. Subtracting $n e_{(\alpha,\beta)}$ leaves that leading coordinate
unchanged. Hence $0<n e_{(\alpha,\beta)}<s$ for every positive integer
$n$, which is exactly the required small-exponent condition.
The single row $\{e_{(\alpha_0,\beta)}:\beta<\lambda\}$ already gives
$\lambda$ distinct elements, and $e_{(\alpha_0,0)}$ is a strict positive
lower bound for $S$. Only the regularity of $\omega_1$, not of $\lambda$,
is used here.
\end{proof}

For $k\in\{\R,\C\}$ and a unital subring $D\subseteq k$, let
$H_{\lambda,k}=\Hc k{\Gamma^{09}_\lambda}$, let
$\Pi^{09}_{\lambda,k}$ be its positive-support part, and put
$A^{09}_{\lambda,D}=D+\Pi^{09}_{\lambda,k}$. Write $A=A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$
and $\Pi_A=\Pi^{09}_{\lambda,k}$ throughout this subsection.
The ambient field is closed under its field operations by
\cref{osq:lem:hcfield}; its real version is real closed and its complex
version is its algebraically closed complexification. The ring $A$ is a
domain, $\ct:A\to D$ is a split surjection with kernel $\Pi_A$, and
$A^\times=D^\times$ by \cref{osq:lem:units}. The subordinate quotients of
\cref{osq:lem:division} remain in $\Pi_A$: their support bound is still
countable. This is a closure assertion for those particular quotients,
not for division by arbitrary nonzero elements of $A$.

Here $|\Gamma^{09}_\lambda|=|L_\lambda|=\lambda$: finite rational
combinations give the upper bound and the basis gives the lower bound.
There are at most $\lambda^{\aleph_0}=\lambda$ countable supports and,
for each one, at most $|k|^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}\le\lambda$
coefficient assignments. Consequently $|H_{\lambda,k}|\le\lambda$.
The $\lambda$ distinct positive basis monomials belong to $\Pi_A$, so
$|\Pi_A|=|A|=|H_{\lambda,k}|=\lambda$, for every allowed $D$.

Regard $\lambda$ as its initial ordinal and set
$j(\alpha,\beta)=\lambda\cdot\alpha+\beta$, using ordinal operations.
This is an order embedding of $L_\lambda$ into the ordinals. Thus
\[
 \iota\Bigl(\sum_\ell q_\ell e_\ell\Bigr)
   =\sum_\ell q_\ell\omega^{-j(\ell)}
\]
is an ordered additive embedding: the finite sum's leading coefficient
is the coefficient at its least index. Reindexing normal forms by
$\iota$ gives a field embedding
\[
 \Phi_\R:H_{\lambda,\R}\longrightarrow\No,\qquad
 \sum_\gamma c_\gamma X^\gamma\longmapsto
 \sum_\gamma c_\gamma\omega^{\iota(\gamma)}.
\]
The support remains reverse well ordered, and injectivity follows from
uniqueness of normal forms. Real and imaginary parts extend this to
$\Phi_\C:H_{\lambda,\C}\to\SC$. These embeddings send
$A^{09}_{\lambda,\Z}$ into $\Oz$ and
$A^{09}_{\lambda,\Z[i]}$ into $\GOz$; the former is the integer part of
$\Phi_\R(H_{\lambda,\R})$ by the truncation and endpoint rule following
\cref{osq:lem:hcfield}. We identify these rings with their images only
after applying $\Phi$. In particular,
$X^{e_\ell}\mapsto\omega^{\omega^{-j(\ell)}}$, and
$X^{e_{(0,0)}}$ maps to the actual $\omega$; the group coordinates describe
the exponents, not the monomials themselves.

\begin{theorem}[Cardinal barrier \src{09}]\label{osq:thm:barrier}
Let $A=A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$ and $\Pi_A=\Pi^{09}_{\lambda,k}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\varphi:A\to B$ is a unital ring map with $\varphi(\Pi_A)\ne0$, then $|\varphi(A)|\ge\lambda$.
\item If $M$ is an $A$-module with $\Pi_AM\ne0$, then $|M|\ge\lambda$.
\item All maps to rings of size $<\lambda$, and all modules of size $<\lambda$, factor through $\ct$.
\item For every ideal $J$, either $\Pi_A\subseteq J$ and $A/J\cong D/\ct(J)$, or $|A/J|=\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, in ZFC there is an explicit $A\subseteq\Oz$ of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (take
$\lambda=2^{\aleph_0}$, $D=\Z$) whose maps to countable rings factor through $\ct$, whose quotients are finite,
countably infinite, or of cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (the last for every quotient not induced from $\Z$), and
whose countable modules are abelian groups with constant-term action.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $f\in\Pi_A$ with $\varphi(f)\ne0$ for (i), or $f\in\Pi_A$
and $v\in M$ with $fv\ne0$ for (ii). Its support is countable, so
\cref{osq:lem:tail} supplies a set $E$ of $\lambda$ positive small
exponents. For distinct $a,b\in E$, \cref{osq:lem:division}, with the
sign changed if necessary, gives $f=(X^a-X^b)q_{a,b}$ with
