$q_{a,b}\in\Pi_A$. Therefore
\[
 a\longmapsto\varphi(X^a),\qquad
 a\longmapsto X^av
\]
are injective into $\varphi(A)$ and $M$, respectively, by
\cref{osq:lem:separation}. Only a finite product identity is transported
by $\varphi$; no infinite sum is transported. The ring argument also
works for nonunital maps and noncommutative targets.

If the target or module has size less than $\lambda$, this forces
annihilation of all of $\Pi_A$. Since $A=D\oplus\Pi_A$ additively,
restriction to $D$ gives the unique factorization in (iii). In (iv),
if $\Pi_A\subseteq J$, the map $a+J\mapsto\ct(a)+\ct(J)$ is a
well-defined ring isomorphism $A/J\to D/\ct(J)$. Otherwise the quotient
map detects some $f\in\Pi_A$, giving $\lambda\le|A/J|\le|A|=\lambda$.

For the final assertion, Cantor's theorem gives
$\aleph_0<2^{\aleph_0}$, so countable targets and modules are below
the threshold without CH. Every ideal of $\Z$ is $n\Z$ with $n\ge0$:
$n=0$ gives the countably infinite quotient $\Z$, $n=1$ the zero ring,
and $n\ge2$ the finite cyclic rings. Conversely these quotients all
occur via $\ct$. A countable module has exactly its underlying abelian
group action pulled back along $\ct$.
\end{proof}

When the continuum exceeds $\aleph_1$ the last statement also excludes all intermediate quotient cardinalities;
this is conditional only on that cardinal inequality (09).

\begin{lemma}[Recovering the coefficient field \src{09}]\label{osq:lem:coefffield}
Let $\varphi:A\to F$ be a unital map to a field with $\varphi(\Pi_A)\ne0$. There is a unique embedding
$\sigma:k\hookrightarrow F$ with $\varphi(rg)=\sigma(r)\varphi(g)$ for $r\in k$, $g\in\Pi_A$, and
$\sigma|_D=\varphi|_D$; in particular $F$ has characteristic $0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $f\in\Pi_A$ with $\varphi(f)\ne0$ and define
$\sigma(r)=\varphi(rf)/\varphi(f)$. Multiplication by a coefficient
preserves positive support, so $rf\in\Pi_A$ even when $r\notin A$.
Additivity follows from $(r+s)f=rf+sf$, and $\sigma(1)=1$.
The identity $(rf)(sf)=(rsf)f$ gives
\[
 \sigma(r)\sigma(s)
 =\frac{\varphi((rf)(sf))}{\varphi(f)^2}
 =\frac{\varphi(rsf)}{\varphi(f)}=\sigma(rs).
\]
Thus $\sigma:k\to F$ is a unital field homomorphism, hence injective.
For $d\in D$, $\varphi(df)=\varphi(d)\varphi(f)$ gives
$\sigma(d)=\varphi(d)$. For any $g\in\Pi_A$, apply $\varphi$ to
$(rg)f=(rf)g$ and divide by $\varphi(f)$ to obtain
$\varphi(rg)=\sigma(r)\varphi(g)$, including when $\varphi(g)=0$.
Any embedding with this property must give the same ratio at the chosen
$f$, proving uniqueness and independence of its choice. The canonical
copy of $k$ is therefore relative to $\varphi$; it is not obtained by
assuming that every coefficient already belongs to $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Residue fields at the threshold \src{09}]\label{osq:thm:residue}
Let $A=A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $0\ne f\in\Pi_A$ there is a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ with $f\equiv1\pmod{\mathfrak m}$ and
$|A/\mathfrak m|=\lambda$.
\item Every maximal ideal not containing $\Pi_A$ has a residue field of cardinality $\lambda$ with a canonical
copy of $k$.
\item For $D=\Z$, the maximal ideals containing $\Pi_A$ are the $pA$, with residue fields $\F_p$, and every other
maximal ideal has a characteristic-zero residue field of cardinality $\lambda$.
\item There are at least $\lambda$ distinct maximal ideals not containing $\Pi_A$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the least cardinality of a field (and of a module) detecting a given $0\ne f\in\Pi_A$ is exactly
$\lambda$; and for $D=\Z$ the intersection of all finite-index ideals is $\Pi_A\ne0$ while $\Jac(A)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) Since $0\ne f\in\Pi_A$, the element $1-f$ is nonconstant, hence a
nonunit by \cref{osq:lem:units}. The ideal $(1-f)A$ is proper. The
ordinary maximal-ideal theorem for the set-sized ring $A$ gives a maximal
ideal $\mathfrak m$ containing it. In the nonzero residue field, $f$ then
has image $1$. The barrier gives $|A/\mathfrak m|\ge\lambda$, and the
quotient upper bound gives equality.

(ii) The quotient map detects an element of $\Pi_A$, so the same
cardinality argument applies. Its canonical coefficient-field embedding
is exactly the one constructed in \cref{osq:lem:coefffield}.
For (iii), every nonzero integer $n$ satisfies $n\Pi_A=\Pi_A$, since
division of its coefficients by $n$ stays in $\Pi_A$. Hence
$pA=p\Z+\Pi_A$ and $A/pA\cong\F_p$. The ideals containing $\Pi_A$
correspond under $\ct$ to ideals of $\Z$; their maximal members are
precisely these $pA$. All remaining maximal ideals have the fields of
(ii), whose embedded $\R$ forces characteristic zero.

(iv) For $\ell<\ell'$ put $\gamma=e_\ell$ and $a=e_{\ell'}$.
Then $na<\gamma$ for every positive integer $n$. The exponents
$\gamma-na$ are positive and strictly decreasing, so they form a
countable reverse well-ordered support. Thus
\[
 q=-\sum_{n\ge1}X^{\gamma-na}\in\Pi_A,\qquad
 (1-X^a)q=X^\gamma,\qquad
 1=(1-X^\gamma)+(1-X^a)q.
\]
The product is a Hahn product: the term at $\gamma$ has coefficient
$1$, and at each $\gamma-na$ the two contributions cancel. No passage
of an infinite sum through a quotient map is used. The principal ideals
$(1-X^{e_\ell})A$ are proper by the units criterion and pairwise
comaximal by this identity. Choose one maximal ideal above each of them.
No maximal ideal can contain two, and none can contain $\Pi_A$, because
it would contain both $X^{e_\ell}$ and $1-X^{e_\ell}$. Since
$|L_\lambda|=\lambda$, this gives at least $\lambda$ distinct maximal
ideals of the required kind, using choice only for a set-indexed family.

For any fixed $0\ne f\in\Pi_A$, (i) gives a field target of size
$\lambda$ and, by restriction of scalars, an $A$-module of that size
on which $f$ acts as the identity. Together with the barrier, this proves
both exact minima.
When $D=\Z$, every finite-index ideal contains $\Pi_A$ by the barrier;
conversely, an element $n+g$ with $n\ne0$ is excluded from $pA$ by
choosing a prime $p$ not dividing $n$. Thus the intersection of all
finite-index ideals is exactly $\Pi_A$, which is nonzero since it
contains the basis monomials. Finally, every nonzero $x=n+g$ is avoided
by a maximal ideal: use such a $pA$ if $n\ne0$, and apply (i) to $g=x$
if $n=0$. This proves $\Jac(A)=0$ despite the nonzero finite residual.
\end{proof}

All of this concerns set-sized rings and is not an application of the maximal-ideal theorem to $\Oz$. The
distinction between finite ring probes and field probes is sharp: the extra information is carried by residue
fields of the full workspace cardinality (09). The number of maximal ideals and the isomorphism types of the
residue fields are not determined; distinct maximal ideals need not give nonisomorphic fields.

The generator count is independent of $\lambda$. If $\alpha<\alpha'$, then
$e_{(\alpha,0)}-e_{(\alpha',0)}>0$, giving inclusion of the corresponding
principal ideals. For every $f\in\Pi_A$, \cref{osq:lem:tail} supplies
$\alpha$ such that shifting its countable support by $-e_{(\alpha,0)}$
still leaves positive support. Consequently
\[
 \Pi^{09}_{\lambda,k}
   =\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1}X^{e_{(\alpha,0)}}A
\]
is an increasing union and gives $\aleph_1$ generators. Conversely, the
union of the supports of a countable family in $\Pi_A$ is countable.
Choose $h$ small relative to that union by \cref{osq:lem:tail}. Every
member then lies in $X^{2h}A$, whereas $X^h$ does not: its only possible
quotient is $X^{-h}$, which has negative support. No countable family
generates $\Pi_A$, so its least number of generators is exactly
$\aleph_1$. Flatness is treated in \cref{osq:thm:homological}.

\begin{remark}[Why the support restriction is real \src{09}]\label{osq:rem:fstar}
In the unrestricted Hahn field over $\Gamma^{09}_\lambda$ the series $f_*=\sum_{\alpha<\omega_1}X^{e_{(\alpha,0)}}$
has reverse well-ordered but uncountable support with no positive lower bound in $\Gamma^{09}_\lambda$ (a late
enough $e_{(\alpha,0)}$ lies below any given $h>0$); it is not divisible by any positive monomial within the
nonnegative-support ring and is not in $A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$. No assertion is made about the quotient
classification of that larger unrestricted ring.
\end{remark}
Indeed, the support is strictly decreasing in $\alpha$, so each nonempty
subset has a greatest element, indexed by its least ordinal. It has
cardinality $\aleph_1$, beyond the allowed support bound. For any $h>0$,
choose $\alpha$ greater than the first coordinate of the leading index
of $h$. Then $0<e_{(\alpha,0)}<h$, and the coefficient of
$X^{e_{(\alpha,0)}-h}$ in $X^{-h}f_*$ is nonzero. Hence division by
$X^h$ produces a negative exponent; uniqueness of the quotient in the
ambient Hahn field rules out any other nonnegative-support quotient.

\subsection{Supports of size \texorpdfstring{$<\kappa$}{< kappa} over a one-armed group \texorpdfstring{\src{11}}{[11]}}\label{osq:sub:model11}

For uncountable $\kappa$, \cref{osq:thm:coinitial} (11) applies to any
divisible ordered abelian set group $\Gamma$ with
$\coin(\Gamma_{>0})\ge\kappa$. The coinitiality condition says that
every set of fewer than $\kappa$ positive elements has a positive strict
lower bound. In the one-arm example below, set
\[
 F_{\kappa,K}=\{f\in\hahn K\Gamma:|\supp f|<\kappa\},\qquad
 I=\{f\in F_{\kappa,K}:\supp f\subseteq\Gamma_{>0}\},\qquad
 A=R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}=D+I,
\]
where $K$ is a set field and $D\subseteq K$ a unital subring. The
subscript on $F$ is a support-cardinality bound; arbitrary reverse
well-ordered supports of that size are allowed.

\begin{proposition}[Long lexicographic groups \src{11}]\label{osq:prop:lex}
For $\kappa$ uncountable and regular and $\Gamma=\bigoplus_{\alpha<\kappa}\Q e_\alpha$ with the least nonzero
index dominant, $|\Gamma|=\kappa$ and $\coin(\Gamma_{>0})=\kappa$. The group $\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$ also has
coinitiality $\kappa$, so $A^{06}_\kappa=R^{11}_{\Gamma^{06}_\kappa,<\kappa}$ with $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ is an instance
of \cref{osq:thm:coinitial}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The group has at least $\kappa$ elements because its basis vectors are
distinct, and at most $\kappa$ because every element is a finite
rational linear combination of them. For $g>0$ with least nonzero
index $\alpha$, every $\beta>\alpha$ satisfies $ne_\beta<g$ for every
positive integer $n$: subtraction leaves the leading coefficient of
$g$ unchanged. Hence the basis vectors form a coinitial family of
size $\kappa$.

If $S\subseteq\Gamma_{>0}$ has size less than $\kappa$, regularity
of $\kappa$ bounds its set of leading indices below some $\beta<\kappa$.
Then $e_\beta<s$ for every $s\in S$; in particular $S$ is not
coinitial. This proves the reverse inequality and hence the exact
coinitiality. For $\Gamma^{06}_\kappa$, \cref{osq:lem:kappagap}
gives the lower bound, and the coinitial family
$(\epsilon_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ gives the upper bound. Substituting
$(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ in the definition of $R^{11}$ gives the asserted
identity of that support-restricted ring with $A^{06}_\kappa$.
\end{proof}

11 proves sharpness under the displayed extra hypotheses $|K|\le\kappa$ and $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$: then
$|R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}|=\kappa$ and its identity map is a target of size $\kappa$ not factoring through $\ct$.
11 states explicitly that these hypotheses are assumptions for the sharpness example, not assertions about all
uncountable regular cardinals, and that regularity enters only the lexicographic example.

\begin{proposition}[Exact size and threshold \merge]\label{osq:prop:card11}
In \cref{osq:prop:lex}, for every set field $K$ and every $c>0$ the field
$L_c=\{f\in\hahn K\Gamma:|\supp f|<\kappa,\ \supp f\subseteq H_c(\Gamma)\}$ has at least $\kappa^{<\kappa}$
elements. If $|K|\le\max(\kappa,2^{\aleph_0})$ (which includes 11's hypothesis $|K|\le\kappa$), then
$|R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}|=\kappa^{<\kappa}$, and the least cardinality of a
ring target or module detecting any nonzero element of the positive-support ideal is exactly $\kappa^{<\kappa}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First $F_{\kappa,K}$ is a field. Finitely many of its series have a
union $S$ of supports of size less than $\kappa$. The subgroup generated
by $S$ has size at most $\max(|S|,\aleph_0)<\kappa$, so the full
Hahn field over that subgroup contains the series and still lies in
$F_{\kappa,K}$. It supplies their field operations and nonzero inverses.
This argument only uses uncountability of $\kappa$, not regularity.
Since $H_c(\Gamma)$ is a subgroup, $L_c$ is the intersection of two
subfields and is therefore a field.

Let $\alpha_0$ be the least nonzero index of $c$. The final segment
$T=(\alpha_0,\kappa)$ has cardinality $\kappa$, and
$e_\alpha\ll c$ for every $\alpha\in T$. Every subset $B\subseteq T$
of size less than $\kappa$ gives
\[
 f_B=\sum_{\alpha\in B}X^{e_\alpha}\in L_c.
\]
The support is reverse well ordered, since its greatest element in a
nonempty subset has the least ordinal index, and its size is $|B|<\kappa$.
The coefficient $1_K\ne0$ recovers $B$, even in positive characteristic.
Thus $B\mapsto f_B$ is injective. The subset count proved in
\cref{osq:lem:card06}, $|[T]^{<\kappa}|=\kappa^{<\kappa}$, gives
the lower bound without any restriction on $|K|$.

Now assume $|K|\le\max(\kappa,2^{\aleph_0})$. Supports of size
$\nu<\kappa$ have at most $\kappa^\nu$ descriptions. For infinite
$\nu$, their coefficient assignments number at most
\[
 |K|^\nu\le\max(\kappa^\nu,2^\nu)=\kappa^\nu.
\]
All finite supports together contribute at most
$\kappa\cdot\max(\kappa,2^{\aleph_0})
\le\kappa^{\aleph_0}\le\kappa^{<\kappa}$ possibilities, including
constant series. There are at most $\kappa$ possible support
cardinalities, so $|F_{\kappa,K}|\le\kappa^{<\kappa}$.
Multiplication by $X^c$ injects $L_c$ into $I$, by
\cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(i). Together with $I\subseteq A\subseteq F_{\kappa,K}$,
this proves
\[
 |L_c|=|I|=|A|=|F_{\kappa,K}|=\kappa^{<\kappa}.
\]

For $0\ne x\in I$, coinitiality gives $g>0$ strictly below its
support. Put $c=g/2$. Then $x=X^{2c}b$ for
$b=X^{-2c}x\in I$, since translation preserves support cardinality.
\Cref{osq:prop:fieldbound}(iii) gives the lower bound
$|L_c|=\kappa^{<\kappa}$ for every ring target or module detecting $x$.
The identity map and the regular module with vector $1$ attain it.
This establishes the threshold directly, independently of the organizing
theorem that summarizes it.
\end{proof}

Thus the exact boundary in this example is $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ under
the stated coefficient-field bound. It specializes to 11's boundary
$\kappa$ when $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$, and sharpens the original
coinitiality estimate when $\kappa^{<\kappa}>\kappa$.

For completeness, the ideal requires exactly $\kappa$ generators,
regardless of $D$. The positive basis monomials give a strictly increasing
chain with
\[
 I=\bigcup_{\alpha<\kappa}X^{e_\alpha}A.
\]
For $\alpha<\beta$, $e_\alpha-e_\beta>0$ gives the inclusion; its
strictness follows because $X^{e_\beta-e_\alpha}$ has negative support.
For any $f\in I$, regularity bounds the leading indices of its fewer
than $\kappa$ support exponents, so some $e_\alpha$ lies strictly
below all of them. The shifted series $X^{-e_\alpha}f\in I$ proves
the union and also $I^2=I$.
If $E\subseteq I$ has size less than $\kappa$, regularity gives
$|\bigcup_{f\in E}\supp f|<\kappa$. A common strict lower bound
$h>0$ then puts every member of $E$, and every finite $A$-linear
combination of them, in $X^hA$. But $X^{h/2}\in I$ is outside that
ideal because its unique quotient is $X^{-h/2}\notin A$.
So no such $E$ generates $I$. The regularity used for this union of
supports is distinct from the field-closure argument above.

With $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ this ring is a Hahn integer part of the kind treated in this section; 11 does not
embed it in $\No$, and no embedding is used in this section. Manuscript~17 supplies one: $e_\alpha\mapsto\omega^{-\alpha}$
embeds $\Gamma$ in $(\No,+)$ as an ordered group, and hence $R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ in $\Oz$ for $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ and in $\GOz$
for $(\Z[i],\C)$ (\cref{osq:rel:lem:embedding}).

\section{Flat ideals and homological reflection}\label{osq:sec:homological}

All rings, modules, resolutions, tensor products and $\Tor$, $\Ext$ groups in this section are
ordinary set-sized objects over the set-sized rings of \cref{osq:sec:models}. No class-sized
resolution is formed, and no directed-colimit theorem is applied to the proper-class union
$\Pi=\bigcup_{a>0}\omega^a\Oz$ (03, 06, 09). The package is 06's, proved there for $A^{06}_\kappa$;
03 and 09 prove its flatness and $\Tor$ parts for their rings. The proofs use only the following
properties, which all five constructions have:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(H1)] $A$ is a commutative domain, $D\subseteq A$ is a unital subring,
$A=D\oplus I$ additively, and $\ct:A\to D$ is the ring retraction
with kernel $I$, identifying $A/I\cong D$;
\item[(H2)] $A$ is built over a divisible exponent group $\Gamma$, and every $f\in I$ has the form
$f=X^gb$ with $g\in\Gamma_{>0}$ and $b\in I$; hence $I=\bigcup_{h\in\Gamma_{>0}}X^hA$, a directed
set-indexed union of principal ideals;
\item[(H3)] $I$ is not finitely generated.
\end{enumerate}
(H2) is the gap property used in \cref{osq:thm:thresholds} (a positive strict lower bound $g$ of
$\supp f$ gives $b=X^{-g}f\in I$). (H3) holds because the least number of generators is $\cf\kappa$,
$\kappa$, $\cf\kappa$, $\aleph_1$, respectively $\kappa$ (\cref{osq:thm:model03}(iv),
\cref{osq:prop:kappachain}, \cref{osq:thm:model08}(iv), the chain after \cref{osq:thm:residue}, and for
$R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ the coinitial chain $(X^{e_\alpha})_{\alpha<\kappa}$ of \cref{osq:prop:lex}:
fewer than $\kappa$ elements have a common monomial divisor $X^h$, and $X^hA$ misses $X^{h/2}$); these
counts are infinite. In particular $I\ne0$, and $I\ne A$ since $A$
is generated by $1$ as an ideal. We use $D$ as an $A$-module via $\ct$.
The constant inclusion $D\hookrightarrow A$ is a ring section and a
$D$-linear additive section, but is not asserted to be $A$-linear.
All splitting claims below specify this latter module structure.

\begin{lemma}[Projective ideals of a domain \src{06}]\label{osq:lem:projideal}
A nonzero projective ideal of a commutative domain is finitely generated.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $0\ne a\in J$. For every $A$-linear $f:J\to A$ and $x\in J$,
\[
 af(x)=f(ax)=xf(a).
\]
If $f(a)=0$, cancellation of $a$ in the domain gives $f(x)=0$ for
every $x$, so $f=0$.

Projectivity gives maps $j:J\to\bigoplus_{s\in S}Ae_s$ and
$p:\bigoplus_{s\in S}Ae_s\to J$ with $pj=\operatorname{id}_J$
\cite[Tag~05CF]{StacksProjective}. Write $f_s$ for the $s$th coordinate
of $j$, and $u_s=p(e_s)$. Each $j(x)$ has finite support, and applying
$p$ yields $x=\sum_s f_s(x)u_s$. The set
$S_0=\{s:f_s(a)\ne0\}$ is finite. For $s\notin S_0$ the first
paragraph gives $f_s=0$ identically, so every $x\in J$ is a linear
combination of the fixed finite family $(u_s)_{s\in S_0}$. No finite
generation assumption on the projective module was used.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Homological package \src{03, 06, 09} \merge]\label{osq:thm:homological}
Let $(A,I,D)$ satisfy (H1)--(H3). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $I$ is flat, $I^2=I$ (each element is a product of two elements of $I$), and $I$ is not projective;
\item for every $D$-module $N$ (inflated along $\ct$), $I\otimes_AN=0$ and $\Tor^A_n(D,N)=0$ for
$n>0$; in particular $\Tor^A_n(D,D)=0$;
\item $D$ is not flat: $\fd_AD=1$, and $\Tor^A_1(D,A/xA)\cong D$ for every $0\ne x\in I$;
\item for all $D$-modules $N,M$ and all $n\ge0$, inflation induces natural isomorphisms
$\Ext^n_A(N,M)\cong\Ext^n_D(N,M)$;
\item $\pd_AD\ge2$;
\item the sequence $0\to I\to A\xrightarrow{\ct}D\to0$ does not split as a sequence of
$A$-modules, so $\Ext^1_A(D,I)\ne0$;
\item if $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ generates $I$, $P=\bigoplus_{\alpha}Ae_\alpha\to I$,
$e_\alpha\mapsto x_\alpha$, and $J$ is its kernel, then $\Ext^2_A(D,J)\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) For every $h>0$, multiplication by $X^h$ identifies $A$ with
$X^hA$, since $A$ is a domain. These are free rank-one $A$-modules.
If $0<h'<h$, then $X^h=X^{h'}X^{h-h'}$ with multiplier in $A$, so
$X^hA\subseteq X^{h'}A$. For two such ideals, any positive exponent
below both indices gives a common larger member. Thus (H2) expresses
$I$ as their set-indexed filtered colimit. It is flat by
\cite[Lemma~10.39.3]{StacksFlat}. The factorization in (H2) puts every
$f\in I$ in $I^2$, while the ideal property gives $I^2\subseteq I$.
Finally $I$ is nonzero; if it were projective,
\cref{osq:lem:projideal} would contradict (H3).

(ii) Let $N$ be a $D$-module with its inflated $A$-action, so $IN=0$.
For a pure tensor $f\otimes n$, factor $f=ab$ with $a,b\in I$ by
(H2). The balancing relation gives
\[
 f\otimes n=b\otimes an=0.
\]
Pure tensors generate, hence $I\otimes_A N=0$. Equivalently this is
the standard identification
$I\otimes_A N\cong(I/I^2)\otimes_D N$ with $I/I^2=0$.
By (i), $0\to I\to A\to D\to0$ is a flat resolution of $D$ of
length one. Tensoring it with $N$ gives the complex
$0\to0\to N$ in positive and zero homological degrees; thus every
positive $\Tor^A_n(D,N)$ vanishes. Flat resolutions compute these
groups \cite[Section~15.60]{StacksDerived}.

(iii) That resolution gives $\fd_A D\le1$. For $0\ne x\in I$, the
domain hypothesis makes
$0\to A\xrightarrow{x}A\to A/xA\to0$ a free resolution.
Tensor it with $D$. The differential $D\xrightarrow{x}D$ is zero
because $x$ acts through $\ct(x)=0$, and therefore
$\Tor^A_1(D,A/xA)\cong D\ne0$. This proves $\fd_A D=1$.
The same obstruction can be seen without derived notation: the injection
$xA\hookrightarrow A$ becomes the zero map $D\to D$ after tensoring
with $D$, so tensoring by $D$ is not left exact.

(iv) Choose a projective $A$-resolution $P_\bullet\to N$ in
nonnegative homological degrees. By (ii), the augmented complex
$D\otimes_A P_\bullet\to D\otimes_A N\cong N$ is exact. Each
term is projective over $D$: tensoring a split realization of $P_j$ as
a summand of a free $A$-module makes it a summand of a free $D$-module.
Consequently this is a projective $D$-resolution of $N$. For every
degree the tensor--Hom adjunction is
\[
 \Hom_A(P_j,M)\cong\Hom_D(D\otimes_A P_j,M),
 \qquad f\longmapsto\bigl(d\otimes p\mapsto d f(p)\bigr),
\]
with inverse $g\mapsto(p\mapsto g(1\otimes p))$. The maps commute
with the differentials, so taking cohomology gives the stated
isomorphisms, including $n=0$.

To identify the map with inflation, take a projective $D$-resolution
$Q_\bullet\to N$. Viewed as an exact complex of $A$-modules, it
admits a comparison map $P_\bullet\to Q_\bullet$ lifting the identity
of $N$. Its adjoint $D\otimes_A P_\bullet\to Q_\bullet$ is a
comparison between projective $D$-resolutions, hence a homotopy
equivalence. The induced cochain map realizes the canonical inflation
map from $\Ext_D$ to $\Ext_A$; the displayed isomorphism in the other
direction is its inverse. Comparison maps for morphisms of $N$ and $M$
give naturality. This does not require $D$ to be flat over $A$.

(v) If $\pd_A D\le1$, choose a projective presentation
$0\to Q_1\to Q_0\to D\to0$ with $Q_0,Q_1$ projective.
Schanuel's lemma, applied alongside $0\to I\to A\to D\to0$,
gives $I\oplus Q_0\cong Q_1\oplus A$
\cite[Tag~00O3]{StacksProjective}. The right side is projective,
so its direct summand $I$ is projective, contradicting (i).

(vi) An $A$-linear section $s:D\to A$ would give $r=s(1)$ with
$\ct(r)=1$. Choose $0\ne x\in I$. Since $x$ acts by zero on $D$,
\[
 xr=s(x\cdot1)=s(0)=0.
\]
The domain hypothesis forces $r=0$, contradicting $\ct(r)=1$.
The nonsplit short exact sequence thus represents a nonzero class in
$\Ext^1_A(D,I)$. The existing ring section is not $A$-linear: it sends
$x\cdot1=0$ to $0$, whereas multiplying its value at $1$ by $x$ gives $x$.

(vii) The prescribed generating family makes $P\to I$ surjective.
If $0\to J\to P\to I\to0$ split, $I$ would be a direct summand
of the free module $P$, again contradicting (i). Let $\eta$ be its
nonzero class in $\Ext^1_A(I,J)$. The long exact sequence from
$0\to I\to A\to D\to0$ contains
\[
 0=\Ext^1_A(A,J)\longrightarrow\Ext^1_A(I,J)
 \longrightarrow\Ext^2_A(D,J)\longrightarrow\Ext^2_A(A,J)=0.
\]
Thus its connecting map is an isomorphism and carries $\eta$ to a
nonzero class. In Yoneda form this is the splice
$0\to J\to P\to A\to D\to0$, where $P\to A$ is the composite
$P\to I\hookrightarrow A$.
\end{proof}

In standard terms, $A\to D$ is a homological ring epimorphism ($D\otimes_AD=D$, all higher self-$\Tor$
vanish) but not a flat one (03, 06); this terminology is optional. The exact value of $\pd_AD$ is not
determined in general: only $\pd_AD\ge2$ and $\fd_AD=1$ are proved
without a generator restriction (06). When $I$ is countably generated,
$\pd_AD=2$ by the telescope described below
(\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(v), from 12).
Hypothesis (H2) is where the totally ordered exponent cone enters: for 12's coordinatewise cones the flat dimension of $D$ is any $d\ge1$, and the two kinds of
statement are compared in \cref{osq:hd:rem:reconcile}. The nonzero $\Tor_1^A(D,A/xA)$ does not
contradict (ii), because $A/xA$ is not a $D$-module with its given
$A$-action. Indeed, $I\subseteq xA$ would imply $I=xA$, since $x\in I$,
contradicting (H3). Hence $I$ acts nontrivially on $A/xA$.
Likewise the nonzero Ext witnesses in (vi) and (vii) are not modules
annihilated by $I$: otherwise (iv), with first variable $D$, would
make their Ext groups zero. Finally, $I/I^2=0$ is not a
finite-presentation or smoothness statement (09).

\paragraph{The countably generated case.}
Choose a decreasing sequence $h_n>0$ so that
$I=\bigcup_{n\ge0}X^{h_n}A$: (H2) and directedness allow each new
principal ideal to contain the preceding one and the next member of a
countable generating family. Divisibility lets the indices decrease
strictly. Put $a_n=X^{h_n-h_{n+1}}$. The transition between the free
rank-one modules is multiplication by $a_n$, and the telescope is
\[
 0\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{n\ge0}Ae_n
 \xrightarrow{\delta}\bigoplus_{n\ge0}Ae_n
 \xrightarrow{\pi} I\longrightarrow0,
\]
where $\delta(e_n)=e_n-a_ne_{n+1}$ and $\pi(e_n)=X^{h_n}$.
The composite is zero. If $\delta(\sum r_ne_n)=0$, its zeroth
coordinate gives $r_0=0$, and consecutive coordinates give every
$r_n=0$, so $\delta$ is injective. Modulo its image, a finite sum
supported through $N$ reduces to a single coefficient times $e_N$.
If its image under $\pi$ vanishes, that coefficient times $X^{h_N}$
is zero; the domain hypothesis makes the coefficient zero. This proves
exactness at the middle term, and the union proves surjectivity of $\pi$.
The telescope is a length-one free resolution of $I$. Splicing with
$0\to I\to A\to D\to0$ gives $\pd_A D\le2$; (v) gives equality.
Among the five families the countably generated case occurs precisely
for 08 with $\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$, by their exact generator counts.
No conclusion $\pd_A D=2$ is drawn for the other cases.

\begin{theorem}[Exact size of cohomological witnesses \src{06} \merge]\label{osq:thm:extthreshold}
Let $A$ be one of the five rings of \cref{osq:sub:organizing}, with $D=\Z$ (or any admissible $D$), and
$\tau=|A|$. For every $A$-module $M$ with $|M|<\tau$ and every $n>0$, $\Ext^n_A(D,M)=0$, and for any two
$A$-modules of size $<\tau$ the $\Ext$ groups over $A$ are those of the underlying $D$-modules. For
$n\in\{1,2\}$,
\[
 \min\{|M|:\Ext^n_A(D,M)\ne0\}=\tau .
\]
For $A^{06}_\kappa$ this minimum is $\kappa^{<\kappa}$ in ZFC; under $\kappa^{<\kappa}=\kappa$ it is $\kappa$,
which is 06's statement. For $A^{03}_\kappa$, $A^{08}_\kappa$ and $A^{09}_{\lambda,D}$ it is $\kappa^{\aleph_0}$,
$\kappa$ and $\lambda$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $|M|<\tau$, the detection theorem \cref{osq:thm:thresholds} gives
$IM=0$. Thus $M$ has the unique induced $D$-module structure, and
\cref{osq:thm:homological}(iv) gives
\[
 \Ext^n_A(D,M)\cong\Ext^n_D(D,M)=0\qquad(n>0),
\]
since $D$ is a free rank-one module over itself. Applying (iv) to two
small modules gives their claimed Ext comparison in every degree.
In particular every coefficient module detecting a nonzero class in
degree $1$ or $2$ must have at least $\tau$ elements.

For degree $1$, take $M=I$. The model-size calculations give
$|I|=|A|=\tau$, and the nonsplit sequence in
\cref{osq:thm:homological}(vi) is a nonzero class.
For degree $2$, choose a generating set $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$
for $I$ with $|\Lambda|\le\tau$, for example all of $I$.
Since $\tau$ is infinite, the free module
$P=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda}Ae_\alpha$ has size at most $\tau$:
its elements are finite lists of indices and coefficients, and
$\sum_{m<\omega}(|\Lambda|\cdot\tau)^m\le\tau$.
Let $J=\ker(P\to I)$. Then $|J|\le\tau$, and (vii) supplies
$\Ext^2_A(D,J)\ne0$. The lower bound already proved forces
$|J|=\tau$. Both minima are therefore attained. Substituting each
model's proved size gives the displayed values; no additional cardinal
arithmetic assumption or minimal generating presentation is needed.
\end{proof}

The $\Ext$ groups are computed in the full category of $A$-modules, not only among small modules; this is why
\cref{osq:thm:homological}(iv) is an ambient derived-functor statement and not merely an equivalence of small
module categories (06). The two witnesses show that a quotient can look homologically projective against every
small coefficient module while failing projectivity in the ambient category. The whole argument works for the
Gaussian versions with $D=\Z[i]$, where $\Ext_D$ means extensions of $\Z[i]$-modules (06). Finally, for
any of the five models and any $0\ne x\in I$, the module $A/xA$ is
detected by $I$, as shown above. The detection theorem and quotient upper
bound give $|A/xA|=|A|$. In particular
$|A^{06}_\kappa/xA^{06}_\kappa|=\kappa^{<\kappa}$; 06 stated a lower
bound with the qualifier ``under the cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis'',
which is not needed. The minima in \cref{osq:thm:extthreshold} concern
the size of the coefficient module $M$, not the cardinality of the Ext
group itself.

\section{Homological and tensor algebra of omnific cores}\label{osq:hd:sec:cores}

This section is the part contributed by manuscripts~12 and~14 (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). Both
study ordinary commutative algebra of rings of the form ``constants plus a tail'' inside $\Oz$ and
$\GOz$, and they share one set-sized model: 14's finite-support ring $A_0$ is 12's rank-one
coordinate-cone core $A_1$, and 12's two-generator relation module is the case $r=2$ of 14's
lattice syzygy. Each is printed once (\cref{osq:hd:lem:cores,osq:tn:thm:syzygy}). Manuscript~12
computes flat and projective dimensions of set-sized finite-support cores
(\cref{osq:hd:sub:cores,osq:hd:sub:resolution,osq:hd:sub:tor,osq:hd:sub:dimensions}); 14 computes
tensor products, symmetric and exterior powers, Rees algebras, homomorphisms and duals of
coefficient-lattice modules, over the full class ring and over $A_0$
(\cref{osq:tn:sub:lattices,osq:tn:sub:tensor,osq:tn:sub:rees,osq:tn:sub:hom}). Manuscript~17 of the third batch
re-derives, independently, 14's matrix, syzygy, $\Hom$, tensor-torsion and power-growth theorems and 12's intersection;
these are printed once, with 17 added to their sources, and 17's new material (presentations and relation counts, the
$\Tor$ identification, moduli, orders, the lexicographic models inside $\Oz$) is \cref{osq:rel:sub:relations}. Manuscript~21 of a
fifth batch determines the projective dimensions that 12 bounds and computes the $\Tor$ algebra of lattice quotients
(\cref{osq:da:sub:derived}). Manuscript~26 of an eighth batch replaces the coordinate cone by an arbitrary rational polyhedral cone
(\cref{osq:pc:sub:polyhedral}). Labels carry the sub-prefixes \texttt{osq:hd:} (12), \texttt{osq:tn:} (14), \texttt{osq:rel:} (17),
\texttt{osq:da:} (21) and \texttt{osq:pc:} (26).

\paragraph{Scope.} The rings of \cref{osq:hd:sub:cores,osq:hd:sub:resolution,osq:hd:sub:tor,osq:hd:sub:dimensions}
and 14's model $A_0$ have \emph{finite} supports. They are therefore outside the universal theorem, like
the finite-support rings of \cref{osq:sec:support}: the augmentation that sends every monomial to $1$
is a unital map to the coefficient field that detects the tail (\cref{osq:hd:prop:finite}). What 12
calls arithmetic invisibility is invisibility to \emph{finite} rings and to modules on which the tail
acts by zero; these rings are not invisible to set-sized rings in the sense of \cref{osq:thm:universal}.

\paragraph{Notation.} 12's augmentation $\varepsilon$ is $\ct$; its tail $M$ is $\Pi_\Lambda$ (the letter $M$ is
14's coefficient lattice); its ordered-cone ring $T=D\oplus P$ with monomials $t^\gamma$ is
$T_\Gamma=D\oplus\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$ with monomials $X^\gamma$ (in this report $t^g$ means $X^{-g}$,
\cref{osq:sub:orientation}); its test modules $N_F$ are $V_F$; its cyclic module $Q=A/(X_1,cX_1)$ is written
$A/H$. 14's ideal $\mathcal I$, its rings $B=k+\mathcal I$, $A=D+\mathcal I$ and its field $F$ are $\Pi_k$,
$\A_{k,k}$, $\A_{D,k}$ and $\hahn k\No$; its set-sized $P$, $A_0$, $B_0$ are $\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Q$,
$T_\Q$ and $k+\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Q$; its multiplication map $\mu_{M,N}$, kernel $K(M,N)$ and carrier $E(M,N)$
are $\mathsf m_{M,N}$, $\mathcal T(M,N)$ and $\mathsf E(M,N)$; its multiplier ring $\mathcal O(M)$ and orders
$\mathcal O$ in number fields $K$ are $\mathfrak o(M)$ and $\mathfrak o\subset K_0$ (the letter $\OO$ denotes the
finite surreal rings); the saturated lattice $L$ of its matrix theorem is $W_D$. 17's positive-support ideal $\mathfrak m$
(which it warns is not the infinitesimal ideal; here $\mm$ is the negative-support ideal) is $\Pi$, its $F=\Frac(D)$ is written
$\Frac(D)$ (14's $F$ was the fraction field $\hahn k\No$), its lattices $L,M$ are $M,N$, its ideals
$J_L^\gamma=\omega^\gamma(L+\mathfrak m)$ are $J_\gamma(M)=X^\gamma L(M)$, its multiplier ring $E(L)$ and conductor $(M:L)$ are
$\mathfrak o(M)$ and $(N:M)$, its multiplication map $\mu_{L,M}$ and kernel $T(L,M)$ are $\mathsf m_{M,N}$ and $\mathcal T(M,N)$
(the letter $\mu$ was 14's generator count), its kernel dimensions $d,r$ are $q,\ell$, and its set-sized models $A_\kappa$,
$\mathfrak m_\kappa$ are $R^{11}_{\Gamma_\kappa,<\kappa}$ and $\Pi^{11}_\kappa$.

\subsection{Coordinate-cone and ordered-cone cores}\label{osq:hd:sub:cores}

Throughout \cref{osq:hd:sub:cores,osq:hd:sub:resolution,osq:hd:sub:tor}, $K$ is a field and $D\subseteq K$ a unital
subring, so $D$ is a domain. Let $\Lambda$ be $[d]=\{1,\dots,d\}$ ($d\ge1$) or $\N_{>0}$, and let
$P_\Lambda=\Q_{\ge0}^{(\Lambda)}$ be the monoid of finitely supported vectors
$\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_i)_{i\in\Lambda}$ with nonnegative rational coordinates. In the monoid algebra
$K[P_\Lambda]$ (finite sums, $X^{\boldsymbol\alpha}X^{\boldsymbol\beta}=X^{\boldsymbol\alpha+\boldsymbol\beta}$) put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:hd:eq:cores}
 \Pi_\Lambda=\bigoplus_{0\ne\boldsymbol\alpha\in P_\Lambda}KX^{\boldsymbol\alpha},\qquad
 A_\Lambda=D\oplus\Pi_\Lambda ,
\end{equation}
and write $A_d,\Pi_d$ for $\Lambda=[d]$ and $X_i=X^{\mathbf e_i}$. The coefficient at $X^{\mathbf 0}$ is a split
surjective ring homomorphism $\ct:A_\Lambda\to D$ with kernel $\Pi_\Lambda$, because a sum of two nonnegative
vectors is zero only when both are. For a nonzero divisible subgroup $\Gamma\subseteq\R$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:hd:eq:T}
 \Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma=\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{>0}}KX^\gamma,\qquad
 T_\Gamma=D\oplus\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma ,
\end{equation}
the finite-support ring of \cref{osq:sec:support} over the fixed ordered group $\Gamma$, again with
$\ct:T_\Gamma\to D$. The difference between the two families is the exponent cone: coordinatewise
nonnegative vectors in $A_\Lambda$, the positive cone of a totally ordered group in $T_\Gamma$.

\begin{lemma}[Domains and embeddings \src{12; 14}]\label{osq:hd:lem:cores}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item $K[P_\Lambda]$, $A_\Lambda$ and $T_\Gamma$ are domains, and $\Pi_\Lambda$ is a nonzero prime ideal.
\item Let $(\gamma_i)_{i\in\Lambda}$ be positive surreals linearly independent over $\Q$. Then
$X^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\mapsto\omega^{\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i}$ defines an injective ring homomorphism
$\R[P_\Lambda]\to\No$, and, applied to real and imaginary parts, $\C[P_\Lambda]\to\SC$; it maps $\Z+\Pi_\Lambda$
into $\Oz$ and $\Z[i]+\Pi_\Lambda$ into $\GOz$. The $\gamma_i$ may be taken real: $\gamma_i=\theta^{i-1}$ for a
transcendental real $\theta>1$. Likewise $X^\gamma\mapsto\omega^\gamma$ embeds $T_\Gamma$ in $\Oz$ or $\GOz$ for
$(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$.
\item If the $\gamma_i$ are positive reals linearly independent over $\Q$ and $\Gamma=\sum_i\Q\gamma_i$, then
$X_i\mapsto X^{\gamma_i}$ is an injective ring homomorphism $A_\Lambda\hookrightarrow T_\Gamma$ compatible with
$\ct$. For $d=1$ and $\gamma_1=1$ it is an isomorphism $A_1\cong T_\Q$; this ring, with $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ or
$(\Z[i],\C)$, is 14's set-sized model $A_0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(i) Given two nonzero elements of $K[P_\Lambda]$, their finite supports
involve only finitely many coordinates $i_1,\ldots,i_s$. Choose a common
positive denominator $n$ for all their rational exponents. Both elements
lie in the subalgebra generated by $X_{i_1}^{1/n},\ldots,X_{i_s}^{1/n}$.
Distinct products of these generators have distinct exponent vectors, so
this subalgebra is a polynomial ring over $K$, hence a domain. Their
product is therefore nonzero in $K[P_\Lambda]$. Its subring $A_\Lambda$
is a domain as well. In $T_\Gamma$, the largest exponents of two nonzero
finite sums add, and the coefficient at that sum is the product of their
nonzero leading coefficients; no other pair reaches that exponent.
This proves that $T_\Gamma$ is a domain. Finally,
$A_\Lambda/\Pi_\Lambda\cong D$ is a nonzero domain, so $\Pi_\Lambda$
is proper and prime, and $X_1\in\Pi_\Lambda$ makes it nonzero.

(ii) The map
$\ell(\boldsymbol\alpha)=\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i$ is defined by a
finite sum, is additive, and is injective by rational linear
independence. It is strictly positive on nonzero vectors of
$P_\Lambda$. Send $\sum c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}X^{\boldsymbol\alpha}$
to $\sum c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\omega^{\ell(\boldsymbol\alpha)}$.
The law $\omega^u\omega^v=\omega^{u+v}$ and finite distributivity
show that this preserves products and the unit. Distinct exponents and
uniqueness of Conway normal forms show that it is injective. For complex
coefficients, the same construction on real and imaginary parts gives
the homomorphism into $\SC=\No[i]$. Positive nonconstant exponents
and an integer, respectively Gaussian-integer, constant coefficient give
the stated omnific memberships.

If $\gamma_i=\theta^{i-1}$, any finite rational relation among the
$\gamma_i$ would give a nonzero rational polynomial vanishing at the
transcendental number $\theta$; hence these positive real choices work
also for countably many indices. For $T_\Gamma$ use the inclusion
$\Gamma\subseteq\R\subseteq\No$ in place of $\ell$, with the
same normal-form argument.

(iii) With real $\gamma_i$, the same $\ell$ is an injective monoid
map $P_\Lambda\to\Gamma_{\ge0}$ and has zero fiber $\{\mathbf0\}$.
Reindexing the finite sum by $\ell$ gives the required embedding over
$D$, and preserves the coefficient at zero. In rank one with
$\gamma_1=1$, every nonnegative rational exponent is reached and every
allowed coefficient is unchanged. The map is therefore onto $T_\Q$,
giving the stated isomorphism. In higher rank only an embedding is
asserted: the coordinate cone need not fill the positive cone of the
ordered group.
\end{proof}

Thus $d$ counts independent monomial directions, not Archimedean scales: with $\gamma_i=\theta^{i-1}$ all exponents lie
in the single Archimedean class of $1$ (12). Every element of every ring in this subsection is a finite sum; no
topology, convergence or infinite summation is involved.

\begin{proposition}[Finite targets only \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:prop:finite}
Let $A$ be $A_\Lambda$ or $T_\Gamma$ with tail $\Pi$, and $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $0\ne a\in D$, $a\Pi=\Pi$ and $A/aA\cong D/aD$. Every unital map from $A$ to a finite ring, and every
finite $A$-module, factors through $\ct$; $\widehat A\cong\widehat D$ for the profinite completions,
$\varprojlim_kA/p^kA\cong\varprojlim_kD/p^kD$ for every ordinary prime $p$, $\bigcap_kp^kA=\Pi$, and
$\Tor^A_{>0}(D,E)=0$ for every finite $A$-module $E$.
\item The augmentation $\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}X^{\boldsymbol\alpha}\mapsto\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$
is a unital ring homomorphism $A\to K$ sending every monomial to $1$; it does not factor through $\ct$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(i) Dividing each of the finitely many tail coefficients by $0\ne a\in D$
stays in $K$ and preserves its positive exponent. Thus $a\Pi=\Pi$,
and the additive decomposition gives $aA=aD\oplus\Pi$. The map
$A\to D/aD$, $f\mapsto\ct(f)\bmod aD$, is surjective with this
kernel, proving $A/aA\cong D/aD$.

Let $\varphi:A\to R$ be unital with $R$ finite. Some positive integer
$n$ annihilates $R$ (including $n=1$ for the zero ring). Since these
coefficient pairs have characteristic zero, $n\Pi=\Pi$. For $x\in\Pi$
write $x=ny$ with $y\in\Pi$; then $\varphi(x)=n\varphi(y)=0$.
The quotient property gives unique factorization through $\ct$.
Likewise the additive group of a finite $A$-module $E$ is annihilated
by some $n\ge1$. For $e\in E$,
$xe=(ny)e=y(ne)=0$, so $\Pi E=0$ and its action factors uniquely
through $D$. This argument does not assume a commutative target ring.

Every finite-index ideal $J$ contains $\Pi$, by applying the preceding
argument to $A/J$, and it contains $nA$ for a positive integer annihilating
that quotient. Conversely $A/nA\cong D/nD$ is finite. The ideals
$nA$ are therefore cofinal among finite-index ideals. The displayed
isomorphisms commute with reduction whenever one integer divides
another, identifying the inverse limits $\widehat A\cong\widehat D$.
Restricting to $n=p^k$ gives the stated $p$-adic limits. Moreover
\[
 \bigcap_{k\ge1}p^kA
 =\left(\bigcap_{k\ge1}p^kD\right)\oplus\Pi=\Pi,
\]
because an ordinary integer divisible by every $p^k$ is zero; apply
this to both integer coordinates for $D=\Z[i]$. Thus $A$ itself is
not separated for the $p$-adic topology: its map to that completion
has kernel $\Pi$.

Finally $E$ is an inflated $D$-module. The $\Tor$ assertion follows
from the face resolution and \cref{osq:hd:cor:arithmeticTor} below for
$A_\Lambda$. For $T_\Gamma$, use the flat tail in
\cref{osq:hd:thm:orderedcone} and
\cref{osq:thm:homological}(ii). These are algebraic resolution
arguments; the completion isomorphisms alone do not compute $\Tor$.

(ii) Every sum is finite, so regrouping the finitely many terms of a
product proves that its coefficient sum is the product of the two
coefficient sums. This gives a unital map to $K$. It sends $X_1$ to
$1$ for $A_\Lambda$, and $X^\gamma$ to $1$ for any $\gamma>0$ in
$T_\Gamma$. Since these monomials have constant term zero, the map
cannot factor through $\ct$. This second augmentation is distinct
from the constant-coefficient retraction.
\end{proof}

Hence all the cores, and 14's $A_0$, have the same finite quotients and profinite completion as $D$, while
\cref{osq:hd:cor:fd} below shows that their homological dimensions differ; this limits any reconstruction of an
omnific subring from its finite arithmetic shadows (12). Item (ii) is the reason the word ``invisible'' must be read
with (i)'s restriction.

\subsection{Flat face ideals and a Boolean resolution}\label{osq:hd:sub:resolution}

For a finite nonempty $S\subseteq\Lambda$ put $p_S=\prod_{i\in S}X_i$ and let
\begin{equation}\label{osq:hd:eq:IS}
 I_S=\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in P_\Lambda,\ \alpha_i>0\ (i\in S)}KX^{\boldsymbol\alpha},
\end{equation}
an ideal of $A_\Lambda$ with $I_S=\bigcap_{i\in S}I_{\{i\}}$ and $\Pi_\Lambda=\sum_iI_{\{i\}}$.

\begin{lemma}[Face ideals \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:lem:faces}
Let $A=A_\Lambda$ and $\Pi=\Pi_\Lambda$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $I_S=\bigcup_{n\ge0}p_S^{2^{-n}}A$, an increasing chain of free rank-one $A$-modules; hence $I_S$ is flat.
\item $\Pi^2=\Pi$, $I_S^2=I_S$ and $\Pi I_S=I_S$; for every $D$-module $E$, regarded as an $A$-module through $\ct$,
$I_S\otimes_AE=0$.
\item Neither $\Pi$ nor any $I_S$ is finitely generated.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(i) Put $u_n=p_S^{2^{-n}}$. Multiplication by $u_n$ identifies $A$
with $u_nA$, because $A$ is a domain. The relation
$u_n=u_{n+1}u_{n+1}$ makes these principal ideals an increasing chain,
each contained in $I_S$. If $f\ne0$ lies in $I_S$, there are only
finitely many positive coordinates $\alpha_i$, with $i\in S$, among
its finitely many exponents. Choose $n$ so that $2^{-n}$ is strictly
below all of them. Subtracting $2^{-n}$ in each coordinate of $S$
leaves nonnegative exponent vectors still positive on $S$. Consequently
$f/u_n$ is a tail in $A$, even if its coefficients are arbitrary in
$K$ rather than in $D$. The zero element lies in every member of the
chain. This proves the exhaustion. Each member is free of rank one,
so the filtered-colimit flatness theorem gives flatness of $I_S$
\cite[Lemma~10.39.3]{StacksFlat}.

(ii) Every nonzero tail monomial admits the factorization
\[
 kX^{\boldsymbol\alpha}
 =(kX^{\boldsymbol\alpha/2})X^{\boldsymbol\alpha/2}.
\]
Both factors belong to $\Pi$, and both belong to $I_S$ when
$\alpha_i>0$ for every $i\in S$. Summing finitely many monomials
gives $\Pi\subseteq\Pi^2$ and $I_S\subseteq I_S^2$; the opposite
inclusions follow from the ideal property. Since $I_S\subseteq\Pi$,
we also obtain $I_S=I_S^2\subseteq\Pi I_S\subseteq I_S$.
For an inflated $D$-module $E$, write each $x\in I_S=\Pi I_S$ as a
finite sum $\sum_j a_jb_j$ with $a_j\in\Pi$, $b_j\in I_S$.
Tensor balancing gives
$x\otimes e=\sum_j b_j\otimes a_je=0$. Pure tensors generate, so
$I_S\otimes_A E=0$.

(iii) Both ideals are nonzero. If a finite family generated either
one, discard its zero members and let $\delta>0$ be the smallest
total degree $|\boldsymbol\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$ among all
monomials occurring in that family. Multiplication by any element of
$A$ adds a nonnegative total degree; addition and cancellation create
no new exponent. Every element of the generated ideal therefore has
all its monomials in total degree at least $\delta$.
Choose a positive rational $q<\delta$ for $\Pi$, or
$0<q<\delta/|S|$ for $I_S$. The monomial $X_1^q\in\Pi$,
respectively $p_S^q\in I_S$, has smaller total degree, a contradiction.
The same argument works when $\Lambda$ is countably infinite, since
the proposed generating family and each of its supports are finite.
\end{proof}

Flatness of every $I_S$ does not imply flatness of their sum $\Pi$; the failure begins at $d=2$
(\cref{osq:hd:cor:fd}). For $p\ge1$ put $C_p=\bigoplus_{S\subseteq\Lambda,\ |S|=p}I_S$ and $C_0=A$; for
$S=\{s_1<\dots<s_p\}$ let $d_p$ send $f$ in the summand $I_S$ to $\sum_{r=1}^p(-1)^{r-1}f$ in the summands
$I_{S\setminus\{s_r\}}$ (for $p=1$ the target is $A$ and the map is the inclusion). Deleting two indices in either
order gives opposite signs, so $d_{p-1}d_p=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Coordinate-intersection resolution \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:thm:resolution}
The augmented complex
\[
 \cdots\longrightarrow C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}A_\Lambda\xrightarrow{\ct}D\longrightarrow0
\]
is exact and every $C_p$ is flat. For $\Lambda=[d]$, $C_p=0$ for $p>d$, and this is a flat resolution of $D$ of
length $d$; also for $\Lambda=\N_{>0}$ the complex is exact.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The inclusions defining the differentials are $A_\Lambda$-linear and
preserve exponent degree. In degree $\mathbf0$ the augmented complex
is just $D\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}}D$. Fix a nonzero exponent
$\boldsymbol\alpha$ and write
$T=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}$, a finite nonempty set even in infinite rank.
The degree-$\boldsymbol\alpha$ part of $A$ is $K$, and that of
$I_S$ is $K$ exactly for $\varnothing\ne S\subseteq T$.
Thus the component is the augmented simplex complex on $T$, with a
$p$-element subset in homological degree $p$ and the empty subset in
degree zero.

Here is an explicit contraction of this component. Let $t=\min T$,
and write $[S]$ for its basis vector, including $[\varnothing]$.
Define
\[
 h[S]=
 \begin{cases}
 [\{t\}\cup S],&t\notin S,\\
 0,&t\in S.
 \end{cases}
\]
The element $t$ is first in the ordered list. If $t\notin S$, the
term deleting $t$ in $dh[S]$ is $[S]$, and each other deletion has the
opposite sign to its counterpart in $hd[S]$. If $t\in S$, only
deleting $t$ survives after applying $h$, and it gives $[S]$.
For the empty subset, $dh[\varnothing]=[\varnothing]$.
Hence $dh+hd=1$ in every nonzero exponent degree.

These are contractions of coefficient complexes. They may depend on
$\boldsymbol\alpha$ and are not claimed to be $A_\Lambda$-linear.
They nevertheless prove exactness of the $A_\Lambda$-module complex:
a cycle has only finitely many exponent components, and its component
preimages under $h$ form a finite sum in the required direct sum.
Each $C_p$ for $p>0$ is a direct sum of the flat ideals $I_S$, hence
flat; $C_0=A$ is free. If $\Lambda=[d]$ there are no subsets of size
greater than $d$, giving the stated length. The same component proof
works for $\Lambda=\N_{>0}$ without forming an infinite-support chain.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Arithmetic modules are $\Tor$-acyclic \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:cor:arithmeticTor}
For every $D$-module $E$, $D\otimes_{A_\Lambda}E\cong E$ and $\Tor^{A_\Lambda}_j(D,E)=0$ for $j>0$; in particular
$A_\Lambda\to D$ is a homological ring epimorphism.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Give $E$ the action $a e=\ct(a)e$. The map
$D\otimes_A E\to E$, $d\otimes e\mapsto de$, has inverse
$e\mapsto1\otimes e$; tensor balancing through the surjection
$A\to D$ verifies both identities. Now tensor the flat resolution
of \cref{osq:hd:thm:resolution} with $E$. Tensor product commutes
with direct sums, and each $I_S\otimes_A E$ vanishes by
\cref{osq:hd:lem:faces}(ii). The resulting complex has only $E$ in
degree zero, so it computes zero $\Tor$ in every positive degree.
This also holds for the unbounded-length resolution in countable
rank: it is still a flat resolution in nonnegative homological degrees
\cite[Section~15.60]{StacksDerived}. Taking $E=D$ gives the
self-$\Tor$ vanishing; together with the multiplication isomorphism
$D\otimes_A D\cong D$, this is the asserted homological epimorphism.
\end{proof}

This concerns every module on which the tail acts by zero; it is why such modules cannot see the flat dimension
computed next (12).

\begin{proposition}[Formal lifting and differentials \src{12; 13}]\label{osq:hd:prop:etale}
Let $A$ be $A_\Lambda$ or $T_\Gamma$ with tail $\Pi$. Then $A\to D$ is formally \'etale for nilpotent lifting
problems, but neither flat nor finitely presented as a ring map, and $\Omega_{A/D}\otimes_AD=0$: every
$D$-derivation of $A$ into a module killed by $\Pi$ vanishes.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Halving each monomial exponent gives $\Pi^2=\Pi$ in either family,
so $\Pi^n=\Pi$ for every $n\ge1$. Consider a commutative
$A$-algebra $R$ with structure map $f:A\to R$, a nilpotent ideal
$J\subseteq R$ with $J^n=0$, and a compatible map $g:D\to R/J$.
Compatibility says that $f(\Pi)\subseteq J$. Thus
$f(\Pi)=f(\Pi^n)\subseteq J^n=0$. The map $f$ factors uniquely
through a ring map $\widetilde g:D\to R$. Its reduction is $g$
because both agree after precomposition with the surjection $A\to D$.
This proves existence and uniqueness of the required lift. It is the
idempotent-ideal mechanism of \cite[Tag~060H]{StacksFormal}.

For nonflatness choose a nonzero monomial $u\in\Pi$. Multiplication
by $u$ is an injective endomorphism of the domain $A$, whereas after
tensoring with $D$ it becomes the zero map $D\to D$. Since $D\ne0$,
tensoring fails to preserve this injection.

The ideal $\Pi_\Lambda$ is not finitely generated by
\cref{osq:hd:lem:faces}(iii). In $T_\Gamma$, a finite nonzero
generating family would have a smallest positive exponent $\delta$
among its monomials. Products with $T_\Gamma$ cannot introduce an
exponent below $\delta$, but $X^{\delta/2}\in\Pi$ has such an
exponent, a contradiction. For completeness, a finitely presented
quotient $A/I$ must have $I$ finitely generated as an ideal. Indeed,
write $A/I=A[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/(r_1,\ldots,r_s)$ as an $A$-algebra
and lift the images of $Y_j$ to elements $a_j\in A$. Substitution
$Y_j\mapsto a_j$ sends the relation ideal onto $I$: it maps into
$I$, and every constant polynomial from $I$ lies in that relation
ideal. Hence the finitely many $r_i(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$ generate $I$.
Apply this with $I=\Pi$ to exclude finite presentation of $A\to D$.

Finally, if $E$ is killed by $\Pi$, a $D$-derivation
$\partial:A\to E$ is zero on $D$ and satisfies
$\partial(uv)=u\partial v+v\partial u=0$ for $u,v\in\Pi$.
Since $\Pi=\Pi^2$, it vanishes on $\Pi$ and therefore on $A$.
Apply this to the universal derivation followed by
$\Omega_{A/D}\to\Omega_{A/D}\otimes_A D$. This target is killed
by $\Pi$ and is generated over $D$ by the images of differentials,
all now zero, so $\Omega_{A/D}\otimes_A D=0$.
The lifting assertion concerns $A\to D$; the displayed differential
module concerns the section $D\to A$, followed by reduction along
$A\to D$. These are different directions of ring maps.
\end{proof}

The mechanism is classical and not a novelty claim (12). Manuscript~13 proves the same statements for the full
omnific ring in a two-universe reading (\cref{osq:hd:rem:reconcile}), and \cref{osq:thm:derivations} is the
class-ring analogue for derivations. ``Nilpotent'' is a test condition on $R$: the cores are domains.

\subsection{The multigraded Tor and exact flat dimensions}\label{osq:hd:sub:tor}

For a finite nonempty $F\subseteq\Lambda$ let $J_F=(X_i:i\in F)A_\Lambda$ and $V_F=A_\Lambda/J_F$. For finite $S$ put
$\mathbf e_S=\sum_{i\in S}\mathbf e_i$; the notation $K\langle\mathbf e_S\rangle$ means a copy of the $D$-module $K$
placed in multidegree $\mathbf e_S$ (not a subring of $A_\Lambda$).

\begin{theorem}[Boolean-face $\Tor$ formula \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:thm:boolean}
For $\Lambda$ finite or countably infinite and $F$ as above,
\begin{align*}
 \Tor_0^{A_\Lambda}(D,V_F)&\cong D\langle\mathbf 0\rangle,\qquad
 \Tor_1^{A_\Lambda}(D,V_F)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in F}D\langle\mathbf e_i\rangle,\\
 \Tor_p^{A_\Lambda}(D,V_F)&\cong\bigoplus_{S\subseteq F,\ |S|=p}K\langle\mathbf e_S\rangle\qquad(p\ge2).
\end{align*}
In particular $\Tor_p=0$ for $p>|F|$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Tensor the flat resolution with $V_F=A/J_F$. The degree-zero term is
$V_F$ and each positive summand becomes
$I_S\otimes_A A/J_F\cong I_S/J_FI_S$. We compute this quotient
complex directly; the preceding degreewise contraction was not an
$A$-linear splitting to which tensoring could be applied.

Fix $\boldsymbol\alpha\ne\mathbf0$ and put
$T=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}$. Only subsets $S\subseteq T$ can contribute
in this degree. If some $j\in F$ has $\alpha_j>1$, subtraction of
$\mathbf e_j$ leaves a nonnegative vector with the same support $T$.
Every coefficient in each contributing $I_S$, and also in $A$, is
therefore a multiple of $X_j$ with cofactor in that same module.
The entire quotient complex is zero in this degree.

Assume now $\alpha_j\le1$ for all $j\in F$, and set
$U=\{j\in F:\alpha_j=1\}\subseteq T$. For nonempty $S\subseteq T$,
the coefficient space $(I_S)_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ is $K$.
The product $X_jI_S$ reaches it exactly when $j\in U\setminus S$:
subtracting $\mathbf e_j$ is nonnegative and retains positivity at
every index of $S$. In that event it reaches all of $K$. Thus
\[
 (I_S/J_FI_S)_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=
 \begin{cases}
 K,&U\subseteq S\subseteq T,\ S\ne\varnothing,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The differentials delete one index, with their original signs, whenever
the target survives. The term $(V_F)_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ must be
computed separately because $A_{\mathbf0}=D$.

\emph{Case $U=\varnothing$.} No generator of $J_F$ reaches this
degree, so $(V_F)_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=K$. All faces survive and the
augmented simplex contraction proves zero homology.

\emph{Case $U\ne\varnothing$ and $T\setminus U\ne\varnothing$.}
Choose $j\in U$. Subtracting $\mathbf e_j$ leaves a nonzero vector,
so the cofactor lies in a full $K$-coefficient tail and
$(V_F)_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=0$. Choose $t\in T\setminus U$.
On surviving faces define $h[S]=0$ if $t\in S$ and otherwise
$h[S]=(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<t\}|}[S\cup\{t\}]$.
The target still contains $U$. Deleting $t$ contributes $[S]$;
all other deletions cancel in $dh+hd$, or both corresponding terms
are zero because they delete an index of $U$. Thus $dh+hd=1$ and
this component is again acyclic.

\emph{Case $T=U$ and $|U|\ge2$.} The only surviving positive
summand is $S=U$, a copy of $K$ in degree $|U|$. There is no larger
face, and deletion of any index kills the target. Also
$(V_F)_{\mathbf e_U}=0$, since removing one of its at least two
unit coordinates leaves a nonzero tail. This gives precisely
$K\langle\mathbf e_U\rangle$ in homology.

\emph{Case $T=U=\{j\}$.} Here $\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf e_j$.
The only way $J_F$ reaches this degree is by multiplying $X_j$ by a
constant in $A$, whose coefficient must lie in $D$. Consequently
$(V_F)_{\mathbf e_j}=K/D$, an additive $D$-module quotient.
The component complex is the quotient map $K\to K/D$, with $K$
in homological degree one. Its kernel is $D$ and its cokernel zero,
giving $D\langle\mathbf e_j\rangle$ in degree one. This includes
$D=K$, when the target is zero and the same kernel formula holds.

In exponent degree $\mathbf0$ only $D$ in homological degree zero
remains. All elements and preimages used above have finite support,
so the homology of the full graded complex is the direct sum of these
component homologies, also in countably infinite rank. The listed
components give exactly the asserted formula and the vanishing above
$|F|$.
\end{proof}

For $|S|=p\ge2$ the class of $k\in K$ is represented by $kX^{\mathbf e_S}$ in $I_S/J_FI_S$; in degree one only
coefficients $d\in D$ give cycles $dX_i$. Treating the constant coefficient as if it lay in $K$ gives a wrong
answer (12). Scaling coordinates by positive rationals $b_i$ ($i\in F$) is an automorphism of $A_\Lambda$ fixing the
coefficients, so the same formula holds for $A_\Lambda/(X_i^{b_i}:i\in F)$ with $\mathbf e_S$ replaced by
$\sum_{i\in S}b_i\mathbf e_i$ (12).

\begin{corollary}[Exact flat dimensions \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:cor:fd}
For $\Lambda=[d]$, $\fd_{A_d}D=d$ and $\fd_{A_d}\Pi_d=d-1$; for $\Lambda=\N_{>0}$ both are infinite. All positive
self-$\Tor$ groups $\Tor^{A_d}_{>0}(D,D)$ vanish.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For finite rank, the flat resolution has length $d$, so $\fd_{A_d}D\le d$.
Take $F=[d]$ in \cref{osq:hd:thm:boolean}. The degree-$d$ group is
$D$ if $d=1$ and $K$ if $d\ge2$, with its displayed multidegree;
either is nonzero. A flat resolution of length less than $d$ would
make this group zero, so $\fd_{A_d}D=d$.

Truncating the resolution at its image $\Pi_d\subset A_d$ gives a
flat resolution of $\Pi_d$ of length $d-1$. For $d\ge2$, the long
exact $\Tor$ sequence of $0\to\Pi_d\to A_d\to D\to0$, with
$A_d$ free, gives
\[
 \Tor_{d-1}^{A_d}(\Pi_d,V_{[d]})
 \cong\Tor_d^{A_d}(D,V_{[d]})\ne0.
\]
This proves the matching lower bound. For $d=1$, the ideal
$\Pi_1=I_{\{1\}}$ is nonzero and flat, so its flat dimension is zero.

In countably infinite rank, choose a finite $F$ of size $n$ for each
$n\ge1$. The same formula gives nonzero $\Tor_n(D,V_F)$ for
arbitrarily large $n$. Taking $n\ge2$ and dimension shifting gives
nonzero $\Tor_{n-1}(\Pi_\Lambda,V_F)$ as well. Neither module can
have a finite-length flat resolution. Finally the vanishing of all
positive self-$\Tor$ groups is
\cref{osq:hd:cor:arithmeticTor}; it is compatible with these lower
bounds because the modules $V_F$ are different test modules.
\end{proof}

For $d=2$ the groups are $D^2$ and $K$ (the latter represented by $kX_1X_2$), and for $d=3$ they are $D^3,K^3,K$:
vertices, edges and the full face (12). The finite audit of 12 checks this formula for $D=\Q\subset K=\Q(\sqrt2)$
(\cref{osq:sub:checks}).

\subsection{Coefficient lattices and their syzygies}\label{osq:tn:sub:lattices}

The next results need only a ring of the following shape, which covers 12's cores, 12's ordered-cone rings and 14's
rings.

\paragraph{Setting (L).} $K$ is a field, $D\subseteq K$ a unital subring, and $A=D\oplus\Pi$ is one of:
(a) $A_\Lambda$ with $\Pi=\Pi_\Lambda$; (b) $T_\Gamma$ with $\Pi=\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$; (c) the class ring
$\A_{D,K}$ with $\Pi=\Pi_K$ (full surreal exponents, $K$ a set field). In each case $B=K\oplus\Pi$ is a ring containing
$A$, $\Pi$ is an ideal of $B$ and a $K$-vector space, $K\cap\Pi=0$, all three lie in a field, and $\Pi$ is not finitely
generated in (a), (b) and not generated by a set in (c) (\cref{osq:hd:lem:faces}(iii), \cref{osq:hd:prop:etale},
\cref{osq:prop:common}(iii)). A \emph{coefficient lattice} is a nonzero module $M=Dm_1+\dots+Dm_r\subseteq K$, with $r\ge1$ and $m_1,\dots,m_r$
linearly independent over $D$ (equivalently over $\Frac D$); $r=\rk M$. Put
\[
 L(M)=M+\Pi\subseteq B,\qquad J_g(M)=X^gL(M)\subseteq A
\]
for a nonzero monomial $X^g\in\Pi$ (a vector $g\ne\mathbf0$ in (a), $g\in\Gamma_{>0}$ in (b), $g>0$ in (c)). For
$(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$, $D$ is a principal ideal domain and every nonzero finitely generated $D$-submodule of
$K$ is free, so these are exactly 14's coefficient lattices.

The direct sums in Setting (L) are additive decompositions. A lattice's
$D$-rank $r$ counts independent constants; it is different from the
fraction-field rank of $L(M)$ as an $A$-module. In the set-sized cases
all modules and tensor products below have their usual meanings. For
the class case, finite free modules, maps and kernels are explicit class
constructions; tensor statements use the balanced carriers specified in
\cref{osq:tn:sub:tensor}. No set of generators for the tail is assumed.

\begin{theorem}[Generators and the first syzygy \src{14; 12; 17} \merge]\label{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}
In Setting (L), let $M$ have basis $m_1,\dots,m_r$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L(M)=\sum_jAm_j$, $\Pi L(M)=\Pi$ and $L(M)/\Pi L(M)\cong M$; the least number of generators of $L(M)$ is $r$,
although $L(M)$ has rank one over the fraction field.
\item The sequence
\begin{gather*}
 0\longrightarrow\Pi^{r-1}\xrightarrow{\ \sigma\ }A^r\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }L(M)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \pi(a)=\sum_ja_jm_j,\\
 \sigma(u_2,\dots,u_r)=\Bigl(-\sum_{j\ge2}\tfrac{m_j}{m_1}u_j,\ u_2,\dots,u_r\Bigr),
\end{gather*}
is exact. For $r=1$, $L(M)\cong A$; for $r\ge2$, $L(M)$ is not finitely presented in (a), (b), and in (c) the kernel is
not generated by any set.
\item \emph{(12's certificate.)} Let $c\in K\setminus\Frac(D)$ and $H=(X^g,cX^g)A$. Then
$X^gA\cap cX^gA=X^g\Pi$ and $0\to\Pi\xrightarrow{m\mapsto(-cm,m)}A^2\xrightarrow{(a,b)\mapsto X^ga+cX^gb}H\to0$ is
exact; in (a) and (b), $A$ is not coherent.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) Every basis vector is nonzero. Since $\Pi$ is a $K$-vector space,
$m_1\Pi=\Pi$, and therefore $\sum_jAm_j$ contains both $M$ and
$\Pi$. Conversely each $a_jm_j$ has its constant part in $Dm_j$
and its tail in $\Pi$, so this sum is exactly $L(M)$. The ideal
property in $B$ gives $\Pi L(M)\subseteq\Pi$, while
$\Pi m_1=\Pi$ gives the reverse inclusion. Taking the constant part
identifies $L(M)/\Pi L(M)$ with $M\cong D^r$, with $A$ acting
through $D$ on this quotient.

Any $q$ generators of $L(M)$ give $q$ generators of $D^r$.
Tensoring the resulting surjection $D^q\to D^r$ with $\Frac(D)$
shows $q\ge r$ by vector-space dimension; the displayed $r$
generators attain this bound. To compare this with fraction-field
rank, choose $0\ne u\in\Pi$. Every $k\in K$ equals $(ku)/u$,
with numerator and denominator in $A$, so $K\subseteq\Frac(A)$.
Thus $L(M)$ is a nonzero submodule of $\Frac(A)$ and spans that
one-dimensional vector space after localization. This is rank one
over $\Frac(A)$, independently of $r$.

(ii) Write $a_j=d_j+u_j$ uniquely with $d_j\in D$, $u_j\in\Pi$.
If $\sum_j a_jm_j=0$, its constant part is
$\sum_jd_jm_j=0$. Independence of the basis over $D$ forces
every $d_j=0$. The remaining relation is
$u_1=-\sum_{j\ge2}(m_j/m_1)u_j$. Its right side lies in $\Pi$
because $\Pi$ is a $K$-space. Conversely every tuple of this form
is a relation. The last $r-1$ coordinates recover the input to
$\sigma$, proving injectivity and the asserted description of the
kernel. Surjectivity of $\pi$ is (i).

For $r=1$, multiplication by $m_1$ gives the isomorphism $A\cong L(M)$.
For $r\ge2$, projection from $\Pi^{r-1}$ onto any coordinate is
surjective. A finite generating family for this kernel would therefore
generate $\Pi$, contradicting Setting (L). In (a) and (b), if
$L(M)$ had any finite presentation, the kernel of its displayed
finite free surjection would be finitely generated. One can see the
independence of the chosen presentation from Schanuel's lemma: comparing
it with a finite presentation makes this kernel a direct summand of
a finitely generated module \cite[Tag~00O3]{StacksProjective}.
In (c), the same coordinate projection shows directly that the displayed
kernel cannot be generated by a set; the stronger statement about
arbitrary presentations is treated in \cref{osq:rel:thm:presentation}.

(iii) The assumption $c\notin\Frac(D)$ gives $c\ne0$ and makes
$1,c$ independent over $D$. Apply (ii) to $M=D+Dc$, and multiply
the presentation by $X^g$. Multiplication is injective in the ambient
field and takes $L(M)$ onto $H$, so the stated sequence is exact.
For the intersection, cancel $X^g$ in
$X^g(d+u)=cX^g(e+v)$. Comparing constant parts gives $d=ce$.
If $e\ne0$, this would put $c=d/e$ in $\Frac(D)$; hence
$e=d=0$. Thus the intersection is contained in $X^g\Pi$.
Conversely $c\Pi=\Pi$ puts every element of $X^g\Pi$ in both
principal ideals. The intersection is therefore exactly $X^g\Pi$,
which is isomorphic to the non-finitely generated module $\Pi$.

For (a) and (b), this rules out coherence: in a coherent ring the
intersection of two finitely generated ideals is finitely generated
\cite[Section~10.90]{StacksCoherent}. Equivalently, the finitely
generated ideal $H\cong L(D+Dc)$ is not finitely presented by (ii),
contradicting the definition of a coherent ring. The existence of
$c\in K\setminus\Frac(D)$ is part of this certificate.
\end{proof}

\Cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(iii) is 12's noncoherence certificate for
$A_\Lambda$ and $T_\Gamma$ whenever $K\ne\Frac(D)$; no principal-ideal
hypothesis on the unital subring $D$ is needed.
(i) and (ii) are 14's theorem for $\Oz$, $\GOz$ and $A_0$ with $D$ a principal ideal domain. Stating both at once in
Setting (L) is the merge's; the proofs are the sources'. All compatible relations between two generators with the same
monomial and incompatible constant lines are forced into the infinitely divisible tail (12). No novelty is attached to
noncoherence as such: rings of the form $D+M$ and their coherence have a long history, including Dobbs--Papick
\cite{DobbsPapick}; 14 uses no valuation-ring hypothesis on $B$, and the useful information is the exact syzygy (14).
Manuscript~17 proves (i), (ii) and the intersection formula of (iii) again, independently, for $\Oz$, $\GOz$ and the models
$R^{11}_{\Gamma_\kappa,<\kappa}$, and adds that in case (c) the module $L(M)$ with $r\ge2$ has no presentation by sets
(\cref{osq:rel:thm:presentation}); it credits the kernel shape $\Pi^{r-1}$ and the flat dimension one of the $D+M$ setting to
Dobbs \cite{Dobbs} and the intersection mechanism to Dobbs--Papick.

\begin{proposition}[Antisymmetric torsion and nonflatness \src{14} \merge]\label{osq:tn:prop:nonflat}
In Setting (L), let $M,N$ be coefficient lattices and $\mathsf m_{M,N}:M\otimes_DN\to K$ the multiplication map. On
$\mathsf E(M,N)=\Pi\oplus(M\otimes_DN)$ the rule
\begin{equation}\label{osq:tn:eq:action}
 (d+h)\cdot(u,t)=\bigl(du+hu+h\,\mathsf m_{M,N}(t),\ dt\bigr)\qquad(d\in D,\ h\in\Pi)
\end{equation}
is an $A$-module structure, and $(m+u)\otimes(n+v)\mapsto(mv+un+uv,\ m\otimes n)$ is a well-defined $A$-linear map
$\beta:L(M)\otimes_AL(N)\to\mathsf E(M,N)$. If $\rk M\ge2$ and $m_1,m_2$ are basis vectors, then
$\tau=m_1\otimes m_2-m_2\otimes m_1$ is a nonzero element of $L(M)\otimes_AL(M)$ with product $0$. Consequently, in
(a) and (b), $L(M)$ and every ideal $J_g(M)$ are not flat, hence neither projective nor invertible.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $\mu=\mathsf m_{M,N}$. The first coordinate in
\eqref{osq:tn:eq:action} lies in $\Pi$, since that is an ideal of
$B$ stable under all $K$-scalars. For $a=d+h$ and $b=e+v$ in $A$,
their product has constant part $de$ and tail $dv+eh+hv$.
Expanding the action twice gives
\[
 a\cdot(b\cdot(u,t))
 =\bigl(ab\,u+(dv+eh+hv)\mu(t),\ de\,t\bigr)
 =(ab)\cdot(u,t).
\]
Here $\mu(et)=e\mu(t)$ accounts for the cross term. Additivity
in both arguments and the identity action follow directly, proving
that this is an $A$-module.

The decompositions $x=m+u$ and $y=n+v$ in $L(M)$ and $L(N)$ are
unique. Define the biadditive map
$b(x,y)=(xy-mn,m\otimes n)$. For $a=d+h\in A$ the constant
part of $ax$ is $dm$, so
\[
 b(ax,y)=(axy-dmn,dm\otimes n)
        =a\cdot b(x,y)=b(x,ay),
\]
where $dm\otimes n=m\otimes dn$ in $M\otimes_DN$.
Thus $b$ is balanced and induces the stated $A$-linear map $\beta$.
The action is generally not the direct-sum action: the term
$h\mu(t)$ couples the two coordinates.

For $N=M$, the image of the antisymmetric tensor is
\[
 \beta(\tau)=(0,m_1\otimes_Dm_2-m_2\otimes_Dm_1).
\]
In the free $D$-module with basis $m_i\otimes_Dm_j$, the coefficient
of $m_1\otimes_Dm_2$ is $1\ne0$. Hence this image, and therefore
$\tau$, is nonzero, including in characteristic two. Multiplication
sends $\tau$ to zero because the ambient field is commutative.

In (a) and (b), multiplication by $X^g$ identifies $L(M)$ with the
ideal $J=J_g(M)\subset A$; both $X^gM$ and $X^g\Pi$ lie in
$\Pi$. The induced tensor isomorphism carries $\tau$ to a nonzero
element of $J\otimes_AJ$ whose product is zero. If $J$ were flat,
tensoring the injection $J\hookrightarrow A$ with $J$ would give
an injection $J\otimes_AJ\to A\otimes_AJ\cong J$. This map is
exactly multiplication, a contradiction. Isomorphism transfers
nonflatness to $L(M)$. Projective modules and invertible ideals are
flat, giving the remaining conclusions. For class carriers the same
balanced-map calculation is interpreted as described immediately below.
\end{proof}

In (c) the tensor product is 14's explicit carrier (\cref{osq:tn:sub:tensor}); there the same element shows that
tensoring $J_g(M)\hookrightarrow A$ with $J_g(M)$ is not injective, which is 14's statement that $L(M)$ is not flat over
$\Oz$. Over $A_0$ this is 14's corollary; allowing any unital $D\subseteq K$ and 12's rings is the merge's (the proof is
14's, and no principal-ideal hypothesis is used in it).

\subsection{Flat and projective dimensions; the ordered cone}\label{osq:hd:sub:dimensions}

\begin{theorem}[Lattice modules and cyclic quotients \src{12, 14} \merge]\label{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice}
Let $A$ be $A_d$ ($d\ge1$) or $T_\Gamma$, and put $\delta=d$, respectively $\delta=1$. Let $M$ be a coefficient lattice of rank
$r\ge2$ and $J=J_g(M)$. Then
\[
 \fd_AL(M)=\delta,\qquad \fd_A(A/J)=\delta+1,
\]
and for every $A$-module $N$ and $j\ge2$,
$\Tor^A_j(L(M),N)\cong\Tor^A_j(D,N)^{r-1}\cong\Tor^A_{j+1}(A/J,N)$. Over $A_{\N_{>0}}$ both dimensions are infinite.
In particular, for $c\in K\setminus\Frac(D)$ and $H=(X^g,cX^g)A$,
$\fd_{A_d}(A_d/H)=d+1$ and $\fd_{T_\Gamma}(T_\Gamma/H)=2$
(with $g=\mathbf e_1$ giving $H=(X_1,cX_1)$ in $A_d$),
and over $A_0=T_\Q$, $\fd L(M)=1$ and $\fd(A_0/J_e(M))=2$. If moreover $c^2\in D$, then
$\Tor_2^A(A/H,A/H)\cong D+cD\cong D\oplus D$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the two exact sequences
\[
 0\to\Pi^{r-1}\to A^r\to L(M)\to0,
 \qquad 0\to J\to A\to A/J\to0,
\]
with $J\cong L(M)$ by multiplication by $X^g$.
For $A_d$, \cref{osq:hd:cor:fd} gives $\fd\Pi=d-1$.
For $T_\Gamma$, the principal-ideal exhaustion in
\cref{osq:hd:thm:orderedcone} makes $\Pi$ flat. Splicing flat
resolutions into the displayed sequences gives
$\fd L(M)\le\delta$ and $\fd(A/J)\le\delta+1$.

For $j\ge2$, the free middle terms make the long exact sequences
give
\[
 \Tor_j(L(M),N)\cong\Tor_{j-1}(\Pi,N)^{r-1}
 \cong\Tor_j(D,N)^{r-1},
\]
where the second comparison uses $0\to\Pi\to A\to D\to0$.
Similarly $\Tor_{j+1}(A/J,N)\cong\Tor_j(J,N)$, and the
isomorphism $J\cong L(M)$ gives the claimed comparison. These maps
are natural in $N$ after the lattice basis and $X^g$ are fixed.

If $\delta=d\ge2$, take $N=V_{[d]}$:
$\Tor_d(D,N)\cong K\ne0$ by \cref{osq:hd:thm:boolean}, and
$r-1\ge1$ ensures that its indicated direct power is nonzero.
This attains both upper bounds. For $\delta=1$, the preceding
antisymmetric tensor gives a concrete degree-one obstruction. With
$N=A/J$, the long exact sequence of $0\to J\to A\to A/J\to0$
tensored with $J$ identifies
$\Tor_1(A/J,J)$ with the kernel of $J\otimes_AJ\to J$.
It is nonzero. Symmetry of $\Tor$ over the commutative ring then
gives $\Tor_1(J,A/J)\ne0$, and dimension shifting gives
$\Tor_2(A/J,A/J)\ne0$. Thus $\fd L(M)=1$ and $\fd(A/J)=2$.
In infinite rank, use $V_F$ with arbitrarily large finite $|F|=n\ge2$
in the same comparison. Both dimensions are infinite.

The two-generator instances use the lattice $U=D+Dc$, of rank two
because $c\notin\Frac(D)$. Assume additionally $c^2\in D$ for
the last assertion. Then
\[
 H=X^gU\oplus X^g\Pi,\qquad H\Pi=X^g\Pi,
 \qquad cH\subseteq H.
\]
For the middle identity use $U\Pi=\Pi$ and $\Pi^2=\Pi$;
for the last, $cU\subseteq U$ follows from $c^2\in D$ and
$c\Pi=\Pi$. Tensor the presentation
$0\to\Pi\xrightarrow{m\mapsto(-cm,m)}A^2\to H\to0$
with $A/H$. Its long exact sequence, together with dimension shifting,
identifies
\[
 \Tor_2(A/H,A/H)\cong\Tor_1(H,A/H)
 \cong\ker\bigl(\Pi/X^g\Pi\longrightarrow(A/H)^2\bigr).
\]
The map sends $m$ to $(-cm,m)$ modulo $H$. Its kernel consists
exactly of the classes with $m\in H$: that condition is necessary
from the second coordinate and sufficient from $cH\subseteq H$.
The kernel is therefore $H/X^g\Pi\cong U$, by taking the
coefficient of $X^g$. The action factors through $D$ since
$H\Pi=X^g\Pi$, and $U\cong D\oplus D$ via its basis $1,c$.
No condition $c^2\in D$ was used in the flat-dimension bounds.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Correction to 12 and the relation to 14.} 12 states $\fd(A_d/H)=d+1$ and $\fd(T_\Gamma/H)=2$ under the extra
hypothesis $c^2\in D$, which it uses only to compute $\Tor_2(A/H,A/H)$; for $d\ge2$ its own shift argument never uses it,
and for $d=1$ and $T_\Gamma$ the lower bound $2$ follows from 14's antisymmetric torsion tensor. The hypothesis is needed only
for the formula $\Tor_2(A/H,A/H)\cong D\oplus D$. 14's flat-dimension proposition for $A_0$ is the case $A=T_\Q=A_1$ of the
theorem. Since a nonzero $\Tor$ in degree $n$ forces weak global dimension at least $n$: if $K\ne\Frac D$ (for instance
$(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$ with $c=\sqrt2$), then $\operatorname{w.gl.dim}A_d\ge d+1$,
$\operatorname{w.gl.dim}T_\Gamma\ge2$, and the countable-rank core has infinite weak global dimension (12, 14). Neither source
claims the exact weak global dimension of any of these rings.

\begin{proposition}[Projective dimensions \src{12} \merge]\label{osq:hd:prop:pd}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Telescope, 12.)} Let $A$ be a domain and $I=\bigcup_{n\ge0}x_nA$ for nonzero $x_n$ with $x_n=x_{n+1}u_n$,
$u_n\in A$. With $F=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}Ae_n$, the sequence
$0\to F\xrightarrow{\Delta}F\xrightarrow{\pi}I\to0$, $\Delta(e_na)=e_na-e_{n+1}u_na$, $\pi(e_na)=x_na$, is exact; so $\pd_AI\le1$.
This applies to every $I_S$ ($x_n=p_S^{2^{-n}}$) and to $\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$ ($x_n=X^{2^{-n}g}$, $g\in\Gamma_{>0}$).
\item \merge\ $\pd_{A_\Lambda}I_S=1$ and $\pd_{T_\Gamma}\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma=1$.
\item $d\le\pd_{A_d}D\le d+1$ (12), and \merge\ $\pd_{A_1}D=\pd_{T_\Gamma}D=2$. (The upper bound is attained for every $d$:
\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd}, 21.)
\item \merge\ Over $T_\Gamma$ (in particular over $A_0$), for a lattice of rank at least two, $\pd L(M)=2$ and
$\pd(T_\Gamma/J_g(M))=3$. Over $A_d$, $d\le\pd L(M)\le d+1$ and $d+1\le\pd(A_d/J_g(M))\le d+2$ (12, for $M=D+Dc$). (The upper
bounds are attained: \cref{osq:da:thm:lattice}, 21.)
\item \merge\ Let $(A,I,D)$ satisfy (H1)--(H3) of \cref{osq:sec:homological}, with $A$ consisting of series of nonnegative
support (as do all rings of \cref{osq:sec:models} and $T_\Gamma$). If $I$ is countably generated, equivalently if $\Gamma_{>0}$ has a
countable coinitial subset, then $\pd_AI=1$ and $\pd_AD=2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(i) The relation $x_n=x_{n+1}u_n$ gives $\pi\Delta=0$, and
the union gives surjectivity of $\pi$. If a finite vector is nonzero,
its least nonzero coordinate is unchanged by $\Delta$, proving
injectivity. Modulo $\operatorname{im}\Delta$ the relation
$e_na=e_{n+1}u_na$ moves every term of a finite vector to one
index $N$. Thus $v\equiv e_Na$, with $x_Na=\pi(v)$.
If $\pi(v)=0$, cancellation in the domain gives $a=0$, proving
exactness at the middle term. Both copies of $F$ are free.
The face ideals have the stated exhaustion by
\cref{osq:hd:lem:faces}(i). For $T_\Gamma$ fix $g>0$.
Since $\Gamma\subseteq\R$, for any finite nonzero tail choose $n$
so large that $2^{-n}g$ is strictly below every exponent in its
support. Dividing by $X^{2^{-n}g}$ then leaves a tail in $T_\Gamma$.
Divisibility ensures these exponents lie in $\Gamma$, and the
Archimedean property gives their coinitiality.

(ii) The ideals in question are nonzero and not finitely generated.
By \cref{osq:lem:projideal} they cannot be projective, while (i)
gives projective dimension at most one. Hence their dimension is one.

(iii) Each $C_p$ for $p>0$ in the finite face resolution has a
length-one free resolution: take direct sums of the telescopes in (i).
Here $C_0=A_d$ is already free. Dimension shifting along the finite
resolution gives $\pd D\le d+1$. Explicitly, in
$0\to U\to V\to W\to0$ one has
$\pd W\le\max(\pd V,\pd U+1)$; iterate this from the leftmost
$C_d$ to $D$. The lower bound is $\pd D\ge\fd D=d$.
For $T_\Gamma$, the sequence $0\to\Pi\to T_\Gamma\to D\to0$
gives $\pd D\le2$. A projective dimension at most one for $D$
would make this kernel $\Pi$ projective by Schanuel's lemma,
contrary to (ii). Thus the dimension is two, also for
$A_1\cong T_\Q$.

(iv) Over $T_\Gamma$ the presentation of $L(M)$ has kernel
$\Pi^{r-1}$ of projective dimension one. It gives
$\pd L(M)\le2$. If this dimension were at most one, Schanuel's
lemma would make $\Pi^{r-1}$ projective, hence also its summand
$\Pi$, a contradiction. Thus $\pd L(M)=\pd J=2$.
The sequence $0\to J\to T_\Gamma\to T_\Gamma/J\to0$ gives
the upper bound three for the quotient. If the quotient had projective
dimension at most two, its first syzygy $J$ would have dimension at
most one, again a contradiction. Over $A_d$, truncation of the face
resolution and the same dimension inequalities give $\pd\Pi_d\le d$,
then $\pd L(M)\le d+1$ and $\pd(A_d/J)\le d+2$.
Their flat dimensions give the displayed lower bounds.

(v) Suppose a countable family generates $I$, and write each generator
as $f_n=X^{g_n}b_n$ with $g_n>0$, $b_n\in I$, by (H2).
For any $h>0$, the monomial $X^h\in I$ is a finite linear
combination of these generators. It therefore lies in $X^gA$ for
$g$ the minimum of the finitely many $g_n$ used. Cancelling the
monomial in the ambient series field shows $X^{h-g}\in A$.
The nonnegative-support hypothesis implies $g\le h$, so the $g_n$
form a coinitial family.
