Conversely, enumerate a countable coinitial family as $q_n>0$.
Divisibility lets us choose recursively $h_n>0$ with $h_n\le q_n$
and $h_{n+1}<h_n$; this sequence is still coinitial. If
$f=X^g b$ as in (H2), choose $n$ with $h_n\le g$. Then
$f=X^{h_n}(X^{g-h_n}b)\in X^{h_n}A$, proving
$I=\bigcup_nX^{h_n}A$. The transition factors are
$X^{h_n-h_{n+1}}\in A$, so (i) applies. Nonfinite generation
and \cref{osq:lem:projideal} exclude projectivity, giving $\pd I=1$.
The same quotient argument as in (iii) gives $\pd D=2$.
\end{proof}

Items (ii)--(v) sharpen 12's bounds $1\le\pd_{A_1}D\le2$ and are consistent with 06's $\pd\ge2$ (\cref{osq:thm:homological}(v)). For
$d\ge2$ these items left the value $\pd_{A_d}D\in\{d,d+1\}$ undetermined; 21 shows that it is $d+1$ for every $d$, and that the lattice
bounds of (iv) are attained (\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd,osq:da:thm:lattice}). Hypothesis (H2) in (v) cannot be dropped: $A_d$ has a countably
generated tail and satisfies (H1) and (H3), but not (H2), and $\pd_{A_d}D=d+1$ (\cref{osq:da:rem:htwo}, a merge remark). Among the five
constructions of \cref{osq:sec:models}, (v) applies
exactly to $A^{08}_\kappa$ with $\cf\kappa=\aleph_0$: the tail of each construction needs as many generators as the length of its
coinitial chain (\cref{osq:rem:reconcile}), namely $\cf\kappa$ for 03 and 08, $\kappa$ for 06 and 11, $\aleph_1$ for 09, and only 08
allows countable cofinality. \Cref{osq:q:pd} is re-scoped accordingly.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[Ordered-cone cores \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:thm:orderedcone}
$(T_\Gamma,\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma,D)$ satisfies (H1)--(H3) of \cref{osq:sec:homological}. Consequently
$\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma=\bigcup_{\delta\in\Gamma_{>0}}X^\delta T_\Gamma$ is flat and idempotent but not projective,
$\Tor^{T_\Gamma}_{>0}(D,N)=0$ for every $D$-module $N$, $\fd_{T_\Gamma}D=1$ with $\Tor_1(D,T_\Gamma/X^\gamma T_\Gamma)\cong D$ for $\gamma>0$, and
the other items of \cref{osq:thm:homological} hold; $T_\Gamma\to D$ is formally \'etale and not flat, $\pd_{T_\Gamma}D=2$, and
$T_\Gamma$ is not coherent if $K\ne\Frac(D)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The domain, additive decomposition and constant-term retraction give
(H1). For a nonzero tail $f$, let $g$ be half the least of its
finitely many positive exponents. Then
$f=X^g(X^{-g}f)$, and the quotient has strictly positive exponents
and arbitrary coefficients in $K$, hence is again a tail. The zero
tail has the same factorization with zero quotient and any $g>0$.
This proves (H2), including the directed principal-ideal exhaustion.
For (H3), a finite nonzero family of tails has a smallest exponent
$\delta>0$ among its monomials. Multiplication by $T_\Gamma$
cannot introduce smaller exponents, so it cannot generate
$X^{\delta/2}\in\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$.

The homological package now gives flatness, idempotence, nonprojectivity,
all the asserted $\Tor$ conclusions and flat dimension one. For the
displayed nonzero $\Tor_1$, use the free resolution given by
multiplication by $X^\gamma$ for $\gamma>0$.
Formal lifting is \cref{osq:hd:prop:etale}, and the countable
exhaustion in \cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(i)--(iii) gives projective
dimension two. Finally, if $K\ne\Frac(D)$, choose
$c\in K\setminus\Frac(D)$ and apply the two-generator
noncoherence certificate of \cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(iii).
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Coefficient hypothesis for noncoherence.}
The final clause above needs the displayed restriction. Without it the
earlier unconditional claim is false: take $D=K$ and $\Gamma=\Q$.
Then $T_\Q=K[\Q_{\ge0}]$. Any finite family lies in a common
polynomial subring $K[X^{1/n}]$. Its ideal there is generated by a
greatest common divisor, with a polynomial B\'ezout identity expressing
that divisor in terms of the family. The same divisibilities and identity
hold after extending to $T_\Q$, so every finitely generated ideal of
$T_\Q$ is principal. A nonzero principal ideal in this domain is
free of rank one; the zero ideal is finitely presented as well. Thus
$T_\Q$ is coherent, despite its non-finitely generated tail and the
projective dimension two of its constant quotient. This counterexample
does not affect the integer/real or Gaussian/complex cases, where
$K\ne\Frac(D)$. No complete coherence classification is asserted.

\begin{theorem}[Same exponent group, different dimension \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:thm:collapse}
Let $(\gamma_i)_{i\in\Lambda}$ be positive reals linearly independent over $\Q$, $\Gamma=\sum_i\Q\gamma_i$, and
$A_\Lambda\hookrightarrow T_\Gamma$ the inclusion of \cref{osq:hd:lem:cores}(iii). Then $\Pi_\Lambda T_\Gamma=\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$
and $T_\Gamma\otimes_{A_\Lambda}D\cong D$. If $|\Lambda|\ge2$ the extension is not flat:
$(X_1A_\Lambda\cap X_2A_\Lambda)T_\Gamma\ne X_1T_\Gamma\cap X_2T_\Gamma$. The flat dimension of $D$ drops from $d$ to $1$ in rank $d$,
and from $\infty$ to $1$ in countable rank.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The image of $\Pi_\Lambda$ lies in the ideal
$\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma$, giving one inclusion. Conversely,
for $\gamma>0$ choose a positive rational $q$ with
$q\gamma_1<\gamma$, using that these are real numbers. Then
\[
 kX^\gamma=X_1^q\,kX^{\gamma-q\gamma_1}
 \in\Pi_\Lambda T_\Gamma.
\]
The second factor is a tail even for $k\notin D$, so the identity
covers every coefficient. Finite sums give equality of the ideals.
The usual base-change identity for a quotient therefore gives
\[
 T_\Gamma\otimes_{A_\Lambda}D
 \cong T_\Gamma/\Pi_\Lambda T_\Gamma
 =T_\Gamma/\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Gamma\cong D.
\]
This identity does not require flatness.

If $|\Lambda|\ge2$, choose and relabel two coordinates so that
$\gamma_1<\gamma_2$; independence excludes equality. Every monomial
in $X_1A_\Lambda\cap X_2A_\Lambda$ has both first and second
coordinates at least one. Its real exponent is therefore at least
$\gamma_1+\gamma_2$. Multiplication by $T_\Gamma$ adds only
nonnegative real exponents, and cancellation cannot create a new smaller
exponent. Thus this lower bound holds throughout the extended
intersection ideal. But
\[
 X^{\gamma_2}=X_1X^{\gamma_2-\gamma_1}
 \in X_1T_\Gamma\cap X_2T_\Gamma
\]
has smaller exponent and does not lie in that ideal.

A flat extension would preserve this intersection: tensor the exact
sequence $0\to I\cap I'\to A\to A/I\oplus A/I'$ and use
flatness also to identify the tensors of ideals with their extended
ideals inside the target ring. Its exactness would give equality of
the two intersections, contrary to the exhibited monomial.
Finally \cref{osq:hd:cor:fd,osq:hd:thm:orderedcone} compute the
two quotient flat dimensions, in finite and countably infinite rank.
The nonflat extension, rather than any change in the constant ring or
ordered exponent group, accounts for their difference.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Two directions inside $\Oz$ \src{12}]\label{osq:hd:ex:cone}
With $\gamma_1=1$, $\gamma_2=\sqrt2$ and $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$, the core $A_2=\Z+\bigoplus_{a,b\in\Q_{\ge0},\,a+b>0}\R\,\omega^{a+b\sqrt2}$
lies in the ring $T_{\Q+\Q\sqrt2}\subseteq\Oz$, which also contains $\omega^{\sqrt2-1}\notin A_2$; the identity
$\omega^{\sqrt2}=\omega\cdot\omega^{\sqrt2-1}$ is the extra intersection element, and the two arithmetic quotients have flat
dimensions $2$ and $1$. Replacing $(\Z,\R)$ by $(\Z[i],\C)$ gives the same example in $\GOz$.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Flat dimension one is a property of the cone \merge]\label{osq:hd:rem:reconcile}
The report now contains two kinds of statements about the flat dimension of the arithmetic quotient, and they concern
different rings.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\fd_AD=1$ holds whenever (H1)--(H3) hold: the tail is a directed union of principal monomial ideals, because the
positive exponents form the positive cone of a totally ordered group and every family of tails of the relevant size
(finite for finite supports, of fewer than $\kappa$ or countably many elements in the constructions, a set for the class ring)
has a common monomial divisor in the ring. This covers the five constructions of \cref{osq:sec:models}
(\cref{osq:thm:homological}), including 06's ring $A^{06}_\kappa$; the full omnific ring in the two-universe reading, where
13 proves that the tail is flat, idempotent and not generated by a family from the smaller universe, that
$\Tor_{>0}(D,D)=0$ and that $D$ is not flat, so $\fd D=1$; 14's $A_0$; and 12's $T_\Gamma$
(\cref{osq:hd:thm:orderedcone}).
\item For the coordinatewise cone $\Q_{\ge0}^d$ the flat dimension is $d$ (\cref{osq:hd:cor:fd}): under the embedding, with
$\gamma_1<\gamma_2$, the quotient $\omega^{\epsilon(\gamma_2-\gamma_1)}$ of $X_2^\epsilon$ by $X_1^\epsilon$ lies in $\Oz$ but not in
$A_d$, so the tail of $A_d$ is not a directed union of principal ideals; it is a sum of $d$ flat ideals that is not flat for
$d\ge2$. (Status (batch 34): 26 proves $\fd D=d$ for the core of every pointed full-dimensional rational polyhedral cone of dimension $d$, and that
its passage to a total-order core, or to $\Oz$, is not flat for $d\ge2$; \cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti,osq:pc:thm:nonflat}.)
\end{itemize}
So ``flat dimension one'' must never be asserted for an arbitrary subring of $\Oz$: $A_d\subseteq T_\Gamma\subseteq\Oz$, with all exponents
in one Archimedean class, have flat dimensions $d$ and $1$, and $A_d\to T_\Gamma$ is not flat. Being a subring of a ring with small
quotient flat dimension imposes no bound on the subring, and conversely these core calculations do not transfer homological
dimensions to the full class ring $\Oz$. The separate flat-dimension-one
assertion for that class ring uses the two-universe interpretation
described above; it does not follow from the embeddings of the cores. The projective dimension of $D$ behaves differently
again: under (H1)--(H3) it is $2$ when the tail is countably generated, in particular for $T_\Gamma$, and is otherwise known only
to be at least~$2$; for $A_d$ it is $d+1$, one more than the flat dimension (\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}, with 21's
\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd}; before 21 it was known only to be $d$ or $d+1$).
\end{remark}

\subsection{The tensor normal form}\label{osq:tn:sub:tensor}

For the rest of this section (14) fix $(D,k)=(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$, and let $(A,\Pi,B)$ be either the class rings
$(\A_{D,k},\Pi_k,\A_{k,k})$, that is $A=\Oz$ or $\GOz$, or the set-sized model $(T_\Q,\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Q,k+\Pi^{\mathrm{fin}}_\Q)$
with $T_\Q=A_0$. Coefficient lattices are those of Setting (L).
The tensor and power results in this subsection hold in both cases (14).
Their proofs use Setting (L), the principal-ideal property of $D$, and the fact that every
$u\in\Pi$ is a product $u=ca$ with $c,a\in\Pi$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}(ii); in $T_\Q$ split off a smaller monomial). This
interface is 14's proposal for a formalization (\cref{osq:sub:formalization}). For the class rings a tensor product means an
explicit carrier with the balanced universal property proved by finite identities (for two lattices,
$\Pi\times(M\otimes_DN)$); no quotient of a proper class by a class relation and no class colimit is used (14).

Here $MN$ denotes the $D$-span of the products $mn$, not just the
set of individual products. It is nonzero and finitely generated inside
$k$, hence free over the principal ideal domain $D$; thus $L(MN)$
is again defined. In a class universal property the target is any fixed
class $A$-module $W$ equipped with a specified map. The proof gives
one explicit factorization into $W$ and proves uniqueness for that map;
it does not form a class of all class modules. Maps called balanced below
are biadditive and satisfy
$b(ax,y)=a\,b(x,y)=b(x,ay)$. The finite formulas also apply to the
ordinary tensor products in the set-sized model.

\begin{lemma}[Absorption \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:lem:absorption}
For every lattice $N$ and $0\ne n_0\in N$, multiplication is an isomorphism $\Pi\otimes_AL(N)\cong\Pi$ with inverse
$u\mapsto(u/n_0)\otimes n_0$; indeed $u\otimes v=(uv/n_0)\otimes n_0$ for $u\in\Pi$, $v\in L(N)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Multiplication maps $\Pi\times L(N)$ to $\Pi$, since $L(N)\subset B$
and $\Pi$ is an ideal of $B$, and is $A$-bilinear. Its proposed
inverse is defined because $u/n_0\in\Pi$ for every $u\in\Pi$.
It is $A$-linear in $u$, and multiplication after this inverse is the
identity.

To prove the other composition, write $u=ca$ with $c,a\in\Pi$.
This includes $u=0$, for which the desired identity is already zero.
For $v\in L(N)$, scalar stability gives $v/n_0\in B$, so
$b=a(v/n_0)\in\Pi\subseteq A$. Only elements of $A$ are moved
between the tensor factors in the calculation
\[
 u\otimes v=c\otimes av
 =c\otimes bn_0=cb\otimes n_0
 =(uv/n_0)\otimes n_0.
\]
In particular this does not move the possibly nonintegral scalar
$v/n_0$ across a tensor sign. Pure tensors generate by finite sums,
so the identity proves that the two maps are inverse. It also shows
that changing the auxiliary choice $n_0$ does not change the inverse
of multiplication.

For the class interpretation, let $b':\Pi\times L(N)\to W$ be
any specified balanced map. Define
$H(u)=b'(u/n_0,n_0)$. This is $A$-linear, and the same sequence
of balancing identities gives $b'(u,v)=H(uv)$. Multiplication is
onto, since $u=(u/n_0)n_0$, so this factorization is unique.
Thus the explicit carrier $\Pi$ has the required universal property
without first constructing a quotient of a class of formal tensors.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact tensor normal form \src{14; 17}]\label{osq:tn:thm:tensor}
The map $\beta$ of \cref{osq:tn:prop:nonflat} is an $A$-module isomorphism $L(M)\otimes_AL(N)\cong\mathsf E(M,N)$. Multiplication
corresponds to $(u,t)\mapsto u+\mathsf m_{M,N}(t)$, and there is an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal T(M,N)\longrightarrow L(M)\otimes_AL(N)\longrightarrow L(MN)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \mathcal T(M,N)=\ker\bigl(M\otimes_DN\to MN\bigr),
\]
with $\mathcal T(M,N)$ embedded as $(0,\mathcal T(M,N))$. This is exactly the $A$-torsion submodule; if it is nonzero its annihilator is
exactly $\Pi$, and $\rk_D\mathcal T(M,N)=\rk M\cdot\rk N-\rk(MN)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\mu=\mathsf m_{M,N}$ and choose $0\ne n_0\in N$.
In the ordinary tensor product define
$j(w)=(w/n_0)\otimes n_0$ for $w\in\Pi$, and let
$s:M\otimes_DN\to L(M)\otimes_AL(N)$ be the $D$-linear map
induced by the constant inclusions. Then
\[
 \beta(j(w))=(w,0),\qquad \beta(s(t))=(0,t).
\]
Consequently $\beta\psi=1$ for $\psi(u,t)=j(u)+s(t)$.
For the other composition expand
$(m+u)\otimes(n+v)$. The terms $u\otimes n$ and $u\otimes v$
become $j(un)$ and $j(uv)$ by absorption. For the remaining mixed
term, factor $v=ca$ with $c,a\in\Pi$. Balancing gives
$m\otimes v=cm\otimes a$, whose first factor is in $\Pi$,
so absorption gives $j(mv)$. The constant term is $s(m\otimes_Dn)$.
Hence $\psi\beta$ is the identity on pure tensors and thus on
every finite tensor sum. Since $\beta$ is $A$-linear, its inverse
$\psi$ is $A$-linear too; the constant map $s$ by itself is only
asserted to be $D$-linear.

We verify the class universal property explicitly as well. For a fixed
balanced map $b:L(M)\times L(N)\to W$, put
$j_b(w)=b(w/n_0,n_0)$ and let $s_b:M\otimes_DN\to W$ be
induced by the restriction of $b$ to the two constant lattices.
This latter map uses the finite free $D$-tensor basis, so it is defined
by finite sums even when $W$ is a class module. Define
\[
 H(u,t)=j_b(u)+s_b(t).
\]
Absorption proves $j_b$ is $A$-linear. For $h\in\Pi$, first
on $t=m\otimes_Dn$ and then by addition, it also gives
\[
 h\,s_b(t)=j_b(h\mu(t)).
\]
Together with $D$-linearity of $s_b$, this is exactly the cross term
needed for $H((d+h)\cdot(u,t))=(d+h)H(u,t)$ under
\eqref{osq:tn:eq:action}. The four-term expansion just used gives
$H\beta(x,y)=b(x,y)$. Finally the elements $(w,0)$ are the images
of $(w/n_0,n_0)$, and $(0,m\otimes_Dn)$ are the images of
$(m,n)$. They generate every pair by finite sums, so a factorization
must have the displayed values and is unique. This proves the claimed
universal property directly on $\mathsf E(M,N)$.

Multiplication is $(u,t)\mapsto u+\mu(t)$ under the normal form.
Its image is $\Pi+MN=L(MN)$. If $u+\mu(t)=0$, the first term
lies in $\Pi$ and the second in $k$; their intersection is zero,
so $u=0$ and $\mu(t)=0$. This proves exactness and identifies the
kernel with $(0,\mathcal T(M,N))$. Its $A$-action is
$(d+h)(0,t)=(0,dt)$, so $\Pi$ annihilates it. Since $\Pi$
contains a nonzero monomial, every element of this kernel is
$A$-torsion. Conversely, any torsion element maps to zero in the
submodule $L(MN)$ of a field, which is torsion free over the domain
$A$. The kernel is therefore exactly the torsion submodule.

The $D$-module $M\otimes_DN$ is finite free, so its submodule
$\mathcal T(M,N)$ is finite free as well. If it is nonzero, no
nonzero $d\in D$ annihilates it. The formula for its action then
shows that its annihilator in $A$ is precisely $\Pi$. If the kernel
is zero its annihilator is all of $A$, which explains the qualification
in the statement. Finally the surjection of finite free $D$-modules
$M\otimes_DN\to MN$ gives
$\rk_D\mathcal T(M,N)=\rk M\,\rk N-\rk(MN)$ by tensoring
with $\Frac(D)$ and taking dimensions.
\end{proof}

For $M=D+D\alpha$ with $\alpha\notin\Frac D$, the tensor
$\tau=1\otimes\alpha-\alpha\otimes1$ is nonzero and is killed
by every $h\in\Pi$. If $\alpha^2=c\in D$, write a constant
tensor in the ordered basis
$1\otimes1,1\otimes\alpha,\alpha\otimes1,\alpha\otimes\alpha$
with coefficients $(a,b,e,f)\in D^4$. Its product is
$(a+cf)+(b+e)\alpha$, which vanishes exactly when $a=-cf$ and
$e=-b$. Thus it equals
$b\tau+f(\alpha\otimes\alpha-c(1\otimes1))$, and these two
generators are independent by their displayed coordinates. This proves
the stated quadratic basis, not just its rank (14).
Manuscript~17 proves the exact sequence and the torsion statement independently over its set-sized models, as a consequence of
its $\Tor$ identification (\cref{osq:rel:thm:tor}).
Here ``torsion'' means $A$-torsion. The kernel is free over $D$
and hence is also free as an abelian group in both the integer and
Gaussian cases (14). Its annihilation by tails is compatible with the
absence of ordinary-integer torsion.

\begin{proposition}[Several factors \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:prop:higher}
For lattices $M_1,\dots,M_n$, $\bigotimes_{j,A}L(M_j)\cong\Pi\oplus\bigotimes_{j,D}M_j$ with the action \eqref{osq:tn:eq:action} for
the $n$-fold product map; the torsion is its kernel, killed by $\Pi$. For equal factors, permutations act trivially on the first
coordinate and by permuting tensor factors on the second.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First let $n\ge1$, put $T_n=\bigotimes_{j,D}M_j$, and let
$\mu_n:T_n\to k$ be the product map. On $\Pi\oplus T_n$ use
\[
 (d+h)\cdot(u,t)=((d+h)u+h\mu_n(t),dt).
\]
The associativity computation of \cref{osq:tn:prop:nonflat} applies
to any $D$-linear $\mu_n$. Define on a tuple $x_j=m_j+u_j$ the map
\[
 \beta_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=
 \left(\prod_jx_j-\prod_jm_j,\ \bigotimes_{j,D}m_j\right).
\]
The first coordinate is in $\Pi$, since expansion removes the
all-constant term. This map is additive in each slot. Multiplying one
slot by $d+h$ multiplies its constant part by $d$; the first
coordinate becomes
$(d+h)\prod_jx_j-d\prod_jm_j$. This is exactly the first
coordinate of $(d+h)\cdot\beta_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, proving
$A$-multilinearity.

Choose $0\ne c_j\in M_j$ and define
\[
 j_n(w)=\frac{w}{c_2\cdots c_n}\otimes c_2\otimes\cdots\otimes c_n,
 \qquad \psi_n(u,t)=j_n(u)+s_n(t),
\]
where $s_n$ is induced by the constant inclusions. For $n=1$ the
empty denominator is $1$, $j_1(w)=w$, and the formula is simply
$L(M_1)=\Pi+M_1$. The map $j_n$ is $A$-linear; $s_n$ is initially
only $D$-linear.

For $n\ge2$, every term in the expansion of a pure tensor either
has all factors constant or contains a tail. If a tail lies in a
slot other than the first, write it as $ab$ with $a,b\in\Pi$
and move the scalar $a\in A$ to the first slot. That first factor
is now in $\Pi$, since $aL(M_1)\subseteq\Pi$. With a tail in
the first slot, apply absorption to that slot and slot $j$, for
$j=2,\ldots,n$, replacing the latter by $c_j$ and multiplying the
first by the old factor divided by $c_j$. The first slot stays in
$\Pi$. The result is $j_n$ of the product of the original factors.
Thus every term with a tail reduces to its product, and the
all-constant term is $s_n$ of its $D$-tensor. This proves
$\psi_n\beta_n=1$, while the definitions give
$\beta_n j_n(w)=(w,0)$ and $\beta_n s_n(t)=(0,t)$.

For a specified class-valued $A$-multilinear map, the same reductions
define its factorization: replace the displayed tensors in $j_n$ and
$s_n$ by values of that map, extended on the finite free $D$-basis
of $T_n$. The identity $h s_n(t)=j_n(h\mu_n(t))$ verifies
$A$-linearity of the factorization, exactly as in the two-factor
proof. The values on $(w,0)$ and constant pure tensors force
uniqueness. Hence no iteration of a class quotient is needed.

Multiplication is $(u,t)\mapsto u+\mu_n(t)$, with image
$L(M_1\cdots M_n)$, where the product lattice is the $D$-span
of all products. Its kernel is $(0,\ker\mu_n)$ because
$\Pi\cap k=0$. The same annihilation and torsion-free-image
argument as before identifies it with the full $A$-torsion.
For equal factors, the two products in the first coordinate of
$\beta_n$ are unchanged by permutation; only the order in the
$D$-tensor coordinate changes. This proves the permutation assertion.
With the empty-family convention, the case $n=0$ reads
$A\cong\Pi\oplus D$ with its usual multiplication action and
zero torsion, separately from the positive-factor construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exterior and symmetric powers \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:thm:powers}
Let $r=\rk M$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $j\ge2$, $\bigwedge^j_AL(M)\cong\bigwedge^j_DM$ with $A$ acting through $\ct$: a free $D$-module of rank $\binom rj$ with
annihilator $\Pi$ when nonzero.
\item For $n\ge1$, $\operatorname{Sym}^n_AL(M)\cong\Pi\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^n_DM$ with the action \eqref{osq:tn:eq:action} for the
product map $\mathsf m_n:\operatorname{Sym}^n_DM\to k$; the product map has image $L(M^n)$ ($M^n$ the $D$-span of $n$-fold products) and
torsion kernel $\ker\mathsf m_n$, of rank $\binom{r+n-1}n-\rk(M^n)$, annihilated by $\Pi$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) We first show that every wedge of at least two factors containing
a tail vanishes. If the other factor is a nonzero constant $m\in M$,
then $u/m\in\Pi\subset A$ and
$u\wedge m=(u/m)(m\wedge m)=0$. If both factors $u,v$ are
tails, choose any $0\ne m_0\in M$ and write them as
$(u/m_0)m_0$ and $(v/m_0)m_0$, with both scalars in $A$.
Their wedge is again zero. A zero factor gives zero directly.
Expanding the remaining factors into constants and tails proves the
claim in every degree $j\ge2$.

It follows that every wedge is represented by constants and that
$\Pi$ acts by zero: multiplying a constant wedge by a tail puts a
tail in its first slot. The constant inclusion therefore induces an
$A$-linear surjection from $\bigwedge_D^j M$, inflated through
$\ct$, onto $\bigwedge_A^j L(M)$. In the other direction use
\[
 (x_1,\ldots,x_j)\longmapsto
 \ct(x_1)\wedge_D\cdots\wedge_D\ct(x_j),
\]
where $\ct(m+u)=m$ on $L(M)$. This map is alternating and
$A$-multilinear into the inflated target, because
$\ct(ax)=\ct(a)\ct(x)$. It is inverse on constant wedges;
the preceding expansion makes the other composition the identity.
For a class target, every alternating multilinear map has the same
tail-vanishing identities. It consequently factors uniquely through
this finite free $D$-exterior carrier, which proves the class
universal property directly.

If $m_1,\ldots,m_r$ is a basis of $M$, the wedges with strictly
increasing indices form a basis of $\bigwedge_D^jM$. Their number
is $\binom rj$ \cite[Section~10.13]{StacksTensor}; for $j>r$ the
module is zero. When it is nonzero, its action through $D$ and its
$D$-freeness make the annihilator exactly $\Pi$. The exclusion of
$j=1$ matters: the first exterior power is $L(M)$ itself and retains
its tail.

(ii) Put $T_n=M^{\otimes_D n}$ and let $R_n$ be the $D$-submodule
generated by all $t-\sigma t$ for permutations $\sigma$.
Then $T_n/R_n=\operatorname{Sym}_D^nM$. By the preceding
proposition, permutation differences in the $A$-tensor power have
the form $(0,t-\sigma t)$. Their product in $k$ is zero, so their
$A$-multiples are
\[
 (d+h)\cdot(0,t-\sigma t)=(0,d(t-\sigma t)).
\]
Thus the entire relation submodule is exactly $0\oplus R_n$.
In particular it imposes no relation on the tail coordinate, and the
quotient is $\Pi\oplus\operatorname{Sym}_D^nM$ with the stated
coupled action. In the class case this is the explicit carrier:
the quotient by $R_n$ is taken only in the set-sized finite free
$D$-module $T_n$. The multilinear factorization just proved descends
to this carrier precisely when the map is symmetric, which verifies
its universal property without a quotient of a proper class.

Multiplication has image $\Pi+M^n=L(M^n)$ and kernel
$(0,\ker\mathsf m_n)$, again by $\Pi\cap k=0$. This kernel is
killed by $\Pi$ and is exactly the $A$-torsion, because the image
lies in a field and $\Pi$ contains a nonzero element. The monomials
$m_1^{a_1}\cdots m_r^{a_r}$ with $a_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i a_i=n$
form a basis of the ordinary symmetric power; there are
$\binom{r+n-1}{n}$ of them. The product lattice $M^n$ is nonzero
and finite free over $D$. Tensoring its surjective product map with
$\Frac(D)$ therefore gives the asserted kernel rank. For $n=1$
the kernel is zero and the formula reduces to $L(M)$; for $n=0$
the usual symmetric power is $A$, outside the displayed range.
\end{proof}

For each $r\ge2$, choose an integer coefficient lattice of rank
$r$, for example the span of $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{r-1}$ for a
transcendental real $\theta$, and scale its module by a positive monomial to obtain a rank-one
ideal of $\Oz$. Its $r$th exterior power is nonzero by (i), while
all its exterior powers above degree $r$ vanish. Thus the assertion
is a family of examples with arbitrarily large nonvanishing degree,
not one finitely generated ideal with nonzero exterior powers in every
degree. After passing to the fraction field, every exterior power of
degree at least two vanishes, in agreement with fraction-field rank
one: each element of the exterior carrier was already killed by a
nonzero tail (14).

\subsection{Rees equations}\label{osq:tn:sub:rees}

Write $F=\Frac(A)$. The Rees algebra of the fractional module $L(M)$ is
\[
 \mathcal R(L(M))=A\oplus\bigoplus_{n\ge1}L(M)^nT^n
 \subseteq F[T].
\]
Here $T$ records the grading; it is independent of the monomial $X^e$
used to place $L(M)$ inside $A$. The powers are finite sums of
products. In fact $L(M)L(N)=L(MN)$: expanding products gives one
inclusion, products of constants span $MN$, and any $u\in\Pi$ is
$m_0(u/m_0)$ for a fixed nonzero $m_0\in M$, with $u/m_0\in\Pi$.
Thus $L(M)^n=M^n+\Pi$ for $n\ge1$.

For $e>0$, the degree-$n$ map $uT^n\mapsto X^{ne}uT^n$,
with the identity in degree zero, identifies this algebra with the
Rees algebra of $J_e(M)$ \cite[Tag~052P]{StacksRees}.
The exponents add under multiplication, so this is a graded
$A$-algebra isomorphism. The module isomorphism
$L(M)\to J_e(M)$ likewise induces a graded isomorphism of symmetric
algebras, compatible with their maps to the Rees algebras.
An ideal is \emph{of linear type} if
$\operatorname{Sym}\to\mathcal R$ is an isomorphism. Its
\emph{first nonlinear degree} is the least degree of a nonzero
element of this kernel, after the linear relations have been imposed
(14). The polynomial variables below are presentation variables,
distinct from the monomials in $A$.

\begin{theorem}[All nonlinear Rees equations are arithmetic \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:thm:rees}
Let $m_1,\dots,m_r$ be a basis of $M$ and $\mathfrak q_M=\ker\bigl(D[X_1,\dots,X_r]\to k[T],\ X_i\mapsto m_iT\bigr)$. The
constant-coefficient map $D[X_1,\dots,X_r]\to\operatorname{Sym}_AL(M)$ is injective, and under it
$\ker(\operatorname{Sym}_AL(M)\to\mathcal R(L(M)))=\mathfrak q_M$; this is all the $A$-torsion of the symmetric algebra, it is killed
by $\Pi$, and it is generated by any set of homogeneous generators of $\mathfrak q_M$, finitely many of which suffice. With
$\mathfrak l_M=\bigl(hX_j-\tfrac{m_j}{m_1}hX_1:h\in\Pi,\ 2\le j\le r\bigr)\subseteq A[X_1,\dots,X_r]$,
\[
 \operatorname{Sym}_AL(M)\cong A[\mathbf X]/\mathfrak l_M,\qquad
 \mathcal R(L(M))\cong A[\mathbf X]/(\mathfrak l_M+\mathfrak q_MA[\mathbf X]).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The linear relations of the generator map are those of
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii). They give the usual symmetric-algebra
presentation \cite[Tag~00DM]{StacksTensor}. We verify the presentation
by a finite reduction, which also explains its meaning for the class
rings in Setting~(L).

Put $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}^n_DM$ and let
$\mathsf m_n:S_n\to M^n$ be multiplication. By
\cref{osq:tn:thm:powers}(ii), the positive-degree carrier is
$G_n=\Pi\oplus S_n$; put $G_0=A$. Elements of the graded carrier
are finite sequences of these components. For $n,m\ge1$, its
multiplication is
\[
 (u,t)(v,s)=
 \bigl(uv+u\mathsf m_m(s)+v\mathsf m_n(t),\ ts\bigr)
 \in G_{n+m}.
\]
Degree zero acts by the coupled $A$-action already established.
The identity $\mathsf m_{n+m}(ts)=\mathsf m_n(t)\mathsf m_m(s)$
verifies associativity by expansion, and the formula agrees with
products of symmetric tensors. Thus it realizes the symmetric algebra
on an explicit carrier, also when $\Pi$ is a proper class.

Send $X_i$ to $(0,m_i)\in G_1$. For a homogeneous polynomial $P$
of positive degree $n$, split each coefficient into its ordinary
constant and its tail, writing $P=P_0+P_\Pi$. Modulo
$\mathfrak l_M$, every tail monomial reduces to
\[
 hX_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_n}
 \equiv h\frac{m_{i_1}\cdots m_{i_n}}{m_1^n}X_1^n.
\]
Indeed, replace one variable at a time using a defining linear
relation; every new coefficient remains in $\Pi$, since $\Pi$ is
a $k$-vector space. Consequently
$P\equiv P_0+(u/m_1^n)X_1^n$, where
$u=P_\Pi(m_1,\ldots,m_r)\in\Pi$. Its image in $G_n$ is
$(u,t_{P_0})$, with $t_{P_0}$ the element of $S_n$ represented by
$P_0$. The ordinary symmetric monomials form a $D$-basis, so this
image vanishes exactly when $P_0=0$ and $u=0$. Every $(u,t)\in G_n$
has such a representative. In degree zero the map is the identity
of $A$. This proves the first presentation and the injection of
$D[\mathbf X]$ degree by degree. For class rings, the displayed
quotient notation denotes this explicit carrier and kernel
description; no quotient of a proper class is needed.

In positive degree the map to the Rees algebra is
$(u,t)\mapsto u+\mathsf m_n(t)$. Since $\Pi\cap k=0$, its kernel
is exactly $(0,\ker\mathsf m_n)$. Under the constant-polynomial
injection this is the degree-$n$ part of $\mathfrak q_M$.
The latter ideal is homogeneous because $X_i\mapsto m_iT$ preserves
degrees. It has no degree-zero or degree-one part, by injectivity
of $D\to k$ and independence of the basis of $M$.

Every kernel element is killed by $\Pi$. Conversely, any
$A$-torsion element maps to zero because $F[T]$ is torsion-free
over $A$. A fixed nonzero element of $\Pi$ kills the whole kernel,
so the kernel is precisely all the $A$-torsion. Moreover, the action
of $A[\mathbf X]$ on it factors through the coefficientwise map
$\operatorname{ct}:A[\mathbf X]\to D[\mathbf X]$. Therefore any
homogeneous ideal generators of $\mathfrak q_M$ generate the Rees
kernel as an ideal of the symmetric algebra. The ring
$D[\mathbf X]$ is Noetherian, so a finite subfamily suffices.
Taking the inverse image of this kernel in $A[\mathbf X]$ gives
$\mathfrak l_M+\mathfrak q_MA[\mathbf X]$, as asserted.
\end{proof}

The nonlinear kernel is finitely generated \emph{as an ideal of the
symmetric algebra}. This is not finite generation as an $A$-module.
In fact, if $0\ne q\in\mathfrak q_M$ is homogeneous, the elements
$qX_1^j$ remain nonzero in the symmetric algebra and have unbounded
degrees. Finitely many $A$-module generators have bounded degrees,
since $A$ acts in degree zero, and hence cannot generate this kernel.
For $r\ge2$, the linear relation module is itself not finitely
(set-) generated (\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}). These are statements
about different scalar actions, and neither gives a finite
presentation of $L(M)$ (14).

\begin{theorem}[The algebraic degree is the first nonlinear degree \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:thm:degree}
Let $\alpha\in k\setminus\Frac(D)$, $M=D+D\alpha$ and $J=(X^e,\alpha X^e)\subseteq A$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\alpha$ is transcendental over $\Frac(D)$, then $J$ is of linear type, although it is not flat and not finitely presented.
\item If $\alpha$ is algebraic of degree $d$ (necessarily $d\ge2$), let $f\in D[Z]$ be primitive irreducible with $f(\alpha)=0$ and
$F_f(X,Y)=X^df(Y/X)$. Then $\mathcal R(J)\cong A[X,Y]/\bigl(hY-\alpha hX\ (h\in\Pi),\ F_f(X,Y)\bigr)$; the kernel of
$\operatorname{Sym}_AJ\to\mathcal R(J)$ is generated by $F_f$, and the first nonlinear degree is exactly $d$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The ideal $\mathfrak q_M$ is homogeneous. For a homogeneous
$G(X,Y)$ of degree $n$, evaluation gives
$G(T,\alpha T)=T^nG(1,\alpha)$, so membership is equivalent to
$g(\alpha)=0$, where $g(Z)=G(1,Z)$ has degree at most $n$.
Dehomogenization is injective on this fixed homogeneous component:
the coefficient of $Z^i$ in $g$ is the coefficient of $X^{n-i}Y^i$
in $G$. Thus transcendence forces $G=0$ in every degree, and
$\mathfrak q_M=0$.

In the algebraic case, clearing denominators in the minimal
polynomial and removing its content gives the primitive $f$ of
degree $d$. It need not be monic; no integrality assumption on
$\alpha$ is required. For nonzero $G\in\mathfrak q_M$, the minimal
polynomial divides $g$ over $\Frac(D)$. Gauss's lemma over the
unique factorization domain $D$ gives $g=fh$ with $h\in D[Z]$.
In particular $n\ge d$ and $\deg h\le n-d$.

If $f(Z)=\sum_{i=0}^d f_iZ^i$, its homogenization means the
polynomial $F_f=\sum_{i=0}^d f_iX^{d-i}Y^i$. Similarly
$H=X^{n-d}h(Y/X)$ is a polynomial, because $\deg h\le n-d$.
Homogenizing the product identity gives $G=F_fH$ in $D[X,Y]$,
without inverting $X$. Conversely $F_f(1,\alpha)=0$, so
$\mathfrak q_M=(F_f)$. There is no nonzero component below degree
$d$, and $F_f$ is nonzero in degree $d$.

By \cref{osq:tn:thm:rees}, $F_f$ remains nonzero after imposing
the linear relations: the constant-polynomial map into the
symmetric algebra is injective. This proves the exact first
nonlinear degree, as well as the presentation. Monomial scaling
transfers the conclusion from $L(M)$ to $J$ and preserves grading.
Finally $1,\alpha$ form a $D$-basis, so nonflatness and failure of
finite presentation follow from
\cref{osq:tn:prop:nonflat,osq:tn:thm:syzygy} in both cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A family of every degree \src{14; 17}]\label{osq:tn:cor:alldegrees}
For $d\ge2$ let $J_d=(\omega,2^{1/d}\omega)\subseteq\Oz$. Then
$\mathcal R_{\Oz}(J_d)\cong\Oz[X,Y]/(hY-2^{1/d}hX\ (h\in\Pi),\ Y^d-2X^d)$, there is no nonlinear equation in degrees $2,\dots,d-1$, and
for $n\ge1$
\begin{gather*}
 \mu_{\Oz}(J_d^n)=\min(n+1,d),\qquad
 \rk_\Z\ker(\operatorname{Sym}^n_{\Oz}J_d\to J_d^n)=\max(0,n-d+1),\\
 \rk_\Z\ker(J_d^{\otimes n}\to J_d^n)=2^n-\min(n+1,d),
\end{gather*}
where $\mu$ is the least number of generators. All these kernels are killed by $\Pi$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $\alpha=2^{1/d}$ be the positive ordinary real root. The
polynomial $Z^d-2$ is Eisenstein at $2$: its nonleading
coefficients are divisible by $2$ and its constant coefficient is
not divisible by $4$. Thus $\alpha$ has degree exactly $d$ over $\Q$,
and \cref{osq:tn:thm:degree} gives the Rees presentation and first
nonlinear degree.

For $M=\Z+\Z\alpha$, products of $n$ basis elements give
\[
 M^n=\sum_{i=0}^n\Z\alpha^i
     =\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\min(n,d-1)}\Z\alpha^i.
\]
The second equality holds as integer lattices, not just after
tensoring with $\Q$: if $i=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$, then
$\alpha^i=2^q\alpha^r$, and the first $d$ powers are independent
over $\Q$. The product law gives
$J_d^n=\omega^n L(M^n)$. Its least number of generators is therefore
$\rk_\Z M^n=\min(n+1,d)$ by \cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(i).

The ordinary symmetric and tensor powers of the rank-two lattice
$M$ have ranks $n+1$ and $2^n$, respectively. Both product maps
surject onto $M^n$. Their kernel ranks are consequently
$n+1-\min(n+1,d)=\max(0,n-d+1)$ and
$2^n-\min(n+1,d)$, by
\cref{osq:tn:thm:powers}(ii) and \cref{osq:tn:prop:higher}.
The same results identify these ordinary kernels with the kernels
over $\Oz$ and show that $\Pi$ kills them. The $\Oz$-linear
isomorphism given by multiplication by $\omega$ transfers these
identifications to the tensor and symmetric powers of $J_d$.
For $n=1$ both kernels vanish. When $d=2$, the excluded range
$2,\ldots,d-1$ is empty and the first nonlinear equation is already
quadratic.
\end{proof}

For $d=5$ the two-generated ideal $(\omega,2^{1/5}\omega)$ has powers needing $2,3,4,5,5,\dots$ generators, a symmetric kernel of ranks
$0,0,0,0,1,2,\dots$, and a nonzero antisymmetric tensor already in its tensor square: symmetric and tensor obstructions occur at different
stages (14). Manuscript~17 proves the generator count $\min(n+1,d)$ independently, from the product law
$J_g(M)J_h(N)=J_{g+h}(MN)$, for every $\alpha$ of degree $d$ over $\Frac(D)$, and adds that it is $n+1$ for every $n$ when $\alpha$ is
transcendental; the lattices $M^n$ need not stabilize when their ranks do, and the count is not a reconstruction theorem (17).
For instance, for $\alpha=\sqrt2/2$ the lattice
$M=\Z+\Z\alpha$ has
$M^2=\tfrac12\Z+\Z\alpha$. Every $M^n$ has rank two for
$n\ge1$, but $\alpha^{2q}=2^{-q}$ supplies unbounded denominators,
so this increasing chain of lattices cannot eventually stabilize.

\subsection{Homomorphisms, ideal classes and duals}\label{osq:tn:sub:hom}

For lattices put $(N:M)=\{c\in k:cM\subseteq N\}$ and
$\mathfrak o(M)=(M:M)$. More generally, for nonzero $A$-submodules
$U,V$ of $F=\Frac(A)$, write
$(V:U)=\{q\in F:qU\subseteq V\}$. The lattice colon is restricted
to the ordinary coefficient field $k$; the module colon permits a
scalar in $F$. Below, $U^*=\Hom_A(U,A)$ is the algebraic $A$-dual,
with its natural $A$-module structure.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[Scalar homomorphisms and isomorphism types \src{14; 17}]\label{osq:tn:thm:hom}
Identifying a scalar with multiplication by it, $\Hom_A(L(M),L(N))=\Pi+(N:M)$, composition is multiplication, and
$L(M)\cong L(N)$ if and only if $N=cM$ for some $c\in k^\times$. Hence $\End_AL(M)=\Pi+\mathfrak o(M)$ and
$\operatorname{Aut}_AL(M)=\mathfrak o(M)^\times$. The ring $\mathfrak o(M)$ is finite free over $D$ and integral over $D$; in the real case
$\Q\,\mathfrak o(M)\subseteq\R$ is a number field of degree at most $\rk M$ (not necessarily totally real).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We first justify the scalar description for arbitrary nonzero
$A$-submodules $U,V\subseteq F$, including $\Pi$ and $B$.
Fix $0\ne u_0\in U$ and an $A$-linear map $\varphi:U\to V$.
For each $u\in U$, choose a nonzero $a\in A$ clearing the two
denominators, so $au_0,au\in A$. By $A$-linearity,
\[
 (au_0)\varphi(u)=\varphi((au_0)u)
 =\varphi((au)u_0)=(au)\varphi(u_0).
\]
Cancelling $au_0$ in $F$ gives
$\varphi(u)=qu$, where $q=\varphi(u_0)/u_0$ is independent of
$u$. Conversely every $q\in(V:U)$ defines such a map, uniquely.
This also includes the zero map, coded by $q=0$. For class modules,
each specified class map therefore has one scalar code; $\Hom$ is
realized by this explicit class of scalars, not by a collection of
arbitrary class functions. Addition and composition become scalar
addition and multiplication.

Now suppose $qL(M)\subseteq L(N)$ and choose $0\ne m_0\in M$.
Since $qm_0\in L(N)\subseteq B$ and $B$ is a $k$-algebra,
$q=(qm_0)/m_0\in B$. Write uniquely $q=c+h$ with $c\in k$,
$h\in\Pi$. For $m\in M$ and $v\in\Pi$,
\[
 (c+h)(m+v)=cm+(cv+hm+hv),
\]
and the parenthesized term lies in $\Pi$. Thus the required
inclusion is equivalent to $cM\subseteq N$, proving the formula
for $\Hom$ and, on taking $N=M$, for $\End$.

If the map is an isomorphism, its inverse is multiplication by
$q^{-1}$. Both scalars lie in $B$, so $q\in B^\times=k^\times$:
the leading-degree argument of \cref{osq:lem:units} applies both
to the full class ring and to the finite-support model. Hence an
isomorphism forces $N=qM$. Conversely any nonzero $c\in k$ with
$N=cM$ gives an isomorphism because $c\Pi=\Pi$.
The automorphisms are exactly the constants $c$ with
$cM=M$, equivalently $c,c^{-1}\in\mathfrak o(M)$.

The map $c\mapsto cm_0$ embeds $\mathfrak o(M)$ as a
$D$-submodule of the finite free module $M$. Since $D$ is a
principal ideal domain, this proves finite generation and freeness.
For $c\in\mathfrak o(M)$, multiplication by $c$ has a matrix over
$D$ on a basis of $M$. Its monic characteristic polynomial
annihilates this endomorphism by Cayley--Hamilton. Applying it to
$m_0\ne0$ shows that the same polynomial vanishes at $c$ in $k$,
proving integrality.

In the real case, $E=\Q\,\mathfrak o(M)$ is a finite-dimensional
$\Q$-algebra inside $\R$, and $c\mapsto cm_0$ embeds it in
$\Q M$, of dimension $\rk M$. Multiplication by a nonzero element
of $E$ is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector
space, hence surjective; its inverse image of $1$ is the
multiplicative inverse. Thus $E$ is a number field with the stated
degree bound.
\end{proof}

Manuscript~17 proves the $\Hom$, isomorphism and automorphism statements independently for $\Oz$ and $\GOz$ (for the ideals
$J_\gamma(M)$, with $\Hom_A(J_\gamma(M),J_\eta(N))=\omega^{\eta-\gamma}((N:M)+\Pi)$), and sharpens the degree bound: the field spanned
by $\mathfrak o(M)$ has degree dividing $\rk M$ (\cref{osq:rel:thm:order}).

The qualification ``not necessarily totally real'' is essential:
for $M=\Z[\sqrt[3]{2}]\subset\R$, the multiplier ring is $M$
itself, since $1\in M$ and $M$ is a ring. Its rational span
$\Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ has two nonreal embeddings, despite its chosen
embedding in $\R$.

For the next theorem and example only, specialize to the real case
$D=\Z$, $k=\R$. Let $K_0\subset\R$ be a number field and
$\mathfrak o\subset K_0$ an order, that is, a subring whose
additive group is a full integer lattice in $K_0$. An invertible
fractional $\mathfrak o$-ideal $P$ is a coefficient lattice:
it is finitely generated over $\mathfrak o$, hence over $\Z$,
and torsion-free inside $K_0$. Its rational span is $K_0$, since
$p\mathfrak o\subseteq P$ for any $0\ne p\in P$; thus its
integer rank is $[K_0:\Q]$.

For these modules put
$U\odot V=(U\otimes_AV)/(A\text{-torsion})$. By
\cref{osq:tn:thm:tensor}, multiplication realizes
$L(M)\odot L(N)$ as $L(MN)$: its kernel is exactly the torsion
and its image is $L(MN)$. In the class case this image is the
explicit carrier intended by the quotient notation.

\begin{theorem}[Ideal classes survive torsion-free multiplication \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:thm:pic}
$P\mapsto L(P)$ distinguishes exactly the ideal classes of invertible fractional $\mathfrak o$-ideals, and under $\odot$ these isomorphism
types form a group isomorphic to $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathfrak o)$ with identity $[L(\mathfrak o)]$. If $[K_0:\Q]\ge2$ this is not a subgroup of
$\operatorname{Pic}(A)$ and its identity is not $[A]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:tn:thm:hom}, $L(P)\cong L(Q)$ exactly when
$Q=cP$ for some $c\in\R^\times$. Choose $0\ne p\in P$.
Then $cp\in Q\subset K_0$, so $c=(cp)/p\in K_0^\times$.
This is precisely equality of the fractional-ideal classes in
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathfrak o)$; the reverse implication is
multiplication by $c$.

The product formula gives $L(P)\odot L(Q)\cong L(PQ)$.
Replacing $P,Q$ by $aP,bQ$ replaces $PQ$ by $abPQ$, so the
operation is well-defined on their isomorphism types. Associativity
and commutativity follow from fractional-ideal multiplication;
$\mathfrak oP=P$ gives the identity and $PP^{-1}=\mathfrak o$
gives the inverse. These statements prove the asserted group
isomorphism, including its identity.

Put $d=[K_0:\Q]$. Each $P$ has integer rank $d$, so
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(i) says that $L(P)$ needs exactly $d$
generators. If $d\ge2$, the nonflatness obstruction of
\cref{osq:tn:prop:nonflat} rules out invertibility over $A$:
an invertible module is finitely generated projective, hence flat
\cite[Tag~0AFW]{StacksPicard}.
For the class ring, invertibility would likewise give a finite
dual basis and hence the equational criterion contradicted there.
Moreover $L(\mathfrak o)$ needs $d\ge2$ generators whereas
$A=L(\Z)$ needs one, so these modules are not isomorphic.
Thus this realization of the ideal-class group does not take its
values in $\operatorname{Pic}(A)$.
\end{proof}

The group has its own idempotent identity inside the multiplicative
semigroup of lattice-module types: $L(\mathfrak o)\odot
L(\mathfrak o)\cong L(\mathfrak o)$. When $[K_0:\Q]\ge2$ this
identity differs from the semigroup identity $A$. In the class setting, choose ordinary
fractional-ideal representatives indexed by the set
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathfrak o)$ and apply $P\mapsto P+\Pi$.
The scalar criterion and product formula express the group law on
this indexed family without forming a collection of all class
modules (14).

\begin{example}[A class of order two \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:ex:sqrt10}
In $K_0=\Q(\sqrt{10})$ with $\mathfrak o=\Z+\Z\sqrt{10}$ let $P=2\Z+\Z\sqrt{10}$. It is an $\mathfrak o$-ideal, $P^2=4\Z+2\sqrt{10}\,\Z+10\Z=2\mathfrak o$,
so $P$ is invertible. It is not principal: $P=c\,\mathfrak o$ with $c=a+b\sqrt{10}\in P$ would give $|a^2-10b^2|=[\mathfrak o:P]=2$, impossible
modulo $5$. Hence $L(P)\not\cong L(\mathfrak o)$ and $L(P)\odot L(P)\cong L(\mathfrak o)$; both have rank one and need two generators, and the
tensor square of $L(P)$ has torsion of rank $4-2=2$. As ideals, $\omega L(P)=(2\omega,\sqrt{10}\,\omega)$ and
$\omega L(\mathfrak o)=(\omega,\sqrt{10}\,\omega)$.
\end{example}

To spell out the arithmetic in the example, multiplication by
$\sqrt{10}$ sends the generators $2,\sqrt{10}$ of $P$ to
$2\sqrt{10},10\in P$, so $P$ is an $\mathfrak o$-ideal.
The constants $4$ and $10$ generate $2\Z$, giving
$P^2=2\mathfrak o$ and the explicit inverse $P^{-1}=\tfrac12P$.
If $P=c\mathfrak o$, then $c\in P\subset\mathfrak o$, since
$1\in\mathfrak o$. For $c=a+b\sqrt{10}$, multiplication on the
basis $1,\sqrt{10}$ has matrix
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&10b\\b&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.
Its determinant has absolute value
$[\mathfrak o:c\mathfrak o]=[\mathfrak o:P]=2$.
But $a^2-10b^2\equiv a^2\pmod5$ cannot be $2$ or $-2$, since
the squares modulo $5$ are $0,1,4$. This proves nonprincipality
and hence exact order two of the ideal class. The rank-one assertion
is over $\Frac(A)$; the rank-two torsion assertion is over $\Z$.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
We now return to both coefficient pairs $(D,k)$ fixed above.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform duals \src{14}]\label{osq:tn:thm:duals}
$(A:\Pi)=B$ and $(A:B)=\Pi$ (in both cases of this subsection). For a lattice $M$ of rank at least two,
$L(M)^*=\Hom_A(L(M),A)=\Pi$, $L(M)^{**}=B$, the canonical bidual map is the inclusion $L(M)\hookrightarrow B$, and $B/L(M)\cong k/M$ with
$A$ acting through $\ct$. Moreover $\Pi^*=B$, $B^*=\Pi$, $\Pi^{**}=\Pi$, $B^{**}=B$, and $J_e(M)^*=X^{-e}\Pi$, $J_e(M)^{**}=X^eB$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The scalar argument in \cref{osq:tn:thm:hom} identifies the dual
of any nonzero $A$-submodule $U\subseteq F$ with $(A:U)$.
First suppose $q\Pi\subseteq A$. Since $X^1\in\Pi$,
$qX^1\in A$, and $q=X^{-1}(qX^1)$ has the corresponding
shifted normal form. In the model $T_\Q$ this proves, before
inspecting exponents, that $q$ has finite rational support;
an arbitrary rational function need not have that property.
If a nonzero coefficient of $q$ occurred at a negative exponent
$\gamma$, choose $0<\delta<-\gamma$ in the same exponent group
(for example $\delta=-\gamma/2$). The coefficient at
$\gamma+\delta<0$ of $qX^\delta$ would be unchanged and nonzero,
contradicting $qX^\delta\in A$. Thus $q$ has only nonnegative
exponents and belongs to $B$. Conversely $B\Pi\subseteq\Pi$
because $\Pi$ is an ideal of $B$. This proves $(A:\Pi)=B$.

If $qB\subseteq A$, then $q=q\cdot1\in A$, so write
$q=d+u$ with $d\in D$ and $u\in\Pi$. Testing all constants
$c\in k\subset B$ gives $dc\in D$. If $d\ne0$, taking
$c=1/(2d)$ would give $1/2\in D$, impossible for either
$D=\Z$ or $D=\Z[i]$. Hence $d=0$ and $q\in\Pi$.
The reverse inclusion is again $\Pi B\subseteq\Pi$, proving
$(A:B)=\Pi$. In particular $\Pi^*=B$ and $B^*=\Pi$.

For a lattice, \cref{osq:tn:thm:hom} gives
$L(M)^*=\Pi+(D:M)$. A nonzero $c\in(D:M)$ would give an
injective $D$-linear map $M\to D$, contradicting $\rk_D M\ge2$
after tensoring with $\Frac(D)$. Thus $(D:M)=0$, the first dual
is $\Pi$, and the second is $B$. Under these scalar
identifications, evaluation at $x\in L(M)$ sends the functional
with scalar $u\in\Pi$ to $ux$. Its scalar code in
$\Hom_A(\Pi,A)=B$ is therefore $x$ itself. This proves that the
canonical bidual map is the stated inclusion. The same evaluation
calculation for $\Pi$ and $B$ gives their displayed bidual
identities and proves both modules reflexive.

The surjective map $B\to k/M$ given by $c+h\mapsto c+M$
has kernel $L(M)$. For $a=d+v\in A$, its value on $a(c+h)$
is $dc+M$, so the $A$-action on $k/M$ is through
$\ct:A\to D$. This is an additive module quotient; no ring
structure on $k/M$ is asserted. In the class case the ordinary
set-sized module $k/M$ explicitly realizes the displayed quotient.

Finally, for $0\ne t\in F$ and $U\subseteq F$,
$(tU)^*=t^{-1}U^*$, since $q(tU)\subseteq A$ is equivalent to
$qt\in U^*$. Applying this twice with $t=X^e$ gives
$J_e(M)^*=X^{-e}\Pi$ and $J_e(M)^{**}=X^eB$.
\end{proof}

The rank restriction matters: if $M=Dm$ has rank one, then
$L(M)=mA$, its dual is $m^{-1}A$, and its bidual is $mA$.
For rank at least two, the two nonisomorphic modules of
\cref{osq:tn:ex:sqrt10} have the same dual and reflexive hull.
Their difference is retained by the coefficient lattice but lost
under double dualization (14).

\begin{theorem}[Common-scale constant matrices \src{14; 17}]\label{osq:tn:thm:matrix}
Let $C\in k^{m\times n}$, $e>0$, $W=\ker_kC$, $q=\dim_kW$, $W_D=W\cap D^n$ and $\ell=\rk_DW_D$. Then
$\ker_A(X^eC)\cong A^\ell\oplus\Pi^{q-\ell}$. The image of $X^eC:A^n\to A^m$ is finitely presented if and only if $\ell=q$, that is,
if and only if $W$ is defined over $\Frac(D)$, and it is then free of rank $n-q$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All entries of $X^eC$ belong to $\Pi\subseteq A$, and the
nonzero common scalar $X^e$ does not change the kernel. Decompose
$x\in A^n$ uniquely as $x=d+u$ with $d\in D^n$ and $u\in\Pi^n$.
Because $Cd$ is constant and $Cu$ is a tail vector,
$Cx=0$ is equivalent to the two equations $Cd=0$ and $Cu=0$.

The submodule $W_D\subseteq D^n$ is saturated: if
$0\ne a\in D$ and $av\in W_D$, then $aCv=0$ in $k^m$,
so $Cv=0$. Hence $D^n/W_D$ is finitely generated and torsion-free
over the principal ideal domain $D$, and is free. The quotient
map therefore splits. Choose a $D$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_\ell$
of $W_D$ and extend it to a $D$-basis of $D^n$.
In particular these first vectors are $k$-independent; extend them
instead to a $k$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_q$ of $W$.

Gaussian elimination over $k$ gives
\[
 \{u\in\Pi^n:Cu=0\}
   =\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q h_jv_j:h_j\in\Pi\right\}.
\]
Indeed, the coordinates in this kernel basis are fixed $k$-linear
combinations of the coordinates of $u$, and hence remain in the
$k$-vector space $\Pi$. Independence remains valid over $F$,
as a nonzero $q$-rowed minor over $k$ remains nonzero in $F$.
Combining constants and tails now gives the explicit $A$-linear
isomorphism
\[
 A^\ell\oplus\Pi^{q-\ell}\longrightarrow\ker_A(X^eC),
 \qquad (a_1,\ldots,a_\ell,h_{\ell+1},\ldots,h_q)
 \longmapsto\sum_{j\le\ell}a_jv_j+\sum_{j>\ell}h_jv_j.
\]
The decomposition above proves surjectivity and the independence
proves injectivity. The construction uses only finite matrices and
also defines the class-module isomorphism.

If $q>\ell$, projection onto one tail coordinate shows that the
kernel is not finitely generated (and not set-generated in the
class case). This excludes every finite presentation of the image,
not just the displayed presentation \cite[Tag~0517]{StacksFiniteModules}. To see this, a hypothetical
finite presentation with finitely generated relation module $R$
and free module $A^a$ would, by the finite-free pullback argument
of Schanuel's lemma, give
\[
 \ker_A(X^eC)\oplus A^a\cong R\oplus A^n.
\]
The right side is finitely generated, so its direct summand
$\ker_A(X^eC)$ would be too. Only finitely many lifts of free
basis vectors are used, so the argument applies to the class
presentation as well.

If $q=\ell$, use the chosen extension of the $D$-basis of $W_D$
to a basis of $D^n$. After this invertible change of columns, the
first $q$ columns of $C$ are zero and the other $n-q$ are
independent over $k$, hence over $F$. Their multiples by $X^e$
form an $A$-basis of the image. Thus the image is free of rank
$n-q$ and in particular finitely presented.

Finally put $F_0=\Frac(D)$. Clearing the finitely many
denominators of a vector gives
$F_0W_D=W\cap F_0^n$. It follows that $\ell$ is the
$F_0$-dimension of this intersection. Equality $\ell=q$ is
therefore equivalent to $W$ having a basis over $k$ consisting
of vectors in $F_0^n$, which is the asserted meaning of ``defined
over $F_0$''. The formulas include $q=0$ (zero kernel) and
$C=0$ (kernel $A^n$ and zero image).
\end{proof}

The matrix theorem concerns constant matrices at one common monomial scale; several support levels need more analysis (14, 17).
Manuscript~17 proves it independently for $\Oz$ and $\GOz$ and adds that $\ell=\dim_{\Frac D}(W\cap\Frac(D)^n)$ (a nonzero vector of
$W\cap\Frac(D)^n$ has a common denominator in $D$), so that the kernel is set-generated exactly when $W$ is spanned by vectors over
$\Frac(D)$; its computation of $q$ and $\ell$ and the relation counts over the models are in \cref{osq:rel:sub:relations}. Its companion,
14's criterion that a point $[r_1:\dots:r_n]\in\mathbb P^{n-1}(k)$ has a unimodular representative in $A^n$ if and only if it is
$\Frac(D)$-rational, is in the real case the rationality theorem for primitive constant directions of the Diophantine report
\cite{RepoOdg}, which 14 does not credit (it credits only that report's example $[1:\sqrt2]$, to a companion manuscript); the Gaussian and
principal-ideal form is printed there with that theorem, not here.

\paragraph{The Gaussian case and the reach of the results (14).}
The tensor, power, Rees, scalar-homomorphism, dual and matrix results
above treat both $(D,k)=(\Z,\R)$ and $(\Z[i],\C)$.
Their proofs use the stated properties of these rings, including
the principal-ideal property of $D$, the common-factor property of
$\Pi$, and, for the scalar and dual descriptions, the support and
unit calculations in $B$. They are not consequences of the
principal-ideal hypothesis alone. Over
$\GOz=\Z[i]+\Pi_\C$, ranks are $\Z[i]$-ranks,
multiplication kernels are killed by $\Pi_\C$, and the degree in
\cref{osq:tn:thm:degree} is taken over $\Q(i)$.

For real algebraic $\alpha$, put $K_0=\Q(\alpha)\subset\R$.
Since $i\notin K_0$, the tower formula gives
$[K_0(i):\Q]=2[K_0:\Q]=2[K_0(i):\Q(i)]$.
Thus the degree of $\alpha$ over $\Q(i)$ equals its degree over
$\Q$. Consequently \cref{osq:tn:cor:alldegrees} holds over
$\GOz$ with the same ranks over $\Z[i]$; in particular
$(\omega,\sqrt2\,\omega)$ has the single nonlinear equation
$Y^2-2X^2$. The ideal-class argument also has a Gaussian version:
take an order over $\Z[i]$ in a finite extension of $\Q(i)$
inside $\C$, and replace its integer rank by its $\Z[i]$-rank.
The displayed $\Q(\sqrt{10})$ example above remains a real
example; no assertion that extending coefficients preserves its
nontrivial ideal class is needed.

Complex conjugation transports the construction for $M$ to that
for $\overline M$. These results concern the omnific \emph{rings}:
after extending scalars to their fraction fields, the modules become
vector spaces and the arithmetic torsion vanishes. They do not
classify arbitrary finitely generated omnific ideals, whose
generators may lie at several support levels.


\subsection{Relations, \texorpdfstring{$\Tor$}{Tor} and moduli of lattice ideals}\label{osq:rel:sub:relations}

This subsection is manuscript~17's new material; its results that repeat 12 and 14 are printed above, with 17 added to
their sources. As in \cref{osq:tn:sub:tensor}, $(D,k)$ is $(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$, so that $\Frac D$ is $\Q$ or $\Q(i)$; a
lattice is a coefficient lattice $M\subset k$ of Setting (L), of rank $r$, and $J_g(M)=X^gL(M)$. The class ring is $A=\A_{D,k}$,
that is $\Oz$ or $\GOz$. 17 works in class theory with global choice; over the class ring, $\Hom$ means the class of scalar codes
of \cref{osq:tn:thm:hom}, and ordinary $\Tor$ groups, flat resolutions and weak dimensions are taken over set-sized rings only
(17). A module $P$ has a \emph{set-presentation} if there is an exact sequence $A^{(T)}\to A^{(S)}\to P\to0$ of finite-support
free modules on sets $S,T$; equivalently, some surjection from a set-indexed free module onto $P$ has a set-generated kernel.
All linear combinations and equational factorizations below are finite.
The adjective ``set-indexed'' restricts the basis, not the coefficients:
when $A$ is a class ring, $A^{(S)}$ is the class of finitely supported
coefficient vectors on the set $S$.

\begin{theorem}[No presentation by sets \src{17}]\label{osq:rel:thm:presentation}
Let $A=\A_{D,k}$, let $M$ be a lattice of rank $r\ge2$ and $g>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $J_g(M)$ and $L(M)$ have no set-presentation. In particular, for $\alpha\in k\setminus\Frac D$ and $\gamma>0$ the
two-generated ideal $(\omega^\gamma,\alpha\omega^\gamma)$ has none, and the intersection
$\omega^\gamma A\cap\alpha\omega^\gamma A=\omega^\gamma\Pi_k$ of two principal ideals has no set of generators. Thus $\Oz$ and $\GOz$
are neither coherent nor finite-conductor domains, in the strong sense that an intersection of two principal ideals need not
be generated by a set.
\item $J_g(M)$ fails the equational criterion of flatness: $a_j=X^gm_j$ and $x=(X^gm_2,-X^gm_1,0,\dots,0)$ satisfy
$\sum_ja_jx_j=0$, but there is no factorization $x_j=\sum_tb_{jt}y_t$ with $y_t\in J_g(M)$, $b_{jt}\in A$ and $\sum_ja_jb_{jt}=0$
for every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) Multiplication by $X^g$ transfers the presentation in
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii) to
\[
 0\longrightarrow K_M\longrightarrow A^r
 \xrightarrow{\pi}J\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 K_M\cong\Pi_k^{r-1},\quad J=J_g(M).
\]
Suppose $\pi':A^{(S)}\to J$ is another surjection, with $S$ a
set and $H=\ker\pi'$ generated by a set. Form the explicit class
pullback
\[
 P=\{(x,y)\in A^r\oplus A^{(S)}:\pi(x)=\pi'(y)\}.
\]
Both projections split, as follows. Every $z\in J$ has a unique
expression $z=X^g(\sum_j d_jm_j+u)$ with $d_j\in D$ and
$u\in\Pi_k$. It has the specified preimage
$\sigma(z)=(d_1+u/m_1,d_2,\ldots,d_r)$ under $\pi$.
This $\sigma$ is a section as a map of classes; it is not asserted
to be $A$-linear. Instead assign to each basis vector $e_s$ the
pair $(\sigma(\pi'(e_s)),e_s)$ and extend by finite
$A$-linear combinations. The resulting map is an $A$-linear
section of $P\to A^{(S)}$, whose kernel is $K_M\oplus0$.
For the projection $P\to A^r$, choose preimages under $\pi'$
of the images of the finitely many standard basis vectors of
$A^r$. Extending those choices linearly gives a section, with
kernel $0\oplus H$.

These splittings are the concrete Schanuel isomorphisms
\[
 K_M\oplus A^{(S)}\cong P\cong H\oplus A^r.
\]
No choice indexed by all elements of a proper class is involved.
The right side is generated by a set, and an image of a
set-generated module is set-generated. Since $r-1\ge1$, project
the left side onto a copy of $\Pi_k$. This contradicts
\cref{osq:prop:common}(iii), proving that no set-presentation
exists. The same holds for $L(M)\cong J$.

For the stated two-generated ideal take $M=D+D\alpha$, whose
rank is two because $\alpha\notin\Frac(D)$. The intersection is
$\omega^\gamma\Pi_k$ by \cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(iii), and
multiplication by $\omega^\gamma$ identifies this module with
$\Pi_k$. Thus it too has no set of generators. In particular
the ideal is not finitely presented and the intersection is not
finitely generated, excluding coherence and the finite-conductor
property, respectively.

(ii) With $a_j=X^gm_j$, the vector in the statement is
$(a_2,-a_1,0,\ldots,0)\in J^r$, and its scalar product with
$(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ is zero by commutativity. In a hypothetical
finite equational factorization, every column $(b_{jt})_j$ lies
in $K_M$. All its coordinates therefore lie in $\Pi_k$, by
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii). Consequently each
$x_j=\sum_t b_{jt}y_t$ belongs to
\[
 \Pi_k J=X^g\Pi_kL(M)=X^g\Pi_k.
\]
But $x_1/X^g=m_2$ is a nonzero ordinary constant, and
$k\cap\Pi_k=0$. This is the required contradiction. The
argument uses only finite equations, so its class-ring assertion
requires no class category of tensor products.
\end{proof}

The kernel shape $\Pi^{r-1}$, flat dimension one and the intersection mechanism are classical for $D+M$ rings (Dobbs
\cite{Dobbs}, Dobbs--Papick \cite{DobbsPapick}); 17 presents neither as new and does not infer any factorization property from
noncoherence. Over a set-sized ring, (ii) is the equational criterion \cite[Lemma~10.39.11]{StacksFlat}; over the class ring it is
stated without a category of class tensor products (17).

\begin{lemma}[The lexicographic models inside $\Oz$ \src{17}; \merge\ for $\kappa=\aleph_0$]\label{osq:rel:lem:embedding}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite regular cardinal and $\Gamma_\kappa=\bigoplus_{\alpha<\kappa}\Q e_\alpha$, ordered by the sign of the
coefficient at the least index where it is nonzero (the group of \cref{osq:prop:lex}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item $e_\alpha\mapsto\omega^{-\alpha}$ extends to an injective order-preserving homomorphism $\iota:\Gamma_\kappa\to(\No,+)$.
\item Every subset of $\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}$ with fewer than $\kappa$ elements has a positive strict lower bound; the $e_\alpha$ are
coinitial in $\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}$, whose coinitiality is exactly $\kappa$.
\item $X^g\mapsto\omega^{\iota(g)}$ embeds $R^{11}_\kappa:=R^{11}_{\Gamma_\kappa,<\kappa}$, with $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$, respectively
$(\Z[i],\C)$, in $\Oz$, respectively $\GOz$, as the ring of normal forms with constant term in $D$ and fewer than $\kappa$
further exponents, all in $\iota(\Gamma_\kappa)_{>0}$. We write $\Pi^{11}_\kappa$ for its positive-support ideal.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
(i) Define
$\iota(\sum_\alpha q_\alpha e_\alpha)=
\sum_\alpha q_\alpha\omega^{-\alpha}$, a finite sum.
Here $-\alpha$ is the additive negative of the ordinal regarded
as a surreal number; differences such as $\beta-\alpha$ use
surreal addition, not ordinal subtraction. The definition is
additive and $\Q$-linear, and $\iota(e_0)=1$.
If $\alpha$ is the least nonzero index, divide the image by
$\omega^{-\alpha}>0$. The result is $q_\alpha$ plus finitely
many terms $q_\beta\omega^{\alpha-\beta}$ with $\beta>\alpha$.
Each latter term is infinitesimal, so the sign is the sign of
the nonzero rational $q_\alpha$. Thus every nonzero vector keeps
its lexicographic sign, proving injectivity and preservation of
the order.

(ii) Let $S\subseteq\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}$ have size less than
$\kappa$. The union $U$ of its finite sets of nonzero coordinate
indices has size less than $\kappa$. Regularity gives
$\beta=\sup\{\alpha+1:\alpha\in U\}<\kappa$, with
$\beta=0$ if $S$ is empty. Every element of $S$ has its leading
positive coordinate before $\beta$, so $0<e_\beta<s$ for every
$s\in S$. The same argument applied to a singleton shows that
the family $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ is coinitial. Conversely
a family $S$ of size less than $\kappa$ cannot be coinitial:
none of its members lies below its positive strict lower bound
$e_\beta$. This proves the exact coinitiality.

(iii) For a series $f=\sum_g c_gX^g$, set
$\Phi(f)=\sum_g c_g\omega^{\iota(g)}$.
An order embedding preserves reverse well-ordering of the support,
and injectivity preserves its cardinality. Thus this is an allowed
set-supported Conway normal form. Uniqueness of coefficients gives
injectivity; coefficientwise addition and the finite convolution
formula for multiplication show that $\Phi$ is a unital ring map,
since $\iota(g+h)=\iota(g)+\iota(h)$
(\cref{osq:sub:orientation,osq:sub:rings}). For supports $S,T$,
the new supports lie in $S\cup T$ and $S+T$, respectively. If
$|S|,|T|<\kappa$, then both have size less than the infinite
cardinal $\kappa$; in the countable case both supports are finite.
Regularity was needed in (ii), not in this two-support estimate.

The coefficient at zero stays in $D$, and every other exponent
stays positive. Conversely a normal form with the stated support
pulls back uniquely along $\iota$ and has the same support bound,
giving the asserted image. For complex coefficients this argument
is applied to the real and imaginary parts; their finite union of
supports still satisfies the bound.
\end{proof}

There are two levels of monomials here: $e_\alpha$ maps to the
surreal exponent $\omega^{-\alpha}$, whereas the ring monomial
$X^{e_\alpha}$ maps to $\omega^{\omega^{-\alpha}}$.
In particular $X^{e_0}$ maps to $\omega$, not to $1$.

11 does not embed its ring in $\No$ (\cref{osq:sub:model11}); (iii) places the ring of \cref{osq:prop:lex,osq:prop:card11} inside
$\Oz$. For $\kappa=\aleph_0$ this notation extends the ring definition
to finite-support series; it does not assert that the corresponding
finite-support ambient collection is a field. Like the finite-support cores of
12 and 14, this ring lies outside \cref{osq:thm:universal}: the coefficient sum is a unital map to $K$ detecting its tail, by the proof of
\cref{osq:hd:prop:finite}(ii). In both cases $R^{11}_\kappa$ has the properties listed in Setting (L) of
\cref{osq:tn:sub:lattices}, with $B=K+\Pi^{11}_\kappa$ and $\Pi^{11}_\kappa$ not finitely generated, so
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(i),(ii) and \cref{osq:tn:prop:nonflat} hold for it with the same proofs (17 proves them for its models).

\begin{theorem}[Exact relation counts \src{17}; \merge\ for $\kappa=\aleph_0$]\label{osq:rel:thm:kappa}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite regular cardinal, $A=R^{11}_\kappa$ and $\Pi=\Pi^{11}_\kappa$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Pi^2=\Pi=\bigcup_{\delta\in\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}}X^\delta A$, a directed union of free modules of rank one; $\Pi$ is flat, and
$\gen_A(\Pi)=\kappa$.
\item For $C\in k^{m\times n}$ and $e\in\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}$, with $q$ and $\ell$ as in \cref{osq:tn:thm:matrix},
$\ker_A(X^eC)\cong A^\ell\oplus\Pi^{q-\ell}$; it needs exactly $\ell$ generators if $q=\ell$ and exactly $\kappa$ if $q>\ell$.
\item For a lattice $M$ of rank $r\ge2$ and $g\in\Gamma_\kappa^{>0}$, the kernel of every surjection from a finite free
$A$-module onto $J_g(M)$ needs exactly $\kappa$ generators; for the natural surjection it is $\Pi^{r-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) Let $0\ne f\in\Pi$. Its support has fewer than $\kappa$
positive exponents, so \cref{osq:rel:lem:embedding}(ii) supplies
a positive strict lower bound $\delta$. Translation by
$-\delta$ preserves reverse well-ordering and support cardinality,
and every translated exponent is still positive. Hence
$X^{-\delta}f\in\Pi$ and
$f=X^\delta(X^{-\delta}f)\in\Pi^2$. The reverse inclusion
follows because $\Pi$ is an ideal, proving idempotence.
This factorization also puts $f$ in $X^\delta A$; the zero
element belongs to every member of the union.

If $0<\delta'<\delta$, then
$X^\delta=X^{\delta'}X^{\delta-\delta'}$, with the last factor
in $A$. Thus $X^\delta A\subseteq X^{\delta'}A$.
For any two indices choose a positive index smaller than both;
the union is directed by inclusion. Each principal ideal is free
of rank one, since its generator is nonzero in a domain. Its
directed union $\Pi$ is therefore flat
\cite[Lemma~10.39.3]{StacksFlat}.

Choose $e_\alpha<\delta$ in the preceding factorization.
Then $f\in X^{e_\alpha}A$, so the $\kappa$ monomials
$X^{e_\alpha}$ generate $\Pi$. For the reverse bound, suppose
a family $\{f_i:i\in I\}$ with $|I|<\kappa$ generated it.
Regularity implies that $\bigcup_i\supp(f_i)$ still has size
less than $\kappa$. Choose a positive strict lower bound
$\delta$ for this union. Each $f_i$ then lies in $X^\delta A$,
so its generated ideal is contained there. However
$X^{\delta/2}\in\Pi$ does not belong to $X^\delta A$:
cancelling $X^\delta$ would put the negative monomial
$X^{-\delta/2}$ in $A$. This proves $\gen_A\Pi=\kappa$.
For $\kappa=\aleph_0$, the regularity step is just the fact
that a finite union of finite supports is finite.

(ii) The kernel construction in \cref{osq:tn:thm:matrix} uses
the additive decomposition $A=D\oplus\Pi$, stability of $\Pi$
under $k$-scalars, and the principal-ideal property of $D$.
These hold in this model, and give the same isomorphism
$A^\ell\oplus\Pi^{q-\ell}$. If $q>\ell$, projection onto one
copy of $\Pi$ forces at least $\kappa$ generators. Conversely,
the union of generating families for its finitely many summands
has cardinality at most $\kappa$, since $\kappa$ is infinite.
If $q=\ell$, the standard basis gives $\ell$ generators and
tensoring with $\Frac(A)$ shows that fewer cannot suffice.
This includes $\ell=0$, when the kernel is zero.

(iii) The natural kernel is $\Pi^{r-1}$ by
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii). For any surjection $A^m\to J_g(M)$
with kernel $H$, the finite-free pullback argument gives
\[
 H\oplus A^r\cong\Pi^{r-1}\oplus A^m.
\]
If $H$ had $\lambda<\kappa$ generators, then the left side
would have at most $\lambda+r<\kappa$ generators. Projecting
the right side onto a copy of $\Pi$ contradicts (i), since
$r-1\ge1$. Conversely the right side has $\kappa$ generators;
transport them to the left side and project onto $H$. This gives
a generating family of size at most $\kappa$, proving equality
for every such surjection.
\end{proof}

For uncountable $\kappa$, (i) is the case $R^{11}_{\Gamma,<\kappa}$ of \cref{osq:thm:homological}(i) together with the generator count
recorded in (H3). Statement (iii) concerns numbers of generators;
for uncountable $\kappa$, the cardinality thresholds
$\kappa^{<\kappa}$ of \cref{osq:prop:card11} are a different
invariant of the same ring. That threshold assertion is not
extended to $\aleph_0$: the coefficient-sum map above already
detects its finite-support tail. In the class ring the relation module needs more than a set of
generators (\cref{osq:rel:thm:presentation}); a set-sized model measures the same obstruction by the regular cardinal $\kappa$ (17).

\begin{remark}[The countable case \merge]\label{osq:rel:rem:alephzero}
17 states \cref{osq:rel:lem:embedding,osq:rel:thm:kappa} for
uncountable regular $\kappa$, but the proofs above also apply to
$\aleph_0$. Put $A=R^{11}_{\aleph_0}$. For $r\ge2$ every
$L(M)$ is countably presented but not finitely presented.
More precisely, every surjection from a finite free $A$-module
onto $L(M)$ has a kernel needing exactly $\aleph_0$ generators.
This is a finite generating map with infinitely many relations,
not a finite presentation. The natural map has kernel
$\Pi^{r-1}$, so choosing its countable generating family gives
a presentation $A^{(\N)}\to A^r\to L(M)\to0$.

The projective dimensions can also be read directly. With
$x_n=X^{e_n}$ one has
$\Pi=\bigcup_nx_nA$ and
$x_n=x_{n+1}X^{e_n-e_{n+1}}$. The transition factor lies in
$A$, since $e_n>e_{n+1}$. Thus the telescope of
\cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(i) gives $\pd_A\Pi\le1$.
Nonfinite generation and \cref{osq:lem:projideal} rule out
projectivity, so $\pd_A\Pi=1$.
The exact sequence $0\to\Pi\to A\to D\to0$ then gives
$\pd_A D=2$: a value at most one would make its first syzygy
$\Pi$ projective. Likewise the natural presentation with kernel
$\Pi^{r-1}$ gives $\pd_A L(M)=\pd_AJ_g(M)=2$, since a smaller
value would make the direct summand $\Pi$ projective.
Finally $0\to J_g(M)\to A\to A/J_g(M)\to0$ gives
$\pd_A(A/J_g(M))=3$ by the same dimension shift.
For uncountable $\kappa$, the tail needs $\kappa$ generators
and these projective dimensions remain open in this report
(\cref{osq:q:pd,osq:rel:q:relations}).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Flat dimensions over the models \src{17}]\label{osq:rel:prop:fd}
Let $\kappa$ be infinite and regular, $A=R^{11}_\kappa$ and $M$ a lattice of rank $r$. Then $\Tor^A_j(J_g(M),-)=0$ for $j\ge2$. If
$r\ge2$, then $\fd_AJ_g(M)=1$ and $\fd_A\bigl(A/J_g(M)\bigr)=2$; hence the weak global dimension of $A$ is at least $2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $J=J_g(M)$. The natural presentation
$0\to\Pi^{r-1}\to A^r\to J\to0$ is a flat resolution by
\cref{osq:rel:thm:kappa}(i). It gives $\fd_AJ\le1$ and
$\Tor_j^A(J,N)=0$ for every $N$ and $j\ge2$. Splicing with
$0\to J\to A\to A/J\to0$ gives $\fd_A(A/J)\le2$.

For $r\ge2$ we exhibit a nonzero obstruction, without using
the general coefficient-$\Tor$ formula below. Put
$a_j=X^gm_j$. In $J\otimes_AJ$ consider
\[
 \tau=a_1\otimes a_2-a_2\otimes a_1.
\]
Its product is zero. The map $J\to M$ given by
$X^g(m+u)\mapsto m$ is $A$-linear when $M$ has action through
$\ct$. Applying it in both factors sends $\tau$ to
$m_1\otimes m_2-m_2\otimes m_1$ in $M\otimes_DM$.
This is nonzero because the two displayed tensors are distinct
members of its $D$-basis. Thus $\tau\ne0$.

The long exact sequence obtained by tensoring
$0\to J\to A\to A/J\to0$ with $J$ identifies
$\Tor_1^A(J,A/J)$ with the kernel of multiplication
$J\otimes_AJ\to J$, since $\Tor_1^A(J,A)=0$.
It is nonzero by $\tau$, proving $\fd_AJ=1$.
The same short exact sequence in the first variable gives
$\Tor_2^A(A/J,A/J)\cong\Tor_1^A(J,A/J)\ne0$.
Hence $\fd_A(A/J)=2$, and the supremum defining weak global
dimension is at least two.
\end{proof}

This is the analogue over $R^{11}_\kappa$ of \cref{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice} for $T_\Gamma$ (14's $A_0$, where 14 proves it); both rings have
a totally ordered exponent cone, as \cref{osq:hd:rem:reconcile} requires. No upper bound on the weak global dimension of $R^{11}_\kappa$
and no global dimension is claimed; Dobbs's global-dimension theorem for valuation pullbacks does not apply, because
$K+\Pi^{11}_\kappa$ is not a valuation ring (17).

\begin{theorem}[$\Tor$ as coefficient multiplication \src{17; 21}; \merge\ over the cores]\label{osq:rel:thm:tor}
Let $A$ be $R^{11}_\kappa$ for an infinite regular $\kappa$ (with $K=k$), or one of the set-sized rings $A_\Lambda$, $T_\Gamma$ of
Setting (L)(a), (b) with any unital $D\subseteq K$. Let $M,N$ be lattices of ranks $r,s$, let $X^g,X^h\in\Pi$ be nonzero monomials,
$I=J_g(M)$ and $J=J_h(N)$. Then, with $A$ acting on the right through $\ct$,
\[
 \Tor^A_1(I,A/J)\cong\Tor^A_2(A/I,A/J)\cong\mathcal T(M,N)=\ker\bigl(\mathsf m_{M,N}:M\otimes_DN\to K\bigr),
\]
a $D$-module of rank $rs-\rk(MN)$ (ranks are dimensions after tensoring with $\Frac D$). There is an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal T(M,N)\longrightarrow I\otimes_AJ\xrightarrow{\ \text{mult}\ }X^{g+h}(MN+\Pi)\longrightarrow0,
\]
whose first term is the torsion submodule of $I\otimes_AJ$ and is killed by $\Pi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $F=\Frac(D)$. A lattice here is finite free by definition;
no principal-ideal or Noetherian hypothesis on $D$ is used.
Fix a basis $m_1,\dots,m_r$ of $M$. Scaling the presentation in
\cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii) by $X^g$ gives
\[
 0\longrightarrow K_M\longrightarrow A^r
 \xrightarrow{(a_j)\mapsto X^g\sum_jm_ja_j}I\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad K_M=\{u\in\Pi^r:\textstyle\sum_jm_ju_j=0\}.
\]
The kernel is a $B$-module and a $K$-vector space: multiplication
preserves both the tail coordinates and their linear relation.
Consequently $JK_M\subseteq X^hK_M$. For the reverse inclusion,
choose $0\ne n\in N$. For every $u\in K_M$,
$X^hu=(X^hn)(u/n)\in JK_M$, since $u/n\in K_M$.
Thus $JK_M=X^hK_M$.

Tensor the presentation with $A/J$. Since $A^r$ is free, its
positive $\Tor$ groups vanish, and the long exact sequence gives
\[
 \Tor^A_1(I,A/J)\cong
 \ker\bigl(K_M/JK_M\longrightarrow(A/J)^r\bigr)
 = (K_M\cap J^r)/X^hK_M.
\]
For $x\in K_M\cap J^r$, write $x=X^hy$ with
$y\in(N+\Pi)^r$. This expression is unique in the ambient field.
Cancellation of $X^h$ gives $\sum_jm_jy_j=0$.
Use the coefficient map on $B=K\oplus\Pi$ coordinatewise to set
$c=\ct(y)\in N^r$. The constant part of that relation is
$\sum_jm_jc_j=0$. Conversely, every such tuple $c$ lifts to
$x=X^hc\in K_M\cap J^r$. The kernel of $x\mapsto c$ is
exactly $X^hK_M$: a zero constant tuple means $y\in\Pi^r$,
and its unchanged relation then means $y\in K_M$.
For $a\in A$, one has $\ct(ay)=\ct(a)c$, so this quotient
map is $A$-linear when the coefficient tuples have action through $\ct$.

The basis isomorphism
\[
 N^r\longrightarrow M\otimes_DN,\qquad
 (c_j)\longmapsto\sum_jm_j\otimes c_j
\]
identifies the equation $\sum_jm_jc_j=0$ with
$\mathcal T(M,N)$. Changes of basis give the same coefficient
tensor. Dimension shifting in $0\to I\to A\to A/I\to0$
now identifies $\Tor^A_2(A/I,A/J)$ with $\Tor^A_1(I,A/J)$.
Finally, localization at $D\setminus\{0\}$ is exact. Applying it to
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal T(M,N)\longrightarrow M\otimes_DN
 \xrightarrow{\mathsf m_{M,N}}MN\longrightarrow0
\]
gives the rank $rs-\rk(MN)$, because $M\otimes_DN\cong D^{rs}$.
Here $MN$ is the $D$-span of the products. Over an arbitrary $D$
this rank computation asserts neither freeness nor finite generation
of the kernel.

Tensoring $0\to J\to A\to A/J\to0$ with $I$ gives an
injection of $\Tor^A_1(I,A/J)$ into $I\otimes_AJ$, whose image
is the kernel of multiplication. The coefficient description sends
$t=\sum_jm_j\otimes c_j\in\mathcal T(M,N)$ to
\[
 \lambda(t)=\sum_j(X^gm_j)\otimes(X^hc_j).
\]
Indeed, the tuple $X^hc\in K_M\cap J^r$ represents the connecting
class just computed. There is also a direct check that this tensor
cannot vanish when $t\ne0$. The $A$-balanced map
\[
 (a,b)\longmapsto\ct(X^{-g}a)\otimes_D\ct(X^{-h}b),
 \qquad a\in I,\ b\in J,
\]
induces $\rho:I\otimes_AJ\to M\otimes_DN$ with
$\rho\lambda(t)=t$. Balancing follows from the coefficient action
through $D$ on both factors.

The image of multiplication is
$IJ=X^{g+h}(MN+\Pi)$. Products with a tail factor lie in $\Pi$;
conversely every tail $u$ is $m(u/m)$ with $0\ne m\in M$ and
$u/m\in\Pi\subseteq N+\Pi$. This proves the stated exact sequence.
Its kernel is killed by $\Pi$, hence by the nonzero element $X^h$
of the domain $A$, so every kernel element is $A$-torsion.
Conversely any torsion tensor maps to zero in $IJ$, since $IJ$ is
a submodule of a field. The kernel is therefore exactly the torsion
submodule. It is nevertheless torsion free over $D$, being a
submodule of $D^{rs}$; the two uses of torsion have different base rings.
\end{proof}

For $R^{11}_\kappa$ with uncountable $\kappa$ this is 17's theorem. Its proof uses only the properties of Setting (L) and the
presentation of \cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii), which is why it applies to 12's cores and to 14's $A_0=T_\Q$; that extension is the
merge's. The exact sequence is 14's \cref{osq:tn:thm:tensor} for the class ring and for $A_0$, where the class tensor product is an
explicit carrier; the $\Tor$ identifications are 17's. The proof shows which coefficient relations survive: a nonzero relation
$\sum_jm_j\otimes c_j$ is represented in $I\otimes_AJ$ by $\sum_j(X^gm_j)\otimes(X^hc_j)$, whose product is zero although the tensor
is not (17). Manuscript~21, whose pin precedes 17's placement, proves the identification of $\Tor_2$ with $\mathcal T(M,N)$, the action
