credits as antecedents the cellular resolutions of Bayer--Sturmfels \cite{BayerSturmfels}, the lcm-lattice homology of Gasharov--Peeva--Welker
\cite{GPW}, the real-exponent global dimensions of Geist--Miller \cite{GeistMiller} and Miller's real polyhedral theory \cite{MillerEssential}, none of
which it claims or reproves. The numbering of 26 cited here is that of its own manuscript.

\paragraph{Notation and renamings.} In this subsection $d\ge1$, $\mathscr C\subseteq\R^d$ is a pointed ($\mathscr C\cap(-\mathscr C)=\{0\}$),
full-dimensional, rational polyhedral cone, $K$ is a field and $D\subseteq K$ a unital subring, as in \cref{osq:hd:sub:cores}. \emph{Faces} of
$\mathscr C$ include $\{0\}$ and $\mathscr C$; the letters $F,G,H$ denote faces (not subsets of $\Lambda$, a field or a group), $F\vee G$ is the least face
containing both, $<$ is strict inclusion, and a face is identified with its rational points where exponents are meant. Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:core}
 P_{\mathscr C}=\mathscr C\cap\Q^d,\qquad \Pi_{\mathscr C}=\bigoplus_{0\ne m\in P_{\mathscr C}}KX^m,\qquad A_{\mathscr C}=D\oplus\Pi_{\mathscr C},
\end{equation}
finite sums, $X^mX^n=X^{m+n}$, graded by $\Q^d$. For $\mathscr C=\R_{\ge0}^d$ these are $P_{[d]}$, $\Pi_d$ and $A_d$. 26's symbols are renamed as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its cone $C$, field $k$, ring $A_D(C)$ (26's $\A$; here $\A$ is $D+\Pi_k$), monoid $M=C\cap\Q^d$ and tail $I_+$ are $\mathscr C$, $K$, $A_{\mathscr C}$,
$P_{\mathscr C}$ and $\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ ($C_p$ are 12's complexes and $M$ a coefficient lattice); its face quotient $A_D(F)$ is $A_{\mathscr C}(F)$.
\item Its face ideal $J_F$ is $I_F$: for a coordinate face on $S$ it is 12's $I_S$ of \eqref{osq:hd:eq:IS}, whereas $J_F=(X_i:i\in F)A$ is 12's ideal
of \cref{osq:hd:sub:tor}. Its radical ideal $I_{\mathcal F}=\sum_iJ_{F_i}$ is $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$, its face primes $P_H$ are $\mathfrak p_H$
($P_\Lambda$ is 12's monoid), and its smallest face $H(m)$ containing $m$ is $\operatorname{fc}(m)$ ($H$ is a group, $H_a$ the scale subgroup).
\item Its $V_G=\{i:F_i\subseteq G\}$ is $\operatorname{At}(G)$ ($V_F$ are 12's test modules), its join complexes $\Delta_{<G}$ are $\mathsf K_{<G}$ ($\Delta$
is 21's telescope map and the difference operator), its $h(\mathcal F;k)$ is $\operatorname{len}(\mathcal F)$, and its complexes $\mathcal C_*$,
$\mathcal R_*$, $E_*$ are $C^{\mathcal F}_*$, $R^{\mathcal F}_*$ and $C^{\mathrm{cell}}_*$ (compare 21's $C^U_*$).
\item Its detecting module $N_{G,b}$, with ring $S_G=k[G\cap\Q^d]$, cap ideal $L_{G,b}$ and facet functionals $\eta_j$, is $\mathcal W_{G,b}$, with
$K[P_G]$, $\mathfrak z_{G,b}$ and $\ell^G_j$ ($N$ is a module, $\mathfrak c$ the continuum, $\eta$ 18's translation); it plays the role of 12's test
modules $V_F$. Its rays $\mathcal R_F$ outside a face are written out ($\mathcal R$ is 14's Rees algebra).
\item Its embedding functional $\lambda$ is $\lambda_\omega$ ($\lambda$ is a cardinal), and its total-order ring $T_D(\lambda)$ is
$T_{\lambda_\omega}$, the finite-support ring over the ordered group $\lambda_\omega(\Q^d)$ (as $T_\Gamma$ of \eqref{osq:hd:eq:T}, but with exponents in
$\No$).
\item Its squarefree ring $R=k[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ and ideal $Q$ are $K[\mathbf x]$ and $\mathfrak q$; its module $E$ acting through $\ct$, with torsion $T$
and quotient $V$, is $N$ with $N_{\mathrm{tor}}$ and $N/N_{\mathrm{tor}}$; its cube cones $C_n$ are $\mathscr C_n$; its $\operatorname{wdim},\operatorname{gldim}$ are
$\operatorname{w.gl.dim},\operatorname{gl.dim}$.
\end{itemize}
The letters $\beta_{p,G}$, $\mu_{\mathscr C}$, $u_F$ and $\ell$ are kept. Four tempting readings are false. (1) $I_F$ is not $J_F$: $I_{\mathscr C}$ for the
orthant is the relative-interior ideal, not $\Pi_d$ unless $d=1$, and $J_{[d]}=(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ is neither. (2) ``Core'' does not mean integer part:
$A_{\mathscr C}$ is a subring of $\Oz$, and a partial exponent cone must not be replaced by the positive cone of the ambient order
(\cref{osq:pc:thm:nonflat}). (3) The numbers $\beta_{p,G}$ count summands of a reduced \emph{flat} resolution, not minimal free ranks, and the reduced
resolution is not unique. (4) ``All radical monomial quotients'' means the coefficient-full geometric ones: arithmetic ideals such as $pA_{\mathscr C}$ and
ideals restricting the coefficient at an admitted exponent are excluded.

\paragraph{The rings.} Pointedness means two nonzero exponents never add to zero, so $\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ is an ideal and $\ct$ is a split surjection
$A_{\mathscr C}\to D$ with kernel $\Pi_{\mathscr C}$; $A_{\mathscr C}\subseteq K[P_{\mathscr C}]$ is a domain (compare least exponents in a total order
of $\Q^d$ compatible with addition). Every sum is finite; this is used in the common-shift argument, in degreewise exactness and in the arguments
against finite generation, and is not shorthand for a Hahn completion (26). For $m\in\mathscr C$, $\operatorname{fc}(m)$ is the smallest face containing
$m$, so $m\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{fc}(m)$, $\operatorname{fc}(0)=\{0\}$, and a supporting functional gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:sumface}
 \operatorname{fc}(m+n)=\operatorname{fc}(m)\vee\operatorname{fc}(n)\qquad(m,n\in\mathscr C),
\end{equation}
since a face contains $m+n$ exactly when it contains $m$ and $n$.

\begin{proposition}[Omnific embeddings \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:prop:embedding}
Choose a rational functional $\ell_1$ strictly positive on $\mathscr C\setminus\{0\}$, extend it to a basis $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_d$ of the rational dual of
$\Q^d$, and put $\lambda_\omega(m)=\ell_1(m)\omega^{d-1}+\ell_2(m)\omega^{d-2}+\dots+\ell_d(m)$, an injective additive map $\Q^d\to\No$, positive on
$\mathscr C\setminus\{0\}$. For $(D,K)=(\Z,\R)$ the rule $c+\sum_ma_mX^m\mapsto c+\sum_ma_m\omega^{\lambda_\omega(m)}$ is an injective ring homomorphism
$A_{\mathscr C}\to\Oz$ preserving $\ct$; for $(D,K)=(\Z[i],\C)$ it is one into $\GOz$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The monomial law gives a homomorphism, distinct $m$ give distinct exponents, so uniqueness of finite normal forms gives injectivity; nonconstant exponents
are positive and the constant term is in $D$. For $\C$ split coefficients into real and imaginary parts.
\end{proof}

This is \cref{osq:hd:lem:cores}(ii) with a lexicographic, rather than a real, functional (26).

\begin{proposition}[A common fraction field \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:prop:fractions}
$\Frac A_{\mathscr C}=\Frac K[\Q^d]$, independently of $\mathscr C$ and of $D\subseteq K$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $0\ne u\in P_{\mathscr C}$ and $a\in K$, $(aX^u)/X^u=a$. Every $g\in\Q^d$ is $m-n$ with $m,n\in P_{\mathscr C}$: take a rational interior point $v$ and a large
integer $N$ with $Nv,Nv+g\in\mathscr C$; then $X^g=X^m/X^n$. The reverse inclusion is $A_{\mathscr C}\subseteq K[\Q^d]$.
\end{proof}

The fraction field forgets the cone, while the face-quotient flat dimensions detect whether it is simplicial (26). All rings and modules used to compute
$\Tor$ and flat or projective dimension are set-sized, flat dimension is taken among all modules, and a nonzero homogeneous $\Tor$ component is a nonzero
component of the ungraded $\Tor$; filtered colimits of flat modules are flat \cite[Lemma~10.39.3]{StacksFlat}, flat resolutions compute $\Tor$, and every
projective-dimension bound below is proved by a telescope or by dimension shifting (26).

\paragraph{Flat ideals indexed by faces.} For a nonzero face $F$ fix a rational $u_F\in\operatorname{relint}F$, for instance the sum of one rational
vector on each ray of $F$.

\begin{lemma}[Face subtraction \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:subtract}
For $m\in\mathscr C$ the following are equivalent: (i) $F\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)$; (ii) $m-\epsilon u_F\in\mathscr C$ for all sufficiently small
positive rational $\epsilon$; (iii) $m-\epsilon u_F\in\mathscr C$ for some positive rational $\epsilon$. Then $\operatorname{fc}(m-\epsilon u_F)=
\operatorname{fc}(m)$ for all small $\epsilon>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $\mathscr C=\{x:\ell_j(x)\ge0,\ j\le s\}$ with facet functionals. If $F\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)$ and $\ell_j(m)=0$, then $\ell_j(u_F)=0$; the
other $\ell_j(m)$ are positive, so for small $\epsilon$ all inequalities hold with the same zero set, which gives (ii) and the last assertion. (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)
is clear. If (iii) holds, $m=(m-\epsilon u_F)+\epsilon u_F$, and a face containing $m$ contains both summands, hence $u_F$ and $F$.
\end{proof}

For a nonzero face $F$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:IF}
 I_F=\bigoplus_{0\ne m\in P_{\mathscr C},\ F\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)}KX^m\subseteq A_{\mathscr C},\qquad I_{\{0\}}=A_{\mathscr C}\ \text{(a convention only)}.
\end{equation}
In the orthant, the face spanned by the coordinate rays in $S$ gives 12's $I_S$: the monomials positive at every index of $S$, possibly zero elsewhere (26).

\begin{theorem}[Principal exhaustion and dimension one \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:exhaustion}
For every nonzero face $F$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:exhaustion}
 I_F=\bigcup_{n\ge1}X^{2^{-n}u_F}A_{\mathscr C},
\end{equation}
an increasing union. So $I_F$ is flat, is not finitely generated, and $\pd_{A_{\mathscr C}}I_F=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $m=2^{-n}u_F+v$ with $v\in\mathscr C$, \eqref{osq:pc:eq:sumface} gives $F\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)$, and
$X^{2^{-n}u_F}=(X^{2^{-n-1}u_F})^2$ makes the union increasing. Conversely, for a finite sum in $I_F$, \cref{osq:pc:lem:subtract} lets one large $n$
subtract $2^{-n}u_F$ from every exponent with every difference nonzero; factoring out $X^{2^{-n}u_F}$ leaves a finite sum in $A_{\mathscr C}$, although its
coefficients lie in $K$, not in $D$ (this is why every difference must be nonzero). Each principal ideal is free of rank one, $A_{\mathscr C}$ being a domain,
so the union is flat. If finitely many elements generated $I_F$, the least value $c>0$ of a functional $\ell$ strictly positive on
$\mathscr C\setminus\{0\}$ on their nonzero exponents would bound below the $\ell$-values of all exponents of $I_F$, but $\ell(2^{-n}u_F)\to0$. With
$P_n=X^{2^{-n}u_F}A_{\mathscr C}$ and the inclusions $\iota_n$, the sequence
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:telescope}
 0\to\bigoplus_{n\ge1}P_n\xrightarrow{\ \tau\ }\bigoplus_{n\ge1}P_n\to I_F\to0,\qquad \tau(e_nx)=e_nx-e_{n+1}\iota_n(x),
\end{equation}
is exact (injectivity at the least nonzero coordinate; the cokernel is the colimit), so $\pd I_F\le1$. A projective ideal of a domain is finitely
generated: with a dual basis $(x_i,f_i)$ and $0\ne a$ in the ideal, $af_i(x)=xf_i(a)$ shows that only the finitely many $f_i$ with $f_i(a)\ne0$ are
nonzero. So $\pd I_F=1$.
\end{proof}

This is \cref{osq:hd:lem:faces}(i), (iii) and \cref{osq:hd:prop:pd}(i), (ii) for arbitrary faces; the dual-basis step is \cref{osq:lem:projideal}.

\begin{theorem}[Intersections, products and tensors \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:products}
For nonzero faces $F,G$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:products}
 I_F\cap I_G=I_{F\vee G}=I_FI_G,\qquad I_F\otimes_{A_{\mathscr C}}I_G\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }I_{F\vee G}\ \text{(multiplication)}.
\end{equation}
In particular $I_F^2=I_F$, and $I_G\subseteq I_F$ if and only if $F\subseteq G$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The intersection is read off the supports, and a product lies in both ideals. For $aX^m\in I_{F\vee G}$ choose a small rational $q>0$ with
$m-qu_F\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{fc}(m)$; then $X^{qu_F}\in I_F$ and $aX^{m-qu_F}\in I_G$. Tensoring $I_F\hookrightarrow A_{\mathscr C}$ with
the flat $I_G$ gives an injection $I_F\otimes I_G\to I_G$, the multiplication map, with image $I_FI_G$. For the last assertion test on $X^{u_G}$.
\end{proof}

None of this needs $D$ to be a field, Noetherian or a principal ideal domain; the constant ring is never replaced by $K$ (26).

\paragraph{Radical monomial ideals.} An ideal $I\subseteq\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ is \emph{geometric monomial} (26: coefficient-full) if it is a direct sum of
some of the spaces $KX^m$, $m\ne0$, so that membership depends on exponents only and admits every coefficient of $K$ at an admitted exponent.

\begin{theorem}[Radical classification \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:radical}
The nonzero radical geometric monomial ideals correspond bijectively to the nonempty upper sets of nonzero faces, equivalently to the nonempty antichains
$\mathcal F$ of nonzero faces, by
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:radicalsum}
 \mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}I_F .
\end{equation}
Every $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ is idempotent and not finitely generated.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $X^m\in I$ and $F=\operatorname{fc}(m)$. For a rational $n\in\operatorname{relint}H$ with $F\subseteq H$, the facet inequalities give $Nn-m\in\mathscr C$ for
large $N$, so $(X^n)^N\in I$ and $X^n\in I$ by radicality, and all of $KX^n$ by coefficient-fullness. So membership is constant on relative interiors and
upward closed, and the minimal admitted faces are the antichain. Conversely an upper set gives an ideal by \eqref{osq:pc:eq:sumface}. For a face $H$ put
$\mathfrak p_H=\bigoplus_{m\in P_{\mathscr C}\setminus H}KX^m$; deleting the exponents outside $H$ is multiplicative (a sum lies in a face only if both summands
do), so $A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak p_H\cong A_{\mathscr C}(H)$, a domain, and $\mathfrak p_H$ is prime. The ideal of an upper set $\mathcal U$ is
$\bigcap\mathfrak p_H$ over the maximal $H$ of the complementary lower set, hence radical. Idempotence follows from $I_F^2=I_F$, and non-finite generation from
the positive functional as in \cref{osq:pc:thm:exhaustion}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Generators of a face prime \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:prop:faceprime}
For a proper face $F<\mathscr C$, $\mathfrak p_F=\sum_\rho I_\rho$ over the rays $\rho$ of $\mathscr C$ not in $F$, which are the minimal faces of its upper set,
and $A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak p_F\cong A_{\mathscr C}(F)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$m\notin F$ exactly when $\operatorname{fc}(m)\not\subseteq F$, and a face not contained in $F$ has a ray not in $F$, faces being generated by their rays.
\end{proof}

For $F=\{0\}$ the generators are all rays and $\mathfrak p_{\{0\}}=\Pi_{\mathscr C}$. An orthant facet excludes one ray; a nonsimplicial facet can exclude
several, and their joins raise the flat dimension (26).

\paragraph{Finite flat resolutions and label reduction.} Fix a nonempty antichain $\mathcal F=\{F_1,\dots,F_r\}$ of nonzero faces, and for
$S\subseteq[r]$ put $G_S=\bigvee_{i\in S}F_i$, $G_\varnothing=\{0\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Face-labelled simplex resolution \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:cech}
The complex with $C^{\mathcal F}_0=A_{\mathscr C}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:cech}
 C^{\mathcal F}_p=\bigoplus_{S\subseteq[r],\ |S|=p}I_{G_S}\quad(1\le p\le r),
\end{equation}
whose differential sends the summand of $S=\{i_1<\dots<i_p\}$ to the summands of $S\setminus\{i_j\}$ by $(-1)^{j-1}$ times the inclusion, is a flat
resolution of $A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The inclusions exist by \cref{osq:pc:thm:products}, and the two ways of deleting two indices cancel. In degree $m\ne0$ put
$T(m)=\{i:F_i\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)\}$; the summand of $S$ contributes $K$ exactly when $S\subseteq T(m)$, so for $T(m)\ne\varnothing$ the degree-$m$
part is the augmented simplex chain complex on $T(m)$, contracted by inserting a fixed vertex, and for $T(m)=\varnothing$ it is the identity of
$(A_{\mathscr C})_m$; in degree $0$ it is $D\to D$. Flatness is \cref{osq:pc:thm:exhaustion}.
\end{proof}

This is a Taylor-type incidence construction, classical in spirit \cite{BayerSturmfels,GPW}, with non-finitely-generated flat summands instead of free
ones; its length $r$ is only a first bound, and $r$ can exceed $d$ (26). For $\mathscr C$ an orthant and $\mathcal F$ its rays it is 12's
\cref{osq:hd:thm:resolution}.

Let $\mathcal L=\{G_S\}$, ordered by inclusion, whose atoms are the $F_i$. For $G\in\mathcal L\setminus\{\{0\}\}$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:deltadef}
 \operatorname{At}(G)=\{i:F_i\subseteq G\},\qquad \mathsf K_{<G}=\{S\subseteq\operatorname{At}(G):G_S<G\},
\end{equation}
a simplicial complex containing the empty face, proper in the full simplex on $\operatorname{At}(G)$; augmented chains place the empty face in degree $-1$.
The part of the differential of \eqref{osq:pc:eq:cech} keeping a label $G$ is a finite complex of $K$-matrices with basis the $p$-subsets $S$ with $G_S=G$.

\begin{lemma}[One diagonal block \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:diagonal}
Its homology in degree $p\ge1$ has dimension
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:beta}
 \beta_{p,G}=\dim_K\widetilde H_{p-2}(\mathsf K_{<G};K);\qquad \beta_{1,F_i}=1 .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The block is the relative augmented chain complex of the full simplex on $\operatorname{At}(G)$ modulo $\mathsf K_{<G}$, with a $p$-subset in degree $p$; the
simplex is contractible, so the relative homology is the reduced homology of $\mathsf K_{<G}$ shifted by two. For $G=F_i$, $\mathsf K_{<G}=\{\varnothing\}$ and
$\widetilde H_{-1}=K$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Triangular cancellation \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:cancellation}
Splitting off finitely many contractible two-term complexes reduces \eqref{osq:pc:eq:cech} to a flat resolution $R^{\mathcal F}_*$ of
$A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:reduced}
 R^{\mathcal F}_0=A_{\mathscr C},\qquad R^{\mathcal F}_p=\bigoplus_{G\in\mathcal L\setminus\{\{0\}\}}I_G^{\,\beta_{p,G}}\quad(p\ge1),
\end{equation}
whose positive differential has every nonzero component a scalar multiple of an inclusion strictly decreasing the face label.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Initially a nonzero component $I_G\to I_H$ needs $H\subseteq G$ and is a scalar times inclusion, a property closed under sums and composites. A nonzero
scalar of $K$ is an automorphism of the $K$-space $I_G$ over $A_{\mathscr C}$, even when it is not in $D$. A nonzero entry $a$ between two copies of the same
label $G$, in row $j$ and column $i$, is isolated by changing coordinates, the other entries becoming
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:schur}
 d'_{uv}=d_{uv}-d_{ui}a^{-1}d_{jv};
\end{equation}
deleting the isolated pair is a chain-homotopy equivalence, and $d^2=0$ keeps the rest a complex. Corrections pass through $G$, so they still decrease labels,
and they can change the diagonal block of $H$ only if $H\supseteq G\supseteq H$. Gaussian elimination inside each block leaves its homology with zero diagonal
differential, and each step removes two summands. $A_{\mathscr C}$ has label $\{0\}$ and is never cancelled.
\end{proof}

``Reduced'' means only that no equal-label contractible pair remains; the remaining maps are not unique, and no finite minimal-generator argument for the
$I_G$ is imported (26).

\begin{lemma}[Crosscut comparison \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:crosscut}
$\mathsf K_{<G}$ is homotopy equivalent to the order complex of the open interval $(\{0\},G)$ of $\mathcal L$ (empty complexes included), so
$\beta_{p,G}=0$ for $p>\dim G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
With $\mathcal S$ the poset of nonempty faces of $\mathsf K_{<G}$, the order maps $f(S)=G_S$ and $g(H)=\{i:F_i\subseteq H\}$ satisfy $fg=\mathrm{id}$ (every
element of $\mathcal L$ is the join of its atoms) and $gf\ge\mathrm{id}$; comparable order maps are homotopic (the prism over the two-element chain), so $f,g$
are homotopy inverses. A chain of nonzero proper faces of $G$ has at most $\dim G-1$ members, so the order complex has dimension at most $\dim G-2$.
\end{proof}

So the reduced resolution has length at most $d$ (26).

\paragraph{Face-isolating modules and the exact formula.} Fix a nonzero face $G$ and a rational $b\in\operatorname{relint}G$, choose facet functionals
$\ell^G_1,\dots,\ell^G_t$ of $G$ in its linear span, so $G=\{x:\ell^G_j(x)\ge0\}$ and $\ell^G_j(b)>0$, let $K[P_G]$ ($P_G=G\cap\Q^d$) be an
$A_{\mathscr C}$-algebra by discarding the monomials outside $G$ and including $D$ in $K$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:detector}
 \mathfrak z_{G,b}=\bigoplus_{m\in P_G,\ \ell^G_j(m)\ge\ell^G_j(b)\text{ for some }j}KX^m,\qquad \mathcal W_{G,b}=K[P_G]/\mathfrak z_{G,b};
\end{equation}
$\mathfrak z_{G,b}$ is an ideal because the $\ell^G_j$ are nonnegative on $G$. The surviving monomials lie below \emph{every} cap: $(\mathcal W_{G,b})_b=0$,
while small inward translates of $b$ survive. $\mathcal W_{G,b}$ is usually not finitely generated, which detection of flat dimension does not need.

\begin{theorem}[Isolation of one face label \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:isolation}
For every nonzero face $H$, $(I_H\otimes_{A_{\mathscr C}}\mathcal W_{G,b})_b$ is $K$ if $H=G$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \eqref{osq:pc:eq:exhaustion} the degree-$b$ component is the colimit of $(\mathcal W_{G,b})_{b-q_nu_H}$, $q_n=2^{-n}$, with transition maps multiplication by
$X^{(q_n-q_{n+1})u_H}$ (the degree shifts must be kept). If $H\not\subseteq G$, a supporting functional of $G$ vanishing on $G$ and positive at $u_H$ is negative at
$b-q_nu_H$, so all terms are zero. If $H\subsetneq G$, some facet of $G$ contains $H$, and its functional has $\ell^G_j(b-q_nu_H)=\ell^G_j(b)$, so the cap kills
every term in $G$. If $H=G$, every $\ell^G_j(u_G)>0$, and for large $n$ the exponent $b-q_nu_G$ lies in $G$ strictly below every cap; late transitions send $a$
to the same coefficient $a$, so the colimit is $K$.
\end{proof}

Faces not in $G$ are excluded by support, proper subfaces of $G$ by equality at a cap; only a move into the relative interior of $G$ leaves all its facets
(26).

\begin{theorem}[Join homology computes flat dimension \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:exactfd}
For $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}\ne0$ put $\operatorname{len}(\mathcal F)=\max\{p:\beta_{p,G}\ne0\text{ for some }G\in\mathcal L\setminus\{\{0\}\}\}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:fdexact}
 \fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}(A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F})=\operatorname{len}(\mathcal F),\qquad \fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}=
 \operatorname{len}(\mathcal F)-1,\qquad 1\le\operatorname{len}(\mathcal F)\le d,
\end{equation}
and for every nonzero $G\in\mathcal L$ and $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:torbeta}
 \Tor_p^{A_{\mathscr C}}(A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F},\mathcal W_{G,b})_b\cong K^{\beta_{p,G}} .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{osq:pc:lem:cancellation,osq:pc:lem:crosscut} give $\fd\le\operatorname{len}\le d$. Tensor $R^{\mathcal F}_*$ with $\mathcal W_{G,b}$ in degree $b$:
the degree-zero term vanishes, only the summands labelled $G$ survive (\cref{osq:pc:thm:isolation}), $\beta_{p,G}$ of them in degree $p$, and the
differentials between them vanish because the reduced differential strictly decreases labels. This is \eqref{osq:pc:eq:torbeta} and the lower bound.
$\beta_{1,F_i}=1$ makes $\operatorname{len}\ge1$. For the ideal shift $\Tor$ in $0\to\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}\to A_{\mathscr C}\to A_{\mathscr C}/
\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}\to0$ if $\operatorname{len}\ge2$; if $\operatorname{len}=1$, truncation shows that $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ is flat.
\end{proof}

A finite incidence calculation alone would give only an upper bound; the detecting module turns diagonal homology into an obstruction to every shorter
flat resolution (26). This is 26's Theorem~B.

\begin{corollary}[A one-step projective interval \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:cor:pdbounds}
With $\ell_0=\operatorname{len}(\mathcal F)$, $\max\{2,\ell_0\}\le\pd_{A_{\mathscr C}}(A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F})\le\ell_0+1$; a one-face
quotient $A_{\mathscr C}/I_F$ has flat dimension one and projective dimension two.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Each $I_G$ has a free resolution of length one \eqref{osq:pc:eq:telescope}, so dimension shifting along the reduced resolution gives $\le\ell_0+1$, and
$\pd\ge\fd$. If $\pd\le1$, the kernel $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ of $A_{\mathscr C}\to A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ would be projective, hence
finitely generated, against \cref{osq:pc:thm:radical}.
\end{proof}

For $\ell_0\ge2$ the argument does not decide the endpoint, and 21's exact value for coordinate cores (\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd}) cannot be transferred to
nonsimplicial quotients without an additional $\Ext$ argument (26). By the isomorphism $A_{\mathscr C}\cong A_d$ for simplicial cones, the upper endpoint
holds for every face quotient of a simplicial cone \merge.

\begin{theorem}[Homological epimorphisms \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:homological}
For every $B=A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ and every $B$-module $N$, $B\otimes_{A_{\mathscr C}}N\cong N$ and $\Tor_j^{A_{\mathscr C}}(B,N)=0$ for $j>0$;
so $A_{\mathscr C}\to B$ is a homological ring epimorphism. Yet $B$ is not flat when $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}\ne0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a positive summand $I_{G_S}$ of \eqref{osq:pc:eq:cech} and $i\in S$, $I_{F_i}I_{G_S}=I_{G_S}$ (\cref{osq:pc:thm:products}), so
$\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}I_{G_S}=I_{G_S}$ and $I_{G_S}\otimes N\cong(I_{G_S}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}I_{G_S})\otimes_BN=0$. For nonflatness, multiplication by a
nonzero monomial of $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ is injective on $A_{\mathscr C}$ and zero on $B$.
\end{proof}

Vanishing self-$\Tor$ and positive flat dimension do not conflict: the former tests only modules killed by $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$, and the cap modules are
not such (26). For $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}=\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ this is 12's \cref{osq:hd:cor:arithmeticTor}.

\paragraph{Face quotients.}

\begin{lemma}[Deleting a face from a polytopal boundary \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:complement}
Let $Q_0$ be a positive-dimensional compact convex polytope and $Q_1$ a nonempty proper face. Then $\partial Q_0\setminus Q_1$ is contractible, and it is
homotopy equivalent to the order complex of $\{H:\varnothing\ne H<Q_0,\ H\not\subseteq Q_1\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Work in the affine span, with $c\in\operatorname{relint}Q_0$ and $q\in\operatorname{relint}Q_1$. Let $\mathsf k=\{t(z-c):t\ge0,z\in Q_1\}$, a pointed convex cone,
and let $r(v)$ be the point where the ray $c+\R_{>0}v$ meets $\partial Q_0$, so $r(v)\in Q_1$ exactly when $v\in\mathsf k\setminus\{0\}$. For
$x\in\partial Q_0\setminus Q_1$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:contraction}
 \mathsf h_t(x)=r\bigl((1-t)(x-c)+t(c-q)\bigr),\qquad0\le t\le1 .
\end{equation}
The vector inside $r$ is never in $\mathsf k$: for $t<1$ membership would put $(1-t)(x-c)$ in $\mathsf k$, against $x\notin Q_1$, and for $t=1$ it is $-(q-c)$
with $0\ne q-c\in\mathsf k$ pointed; in particular it never vanishes. So $\mathsf h$ contracts $\partial Q_0\setminus Q_1$ to $r(c-q)$. In the barycentric
subdivision of $\partial Q_0$, whose vertices are the nonempty proper faces, a point outside $Q_1$ has positive total weight on vertices not contained in $Q_1$;
decreasing the other weights to zero and renormalizing retracts onto the full subcomplex on those vertices, the stated order complex.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The outside-vertex complex \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:outside}
Let $Q_0$ be a convex polytope, $Q_1$ a proper face (possibly empty), $V$ the vertices of $Q_0$ not in $Q_1$, and $\mathsf K$ the subsets of $V$ lying in a proper
face of $Q_0$. If $Q_1=\varnothing$ then $\mathsf K\simeq\partial Q_0$; if $Q_1\ne\varnothing$ then $\mathsf K$ is contractible. (For a point $Q_0$ and empty
$Q_1$ both are $\{\varnothing\}$.)
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Send a simplex to the smallest face containing it, and a face $H$ with $\varnothing\ne H<Q_0$, $H\not\subseteq Q_1$, to its vertices outside $Q_1$ (nonempty,
faces being spanned by vertices); the composites are below, respectively above, the identities, so the order-map homotopy of \cref{osq:pc:lem:crosscut} applies.
For $Q_1=\varnothing$ the face poset gives the barycentric subdivision of $\partial Q_0$; otherwise use \cref{osq:pc:lem:complement}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Face-quotient multiplicities \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:facebetti}
For a face $F<\mathscr C$, use the antichain of rays outside $F$ (\cref{osq:pc:prop:faceprime}) and extend $\beta_{p,G}$ by zero. Then for every nonzero face
$G$ and $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:facebetti}
 \beta_{p,G}=1\ \text{if }G\cap F=\{0\}\text{ and }p=\dim G,\qquad \beta_{p,G}=0\ \text{otherwise}.
\end{equation}
So $A_{\mathscr C}(F)$ has a reduced flat resolution with $\bigoplus_{G\cap F=\{0\},\ \dim G=p}I_G$ in degree $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:mainface}
 \fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}A_{\mathscr C}(F)=\mu_{\mathscr C}(F)=\max\{\dim G:G\text{ a face},\ G\cap F=\{0\}\},
\end{equation}
the maximum including $G=\{0\}$, and $\Tor^{A_{\mathscr C}}_{\dim G}(A_{\mathscr C}(F),\mathcal W_{G,b})_b\cong K$ for every nonzero face $G$ with $G\cap F=\{0\}$.
In particular $\fd D=d$ and $\fd A_{\mathscr C}=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
With $\ell$ strictly positive on $\mathscr C$, $Q_0=G\cap\{\ell=1\}$ is a polytope of dimension $\dim G-1$ whose vertices are the rays of $G$, and the active rays are
the vertices outside $Q_1=(G\cap F)\cap\{\ell=1\}$. If $G\subseteq F$ there are no active rays and $G$ is not a label. Otherwise $\mathsf K_{<G}$ is the
outside-vertex complex of \cref{osq:pc:lem:outside}: for $G\cap F=\{0\}$, $Q_1=\varnothing$, $G$ is a join label and $\mathsf K_{<G}$ has the homology of the
sphere $\partial Q_0$ of dimension $\dim G-2$ (degree $-1$ for a ray); for $\{0\}<G\cap F<G$ it is contractible; and if $G$ is not a join label the active rays
join below $G$ and their complex is a full simplex. Substitute into \eqref{osq:pc:eq:beta} and apply \cref{osq:pc:lem:cancellation,osq:pc:thm:exactfd}. For
$F=\mathscr C$ the only disjoint face is $\{0\}$.
\end{proof}

The equality involves the dimension of the disjoint face, not the number of its rays: a nonsimplicial face with many rays contributes one top class, which is
what equal-label cancellation measures (26). This is 26's Theorem~A.

\begin{proposition}[The face complex resolves $D$ \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:prop:cellular}
Orient the faces of $Q_0=\mathscr C\cap\{\ell=1\}$. There is a flat resolution of $D$ with $C^{\mathrm{cell}}_0=A_{\mathscr C}$,
$C^{\mathrm{cell}}_p=\bigoplus_{\dim G=p}I_G$ ($1\le p\le d$), cellular incidence numbers times inclusions as differentials and $\ct$ as augmentation; hence
$\fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}D=d$ independently of the cancellation.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In degree $m\ne0$ the summands present are the nonzero faces $G\subseteq\operatorname{fc}(m)$, and the complex is the augmented cellular chain complex of the
convex, contractible $Q_0\cap\operatorname{fc}(m)$; in degree $0$ it is $D\to D$. Tensoring with $\mathcal W_{\mathscr C,b}$ in degree $b$ leaves only $I_{\mathscr
C}$ in degree $d$, so $\Tor_d(D,\mathcal W_{\mathscr C,b})_b=K$.
\end{proof}

For a simplicial cone the numbers of summands are $\binom d0,\dots,\binom dd$, the Boolean pattern of \cref{osq:hd:thm:resolution}; for the cone over a square
$1,4,4,1$, over a cube $1,8,12,6,1$. The method is cellular in the sense of \cite{BayerSturmfels}, but flatness comes from rational root exhaustion, not from
free cellular summands (26).

\paragraph{Flatness detects simpliciality.}

\begin{theorem}[Only single-face ideals are flat \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:flatclass}
For an irredundant antichain $\mathcal F=\{F_1,\dots,F_r\}$ the following are equivalent: $\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F}$ is flat; $\fd(A_{\mathscr C}/
\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F})=1$; $r=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first two are equivalent because the nonzero quotient is not flat (\cref{osq:pc:thm:homological}), and $r=1$ gives flatness
(\cref{osq:pc:thm:exhaustion}). If $r\ge2$, take $G$ minimal among the joins $F_i\vee F_j$, $i\ne j$; the $t\ge2$ generators inside $G$ join pairwise to $G$ and
none equals $G$, so $\mathsf K_{<G}$ is $t$ isolated vertices, $\beta_{2,G}=t-1>0$, and the flat dimension is at least two.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A marked face lattice \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:cor:reconstruct}
Among the nonzero radical geometric monomial ideals the flat ones are exactly the $I_F$; with $A_{\mathscr C}=I_{\{0\}}$, their inclusion order is
anti-isomorphic to the face lattice and tensor product corresponds to join.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{osq:pc:thm:flatclass,osq:pc:thm:products}.
\end{proof}

This reconstructs the face lattice from the ring \emph{with its geometric monomial structure marked}; it does not show that an abstract ring isomorphism of
cores preserves the monomials or the face lattice (26).

\begin{theorem}[A homological characterization of simplicial cones \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:simplicial}
The following are equivalent: (i) $\mathscr C$ is simplicial; (ii) every facet omits exactly one ray; (iii) $\mathfrak p_F$ is flat for every facet $F$;
(iv) $\fd A_{\mathscr C}(F)=1$ for every facet $F$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is clear, and (ii), (iii), (iv) are equivalent by \cref{osq:pc:prop:faceprime,osq:pc:thm:flatclass}. Assume (ii). Every ray $\rho$ is
omitted by some facet, since the facets meet in $\{0\}$; that facet's functional is positive on $\rho$ and zero on the other rays, so in a linear relation among
ray vectors the coefficient of $\rho$ vanishes. The rays are linearly independent and span $\R^d$, so there are $d$ of them.
\end{proof}

The criterion concerns all facets: a nonsimplicial cone can have one facet omitting a single ray (26).

\begin{corollary}[Simplicial face dimensions \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:cor:simplicialface}
If $\mathscr C$ is simplicial, $\fd A_{\mathscr C}(F)=d-\dim F$ for every face $F$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The largest face disjoint from $F$ is spanned by the complementary rays; apply \cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti}.
\end{proof}

Through $A_{\mathscr C}\cong A_d$ this is 21's $\fd\mathsf F_U=|U|$ (\cref{osq:da:prop:faces}) with $|U|=d-\dim F$, and 21's
\cref{osq:da:cor:exactpd} adds $\pd A_{\mathscr C}(F)=d-\dim F+1$ \merge.

\paragraph{Examples, sharpness and coefficients.} Let $\mathscr C=\{(x,y,z):z\ge|x|,\ z\ge|y|\}$, the cone over a square, with rays through
$v_1=(1,1,1)$, $v_2=(1,-1,1)$, $v_3=(-1,-1,1)$, $v_4=(-1,1,1)$ and adjacent two-faces $F_{ij}=\rho_i\vee\rho_j$. The augmentation has the flat resolution
\[
 0\to I_{\mathscr C}\to I_{F_{12}}\oplus I_{F_{23}}\oplus I_{F_{34}}\oplus I_{F_{41}}\to\textstyle\bigoplus_{i=1}^4I_{\rho_i}\to A_{\mathscr C}\to D\to0
\]
of length three, where the unreduced simplex complex on four rays has length four. For the facet $F_{12}$, $\mathfrak p_{F_{12}}=I_{\rho_3}+I_{\rho_4}$, whose join
is the opposite facet $F_{34}$, disjoint from $F_{12}$, so
\[
 0\to I_{F_{34}}\xrightarrow{u\mapsto(u,-u)}I_{\rho_3}\oplus I_{\rho_4}\to A_{\mathscr C}\to A_{\mathscr C}(F_{12})\to0,
\]
and a cap module in the interior of $F_{34}$ gives $\Tor_2\ne0$: a facet quotient of flat dimension two although its codimension is one. For the ray
$F=\rho_1$ the disjoint nonzero faces are $\rho_2,\rho_3,\rho_4,F_{23},F_{34}$, the multiplicities are $(1,3,2)$ and the flat dimension is two; the top cone meets
$F$ (26, with a figure of the square section).

\begin{theorem}[Cube cones \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:cubes}
For $n\ge1$ let $\mathscr C_n=\{(x_1,\dots,x_n,z):z\ge|x_i|\ (1\le i\le n)\}$ and $F_\pm=\mathscr C_n\cap\{x_1=\pm z\}$. Then $\dim\mathscr C_n=n+1$, the $F_\pm$
are facets, and $\fd_{A_{\mathscr C_n}}A_{\mathscr C_n}(F_+)=n$, in the omnific and in the Gaussian omnific cores.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The section $z=1$ is the $n$-cube and $F_\pm$ are cones over opposite facets; $x_1=z=-x_1$ forces $z=0$ and then all $x_i=0$, so $F_+\cap F_-=\{0\}$ and
\cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti} gives $\ge n$; the only face of dimension $n+1$ is $\mathscr C_n$, which meets $F_+$. The embeddings are
\cref{osq:pc:prop:embedding}.
\end{proof}

By \cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti} a nonzero proper face quotient has flat dimension at most $d-1$, and the cube cones attain it on a facet (26). The multiplicities
of the reduced face-labelled flat resolutions, starting with the single $A_{\mathscr C}$ in degree $0$, are: $d$-orthant and $D$: $\binom d0,\dots,\binom dd$
($\fd=d$); square cone and $D$: $(1,4,4,1)$ ($3$); square cone and a facet: $(1,2,1)$ ($2$); square cone and a ray: $(1,3,2)$ ($2$); any cone and
$A_{\mathscr C}/I_{\mathscr C}$: $(1,1)$ ($1$); cone over a $3$-cube and $D$: $(1,8,12,6,1)$ ($4$); cone over a $3$-cube and a facet: $(1,4,4,1)$ ($3$); cone
over an octahedron and $D$: $(1,6,12,8,1)$ ($4$). The quotient $A_{\mathscr C}/I_{\mathscr C}$ keeps the boundary faces, usually has zero divisors, and is
radical but not a face-prime quotient (26).

\begin{corollary}[Squarefree homology survives rational roots \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:cor:squarefree}
Let $\mathfrak q\subsetneq K[\mathbf x]=K[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ be a nonzero squarefree monomial ideal with irredundant supports $S_1,\dots,S_r$, and in $A_d$ let
$\mathfrak r=\sum_iI_{S_i}$. Then $\fd_{A_d}(A_d/\mathfrak r)=\pd_{K[\mathbf x]}(K[\mathbf x]/\mathfrak q)$, and the face-labelled multiplicities equal the
multigraded Betti numbers of $K[\mathbf x]/\mathfrak q$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Both join semilattices are the unions of the $S_i$, and the lcm-lattice formula \cite{GPW} gives the Betti numbers by the same interval (crosscut) homology as
\eqref{osq:pc:eq:beta}; take the top degree (\cref{osq:pc:thm:exactfd}).
\end{proof}

Projective dimension is not preserved: for one generator the ordinary quotient has projective dimension one, the root-face quotient two
(\cref{osq:pc:cor:pdbounds}); only the flat dimension and its face topology survive (26).

\begin{corollary}[Coefficient independence \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:cor:coefficients}
For fixed $\mathscr C$ and $\mathcal F$, the $\beta_{p,G}$ and $\fd(A_{\mathscr C}/\mathfrak r_{\mathcal F})$ do not depend on $D\subseteq K$, and depend on $K$
only through its characteristic; the real omnific and Gaussian omnific realizations agree.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The boundary matrices have entries $0,\pm1$, so their ranks depend only on the prime field, and \cref{osq:pc:thm:exactfd} holds for every unital $D\subseteq K$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Arithmetic modules.}

\begin{proposition}[A nonzero scalar removes the tail \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:prop:scalar}
For $0\ne a\in D$, $aA_{\mathscr C}=aD\oplus\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ and $A_{\mathscr C}/aA_{\mathscr C}\cong D/aD$; if $a\notin D^\times$,
$\fd(D/aD)=\pd(D/aD)=1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$a\Pi_{\mathscr C}=\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ since $\Pi_{\mathscr C}$ is a $K$-space. $0\to A_{\mathscr C}\xrightarrow{a}A_{\mathscr C}\to D/aD\to0$ is a free resolution,
and $D/aD$ is not flat, multiplication by $a$ becoming zero.
\end{proof}

This is 12's \cref{osq:hd:prop:finite}(i) for cones, and an elementary consequence of divisible tail coefficients, not a new finite-quotient theorem for $\Oz$
(26; compare \cref{osq:thm:quotients}).

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic modules over a principal-ideal core \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:arithmetic}
Let $D$ be a principal ideal domain, not a field, and $N\ne0$ a $D$-module regarded as an $A_{\mathscr C}$-module through $\ct$. Then $\fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}N=1$
if $N$ is torsion over $D$ and $\fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}N=d$ otherwise. This applies to $D=\Z$ and $D=\Z[i]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Finitely generated torsion $D$-modules are finite sums of $D/aD$, so the filtered union $N_{\mathrm{tor}}$ has $\fd\le1$, and $\fd N_{\mathrm{tor}}=1$ if
$N_{\mathrm{tor}}\ne0$ because some $a\ne0$ kills a nonzero element. If $V=N/N_{\mathrm{tor}}\ne0$, $V$ is flat over the principal ideal domain $D$, so
tensoring \cref{osq:pc:prop:cellular} over $D$ with $V$ stays exact, $A_{\mathscr C}\otimes_DV$ is flat and $I_G\otimes_DV\cong I_G\otimes_K(K\otimes_DV)$ is a
sum of copies of $I_G$: a flat resolution of $V$ of length $d$. With $\mathcal W=\mathcal W_{\mathscr C,b}$, degree $b$ leaves
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:arithmeticdetector}
 \Tor_d^{A_{\mathscr C}}(V,\mathcal W)_b\cong K\otimes_DV\ne0,
\end{equation}
nonzero because localizing the torsion-free $V$ at $D\setminus\{0\}$ and extending scalars to $K$ is faithful. Since $a$ acts invertibly on the $K$-space
$\mathcal W$, $\Tor_j(D/aD,\mathcal W)=0$ for all $j\ge0$, hence for $N_{\mathrm{tor}}$, and the long exact sequence of $0\to N_{\mathrm{tor}}\to N\to V\to0$
gives $\Tor_d(N,\mathcal W)\cong\Tor_d(V,\mathcal W)$ and the upper bound $d$.
\end{proof}

All these modules have $\Tor_{>0}(D,N)=0$ (\cref{osq:pc:thm:homological}); the theorem classifies modules acting through $\ct$ only, not all modules over a core or
the class ring (26). For the orthant the non-torsion value $d$ contains 12's $\fd D=d$ (\cref{osq:hd:cor:fd}).

\begin{remark}[Lattice modules over every cone \merge]\label{osq:pc:rem:lattice}
The proof of \cref{osq:tn:thm:syzygy}(ii) uses only that $A=D\oplus\Pi$ with $\Pi$ a $K$-space ideal of $K\oplus\Pi$ inside a field and $K\cap\Pi=0$; so it applies
to $A_{\mathscr C}$ with $\Pi=\Pi_{\mathscr C}$, not finitely generated by \cref{osq:pc:thm:radical}. For a coefficient lattice $M$ of rank $r\ge2$ and
$J=X^gL(M)$, $0\ne g\in P_{\mathscr C}$, the argument of \cref{osq:hd:thm:fdlattice}, with $\fd\Pi_{\mathscr C}=d-1$ (\cref{osq:pc:thm:facebetti,osq:pc:thm:exactfd}
for the rays) and the cap module $\mathcal W_{\mathscr C,b}$ in place of $V_{[d]}$, gives for $d\ge2$
\[
 \fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}L(M)=d,\qquad \fd_{A_{\mathscr C}}(A_{\mathscr C}/J)=d+1,
\]
so $\operatorname{w.gl.dim}A_{\mathscr C}\ge d+1$ whenever $K\ne\Frac D$ (take $M=D+Dc$, $c\in K\setminus\Frac D$). This improves the lower bound $d$ of 26's
Question~13.2, as 12 and 21 do for $A_d$ (\cref{osq:hd:sub:dimensions,osq:da:thm:lattice}). For $d=1$, $A_{\mathscr C}\cong A_1=T_\Q$.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Passage to the omnific ring is not flat.} The injection $\lambda_\omega$ pulls back the order of $\No$ to a total order on $\Q^d$ whose positive
cone contains $P_{\mathscr C}\setminus\{0\}$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pc:eq:totalcore}
 T_{\lambda_\omega}=D\oplus\bigoplus_{g\in\Q^d,\ \lambda_\omega(g)>0}KX^g\supseteq A_{\mathscr C},
\end{equation}
a set-sized ring with the same fraction field (\cref{osq:pc:prop:fractions}) and a compatible $\ct$.

\begin{lemma}[Two-ray syzygies have zero constants \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:lem:syzygy}
If $u,v$ are nonzero rational vectors on distinct rays and $rX^u+sX^v=0$ in $A_{\mathscr C}$, then $\ct(r)=\ct(s)=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Neither $u-v$ nor $v-u$ is in $\mathscr C$ (else the face of $u$ would contain $v$). The coefficient of degree $u$ in $rX^u+sX^v$ is $\ct(r)$, the degree $u-v$
being absent from $A_{\mathscr C}$; similarly for $v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A two-monomial nonflatness certificate \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:thm:nonflat}
If $d\ge2$, $A_{\mathscr C}\hookrightarrow T_{\lambda_\omega}$ is not flat, and in the real and Gaussian realizations the inclusion into $\Oz$ or $\GOz$ fails
the same finite equational criterion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $u,v$ on distinct rays with $\lambda_\omega(u)>\lambda_\omega(v)$; then $z=X^{u-v}\in T_{\lambda_\omega}$ and $X^u-zX^v=0$. If the inclusion were flat,
the relation vector $(1,-z)$ would be a finite combination, with coefficients in $T_{\lambda_\omega}$, of relation vectors of $(X^u,X^v)$ over $A_{\mathscr C}$
\cite[Tag~00HK]{StacksFlat}; by \cref{osq:pc:lem:syzygy} all their coordinates have constant term zero, and the zero-constant elements form an ideal of
$T_{\lambda_\omega}$, so the first coordinate cannot be $1$. In $\Oz$, $z$ is the monomial $\omega^{\lambda_\omega(u)-\lambda_\omega(v)}$ and $\Pi$ is an ideal
(for $\GOz$, $\Pi_\C$), so the same contradiction applies to finite combinations in the full target; this is a finite relation, with no proper-class tensor
category.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[An explicit pair in $\Oz$ \src{26}]\label{osq:pc:ex:pair}
For the orthant $\R_{\ge0}^2$ with $\lambda_\omega(x,y)=(x+y)\omega+y$, the coordinate monomials become $b=\omega^\omega$ and $a=\omega^{\omega+1}$, and
$a-\omega b=0$ in $\Oz$; every syzygy of the pair in the core has zero constant terms, so this relation with first coefficient $1$ does not descend.
\end{example}

For the orthant the conclusion is the nonflatness in 12's \cref{osq:hd:thm:collapse}, proved there by an intersection certificate in $T_\Gamma$ with a real
embedding; 26's equational certificate, with a lexicographic embedding and the explicit failure in $\Oz$, is a second route. Partial exponent order creates
independent directions of divisibility, which the total order of $\No$ compares; so the flat dimensions of cores do not transfer to $\Oz$ by flat base change.
The obstruction does not deny the embeddings, the fraction field or the retraction $\ct$, and it says nothing about embeddings of one-dimensional cores; it
is exactly the failure of the displayed finite test for $d\ge2$ (26).

\paragraph{Dependencies and pitfalls (26).} Flat face ideals rest on facet subtraction, finite supports, principal exhaustion and filtered colimits; the
reduced resolution on degreewise simplex exactness and same-label scalar cancellation; the exact dimension on the cap module and its degree-shifted colimit;
the face formula on the outside-vertex complex and the explicit contraction of a polytopal boundary minus a face; simpliciality on a minimal pair join and
facet normals; the arithmetic dichotomy on scalar resolutions, torsion theory over a principal ideal domain and the full-face cap; nonflatness on the
absence of a positive difference between two rays. 26 records these obligations: a principal ideal $X^qA_{\mathscr C}$ has coefficient space $D$, not $K$,
at $q$, so the exhaustion always uses a strictly smaller shift; the $I_G$ are flat but not projective, and a scalar cancellation does not make them free;
the cap module is defined before use and its late transition maps are identities on $K$; only nonzero joins are labels, and a face inside the retained face
gets no spurious degree-one class, while a ray disjoint from it correctly contributes $\widetilde H_{-1}(\{\varnothing\};K)=K$; and all rings, resolutions and test
modules are sets, the statement about $\Oz$ being a finite relation. The main theorems use no unrefereed repository theorem as a premise.

\section{Large internal fields and the binomial quotient}
\label{osq:sec:internal}

The universal theorem (\cref{osq:thm:universal}) describes what a set-sized target
can see of $\Oz$: every purely infinite element dies, and only the constant term
survives. This section, taken from manuscript~07 together with one proposition of
manuscript~06, shows how much survives in a large target once a single purely infinite
element becomes a \emph{unit}. The answer is a great deal: the target then contains a
real closed Hahn field into which all of $\No$ embeds as an ordered field. In the
nonzero binomial quotient $\Qa_a=\Oz/(1+\omega^a)$, which has no nonzero set-sized ring
image at all, the same mechanism produces an algebraically closed class field containing
a copy of $\SC$, exact finite cyclotomic algebras over it, and an atomless Boolean
algebra of idempotents.

The dependence of the results is as follows (07). An ordered additive compression of
$\No$ and the closedness of set-sized Hahn fields give a copy of $\No$ inside the
compressed field $\FF_a$ (\cref{osq:if:prop:closed,osq:if:thm:compression});
localization transfers $\FF_a$ into every quotient in which a suitable purely infinite
element is invertible (\cref{osq:if:thm:transfer}); a support argument gives exact
binomial kernels (\cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel}); and finite Chinese remainder
decompositions give the internal field $\EE_a$ and the Cantor algebra
(\cref{osq:if:cor:Ea,osq:if:thm:cantor}). The absence of small images of $\Qa_a$
comes from the other branch, \cref{osq:thm:universal,osq:thm:reflection}. No
factorization conjecture enters either chain. What manuscript~07 calls its Main
Theorem~B is \cref{osq:if:thm:transfer} together with \cref{osq:if:thm:compression},
and its Main Theorem~C is the combination of
\cref{osq:if:lem:localization,osq:if:cor:Ea,osq:if:thm:cantor} with the absence of
small images of $\Qa_a$ recorded before \cref{osq:if:lem:localization}.

\subsection{Compressed exponent fields}\label{osq:if:sub:compressed}

Fix $a>0$. Recall from \eqref{osq:eq:Ha} and \cref{osq:lem:Ha} that
$H_a=\{h\in\No:n|h|<a\text{ for all ordinary }n\ge1\}$ is a convex divisible
subgroup of $(\No,+)$ containing a proper class of positive elements, and that
$\FF_a(k)=\hahn{k}{H_a}$ is a field for every set field $k$. For $k=\R$ and $k=\C$ we
realize these fields inside the surreals and surcomplex numbers,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:Fa}
\begin{aligned}
 \FF_a&=\FF_a(\R)=\{f\in\No:\supp f\subseteq H_a\},\\
 \FF_a(i)&=\FF_a(\C)=\{f\in\SC:\supp f\subseteq H_a\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Taking real and imaginary parts of coefficients shows $\FF_a(i)=\FF_a+i\FF_a$.
Manuscript~07 calls them \emph{compressed exponent fields}; the phrase refers to the
restriction on exponents, not to finiteness of supports. Both are proper classes.
Manuscript~07 checks directly that $H_a$ is a subgroup by the inequality
$n|h+h'|\le n|h|+n|h'|<a/2+a/2$, using the defining inequalities at $2n$; this is
part of \cref{osq:lem:Ha}.

\begin{proposition}[Closedness of the compressed fields \src{07, 24}]\label{osq:if:prop:closed}
The class $\FF_a$ is a real closed subfield of $\No$, and $\FF_a(i)$ is an algebraically
closed subfield of $\SC$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Since $H_a$ is a subgroup, sums and products of series supported in $H_a$ are supported
in $H_a$; the inverse of a nonzero Hahn series has support in the subgroup generated by
its own support (factor out the leading monomial and use the Hahn geometric series), so
it stays in $H_a$ as well. Hence $\FF_a$ and $\FF_a(i)$ are subfields
(\cref{osq:lem:Ha}).

Let $P$ be a nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in $\FF_a(i)$. The union of the
supports of its finitely many coefficients is a set; its rational span is a set-sized
divisible ordered subgroup $G\subseteq H_a$, because $H_a$ is a divisible subgroup. The
series with support in $G$ form the set-sized Hahn fields $\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)\subseteq
\FF_a$ and $\C(\!(\omega^G)\!)\subseteq\FF_a(i)$, whose operations are those of $\No$ and
$\SC$, and $P$ has coefficients in $\C(\!(\omega^G)\!)$. For divisible $G$ this field is
algebraically closed by the Hahn-field theorem \cite[Corollary~4]{Poonen} (stated there
for well-ordered supports; the substitution $t^g=\omega^{-g}$ converts). So $P$ has a root
in $\C(\!(\omega^G)\!)\subseteq\FF_a(i)$, and $\FF_a(i)$ is algebraically closed.

For the real field, note first that $\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)$ is real closed. If
$0<f\in\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)$, write a square root of $f$ in $\C(\!(\omega^G)\!)$ as $u+iv$
with $u,v\in\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)$; then $u^2-v^2=f$ and $2uv=0$. If $u=0$ then
$f=-v^2\le0$, which is impossible; so $v=0$ and $u^2=f$. If $Q$ has odd degree and
coefficients in $\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)$, coefficientwise conjugation is an automorphism of
$\C(\!(\omega^G)\!)$ fixing $Q$, so the nonreal roots of $Q$ occur in conjugate pairs
with equal multiplicities, and an odd number of roots counted with multiplicity must be
real. An ordered field in which positive elements are squares and odd-degree polynomials
have roots is real closed. Now let $0<f\in\FF_a$, or let $Q$ be of odd degree over
$\FF_a$; choosing $G$ as above for $f$ or for the coefficients of $Q$, the required square
root or root lies in $\R(\!(\omega^G)\!)\subseteq\FF_a$. Hence $\FF_a$ is real closed.
Only set-sized instances of the classical theorem have been used.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Bounded in the ambient field, yet a proper class \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:rem:bounded}
Every positive $f\in\FF_a$ satisfies $\omega^{-a}<f<\omega^a$: its leading exponent $h$
satisfies $|h|<a/2$ and its leading coefficient is a positive real. A field contained in
such an ambient interval need not be small, since the interval is itself a proper class;
$\FF_a$ is a proper class, and by \cref{osq:if:thm:compression} it even contains an
ordered-field copy of $\No$. Bounds in the surrounding field do not give bounds inside an
isomorphic copy of $\No$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{An ordered additive compression of the surreals}\label{osq:if:sub:compression}

Knowing that $\FF_a$ contains Hahn fields of every set size (\cref{osq:lem:Ha}) would
already show considerable largeness. Manuscript~07 does more: it embeds all of $\No$ into
$\FF_a$ as an ordered field. Define
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:theta}
 \vartheta(x)=\frac12\Bigl(\frac{x}{1+|x|}-3\Bigr),\qquad
 \vartheta:\No\longrightarrow(-2,-1).
\end{equation}
For $x\ge0$ the inner fraction is $x/(1+x)=1-1/(1+x)\in[0,1)$, and for $x<0$ it is
$x/(1-x)=-1+1/(1-x)\in(-1,0)$. Each branch is strictly increasing and they agree at $0$,
so $\vartheta$ is strictly increasing with values in $(-2,-1)$. For a real-coefficient
normal form put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:Psi}
 \Psi\Bigl(\sum_\gamma r_\gamma\omega^\gamma\Bigr)=\sum_\gamma r_\gamma\omega^{\vartheta(\gamma)},
 \qquad \Psi_a(x)=a\Psi(x).
\end{equation}
(Manuscript~07 writes $E_a$ for $\Psi_a$; the letter $\EE_a$ is reserved here for the
internal field of \cref{osq:if:cor:Ea}.)

\begin{lemma}[Ordered additive compression \src{07}]\label{osq:if:lem:compression}
The map $\Psi_a:(\No,+)\to(H_a,+)$ is an injective, order-preserving, $\R$-linear
homomorphism of additive groups.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A strictly increasing map sends a reverse well-ordered set to a reverse well-ordered set,
so the support $\vartheta(\supp x)$ is a reverse well-ordered set and $\Psi(x)$ exists.
Since $\vartheta$ is injective, distinct exponents stay distinct, and the coefficient of
$\Psi(x)$ at $\vartheta(\gamma)$ is $x_\gamma$; hence coefficientwise addition, with all
cancellations, and multiplication by real scalars are preserved. If $x\ne0$, the greatest
exponent $\gamma_0$ of $\supp x$ is sent to the greatest exponent $\vartheta(\gamma_0)$ of
$\supp\Psi(x)$ with the same coefficient; since the sign of a nonzero normal form is the
sign of its leading coefficient, $\Psi$ maps positive elements to positive elements, and
being additive it is injective and order preserving. The leading exponent of a nonzero
$\Psi(x)$ lies in $(-2,-1)$, so $\Psi(x)$ is infinitesimal and $n|\Psi(x)|<1$ for every
ordinary $n\ge1$. Multiplying by $a>0$ gives $n|\Psi_a(x)|<a$, that is,
$\Psi_a(x)\in H_a$, and multiplication by the positive surreal $a$ preserves additivity,
$\R$-linearity and order.
\end{proof}

The map $\vartheta$ is not additive, and $\Psi$ is not asserted to be multiplicative. The
construction deliberately has two levels: first an additive exponent group is compressed,
and only then is the additive map used as a substitution on monomials.

\begin{theorem}[A full surreal field in every compressed field \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:thm:compression}
The formula
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:Theta}
 \Theta_a\Bigl(\sum_\gamma r_\gamma\omega^\gamma\Bigr)=\sum_\gamma r_\gamma\omega^{\Psi_a(\gamma)}
\end{equation}
defines an injective ordered-field homomorphism $\Theta_a:\No\hookrightarrow\FF_a$ fixing
$\R$. It preserves every set-indexed strongly summable family. Extending coefficients,
$x+iy\mapsto\Theta_a(x)+i\Theta_a(y)$, gives an injective field homomorphism
$\SC\hookrightarrow\FF_a(i)$ fixing $\C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The support of the right side of \eqref{osq:if:eq:Theta} is $\Psi_a(\supp x)$, the image of
a reverse well-ordered set under a strictly increasing map into $H_a$
(\cref{osq:if:lem:compression}); so the output exists and lies in $\FF_a$. If
$(x_\lambda)$ is a strongly summable set-indexed family, the union of the supports is
reverse well ordered and each exponent receives finitely many contributions; since
$\Psi_a$ is injective and strictly increasing, the same holds for the family
$(\Theta_a(x_\lambda))$ with the same contributions at $\Psi_a(\gamma)$ as at $\gamma$,
so $\Theta_a(\sum_\lambda x_\lambda)=\sum_\lambda\Theta_a(x_\lambda)$.

For multiplication, write $x=\sum r_\gamma\omega^\gamma$ and $y=\sum s_\delta\omega^\delta$.
Because $\Psi_a$ is additive and injective,
$\Psi_a(\gamma)+\Psi_a(\delta)=\Psi_a(\varepsilon)$ holds exactly when
$\gamma+\delta=\varepsilon$, and every sum $\Psi_a(\gamma)+\Psi_a(\delta)$ lies in the image
of $\Psi_a$. Hence the coefficient of $\Theta_a(x)\Theta_a(y)$ at $\Psi_a(\varepsilon)$ is
$\sum_{\gamma+\delta=\varepsilon}r_\gamma s_\delta=(xy)_\varepsilon$, and its coefficients
at exponents outside the image vanish; so $\Theta_a(xy)=\Theta_a(x)\Theta_a(y)$.
Additivity is clear, and constants are fixed because $\Psi_a(0)=0$. A nonzero $x$ has a
nonzero image whose leading coefficient is that of $x$, so $\Theta_a$ is injective and
preserves signs, hence order. It is an injective unital ring map between fields, hence a
field embedding. The complex extension is the same coefficient-and-support argument with
complex coefficients.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[\src{07}]\label{osq:if:ex:Theta}
Since $\vartheta(0)=-3/2$, one has $\Psi_a(1)=a\omega^{-3/2}$ and
\[
 \Theta_a(\omega)=\omega^{a\omega^{-3/2}} .
\]
\end{example}

No preservation of the ordinal embedding, of birthdays or simplicity, or of the surreal
exponential is asserted or needed: $\Theta_a$ is an explicit ordered-field embedding with a
controlled normal-form support image. Constructions of self-similar surreal subclasses and
strongly linear maps have a substantial prior literature, notably the surreal
substructures of Bagayoko and van der Hoeven \cite{BagayokoHoeven}. Manuscript~07 uses the
elementary construction above to make the transfer theorem independent of a general
classification of surreal substructures, and does not claim that surreal self-similarity
itself is new.

\subsection{Transfer by inverting a purely infinite element}\label{osq:if:sub:transfer}

\begin{lemma}[Multiplication by a purely infinite denominator \src{07}]\label{osq:if:lem:gf}
Let $0\ne g\in\Pi$ and choose $a>0$ with $a<\gamma$ for every $\gamma\in\supp g$ (possible
by \cref{osq:lem:gap}). If $f\in\FF_a$, then $gf\in\Pi$. The same holds for
$0\ne g\in\Pi_\C$ and $f\in\FF_a(i)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every $h\in\supp f$ satisfies $|h|<a/2$. Every exponent occurring in the product before
cancellation has the form $\gamma+h$ with $\gamma\in\supp g$, and
$\gamma+h>a-a/2>0$. Hahn multiplication is defined and cancellation cannot create an
exponent outside the sum of the supports, so $gf$ has strictly positive support and real
(respectively complex) coefficients.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Localization and quotient transfer \src{07}]\label{osq:if:thm:transfer}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{osq:if:lem:gf}, the subfield $\FF_a$ of $\No$ lies in the
localization $\Oz[1/g]\subseteq\No$. If $q:\Oz\to B$ is a unital homomorphism to a nonzero
class ring and $q(g)$ is invertible in $B$, then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:transfer}
 \iota_g(f)=q(gf)\,q(g)^{-1}\qquad(f\in\FF_a)
\end{equation}
is an injective field homomorphism $\FF_a\hookrightarrow B$, and $\iota_g\circ\Theta_a$ is
an injective field homomorphism $\No\hookrightarrow B$. For $q:\GOz\to B$ and
$0\ne g\in\Pi_\C$ with $q(g)$ invertible, the same formula gives an injective field
homomorphism $\FF_a(i)\hookrightarrow B$, and hence a copy of $\SC$ in $B$. In either case
$B$ is a proper class.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Inside $\No$, $f=(gf)/g$ with $gf\in\Pi\subseteq\Oz$ by \cref{osq:if:lem:gf}, so
$f\in\Oz[1/g]$. The elements of $q(\Oz)$ commute pairwise, and $q(g)^{-1}$ commutes with
every element $y$ commuting with $q(g)$ (multiply $q(g)y=yq(g)$ on both sides by
$q(g)^{-1}$). Hence $q(\Oz)$ and $q(g)^{-1}$ generate a commutative subring of $B$, and all
computations below take place there; no commutativity of $B$ is needed. The map
\eqref{osq:if:eq:transfer} is additive and $\iota_g(1)=1$. For $f,f'\in\FF_a$ the
elements $gf$, $gf'$, $gff'$ lie in $\Oz$ and $(gf)(gf')=g\cdot(gff')$, so
\[
 \iota_g(f)\iota_g(f')=q(gf)q(gf')q(g)^{-2}=q(g)q(gff')q(g)^{-2}=\iota_g(ff').
\]
(Equivalently, $\iota_g$ is the restriction to $\FF_a$ of the extension of $q$ to
$\Oz[1/g]$ given by the universal property of localization.) If $f\ne0$ and
$\iota_g(f)=0$, then $1_B=\iota_g(f)\iota_g(f^{-1})=0$, contradicting $B\ne0$; so
$\iota_g$ is injective. Composing with \cref{osq:if:thm:compression} gives the copy of
$\No$. The complex case is identical, with \cref{osq:if:lem:gf} for $\Pi_\C$ and the
complex extension of $\Theta_a$. Finally, if $B$ were set-sized,
\cref{osq:thm:universal} would give $q(g)=0$, which is not invertible in a nonzero ring.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[\src{07}]\label{osq:if:rem:transfer}
If the target $B$ is noncommutative, the image of the localization still lies in a
commutative subring, as the proof shows; no commutativity condition on all of $B$ is
needed. The hypothesis on $a$ is always available in the full surreal exponent class, even
when the exponents of $g$ approach zero inside a smaller ordered group
(\cref{osq:lem:gap}). No inference of this kind is valid for an arbitrary fixed
set-sized exponent group without an additional lower-bound hypothesis.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Quotients by a unit-constant perturbation \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:cor:unitconstant}
If $0\ne g\in\Pi$, then $\Oz/(1+g)$ is nonzero and contains a class copy of $\No$. If
$0\ne g\in\Pi_\C$, then $\GOz/(1+g)$ is nonzero and contains a class copy of $\SC$. Neither
quotient has a unital homomorphism to a nonzero set-sized ring.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The element $1+g$ is nonconstant, hence a nonunit by \cref{osq:lem:units}, so the
quotients are nonzero. In the quotient $g=-1$ is a unit, so
\cref{osq:if:thm:transfer} applies. Since $\ct(1+g)=1$, the ideal $(1+g)$ has constant-term
image all of $\Z$ (respectively $\Z[i]$), and \cref{osq:thm:reflection} makes the
universal set-sized image the zero ring; a unital map from the zero ring exists only to the
zero ring.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A conditional statement about nonarithmetic primes \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:cor:primefield}
Let $P$ be a prime ideal of $\Oz$ such that $P\cap\Z=0$ and $P\not\subseteq\Pi$. Then
$\Oz/P$ contains a class copy of $\No$ and is a $\Q$-algebra. Likewise, if $P$ is a prime
ideal of $\GOz$ with $P\cap\Z[i]=0$ and $P\not\subseteq\Pi_\C$, then $\GOz/P$ contains a class
copy of $\SC$ and is a $\Q(i)$-algebra.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose $f\in P$ with nonzero constant term $c$. The series $f/c$ still lies in the omnific
ring: its constant term is $1$ and its other coefficients are real (respectively complex).
Since $f=c\cdot(f/c)$, $P$ is prime and $c\notin P$, we get $f/c\in P$. Write $f/c=1+g$
with $g$ purely infinite; $g\ne0$ because $c\notin P$. In the quotient $g=-1$ is a unit, and
\cref{osq:if:thm:transfer} applies. For every nonzero ordinary coefficient $d$ ($d\in\Z$,
respectively $d\in\Z[i]$), $g/d$ lies in the ring, and in the quotient
$d\cdot(-g/d)=-g=1$; so $d$ is invertible, which gives the $\Q$-, respectively
$\Q(i)$-, algebra structure.
\end{proof}

The corollary is deliberately conditional. Manuscript~07 does not assert that prime ideals
with these properties exist; see \cref{osq:if:sub:boundaries}. (Status (batch 34): with global choice they exist. Every maximal class ideal
containing $1+\omega^a$ is one (\cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax,osq:cr:prop:arithmetic}), and 24 proves this corollary again, with a proper-class
Hahn field in place of $\No$ (\cref{osq:cr:sub:residues}).)

\begin{example}[Invertibility cannot be replaced by nonvanishing \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:ex:nilpotent}
The quotient $\Oz/(\omega^a)$ is nonzero, and the class of $\omega^{a/2}$ is a nonzero
element of square zero: it is nonzero because $\omega^{a/2}/\omega^a=\omega^{-a/2}\notin\Oz$.
Since $(\omega^a)\subseteq\Pi$, this quotient still maps onto $\Z$ by constant terms, and so
it cannot contain a unital copy of $\Q$: composing such a copy with that map would give a
unital map $\Q\to\Z$. A surviving nilpotent and a surviving unit are therefore
substantively different.
\end{example}

The same mechanism, with a fraction field in place of the quotient, applies to every prime
ideal not containing the purely infinite ideal. Here $X^g$ is the monomial of
$\hahn{k}{\No}$, which is $\omega^g$ when $k=\R$ or $k=\C$.

\begin{proposition}[A scaled field in every non-arithmetic residue field \src{06}]
\label{osq:if:prop:reservoir}
Let $k$ be a set field, $D\subseteq k$ a unital subring, $A=\A_{D,k}$, and let $P$ be a
prime class ideal of $A$ with $\Pi_k\not\subseteq P$. There exists $a>0$ for which the
class field $\FF_a(k)=\hahn{k}{H_a}$ embeds in $\Frac(A/P)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose $f\in\Pi_k\setminus P$ and write $f=X^gh$ with $g>0$ and $h\in\Pi_k$
(\cref{osq:lem:gap} applied to $\supp f$). Then $X^g\notin P$, since otherwise $f\in P$.
Put $a=g/2$ and $m=X^a$. As $m^2=X^g\notin P$ and $P$ is prime, $\bar m\ne0$ in the domain
$A/P$. Since $m\FF_a(k)\subseteq\Pi_k\subseteq A$ (\cref{osq:lem:Ha}), we may define
\[
 \iota(x)=\frac{\overline{mx}}{\bar m}\in\Frac(A/P)\qquad(x\in\FF_a(k)).
\]
Additivity and $\iota(1)=1$ are immediate. Multiplicativity follows by reducing the
identity $(mx)(my)=m(mxy)$ in $A$ and dividing by $\bar m^2$. For $x\ne0$, the identity
$(mx)(m/x)=m^2$ in $A$ shows $\overline{mx}\ne0$, because $\overline{m^2}\ne0$. Thus the
unital field homomorphism $\iota$ is injective.
\end{proof}

This is the scaled-field collision mechanism of \cref{osq:lem:collision} in a fraction
field. The conclusion says more than that the residue field is large: it contains a
specific Hahn field built on all exponent scales infinitesimal relative to one positive
$a$. It is a necessary structural condition on such residue fields; manuscript~06 states
that it does not classify those prime ideals, assert that they exist, or assert that
every field of this form is a residue field.

\begin{remark}[The composed embedding \merge]\label{osq:if:rem:composition}
Let $P$ be a prime class ideal of $\Oz$ with $\Pi\not\subseteq P$. Then there is an
injective field homomorphism $\No\hookrightarrow\Frac(\Oz/P)$ whose first factor is an
ordered-field embedding,
\[
 \No\xrightarrow{\ \Theta_a\ }\FF_a\xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }\Frac(\Oz/P).
\]
Indeed, \cref{osq:if:prop:reservoir} with $(D,k)=(\Z,\R)$ gives $a>0$ and an injective field
homomorphism $\iota:\FF_a\to\Frac(\Oz/P)$, and \cref{osq:if:thm:compression} gives
$\Theta_a$; a composite of injective field homomorphisms is one. With $(D,k)=(\Z[i],\C)$ and
the complex extension of $\Theta_a$, every prime $P$ of $\GOz$ with $\Pi_\C\not\subseteq P$
gives $\SC\hookrightarrow\Frac(\GOz/P)$. Neither source states this composition.

The hypotheses of \cref{osq:if:prop:reservoir} and \cref{osq:if:cor:primefield} are
different. If $P\cap\Z=0$ and $P\not\subseteq\Pi$, then $\Pi\not\subseteq P$: otherwise,
for $x\in P$ we would have $x-\ct(x)\in\Pi\subseteq P$, hence $\ct(x)\in P\cap\Z=0$, so
$P\subseteq\Pi$. Conversely, $\Pi\not\subseteq P$ forces $P\cap\Z=0$, since a nonzero
$n\in P$ would give $\Pi=n\Pi\subseteq P$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}), but it allows
$P\subseteq\Pi$, for instance $P=0$, where the statement is the trivial
$\Frac(\Oz)=\No$ (\cref{osq:prop:fractions}). Thus 07's hypothesis is the stronger one and
yields the stronger conclusion (a copy of $\No$ inside $\Oz/P$ itself, and a
$\Q$-algebra structure), while 06's hypothesis also covers primes contained in $\Pi$, with
the conclusion only in the fraction field.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The binomial quotient and its localization}\label{osq:if:sub:binomial}

Fix $a>0$ and write
\[
 \Qa_a=\Oz/(1+\omega^a),\qquad q_a:\Oz\longrightarrow\Qa_a
\]
for the quotient map (07's $B_a$). The element $1+\omega^a$ is a nonunit
(\cref{osq:lem:units}), so $\Qa_a\ne0$; and since $\ct(1+\omega^a)=1$,
\cref{osq:thm:reflection} shows that $\Qa_a$ has no unital homomorphism to a nonzero
set-sized ring. A purely arithmetic calculation shows why: in a set-sized target
$\omega^a$ becomes $0$ (\cref{osq:thm:universal}), so $1+\omega^a$ becomes $1$, and a
target in which it vanishes has $1=0$. Its failure to have small ring images is therefore
not caused by its being zero, a field, or a domain; it is none of these by
\cref{osq:if:cor:boolean}. By \cref{osq:if:cor:unitconstant} it contains a copy of $\No$;
the rest of this section identifies much more of its internal structure.

The support description of the localization
\[
 \Oz[\omega^{-a}]=\{f\in\No:\supp f\subseteq[-Na,\infty)\text{ for some ordinary }N\ge0\}
\]
is \cref{osq:prop:locsupport}; manuscripts~04 and~07 both prove it. (07 calls this ring
$L_a$.)

\begin{lemma}[Localization of the binomial quotient \src{07}]\label{osq:if:lem:localization}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\omega^a\FF_a\subseteq\Pi$; in particular $\FF_a\subseteq\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$.
\item There is a unique ring homomorphism $\widetilde q_a:\Oz[\omega^{-a}]\to\Qa_a$
extending $q_a$. It is surjective with kernel $(1+\omega^a)\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$, so
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:localquotient}
 \Qa_a\cong\Oz[\omega^{-a}]/(1+\omega^a)\Oz[\omega^{-a}] .
\end{equation}
\item The restriction of $\widetilde q_a$ to $\FF_a$ is the injective field homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:iota}
 \iota_a(f)=-q_a(\omega^af)\qquad(f\in\FF_a).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Every $h\in H_a$ satisfies $a+h>0$, so translating a support in $H_a$ by $a$ gives a
strictly positive support (\cref{osq:lem:Ha}); then $f=\omega^{-a}(\omega^af)$.

(ii) The subring of $\No$ generated by $\Oz$ and $\omega^{-a}$ consists of the finite sums
$\sum_{j\le N}h_j\omega^{-ja}=\omega^{-Na}\sum_{j\le N}h_j\omega^{(N-j)a}$, so every element
has the form $\omega^{-Na}h$ with $N\ge0$ and $h\in\Oz$. Any extension of $q_a$ sends
$\omega^{-a}$ to $q_a(\omega^a)^{-1}=-1$, which proves uniqueness; define
$\widetilde q_a(\omega^{-Na}h)=(-1)^Nq_a(h)$. This is well defined: if
$\omega^{-Na}h=\omega^{-Ma}h'$ with $N\le M$, then $h'=\omega^{(M-N)a}h$ and
$(-1)^Mq_a(h')=(-1)^M(-1)^{M-N}q_a(h)=(-1)^Nq_a(h)$. Writing two elements over a common
power $\omega^{-Na}$ shows that $\widetilde q_a$ is a ring homomorphism; it extends $q_a$
and is surjective. If $\widetilde q_a(\omega^{-Na}h)=0$, then $q_a(h)=0$, so
$h=(1+\omega^a)y$ with $y\in\Oz$ and
$\omega^{-Na}h=(1+\omega^a)\omega^{-Na}y\in(1+\omega^a)\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$. Conversely
$\widetilde q_a((1+\omega^a)\omega^{-Na}y)=(-1)^Nq_a((1+\omega^a)y)=0$ for $y\in\Oz$.

(iii) By (i) and (ii), $\widetilde q_a(f)=\widetilde q_a(\omega^{-a}\cdot\omega^af)
=-q_a(\omega^af)$. A unital ring homomorphism from a field to a nonzero ring is injective.
\end{proof}

Henceforth $\FF_a$ is identified with its image $\iota_a(\FF_a)\subseteq\Qa_a$ whenever we
work inside $\Qa_a$; all coefficient fields below are embedded with the identity of
$\Qa_a$. This identification is not constant-term extraction: a nonintegral real scalar
$r$ is represented in $\Qa_a$ by the omnific integer $-r\omega^a$.

\subsection{Exact binomial kernels}\label{osq:if:sub:kernel}

For an ordinary integer $n\ge1$ put $x_n=q_a(\omega^{a/n})\in\Qa_a$. Certainly
$x_n^n=q_a(\omega^a)=-1$. The substantive question is whether the full ambient omnific
ring, with its arbitrary surreal exponents, creates additional polynomial relations over
$\FF_a$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact binomial kernel \src{07}]\label{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel}
For every $n\ge1$, evaluation at $x_n$ induces an injective ring homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:binomialinjection}
 \FF_a[T]/(T^n+1)\hookrightarrow\Qa_a .
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the kernel of $\FF_a[T]\to\Qa_a$, $T\mapsto x_n$, is exactly $(T^n+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The polynomial $T^n+1$ lies in the kernel. Dividing by this monic polynomial over the
field $\FF_a$, it suffices to show that no nonzero remainder
\[
 R(T)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r_jT^j\qquad(r_j\in\FF_a)
\]
vanishes at $x_n$. Put $\xi=\omega^{a/n}\in\Oz$; then $R(\xi)\in\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$ by
\cref{osq:if:lem:localization}(i), and $\widetilde q_a(R(\xi))=R(x_n)$.

\emph{The quotient in $\No$.} The series $U=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\omega^{-(k+1)a}$ has the
decreasing support $\{-(k+1)a\}$, and $(1+\omega^a)U=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\omega^{-(k+1)a}
+\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\omega^{-ka}=1$, each exponent receiving at most two contributions that
cancel except at exponent $0$. Hence $U=(1+\omega^a)^{-1}$ in $\No$, and multiplying the
finite sum $R(\xi)=\sum_jr_j\omega^{ja/n}$ by $U$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision}
 \frac{R(\xi)}{1+\omega^a}=\sum_{k\ge0}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^kr_j\,\omega^{(j/n-k-1)a},
\end{equation}
provided the right side is a strongly summable family, which we now check together with
the absence of cancellation between blocks.

\emph{Block cosets.} The support of the block indexed by $(j,k)$ lies in the coset
$c_{j,k}+H_a$ with centre $c_{j,k}=(j/n-k-1)a$, because $\supp r_j\subseteq H_a$. Distinct
pairs give distinct cosets. Indeed, $c_{j,k}-c_{j',k'}=(m/n)a$ with
$m=j-j'-n(k-k')\in\Z$, and $(m/n)a\in H_a$ only for $m=0$, since for $m\ne0$ one has
$n\cdot|(m/n)a|=|m|a\ge a$. From $j-j'=n(k-k')$ and $|j-j'|<n$ we get $j=j'$ and $k=k'$.
Cosets of $H_a$ are disjoint, so distinct blocks have disjoint supports, and each exponent
receives a contribution from at most one block.

\emph{Reverse well-ordering.} As $(j,k)$ runs over $\{0,\dots,n-1\}\times\N$, the integer
$j-n(k+1)$ runs bijectively over the integers $m\le-1$, so the centres are the points
$(m/n)a$, $m\le-1$, a strictly descending discrete progression with step $a/n$. Every
offset $h\in H_a$ satisfies $4n|h|<a$, that is, $|h|<a/(4n)$, so the block with centre
$(m/n)a$ lies in the open interval of radius $a/(4n)$ about its centre; these intervals are
pairwise disjoint and ordered as their centres. Given a nonempty subset $S$ of the union of
the supports, the set of $m$ whose block meets $S$ is a nonempty set of integers bounded
above by $-1$, so it has a largest element $m^*$; the elements of $S$ in block $m^*$
exceed all other elements of $S$, and since that block has reverse well-ordered support,
$S$ has a greatest element. All supports and the index family are sets. Hence the right
side of \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision} is a legitimate strongly summable Hahn
expression, and \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision} holds because Hahn multiplication
distributes over strongly summable families. (Equivalently, multiplying the right side by
$1+\omega^a$ cancels consecutive $k$-blocks and leaves exactly $R(\xi)$.)

\emph{Unbounded-below support.} Choose $j$ with $r_j\ne0$ and $h\in\supp r_j$. For every
$k\ge0$ the exponent $h+(j/n-k-1)a$ lies only in block $(j,k)$, so it occurs in
\eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision} with the nonzero coefficient $(-1)^k(r_j)_h$. Since
$h<a$ and $j/n<1$, this exponent is less than $a+a-(k+1)a=(1-k)a$, which is below $-Na$
as soon as $k\ge N+1$. Thus the support of \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision} is not
contained in $[-Na,\infty)$ for any ordinary $N$, and by \cref{osq:prop:locsupport} the
quotient $R(\xi)/(1+\omega^a)$ does not belong to $\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$.

\emph{Conclusion.} If $R(x_n)=0$, then $R(\xi)\in\ker\widetilde q_a
=(1+\omega^a)\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$ by \cref{osq:if:lem:localization}(ii), so
$R(\xi)=(1+\omega^a)u$ with $u\in\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$. Division in the field $\No$ identifies
$u$ with \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision}, a contradiction. Hence $R(x_n)\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[\src{07}]\label{osq:if:rem:hiddenfactors}
The proof does not restrict the exponents of an alleged ambient factor $u$ to rational
multiples of $a$; the full support characterization of $\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$ is exactly what
rules out such hidden factors. A calculation solely in a finite group algebra (the span of
the monomials $\omega^{ja/n}$) would not establish the theorem.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Internal algebraically closed field \src{07}]\label{osq:if:cor:Ea}
Let $u=x_2=q_a(\omega^{a/2})$. The subring $\EE_a=\FF_a[u]\subseteq\Qa_a$ is a field,
isomorphic over $\FF_a$ to $\FF_a(i)$ by $i\mapsto u$. It is algebraically closed and
contains a class copy of $\SC$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel} with $n=2$, $\EE_a\cong\FF_a[T]/(T^2+1)$. Since $\FF_a$
is real closed (\cref{osq:if:prop:closed}), $-1$ is not a square in it, $T^2+1$ is
irreducible, and the quotient is the field $\FF_a+i\FF_a=\FF_a(i)$, which is algebraically
closed by \cref{osq:if:prop:closed}. The complex extension of $\Theta_a$
(\cref{osq:if:thm:compression}) embeds $\SC$ in it.
\end{proof}

There is no order contradiction. Although $\omega^{a/2}$ is positive in $\Oz$, its square
becomes $-1$ in $\Qa_a$; the order of $\Oz$ does not descend to $\Qa_a$. The corollary is a
statement about rings and fields, not about ordered quotients.

More generally, finite real factorization and the Chinese remainder theorem give
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:finiteCRT}
 \FF_a[T]/(T^n+1)\cong
 \begin{cases}
 \EE_a^{\,m}, & n=2m,\\[2pt]
 \FF_a\times\EE_a^{\,m}, & n=2m+1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The roots of $T^n+1$ are the $n$ distinct ordinary complex numbers
$\exp(i\pi(2k+1)/n)$, which lie in $\C\subseteq\FF_a(i)$. For even $n$ none is real, and
the $m$ conjugate pairs give $m$ distinct monic quadratic factors with real coefficients,
irreducible over $\FF_a$ because their roots are not in $\FF_a$. For odd $n$ the only real
root is $-1$, and the remaining roots give $m$ such quadratics. All roots are simple, so
the factors are pairwise coprime, and each quadratic quotient is isomorphic to
$\FF_a(i)\cong\EE_a$. The isomorphisms in \eqref{osq:if:eq:finiteCRT} need not identify a
chosen imaginary unit in the same way at different stages; the dyadic tower below makes
coherent choices.

\subsection{The dyadic tower and its Cantor algebra}\label{osq:if:sub:cantor}

For $r\ge1$ define
\[
 \xi_r=q_a(\omega^{a/2^r})=x_{2^r},\qquad \mathcal S_r=\FF_a[\xi_r]\subseteq\Qa_a
\]
(07's $S_r$). Then $\xi_r^2=\xi_{r-1}$ for $r\ge2$, $\mathcal S_r\subseteq\mathcal S_{r+1}$,
and $\mathcal S_1=\EE_a$, so each $\mathcal S_r$ is an $\EE_a$-algebra. In this subsection
$i$ denotes the element $u=\xi_1$ of $\EE_a$; under $\EE_a\cong\FF_a(i)$ the ordinary
complex field $\C\subseteq\FF_a(i)$ corresponds to $\R+\R u\subseteq\EE_a$, and ordinary
complex numbers are read in $\EE_a$ through this identification.

\begin{lemma}[A single stage over the fixed complex field \src{07}]\label{osq:if:lem:stage}
Let $m=2^{r-1}$. As $\EE_a$-algebras,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:stage}
 \mathcal S_r\cong\EE_a[T]/(T^m-i),\qquad T\mapsto\xi_r .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The $\EE_a$-algebra map $\EE_a[T]\to\mathcal S_r$, $T\mapsto\xi_r$, is surjective, since
$\EE_a[\xi_r]=\FF_a[\xi_r^m,\xi_r]=\mathcal S_r$, and it kills $T^m-i$ because
$\xi_r^m=\xi_1=i$. For injectivity on the quotient, suppose
$\sum_{j<m}(a_j+b_ji)\xi_r^j=0$ with $a_j,b_j\in\FF_a$. Substituting $i=\xi_r^m$ gives
$\sum_{j<m}a_j\xi_r^j+\sum_{j<m}b_j\xi_r^{j+m}=0$, a polynomial relation over $\FF_a$ of
degree less than $2m=2^r$ satisfied by $\xi_r=x_{2^r}$. By
\cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel} with $n=2^r$ all its coefficients vanish, so all $a_j$ and
$b_j$ are zero.
\end{proof}

The roots of $T^m-i$ can be chosen in the ordinary complex subfield of $\EE_a$:
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:zetas}
 \zeta_{r,k}=\exp\Bigl(i\,\frac{\pi/2+2\pi k}{2^{r-1}}\Bigr)\qquad(k\in\Z/2^{r-1}\Z).
\end{equation}
The expression is evaluated in $\C$ and then embedded in $\EE_a$; no exponential function
on surcomplex arguments is assumed. These $m$ roots are distinct, and
\[
 \zeta_{r+1,k}^{\,2}=\zeta_{r,\,k\bmod 2^{r-1}}\qquad(k\in\Z/2^r\Z).
\]
Since the roots are distinct, the Chinese remainder theorem and \eqref{osq:if:eq:stage}
