give an isomorphism of $\EE_a$-algebras
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:stageCRT}
 \Phi_r:\mathcal S_r\longrightarrow\EE_a^{\Z/2^{r-1}\Z},\qquad
 P(\xi_r)\longmapsto\bigl(P(\zeta_{r,k})\bigr)_k\qquad(P\in\EE_a[T]).
\end{equation}
The inclusion $\mathcal S_r\subseteq\mathcal S_{r+1}$ replaces $\xi_r$ by $\xi_{r+1}^2$, so
$P(\xi_r)=P(\xi_{r+1}^2)$ has stage-$(r+1)$ coordinates
$P(\zeta_{r+1,k}^2)=P(\zeta_{r,k\bmod m})$. In coordinates the transition map is therefore
exactly
\[
 (c_k)_{k\bmod m}\longmapsto(c_{k\bmod m})_{k\bmod 2m},
\]
which repeats each coordinate on its two lifts. This compatibility, and not merely the
existence of separate finite product decompositions, is what identifies the direct limit.

\begin{theorem}[Cantor algebra theorem \src{07}]\label{osq:if:thm:cantor}
Let $\LC(\Z_2,\EE_a)$ be the class of functions from the $2$-adic integers $\Z_2$ to $\EE_a$
that factor through some finite quotient $\Z/2^N\Z$, with pointwise operations; thus
$\LC(\Z_2,\EE_a)=\bigcup_{N\ge0}\EE_a^{\Z/2^N\Z}$ with the transition maps repeating each
coordinate on its two lifts. There is an explicit $\EE_a$-algebra isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:cantor}
 \bigcup_{r\ge1}\mathcal S_r\;\cong\;\LC(\Z_2,\EE_a),
\end{equation}
under which $\xi_r$ corresponds to the function $z\mapsto\zeta_{r,\,z\bmod 2^{r-1}}$. The
left side is the subalgebra of $\Qa_a$ generated by $\FF_a$ and the classes of
$\omega^{a/2^r}$, $r\ge1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Identify $\EE_a^{\Z/2^{r-1}\Z}$ with the functions $\Z_2\to\EE_a$ factoring through
$\Z/2^{r-1}\Z$, via $c\mapsto(z\mapsto c_{z\bmod 2^{r-1}})$. By the computation of the
transition maps, the function attached to an element of $\mathcal S_r$ by $\Phi_r$ is the
same as the one attached by $\Phi_{r+1}$, so the $\Phi_r$ combine into a map $\Phi$ on the
increasing union; it is an $\EE_a$-algebra homomorphism, and it is injective because each
$\Phi_r$ is. Conversely, every function factoring through $\Z/2^N\Z$ lies in the image of
the bijection $\Phi_{N+1}$, so $\Phi$ is surjective. Evaluating $T$ at the roots gives the
function attached to $\xi_r$. Finally, $\xi_{r'}=\xi_r^{2^{r-r'}}\in\mathcal S_r$ for
$r'\le r$, so the union of the $\mathcal S_r$ is the subalgebra generated by $\FF_a$ and all
$\xi_r$.
\end{proof}

The isomorphism is an algebraic statement about a specified subalgebra; it is not a
classification of all of $\Qa_a$.

\begin{remark}[Locally constant functions \src{07}]\label{osq:if:rem:lc}
The topological terminology is justified: a locally constant function on the ordinary
compact space $\Z_2$ has a finite subcover of neighbourhoods of constancy and hence factors
through one finite quotient, and conversely such a factorization is locally constant. This
uses only the ordinary Cantor space; no topology is imposed on the proper-class field
$\EE_a$, and one can equally take the finite-factorization condition as the definition.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Evaluation at a point \src{07}]\label{osq:if:rem:evaluation}
Evaluation at a point $z\in\Z_2$ is a homomorphism from the subalgebra
\eqref{osq:if:eq:cantor} onto $\EE_a$. Its target is a proper-class field, not a set-sized
ring, and no assertion is made that it extends to all of $\Qa_a$. The construction is
therefore fully compatible with the absence of small ring images of $\Qa_a$. (Status (batch 34): with global choice, evaluation at $z$ does
extend, not onto $\EE_a$ but to a homomorphism of $\Qa_a$ onto a proper-class field containing $\EE_a$, through the maximal ideal $\mathfrak M_{a,z}$ of
\cref{osq:cr:thm:cantor}; see \cref{osq:cr:rem:evaluation}.)
\end{remark}

For $m=2^{r-1}$ and $k\in\Z/m\Z$ define, in $\mathcal S_r$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:idempotent}
 e_{r,k}=\frac1m\sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}\Bigl(\frac{\xi_r}{\zeta_{r,k}}\Bigr)^{\ell}.
\end{equation}
At the root $\zeta_{r,j}$ the sum has value $1$ for $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, by the finite
geometric-sum identity for the $m$th root of unity $\zeta_{r,j}/\zeta_{r,k}$. Thus
$\Phi_r(e_{r,k})$ is the indicator of the coordinate $k$, and
\begin{align}
 e_{r,k}^2&=e_{r,k},\qquad e_{r,k}e_{r,j}=0\ (k\ne j),\qquad
 \sum_{k\bmod m}e_{r,k}=1,\label{osq:if:eq:idempotentlaws}\\
 e_{r,k}&=e_{r+1,k}+e_{r+1,k+m}.\label{osq:if:eq:refine}
\end{align}
Each $e_{r,k}$ is nonzero because $\Phi_r$ is injective, which rests on
\cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel}. The refinement formula \eqref{osq:if:eq:refine} follows
from the coordinate transition, or by checking values at all roots of stage $r+1$.

The first nontrivial instance can be written without trigonometric notation. Put
\[
 y=\xi_2,\qquad u=\xi_1=y^2,\qquad \zeta=\frac{1+u}{\sqrt2}\in\EE_a .
\]
Then $u^2=-1$ and $\zeta^2=(1+2u+u^2)/2=u=y^2$, so $(y/\zeta)^2=1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:if:eq:firstidempotents}
 e_+=\frac12\Bigl(1+\frac y\zeta\Bigr),\qquad e_-=\frac12\Bigl(1-\frac y\zeta\Bigr)
\end{equation}
satisfy $e_\pm^2=e_\pm$, $e_+e_-=\frac14(1-(y/\zeta)^2)=0$ and $e_++e_-=1$. Nonvanishing is
not inferred from the suggestive formula: the roots at stage $2$ are
$\zeta_{2,0}=\zeta$ and $\zeta_{2,1}=-\zeta$, so $e_+=e_{2,0}$, $e_-=e_{2,1}$, and
$\Phi_2$ identifies $\mathcal S_2\cong\EE_a\times\EE_a$ and sends $e_+,e_-$ to $(1,0)$ and
$(0,1)$. This is why the exact-kernel theorem is an essential part of the argument.

\begin{corollary}[Boolean algebra and failure of finiteness conditions \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:cor:boolean}
The idempotents of $\bigcup_r\mathcal S_r$ form precisely the Boolean algebra of clopen
subsets of $\Z_2$, and this Boolean algebra is atomless. The ring $\Qa_a$ has an infinite
sequence of pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents, is neither a domain nor a local ring,
and fails the ascending chain condition on ideals.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
A field has only the idempotents $0$ and $1$, so an idempotent of $\LC(\Z_2,\EE_a)$ is the
indicator of a set that is a union of residue classes modulo some $2^N$, that is, of a
clopen subset of $\Z_2$; conversely, by compactness every clopen subset is a finite union
of such residue classes, and its indicator is idempotent. Every nonempty clopen set
contains a residue class modulo some $2^N$, which splits into two nonempty residue classes
modulo $2^{N+1}$; so there are no atoms.

For $j\ge0$ the sets $C_j=\{z\in\Z_2:z\equiv2^j\pmod{2^{j+1}}\}$ (the $z$ of $2$-adic
valuation exactly $j$) are nonempty, clopen and pairwise disjoint. Their indicators give
pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents $f_j\in\Qa_a$. The ideals
\[
 (f_0)\subsetneq(f_0,f_1)\subsetneq(f_0,f_1,f_2)\subsetneq\cdots
\]
of $\Qa_a$ strictly increase: if $f_{n+1}=\sum_{j\le n}c_jf_j$ with $c_j\in\Qa_a$,
multiplication by $f_{n+1}$ would give $f_{n+1}=0$. This proves the failure of the
ascending chain condition without forming any class-sized generating family. A nontrivial
idempotent $e$ satisfies $e(1-e)=0$, so $\Qa_a$ is not a domain; and in a local ring (for
every $x$, one of $x$ and $1-x$ is a unit) either $e$ or $1-e$ is a unit, which forces
$e=1$ or $e=0$.
\end{proof}

Grouping a sufficiently fine dyadic partition of $\Z_2$ into any prescribed number $d\ge1$
of nonempty blocks yields a unital subalgebra of $\Qa_a$ isomorphic to $\EE_a^d$.
Manuscript~07 claims neither that all idempotents of $\Qa_a$ lie in the Cantor algebra
\eqref{osq:if:eq:cantor} nor that $\Qa_a$ itself is a ring of locally constant functions.
No infinite sum of the orthogonal sequence $(f_j)$ is used.

\subsection{Gaussian binomial quotients}\label{osq:if:sub:gaussian}

Let
\[
 \Qa_a^\C=\GOz/(1+\omega^a),\qquad q_a^\C:\GOz\to\Qa_a^\C .
\]
Since $\GOz=\Oz+i\Oz$ and $\omega^{-a}$ is real, $\GOz[\omega^{-a}]=\Oz[\omega^{-a}]
+i\,\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$, so by \cref{osq:prop:locsupport} it consists of the surcomplex normal
forms whose supports are bounded below by some $-Na$. It contains $\FF_a(i)$, and the proof of
\cref{osq:if:lem:localization} applies verbatim with $\GOz$ in place of $\Oz$: the
extension $\widetilde q_a^\C$ of $q_a^\C$ has kernel $(1+\omega^a)\GOz[\omega^{-a}]$, and
it embeds the coefficient field by
\[
 f\longmapsto-q_a^\C(\omega^af)\qquad(f\in\FF_a(i)).
\]
For $f=i$ this is the Gaussian imaginary unit of the quotient, since
$-q_a^\C(\omega^ai)=-q_a^\C(\omega^a)q_a^\C(i)=q_a^\C(i)$.

\begin{theorem}[Complex exact kernels and dyadic algebra \src{07}]
\label{osq:if:thm:complexkernel}
For every $n\ge1$ there is an injective ring homomorphism
\[
 \FF_a(i)[T]/(T^n+1)\hookrightarrow\Qa_a^\C,\qquad T\mapsto q_a^\C(\omega^{a/n}),
\]
and its source is isomorphic to $\FF_a(i)^n$. The increasing union of the dyadic stages
$n=2^r$, $r\ge0$, is isomorphic to $\LC(\Z_2,\FF_a(i))$. The ring $\Qa_a^\C$ is nonzero,
has no unital homomorphism to a nonzero set-sized ring, and contains a class copy of $\SC$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The proof of \cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel} uses only supports and the nonvanishing of
coefficients, not their reality, so it applies verbatim over $\FF_a(i)$ and
$\GOz[\omega^{-a}]$: a nonzero remainder $R$ with coefficients in $\FF_a(i)$ gives the
expansion \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision}, whose blocks lie in the distinct cosets
$(j/n-k-1)a+H_a$, whose union of supports is reverse well ordered, and whose support is
not bounded below by any $-Na$; so $R(\omega^{a/n})\notin(1+\omega^a)\GOz[\omega^{-a}]$.
The polynomial $T^n+1$ has $n$ distinct roots $\exp(i\pi(2k+1)/n)$ in $\C\subseteq\FF_a(i)$,
so the Chinese remainder theorem gives $\FF_a(i)[T]/(T^n+1)\cong\FF_a(i)^n$ by evaluation
at the roots.

For $n=2^r$ label the roots $\eta_{r,k}=\exp(i(\pi+2\pi k)/2^r)$, $k\in\Z/2^r\Z$. Then
$\eta_{r,k}^2=\eta_{r-1,\,k\bmod 2^{r-1}}$, and the stage-$(r-1)$ generator
$q_a^\C(\omega^{a/2^{r-1}})$ is the square of the stage-$r$ generator; so, exactly as in
\cref{osq:if:thm:cantor}, the coordinate transitions repeat each entry on its two lifts,
and the union is $\LC(\Z_2,\FF_a(i))$. The ring is nonzero because $1+\omega^a$ is not
among the units $\pm1,\pm i$ of $\GOz$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}); it has no nonzero set-sized
image by \cref{osq:thm:reflection}, since $\ct(1+\omega^a)=1$ generates $\Z[i]$; and it
contains a copy of $\SC$ by the complex extension of $\Theta_a$
(\cref{osq:if:thm:compression}).
\end{proof}

Coefficientwise complex conjugation preserves $\GOz$ and, because $1+\omega^a$ is real,
the ideal $(1+\omega^a)$; hence it descends to an involution of $\Qa_a^\C$. It commutes
with the coefficient-field embedding $f\mapsto-q_a^\C(\omega^af)$ because the multiplier
$-\omega^a$ is real. This supplies a compatible involution without requiring an order or an
analytic interpretation of the quotient.

\subsection{Boundaries of the large-field results}\label{osq:if:sub:boundaries}

The small-image theorem and the large-field results concern different hypotheses and
reinforce one another (07). A homomorphism to a set-sized ring kills every purely infinite
element (\cref{osq:thm:universal}); a homomorphism to a nonzero ring that makes even one
purely infinite element invertible has a huge field in its target
(\cref{osq:if:thm:transfer}). That target is necessarily a proper class, but the explicit
field embedding gives considerably more than this size conclusion, and the Cantor algebra
describes zero-divisor structure that no cardinality argument captures. Manuscript~07
insists on the following distinctions.

\paragraph{A nonzero element versus a unit.} A nonzero nilpotent, as in
\cref{osq:if:ex:nilpotent}, does not produce a field. Invertibility is what allows the
formula $f=(gf)/g$ to be transported to a quotient. No cancellation in a ring with zero
divisors has been used.

\paragraph{A specified subalgebra versus the entire quotient.} The exact kernel theorem
identifies the subalgebras $\FF_a[x_n]$, and their dyadic union is a Cantor algebra.
Surreal normal forms with other supports can still create further elements of $\Qa_a$.
Neither a classification of all idempotents of $\Qa_a$ nor a description of its prime
ideals has been proved.

\paragraph{Class ideals versus set-theoretic Zorn arguments.} Zorn's lemma applies to sets
of candidates. The ring $\Qa_a$ is a proper class, so the usual existence argument for
maximal ideals cannot simply be repeated over its class of ideals. Statements such as
\cref{osq:if:cor:primefield} are deliberately conditional: it is not concluded that a
proper-class nonarithmetic maximal ideal exists merely because $(1+\omega^a)$ is proper.
Likewise (06) \cref{osq:if:prop:reservoir} is a necessary condition on residue fields, not an
existence theorem. (Status (batch 34): the existence question is settled with global choice. A proper class of ideals is not searched: 24's
recursion (\cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}) enumerates the \emph{elements} of the ring along a global well-order and stores a set of accepted generators at
each stage, keeping finite witnesses of improperness, so $(1+\omega^a)$ does lie in maximal class ideals, all nonarithmetic
(\cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}), and which monomials lie in a proper ideal containing $1+\omega^a$ is decided by \cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}. 07's and 06's statements
remain necessary conditions, now on ideals that exist; the prime ideals of $\Qa_a$ are still not described.)

\paragraph{Strong sums versus limits.} Every infinite sum used above, namely the geometric
series for $(1+\omega^a)^{-1}$ and the block expansion \eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision},
has a set-sized reverse well-ordered support and finitely many contributions at each
exponent, and is verified coefficientwise. Finite geometric remainders of the kind in
\cref{osq:lem:telescope} do not tend to zero, and no limit argument is used.

\paragraph{Finite checks.} The program accompanying manuscript~07 checks exact finite
geometric identities, finite binomial remainders, the first nontrivial idempotents
\eqref{osq:if:eq:firstidempotents} and finite coordinate refinement maps (07 records that
all $621$ named checks passed). It does not represent arbitrary surreal normal forms, and
it does not verify the ambient support argument, namely that the infinite expansion
\eqref{osq:if:eq:remainderdivision} lies outside $\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$; that is a
mathematical proof in the text. For a formalization, 07 recommends keeping the support
characterization of $\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$ and the exact binomial kernel separate from the
routine finite Chinese remainder calculations; no corresponding Lean declarations are
claimed.

\subsection{Class residue fields beyond the constant term}\label{osq:cr:sub:residues}

This subsection is manuscript~24's (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). Its subject is the maximal class ideals of $\Oz$ and $\GOz$ that the universal
theorem cannot see. Working in G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice, 24 proves that every proper class ideal of a commutative class
ring lies in a maximal class ideal (\cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}), by a recursion that stores only sets of generators, and that the unrestricted form of
this principle is equivalent to global choice (\cref{osq:cr:thm:equivalence}). Consequently $1+\omega^a$ lies in a characteristic-zero maximal ideal
of $\Oz$ and of $\GOz$ for every $a>0$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}): this answers, with global choice, the existence clause of
\cref{osq:q:primes}, whose classification clause stays open. In the binomial quotient a monomial $\omega^b$, $b\ge0$, is zero exactly when $a\ll b$
and is a unit otherwise (\cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}); separated scales are comaximal by an explicit B\'ezout identity (\cref{osq:cr:cor:comaximal});
every branch of 07's dyadic idempotent tree lies in its own maximal ideal, which gives at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ maximal ideals above each $1+\omega^a$
and a family indexed by $\On\times\Z_2$ across scales (\cref{osq:cr:thm:cantor,osq:cr:thm:twoaxes}); characteristic-zero maximal ideals separate
the points of $\Oz$, and their residue fields embed in $\SC$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:separation,osq:cr:thm:residually}), the specializations that
vanish on a binomial $1+\omega^a$ not preserving strong summability (\cref{osq:cr:thm:nonstrong}); and the primes that are both term-closed and strongly sum-closed are
classified (\cref{osq:cr:thm:termprimes}). Where the universal theorem says that every \emph{set-sized} image of $\Oz$ sees only $\ct$, these
class-sized field images together see every element.

\paragraph{Foundations, notation and renamings.} Every statement of this subsection that asserts the existence of a maximal class ideal, or of a
map built from one, is proved in $\mathsf{GBC}$: G\"odel--Bernays class theory $\mathsf{GB}$, which here includes no choice principle, together with
global choice $\mathsf{GC}$. This is stronger than the base theory of \cref{osq:sub:foundations}, NBG with choice for sets, and 24 never substitutes
choice for sets for global choice. Over $\mathsf{GB}$, global choice is equivalent to a set-like global well-ordering of the universe and to an
enumeration of every proper class in order type $\On$ \cite{HamkinsGC}. A \emph{class ring} has a class of set-valued elements and class functions as
operations; a class ideal satisfies the finite ideal axioms; \emph{maximal} means maximal among proper class ideals, which for a proper class ideal
$M$ of a commutative unital class ring $R$ is equivalent to the finite criterion
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:maxcriterion}
 x\notin M\ \Longrightarrow\ 1-rx\in M\ \text{for some }r\in R,
\end{equation}
since \eqref{osq:cr:eq:maxcriterion} follows from $M+(x)=R$ and implies maximality; so no collection of class ideals is ever formed. A quotient
$R/I$ is coded in $\mathsf{GBC}$ by the least representative of each coset in a fixed set-like global well-order, with the operations computed on
representatives and reduced, and over $\mathsf{GB}$ by Scott codes, the members of a coset of least rank, as in \cref{osq:sub:foundations}. Every
recursion below has a \emph{set} as its state at each ordinal stage: for each set ordinal, ordinary transfinite recursion with class parameters
applies, uniqueness makes the runs of different lengths compatible, and elementary comprehension collects them into one class relation. No recursion
with proper-class values, and no unrestricted elementary transfinite recursion for class-valued stages, is used; such principles need separate
attention in class set theory \cite{GHHSW}.

Throughout, $(D,k)$ is $(\Z,\R)$ or $(\Z[i],\C)$, $A=\A_{D,k}$ is $\Oz$ or $\GOz$, and $a>0$. We write $\Qa_a^k=A/(1+\omega^a)A$, so that
$\Qa_a^\R=\Qa_a$ and $\Qa_a^\C$ are the rings of \cref{osq:if:sub:binomial,osq:if:sub:gaussian}, and $q_a$ for the quotient map (07's $q_a^\C$ for the
Gaussian pair). Every series has a set-sized support, even when its ambient ring or exponent group is a proper class. $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)=\{g\in\No:
|g|\le na\text{ for some ordinary }n\ge1\}$ is the convex subgroup of $\No$ generated by $a$, the class form of $\operatorname{cvx}_\Gamma(G)$ of
\cref{osq:ft:prop:relative}, and $a\ll b$ is the relation of \eqref{osq:eq:Ha}: $b>na$ for every ordinary $n\ge1$; for $b>0$ this says $b\notin
\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$. 24's symbols are renamed as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its $(D,K)$, $\Pi_K$, $A_D$, $B_K=K\oplus\Pi_K$ and $Q_a$ are $(D,k)$, $\Pi_k$, $\A_{D,k}$, $\A_{k,k}$ and $\Qa^k_a$ ($\B$ is the ring $D+\mm_k$);
its classes $[x]$ are $q_a(x)$. Its relation $b\gg a$ is $a\ll b$, the same relation written with the opposite symbol.
\item Its convex subgroup $C_a$ is $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ ($C_j$ are clopen sets in \cref{osq:if:cor:boolean}, $C_{d+1}$ a Gaussian grid and
$\mathsf C(G)$ a reduced fibre); its support ideal $J_a$ is $\Pi_k^{\gg a}$, its truncation $\tau_a$ is $\operatorname{tr}_a$ and its ring $A_D(C_a)$ is
$\A_{D,k}(\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a))$ (\eqref{osq:cr:eq:tails}; $J$ and $\mathsf J$ are other ideals and $\tau$ an exponent automorphism). For a convex
subgroup $H\subseteq\No$ its $\Pi_K(H)$ is $\Pi_k(H)$ of \eqref{osq:eq:ideals} and its support ideal $P_H$ is $\Pi_k^{>H}$ (\eqref{osq:cr:eq:PH}).
\item Its geometric series $q_{a,b}$ is $\mathsf g_{a,b}$ ($q_a$ is the quotient map); its scales $a_\alpha=\omega^\alpha$ are written out, since
$a_\alpha$ denotes the small scales of \eqref{osq:eq:scales}, and its binomials $f_\alpha$ are $\mathsf f_\alpha$; its rescaling automorphism $\sigma_{b/a}$ is
$\operatorname{sc}_{b/a}$ ($\sigma$ is an endomorphism of $\Oz$ in \cref{osq:sub:consequences} and 20's specialization).
\item Its field $F_a$ and group $H_a$ are $\FF_a$ and $H_a$, the same objects (the Hahn field over the scale subgroup \eqref{osq:eq:Ha}), and its
$F_a[i]$ is $\FF_a(i)$. Its shifted embedding $\Theta_a(x)=-[\omega^ax]$ is 07's $\iota_a$ of \eqref{osq:if:eq:iota}; $\Theta_a$ is 07's compression
$\No\hookrightarrow\FF_a$ of \eqref{osq:if:eq:Theta}, a different map.
\item Its dyadic classes $u_n=[\omega^{a/2^n}]$ are 07's $\xi_n$, and $u=u_1$ is 07's $u=\xi_1$; 07's $x_n=q_a(\omega^{a/n})$ has $x_{2^n}=\xi_n$. Its
family $z_n=\omega^{a/2^n}$ in Theorem~9.6 is written out ($\mathsf z_n$ are 23's branches and $z$ is a $2$-adic integer here). Its
binary idempotent tree $(e_s)$ is 07's $(e_{r,k})$, a branch $\eta\in2^{\N}$ being read as the $2$-adic integer $z=\sum_j\eta_j2^j$; its maximal ideals
$M_{a,\eta}$, $M_{\alpha,\eta}$, $M_x$ and quotient maps $\pi_{\beta,\eta}$ are $\mathfrak M_{a,z}$, $\mathfrak M_{\alpha,z}$, $\mathfrak M_x$ and
$\varpi_{\beta,z}$ ($M$ is a coefficient lattice and $\pi_b$ a detecting map).
\item Its multiplicative class $T$ (its Proposition~3.3 and Lemma~4.3) is $\Sigma$, and its class poset $X$, with a variable for each element and
the ideals $I_x$, is $\mathcal P$, with variables $v_p$ and ideals $I_p$ ($X^g$ are formal monomials; $T$ is a polynomial variable in
\cref{osq:if:sub:kernel} and the monomial $\omega^a$ in \cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}).
\item Its class field $L$ and set subfield $E_0$ in Theorem~9.2 are $\mathbb K$ and $\mathbb K_0$ ($L$ is a set field or a lower set elsewhere and $E$ an
ambient field), and its specialization $\varphi_a:\Oz\to\SC$ is $\operatorname{sp}_a$ ($\varphi$ is a general map in \cref{osq:thm:universal} and a
branch map in \cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}).
\end{itemize}
Five tempting readings are false. (1) $a\ll b$ is not $b>a$: $\omega^{2a}$ is infinitely larger than $\omega^a$, but $q_a(\omega^{2a})=1$ is a unit;
only $a\ll b$ kills $\omega^b$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}). (2) $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ is not $H_a$: $H_a$ collects the exponents infinitesimal
relative to $a$, $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ those bounded by a multiple of $a$, and $H_a\subsetneq\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$; manuscript~25 writes $H_a$ for
$\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ (\cref{osq:sa:sub:semialgebraic}). (3) A residue field containing an algebraically closed class subfield need not be
algebraically closed (\cref{osq:cr:q:closed}). (4) $\operatorname{sp}_a$ is a ring homomorphism, not an ordered or strongly additive map
(\cref{osq:cr:thm:nonstrong}). (5) ``Nonarithmetic'' is a predicate on individual ideals, and a family of maximal ideals is one class relation on
parameters and ring elements; no class of all class ideals is formed.

\paragraph{Maximal class ideals under global choice.}

\begin{theorem}[Maximal class extensions \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:krull}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, let $R$ be a nonzero commutative unital class ring and $I\subsetneq R$ a class ideal. There is a maximal class ideal $M$ of $R$
containing $I$. With a fixed global well-order, $M$ can be defined uniformly from the class parameters coding $R$ and $I$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose an ordinal-indexed enumeration $(r_\alpha)$ of $R$ (for a set ring a set ordinal suffices) and define sets $S_\alpha$ of accepted
generators by $S_0=\varnothing$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:greedy}
 S_{\alpha+1}=\begin{cases}
 S_\alpha\cup\{r_\alpha\},&1\notin I+(S_\alpha\cup\{r_\alpha\})R,\\
 S_\alpha,&1\in I+(S_\alpha\cup\{r_\alpha\})R,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
and $S_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}S_\alpha$ at limits; $S_\lambda$ is a set, being a set-indexed union of sets contained in the set of elements
enumerated before $\lambda$. For a set $T_0$, the assertion $1\in I+T_0R$ says that there are an ordinary $m$, elements $t_1,\dots,t_m\in T_0$,
coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in R$ and $z\in I$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:finitewitness}
 1=z+\sum_{j=1}^mc_jt_j ;
\end{equation}
this is an elementary formula with class parameters, all of whose quantified objects are sets, so the set-length recursions described above apply,
and the usually proper-class ideal $I+S_\alpha R$ is never stored. Let $S$ be the class of all accepted generators and $M=I+SR$, defined by the same
finite-sum formula; it is a class ideal. It is proper: an equation \eqref{osq:cr:eq:finitewitness} with $t_j\in S$ involves finitely many acceptance
stages, all below one ordinal, and would already make an earlier $I+S_\alpha R$ improper, contrary to the recursion; at limit stages the same
finite-witness argument preserves properness. If $x\notin M$, its occurrence in the enumeration was rejected, so
$1\in I+(S_\alpha\cup\{x\})R\subseteq M+(x)$ at that stage, and \eqref{osq:cr:eq:maxcriterion} proves maximality. Every decision is definable from
the global well-order and the class parameters, which proves uniformity.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What has been made constructive \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:constructive}
The recursion is explicit as a class definition, not an effective algorithm: the finite-equation test quantifies over all ring elements and can be
undecidable. The method is the familiar greedy proof of Krull's theorem with its size obligations checked; recursive approaches for set-sized rings are
classical and appear in constructive work \cite{BlechschmidtSchuster}. No new general algorithm for ideal membership is claimed (24).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Prime extension avoiding a multiplicative class \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:prop:avoid}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, let $\Sigma\subseteq R$ be a multiplicatively closed class containing $1$ with $I\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$. There is a prime class
ideal $P\supseteq I$ disjoint from $\Sigma$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Accept $r_\alpha$ exactly when $\bigl(I+(S_\alpha\cup\{r_\alpha\})R\bigr)\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$. A violation again has one element of $\Sigma$ and a
finite membership witness, so the resulting ideal $P$ is disjoint from $\Sigma$, and rejection shows that it is maximal among ideals disjoint from
$\Sigma$. If $xy\in P$ with $x,y\notin P$, maximality gives $t=p+rx\in\Sigma$ and $u=p'+sy\in\Sigma$ with $p,p'\in P$, and then $tu\in P\cap\Sigma$, a
contradiction. So $P$ is prime; it is not asserted to be a maximal ideal of $R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Compatible prescribed equations \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:cor:prescribe}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, if a class family $(f_t)_{t\in T_0}$ of elements of $R$ has no finite subfamily generating $1$, then all the equations $f_t=0$
hold in some maximal class quotient of $R$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The ideal generated by the family is proper because its membership relation uses finite sums; apply \cref{osq:cr:thm:krull} and code the quotient
as above.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Class ultrafilters as the Boolean case \merge]\label{osq:cr:rem:ultrafilters}
For a Boolean algebra $\mathcal A$ whose elements are sets, viewed as the Boolean ring with addition the symmetric difference, the ideal generated by
finitely many complements $\neg s_1,\dots,\neg s_n$ is principal, generated by $\neg s_1\vee\cdots\vee\neg s_n$, so it contains $1$ exactly when
$s_1\wedge\cdots\wedge s_n=0$. A class family with the finite intersection property therefore has complements generating a proper ideal, and a
maximal class ideal $M$ containing them (\cref{osq:cr:cor:prescribe}) has residue field $\F_2$, so $\{x:x\notin M\}$ is an ultrafilter containing the
family. Thus 19's and 20's class-ultrafilter lemmas (\cref{osq:nf:lem:classultra,osq:bb:lem:classultra}) are the Boolean-ring case of
\cref{osq:cr:cor:prescribe}, and 20's lemma holds for a class family with the finite intersection property, not only a set. Their proofs decide $b$
or $\neg b$ at each stage; \cref{osq:cr:thm:krull} accepts or rejects a generator. The foundation is the same.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[\src{24}]\label{osq:cr:def:cmit}
The \emph{class maximal ideal principle} $\mathsf{CMIT}$ asserts that every nonzero commutative unital class ring has a maximal class ideal. It
quantifies over class rings, not only over rings whose carriers are sets.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Class Krull and global choice \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:equivalence}
Over $\mathsf{GB}$, $\mathsf{CMIT}$ is equivalent to $\mathsf{GC}$. Equivalently, global choice is equivalent to the assertion that every proper
class ideal of every commutative unital class ring has a maximal class extension.
\end{theorem}

The reverse implication uses the finite-polynomial mechanism of the classical proofs that Krull's theorem implies choice, following the
maximal-small-ideal argument in the corrected (third) version of Entin's exposition, with antecedents in Ern\'e and Hodges
\cite{Entin,Erne,Hodges}. 24's contribution is the passage to classes and the choice of a class poset encoding a \emph{global} choice function;
the finite algebraic lemma is not offered as new (24).

\begin{lemma}[Finite-polynomial compatibility \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:lem:compat}
Assume $\mathsf{CMIT}$. Every nonempty class poset $\mathcal P$ has a subclass $\mathcal Y$ maximal with the property that every finite subset of
$\mathcal Y$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal P$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $R=\F_2[v_p:p\in\mathcal P]$ be the class polynomial ring with finite supports, and for $p\in\mathcal P$ let $I_p$ be the ideal generated by the
variables $v_q$ with $q\le p$. Call a polynomial \emph{small} if it lies in some $I_p$. Each $I_p$ is a monomial prime ideal, so the nonsmall
polynomials form a multiplicative class $\Sigma$ with $1\in\Sigma$ and $0\notin\Sigma$. A maximal ideal of $\Sigma^{-1}R$, which exists by
$\mathsf{CMIT}$, contracts to a prime ideal $P$ of $R$ maximal among ideals consisting of small polynomials; the localization uses finite fractions and
Scott codes, so needs no global choice.

A small polynomial has zero constant term. If a monomial $m$ occurs in some $f\in P$, choose a variable $v$ dividing $m$; given $g\in P$, take an
ordinary $d>\deg g$. Then $v^df+g\in P$ is small, say in $I_{p'}$, and there is no cancellation between the terms of $g$ and those of $v^df$ (the latter
have degree above $\deg g$). As $I_{p'}$ is a monomial ideal, $g\in I_{p'}$ and $v^dm\in I_{p'}$; every variable dividing $v^dm$ divides $m$, so $m\in
I_{p'}$ and $g+hm$ is small for every polynomial $h$. So $P+(m)$ consists of small polynomials, maximality gives $m\in P$, and primality puts a
variable of $m$ in $P$. Hence $P=(\mathcal Y)$ for the class $\mathcal Y$ of $p$ with $v_p\in P$.

A sum of finitely many distinct variables from $\mathcal Y$ lies in $P$, hence in some $I_p$, so they have the common upper bound $p$. Conversely, if
$\mathcal Y'\supseteq\mathcal Y$ has the finite-upper-bound property, every element of the ideal $(\mathcal Y')$ lies in some $I_p$; maximality of $P$
gives $(\mathcal Y')=P$ and then $\mathcal Y'=\mathcal Y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{osq:cr:thm:equivalence}]
Global choice implies the maximal-extension assertion by \cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}, and that assertion implies $\mathsf{CMIT}$ (take the zero ideal).
Conversely assume $\mathsf{CMIT}$ and let $\mathcal P$ be the class of all \emph{finite} partial choice functions, finite functions $p$ on sets of
nonempty sets with $p(B)\in B$ for $B$ in their domain, ordered by extension; it contains the empty function, and a finite subset of $\mathcal P$ has an
upper bound exactly when its members agree on overlapping domains, the union then being a finite upper bound. Let $\mathcal Y$ be given by
\cref{osq:cr:lem:compat}. Pairwise compatibility makes $h=\bigcup\mathcal Y$ a class function. If a nonempty set $B$ were not in its domain, fix
$b\in B$: the singleton function $\{(B,b)\}$ is compatible with every finite subfamily of $\mathcal Y$ (the union of such a subfamily and
$\{(B,b)\}$ is a finite upper bound), so it could be adjoined to $\mathcal Y$, and maximality would put it in $\mathcal Y$, contradicting the omission of
$B$. Hence $h(B)\in B$ for every nonempty set $B$, and $h$ is a global choice function.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The quantifier restriction matters \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:restricted}
\Cref{osq:cr:thm:equivalence} does \emph{not} show that the existence of one nonarithmetic maximal ideal of $\Oz$, or even of one above every
$1+\omega^a$, implies global choice: the converse uses arbitrary, specially built class rings, and necessity for the restricted omnific problem is a
separate question (\cref{osq:cr:q:choice}). Likewise the ordinary maximal-ideal theorem for set rings yields choice for sets; it is the class-uniform
version that yields global choice (24).
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Nonarithmetic maximal ideals exist.}

\begin{proposition}[The arithmetic maximal ideals \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:prop:arithmetic}
A maximal class ideal $M$ of $A$ with $M\cap D\ne0$ is $\ct^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak pA$ for a nonzero prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $D$, with
quotient $D/\mathfrak p$. Every other maximal class ideal has $M\cap D=0$, a residue field of characteristic $0$, and $M\not\subseteq\Pi_k$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $0\ne d\in M\cap D$, then $\Pi_k=d\Pi_k\subseteq M$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}), so $M$ is the preimage of a maximal ideal of $D$
(\cref{osq:thm:quotients}); for $D=\Z$ or $\Z[i]$ these are the nonzero prime ideals. Conversely each such preimage is maximal, since its quotient is the
field $D/\mathfrak p$, and coefficient division gives $\ct^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak pA$. If $M\cap D=0$, the quotient contains a copy of $D$ and has
characteristic $0$; and $M\subseteq\Pi_k$ would force $M=\Pi_k$ by maximality, which is impossible because $A/\Pi_k\cong D$ is not a field.
\end{proof}

For $\Oz$ the arithmetic maximal ideals are the $p\Oz$ of \cref{osq:cor:smallprimes}, and for $\GOz$ they are generated by the Gaussian primes. A
maximal class ideal is \emph{nonarithmetic} if it is not of this form; by \cref{osq:cr:prop:arithmetic} it then satisfies the hypotheses of
\cref{osq:if:cor:primefield}. This defines a predicate on single ideals, not a set of ideals (24).

\begin{theorem}[Binomial maximal extensions \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, for every $a\in\No_{>0}$ there is a maximal class ideal $M$ of $A$ with $1+\omega^a\in M$ and $M\cap D=0$. Every maximal
class ideal containing $1+\omega^a$ is nonarithmetic, with a residue field of characteristic $0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$1+\omega^a$ is a nonunit (\cref{osq:lem:units}), so $(1+\omega^a)$ is proper and \cref{osq:cr:thm:krull} gives $M$. If some maximal $M\ni1+\omega^a$
met $D$ nontrivially, \cref{osq:cr:prop:arithmetic} would give $\omega^a\in\Pi_k\subseteq M$ and then $1\in M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Unit-constant fibres \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:cor:unitconstant}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, every nonconstant $f\in A$ with $\ct(f)\in D^\times$ lies in a maximal class ideal, and every maximal class ideal containing $f$
has characteristic $0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Positive degree makes $f$ a nonunit (\cref{osq:lem:units}); an arithmetic maximal ideal contains $\Pi_k$, hence $\ct(f)$, and cannot contain an element
with unit constant term. Apply \cref{osq:cr:thm:krull}.
\end{proof}

So the quotients $\Oz/(1+g)$ and $\GOz/(1+g)$ of \cref{osq:if:cor:unitconstant}, which contain copies of $\No$ and $\SC$ and have no nonzero
set-sized image, have characteristic-zero maximal class quotients. In 08's set-sized ring $A^{08}_\kappa$ the same element $1+X^{e_0}$ lies in a
characteristic-zero maximal ideal by the ordinary maximal-ideal theorem, with a residue field of size $\kappa$ (\cref{osq:thm:model08}(vi) and the
paragraph after it); 08 notes that this quotient map cannot extend to $\Oz$ with a set-sized target, and \cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax} supplies class-sized
targets instead.

\begin{lemma}[The same binomial quotient over $D$ and over $k$ \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:lem:coefficients}
Inclusion induces an isomorphism of class rings
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:coefficients}
 \A_{D,k}/(1+\omega^a)\A_{D,k}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \A_{k,k}/(1+\omega^a)\A_{k,k}.
\end{equation}
The quotient is nonzero, the natural map from $k$ to it is injective, and $k$ stays embedded in every proper quotient.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $c\in k$ and $s\in\Pi_k$, the relation $\omega^a=-1$ identifies the class of $c+s$ with that of $s-c\omega^a\in\A_{D,k}$, which proves
surjectivity. If $x\in\A_{D,k}$ and $x=(1+\omega^a)y$ with $y\in\A_{k,k}$, then $\ct(y)=\ct(x)\in D$ because $\ct$ is multiplicative on $\A_{k,k}$, so
$y\in\A_{D,k}$; this proves injectivity. The binomial is a nonunit of $\A_{k,k}$, so the quotient is nonzero, and a nonzero $c\in k$ is a unit of
$\A_{k,k}$, which stays a unit, hence nonzero, in every proper quotient.
\end{proof}

Both sides of \eqref{osq:cr:eq:coefficients} are $\Qa_a^k$. The embedded scalar $c\in k$ is represented in $\A_{D,k}$ by $-c\omega^a$, as after
\cref{osq:if:lem:localization}; the embedding is a feature of the quotient and does not put $k$ inside $\A_{D,k}$. \Cref{osq:if:lem:localization}(ii)
presents the same ring as $\Oz[\omega^{-a}]/(1+\omega^a)$, by the other inclusion.

\paragraph{The exact monomial kernel at one scale.}

\begin{theorem}[Exact monomial dichotomy \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}
Let $a>0$ and $b\ge0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $a\ll b$, then $q_a(\omega^b)=0$.
\item Otherwise $b\le Na$ for some ordinary $N\ge1$, and $q_a(\omega^b)$ is a unit of $\Qa^k_a$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:monomialinverse}
 q_a(\omega^b)^{-1}=(-1)^Nq_a(\omega^{Na-b}).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, for every proper ideal $J$ of $A$ containing $1+\omega^a$, prime or not,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:exactmembership}
 \omega^b\in J\iff a\ll b .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $a\ll b$, the series
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:g}
 \mathsf g_{a,b}=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n\omega^{b-(n+1)a}
\end{equation}
has strictly decreasing, strictly positive exponents, so $\mathsf g_{a,b}\in\Pi_k$, and multiplying by the two-term series $1+\omega^a$, with at most two
contributions at each exponent, gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:telescope}
 (1+\omega^a)\,\mathsf g_{a,b}=\omega^b ;
\end{equation}
this is membership in the principal ideal, not only in its radical. If $0\le b\le Na$, then $\omega^{Na-b}\in A$ and
$q_a(\omega^b)\,(-1)^Nq_a(\omega^{Na-b})=(-1)^Nq_a(\omega^a)^N=1$. A unit of a nonzero ring is not zero, and every proper quotient of $\Qa^k_a$ keeps
both the zeros of (i) and the inverse equations of (ii), which gives \eqref{osq:cr:eq:exactmembership}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A second route through the localization \merge]\label{osq:cr:rem:cutofflocal}
By \cref{osq:if:lem:localization}(ii) and \cref{osq:prop:locsupport}, $q_a(\omega^b)=0$ if and only if $\omega^b/(1+\omega^a)=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n
\omega^{b-(n+1)a}$ has support bounded below by some $-Na$, that is, $b-(n+1)a\ge-Na$ for every $n$, which holds exactly when $a\ll b$. This gives
(i) and its converse without the inverse formula; the inverse \eqref{osq:cr:eq:monomialinverse} is the finer information of (ii).
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[The fibre $1+\omega=0$ \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:ex:omega}
For $a=1$ the relation is $q_1(\omega)=-1$. Every monomial $\omega^b$ with $0\le b\le N$ for an ordinary $N$ is a unit, for instance $b=\sqrt2$,
$b=1/\omega$ and every ordinary $b\ge0$; every monomial with positive infinite exponent vanishes, for instance $q_1(\omega^\omega)=0$ and
$q_1(\omega^{\sqrt\omega})=0$. The square root $u=q_1(\omega^{1/2})$ satisfies $u^2=-1$, so $\Qa^k_1$ is not ordered by the order inherited from $\Oz$.
\end{example}

Truncation to $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ removes entire tails. Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:tails}
 \Pi_k^{\gg a}=\{s\in\Pi_k:\ a\ll g\text{ for every }g\in\supp s\},\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}_a\Bigl(\sum_gc_g\omega^g\Bigr)=\sum_{g\in\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}c_g\omega^g .
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Discarding all exponents above the scale \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:prop:tails}
$\Pi_k^{\gg a}\subseteq(1+\omega^a)A$. The truncation $\operatorname{tr}_a:A\to\A_{D,k}(\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a))$, onto the elements of $A$ supported in
$\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $\Pi_k^{\gg a}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:truncatequotient}
 \Qa^k_a\cong\A_{D,k}(\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a))/(1+\omega^a)\A_{D,k}(\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $s\in\Pi_k^{\gg a}$ multiply $s$ in the ambient Hahn field by $(1+\omega^a)^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^n\omega^{-(n+1)a}$; the Hahn product is defined,
and every exponent that can occur is $g-(n+1)a$ with $a\ll g$, which is positive. So $s/(1+\omega^a)\in\Pi_k$. If $g,h\ge0$ and $g+h\in
\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, convexity gives $g,h\in\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, and if one of $g,h$ lies outside, so does $g+h$; so truncation is
multiplicative on nonnegative supports, with the stated kernel and image. It fixes $1+\omega^a$ and induces the map \eqref{osq:cr:eq:truncatequotient},
which is surjective, and injective because $\Pi_k^{\gg a}$ is already in the binomial ideal: if $x=(1+\omega^a)y$ is supported in
$\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, then $x=\operatorname{tr}_a(x)=(1+\omega^a)\operatorname{tr}_a(y)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[\src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:tails}
The reduction does not replace the exponent group by a set: $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, and the much smaller $H_a$, are proper classes. Nor does it
classify the elements of the binomial ideal: inside $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ different terms can cancel modulo the binomial, and the dyadic
idempotents show substantial branching (24). The ring $\A_{D,k}(\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a))$ is $\A_{D,k}(G)$ of \eqref{osq:eq:rings} for the class group
$G=\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A B\'ezout identity between separated scales \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:cor:comaximal}
If $a\ll b$, then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:bezout}
 1=(1+\omega^b)-(1+\omega^a)\,\mathsf g_{a,b},
\end{equation}
so the principal ideals $(1+\omega^a)$ and $(1+\omega^b)$ are comaximal and no proper ideal contains both.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Subtract \eqref{osq:cr:eq:telescope} from $1+\omega^b$.
\end{proof}

For an ordinal $\alpha$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:ordinalscales}
 \mathsf f_\alpha=1+\omega^{\omega^\alpha}.
\end{equation}
If $\alpha<\beta$, then $\omega^\beta=\omega^\alpha\omega^{\beta-\alpha}$ with $\omega^{\beta-\alpha}$ infinite, so $\omega^\alpha\ll\omega^\beta$, and the
ideals $(\mathsf f_\alpha)$ are pairwise comaximal: a proper-class range of scales, obtained without counting a putative set of ideals (24). 09's
comaximal ideals $(1-X^{e_\ell})$ in a set-sized ring are the same identity (\cref{osq:thm:residue}(iv)).

\begin{proposition}[The abstract binomial ring does not depend on $a$ \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:prop:rescale}
For $a,b>0$ the coefficient-fixing strong automorphism
\[
 \operatorname{sc}_{b/a}\Bigl(\sum_gc_g\omega^g\Bigr)=\sum_gc_g\omega^{(b/a)g}
\]
of $\No$ (of $\SC$ for $k=\C$) preserves $A$ and induces $\Qa^k_a\cong\Qa^k_b$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Multiplication by the positive surreal $b/a$ is an order-preserving automorphism of the additive exponent group, with inverse multiplication by $a/b$;
it preserves reverse well-ordering and the finite-decomposition property of Hahn products, positive exponents and the constant coefficient, and it sends
$1+\omega^a$ to $1+\omega^b$.
\end{proof}

This is the standard Hahn rescaling, not a novelty claim; it shows that the monomial cutoff is an invariant of the embedded fibre at a chosen scale,
not evidence that the abstract quotient rings are pairwise nonisomorphic (24).

\paragraph{The field core.} As explained at the start of this subsection, 24's Lemma~7.1, Theorem~7.2 and Proposition~7.4 are printed once, as
\cref{osq:if:prop:closed,osq:lem:Ha,osq:if:lem:localization,osq:if:cor:Ea,osq:if:thm:complexkernel,osq:if:cor:primefield}. 24's proofs are the same as
07's: the closure of $\FF_a$ and $\FF_a(i)$ is reduced polynomial by polynomial to set-sized divisible support groups, the shifted map is multiplicative
because $\omega^axy(1+\omega^a)$ lies in the binomial ideal, $T^2+1$ is irreducible over the real closed $\FF_a$, and a unital map from a field to a nonzero
ring is injective. 24's reservoir argument for a prime $P$ with $P\cap D=0$ and $P\not\subseteq\Pi_k$ takes $c+s\in P$ with $0\ne c\in D$, puts $v=s/c$ and
$a$ below $\supp v$, and embeds the Hahn field over $H_a$ by $x\mapsto-q(vx)$, which is 07's transfer with $g=v$; in the real case it asserts no square
root of $-1$ in $A/P$. Its purpose in 24, making the size statements independent of the universal theorem, is served equally by 07's versions.

\begin{corollary}[Residue fields above the binomial \src{24} \merge]\label{osq:cr:cor:properfield}
Let $M$ be a maximal class ideal of $A$ containing $1+\omega^a$, which exists in $\mathsf{GBC}$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}). Then $A/M$ is a
proper-class field of characteristic $0$ containing an isomorphic copy of $\EE_a\cong\FF_a(i)$, an algebraically closed proper-class Hahn field, and hence
of $\SC$. No maximal ideal containing $1+\omega^a$ has a set-sized residue field.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$A/M$ is a proper quotient of $\Qa^k_a$. For $k=\R$ it receives the field $\EE_a\subseteq\Qa_a$ of \cref{osq:if:cor:Ea}; for $k=\C$ it receives
$\FF_a(i)$ by the coefficient embedding of \cref{osq:if:sub:gaussian}. A unital map from a field to a nonzero ring is injective, and $\SC$ embeds in
$\FF_a(i)$ by \cref{osq:if:thm:compression}. The characteristic is $0$ by \cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}.
\end{proof}

24 states the corollary with ``an algebraically closed proper-class Hahn subfield''; the copy of $\SC$ is the merge's addition from 07's compression.
Neither says that $A/M$ is algebraically closed: a field can be a proper transcendental extension of an algebraically closed subfield
(\cref{osq:cr:q:closed}).

\paragraph{Continuum branching at one scale.} 24's Lemma~8.1 states that $\R[\xi_n]\cong\R[T]/(T^{2^n}+1)\cong\C^{2^{n-1}}$ inside $\Qa_a$, that
$\R[\xi_n]\subseteq\R[\xi_{n+1}]$ via $\xi_n=\xi_{n+1}^2$ splits every primitive idempotent into two nonzero orthogonal ones, and that for $\GOz$ the
corresponding rings are $\C^{2^n}$ from $n=0$. This is the restriction to constant coefficients of \cref{osq:if:thm:binomialkernel} (with
\eqref{osq:if:eq:finiteCRT}, \eqref{osq:if:eq:refine}) and \cref{osq:if:thm:complexkernel}.

\begin{remark}[A degree proof for constant coefficients \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:dyadic}
Work in $\A_{\R,\R}/(1+\omega^a)$, which is $\Qa_a$ by \cref{osq:cr:lem:coefficients}. A nonzero remainder $r(T)\in\R[T]$ of degree less than $2^n$ gives
$\degw r(\omega^{a/2^n})<a$, while every nonzero multiple of $1+\omega^a$ in $\A_{\R,\R}$ has degree at least $a$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}); so the kernel of
$T\mapsto\xi_n$ on $\R[T]$ is exactly $(T^{2^n}+1)$. The roots of $T^{2^n}+1$ are simple and form $2^{n-1}$ conjugate pairs, and under squaring each pair
has two pairs of preimages; over $\C$ every root is its own factor with two square roots. This route needs no support description of
$\Oz[\omega^{-a}]$, but it does not cover coefficients in $\FF_a$, which have negative exponents; 07's proof does. At $n=2$, $T^4+1=(T^2-\sqrt2T+1)
(T^2+\sqrt2T+1)$, and 24's idempotents
\[
 e_\pm=\tfrac12\pm\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\,(\xi_2-\xi_2^3),\qquad (\xi_2-\xi_2^3)^2=2\ \text{modulo }\xi_2^4+1,
\]
are 07's $e_\pm$ of \eqref{osq:if:eq:firstidempotents} \merge: with $y=\xi_2$ and $\zeta=(1+y^2)/\sqrt2$, $y^4=-1$ gives $(1+y^2)(1-y^2)=2$, so
$y/\zeta=\frac{\sqrt2}2(y-y^3)$.
\end{remark}

A \emph{branch} of 07's tree is a $2$-adic integer $z\in\Z_2$; its idempotent at stage $r$ is $e_{r,z\bmod 2^{r-1}}$, and by \eqref{osq:if:eq:refine}
these form a decreasing chain of nonzero idempotents, $e_{r+1,z\bmod2^r}e_{r,z\bmod2^{r-1}}=e_{r+1,z\bmod2^r}$. 24 indexes the same tree by finite
binary strings, with $e_\varnothing=1$, $e_s=e_{s0}+e_{s1}$, $e_{s0}e_{s1}=0$ and $e_s\ne0$, rooted at the first complex factor in the real case and at the
scalar field in the Gaussian case. For $\GOz$ the stages are those of \cref{osq:if:thm:complexkernel}, $n=2^r$ with $r\ge0$, and the idempotent of $z$
at stage $r$ is the indicator of the residue class $z\bmod2^r$; the statements below hold verbatim with this indexing.

\begin{theorem}[Continuum many maximal extensions at a fixed scale \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:cantor}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, for each $a>0$ there is a family $(\mathfrak M_{a,z})_{z\in\Z_2}$ of pairwise distinct maximal class ideals of $A$ containing
$1+\omega^a$, encoded by a single class membership relation on $\Z_2\times A$, with $e_{r,z\bmod2^{r-1}}\equiv1$ modulo $\mathfrak M_{a,z}$ for every
$r\ge1$. Every residue field $A/\mathfrak M_{a,z}$ has the properties of \cref{osq:cr:cor:properfield}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $z\in\Z_2$ let $I_z$ be the ideal of $\Qa^k_a$ generated by the $1-e_{r,z\bmod2^{r-1}}$, $r\ge1$. It is proper: an equation for $1$ uses finitely
many generators; multiplying by $e_{N,z\bmod2^{N-1}}$ for $N$ at least all stages occurring annihilates every generator used, since $e_{N,z\bmod2^{N-1}}
(1-e_{r,z\bmod2^{r-1}})=0$ for $r\le N$, and leaves the nonzero idempotent $e_{N,z\bmod2^{N-1}}$ on the left. \Cref{osq:cr:thm:krull} extends $I_z$ to a
maximal class ideal of $\Qa^k_a$, whose preimage in $A$ is $\mathfrak M_{a,z}$. For $z\ne z'$ choose $r$ with $z\not\equiv z'\bmod2^{r-1}$; the two
idempotents at stage $r$ are orthogonal, and one maximal ideal containing both sets of branch equations would make their product both $0$ and $1$. With
the global well-order the extension is a uniform class definition with the set parameters $a,z$, so the membership predicates form one class relation;
no choice from a set of maximal class ideals is made.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Evaluation at a point extends \merge]\label{osq:cr:rem:evaluation}
For $f$ in the Cantor subalgebra \eqref{osq:if:eq:cantor}, factoring through $\Z/2^N\Z$, write $f=\sum_kc_ke_{N+1,k}$ with $c_k\in\EE_a$. Modulo
$\mathfrak M_{a,z}$ the idempotent $e_{N+1,z\bmod2^N}$ becomes $1$ and the others, orthogonal to it, become $0$, so $f\equiv c_{z\bmod2^N}=f(z)$. Hence
the quotient map $\Qa_a\to A/\mathfrak M_{a,z}$ restricts on the Cantor subalgebra to evaluation at $z$ (\cref{osq:if:rem:evaluation}) followed by the
embedding of $\EE_a$ in the residue field (\cref{osq:cr:cor:properfield}). So with global choice every point evaluation of \cref{osq:if:rem:evaluation}
extends to a homomorphism of all of $\Qa_a$ onto a field containing $\EE_a$; the extension is not unique or canonical, and its target is not $\EE_a$.
The same holds for $\Qa_a^\C$ with $\FF_a(i)$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Ordinal scales and binary branches together \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:twoaxes}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$ there is a class relation encoding pairwise distinct maximal class ideals $\mathfrak M_{\alpha,z}$ of $A$, $(\alpha,z)\in\On\times\Z_2$,
with $\mathsf f_\alpha\in\mathfrak M_{\alpha,z}$, and with the quotient maps $\varpi_{\beta,z}$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:triangular}
 \varpi_{\beta,z}\bigl(\omega^{\omega^\alpha}\bigr)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&\alpha>\beta,\\
 -1,&\alpha=\beta,\\
 \text{a nonzero unit},&\alpha<\beta.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{osq:cr:thm:cantor} with $a=\omega^\alpha$. Different branches at one scale give different ideals; at different scales the base ideals are
comaximal (\cref{osq:cr:cor:comaximal}), so no proper ideal contains both. The pattern \eqref{osq:cr:eq:triangular} is \cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff} with the
relation $\omega^{\omega^\beta}=-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Lower bounds, not a spectrum \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:lower}
\Cref{osq:cr:thm:cantor} is a continuum lower bound within one fibre: it does not say that all maximal ideals of the fibre are indexed by $\Z_2$, nor that
$\Qa^k_a$ is a ring of functions on Cantor space. \Cref{osq:cr:thm:twoaxes} is a uniform class-family statement. In two-sorted class theory the
collection of \emph{all} proper class ideals is not a class of set-valued elements, so no cardinality of it and no class-sized Zariski space with it as
points is asserted (24). The ordinal family changes the embedded scale, and by \cref{osq:cr:prop:rescale} the abstract fibres are isomorphic, so it
gives no larger same-fibre bound (\cref{osq:cr:q:branching}).
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Separation and realization in the surcomplex field.}

\begin{theorem}[Characteristic-zero maximal separation \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:separation}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, for every $0\ne x\in A$ there is a characteristic-zero maximal class ideal $\mathfrak M_x$ with $x\notin\mathfrak M_x$ and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:separating}
 1-\omega x\in\mathfrak M_x .
\end{equation}
Its residue field is a proper class. So every nonzero element of $A$ lies outside some nonarithmetic maximal class ideal: the nonarithmetic maximal
ideals have zero intersection in this elementwise sense.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
As $x\ne0$ has nonnegative support, $\omega x$ is a nonzero purely infinite element, so $1-\omega x$ is nonconstant with constant term $1$ and
\cref{osq:cr:cor:unitconstant} gives a characteristic-zero maximal ideal containing it; if it contained $x$ it would contain $\omega x$ and $1$.
By \eqref{osq:cr:eq:separating} the image of $\omega$ is the inverse of the image of $x$. The residue field contains a copy of $\No$ by
\cref{osq:if:cor:primefield}, since the ideal is nonarithmetic (\cref{osq:cr:prop:arithmetic}); 24 cites its reservoir Proposition~7.4.
\end{proof}

The intersection of the arithmetic maximal ideals is $\Pi_k$, since their membership conditions are divisibility conditions on the constant term and
the nonzero primes of $D$ intersect in $0$; the tails invisible to every arithmetic residue field are separated by the nonarithmetic class residue fields.
The Jacobson radical, expressed by the unit criterion without forming a collection of ideals, is
\[
 \Jac(A)=\{x\in A:1-rx\text{ is a unit for every }r\in A\}=0,
\]
already because $1-\omega x$ is a nonunit for $x\ne0$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}); 24 regards this as an elementary consequence. \Cref{osq:cr:thm:separation}
realizes it by nonarithmetic maximal ideals, with the foundation stated. 09 proves the set-sized analogue for its rings (\cref{osq:thm:residue}).

\begin{theorem}[Embedding a class field in $\SC$ \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:universalfield}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, every set or class field $\mathbb K$ of characteristic $0$ has a unital field embedding into $\SC$, and every embedding into $\SC$ of a
set-sized subfield $\mathbb K_0\subseteq\mathbb K$ extends to one of $\mathbb K$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix a set-like enumeration $(x_\alpha)$ of $\mathbb K$ and build compatible embeddings $e_\alpha:\mathbb K_\alpha\to\SC$ of set-sized subfields, starting
from the prescribed one (or from the canonical embedding of $\Q$). At a successor stage do nothing if $x_\alpha\in\mathbb K_\alpha$. If $x_\alpha$ is
algebraic over $\mathbb K_\alpha$, transport its minimal polynomial by $e_\alpha$ and send $x_\alpha$ to the least root in $\SC$ in the global
well-order; $\SC$ is algebraically closed. If $x_\alpha$ is transcendental, send it to an element of $\SC$ transcendental over $e_\alpha(\mathbb K_\alpha)$:
the polynomials over a set field form a set, each nonzero one has finitely many roots, and the proper class $\SC$ is not exhausted by this set of
algebraic elements. At limits take unions; a set ordinal indexes a set of sets, and each $\mathbb K_\alpha(x_\alpha)$ is a set, described by finite
rational expressions. These are set-valued recursions as above, and the union is the required class embedding.
\end{proof}

This is the standard universality argument for an algebraically closed field with more than set-many transcendence resources; 24 includes it so as not to
assume a classification of the residue fields or that they are algebraically closed.

\begin{corollary}[Algebraically closed class fields \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:cor:acfiso}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, every proper-class algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ is isomorphic, as an abstract class field, to $\SC$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Run the construction of \cref{osq:cr:thm:universalfield} back and forth along ordinal enumerations of both fields, alternately putting the next source
element in the domain and the next target element in the range; both fields are algebraically closed and have elements transcendental over each
set-sized subfield, every stage is a set partial isomorphism, and the union is bijective.
\end{proof}

This is the class back-and-forth of the surcomplex-automorphism report (\nolinkurl{saut:thm:acfhomogeneity} \cite{RepoSaut}, which extends every isomorphism
between set-sized subfields of two proper-class algebraically closed fields of the same characteristic) and of \nolinkurl{fkc:sb:lem:backforth}
\cite{RepoFKC}; 24's corollary is the case of prime subfields in characteristic $0$.

\begin{theorem}[Residual surcomplexity \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:residually}
In $\mathsf{GBC}$, every nonarithmetic maximal class ideal of $A$ is the kernel of a unital class ring homomorphism $A\to\SC$ whose image is a
proper-class field, and these homomorphisms together separate the points of $A$. In particular, for every $a>0$ there is a unital homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:complexspecial}
 \operatorname{sp}_a:\Oz\longrightarrow\SC,\qquad \operatorname{sp}_a(\omega^a)=-1,
\end{equation}
which can be chosen with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:scalarspecial}
 \operatorname{sp}_a(\omega^{a/2})=i,\qquad \operatorname{sp}_a(r\omega^a)=-r\quad(r\in\R).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Code the maximal quotient as a class field and compose the quotient map with an embedding from \cref{osq:cr:thm:universalfield}; the kernel is the given
ideal, and the image is a proper class by \cref{osq:if:cor:primefield}. \Cref{osq:cr:thm:separation}, applied to a nonzero difference, separates points.
For \eqref{osq:cr:eq:complexspecial} take a maximal ideal containing $1+\omega^a$. For \eqref{osq:cr:eq:scalarspecial} note that its residue field
contains the set-sized field $\C$ formed from the embedded $\R$ of \cref{osq:cr:lem:coefficients} and the class $u$ of $\omega^{a/2}$, with
$u^2=-1$; prescribe its embedding into $\C\subseteq\SC$ by $u\mapsto i$ and the identity on $\R$, and use the extension clause of
\cref{osq:cr:thm:universalfield}. Since the class of $r\omega^a$ is the embedded scalar $-r$, all the identities follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What ``residually surcomplex'' means \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:rem:residually}
The phrase means the separating family of \cref{osq:cr:thm:residually}. It is not residual finiteness, not a representation in a set-indexed product,
and not a single injective homomorphism with maximal kernel; a product indexed by a proper class of class fields would need further foundations and is
not used. It is not asserted that each residue field is isomorphic to $\SC$, nor that an embedding of a residue field is surjective (24).
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Failure to preserve Hahn summability \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:nonstrong}
Let $\varphi:A\to\SC$ be a unital ring homomorphism with $\varphi(1+\omega^a)=0$ for some $a>0$. Then $\varphi$ does not send every strongly summable
family in $A$ to a strongly summable family in $\SC$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The family $(\omega^{a/2^n})_{n\ge1}$ is strongly summable: its supports are distinct points of a strictly decreasing sequence. But
$\varphi(\omega^{a/2^n})^{2^n}=-1$, and $T^{2^n}+1$ splits over the ordinary complex numbers, so every $\varphi(\omega^{a/2^n})$ is a nonzero ordinary
complex number, with
support $\{0\}$. The exponent $0$ then occurs in infinitely many members of the image family.
\end{proof}

No sum in the source is missing, since $\sum_{n\ge1}\omega^{a/2^n}$ is a valid omnific integer; its image is simply not the strong sum of the images. So the specializations
do not contradict rigidity theorems for strong maps: they have nonzero kernels and fail even to preserve summability. A homomorphism satisfying
\eqref{osq:cr:eq:complexspecial} cannot take values in an ordered field, since the image of $\omega^{a/2}$ squares to $-1$; the inclusion
$\Oz\hookrightarrow\No$ is a different homomorphism (24).

\paragraph{Primes read term by term.} The monomial-prime and convex-face mechanism of ordered monoid algebras is standard; 24 uses it to delimit the
support-controlled part of the prime ideals, not to suggest that every omnific prime is a monomial prime.

\begin{definition}[\src{24}]\label{osq:cr:def:termclosed}
An ideal $P\subseteq A$ is \emph{term-closed} if for every $x\in P$ every nonzero normal-form term of $x$, including its constant term, lies in $P$; it
is \emph{strongly sum-closed} if the strong sum of every set-indexed strongly summable family of elements of $P$ lies in $P$.
\end{definition}

For a convex subgroup $H\subseteq\No$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:PH}
 \Pi_k^{>H}=\{s\in\Pi_k:\supp s\cap H=\varnothing\}=\{s\in\Pi_k:g>H\text{ for every }g\in\supp s\};
\end{equation}
the two descriptions agree because a positive element outside a convex subgroup lies above it. The endpoints are $\Pi_k^{>\{0\}}=\Pi_k$ and
$\Pi_k^{>\No}=0$, and $\Pi_k^{\gg a}=\Pi_k^{>\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$.

\begin{theorem}[Support-closed primes \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:thm:termprimes}
The prime class ideals of $A$ that are both term-closed and strongly sum-closed are exactly
\begin{enumerate}
\item the ideals $\mathfrak pA$ for a nonzero prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of $D$, and
\item the ideals $\Pi_k^{>H}$ for a convex subgroup $H\subseteq\No$, with $H$ unique.
\end{enumerate}
None of the characteristic-zero primes in this list is maximal.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $P$ meets $D$ nontrivially, $\Pi_k\subseteq P$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}), $P\cap D$ is a nonzero prime of $D$ and $P=\ct^{-1}(P\cap D)=(P\cap D)A$;
such ideals have both closure properties, their only condition being divisibility of the constant term. Suppose $P\cap D=0$. Term-closedness gives
$P\subseteq\Pi_k$. For $g>0$ and $r\in k^\times$ the identities $(r\omega^g)^2=\omega^g(r^2\omega^g)$ and $(\omega^g)^2=(r\omega^g)(r^{-1}\omega^g)$, all of
whose factors lie in $A$, and primality give
\begin{equation}\label{osq:cr:eq:coeffindependence}
 r\omega^g\in P\iff\omega^g\in P .
\end{equation}
Let $F=\{g\ge0:\omega^g\notin P\}$. It contains $0$, is closed under addition by primality, and is downward closed: if $0\le h\le g\in F$ and
$\omega^h\in P$, then $\omega^g=\omega^h\omega^{g-h}\in P$. So $H=F-F$ is a convex subgroup with $H\cap\No_{\ge0}=F$ (a nonnegative difference $f_1-f_2$ is
at most $f_1\in F$). Term-closedness and \eqref{osq:cr:eq:coeffindependence} make every support in $P$ avoid $H$; conversely, if $s\in\Pi_k$ has support
avoiding $H$, its terms lie in $P$ by \eqref{osq:cr:eq:coeffindependence}, they form a strongly summable set-indexed family, and $s\in P$. So
$P=\Pi_k^{>H}$. Conversely, deleting the exponents outside $H$ is, as in \cref{osq:cr:prop:tails}, a ring retraction $A\to D\oplus\Pi_k(H)$ onto a domain
with kernel $\Pi_k^{>H}$, so $\Pi_k^{>H}$ is prime, and both closure properties are clear from the support description. $H$ is recovered from the
nonnegative monomials outside the ideal. Finally $\Pi_k^{>H}\subseteq\Pi_k$, which is proper and not maximal since $A/\Pi_k\cong D$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A maximal binomial kernel is not a support ideal \src{24}]\label{osq:cr:cor:notsupport}
A maximal ideal containing $1+\omega^a$ is not term-closed: it contains the two-term series $1+\omega^a$ and neither of its terms. Its monomials are
nevertheless exactly the $\omega^b$ with $a\ll b$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}).
\end{corollary}

There is no tension: a monomial kernel records what happens to isolated scales, not how sums of surviving terms cancel, and the dyadic branch choices
and the binomial equation live in that additional information (24).

\paragraph{Dependencies and plausible but incorrect arguments (24).} The existence theorem is short only after the foundations are supplied; its chain is
$\mathsf{GC}\Rightarrow$ a set-like enumeration $\Rightarrow$ finite-witness recursion $\Rightarrow$ maximal class extension, and normal-form degree
(properness of the binomial ideal) and scalar divisibility of $\Pi_k$ (no arithmetic extension) connect it to $\Oz$ and $\GOz$. The monomial cutoff is
independent of the maximal-ideal construction: it concerns the concrete principal ideal, and its only infinite calculation is the strongly summable
identity \eqref{osq:cr:eq:telescope}. The continuum branching needs the finite dyadic algebras and one maximal extension per branch; the surcomplex
realization needs algebraic closedness of $\SC$ and set-valued field recursion; the support-prime classification uses primality, coefficient identities,
convexity and the two closure hypotheses, and is not used to construct maximal ideals. 24 lists eight distinctions on which its proofs depend.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A proper ideal is not a set of generators: $I$ and the ideals at the stages may be proper classes; the recursive state is the set $S_\alpha$, and
membership is a finite formula with $I$ as a class parameter.
\item A class quotient is not a collection of literal cosets; least-representative coding in $\mathsf{GBC}$, or Scott coding in $\mathsf{GB}$, keeps its
elements set-valued.
\item The converse choice theorem has universal scope: it concerns every class ring and gives no lower bound for the choice strength of the omnific ring.
\item Infinite telescoping is a support assertion: every exponent in \eqref{osq:cr:eq:g} must stay positive, so $b>a$ in place of $a\ll b$ would invalidate
it, and for $b\le Na$ the opposite holds, the monomial being a unit.
\item Finite product factors do not become prime by declaration: a dyadic branch first gives a proper ideal, and the class Krull construction extends it
to a maximal one.
\item Containing an algebraically closed field is not algebraic closedness.
\item An algebraic homomorphism is not a strong homomorphism: the source sum in \cref{osq:cr:thm:nonstrong} is valid, its image family is not strongly
summable, and no interchange of the map with the sum is allowed.
\item Computations certify only finite examples: 24's checks test finite greedy constructions, polynomial identities, finite dyadic product algebras and
finite-rank support examples, not class recursion, all surreal supports, global choice or priority.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Integral closure, complete integral closure, and invisible equations}
\label{osq:sec:closure}

The universal theorem uses exponent scales \emph{below} the supports of purely infinite
elements. This section uses a scale \emph{above} all negative exponents, which yields one
denominator for a whole set-generated algebra (03). The consequences separate three
notions that coincide for Noetherian domains: membership in $\Oz$, integrality over
$\Oz$, and almost integrality over $\Oz$. The complete integral closure of $\Oz$ is all
of $\No$, while its integral closure $\NN$ is a proper, fine-dense subring that no set of
generators produces (03). A monic equation of 08 has no root in
$\GOz$ although its image in every set-sized ring has the root $1$; its positive root is an
explicit element of $\NN\setminus\Oz$. The section ends with 19's description of $\NN$ and $\NN_\C$
modulo the ideals generated by $\Pi$, which classifies their set-sized domain images
(\cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}), and with 20's proof that the Boolean algebra of that description is atomless and a proper
class (\cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}), and with 23's fixed cyclic workspace, whose extended ideal is not radical although the Boolean algebra
of its reduced fibre is still atomless (\cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}), and with 27's henselization at the constant-term ideal of a set-sized omnific integer
part, which has the maximal number of generic branches (\cref{osq:hb:sub:henselian}).

\paragraph{Standing notation.}
As in \cref{osq:sec:model03}, $\kappa$ is an infinite cardinal with
$\mu=\cf(\kappa)>\aleph_0$, $\theta=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$, $G_\kappa$ is the two-armed
lexicographic group of 03, $F^{03}_\kappa=\Hc{\R}{G_\kappa}$ is the field of
countably supported Hahn series over $G_\kappa$, identified with its image in $\No$, and
\[
 A^{03}_\kappa=F^{03}_\kappa\cap\Oz=\Z+\Pi^{03}_\kappa,
\]
where $\Pi^{03}_\kappa$ consists of the elements of $F^{03}_\kappa$ with strictly positive
support. We write $X^g$ ($g\in G_\kappa$) for the monomials of $F^{03}_\kappa$; under the
identification they are surreal monomials. The Gaussian versions are
$F^{03}_\kappa[i]=\Hc{\C}{G_\kappa}$, $A^{03}_\kappa[i]=\Z[i]+\Pi^{03}_\kappa+i\Pi^{03}_\kappa$
and the ideal $\Pi^{03}_\kappa+i\Pi^{03}_\kappa$. The field $F^{03}_\kappa$ is real closed
and $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$ is algebraically closed (\cref{osq:sec:model03}). We write
$\overline\Z$ for the ring of complex algebraic integers and
$\overline\Z_\R=\overline\Z\cap\R$ for the real ones. For an inclusion of rings
$A\subseteq R$ the \emph{conductor} is $(A:R)=\{a\in A:aR\subseteq A\}$.

\subsection{Uniform denominators}\label{osq:nm:sub:denominators}

The clearing statement \cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i) clears one set of surreals. Applied to
a well-chosen set it clears a whole algebra.

\begin{theorem}[One denominator for a set-generated algebra \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:onedenominator}
For every set $S\subseteq\No$ there is a positive monomial $d=\omega^h\in\Pi$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:fullabsorption}
 d\,\Oz[S]\subseteq\Pi .
\end{equation}
For every set $S\subseteq\SC$ there is such a $d$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:complexabsorption}
 d\,\GOz[S]\subseteq\Pi_\C .
\end{equation}
In particular $d$ is a nonzero element of the conductor $(\Oz:\Oz[S])$, respectively
$(\GOz:\GOz[S])$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Although $\Oz[S]$ is in general a proper class, the ring $\Z[S]$ is a set: it consists of
the values of ordinary integer polynomials in finitely many members of $S$. By
\cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i) there is $h>0$ with $\omega^h\Z[S]\subseteq\Pi$. Every element
of $\Oz[S]$ is a finite sum $\sum_ja_jb_j$ with $a_j\in\Oz$ and $b_j\in\Z[S]$, and
\[
 \omega^h\sum_ja_jb_j=\sum_ja_j(\omega^hb_j)\in\Pi
\]
because $\Pi$ is an ideal of $\Oz$ (\cref{osq:lem:ct}). The complex statement is the same
argument with the set $\Z[i][S]$, the complex clause of \cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i) and
the ideal $\Pi_\C$ of $\GOz$. Finally $\Pi\subseteq\Oz$ and $\Pi_\C\subseteq\GOz$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Conductors \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:rem:conductor}
The theorem gives more than a nonzero element of the conductor $(\Oz:\Oz[S])$: it gives
a monomial whose products with the whole algebra land in the strictly positive-support
ideal $\Pi$. The real clearing statement and its proof are due to manuscript~05 (now in
the sibling report \cite{RepoOdg}); the algebra formulation and the closure consequences
below are 03's.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The bounded-size version \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption}
Let $A$ be $A^{03}_\kappa$ or $A^{03}_\kappa[i]$, with ambient field $F=F^{03}_\kappa$,
respectively $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$, constant ring $D=\Z$, respectively $\Z[i]$, and ideal
$P=\Pi^{03}_\kappa$, respectively $\Pi^{03}_\kappa+i\Pi^{03}_\kappa$. For every set
$S\subseteq F$ with $|S|<\mu=\cf(\kappa)$ there is $h>0$ in $G_\kappa$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:smallabsorption}
 X^h A[S]\subseteq P .
\end{equation}
In particular $\Frac(A^{03}_\kappa)=F^{03}_\kappa$ and
$\Frac(A^{03}_\kappa[i])=F^{03}_\kappa[i]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The ring $D[S]$ has cardinality at most $\max(|S|,\aleph_0)<\mu$, since $\mu$ is
uncountable. Each of its elements has countable support (in the complex case, take the
union of the supports of the real and imaginary coordinates). The union $U$ of these
supports is a union of fewer than $\mu$ countable sets, so $|U|<\mu$ because $\mu$ is
regular and uncountable. By \cref{osq:lem:twosided}(i) the family
$\{-g:g\in U\}\cup\{0\}$, which has fewer than $\mu$ members, has an upper bound
$b\in G_\kappa$; put $h=b+e$ for any $e>0$ in $G_\kappa$. Then $h>0$ and $h>-g$ for every
$g\in U$. Multiplication by $X^h$ translates each support by $h$, so it maps every element
of $D[S]$ to a countably supported series with strictly positive support, that is, into
$P$. Every element of $A[S]$ is a finite sum $\sum_ja_jb_j$ with $a_j\in A$ and
$b_j\in D[S]$, and $X^h\sum_ja_jb_j=\sum_ja_j(X^hb_j)\in P$ because $P$ is an ideal of $A$.

For $x\in F$ apply this to $S=\{x\}$: then $x=(X^hx)/X^h$ is a quotient of elements of
$A$, and $X^h\in P\subseteq A$ is nonzero.
\end{proof}

This supplies the fraction-field clause $\Frac(A^{03}_\kappa)=F^{03}_\kappa$ of 03's
cardinal realization (compare \cref{osq:thm:model03}). Clearing one element is weaker than
clearing \emph{all powers} of that element by the same denominator; both theorems supply
the latter as well, since $x^n\in A[x]$ for every $n$.

\subsection{Almost integrality and complete integral closure}\label{osq:nm:sub:complete}

\begin{definition}[\src{03}]\label{osq:nm:def:almost}
Let $A$ be a domain contained in a field $F$. An element $x\in F$ is \emph{almost integral}
over $A$ if there is $0\ne d\in A$ with $dx^n\in A$ for every ordinary $n\ge0$. When
$F=\Frac(A)$, the set $A^*$ of these elements is the \emph{complete integral closure} of
$A$. The \emph{integral closure} $\IC_F(A)$ consists instead of the roots in $F$ of monic
polynomials in $A[T]$.
\end{definition}

These are the standard notions of commutative algebra; they differ in non-Noetherian
settings, and we take the terminology from \cite{BGR} without importing any result of
that paper as a proof. The quantifier over powers ranges over ordinary finite powers, not
over ordinal iterations or surreal exponentiation. Each individual witness $d$ and each
monic polynomial is set-sized data, so the definitions apply verbatim to the class rings
$\Oz$ and $\GOz$.

\begin{theorem}[Every ambient element is almost integral \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:complete}
Relative to their fraction fields,
\begin{align}
 \Oz^*&=\No,& \GOz^*&=\SC,\label{osq:nm:eq:fullcic}\\
 (A^{03}_\kappa)^*&=F^{03}_\kappa,& (A^{03}_\kappa[i])^*&=F^{03}_\kappa[i].\label{osq:nm:eq:localcic}
\end{align}
More generally, every ring $R$ with $A\subseteq R\subseteq F$, where $(A,F)$ is one of
the four pairs $(\Oz,\No)$, $(\GOz,\SC)$, $(A^{03}_\kappa,F^{03}_\kappa)$,
$(A^{03}_\kappa[i],F^{03}_\kappa[i])$, has $\Frac(R)=F$ and $R^*=F$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The fraction fields are the indicated ambient fields by \cref{osq:prop:fractions}(ii) and
\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption}, so there are no further elements to consider. For $x$
in the ambient field apply \cref{osq:nm:thm:onedenominator} or
\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption} to $S=\{x\}$. The single nonzero denominator $d$
supplied there satisfies $dx^n\in dA[x]\subseteq A$ for every ordinary $n\ge0$, so $x$ is
almost integral. If $A\subseteq R\subseteq F$, then $F=\Frac(A)\subseteq\Frac(R)\subseteq
F$, and the same $d\in A\subseteq R$ gives $dx^n\in A\subseteq R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Two explicit denominators \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:ex:almost}
The rational $1/2$ is almost integral over $\Oz$, witnessed by $d=\omega$: indeed
$\omega/2^n\in\Pi$ for all $n\ge0$. The monomial $\omega^{-1}$ is almost integral,
witnessed by $d=\omega^\omega$: indeed $\omega^{\omega-n}\in\Pi$ for every ordinary $n$,
since $\omega-n>0$. Neither claim uses a limit as $n$ tends to an infinite ordinal.
Neither element is integral (\cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal} below).
\end{example}

\subsection{Integral closure: reciprocals, small units and density}\label{osq:nm:sub:integral}

The geometric statements are proved first for an arbitrary integer part of a real closed
field; this isolates what is a consequence of integer-part geometry rather than of the
proper-class size of $\No$ (03).

\begin{lemma}[An integral reciprocal was already present \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}
Let $A$ be a domain in a field $F$ and $0\ne a\in A$. If $a^{-1}$ is integral over $A$,
then $a^{-1}\in A$. Hence the integral closure of $A$ in $F$ contains the inverse of no
nonunit of $A$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $(a^{-1})^n+c_{n-1}(a^{-1})^{n-1}+\dots+c_0=0$ with $c_j\in A$ and $n\ge1$.
Multiplying by $a^{n-1}$ gives
\[
 a^{-1}=-c_{n-1}-c_{n-2}a-\dots-c_0a^{n-1}\in A. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Consequently $1/2$ is not integral over $\Oz$, $A^{03}_\kappa$, $\GOz$ or
$A^{03}_\kappa[i]$, despite \cref{osq:nm:ex:almost}: $2$ is a nonunit of each of these
rings by \cref{osq:lem:units} (the units of $A^{03}_\kappa\subseteq\Oz$ are among
$\Oz^\times=\{\pm1\}$, and similarly in the Gaussian case). More generally, for $h>0$ and
$0\ne c\in\R$ the negative monomial $c\,\omega^{-h}$ is not integral over $\Oz$, and for
$0\ne c\in\C$ it is not integral over $\GOz$: its reciprocal $c^{-1}\omega^h$ lies in the
purely infinite ideal $\Pi$, respectively $\Pi_\C$, and is a nonunit. The same holds for
$cX^{-h}$ over $A^{03}_\kappa$ and $A^{03}_\kappa[i]$ when $h>0$ in $G_\kappa$.

\begin{lemma}[Integer parts \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:lem:intpart}
Recall that a subring $A$ of an ordered field $F$ is an \emph{integer part} if for every
$x\in F$ there is a unique $\lfloor x\rfloor\in A$ with $\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor
x\rfloor+1$. Then $\Oz$ is an integer part of $\No$ and $A^{03}_\kappa$ is an integer part
of $F^{03}_\kappa$. Every nonzero element of $\Oz$ has absolute value at least $1$, and
every nonzero element of $\GOz$ has surreal modulus $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ at least $1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A nonzero element of $\Oz$ is either a nonzero ordinary integer or has positive degree
(\cref{osq:lem:units}); in the second case its absolute value exceeds every real number.
Hence $|a|\ge1$ for $0\ne a\in\Oz$, and for $a+ib\in\GOz$ with $a,b\in\Oz$ not both zero,
$\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\ge\max(|a|,|b|)\ge1$. This lower bound also gives uniqueness of floors:
two elements of $\Oz$ in a half-open interval of length $1$ differ by an element of
absolute value less than $1$. For existence, write the normal form of $x\in\No$ uniquely
as $x=P+r+\epsilon$ with $P\in\Pi$, $r\in\R$ and $\supp\epsilon$ strictly negative, so
that $\epsilon$ is zero or infinitesimal. Take $\lfloor x\rfloor=P+\lfloor r\rfloor$,
except when $r\in\Z$ and $\epsilon<0$, where $\lfloor x\rfloor=P+r-1$. In every case
$\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1$. For $x\in F^{03}_\kappa$ the same decomposition
has $P\in\Pi^{03}_\kappa$, so the floor lies in $A^{03}_\kappa$.
\end{proof}

The exceptional case in the floor formula matters: discarding all negative exponents sends
$-\omega^{-1}$ to $0$, which is not its floor.

\paragraph{Why integral elements form a ring.}
That the integral elements over a commutative ring $A$ form a ring, and that integrality is
transitive, is finite algebra, which we recall because it is applied to class rings. If
$x$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $n$ over $A$, then $A[x]=A+Ax+\dots+Ax^{n-1}$ is
