a finitely generated $A$-module, by reducing powers with that equation. If $x$ and $y$ are
integral, $A[x,y]$ is generated by finitely many monomials $w_1=1,w_2,\dots,w_N$ in $x$
and $y$. For $z\in A[x,y]$ write $zw_k=\sum_la_{kl}w_l$ with $a_{kl}\in A$; the determinant
trick shows that $\det(zI-(a_{kl}))$ annihilates every $w_l$, in particular $w_1=1$, so it
is zero, and this is a monic equation for $z$. The same argument, applied to the finitely
many coefficients of a monic equation and to the element, proves transitivity. Only
finitely many elements are involved at each step, so the arguments apply unchanged to
$\Oz$, $\GOz$ and their overrings in $\No$ and $\SC$ (03).

\begin{theorem}[Small integral units \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}
Let $F$ be a real closed ordered field, $A\subseteq F$ an integer part, and $N$ the
integral closure of $A$ in $F$. For every $H\in A_{>0}$ the element
$u_H=\sqrt{H^2+1}-H$ is a positive unit of $N$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:smallunit}
 u_H^2+2Hu_H-1=0,\qquad u_H^{-1}=u_H+2H,\qquad 0<u_H<\frac1{2H}.
\end{equation}
For every $\epsilon\in F_{>0}$ there is such a unit with $0<u_H<\epsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\sqrt{H^2+1}>H>0$, the element $u_H$ is positive. Squaring
$u_H+H=\sqrt{H^2+1}$ gives the first equation, which is monic over $A$; so $u_H\in N$.
The same equation says $u_H(u_H+2H)=1$, and $u_H+2H\in N$ because $N$ is a ring containing
$A$; so $u_H$ is a unit of $N$. Rationalizing,
\[
 u_H=\frac{1}{\sqrt{H^2+1}+H}<\frac1{2H}.
\]
An integer part is cofinal in $F$: $\lfloor 1/(2\epsilon)\rfloor+1\in A$ is positive and
exceeds $1/(2\epsilon)$. Taking $H$ to be this element gives $u_H<1/(2H)<\epsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dense normalization of an integer part \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:density}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}, $N$ is dense in $F$ for the order
topology. More precisely, for every $x\in F$ and every $\epsilon\in F_{>0}$ there is
$y\in N$ with
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:density}
 0\le x-y<\epsilon .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose a positive unit $u<\epsilon$ of $N$ by \cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits} and let
$n=\lfloor x/u\rfloor\in A$. Multiplying $n\le x/u<n+1$ by $u>0$ gives $0\le x-un<u<\epsilon$;
put $y=un\in N$. To meet a prescribed open interval $(a,b)$, apply this with
$x=(a+b)/2$ and $\epsilon<(b-a)/2$; then $y\in(x-\epsilon,x]\subseteq(a,b)$.
\end{proof}

No completion and no sequential argument is used. The same proof is valid for the order
topology of $\No$ (the fine topology), with all positive surreal radii. Results on dense
subfields and integer parts in other settings provide context \cite{Kuhlmann}; the object
here is the integral closure of a specified integer part, not an arbitrary dense subfield,
and the normalization theorem is not attributed to that work. The small-unit argument is
a general elementary lemma about integer parts, and 03 makes no priority claim for it.

\paragraph{The normalizations.}
We write
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:normalizations}
 \NN=\IC_{\No}(\Oz),\qquad \NN_\kappa=\IC_{F^{03}_\kappa}(A^{03}_\kappa).
\end{equation}
These are 03's $B$ and $B_\kappa$. Manuscript~03 wrote $\Int_F(A)$ for the integral
closure of $A$ in $F$; we write $\IC_F(A)$ because $\Int$ denotes rings of integer-valued
polynomials, such as $\Int(\Z^r)$, elsewhere in this report. Note that $\NN_\kappa$ is
defined relative to $F^{03}_\kappa$; only $\NN_\kappa\subseteq\NN\cap F^{03}_\kappa$ is
automatic, and 03 claims no descent equality. The equality $\NN\cap F^{03}_\kappa=\NN_\kappa$ does hold: it follows from
20's support projection (\cref{osq:bb:cor:descent03}, a merge result).

\begin{theorem}[Set-generated intermediate algebras are uniformly discrete \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:discrete}
For every set $S\subseteq\No$ the algebra $C=\Oz[S]$ has a positive surreal separation
bound $r$:
\[
 |x-y|\ge r\qquad\text{for all distinct }x,y\in C .
\]
It is a closed, uniformly discrete subclass of $\No$ in the fine order topology. The same
holds for $A^{03}_\kappa[S]\subseteq F^{03}_\kappa$, in the order topology of
$F^{03}_\kappa$, whenever $|S|<\mu$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose the positive monomial $d$ of \cref{osq:nm:thm:onedenominator}, respectively
$d=X^h$ of \cref{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption}. For distinct $x,y\in C$ the product
$d(x-y)$ is a nonzero element of $\Pi$ (respectively $\Pi^{03}_\kappa$), hence of the
integer part, so $|d(x-y)|\ge1$ by \cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}. Thus $|x-y|\ge1/d=:r$.

Uniform discreteness gives an isolating interval of radius $r/3$ around each point. For
closedness, let $z\notin C$. If no point of $C$ lies within $r/3$ of $z$, that
neighbourhood misses $C$. Otherwise let $c\in C$ be such a point; every other point of $C$
is at distance greater than $2r/3$ from $z$ by the triangle inequality, so a radius
smaller than both $r/3$ and $|z-c|$ gives a neighbourhood of $z$ disjoint from $C$.
\end{proof}

This is a class-size statement about a proper-class base ring; it is not the familiar
assertion that a finite extension of a discrete ring is discrete in an Archimedean
topology (03).

\begin{theorem}[Proper dense normalization, zero conductor, no set of generators \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:normalization}
For the full omnific ring,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:normalization}
 \Oz\subsetneq\NN\subsetneq\No,\qquad \overline{\NN}^{\,\mathrm{fine}}=\No,\qquad
 (\Oz:\NN)=0,
\end{equation}
and $\NN$ is not generated as an $\Oz$-algebra by any set of its elements. For the
set-sized ring $A^{03}_\kappa$, the normalization $\NN_\kappa$ satisfies
$A^{03}_\kappa\subsetneq\NN_\kappa\subsetneq F^{03}_\kappa$, is dense in $F^{03}_\kappa$,
has conductor $(A^{03}_\kappa:\NN_\kappa)=0$, and requires at least $\mu$ algebra
generators over $A^{03}_\kappa$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The element $\sqrt2\in\R\subseteq F^{03}_\kappa$ is integral, being a root of $T^2-2$,
and it is in neither integer part, whose real elements are the ordinary integers; so the
first inclusions are strict. The element $1/2$ is not integral by
\cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}, so the second inclusions are strict. The fields $\No$ and
$F^{03}_\kappa$ are real closed and $\Oz$, $A^{03}_\kappa$ are integer parts
(\cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}); density is \cref{osq:nm:thm:density}.

For the conductor, fix $a\ne0$ in the integer part. Choose a positive unit $u$ of the
normalization with $u<1/|a|$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}). Then $au$ lies in the
normalization and $0<|au|<1$, so $au$ is not in the integer part by
\cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}. Hence $a$ is not in the conductor, and this holds for every
$a\ne0$.

If $\NN=\Oz[S]$ for a set $S$, then \cref{osq:nm:thm:onedenominator} would give a nonzero
element $d$ of the conductor, a contradiction. (Equivalently, $\NN$ would be uniformly
discrete by \cref{osq:nm:thm:discrete}, contradicting density.) The same argument with
\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption} shows that $\NN_\kappa\ne A^{03}_\kappa[S]$ whenever
$|S|<\mu$.
\end{proof}

Integral closure therefore changes the fine geometry of the ring, although $\NN$ still
contains neither $1/2$ nor any nonzero negative monomial $c\,\omega^{-h}$. For
$\kappa=\aleph_1$ the theorem says, without the continuum hypothesis, that the
normalization cannot be obtained by adjoining countably many elements to the
continuum-sized ring $A^{03}_{\aleph_1}$ (here $\theta=\aleph_1^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$).
For general $\kappa$ the theorem gives only the \emph{lower bound} $\mu$ on the number of
algebra generators of $\NN_\kappa$, not an exact generation number; the exact count $\mu$
of 03's cardinal realization (\cref{osq:thm:model03}) concerns the ideal
$\Pi^{03}_\kappa$, not the normalization.

\begin{remark}[Dense does not mean sequentially approximable \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:rem:dense}
The fine topology of $\No$ has the size obstructions discussed in the foundations report
\cite{RepoFound}. The density statement chooses a point separately for each positive
surreal radius; it does not produce a nonconstant convergent set-indexed net. Indeed, every
fixed set of elements of $\NN$ lies in a single uniformly discrete algebra $\Oz[S]$ by
\cref{osq:nm:thm:discrete}. The dense normalization requires access to more than any
fixed set of its additional generators.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Constant slices, truncation, and a unit equation}\label{osq:nm:sub:slices}

The results above do not give a complete normal-form test for integrality. They do give
exact tests on the nonnegative-support slice, and they show why leading-term tests fail
(03). Recall $\A_{\R,\R}=\R+\Pi$ (03's $P_\R$), on which $\ct$ is a ring homomorphism onto
$\R$ by \cref{osq:lem:ct}, although $\A_{\R,\R}$ is not an integer part; its countable
version is $\R+\Pi^{03}_\kappa$.

\begin{theorem}[The real constant and support slices \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:realslice}
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:realslice}
 \NN\cap\A_{\R,\R}=\overline\Z_\R+\Pi=\A_{\overline\Z_\R,\R},\qquad
 \NN\cap\R=\overline\Z_\R,\qquad \NN\cap\Q=\Z .
\end{equation}
The same formulas hold for $\NN_\kappa$, with $\A_{\R,\R}$ and $\Pi$ replaced by
$\R+\Pi^{03}_\kappa$ and $\Pi^{03}_\kappa$ in the first formula.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $x=r+P$ with $r\in\R$ and $P\in\Pi$, and suppose
$x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=0$ with $a_j\in\Oz$. All terms lie in $\A_{\R,\R}$, and
applying the ring homomorphism $\ct$ gives $r^n+\ct(a_{n-1})r^{n-1}+\dots+\ct(a_0)=0$, a
monic equation over $\Z$. So $r\in\overline\Z_\R$. Conversely, a real algebraic integer $r$
is integral over $\Z\subseteq\Oz$, and $P\in\Pi\subseteq\Oz$, so $r+P$ is integral over
$\Oz$ because integral elements form a ring. This is the first equality; intersecting with
$\R$ gives the second, and the third holds because a rational root of a monic integer
polynomial is an integer. For $\NN_\kappa$ the coefficients lie in
$A^{03}_\kappa\subseteq\Oz$, the element lies in $\R+\Pi^{03}_\kappa$, and the same
argument applies; conversely $\overline\Z_\R\subseteq\R\subseteq F^{03}_\kappa$ and
$\Pi^{03}_\kappa\subseteq A^{03}_\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[\src{03}]\label{osq:nm:ex:slice}
The element $\pi\omega+\sqrt2$ is integral over $\Oz$, whereas $\pi\omega+\pi$ is not. The
nature of a coefficient at a \emph{positive} exponent is irrelevant to the test; only the
ordinary constant coefficient is constrained. The element $\omega+1/2$ is almost integral
(\cref{osq:nm:thm:complete}) but not integral, since $1/2\notin\overline\Z_\R$.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[Normalization is not truncation closed \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:prop:truncation}
Let $h>0$ and $H=\omega^h$ (or $H=X^h$ with $h>0$ in $G_\kappa$). The integral unit $u_H$
of \cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits} has the normal form
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:binomialunit}
 u_H=\sum_{n\ge1}\binom{1/2}{n}\omega^{-(2n-1)h}
 =\tfrac12\omega^{-h}-\tfrac18\omega^{-3h}+\tfrac1{16}\omega^{-5h}
 -\tfrac5{128}\omega^{-7h}+\tfrac7{256}\omega^{-9h}-\cdots .
\end{equation}
Its leading monomial $\frac12\omega^{-h}$ is not integral over the integer part.
Therefore neither $\NN$ nor $\NN_\kappa$ is closed under leading normal-form truncation.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:nm:lem:binomial} below with $m=2$ and $\gamma=2h$, the series
$s=\omega^h\mathsf b_2(\omega^{-2h})$ satisfies $s^2=\omega^{2h}(1+\omega^{-2h})=H^2+1$.
Its leading term is $\omega^h>0$, so $s$ is the positive square root $\sqrt{H^2+1}$ (an
ordered field has at most one positive square root of a given element). Hence
\[
 u_H=s-\omega^h=\omega^h\bigl(\mathsf b_2(\omega^{-2h})-1\bigr)
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\binom{1/2}{n}\omega^{h-2nh},
\]
a series with countable, reverse well-ordered support $\{-(2n-1)h:n\ge1\}$. The first five
binomial coefficients are $\binom{1/2}{1}=\frac12$, $\binom{1/2}{2}=-\frac18$,
$\binom{1/2}{3}=\frac1{16}$, $\binom{1/2}{4}=-\frac5{128}$ and
$\binom{1/2}{5}=\frac7{256}$. In the countable model the same computation takes place in
$F^{03}_\kappa$. The leading monomial $\frac12\omega^{-h}$ is the reciprocal of the nonunit
$2\omega^h$ of the integer part, so it is not integral by \cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}.
\end{proof}

This is stronger than the statement that some integral elements have negative exponents:
their negative tails can be essential, since deleting all but the leading term destroys
integrality. In the opposite direction, \cref{osq:nm:thm:realslice} gives a complete
constant-term criterion when negative exponents are absent (03).

\begin{proposition}[A unit equation acquires solutions only after normalization \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:prop:unitdioph}
Let $A$ be $\Oz$ or $A^{03}_\kappa$ and $0\ne H\in A$. The equation
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:unitdioph}
 U^2+2HU-1=0
\end{equation}
has no solution in $A$. For $H>0$ its two roots in the real closed ambient field are
$u_H$ and $-2H-u_H$; both are integral units and belong to the normalization.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A solution in $A$ would satisfy $U(U+2H)=1$, so $U$ would be a unit of $A$, hence
$U=\pm1$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}; $A^{03}_\kappa\subseteq\Oz$). Substituting $U=1$ gives
$2H=0$ and substituting $U=-1$ gives $-2H=0$, both contrary to $H\ne0$. The two roots are
$u_H$ and $-2H-u_H$ because their sum is $-2H$. Each is integral by the monic equation, and
their product is $-1$, so each is a unit of the normalization.
\end{proof}

Thus membership, integrality and almost integrality give three different arithmetic
environments even for a single quadratic equation with a parameter. This does not
contradict constant-term transfer for systems with ordinary integer coefficients: here a
possibly infinite coefficient $H$ is fixed, and changing the ambient ring changes the
allowed witnesses (03).

\subsection{The surcomplex and Gaussian versions}\label{osq:nm:sub:complex}

The Gaussian omnific ring $\GOz=\Oz+i\Oz=\Z[i]\oplus\Pi_\C$ is the natural Gaussian
analogue of $\Oz$; it is not discretely ordered. It has the split Gaussian constant term
$\ct:\GOz\to\Z[i]$ (\cref{osq:lem:ct}), its units are $\pm1,\pm i$ (\cref{osq:lem:units}),
and each nonzero element has surreal modulus at least $1$ (\cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}). Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:complexnormalization}
 \NN_\C=\IC_{\SC}(\GOz),\qquad
 \NN_{\kappa,\C}=\IC_{F^{03}_\kappa[i]}(A^{03}_\kappa[i]),
\end{equation}
03's $C$ and $C_\kappa$. Since $i$ is integral over $\Oz$, transitivity shows that these are
also the integral closures of $\Oz$ in $\SC$ and of $A^{03}_\kappa$ in $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$.
Complex conjugation is a ring automorphism of $\SC$ preserving $\GOz$ (and of
$F^{03}_\kappa[i]$ preserving $A^{03}_\kappa[i]$), so it preserves $\NN_\C$ and
$\NN_{\kappa,\C}$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:realintersection}
 \NN_\C\cap\No=\NN,\qquad \NN_{\kappa,\C}\cap F^{03}_\kappa=\NN_\kappa .
\end{equation}
Complexification nevertheless does not commute with normalization, and the failure is
located at the prime $2$.

\begin{proposition}[The complexification defect is killed by $2$ \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:prop:complexdefect}
There are strict inclusions of additive subclasses
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:complexdefect}
 \NN[i]\subsetneq\NN_\C\subsetneq\tfrac12\NN[i],\qquad \NN_\C[1/2]=\NN[1/2][i].
\end{equation}
The last object of the chain is a fractional module, not asserted to be a ring. In
particular $2\NN_\C\subseteq\NN[i]$ although $\NN_\C\ne\NN[i]$. The same inclusions hold
for $\NN_\kappa$ and $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$, and the set-sized quotient
$\NN_{\kappa,\C}/\NN_\kappa[i]$ is a nonzero $\NN_\kappa$-module annihilated by $2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Every element of $\NN[i]$ is integral over $\GOz$, so $\NN[i]\subseteq\NN_\C$. If
$z=x+iy\in\NN_\C$ with $x,y\in\No$, then $\bar z\in\NN_\C$, so
\[
 2x=z+\bar z\in\NN_\C\cap\No=\NN,\qquad 2y=-i(z-\bar z)\in\NN_\C\cap\No=\NN
\]
by \eqref{osq:nm:eq:realintersection}. Hence $2\NN_\C\subseteq\NN[i]$, that is,
$\NN_\C\subseteq\frac12\NN[i]$. Inverting $2$ in $2\NN_\C\subseteq\NN[i]\subseteq\NN_\C$
gives $\NN_\C[1/2]=\NN[i][1/2]=\NN[1/2][i]$.

The root of unity $\zeta=(-1+i\sqrt3)/2$ satisfies $\zeta^2+\zeta+1=0$, so
$\zeta\in\NN_\C$; its real coordinate $-1/2$ is not in $\NN$ by
\cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}, so $\zeta\notin\NN[i]$. Finally $1/2\in\frac12\NN[i]$ is not
in $\NN_\C$, again by the reciprocal lemma, since $2$ is a nonunit of $\GOz$. The proof is
unchanged in $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$, which contains $\zeta$; there $\zeta$ represents a nonzero
class of $\NN_{\kappa,\C}/\NN_\kappa[i]$, and this quotient of $\NN_\kappa$-modules is
annihilated by $2$ because $2\NN_{\kappa,\C}\subseteq\NN_\kappa[i]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dense Gaussian normalization and its constant slice \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:complexnormal}
The ring $\NN_\C$ is a proper dense subring of $\SC$ for the surreal-modulus topology, its
conductor $(\GOz:\NN_\C)$ is zero, and it cannot be generated over $\GOz$ by a set.
Moreover, with $\A_{\C,\C}=\C+\Pi_\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:complexslice}
 \NN_\C\cap\A_{\C,\C}=\overline\Z+\Pi_\C=\A_{\overline\Z,\C},\qquad
 \NN_\C\cap\C=\overline\Z .
\end{equation}
For $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$ the analogous properness, density, slice (with
$\Pi^{03}_\kappa+i\Pi^{03}_\kappa$ in place of $\Pi_\C$) and zero-conductor statements
hold, and fewer than $\mu$ algebra generators over $A^{03}_\kappa[i]$ do not suffice.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $z=x+iy\in\SC$ and $\epsilon>0$. Choose a positive real integral unit
$u<\epsilon/2$ of $\NN$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}) and put
\[
 n=\lfloor x/u\rfloor,\qquad m=\lfloor y/u\rfloor,\qquad w=u(n+im).
\]
The floors lie in $\Oz$ and $u\in\NN\subseteq\NN_\C$, so $w\in\NN_\C$. Each coordinate of
$z-w$ lies in $[0,u)$, hence $|z-w|<\sqrt2\,u<\epsilon$. This proves density. The element
$1/2$ is excluded by \cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}, which proves properness.

For $0\ne a\in\GOz$ choose such a $u$ with $0<u<1/|a|$. Then $au\in\NN_\C$ and
$0<|au|<1$, so $au\notin\GOz$ by \cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}; thus the conductor is zero.
If $\NN_\C=\GOz[S]$ for a set $S$, \cref{osq:nm:thm:onedenominator} would give a nonzero
element of the conductor; for $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$ and fewer than $\mu$ generators,
\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallabsorption} does the same. The two absorption theorems also show
directly that every such small-generated algebra has a uniform modulus separation bound,
as in \cref{osq:nm:thm:discrete}.

Finally, let $z=c+P$ with $c\in\C$ and $P\in\Pi_\C$, integral over $\GOz$. All terms of its
monic equation lie in $\A_{\C,\C}$, and applying the ring homomorphism
$\ct:\A_{\C,\C}\to\C$ shows that $c$ is integral over $\Z[i]$; since $\Z[i]$ is integral
over $\Z$, $c\in\overline\Z$. Conversely such a $c$ is integral over the base, and $P$
already belongs to it. Restricting to constants gives the second equality. The same
arguments work in $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$, using the real integer part $A^{03}_\kappa$ of
$F^{03}_\kappa$ for the floors.
\end{proof}

The original integer-part rings have many finite quotients:
$\Oz/n\Oz\cong\Z/n\Z$ for ordinary $n\ge1$ by \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}, and likewise
$A^{03}_\kappa/nA^{03}_\kappa\cong\Z/n\Z$, because the purely infinite ideal is divisible
by every nonzero ordinary integer (compare \cref{osq:thm:quotients}). Their
normalizations behave oppositely.

\begin{theorem}[No nonzero finite ring targets \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:nofinite}
None of $\NN$, $\NN_\kappa$, $\NN_\C$, $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$ admits a unital homomorphism to a
nonzero finite ring. In particular none of them has a proper ideal of finite index.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose such a homomorphism exists. Its image is a nonzero finite commutative ring, even
if the target is not commutative, and a maximal ideal of the image gives a unital
homomorphism onto a finite field $\F_q$. The ordinary monic polynomial $T^q-T-1$ is
negative at $0$ and positive at $2$, so it has a real root $\alpha\in(0,2)$. This $\alpha$
is a real algebraic integer and belongs to all four normalizations by
\cref{osq:nm:thm:realslice,osq:nm:thm:complexnormal}. Its image $\bar\alpha$ would satisfy
$\bar\alpha^q-\bar\alpha-1=0$ in $\F_q$, whereas every element of $\F_q$ satisfies
$\bar\alpha^q-\bar\alpha=0$; so $1=0$ in $\F_q$, which is impossible. A proper ideal of
finite index would give a unital homomorphism onto a nonzero finite ring.
\end{proof}

The proof uses only the real algebraic integer constants. Accordingly this finite-quotient
obstruction is a general consequence of containing those constants, not a phenomenon
specific to surreal supports. It says nothing about infinite set-sized homomorphic images
of the normalizations, and 03 classifies none (03). Manuscript~19 classifies the domain
images and factors every set-sized image through $\NN/\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:domainimages,osq:nf:cor:small}).

\subsection{Set-valued valuations cannot contain the omnific ring}\label{osq:nm:sub:valuations}

A \emph{valuation} of a field $F$ (possibly a proper class, such as $\No$ or $\SC$) is a
map $v:F^\times\to\Gamma$ to an ordered abelian group with $v(xy)=v(x)+v(y)$ and
$v(x+y)\ge\min(v(x),v(y))$ whenever $x+y\ne0$; its valuation ring consists of $0$ and the
elements of nonnegative value. No compatibility with the ordering of $F$ is assumed. The
value group is \emph{set-sized} if $\Gamma$ is a set.

\begin{lemma}[No nonzero set-valued ordered quotient of $(\No,+)$ \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:lem:orderedmap}
Every order-preserving additive class map $w:(\No,+)\to\Gamma$ into a set-sized ordered
abelian group is zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $w(x)\ne0$ for some $x$. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ if necessary, $w(x)>0$; then $x\ne0$,
and $x<0$ would give $w(x)\le w(0)=0$, so $h:=x>0$ and $w(h)>0$. Choose a cardinal
$\lambda>|\Gamma|$ and consider the set of surreals $\alpha h$ (surreal products) for
ordinals $\alpha<\lambda$. If $\alpha<\beta$, then $\beta\ge\alpha+1$ in the surreal
order, the ordinal successor being the surreal sum with $1$. Hence
$\beta h-\alpha h\ge h$ and, by additivity and monotonicity,
\[
 w(\beta h)-w(\alpha h)=w(\beta h-\alpha h)\ge w(h)>0 .
\]
So the $\lambda$ elements $\alpha h$ have pairwise distinct images in $\Gamma$, contradicting
$\lambda>|\Gamma|$. Only a set of ordinals was used.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Full-class valuation obstruction \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:thm:valuation}
Let $v:\No^\times\to\Gamma$ be a valuation with set-sized value group. If $v(a)\ge0$ for
every $0\ne a\in\Oz$, then $v$ is trivial. Likewise, a valuation of $\SC$ with set-sized
value group whose valuation ring contains $\GOz$ is trivial.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define $w(g)=v(\omega^g)$ for $g\in\No$. The monomial law $\omega^{g+g'}=\omega^g\omega^{g'}$
makes $w$ additive. If $g>0$ then $\omega^g\in\Pi\subseteq\Oz$, so $w(g)\ge0$; hence
$g\le g'$ implies $w(g')-w(g)=w(g'-g)\ge0$, and $w$ is order preserving. By
\cref{osq:nm:lem:orderedmap}, $w=0$.

For $x\ne0$, clear the set $\{x,x^{-1}\}$ by \cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i): there is a
monomial $d=\omega^h$ with $dx,dx^{-1}\in\Pi\subseteq\Oz$. Since $v(d)=w(h)=0$,
\[
 v(x)=v(dx)\ge0,\qquad -v(x)=v(x^{-1})=v(dx^{-1})\ge0,
\]
so $v(x)=0$. The complex proof uses the same real monomials and the complex clause of
\cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i), with $dx,dx^{-1}\in\Pi_\C\subseteq\GOz$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the size restriction is essential \src{03}]\label{osq:nm:rem:valsize}
The theorem does not say that $\No$ has no interesting valuations. Its normal-form
valuation $x\mapsto-\max\supp x$ takes values in the proper-class group $(\No,+)$ and is
negative on positive-exponent monomials, so it does not satisfy the containment hypothesis
anyway. Nor is the theorem a consequence of complete integral closure alone: in the
lexicographically ordered group $\Z\oplus\Z$, the values $v(d)=(1,0)$ and $v(x)=(0,-1)$
would give $v(dx^n)=(1,-n)>0$ for every ordinary $n$ although $v(x)<0$. Almost integrality
by itself cannot eliminate valuations of higher rank.

For ordinary set-sized domains the integral closure is characterized by valuation
overrings with set-sized value groups \cite[Lemmas 10.50.3 and 10.50.11]{StacksVal}. That
valuative criterion of integrality cannot be imported to a class ring while retaining only
set-sized value groups: $1/2$ is not integral over $\Oz$, yet
\cref{osq:nm:thm:valuation} rules out every nontrivial valuation of that restricted kind
whose ring contains $\Oz$. No assertion is made about the existence or classification of
\emph{proper-class-valued} valuation overrings separating nonintegral surreal elements.
\end{remark}

\subsection{An equation invisible to every set-sized image}\label{osq:nm:sub:invisible}

Manuscript~08 writes $B_m(t)$ for the binomial series; we write $\mathsf b_m(t)$.

\begin{lemma}[The binomial identity \src{08}]\label{osq:nm:lem:binomial}
For an ordinary integer $m\ge2$ the formal power series
\[
 \mathsf b_m(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}\binom{1/m}{n}t^n\in\Q[[t]]
\]
satisfies $\mathsf b_m(t)^m=1+t$. For every $\gamma\in\No_{>0}$ the substitution
$t=\omega^{-\gamma}$ is a valid Hahn substitution, and
$\mathsf b_m(\omega^{-\gamma})^m=1+\omega^{-\gamma}$ in $\No$. The same holds for
$t=X^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma>0$ in any ordered abelian group, in particular in
$F^{03}_\kappa$ (this last sentence is 03's use of the binomial expansion in its Hahn fields, not 08's).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $b_n=\binom{1/m}{n}$; then $b_0=1$ and $(n+1)b_{n+1}=(1/m-n)b_n$. The coefficient of
$t^n$ in $(1+t)\mathsf b_m'$ is $(n+1)b_{n+1}+nb_n=b_n/m$, so
$(1+t)\mathsf b_m'=\frac1m\mathsf b_m$. Put $c=\mathsf b_m^m=\sum_nc_nt^n$. Then
$(1+t)c'=m\,\mathsf b_m^{m-1}(1+t)\mathsf b_m'=c$ and $c_0=1$. Comparing coefficients gives
$(n+1)c_{n+1}=(1-n)c_n$ for $n\ge0$, so $c_1=1$, $c_2=0$ and hence $c_n=0$ for all $n\ge2$.
Thus $c=1+t$.

After substitution the support lies in $\{-n\gamma:n\ge0\}$, which is reverse well
ordered. In any fixed finite product each exponent $-n\gamma$ receives finitely many
contributions, because an ordinary integer $n\ge0$ has only finitely many ordered
decompositions into a fixed number of nonnegative integers. Hence
$\sum_nc_nt^n\mapsto\sum_nc_n\omega^{-n\gamma}$ is a ring homomorphism
$\Q[[t]]\to\No$, and the formal identity remains a Hahn identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Universal small-target failure of root detection \src{08}]\label{osq:nm:thm:invisible}
Fix $\gamma\in\No_{>0}$ and an ordinary integer $m\ge2$. The equation
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:invisible}
 T^m=\omega^\gamma+1
\end{equation}
has no root in $\GOz$, and therefore none in $\Oz$. Nevertheless, for every unital ring
homomorphism $\varphi:\Oz\to R$ with $R$ set-sized, the image equation
$T^m=\varphi(\omega^\gamma)+1_R$ has the solution $T=1_R$. The same holds for unital
homomorphisms with domain $\GOz$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $r=\omega^{\gamma/m}\mathsf b_m(\omega^{-\gamma})\in\No$. By
\cref{osq:nm:lem:binomial}, $r^m=\omega^\gamma(1+\omega^{-\gamma})=\omega^\gamma+1$. For
every ordinary complex $m$th root of unity $\zeta$, the element $\zeta r\in\SC$ is a
root. These are $m$ distinct roots (as $r\ne0$), so they exhaust the roots of the
degree-$m$ polynomial $T^m-\omega^\gamma-1$ in the field $\SC$; no algebraic-closedness
argument is needed. The complex normal form of each root begins
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nm:eq:rootexpansion}
 \zeta r=\zeta\omega^{\gamma/m}+\frac{\zeta}{m}\,\omega^{\gamma/m-\gamma}
 +\sum_{n\ge2}\zeta\binom{1/m}{n}\omega^{\gamma/m-n\gamma}.
\end{equation}
The exponent $\gamma/m-\gamma$ is strictly negative because $m\ge2$, its coefficient
$\zeta/m$ is nonzero, and it differs from every other exponent $\gamma/m-n\gamma$
($n\ne1$) of the expansion. So this negative-exponent term cannot cancel, and no root lies
in $\GOz=\Z[i]\oplus\Pi_\C$, whose elements have nonnegative support.

On the other hand, by \cref{osq:thm:universal} every unital homomorphism $\varphi$ from
$\Oz$ to a set-sized ring kills $\Pi$, so $\varphi(\omega^\gamma)=0$ and the image equation
is $T^m=1_R$, solved by $1_R$. For a unital homomorphism with domain $\GOz$, the universal
theorem with $D=\Z[i]$ and $k=\C$ (see \cref{osq:cor:gaussian} for the description of these
maps) again gives $\varphi(\omega^\gamma)=0$.
\end{proof}

The nonexistence of a root in $\GOz$ is also a case of 16's image-gap theorem
(\cref{osq:fs:rem:special}(c)). This is not merely a failure of a local--global test by congruences
modulo ordinary primes.
Even allowing \emph{every set-sized ring} as a target does not reveal the missing negative
tail in \eqref{osq:nm:eq:rootexpansion}. The obstruction belongs to the full normal-form
arithmetic and survives in the proper-class ring itself (08).

\begin{corollary}[\src{08; 03}]\label{osq:nm:cor:notintclosed}
The ring $\Oz$ is not integrally closed in its fraction field $\No$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The positive square root of $\omega+1$ lies in $\No=\Frac(\Oz)$
(\cref{osq:prop:fractions}(ii)). It is integral over $\Oz$, being a root of the monic
polynomial $T^2-(\omega+1)$, but it is not in $\Oz$ by \cref{osq:nm:thm:invisible} with
$m=2$ and $\gamma=1$.
\end{proof}

The same corollary is contained in 03's \cref{osq:nm:thm:normalization}, with the witness
$\sqrt2$, and manuscript~05 of the sibling report \cite{RepoOdg} proves it with the same
witness $\sqrt2$. This elementary corollary is included to clarify the distinction between
an integer part and an integral closure; it is not offered as a new factorization theorem
(08).

\begin{remark}[Explicit elements of $\NN\setminus\Oz$ \merge]\label{osq:nm:rem:rootinN}
Let $r$ be the positive root of $T^m-(\omega^\gamma+1)$ in $\No$, for $\gamma>0$ and
$m\ge2$; it is the element $r=\omega^{\gamma/m}\mathsf b_m(\omega^{-\gamma})$ of the proof
of \cref{osq:nm:thm:invisible}. Then
\[
 r\in\NN\setminus\Oz,\qquad \zeta r\in\NN_\C\setminus\GOz\quad(\zeta^m=1).
\]
Indeed $r$ is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $\Oz$, so it lies in $\NN$
by definition, and $\zeta r$ lies in $\NN_\C$ for the same reason; neither lies in the
respective integer ring by \cref{osq:nm:thm:invisible}. Thus 08's equation exhibits
explicit elements of the normalization whose absence from $\Oz$ is invisible to every
set-sized image: under every unital homomorphism from $\Oz$ to a set-sized ring the
defining equation of $r$ becomes $T^m=1$, which already has the root $1$. Equivalently, if
$\psi$ is a unital homomorphism from $\NN$ (or from $\Oz[r]$) to a set-sized ring, then its
restriction to $\Oz$ kills $\omega^\gamma$ by \cref{osq:thm:universal}, so $\psi(r)^m=1$.
Unlike $\sqrt2$, the elements $r$ are not constants: by
\eqref{osq:nm:eq:rootexpansion} they have infinite leading term $\omega^{\gamma/m}$ and a
nonzero negative tail. Nothing is claimed in this remark about the set-sized images of $\NN$
themselves; they are the subject of \cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre}, where
\cref{osq:nf:rem:rootimages} sharpens $\psi(r)^m=1$ for domain targets.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The arithmetic fibre of the normalization}\label{osq:nf:sub:fibre}

This subsection is manuscript~19's. It studies the normalizations $\NN$ and $\NN_\C$ (19's $N_\R$ and $N_\C$) modulo the ideals
that $\Pi$ generates in them, and it answers part of \cref{osq:q:normalization}. We write $\NN_\bullet$ for $\NN_\R=\NN$ or $\NN_\C$,
$\Pi\NN_\bullet$ for the extended ideal of finite sums of products (19's $K_\R,K_\C$), and
\[
 \mathsf B_\bullet=\NN_\bullet/\Pi\NN_\bullet,\qquad \mathsf B^\Q_\bullet=\mathsf B_\bullet\otimes_\Z\Q
\]
(19's $B_\epsilon$, $E_\epsilon$; 03 had used $B$ for the normalization itself, here $\NN$, and the letters $\EE$ and $\mathsf E$ are taken).
$\Idem(R)$ is the Boolean algebra of idempotents of a commutative ring $R$ (19's $\mathcal E$), $\overline\Z$ is the ring of all complex
algebraic integers, $\overline\Q$ its fraction field and $\Fpbar$ an algebraic closure of $\F_p$. Quotients by class ideals are read
as in \cref{osq:sub:foundations}. 19 did not see 03's text (\cref{osq:sub:sources}), and four of its results are 03's, printed above and
credited here: the constant slices $\NN\cap\R=\overline\Z_\R$ and $\NN_\C\cap\C=\overline\Z$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:realslice,osq:nm:thm:complexnormal}),
the absence of nonzero finite images (\cref{osq:nm:thm:nofinite}; a different proof is \cref{osq:nf:thm:domainimages} below), the strict
inclusion $\NN[i]\subsetneq\NN_\C$ (\cref{osq:nm:prop:complexdefect}; 19's witness is $w_\pm$ of \cref{osq:nf:prop:idempotents} in place of
$\zeta_3$), and infinitesimal integral units (\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}; 19's unit of \cref{osq:nf:prop:unit} has a different residue). Its
reproof of the universal theorem for $\Oz$ is credited in \cref{osq:sub:universalthm}.

\begin{lemma}[Contraction \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:lem:contraction}
$\Pi\NN_\bullet\cap\Oz=\Pi$, and $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ is divisible by every nonzero ordinary integer. Hence $\mathsf B_\bullet$ is a nonzero
ring containing $\Z$, torsion free over $\Z$, and integral over $\Z$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $0\ne n\in\Z$ lies in $\Pi\NN_\bullet$, say $n=\sum_{j\le r}a_jb_j$ with $a_j\in\Pi$ and $b_j\in\NN_\bullet$. The ring
$C=\Oz[b_1,\dots,b_r]$ is generated as an $\Oz$-module by finitely many elements $c_1=1,c_2,\dots,c_s$, and $nc_l=\sum_mh_{lm}c_m$ with all
$h_{lm}\in\Pi$ because $n\in\Pi C$. The adjugate of $nI-(h_{lm})$ shows that $\det(nI-(h_{lm}))$ kills every $c_l$, in particular $c_1=1$;
expanding, $n^s+j_{s-1}n^{s-1}+\dots+j_0=0$ with $j_\nu\in\Pi$, and $\ct$ gives $n^s=0$, which is absurd. If $a\in\Pi\NN_\bullet\cap\Oz$,
then $\ct(a)=a-(a-\ct(a))\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$, so $\ct(a)=0$. Divisibility: $\sum_ja_jb_j/n=\sum_j(a_j/n)b_j$. So $nx\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$
with $x\in\NN_\bullet$ forces $x\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$, which is torsion freeness. Reducing a monic equation of $x\in\NN_\bullet$ over $\Oz$
modulo $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ replaces each coefficient $a$ by $\ct(a)\in\Z$.
\end{proof}

A large normal overring need not preserve the contraction of an ideal; the determinant argument prevents $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ from
containing $1$, although it contains elements that differ from $1$ by an infinitesimal (19).

\begin{theorem}[Radicality \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:thm:radical}
If $x\in\NN_\bullet$ and $x^m\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$ for some ordinary $m\ge1$, then $x\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$. Hence $\mathsf B_\bullet$ and
$\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ are reduced, $\mathsf B_\bullet\to\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ is injective, and $\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ is algebraic over $\Q$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $x^m=\sum_ja_jb_j$ with $a_j\in\Pi$, $b_j\in\NN_\bullet$. By \cref{osq:prop:common}(i) there is $a>0$ with every $a_j\in\omega^a\Pi$;
put $d=\omega^{a/m}$, so that $a_j/d^m\in\Pi$ for all $j$. Then $(x/d)^m=\sum_j(a_j/d^m)b_j\in\NN_\bullet$, so
$x/d$ is a root of a monic polynomial over $\NN_\bullet$ and lies in $\NN_\bullet$; hence $x=d(x/d)\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$. Reducedness passes
to the localization, injectivity is torsion freeness, and a rational multiple of an element integral over $\Z$ is algebraic.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rational saturation \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:thm:saturation}
$\mathsf B_\bullet$ is integrally closed in $\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$, and $\mathsf B_\bullet=\{y\in\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet:y\text{ is integral over }\Z\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Represent $y$ by $x/n$ with $x\in\NN_\bullet$ and $0\ne n\in\Z$, and let $y$ satisfy a monic equation over $\mathsf B_\bullet$; lift it to a
monic $f\in\NN_\bullet[X]$. The kernel of $\NN_\bullet\otimes\Q\to\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ is the localization of $\Pi\NN_\bullet$, which is
$\Pi\NN_\bullet$ itself by divisibility (\cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction}); so $c=f(x/n)\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$, and $x/n$ is a root of the monic
$f(X)-c\in\NN_\bullet[X]$, hence lies in $\NN_\bullet$. Elements of $\mathsf B_\bullet$ are integral over $\Z$ by \cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction},
and an element of $\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ integral over $\Z$ is integral over $\mathsf B_\bullet$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The extended ideal \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:prop:ideal}
$\Pi\NN_\bullet=(\Pi\NN_\bullet)^2=\bigcup_{\delta>0}\omega^\delta\NN_\bullet$, and $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ is not generated by any set of its elements.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $x=\sum_ja_jb_j$ choose a positive monomial $d$ with $a_j/d\in\Pi$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}(i)); then $x/d\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$ and $x=d\cdot(x/d)$.
If a set $G$ generated $\Pi\NN_\bullet$, then for each $g\in G$ the class $D_g=\{\delta>0:g\in\omega^\delta\NN_\bullet\}$ is nonempty and
downward closed, and its elements of least birthday form a set; a positive $\delta$ below the union of these sets lies in every $D_g$, so
$G\subseteq\omega^\delta\NN_\bullet$. Then $\omega^{\delta/2}\in\Pi$ would lie in $\omega^\delta\NN_\bullet$, so $\omega^{-\delta/2}$ and hence
$\omega^{-\delta}$ would lie in $\NN_\bullet$, and $1\in\omega^\delta\NN_\bullet\subseteq\Pi\NN_\bullet$, contrary to \cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction}.
\end{proof}

19 chooses one expression per generator with global choice; the least-birthday selection makes the argument choice free. This parallels
03's statement that $\NN$ is not set-generated as an $\Oz$-algebra (\cref{osq:nm:thm:normalization}), which concerns a different object.

\begin{theorem}[Real-rooted lifting \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:thm:rootlift}
Let $P(X)=X^d+\sum_{k<d}a_kX^k\in\NN[X]$ with $d\ge1$, let $M\in\No$ with $M\ge1$ and $M\ge|a_k|$ for all $k$, put
$\eta_d=\frac14\bigl(\frac34\bigr)^{d-1}$ and $C_d=d(d+1)^{d-1}$, and let $T\in\Pi$ be a positive monomial with $T>C_dM/\eta_d$. Then
\[
 Q(X)=P(X)+\prod_{j=1}^d(X-jT)-X^d
\]
satisfies $Q-P\in\Pi[X]$ and has exactly one root in each interval $\bigl((j-\frac14)T,(j+\frac14)T\bigr)$, $1\le j\le d$; these are $d$ distinct,
positive, infinite roots, and they lie in $\NN$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $R_T=\prod_j(X-jT)$. At an endpoint $x=(j\pm\frac14)T$ the factor $x-jT$ has modulus $T/4$ and the others at least $3T/4$, so
$|R_T(x)|\ge\eta_dT^d$, and $R_T$ has opposite signs at the two endpoints of the $j$th interval. Since $|x|\le(d+1)T$ and $T>1$,
$|P(x)-x^d|\le\sum_{k<d}|a_k||x|^k\le C_dMT^{d-1}<\eta_dT^d$, so $Q$ has the sign of $R_T$ at every endpoint, and the intermediate value
property of polynomials over the real closed field $\No$ gives a root in each of the $d$ disjoint intervals; there are no others. The
roots exceed $\frac34T$, which is infinite; they are integral over $\NN$, hence in $\NN$. The coefficients of $R_T-X^d$ are integer
multiples of positive powers of $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Absolute integral closedness \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:cor:aic}
$\mathsf B_\R$, $\NN_\C$ and $\mathsf B_\C$ are absolutely integrally closed: every monic polynomial over them splits into linear factors.
$\NN$ itself is not, since $X^2+1$ has no root in $\NN\subseteq\No$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Lift a monic polynomial over $\mathsf B_\R$ to $\NN$, apply \cref{osq:nf:thm:rootlift} and reduce the factorization; the change of coefficients
lies in $\Pi[X]$. Over $\NN_\C$ the roots in the algebraically closed field $\SC$ are integral, hence in $\NN_\C$; reduce for $\mathsf B_\C$.
\end{proof}

The lifted roots need not stay distinct modulo $\Pi\NN$: the lifting preserves the factorization, not the separation of residues (19).

\begin{proposition}[An infinitesimal unit whose residue squares to $-1$ \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:prop:unit}
Let $T\in\Pi$ be a positive monomial and $\upsilon_T=\bigl(T-\sqrt{T^2-4}\bigr)/2=2/\bigl(T+\sqrt{T^2-4}\bigr)$. Then
$\upsilon_T^2-T\upsilon_T+1=0$, $\upsilon_T$ is a positive infinitesimal unit of $\NN$ with inverse $T-\upsilon_T$, $\upsilon_T\notin\Oz$, and its image
$\mathsf v\in\mathsf B_\R$ satisfies $\mathsf v^2=-1$. For $T=\omega$,
\[
 \upsilon_\omega=\omega^{-1}+\omega^{-3}+2\omega^{-5}+5\omega^{-7}+14\omega^{-9}+\cdots=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}n\omega^{-(2n+1)} .
\]
Consequently $\NN\to\mathsf B_\R$ is not compatible with any ordered-ring quotient, and $\Pi\NN$ is not convex in $\No$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The equation is the quadratic formula; it is monic over $\Oz$ and says $\upsilon_T(T-\upsilon_T)=1$. The second expression gives
$0<\upsilon_T<2/T$, and $\Oz$ has no positive element below $1$. Modulo $\Pi\NN$, $\upsilon_T^2+1=T\upsilon_T\in\Pi\NN$. Writing
$\upsilon_\omega=\omega^{-1}C(\omega^{-2})$ turns the equation into $C=1+zC^2$, whose solution in $\Q[[z]]$ has the Catalan coefficients;
the substitution $z=\omega^{-2}$ is a Hahn substitution as in \cref{osq:nm:lem:binomial}, and the sum is a strong sum, not a limit of
partial sums. Finally $0<1<T\upsilon_T=1+\upsilon_T^2$ with $T\upsilon_T\in\Pi\NN$ and $1\notin\Pi\NN$.
\end{proof}

03's unit $u_H=\sqrt{H^2+1}-H$ with $H\in\Pi$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}) has a residue $\bar u_H$ with $\bar u_H^2=1$; 19's residue squares
to $-1$. Normalization adds a real infinitesimal whose arithmetic residue behaves like an imaginary unit; no imaginary surreal is
inserted into the real field, and it is the quotient that loses the order (19).

\begin{lemma}[A coefficient copy of $\overline\Q$ \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:lem:coefficients}
There is an embedding $\overline\Q\hookrightarrow\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ whose restriction to $\overline\Z$ lands in $\mathsf B_\bullet$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Real algebraic integers lie in $\NN$. A nonzero one, $a$, satisfies $ab=m$ for a real algebraic integer $b$ and some $0\ne m\in\Z$; as
$\Z\subseteq\mathsf B_\bullet$ is torsion free, the image of $a$ is a unit of $\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$. So the field $k_0=\overline\Q\cap\R$ of real
algebraic numbers embeds. In the real case $X\mapsto\mathsf v$ defines $k_0[X]/(X^2+1)\to\mathsf B^\Q_\R$, injective because its source is the
field $k_0(i)\cong\overline\Q$; in the complex case use $i\in\NN_\C$. Algebraic integers map into $\mathsf B_\bullet$ by
\cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation}.
\end{proof}

In the real case the embedding depends on the choice of $\mathsf v$; it is an embedding of algebraic numbers into the quotient
rationalization, not an embedding of $\C$ into $\No$, whose existence is not asserted (19).

\begin{lemma}[Spectral idempotents \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:lem:spectral}
Let $E$ be a reduced algebraic $\Q$-algebra containing a unital copy of $\overline\Q$. Every $x\in E$ is $\sum_{j\le r}\lambda_je_j$ with distinct
$\lambda_j\in\overline\Q$ and orthogonal idempotents $e_j$ with $\sum_je_j=1$, and finitely many elements have such expressions on one common
partition.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $p$ be the squarefree part of a nonzero rational polynomial killing $x$; $p(x)$ is nilpotent, hence $0$. Factor
$p=c\prod_j(X-\lambda_j)$ over $\overline\Q$ and put $e_j=L_j(x)$ with the Lagrange polynomials
$L_j=\prod_{k\ne j}(X-\lambda_k)/(\lambda_j-\lambda_k)$; modulo $p$, $L_j^2\equiv L_j$, $L_jL_k\equiv0$, $\sum_jL_j\equiv1$ and
$X\equiv\sum_j\lambda_jL_j$. For several elements multiply their partitions.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Finite-partition Boolean powers \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:def:boolean}
For a Boolean algebra $\mathfrak E$ (possibly a proper class) and a commutative ring $R$, an element of $R[\mathfrak E]$ is a finite partition
$1=e_1\vee\dots\vee e_r$ into disjoint elements of $\mathfrak E$ with values $d_1,\dots,d_r\in R$; values on zero parts are ignored, two such
objects are equal when their values agree on every nonzero intersection of parts, and the ring operations are computed on a common
refinement. For idempotents, $e\wedge f=ef$, $\neg e=1-e$ and $e\vee f=e+f-ef$. No infinite sums occur.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The fibre is a Boolean power of the algebraic integers \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:thm:boolean}
With the coefficient embedding of \cref{osq:nf:lem:coefficients}, $\Idem(\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet)=\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)$, and evaluation
$(\lambda_j,e_j)_j\mapsto\sum_j\lambda_je_j$ gives isomorphisms
\[
 \mathsf B^\Q_\bullet\cong\overline\Q[\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)],\qquad \mathsf B_\bullet\cong\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)].
\]
Every finite family of elements of $\mathsf B_\bullet$ lies in a subring isomorphic to $\overline\Z^r$, embedded by an orthogonal partition of $1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Idempotents are roots of $X^2-X$, so \cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation} puts those of $\mathsf B^\Q_\bullet$ in $\mathsf B_\bullet$. Evaluation is onto by
\cref{osq:nf:lem:spectral} and \cref{osq:nf:thm:radical}. On a nonzero common part $e$ of two representations, equality gives $(\lambda-\mu)e=0$, and
a nonzero $\lambda-\mu\in\overline\Q$ is a unit; so evaluation is injective. If $x=\sum_j\lambda_je_j\in\mathsf B_\bullet$ with every $e_j\ne0$ and
$f\in\Z[X]$ is monic with $f(x)=0$, then $f(\lambda_j)e_j=0$, so $f(\lambda_j)=0$ and $\lambda_j\in\overline\Z$; conversely a finite sum of commuting
integral elements is integral, and lies in $\mathsf B_\bullet$ by \cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation}. On a common partition with nonzero parts, the map
from $\overline\Z^r$ is injective.
\end{proof}

The Boolean description gives \cref{osq:nf:cor:aic} again: refine the coefficients of a monic polynomial to one partition and split it over
$\overline\Z$ on each part. $\mathsf B_\bullet$ is neither one finite product of copies of $\overline\Z$ nor an unrestricted product; the finite-partition
restriction is part of the theorem, and 19 does not determine $\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$ (19). 20 shows that it is nontrivial,
atomless and a proper class with explicit independent families (\cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal,osq:bb:thm:atoms}); its isomorphism type
is not determined.

\begin{theorem}[Finitely generated ideals of the fibre \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:thm:bezout}
Every finitely generated ideal of $\overline\Z$ is principal (a classical fact \cite{Cohn}). Every finitely generated ideal $I$ of
$\mathsf B_\bullet$ is principal, $I=g\mathsf B_\bullet$, and there is an idempotent $e$ with $\Ann(g)=(1-e)\mathsf B_\bullet$ and
$I\cong e\mathsf B_\bullet$; so $I$ is projective and $\mathsf B_\bullet$ is semihereditary.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $I=(a_1,\dots,a_r)\overline\Z\ne0$ choose a number field $L$ containing the $a_j$, put $I_0=(a_1,\dots,a_r)O_L$, and use finiteness of the class
group \cite[Theorem~4.4]{Milne} to get $h\ge1$ and $c\in O_L$ with $I_0^h=cO_L$. With $t\in\overline\Z$, $t^h=c$, every $x\in I_0$ has
$(x/t)^h=x^h/c\in O_L$, so $I\subseteq t\overline\Z$; and $(I/t)^h=\overline\Z$ forces $I/t=\overline\Z$. For $\mathsf B_\bullet$ put the generators on
a common partition $e_1,\dots,e_q$, write $x_i=\sum_ja_{ij}e_j$, choose generators $g_j$ of $(a_{1j},\dots,a_{rj})\overline\Z$ and put
$g=\sum_jg_je_j$ and $e=\sum_{g_j\ne0}e_j$. The coefficient identities on each part show $I=g\mathsf B_\bullet$; since $\overline\Z$ is a domain,
$\Ann(g)=(1-e)\mathsf B_\bullet$, and multiplication by $g$ identifies $e\mathsf B_\bullet$ with $I$.
\end{proof}

No B\'ezout property of $\Oz$ or of $\NN_\bullet$ is claimed; the theorem concerns their arithmetic fibre (19).

\begin{proposition}[Nilpotents modulo a prime \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:prop:nilpotents}
For every ordinary prime $p$ and $n\ge2$, $\mathsf B_\bullet/p\mathsf B_\bullet$ has an element of nilpotence index exactly $n$; it is nonzero and not
reduced.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $\alpha=p^{1/n}\in\overline\Z\subseteq\mathsf B_\bullet$. If $\alpha^k\in p\mathsf B_\bullet$ with $1\le k<n$, then $\alpha^k/p\in\mathsf B_\bullet$ is integral
over $\Z$, and so is its $n$th power $p^{k-n}\in\Q\setminus\Z$, which is absurd; the case $k=0$ is $1\notin p\mathsf B_\bullet$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Rational comparison \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:lem:rationalcomplex}
$\NN_\C\otimes\Q=(\NN\otimes\Q)[i]$ and $\mathsf B^\Q_\C\cong\mathsf B^\Q_\R[X]/(X^2+1)$; the map $\mathsf B_\R\to\mathsf B_\C$ is injective, that is,
$\Pi\NN_\C\cap\NN=\Pi\NN$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $z\in\NN_\C$, $z+\bar z$ and $(z-\bar z)/i$ are real and integral, so lie in $\NN$, and $2z$ is in $\NN[i]$ (as in
\cref{osq:nm:prop:complexdefect}); with $\NN[i]\subseteq\NN_\C$ this gives the first equality, and $1,i$ are independent over $\NN\otimes\Q$.
Since $\Pi\NN$ is rationally divisible, $\Pi\NN_\C\otimes\Q=\Pi\NN\otimes\Q+i(\Pi\NN\otimes\Q)$, and the quotient is $\mathsf B^\Q_\R[i]$, into which
$\mathsf B^\Q_\R$ injects.
\end{proof}

With $\mathsf v$ from \cref{osq:nf:prop:unit}, $\mathsf B^\Q_\R$ contains $\frac12$ and the unit $\mathsf v$, and the Chinese remainder map
\begin{equation}\label{osq:nf:eq:crt}
 \Psi:\mathsf B^\Q_\R[i]\to\mathsf B^\Q_\R\times\mathsf B^\Q_\R,\qquad a+ib\mapsto(a+\mathsf vb,\ a-\mathsf vb),
\end{equation}
is an isomorphism with inverse $(r,s)\mapsto\frac12(r+s)+\frac i{2\mathsf v}(r-s)$.

\begin{theorem}[Integral doubling \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:thm:doubling}
$\Psi$ restricts to an isomorphism $\mathsf B_\C\cong\mathsf B_\R\times\mathsf B_\R$ of $\mathsf B_\R$-algebras, with $\mathsf B_\R$ acting diagonally and
complex conjugation exchanging the factors. Hence $\mathsf B_\C/m\mathsf B_\C\cong(\mathsf B_\R/m\mathsf B_\R)^2$ for every ordinary $m\ge2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation}, $\mathsf B_\C$ is the set of elements of $\mathsf B^\Q_\C$ integral over $\Z$. A pair is integral over the diagonal $\Z$
exactly when both coordinates are (multiply two monic annihilators), and the integral elements of $\mathsf B^\Q_\R$ are $\mathsf B_\R$. The rest is read
off from \eqref{osq:nf:eq:crt}.
\end{proof}

Factoring $X^2+1$ over $\mathsf B_\R$ and applying the Chinese remainder theorem there would not prove this, because $2$ need not be a unit;
rationalization followed by the characterization of integral elements is what gives the integral statement (19).

\begin{proposition}[The integral idempotents \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:prop:idempotents}
With $\upsilon=\upsilon_T$ as in \cref{osq:nf:prop:unit}, $w_\pm=(1\mp i\upsilon)/2$ lie in $\NN_\C$; their residues are complementary nonzero
idempotents of $\mathsf B_\C$, sent by $\Psi$ to $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. They are not in $\NN[i]$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
From $\upsilon^2+1=T\upsilon$: $w_\pm^2-w_\pm=-T\upsilon/4$, $w_++w_-=1$ and $w_+w_-=T\upsilon/4$, where $T\upsilon/4=(T/4)\upsilon\in\Pi\NN$. So each
$w_\pm$ is integral over $\NN$, hence over $\Oz$, and the residues are complementary idempotents; $\Psi$ gives the coordinate vectors, using
$\mathsf v^2=-1$. The real coordinate of $w_\pm$ is $\frac12\notin\NN$ (\cref{osq:nm:lem:reciprocal}).
\end{proof}

So $w_\pm$ is a second witness for $\NN[i]\subsetneq\NN_\C$ (03's is $\zeta_3$): normalization adds integral elements written with a
denominator $2$, certified by $T\upsilon/4\in\Pi\NN$ (19).

\begin{corollary}[Characteristic two, trace and norm \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:cor:tracenorm}
Modulo $2$ the residues of $w_\pm$ still split $\mathsf B_\C/2\mathsf B_\C\cong(\mathsf B_\R/2\mathsf B_\R)^2$ into two nonzero factors, although
$i\mapsto(\mathsf v,-\mathsf v)$ has equal coordinates modulo $2$. Field trace and norm induce $\operatorname{Tr},\operatorname{Nm}:\mathsf B_\C\to\mathsf B_\R$,
equal to $(r,s)\mapsto r+s$ and $(r,s)\mapsto rs$; the fixed ring of conjugation is the diagonal $\mathsf B_\R$, and the trace is onto, also
modulo $2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The factors are nonzero by \cref{osq:nf:prop:nilpotents}. For $z\in\NN_\C$, $z+\bar z$ and $z\bar z$ lie in $\NN$, and changing $z$ modulo
$\Pi\NN_\C$ changes them by elements of $\Pi\NN_\C\cap\NN=\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:nf:lem:rationalcomplex}). Conjugation swaps the coordinates, and
$(r,0)$ has trace $r$.
\end{proof}

The mod-2 splitting is a product of two nonreduced rings, not of fields. The norm-one units of $\mathsf B_\C$ form a group isomorphic to
$\mathsf B_\R^\times$ via $r\mapsto(r,r^{-1})$, on which conjugation acts by inversion; it is not asserted that such units lift to norm-one units of
$\NN_\C$ (19).

\begin{corollary}[Set-sized images factor through the fibre \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:cor:small}
Every unital homomorphism from $\NN_\bullet$ to a set-sized ring kills $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ and factors uniquely through $\mathsf B_\bullet$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Its restriction to $\Oz$ kills $\Pi$ (\cref{osq:thm:universal}), hence it kills every finite sum of products in $\Pi\NN_\bullet$.
\end{proof}

$\mathsf B_\bullet$ is not asserted to be a set: this is a factorization property for each set-sized target, not a universal object in a category of
set-sized rings (19). In fact $\mathsf B_\bullet$ is a proper class, and no set-indexed family of set-sized targets is jointly faithful on it
(20; \cref{osq:bb:thm:atoms,osq:bb:cor:complex,osq:bb:thm:noseparating,osq:bb:cor:complexmaps}).

\begin{theorem}[Domain images \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:thm:domainimages}
Let $\varphi:\NN_\bullet\to S$ be a unital homomorphism to a set-sized ring whose image $R$ is a nonzero domain. Then $R\cong\overline\Z$ if
$\Char R=0$ and $R\cong\Fpbar$ if $\Char R=p>0$. In particular every such image is countable, no nonzero finite ring is a unital image of
$\NN_\bullet$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:nofinite}), and no set-sized formally real field is a unital target.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:nf:cor:small} and \cref{osq:nf:thm:boolean}, $\varphi$ factors through $\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)]$. In a domain each idempotent
goes to $0$ or $1$, so exactly one part of each finite partition goes to $1$, and $R$ is the image of $\overline\Z$. In characteristic $0$ this map is
injective: a nonzero $\alpha\in\overline\Z$ divides a nonzero ordinary integer. In characteristic $p$, $R$ is a domain algebraic over $\F_p$, hence a
field, and it is algebraically closed because monic polynomials over $\overline\Z$ split; so $R\cong\Fpbar$. A nonzero finite image, which is
commutative, has a finite field as a quotient, and that would be a finite domain image; in a formally real field the image of $\mathsf v$ (or of
$i$) would square to $-1$.
\end{proof}

This answers, for domain targets, the clause of \cref{osq:q:normalization} asking for the infinite set-sized images of $\NN$, and it
contains 03's absence of finite images with a different proof (03's uses a root of $T^q-T-1$). Images with zero divisors are not
classified beyond the factorization through $\mathsf B_\bullet$, and it is not claimed that all set-sized images are countable (19).

\begin{remark}[Images of 08's invisible roots \merge]\label{osq:nf:rem:rootimages}
Let $r=\omega^{\gamma/m}\mathsf b_m(\omega^{-\gamma})\in\NN$ be the root of $T^m=\omega^\gamma+1$ of \cref{osq:nm:rem:rootinN}. Its residue in
$\mathsf B_\R$ satisfies $\bar r^m=1$, so under \cref{osq:nf:thm:boolean} it is $\sum_j\zeta_je_j$ with $\zeta_j^m=1$ on every nonzero part; under every
unital map from $\NN$ to a set-sized domain, $r$ goes to an $m$th root of unity of $\overline\Z$ or $\Fpbar$. This sharpens ``$\psi(r)^m=1$'' of
\cref{osq:nm:rem:rootinN} for domain targets.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Class ultrafilters \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:lem:classultra}
In G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice, every Boolean algebra whose elements are sets, even a proper class, has an
ultrafilter (a class) containing any prescribed nonzero element.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the algebra along a global well-order, by an ordinal or by the class of ordinals, starting from the prescribed element $e$. At stage
$\alpha$ add $b_\alpha$ if the decisions so far together with $b_\alpha$ have the finite intersection property, and otherwise $\neg b_\alpha$. If both
failed, finite meets $c,d$ of earlier decisions would have $c\wedge b_\alpha=0=d\wedge\neg b_\alpha$, hence $c\wedge d=0$, which is impossible; limit
stages preserve the finite intersection property. The history at each stage is a set, so ordinary transfinite recursion with the global well-order
as a class parameter defines the class of decisions, which generates an ultrafilter containing $e$.
\end{proof}

No class form of Zorn's lemma and no measurable cardinal is used; one part of each finite partition is chosen, without any countable
completeness (19).

\begin{theorem}[Detection by maps to $\overline\Z$ \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:nf:thm:kernel}
Assume global choice. For an ultrafilter $U$ on $\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)$, $\sum_j\lambda_je_j\mapsto\lambda_{j_0}$ with $e_{j_0}\in U$ is a surjective
unital homomorphism $\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf B_\bullet)]\to\overline\Z$. Every $x\in\NN_\bullet\setminus\Pi\NN_\bullet$ is sent to a nonzero element by a
surjective class homomorphism $\NN_\bullet\to\overline\Z$. So $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ is the common kernel of the unital maps from $\NN_\bullet$ to countable
domains, and already of those to $\overline\Z$, in the pointwise sense (no set or class of all such maps is formed).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Exactly one part of a finite partition lies in $U$, and refinement preserves the selected value; so evaluation is a well-defined surjective
homomorphism. If $x\notin\Pi\NN_\bullet$, its image has a nonzero part $e$ with a nonzero coefficient $\alpha$; take $U\ni e$ by
\cref{osq:nf:lem:classultra}, and $x\mapsto\alpha$. Conversely maps to countable domains kill $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ by \cref{osq:nf:cor:small}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Field targets \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:cor:fieldtargets}
Assume global choice. A set-sized field $L$ receives a unital homomorphism from $\NN_\bullet$ if and only if $L$ contains an algebraic closure of
its prime field.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A map forces a copy of $\overline\Z$, hence of $\overline\Q$, or a copy of $\Fpbar$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:domainimages}). Conversely compose an evaluation
$\NN_\bullet\to\overline\Z$ with $\overline\Z\subseteq\overline\Q\subseteq L$, or with $\overline\Z\to\overline\Z/\mathfrak p\cong\Fpbar$ for a prime
$\mathfrak p$ of $\overline\Z$ over $p$ (lying over), followed by an inclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A finite-axiom form \src{19}]\label{osq:nf:thm:abstract}
Let $F$ be a real closed field (a set or a class) containing the real algebraic numbers and $A\subseteq F$ a unital subring with a ring
retraction $c:A\to\Z$ and kernel $J$ such that (i) $J$ is divisible by every nonzero integer; (ii) for all $a_1,\dots,a_r\in J$ and $m\ge1$ there is
$0\ne d\in J$ with $a_j/d^m\in A$ for all $j$; (iii) the positive elements of $J$ are cofinal in $F_{>0}$. Let $N_\R$, $N_\C$ be the integral
closures of $A$ in $F$ and $F(i)$ and $\mathsf B_\bullet=N_\bullet/JN_\bullet$. Then \cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction,osq:nf:thm:radical,osq:nf:thm:saturation,osq:nf:thm:boolean,osq:nf:thm:doubling}
and \cref{osq:nf:cor:aic} hold with $(\Oz,\Pi,\ct)$ replaced by $(A,J,c)$, and \cref{osq:nf:thm:rootlift} holds with $T$ any sufficiently large
positive element of $J$, the roots being positive and distinct but not necessarily infinite.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The contraction uses only the retraction and finite integrality, torsion freeness uses (i), radicality uses exactly (ii), and saturation uses (i)
and normality. By (iii) there is $T\in J$ with $T>2$ for \cref{osq:nf:prop:unit} and as large as needed for the lifting; $\upsilon_T$ is a unit with
residue square $-1$ whether or not it is infinitesimal. Real algebraic integers are integral over $\Z\subseteq A$, so the coefficient embedding,
the spectral idempotents, the Boolean description and the doubling apply unchanged.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not give that $\upsilon_T$ is infinitesimal, nor that $JN_\bullet$ has no set of generators (that needs the set-family divisibility of
the full class), nor \cref{osq:nf:cor:small}, which needs arbitrarily large sets of exponent scales below a fixed exponent, a cardinal condition absent
from (i)--(iii). In a fixed real-exponent Hahn integer part the support $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ blocks the monomial proof of (ii); this is a failure of the
argument, not a counterexample to any conclusion (19). (Status (batch 32): the cyclic workspace $\Z+\omega^a\R[\omega^a]$ lies outside the
theorem, since its Laurent field is not real closed and (ii) fails there, and in it the conclusion of \cref{osq:nf:thm:radical} does fail:
the extended ideal is not radical, \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:rem:fullclass}; for real closed fixed workspaces such as the Hahn field
over $\Q a$ the question stays open, \cref{osq:rm:q:fullQ}, while the bounded-denominator Puiseux ring satisfies (i)--(iii),
\cref{osq:rm:rem:puiabstract}.) For the reduced fibre $\mathsf C(G)$ of the full Hahn field over a nonzero set group
(defined in \eqref{osq:bb:eq:local} below), 20 obtains the Boolean-power form without (ii) and without deciding radicality (\cref{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean}).

\begin{remark}[Candidates for idempotents \merge]\label{osq:nf:rem:candidates}
$\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$ is nontrivial exactly when some $x\in\NN$ has $x^2-x\in\Pi\NN$ while $x,1-x\notin\Pi\NN$. For $s=\sqrt{1+\omega}$ and
$x=(1+s)/2$ one has $x^2-x=\omega/4$, so $x\in\NN$ (a root of $X^2-X-\omega/4$) and its residue is an idempotent. By
\cref{osq:nf:prop:ideal}, $x\in\Pi\NN$ exactly when $x/\omega^\delta\in\NN$ for some $\delta>0$; so this residue is nontrivial exactly when neither
$x/\omega^\delta$ nor $(1-x)/\omega^\delta$ lies in $\NN$ for any $\delta>0$, an instance of the open membership question. Likewise 03's unit gives the
idempotent $(1+\bar u_H)/2$ of $\mathsf B_\R$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation}), nontrivial exactly when $u_H\mp1\notin\Pi\NN$. Neither case is decided by this
remark (\cref{osq:nf:q:fibre}).
\end{remark}

This reduction to the membership question is superseded: 20 proves nontriviality, and much more, by support projection and
two specializations, without a membership test (\cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}), and both candidates are nontrivial, the first
being the second for $H=\omega^{1/2}$ (\cref{osq:bb:prop:candidates}, a merge result).

\subsection{Proper-class Boolean branching of the fibre}\label{osq:bb:sub:branching}

This subsection is manuscript~20's (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). It answers \cref{osq:nf:q:fibre}(a): $\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$ is
nontrivial and atomless, it is a proper class with no set-sized order-dense subset, it contains an explicit independent family
indexed by all ordinals, and one idempotent splits every nonzero element of any prescribed set-sized subring of $\mathsf B_\R$. The
tool is a support projection that makes integrality and radical membership local to the exponent group of an element, followed by
two specializations of a quadratic branch algebra at one fresh scale. The splitting theorems use neither the Boolean-power theorem
nor the universal theorem; only the statements about maps at the end of the subsection do (20).

20 read 19 as a preceding draft (it was not in the repository at 20's pin) and reproves what it needs of it, with the same
constructions. Those results are printed once, above, and carry the tag \src{19, 20} where 20 proves the whole statement: the
contraction, radicality and saturation (\cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction,osq:nf:thm:radical,osq:nf:thm:saturation}), the coefficient
copy, spectral idempotents and Boolean power (\cref{osq:nf:lem:coefficients,osq:nf:lem:spectral,osq:nf:def:boolean,osq:nf:thm:boolean}),
the rational comparison and integral doubling (\cref{osq:nf:lem:rationalcomplex,osq:nf:thm:doubling}), the factorization of
set-sized images, class ultrafilters and detection (\cref{osq:nf:cor:small,osq:nf:lem:classultra,osq:nf:thm:kernel}). 20 also
proves most of \cref{osq:nf:prop:unit} (all but the Catalan expansion), of \cref{osq:nf:prop:idempotents} (all but $w_\pm\notin\NN[i]$)
and of \cref{osq:nf:thm:domainimages} (the classification, not the consequences for finite and formally real targets), and the part of
\cref{osq:nf:cor:tracenorm} saying that $w_\pm$ separate the two nonzero factors modulo $2$. 20's set bounds and common
monomial division are \cref{osq:lem:gap,osq:prop:common}(i), its constant term and $\Pi^2=\Pi$ are \cref{osq:lem:ct} and
\cref{osq:prop:common}(ii), and its proof of the universal theorem for $\Oz$ is credited at \cref{osq:thm:universal}. Its
dominant-scale lemma is 16's Laurent-block theorem, which was not in the repository at 20's pin; it is credited in
\cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent}.

\paragraph{Notation.} For a set-sized additive subgroup $G\subseteq\No$ let $K_G=\hahn\R G\subseteq\No$ be the real Hahn field with
supports in $G$, as in \cref{osq:fs:sub:gaps} with $k=\R$ (20's $F_G$), and put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:bb:eq:local}
 \begin{gathered}
 \A(G)=\Oz\cap K_G,\qquad \Pi(G)=\Pi\cap K_G,\\
 \NN(G)=\IC_{K_G}(\A(G)),\qquad \mathsf C(G)=\NN(G)\big/\sqrt{\Pi(G)\NN(G)}
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
(20's $A_G$, $J_G$, $N_G$, $C_G$). Thus $\A(G)=\A_{\Z,\R}(G)$ and $\Pi(G)=\Pi_\R(G)$ in the notation of \cref{osq:sub:rings}; the
parentheses keep $\NN(G)$ apart from 03's $\NN_\kappa$ and from $\NN_\bullet$, and the letter $C$ is 03's (for $\Oz[S]$ and for its
complex normalization). 20's $N_\R,N_\C,\mathcal J,K_\R,K_\C,B_\R,B_\C,E,\mathcal E$ are
$\NN,\NN_\C,\Pi,\Pi\NN,\Pi\NN_\C,\mathsf B_\R,\mathsf B_\C,\mathsf B^\Q_\R,\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$; its unit $u$ and residue $v$ are
$\upsilon_T$ and $\mathsf v$. Its coefficient projection $\pi_G$ is written $\operatorname{pr}_G$ ($\pi_b$ is a detecting map in
\cref{osq:thm:residual}); its dominant exponent $a$ and group $H=G\oplus\Z a$ are 16's fresh exponent $b$ and
$\widetilde G=G\oplus\Z b$ ($H_a$ is the scale subgroup \eqref{osq:eq:Ha}, and $H$ is 03's parameter in $u_H$); its monomial
$T=\omega^a$ is $t=\omega^b$, with $T$ the formal Laurent variable as in \cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding}; its branches $s_0,s_1,s_r$
are $\varrho_0,\varrho_1,\varrho_r$ ($s$ is 16's centre and the root of \cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates}); its specializations
$\theta_\pm$ are $\sigma_\pm$ ($\theta=\kappa^{\aleph_0}$ in 03's construction); its splitting element $w(T)$ is $\mathsf w_t$
($w_\pm$ are 19's idempotents). Square roots are the positive ones in $\No$, and extended ideals consist of finite sums of
products.

\begin{lemma}[Monic radical certificates \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:lem:certificate}
Let $D\subseteq C$ be an integral extension of commutative rings (sets or classes) and $I\subseteq D$ an ideal. An element $x\in C$
lies in $\sqrt{IC}$ if and only if $x^m+c_{m-1}x^{m-1}+\dots+c_0=0$ for some ordinary $m\ge1$ and $c_0,\dots,c_{m-1}\in I$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $x^q=\sum_{l\le r}a_lb_l$ with $a_l\in I$ and $b_l\in C$. The ring $C_0=D[x,b_1,\dots,b_r]$ is generated as a $D$-module by
finitely many elements $c_1=1,c_2,\dots,c_s$, and $x^qc_\nu=\sum_la_l(b_lc_\nu)\in IC_0=\sum_\mu Ic_\mu$, so
$x^qc_\nu=\sum_\mu h_{\nu\mu}c_\mu$ with all $h_{\nu\mu}\in I$. The adjugate of $x^q\mathbf 1_s-(h_{\nu\mu})$ shows that $P(x^q)=0$ for the
characteristic polynomial $P$ of $(h_{\nu\mu})$, using $c_1=1$; the coefficient of $X^{s-j}$ in $P$ ($j\ge1$) is a sum of products of
$j$ entries, hence in $I$. Then $P(X^q)$ is a
monic polynomial of degree $qs$ killing $x$ whose nonleading coefficients lie in $I$ (or are $0$). Conversely the displayed
relation gives $x^m=-\sum_jc_jx^j\in IC$. Only finitely many elements occur, so the argument applies to class rings.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact membership certificate \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:cor:certificate}
For $x\in\NN_\bullet$: $x\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$ if and only if $x^m+\sum_{j<m}c_jx^j=0$ for some $m\ge1$ and $c_j\in\Pi$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$\NN_\bullet$ is integral over $\Oz$; apply \cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate} with $(D,C,I)=(\Oz,\NN_\bullet,\Pi)$ and the radicality
of $\Pi\NN_\bullet$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:radical}).
\end{proof}

The certificate lets one project the coefficients of a vanishing relation without projecting a homomorphism or an ideal
expression (20).

\begin{lemma}[Support projection \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:lem:projection}
For a set-sized subgroup $G\subseteq\No$ put $\operatorname{pr}_G\bigl(\sum_gr_g\omega^g\bigr)=\sum_{g\in G}r_g\omega^g$ on $\SC$
(coefficients in $\C$). Then $\operatorname{pr}_G$ is additive, fixes $K_G[i]$ pointwise, and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:bb:eq:linear}
 \operatorname{pr}_G(yx)=\operatorname{pr}_G(y)\,x\qquad(y\in\SC,\ x\in K_G[i]).
\end{equation}
Moreover $\operatorname{pr}_G(\Oz)=\A(G)$ and $\operatorname{pr}_G(\Pi)=\Pi(G)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A subset of a reverse well-ordered set is reverse well ordered, and additivity and the fixing are coefficientwise. A contribution to
an exponent $h\in G$ of $yx$ comes from exponents $g$ of $y$ and $s$ of $x$ with $g+s=h$; since $s\in G$ and $G$ is a group,
$g=h-s\in G$. So exactly the terms of $y$ kept by $\operatorname{pr}_G$ contribute to the exponents in $G$, and each coefficient of a
Hahn product is a finite sum, so no exchange of infinite sums is needed. Selection keeps positive exponents and the constant
coefficient, and it fixes $\A(G)$ and $\Pi(G)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Not a ring retraction \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:rem:notretraction}
$\operatorname{pr}_{\{0\}}(\omega)=\operatorname{pr}_{\{0\}}(\omega^{-1})=0$ although $\operatorname{pr}_{\{0\}}(\omega\cdot\omega^{-1})=1$; only
\eqref{osq:bb:eq:linear}, with one factor supported in $G$, is used. This is the warning of \cref{osq:rem:ctnot} for $G=\{0\}$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Exact support descent \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:descent}
For set-sized subgroups $G\subseteq G'\subseteq\No$,
\begin{align}
 \NN\cap K_G&=\NN(G),& \Pi\NN\cap K_G&=\sqrt{\Pi(G)\NN(G)},\label{osq:bb:eq:descent}\\
 \NN(G')\cap K_G&=\NN(G),& \sqrt{\Pi(G')\NN(G')}\cap K_G&=\sqrt{\Pi(G)\NN(G)}.\label{osq:bb:eq:localdescent}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $x\in K_G$ satisfy $x^m+\sum_{j<m}a_jx^j=0$ with $a_j\in\Oz$. Every $x^j$ lies in $K_G$, so \eqref{osq:bb:eq:linear} gives
$x^m+\sum_{j<m}\operatorname{pr}_G(a_j)x^j=0$ with coefficients in $\A(G)$; hence $x\in\NN(G)$. The reverse inclusion is clear, and
the same argument with $a_j\in\A(G')$ gives $\NN(G')\cap K_G=\NN(G)$. If $x\in\Pi\NN\cap K_G$, project the certificate of
\cref{osq:bb:cor:certificate}: its coefficients go to $\Pi(G)$, $x\in\NN(G)$ by the first part, and \cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate}
with $(\A(G),\NN(G),\Pi(G))$ gives $x\in\sqrt{\Pi(G)\NN(G)}$. Conversely $\Pi(G)\NN(G)\subseteq\Pi\NN$, which is radical. The local
radical equality is the same argument with \cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate} applied to $(\A(G'),\NN(G'),\Pi(G'))$ and then to
$(\A(G),\NN(G),\Pi(G))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Reduced fibres embed \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:cor:localinjection}
For $G\subseteq G'$ inclusion induces injections $\mathsf C(G)\hookrightarrow\mathsf C(G')\hookrightarrow\mathsf B_\R$. Larger surreal
supports cannot annihilate a nonzero reduced-fibre class from a smaller support group.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
These are the contracted-ideal equalities of \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent}.
\end{proof}

So an integrality witness using arbitrary surreal scales can be replaced by one using only the exponent group of the element: in
19's membership question, which allows witnesses at larger scales, larger scales never help. \Cref{osq:bb:thm:descent} is a
descent statement, not a decision procedure for $\NN(G)$ (20). The second equality in \eqref{osq:bb:eq:descent} deliberately keeps
the radical: it is not asserted that $\Pi(G)\NN(G)$ is radical in a fixed workspace (20). (Status (batch 32): for $G=\Z a$ it is
not radical, so there the radical cannot be removed, \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:rem:fullclass}.) The same projection decides the descent
asked in \cref{osq:q:normalization}.

\begin{corollary}[Descent for 03's fields \merge]\label{osq:bb:cor:descent03}
With the notation of \cref{osq:sec:closure},
\[
 \NN\cap F^{03}_\kappa=\NN_\kappa,\qquad \Pi\NN\cap F^{03}_\kappa=\sqrt{\Pi^{03}_\kappa\NN_\kappa},\qquad
 \NN_\C\cap F^{03}_\kappa[i]=\NN_{\kappa,\C},\qquad \Pi\NN_\C\cap F^{03}_\kappa[i]=\sqrt{\Pi^{03}_\kappa\NN_{\kappa,\C}},
\]
the radicals being taken in $\NN_\kappa$ and $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Identify $F^{03}_\kappa$ with its image in $\No$ (\cref{osq:sec:model03}): the series with countable support in the subgroup
$\iota(G_\kappa)$. Let $x\in F^{03}_\kappa[i]$ be integral over $\Oz$, and let $G'$ be the subgroup generated by the supports of its
real and imaginary parts. It is countable and contained in $\iota(G_\kappa)$, so every element of $K_{G'}$ has countable support in
$\iota(G_\kappa)$: $K_{G'}\subseteq F^{03}_\kappa$ and $\A(G')\subseteq\Oz\cap F^{03}_\kappa=A^{03}_\kappa$. Projecting a monic
equation of $x$ over $\Oz$ by $\operatorname{pr}_{G'}$ (\cref{osq:bb:lem:projection}) gives one over $\A(G')\subseteq A^{03}_\kappa$,
so $x$ is integral over $A^{03}_\kappa$. By \eqref{osq:nm:eq:normalizations} and \eqref{osq:nm:eq:complexnormalization} (and the
remark after it that $\NN_{\kappa,\C}$ is the integral closure of $A^{03}_\kappa$ in $F^{03}_\kappa[i]$) this proves the first and
third equalities; the reverse inclusions hold because $A^{03}_\kappa\subseteq\Oz$. If moreover $x\in\Pi\NN_\bullet$, the
certificate of \cref{osq:bb:cor:certificate} has coefficients in $\Pi$, and its projection has coefficients in
$\Pi(G')\subseteq\Pi^{03}_\kappa$; \cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate}, applied to $A^{03}_\kappa$ and the ring $\NN_\kappa$ or
$\NN_{\kappa,\C}$, which is integral over it, puts $x$ in the stated radical. Conversely
$\Pi^{03}_\kappa\NN_\kappa\subseteq\Pi\NN$ and $\Pi^{03}_\kappa\NN_{\kappa,\C}\subseteq\Pi\NN_\C$, and these are radical.
\end{proof}

The proof uses only that $F^{03}_\kappa$ contains the full Hahn field over the subgroup generated by the support of each of its
elements; it is a descent, not a membership test for $\NN_\kappa$.

\begin{theorem}[One-scale rational functions \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:rational}
For $a>0$ and $T=\omega^a$,
\[
 \NN\cap\R(T)=\overline\Z_\R+T\R[T],\qquad \Pi\NN\cap\R(T)=T\R[T].
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A rational function of $T$ expands at infinity with support in $\Z a$, so $\R(T)\subseteq K_{\Z a}$. A reverse well-ordered subset
of $\{na:n\ge0\}$ is finite, so $\A(\Z a)=\Z+T\R[T]$ and $\Pi(\Z a)=T\R[T]$. If $f\in\R(T)$ is integral over $\Oz$, it is integral
over $\Z+T\R[T]\subseteq\R[T]$ by \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent}, hence lies in $\R[T]$, which is integrally closed (a monic equation for
$p/q$ in lowest terms, multiplied by $q^m$, forces $q\mid p^m$). Evaluating the monic equation at $T=0$ makes $f(0)$ a real
algebraic integer. Conversely $f(0)\in\overline\Z_\R\subseteq\NN$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:realslice}) and $f-f(0)\in T\R[T]\subseteq\Pi$.
If also $f\in\Pi\NN$, project its certificate onto $\Z a$: the coefficients lie in $T\R[T]$, and evaluation at $0$ gives
$f(0)^m=0$. Finally $T\R[T]\subseteq\Pi\subseteq\Pi\NN$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[\src{20}]\label{osq:bb:ex:rational}
$(\omega^2-1)^{-1}$ is not integral over $\Oz$, although a monic witness over $\Oz$ could use coefficients at arbitrary surreal scales; 19's
$\upsilon_\omega=(\omega-\sqrt{\omega^2-4})/2$ (\cref{osq:nf:prop:unit}) is integral, and its infinite Laurent tail is algebraic but not
rational in $\omega$, as \cref{osq:bb:thm:rational} requires.
\end{example}

\begin{lemma}[Laurent blocks exhaust the enlarged field \src{16, 20}]\label{osq:bb:lem:laurent}
Let $G\subseteq\No$ be a set-sized subgroup, $b>G$ fresh (\cref{osq:fs:lem:fresh}), $\widetilde G=G\oplus\Z b$ and $t=\omega^b$. The
map $\iota_b$ of \cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding} is a field isomorphism $K_G(\!(T^{-1})\!)\to K_{\widetilde G}$ with $\iota_b(T)=t$, and
\[
 \iota_b^{-1}\bigl(\A(\widetilde G)\bigr)=\A(G)+TK_G[T],\qquad \iota_b^{-1}\bigl(\Pi(\widetilde G)\bigr)=\Pi(G)+TK_G[T].
\]
In particular a coefficient in $\Pi(\widetilde G)$ is a polynomial in $t$ over $K_G$ whose value at $T=0$ lies in $\Pi(G)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding} (16) gives an injective field homomorphism into $K_{\widetilde G}$. It is onto (20): an exponent of
$\widetilde G$ is uniquely $g+jb$ with $g\in G$, $j\in\Z$; in a reverse well-ordered support the occurring $j$ are bounded above,
since increasing $j$ gives larger exponents by freshness, and the part with a fixed $j$ is $\omega^{jb}$ times an element of $K_G$.
The ring statements are \cref{osq:fs:cor:blocktest} with $D=\Z$: $\iota_b(\sum_jc_jT^j)\in\Oz$ exactly when $c_j=0$ for $j<0$ and
$c_0\in\Oz$, and the positive-index blocks are purely infinite, so the constant term is $\ct(c_0)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Independent quadratic branches \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:lem:quadratic}
Let $k$ be an ordered field and, in $k(\!(T^{-1})\!)$, let $\varrho_0=T(1-T^{-2})^{1/2}$ and $\varrho_1=\frac T2(1-4T^{-2})^{1/2}$ be the
binomial branches. Then
\[
 k[T,\varrho_0,\varrho_1]\cong k[T,U,V]/(U^2-T^2+1,\ V^2-T^2/4+1),
\]
a free $k[T]$-module with basis $1,\varrho_0,\varrho_1,\varrho_0\varrho_1$, and there are $k$-algebra homomorphisms
\[
 \sigma_\pm:k[T,\varrho_0,\varrho_1]\to k[i]=k[X]/(X^2+1),\qquad T\mapsto0,\quad\varrho_0\mapsto i,\quad\varrho_1\mapsto\pm i .
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The binomial series exist in characteristic $0$, and $\varrho_0^2=d_0=T^2-1$, $\varrho_1^2=d_1=T^2/4-1$. At $T=1$, $d_0$ has a simple
zero and $d_1\ne0$; at $T=2$ the roles are reversed. So $d_0$, $d_1$ and $d_0d_1$ are not squares in $k(T)$, since a square has
even order at every linear factor. If $d_1$ were a square $(x+y\varrho_0)^2$ in $k(T)(\varrho_0)$, then $2xy=0$, and $y=0$ or $x=0$
would make $d_1$ or $d_0d_1$ a square in $k(T)$. Hence $[k(T)(\varrho_0,\varrho_1):k(T)]=4$. The presented algebra is free over
$k[T]$ on the four monomials, by reduction with the two monic relations, and their images are linearly independent over $k(T)$; so
the map is injective. The substitutions respect both relations, which defines $\sigma_\pm$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Specializations, not evaluations \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:rem:specialization}
$\sigma_\pm$ are specializations of a finite branch algebra whose presentation has been proved. They are not evaluations of Laurent
series at $T=0$, where these have no meaning, nor maps $K_{\widetilde G}\to k[i]$, and no evaluation map on all surreal numbers is
used.
\end{remark}

For a fresh $b$ and $t=\omega^b$ put, with $\varrho_0,\varrho_1$ read through $\iota_b$ (they are the positive roots in $\No$, having
positive leading coefficients),
\begin{equation}\label{osq:bb:eq:splitter}
 \varrho_0=\sqrt{t^2-1},\qquad \varrho_1=\sqrt{t^2/4-1},\qquad \mathsf w_t=\frac{1-\varrho_0\varrho_1}2,\qquad
 \mathsf w_t^2-\mathsf w_t=\frac{t^4-5t^2}{16}\in\Pi .
\end{equation}
So $\mathsf w_t\in\NN$, and $\mathsf e_t=[\mathsf w_t]$ is an idempotent of $\mathsf B_\R$. The element $\mathsf w_t=-t^2/4+9/8+9t^{-2}/32+\cdots$
has an infinite Laurent tail, but its certificate is a polynomial in $t$ with zero constant coefficient (20).

\begin{theorem}[One-scale uniform splitting \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:split}
Let $G\subseteq\No$ be a set-sized subgroup, $b>G$ fresh and $t=\omega^b$. For every $x\in\NN\cap K_G$,
\[
 x\mathsf w_t\in\Pi\NN\iff x\in\Pi\NN\iff x(1-\mathsf w_t)\in\Pi\NN .
\]
Equivalently, multiplication by $\mathsf e_t$ and by $1-\mathsf e_t$ kills no nonzero element of $\mathsf C(G)\subseteq\mathsf B_\R$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The implications from the middle hold because $\Pi\NN$ is an ideal. Suppose $z=x\mathsf w_t\in\Pi\NN$ and take a certificate
$z^m+\sum_{j<m}c_jz^j=0$, $c_j\in\Pi$ (\cref{osq:bb:cor:certificate}). Since $z\in K_{\widetilde G}$, \cref{osq:bb:lem:projection}
gives $z^m+\sum_{j<m}p_jz^j=0$ with $p_j=\operatorname{pr}_{\widetilde G}(c_j)\in\Pi(\widetilde G)$, and by \cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent} each
$p_j$ is $\iota_b$ of a polynomial in $\Pi(G)+TK_G[T]$. So the relation holds in $\iota_b(K_G[T,\varrho_0,\varrho_1])$, and
\cref{osq:bb:lem:quadratic} with $k=K_G$ lets us apply $\sigma_+$. It fixes $x$ and sends $\mathsf w_t$ to $(1-i^2)/2=1$, so
$x^m+\sum_{j<m}p_j(0)x^j=0$ in $K_G$, with $p_j(0)\in\Pi(G)\subseteq\Pi$; hence $x\in\Pi\NN$ by \cref{osq:bb:cor:certificate}. If
