instead $x(1-\mathsf w_t)\in\Pi\NN$, use $\sigma_-$, which sends $\mathsf w_t$ to $(1-i(-i))/2=0$ and $1-\mathsf w_t$ to $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform splitting \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:uniform}
For every set-sized unital subring $R\subseteq\mathsf B_\R$ there is an idempotent $e\in\mathsf B_\R$ with $re\ne0$ and $r(1-e)\ne0$
for every $0\ne r\in R$. Consequently $R\times R\to\mathsf B_\R$, $(r,s)\mapsto re+s(1-e)$, is an injective unital homomorphism
extending the diagonal copy of $R$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Represent the elements of $R$ by elements of $\NN$ (a set of representatives exists, for instance the least-rank ones of
\cref{osq:sub:foundations}), let $G$ be the group generated by the union of their supports, choose $b>G$ and put
$e=\mathsf e_{\omega^b}$. \Cref{osq:bb:thm:split} gives $re\ne0\ne r(1-e)$. The map is a unital homomorphism because $e(1-e)=0$, and
if $re+s(1-e)=0$, multiplying by $e$ and by $1-e$ gives $re=0=s(1-e)$, so $r=s=0$.
\end{proof}

This splits all nonzero elements of a prescribed set at once, with no exception caused by zero divisors of $R$ (20).

\begin{example}[A nontrivial idempotent at $t=\omega$ \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:ex:omega}
With $G=\{0\}$ and $t=\omega$, the residue $\bigl[\bigl(1-\sqrt{\omega^2-1}\sqrt{\omega^2/4-1}\bigr)/2\bigr]$ is neither $0$ nor $1$:
apply \cref{osq:bb:thm:split} to $x=1\notin\Pi\NN$. The identity \eqref{osq:bb:eq:splitter} proves idempotence; the two
specializations prove the separately needed nontriviality.
\end{example}

One radical suffices, and it can be 03's. This decides the two candidates of \cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates}.

\begin{proposition}[03's unit splits, and the candidates are nontrivial \merge]\label{osq:bb:prop:candidates}
Let $G$, $b$, $t$ be as in \cref{osq:bb:thm:split}, let $h\in TK_G[T]$ be nonzero with positive leading coefficient, and put
$H=\iota_b(h)$, a positive element of $\Pi$. With 03's unit $u_H=\sqrt{H^2+1}-H$ (\cref{osq:nm:thm:smallunits}), the element
$y_H=(1+u_H)/2$ lies in $\NN$, its residue $e_H$ is an idempotent of $\mathsf B_\R$, and for every $x\in\NN\cap K_G$
\[
 xy_H\in\Pi\NN\iff x\in\Pi\NN\iff x(1-y_H)\in\Pi\NN .
\]
In particular, for every $a>0$ and every positive $H\in\Pi$ with $\supp H\subseteq\Z a$, the idempotent $(1+\bar u_H)/2$ of
\cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates} is neither $0$ nor $1$, that is, $u_H\mp1\notin\Pi\NN$; and $x=(1+\sqrt{1+\omega})/2$ has a residue that
is neither $0$ nor $1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
From $u_H^2+2Hu_H-1=0$, $y_H^2-y_H=(u_H^2-1)/4=-Hu_H/2$, and $H/2\in\Pi$, $u_H\in\NN$; so $y_H$ is a root of
$X^2-X+Hu_H/2\in\NN[X]$, hence in $\NN$, and $e_H$ is idempotent. Put $\varrho=\iota_b\bigl(h(1+h^{-2})^{1/2}\bigr)=\sqrt{H^2+1}$ (the
binomial series in $h^{-2}\in T^{-2}K_G[[T^{-1}]]$). The polynomial $h^2+1$ is not a square in $K_G(T)$: a square root would lie in
$K_G[T]$, and $(g-h)(g+h)=1$ would make $g\pm h$ constant and $h$ constant. So $1,\varrho$ are linearly independent over $K_G(T)$,
$K_G[T,\varrho]\cong K_G[T,U]/(U^2-h^2-1)$ is free over $K_G[T]$ with basis $1,U$, and since $h(0)=0$ there are $K_G$-algebra maps
$\sigma'_\pm:K_G[T,\varrho]\to K_G$ with $T\mapsto0$, $\varrho\mapsto\pm1$; they send $u_H=\varrho-h$ to $\pm1$ and $y_H$ to $1$, respectively
$0$. The proof of \cref{osq:bb:thm:split} now applies verbatim with $\mathsf w_t$ replaced by $y_H$ and $\sigma_\pm$ by $\sigma'_\pm$.
For the candidates take $G=\{0\}$ and $b=a$, so that $H=h(\omega^a)$ with $h\in T\R[T]$, and $x=1$: then $e_H\ne0,1$, and
$e_H=(1+\bar u_H)/2$ differs from $0$ and $1$ exactly when $u_H\mp1\notin\Pi\NN$ (both $\Pi\NN$ and $\mathsf B_\R$ are torsion free,
\cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction}). Finally $(1+\sqrt{1+\omega})/2=y_H+H/2$ for $H=\omega^{1/2}$, and $H/2\in\Pi$, so its residue is $e_H$.
\end{proof}

The two candidates are therefore one idempotent (for $H=\omega^{1/2}$), and \cref{osq:nf:rem:candidates}'s reduction to the
membership question is superseded: nontriviality follows from support projection and two specializations, without a membership
test. For $H\in\Pi$ whose support is not contained in one cyclic group the method needs $H$ to be a polynomial in a fresh monomial
over a group containing the rest of its support, and general $H$ is not decided here. 20's two-radical splitter
\eqref{osq:bb:eq:splitter} is not minimal in this sense, which is not an error.

\begin{lemma}[Multiquadratic extensions \src{20, 23}]\label{osq:bb:lem:multiquadratic}
Over a field $L$ of characteristic different from $2$, classes $d_1,\dots,d_n$ independent in $L^\times/L^{\times2}$ give an extension
$L(\sqrt{d_1},\dots,\sqrt{d_n})$ of degree $2^n$, with the square-root monomials as a basis and all $2^n$ independent sign
automorphisms.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $n$. If $y^2=d_n$ in the extension by the first $n-1$ roots, every sign automorphism sends $y$ to $\pm y$, so $y$ is a
common eigenvector; the monomial basis has distinct sign characters, so $y$ is a scalar multiple of one monomial, and squaring
expresses the class of $d_n$ as a product of earlier classes, a contradiction. So the last step has degree $2$ and supplies the new
basis elements and sign change.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rank extension of set-sized Hahn fibres \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:rank}
Let $G$ be a set-sized ordered abelian group, $K_G=\hahn\R G$, and define $\A(G)=\Z+\Pi_\R(G)$, $\Pi(G)=\Pi_\R(G)$, $\NN(G)$ and
$\mathsf C(G)$ as in \eqref{osq:bb:eq:local}. Let $\widetilde G=G\oplus\Z$ with the new coordinate dominant, and make the same
definitions for $\widetilde G$. Then $\mathsf C(G)\to\mathsf C(\widetilde G)$ is injective, there is a diagonal-extending injection
$\mathsf C(G)\times\mathsf C(G)\hookrightarrow\mathsf C(\widetilde G)$, and for every set $P\subseteq K_G^{>0}\setminus\{1\}$ there is an
injective $\mathsf C(G)$-algebra map
\[
 \mathsf C(G)[X_r:r\in P]/(X_r^2-X_r:r\in P)\hookrightarrow\mathsf C(\widetilde G).
\]
So one dominant coordinate gives a free Boolean family of cardinality $|K_G|$ over the smaller reduced fibre.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A monic $\Pi(G)$-certificate for $1$ (\cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate}) would give $1=0$ after $\ct$; so $\mathsf C(G)\ne0$. The
proofs of \cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding,osq:bb:lem:laurent,osq:bb:lem:projection} apply verbatim to $G\subseteq\widetilde G$, with $T$ the
monomial of the new coordinate and $k=K_G$; the local equality \eqref{osq:bb:eq:localdescent} then gives the first injection, using
radical ideals only and no global radicality. The second is proved exactly as \cref{osq:bb:thm:split}. For the third put
$\varrho_0=\sqrt{T^2-1}$, $\varrho_r=\frac Tr(1-r^2T^{-2})^{1/2}$ and $\mathsf w_r=(1-\varrho_0\varrho_r)/2$ ($r\in P$), binomial branches
with positive leading coefficients, so that
\[
 \mathsf w_r^2-\mathsf w_r=\frac{T^4/r^2-(1+r^{-2})T^2}{4}\in Tk[T]\subseteq\Pi(\widetilde G),
\]
and $\mathsf w_r\in\NN(\widetilde G)$ has an idempotent residue $e_r$. For finite $P_0\subseteq P$ the radicands $T^2-1$ and $T^2/r^2-1$
($r\in P_0$) have the simple zeros $\pm1$ and $\pm r$, pairwise disjoint because the $r$ are positive, distinct and $\ne1$; so every
nonempty product of them has a simple zero and is not a square, and \cref{osq:bb:lem:multiquadratic} gives degree $2^{1+|P_0|}$. As
in \cref{osq:bb:lem:quadratic}, the branch algebra has only its monic quadratic relations, and $T\mapsto0$, $\varrho_0\mapsto i$,
$\varrho_r\mapsto\pm i$ can be chosen independently in $k[i]$, realizing every assignment of $0$ and $1$ to the $e_r$. If $0\ne\bar x\in\mathsf C(G)$
and $p$ is a finite word in the $e_r$ and their complements, a certificate for $xp\in\sqrt{\Pi(\widetilde G)\NN(\widetilde G)}$ specialized with
$p\mapsto1$ would be a $\Pi(G)$-certificate for $x$; so $\bar xp\ne0$. An element of the source uses finitely many variables and
has a unique expansion on their Boolean atoms, and multiplying a vanishing image by each atom kills its coefficient; so the map is
injective. The positive part of an infinite ordered field minus one point has the cardinality of the field.
\end{proof}

Neither $K_G$ nor $K_{\widetilde G}$ need be real closed, and $\Pi(G)\NN(G)$ is not assumed radical; the theorem concerns reduced
fibres. For $G=\{0\}$, $K_G=\R$ and $\mathsf C(G)=\overline\Z_\R$, so one Laurent scale already carries continuum many independent
idempotents over $\overline\Z_\R$ (20). 23 shows that $\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))$ is atomless, of cardinality and order density exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$,
with another explicit independent family (\cref{osq:rm:cor:atomless,osq:rm:thm:cardinality}).

\begin{theorem}[Relative Boolean freeness \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:free}
For every set-sized unital subring $R\subseteq\mathsf B_\R$ and every set $I$ there is an injective $R$-algebra homomorphism
\[
 R[X_i:i\in I]/(X_i^2-X_i:i\in I)\hookrightarrow\mathsf B_\R .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Well-order $I$ as an ordinal $\kappa$. At stage $\alpha<\kappa$ let $R_\alpha$ be the ring generated by $R$ and the $e_\beta$, $\beta<\alpha$;
it is a set, and \cref{osq:bb:thm:uniform} gives a splitter $e_\alpha$ for it. For $0\ne r\in R$ the product of $r$ with any finite
choice of $e_\alpha$ or $1-e_\alpha$, in increasing order of indices, stays nonzero, since each partial product lies in the ring present
before the next index. In finitely many variables the polynomials $p_\varepsilon=\prod_jX_j^{\varepsilon_j}(1-X_j)^{1-\varepsilon_j}$
($\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^n$) are orthogonal idempotents summing to $1$, and every element is uniquely $\sum_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon p_\varepsilon$
(evaluate at zero--one vectors); a vanishing image, multiplied by the image of each $p_\varepsilon$, forces every $r_\varepsilon=0$. A
polynomial in infinitely many variables uses finitely many.
\end{proof}

For $|I|=n$ the source is $R^{2^n}$; for infinite $I$ it is the directed union of these finite products, not the unrestricted
product $R^{\{0,1\}^I}$ (20).

\begin{theorem}[An explicit independent class \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:ordinal}
For every ordinal $\alpha$ put $t_\alpha=\omega^{\omega^\alpha}$ and $e_\alpha=\mathsf e_{t_\alpha}=\Bigl[\bigl(1-\sqrt{t_\alpha^2-1}\,\sqrt{t_\alpha^2/4-1}\bigr)/2\Bigr]$.
Every finite Boolean word in distinct $e_\alpha$ and their complements is nonzero in $\mathsf B_\R$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}$ has support in $\Z\omega^\alpha$. The group generated by the supports for $\beta<\alpha$ lies in the rational span of
$\{\omega^\beta:\beta<\alpha\}$ in the exponent field, whose members are finite combinations with leading exponent below $\alpha$; so
$\omega^\alpha$ exceeds them all and is fresh over that group. \Cref{osq:bb:thm:split}, applied inductively along increasing indices,
proves every finite word nonzero. Only individual earlier supports are used, never an infinite Boolean product, and the family is
defined by a formula, without class-valued recursion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Atomless, a proper class, no set-sized dense core \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:atoms}
$\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$ is atomless and a proper class, and no set $\mathcal D\subseteq\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)\setminus\{0\}$ has the property that
every nonzero idempotent lies above a member of $\mathcal D$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $f\ne0$ split the set-sized ring $\Z[f]$: $fe$ and $f(1-e)$ are nonzero orthogonal idempotents with sum $f$. If $\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$
were a set, the ring it generates would be a set; a splitter $e$ of that ring lies in it and is nonzero, and splitting $r=e$ would
give $e(1-e)\ne0$. (Alternatively \cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal} injects the ordinals.) If $\mathcal D$ were such a set, a splitter $e$ of
the ring it generates is nonzero, and no $d\in\mathcal D$ has $d\le e$, since $d(1-e)\ne0$.
\end{proof}

With \cref{osq:nf:thm:boolean} this sharpens 19's description: $\mathsf B_\R\cong\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)]$ with the ring of all
complex algebraic integers as coefficients and an atomless proper-class Boolean parameter with no set-sized dense core; the
complexity lies in how arithmetic branches are organized, not in new algebraic numbers on one branch (20). Free subalgebras of every
set size do not make the whole class algebra free or complete, nor show that it realizes every set-sized Boolean type (20).

\begin{corollary}[Idempotent matrices split \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:cor:matrix}
Every nonzero idempotent matrix $P\in M_n(\mathsf B_\R)$ is $eP+(1-e)P$ with $eP$, $(1-e)P$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents, for a scalar
idempotent $e$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Split the set-sized ring generated by the entries of $P$; a nonzero entry survives multiplication by $e$ and by $1-e$, and
centrality of $e$ with $P^2=P$ gives idempotence and orthogonality.
\end{proof}

In the idempotent-matrix description of finitely generated projective modules, every nonzero one therefore decomposes
nontrivially. This is a finite matrix statement over a class ring; no category of class-sized modules is formed, and no
projective or global dimension is computed (20).

\begin{remark}[No global choice in the splitting results \merge]\label{osq:bb:rem:choice}
20 works in G\"odel--Bernays class theory with global choice, but \cref{osq:bb:thm:uniform,osq:bb:thm:free,osq:bb:thm:ordinal,osq:bb:thm:atoms,osq:bb:cor:matrix}
need only choice for sets (for well-ordering $I$ in \cref{osq:bb:thm:free}). The splitter can be chosen canonically: take as
representatives of the elements of $R$ all their members of least rank (a set), let $G$ be the group generated by all their
supports and $b$ the simplest surreal above $G\cup\{0\}$; \cref{osq:bb:thm:split} applies to every representative. The recursion in
\cref{osq:bb:thm:free} then makes no choices, and \cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal} is explicit. \Cref{osq:bb:thm:noseparating} below uses no
global choice either; \cref{osq:bb:thm:manymaps}, like \cref{osq:nf:thm:kernel}, uses class ultrafilters.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Reduced fibres of fixed Hahn fields \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean}
For a nonzero set-sized ordered abelian group $G$, with the notation of \cref{osq:bb:thm:rank}, $\mathsf C(G)\cong\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf C(G))]$.
For $G=\{0\}$, $\mathsf C(G)=\overline\Z_\R$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $I=\Pi(G)\NN(G)$ and $L=\sqrt I$. $I$ is divisible by nonzero integers, and so is $L$: if $x^m\in I$, then $(x/n)^m\in I\subseteq\NN(G)$,
so $x/n\in\NN(G)$ by normality and then $x/n\in L$. A monic $\Pi(G)$-certificate for a nonzero integer, followed by $\ct$, would make a
nonzero power of it vanish; so $L\cap\Z=0$, and $\mathsf C(G)$ is nonzero, reduced, torsion free and integral over $\Z$. The proof of
\cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation} applies unchanged. A positive monomial $T=\omega^g$, $0<g\in G$, gives $\upsilon_T\in K_G$ by its binomial
Laurent expansion, whether or not $K_G$ is real closed, with $\upsilon_T^2+1=T\upsilon_T\in I$; so the coefficient embedding and the
spectral argument of \cref{osq:nf:lem:coefficients,osq:nf:lem:spectral,osq:nf:thm:boolean} apply. For $G=\{0\}$: $K_G=\R$, $\A(G)=\Z$
and $\Pi(G)=0$.
\end{proof}

This complements \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}, which describes the unreduced $N_\bullet/JN_\bullet$ under the divisibility axiom (ii) that a
fixed Hahn field may fail. No atomlessness of $\Idem(\mathsf C(G))$ for a fixed $G$ follows: the proof for $\No$ gains a fresh scale beyond
a prescribed set of supports, which a fixed workspace need not supply, and reduction by $\sqrt{\Pi(G)\NN(G)}$ cannot silently be replaced
by reduction by $\Pi(G)\NN(G)$ (20). (Status (batch 32): for cyclic $G$ both points are decided by 23 without a
fresh scale: $\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))$ is atomless, by ramification at unused finite places, and the replacement is impossible because
$\Pi(\Z a)\NN(\Z a)$ is not radical, \cref{osq:rm:cor:atomless,osq:rm:thm:explicit}; see also \cref{osq:rm:rem:booleanform}.)

\begin{corollary}[The surcomplex fibre \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:cor:complex}
Every set-sized subring of $\mathsf B_\C$ has a uniform splitter, and \cref{osq:bb:thm:free,osq:bb:thm:atoms,osq:bb:cor:matrix} hold for
$\mathsf B_\C$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Identify $\mathsf B_\C=\mathsf B_\R\times\mathsf B_\R$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:doubling}). For a set-sized subring $S$ let $R$ be the ring generated by
both coordinate projections of $S$ and $e$ a splitter of $R$; the diagonal idempotent $(e,e)$ splits every nonzero pair, since some
coordinate is nonzero. The other proofs use only uniform splitting.
\end{proof}

Atomlessness does not give $\mathsf B_\R\cong\mathsf B_\R\times\mathsf B_\R$, which would need more information about the global Boolean
algebra; the integral doubling is $\mathsf B_\C\cong\mathsf B_\R\times\mathsf B_\R$ (20).

\paragraph{Maps to set-sized rings.} The remaining results use the universal theorem through \cref{osq:nf:cor:small}, and the last
one uses class ultrafilters. For a class ultrafilter $U$ on $\Idem(\mathsf B_\R)$, the evaluation $\operatorname{ev}_U$ of
\cref{osq:nf:thm:kernel} is a surjective unital map $\mathsf B_\R\to\overline\Z$ fixing the coefficient copy; 20 calls it a
\emph{branch map}.

\begin{lemma}[Class ultrafilters through a prescribed set \src{19, 20}]\label{osq:bb:lem:classultra}
With global choice, a set of elements of a Boolean algebra (possibly a proper class) with the finite intersection property is
contained in an ultrafilter (a class).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
As for \cref{osq:nf:lem:classultra}, adding the prescribed set to the decisions: at stage $\alpha$ add $b_\alpha$ if the prescribed set
and the earlier decisions together with $b_\alpha$ keep the finite intersection property, and $\neg b_\alpha$ otherwise; if both failed,
finite meets $c,d$ from the prescribed set and the earlier decisions would satisfy $c\wedge b_\alpha=0=d\wedge\neg b_\alpha$, hence $c\wedge d=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[An idempotent invisible to every set of small targets \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:noseparating}
Let $(\varphi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a set-indexed family, given by one class relation, of unital homomorphisms $\varphi_i:\NN\to S_i$ to
set-sized rings. There is $x\in\NN$ whose residue is a nonzero idempotent of $\mathsf B_\R$ with $\varphi_i(x)=0$ for all $i$. Hence
$\bigcap_i\ker\varphi_i\supsetneq\Pi\NN$, and $\mathsf B_\R$ does not embed in a set-indexed product of set-sized rings.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The maps factor through $\mathsf B_\R$ (\cref{osq:nf:cor:small}), and together give $\psi:\mathsf B_\R\to S=\prod_iS_i$, a set. Take a
cardinal $\kappa>|S|$ and the independent family $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ of \cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal}; two members $e_\alpha\ne e_\beta$ have
the same image $p$, an idempotent. Their symmetric difference $d=e_\alpha+e_\beta-2e_\alpha e_\beta=e_\alpha(1-e_\beta)+(1-e_\alpha)e_\beta$ is an
idempotent, nonzero by independence, and $\psi(d)=2p-2p^2=0$ in every characteristic. Any lift $x\in\NN$ of $d$ works.
\end{proof}

Each nonzero residue is detected by a map to the countable domain $\overline\Z$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:kernel}), so in the elementwise sense of
\cref{osq:thm:residual} $\mathsf B_\R$ is residually set-sized \merge; but no set-indexed family is jointly faithful. The obstruction
concerns the size of the index set, not of any one target, and it exhibits a nonzero idempotent in every such common kernel (20).

\begin{theorem}[Many branches through prescribed data \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:thm:manymaps}
Assume global choice. Fix a coefficient copy $\overline\Z\subseteq\mathsf B_\R$ and a branch map $\varphi:\mathsf B_\R\to\overline\Z$ fixing
it. For every set $S\subseteq\mathsf B_\R$ and every cardinal $\kappa$ there are at least $2^\kappa$ branch maps agreeing with $\varphi$
on $S$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose finite-partition representations of the elements of $S$, let $\mathfrak E_0$ be the set-sized Boolean algebra generated by the
parts used and $B_0=\overline\Z[\mathfrak E_0]$, a set-sized subring containing $S$ and the coefficient copy; $\varphi$ restricted to
$\mathfrak E_0$ is an ultrafilter $U_0$. Take $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ free over $B_0$ (\cref{osq:bb:thm:free}). For
$\eta:\kappa\to\{0,1\}$, the set $U_0\cup\{e_\alpha:\eta(\alpha)=1\}\cup\{1-e_\alpha:\eta(\alpha)=0\}$ has the finite intersection property: a
finite meet from $U_0$ is a nonzero idempotent of $B_0$, and its product with any finite assignment word stays nonzero by relative
freeness. Extend it to a class ultrafilter (\cref{osq:bb:lem:classultra}) and evaluate. The map selects the same part as $\varphi$ in
every partition from $\mathfrak E_0$, so it agrees with $\varphi$ on $B_0$; different $\eta$ give maps differing on some $e_\alpha$. The
recursion is uniform in the set parameter $\eta$, so this is a set-indexed class family of maps.
\end{proof}

Fixing the coefficient copy only removes an irrelevant automorphism of $\overline\Z$: an arbitrary characteristic-zero domain map
can be normalized by composing with the inverse of the automorphism it induces on the copy (20).

\begin{corollary}[Surcomplex maps \src{20}]\label{osq:bb:cor:complexmaps}
\Cref{osq:bb:thm:noseparating,osq:bb:thm:manymaps} hold for $\NN_\C$, $\Pi\NN_\C$ and $\mathsf B_\C$; in the extension statement the factor of
$\mathsf B_\C\cong\mathsf B_\R\times\mathsf B_\R$ selected by the given branch can be kept fixed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{osq:bb:cor:complex} gives uniform splitting and relative freeness in $\mathsf B_\C$, and the proof of \cref{osq:bb:thm:noseparating}
is unchanged. A domain map out of a product selects one factor; keep it, project the prescribed set into it, and apply
\cref{osq:bb:thm:manymaps}.
\end{proof}

$\NN\subseteq\No$ has no idempotents other than $0,1$, while $\mathsf B_\R$ has a proper class of them and contains the residue $\mathsf v$ with
$\mathsf v^2=-1$; this is possible because $\Pi\NN$ is not convex (\cref{osq:nf:prop:unit}). The quotient is not standard part, and an
idempotent residue does not say that its chosen representative is idempotent (20). What 20 leaves open is recorded in
\cref{osq:nf:q:fibre,osq:bb:q:structure} and its limitations in \cref{osq:sub:nonclaims}.

\subsection{Ramification in a cyclic workspace}\label{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}

This subsection is manuscript~23's (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). It settles the fixed-group clause of \cref{osq:nf:q:fibre}(b) for every nonzero
cyclic exponent group $G=\Z a$, with opposite answers for its two parts: the extended ideal $\Pi(\Z a)\NN(\Z a)$ is \emph{not} radical, since
the branch $\mathsf z_n=T(1+T^{1-n})^{1/n}$ has nilpotency index exactly $n$ modulo it (\cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit}), whereas $\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))$
\emph{is} atomless, of cardinality and order density $\mathfrak c=2^{\aleph_0}$ (\cref{osq:rm:cor:atomless,osq:rm:thm:cardinality}). It describes
$\NN(\Z a)$ completely by a residue test at the finitely many branches over $T=0$ of each finite subextension
(\cref{osq:rm:thm:residues,osq:rm:thm:span}); this answers the fixed-group clause of \cref{osq:q:normalization} for cyclic groups, as a criterion and
not as an algorithm. The mechanism is a distinction between two places. The elements are Laurent series at $T=\infty$, where $T=\omega^a$ is
infinitely large, while integrality and nilpotence modulo the extended ideal are governed by the algebraic places over $T=0$; a series at
infinity is never evaluated term by term at zero (23). Atomlessness needs no fresh dominant scale, which 20's argument uses and a fixed
workspace lacks (the paragraph after \cref{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean}): the new idempotents come from ramification at unused finite places of
$k(T)$. 23 adds exact thresholds for the refinement $T=U^m$, a reduced bounded-denominator Puiseux limit with no reduced finite stage, the local
structure of the coefficient normalization, the associated graded ring and the completion, a periodic free resolution over the coefficient
fibre that fails over the arithmetic fibre, and a countable fragment whose Boolean algebra is the Cantor algebra. Every result holds for the
real pair and for its Gaussian counterpart.

23 pins \texttt{343dc2c} (23 September 2026), which contains the writing of 20's subsection but not that of 22's; it read this report's
normalization, fibre and branching material (its audit names \cref{osq:nf:q:fibre,osq:q:normalization,osq:bb:thm:descent,osq:bb:thm:rational}).
Printed once, under the existing label and with 23 added as a proving source, is 20's multiquadratic lemma (\cref{osq:bb:lem:multiquadratic};
23's Lemma~7.4, with the same proof). 23's Corollary~4.5 (\cref{osq:rm:cor:rational}) contains, for the real pair, the first equality of 20's
\cref{osq:bb:thm:rational}, which 23 credits and recovers as a check; its Gaussian form and its statement for the fixed ideal are new. At its pin this report also contained, after \cref{osq:bb:thm:rank},
the remark that one Laurent scale carries continuum many independent idempotents over $\overline\Z_\R$: with $G=\{0\}$, \cref{osq:bb:thm:rank}
gives an independent family of size $\mathfrak c$ in $\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))$ (20). 23 does not cite it. The lower-bound half of 23's cardinality
statement for the reduced fibre is therefore 20's; 23's family, its independence in the unreduced and coefficient fibres, the exact value
$\mathfrak c$, atomlessness, order density, uniform splitting and the count $2^{\mathfrak c}$ are new. The radicality of the Puiseux limit also
follows from 19's finite-axiom theorem \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}, which was in the report at 23's pin and which 23 does not cite
(\cref{osq:rm:rem:puiabstract}, a merge observation); 23's refinement proof is kept as the first route, and the stage-by-stage statements of
\cref{osq:rm:thm:pui} are new. The numbering of 23 cited here is that of its own manuscript.

\paragraph{Notation and renamings.} Throughout, $(k,D)$ is $(\R,\Z)$ or $(\C,\Z[i])$, $a>0$ is a fixed surreal exponent, and $T=\omega^a$ is the
actual monomial, as in \cref{osq:bb:thm:rational}. $K_{\Z a}=\hahn k{\Z a}$ is 16's Hahn field with coefficients $k$ and supports in $\Z a$ (for
$k=\R$ it is 20's $K_{\Z a}$); by \cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent} with $G=\{0\}$ and $b=a$ it is the Laurent field $k(\!(T^{-1})\!)$, the Laurent variable being identified with $\omega^a$, so its elements
are actual surreal, respectively surcomplex, numbers, and $\mathfrak c=|K_{\Z a}|$. For the real pair \eqref{osq:bb:eq:local} gives
$\A(\Z a)=\Z+T\R[T]$, $\Pi(\Z a)=T\R[T]$, $\NN(\Z a)=\IC_{K_{\Z a}}(\A(\Z a))$ and $\mathsf C(\Z a)$. For the Gaussian pair the same symbols
denote $\A(\Z a)=\GOz\cap K_{\Z a}$, $\Pi(\Z a)=\Pi_\C\cap K_{\Z a}$, the integral closure $\NN(\Z a)$ of $\A(\Z a)$ in $K_{\Z a}$, and
$\mathsf C(\Z a)$ defined by \eqref{osq:bb:eq:local} verbatim; the pair is fixed and not shown in the notation. Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:rings}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathscr B=\IC_{K_{\Z a}}(k[T]),\qquad \mathsf I=\Pi(\Z a)\NN(\Z a),\qquad \mathsf J=\sqrt{T\mathscr B}\subseteq\mathscr B,\\
 \mathsf B(\Z a)=\NN(\Z a)/\mathsf I,\qquad \mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)=\mathscr B/T\mathscr B,\qquad \mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)=\mathscr B/\mathsf J,
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
the radical $\mathsf J$ being taken in $\mathscr B$. \Cref{osq:rm:thm:residues,osq:rm:thm:span} show $\mathsf J\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$, $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ and
$\mathsf C(\Z a)=\NN(\Z a)/\mathsf J$. $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ is the \emph{arithmetic fibre}, the fixed-workspace analogue of 19's $\mathsf B_\bullet$,
and $\mathsf C(\Z a)$ is its reduction; $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ is the \emph{coefficient fibre}, with reduction $\mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$.
The coefficient fibre is the arithmetic fibre of the pair $(k,k)$, since $k[T]=\A_{k,k}(\Z a)$ and $T\mathscr B=\Pi_k(\Z a)\mathscr B$.
$K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ is the subfield of $K_{\Z a}$ of elements algebraic over $k(T)$. For a finite extension $k(T)\subseteq L\subseteq K^{\mathrm{alg}}$
put $\mathscr B_L=\IC_L(k[T])$; for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $\mathscr B_L$ write $\mathfrak q\mid T$ if $\mathfrak q\cap k[T]=(T)$,
$\ell_{\mathfrak q}=\mathscr B_L/\mathfrak q$ for its residue field, $f\bmod\mathfrak q$ for the residue of $f$, and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:valuation}
 v_{\mathfrak q}(f)=\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak q}(f)}{\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak q}(T)},\qquad v_{\mathfrak q}(T)=1 .
\end{equation}
For an integer $m\ge1$, $U=\omega^{a/m}$, so $T=U^m$, and $\Z a/m$ is the group generated by $a/m$; the objects defined with $U$ in place of $T$ are
$K_{\Z a/m}$, $\A(\Z a/m)$, $\Pi(\Z a/m)$, $\NN(\Z a/m)$, $\mathsf I(\Z a/m)$ and $\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$, so that $\mathsf I=\mathsf I(\Z a)$. 23's symbols
are renamed as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its $F$, $A$, $P$, $N$, $B$, $I$, $E$ are $K_{\Z a}$, $\A(\Z a)$, $\Pi(\Z a)$, $\NN(\Z a)$, $\mathscr B$, $\mathsf I$, $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ ($\B$ is the ring
$D+\mm_k$ and $\mathsf B_\bullet$ the full-class fibre; $I$ and $J$ are local ideals in \cref{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean,osq:nf:thm:abstract}; $\EE$ is
07's field and $E$ an ambient field). Its arithmetic fibre $\mathcal R=N/I$, its reduction $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{red}}$, its coefficient fibre
$\mathcal C=B/TB$ and $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{red}}$ are $\mathsf B(\Z a)$, $\mathsf C(\Z a)$, $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ and $\mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$
($\mathcal R$ is 14's Rees algebra). Its $J$ and its nilradical $\mathfrak n=J/TB$ are $\mathsf J$ and $\mathsf J/T\mathscr B$.
\item Its $B_L$ and residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ are $\mathscr B_L$ and $\ell_{\mathfrak q}$ ($\kappa$ is a cardinal); its minimum order $\mu_T$ and
truncated order $h_T$ are $\nu_T$ and $\hat\nu_T$ ($\mu$ is a cardinal letter, $h$ an exponent); its filtration $\mathcal F^r\mathcal R$ is
$\operatorname{Fil}^r$ ($\mathcal F$ is a family in \cref{osq:prop:common}); its $V=B_{\mathfrak q}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ is $\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$
with maximal ideal $\mathfrak q\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$ ($\mm$ is the negative-support ideal).
\item Its branches $z_n$, $h_c$, $e_c$ and $w$ are $\mathsf z_n$, $\varsigma_c$, $\mathsf y_c$ and 20's $\varrho_0$ of \cref{osq:bb:lem:quadratic} (a
sequence $z_n$ occurs in the proof of \cref{osq:da:thm:ext}; $e_r$, $\mathsf e_t$, $e_\alpha$, $e_H$, $w_\pm$ and $\mathsf w_t$ are 19's and 20's
idempotents and splitters); the residue of $\mathsf y_c$ is $\bar{\mathsf y}_c$.
\item Its refined rings $F_m,A_m,P_m,N_m,I_m,\mathcal R_m$ are the objects over $\Z a/m$ above; its Puiseux rings
$F_{\mathrm{Pui}},A_{\mathrm{Pui}},P_{\mathrm{Pui}},N_{\mathrm{Pui}},I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ are $K_{\mathrm{Pui}},\A_{\mathrm{Pui}},\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}},\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}},\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$;
its $F_\Q,A_\Q,P_\Q$ are $K_{\Q a}$, $\A(\Q a)$, $\Pi(\Q a)$.
\item Its $D_k^{\mathrm{int}}$ is $\overline\Z_\R$ or $\overline\Z$; its coefficient fragments $k_{\mathrm r}$, $k_{\mathrm c}$ are 19's $k_0=\overline\Q\cap\R$ and
$\overline\Q$; its module $M=\mathcal C/(x)$ is $\mathscr M_n$ ($M$ is a lattice); its graded variable $X$ is $W$ ($X^g$ are formal monomials).
\end{itemize}
23's finite extensions $L$ keep their letter (as the set-sized field of \cref{osq:nf:cor:fieldtargets}; not 14's module $L(M)$, 16's lower set or
03's $L_c(F)$), and so do its primes $\mathfrak q$ (not 14's kernels $\mathfrak q_M$). The letter $c$ is a positive real parameter, $\mathfrak c$ the
continuum. Four tempting readings are false. (1) The Laurent constant coefficient is not a residue at a place over zero: $\mathsf z_2=T+\frac12-\cdots$
lies in $\NN(\Z a)$ although $\frac12$ is not an algebraic integer (\cref{osq:rm:ex:sqrt}). (2) The valuations $v_{\mathfrak q}$ have $v_{\mathfrak q}(T)=1$;
the Laurent valuation at infinity has value $-1$ at $T$, and neither extends the other (\cref{osq:rm:rem:twoplaces}). (3) $k\NN(\Z a)=\mathscr B$ is a finite
$k$-linear span: it does not say $k\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$, and $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ is larger than $T\NN(\Z a)$. (4) The injection
$\mathsf C(\Z a)\hookrightarrow\mathsf B_\R$ of \cref{osq:bb:cor:localinjection} concerns the reduced fibre; on $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ the map to $\mathsf B_\R$
kills exactly the nilradical (\cref{osq:rm:rem:fullclass}).

\paragraph{The workspace and its finite normalizations.}

\begin{proposition}[The cyclic integer part \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:prop:cyclic}
$\Oz\cap K_{\Z a}=\Z+T\R[T]$ for the real pair and $\GOz\cap K_{\Z a}=\Z[i]+T\C[T]$ for the Gaussian pair. In both cases $\Pi(\Z a)=Tk[T]$ and
$\Frac(\A(\Z a))=k(T)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
An omnific normal form has no negative exponents and an integer constant coefficient, and a reverse well-ordered subset of $\{na:n\ge1\}$ is finite;
so the positive part is a polynomial in $T$ without constant term (as in the proof of \cref{osq:bb:thm:rational}). The Gaussian case applies this to
both coordinates. Finally $T$ and $cT$ lie in $\A(\Z a)$ for $c\in k$, so $c=(cT)/T\in\Frac(\A(\Z a))$ and $k(T)\subseteq\Frac(\A(\Z a))$; the reverse
inclusion is clear.
\end{proof}

For the real pair $\A(\Z a)$ is an integer part of $K_{\Z a}$, although $K_{\Z a}$ is not real closed: keep the positive powers of $f$, round its real
constant down, and subtract one more if the constant was an integer and the negative-power tail is negative; this is the unique $u\in\A(\Z a)$ with
$u\le f<u+1$. It does not extend $\ct$ from $\A(\Z a)$ to $\NN(\Z a)$ (23).

For every finite extension $k(T)\subseteq L\subseteq K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ (separable, in characteristic $0$), $\mathscr B_L$ is a finite $k[T]$-module and a
Dedekind domain whose nonzero prime localizations are discrete valuation rings, its residue fields are finite over those of $k[T]$, and every prime of
$k[T]$ has a prime above it \cite{StacksIntClosure,StacksDedekind,Sutherland}. There are finitely many $\mathfrak q\mid T$, and $\ell_{\mathfrak q}$ is
$\C$ if $k=\C$ and is $\R$ or $\C$ if $k=\R$.

\begin{lemma}[Finite detection and descent \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:lem:finite}
The rings $\mathscr B_L$ form a directed system with $\mathscr B=\bigcup_L\mathscr B_L$, $\mathscr B\cap L=\mathscr B_L$ and $\Frac(\mathscr B)=K^{\mathrm{alg}}$.
For $f\in\mathscr B_L$ and an integer $r\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:finitetest}
 f\in T^r\mathscr B\iff f\in T^r\mathscr B_L\iff v_{\mathfrak q}(f)\ge r\ \text{for every }\mathfrak q\mid T .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An integral element is algebraic and lies in a finite extension, and integrality over $k[T]$ is a property of the element, so $\mathscr B\cap L=\mathscr B_L$.
Clearing the denominators of a monic equation, a nonzero polynomial multiple of any element of $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ is integral over $k[T]$. Next,
$f\in T^r\mathscr B$ means $f/T^r\in\mathscr B\cap L=\mathscr B_L$. A Dedekind domain is the intersection of its localizations at nonzero primes; at primes
not above $T$ the element $T$ is a unit, and at the primes above $T$ regularity of $f/T^r$ is the stated inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite branch locus \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:lem:branchlocus}
A finite extension $L/k(T)$ is unramified at all but finitely many nonzero primes of $k[T]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Multiply a primitive element by a nonzero polynomial to make it integral over $k[T]$. Its minimal polynomial is monic and separable, with nonzero
discriminant $\Delta$. After inverting $\Delta$ the finite free algebra it generates is \'etale over $k[T][\Delta^{-1}]$, hence normal, hence the
normalization there; only the finitely many prime divisors of $\Delta$ can ramify \cite{StacksRamification}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Two unrelated valuations \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:rem:twoplaces}
The Laurent valuation at infinity has value $-1$ at $T$, the valuations \eqref{osq:rm:eq:valuation} have value $1$. The latter are valuations of finite
algebraic function fields, not continuous extensions of the Laurent topology to an evaluation at $T=0$. An expansion with infinitely many negative
powers can be regular at a place over zero, and an element finite in the surreal order, such as $\mathsf z_2/T$ below, can have a pole there.
Confusing the two would invalidate every argument below (23).
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Explicit nilpotents of every finite order.} For an ordinary integer $n\ge2$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:zn}
 \mathsf z_n=T\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{1/n}jT^{j(1-n)},\qquad \mathsf z_n^n=T^n+T=T(1+T^{n-1}).
\end{equation}
The exponents are integers decreasing to $-\infty$, the formal binomial identity holds in characteristic $0$, and the coefficients are rational;
in $K_{\Z a}$ for $k=\R$ this is the positive root with leading term $T$, and the same branch is used for $k=\C$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact cyclic nilpotency \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:explicit}
$\mathsf z_n\in\NN(\Z a)$, $\mathsf z_n^n\in\mathsf I$, and $\mathsf z_n^j\notin\mathsf I$ for $1\le j<n$. Hence $\mathsf I=\Pi(\Z a)\NN(\Z a)$ is not radical,
and the residue of $\mathsf z_n$ in $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ has nilpotency index exactly $n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\eqref{osq:rm:eq:zn} is a monic equation over $\A(\Z a)$ with right side in $\Pi(\Z a)$, so $\mathsf z_n\in\NN(\Z a)$ and $\mathsf z_n^n\in\mathsf I$. Suppose
$\mathsf z_n^j=\sum_{\ell\le r}p_\ell b_\ell$ with $1\le j<n$, $p_\ell\in Tk[T]$ and $b_\ell\in\NN(\Z a)$. Choose a finite $L$ containing $\mathsf z_n$ and all
$b_\ell$; each $b_\ell$ is integral over $k[T]$, hence in $\mathscr B_L$. At any $\mathfrak q\mid T$ every summand has value at least $1$, while
$1+T^{n-1}$ is a unit and \eqref{osq:rm:eq:zn} gives $v_{\mathfrak q}(\mathsf z_n^j)=j/n<1$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

This proof uses only a finite ideal expression, the normalization of one finite function field and one valuation; it does not use the identity
$\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ of \cref{osq:rm:thm:span}, and it is a self-contained negative answer to fixed-cyclic radicality (23).

\begin{example}[The first obstruction \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:ex:sqrt}
For $n=2$,
\[
 \mathsf z_2=\sqrt{T^2+T}=T+\frac12-\frac1{8T}+\frac1{16T^2}-\frac5{128T^3}+\cdots,
\]
and its residue in $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ is nonzero with square zero. Although $\mathsf z_2$ is integral over $\A(\Z a)$, its Laurent constant coefficient
$\frac12$ is not an algebraic integer, so integrality over $\A(\Z a)$ cannot be tested on the constant coefficient at infinity. And $\mathsf z_2/T$ is
infinitesimally close to $1$ but not integral over $\A(\Z a)$: it has value $-\frac12$ at every place over zero. In the full class
$\mathsf z_2=\omega^{a/2}\sqrt{1+\omega^a}$ with $\sqrt{1+\omega^a}\in\NN$, so $\mathsf z_2\in\Pi\NN$, in accordance with \cref{osq:nf:thm:radical}
\merge.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}[Unbounded nilpotence \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:unbounded}
The nilradical of $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ is not nilpotent and not finitely generated; $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ and $\NN(\Z a)$ are not Noetherian.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The nilpotency indices of \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit} are unbounded. A nil ideal generated by $x_1,\dots,x_s$ with $x_i^{d_i}=0$ has vanishing
$(1+\sum_i(d_i-1))$th power, since every monomial of that degree contains some $x_i^{d_i}$. A quotient of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact order after refinement \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:explicitrefinement}
For $n\ge2$, $m\ge1$ and $j\ge1$, $\mathsf z_n^j\in\mathsf I(\Z a/m)$ if and only if $mj\ge n$. So under $\mathsf B(\Z a)\to\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$, induced by
$\A(\Z a)\subseteq\A(\Z a/m)$, the residue of $\mathsf z_n$ has index $\lceil n/m\rceil$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At a place above $U=0$, normalized by $v(U)=1$, the relation $\mathsf z_n^n=U^m(1+U^{m(n-1)})$ gives $v(\mathsf z_n^j)=mj/n$, while every element of
$\mathsf I(\Z a/m)$ has value at least $1$, as in \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit}. Conversely, if $mj\ge n$, then $y=\mathsf z_n^j/U$ satisfies
$y^n=U^{mj-n}(1+U^{m(n-1)})^j$, a polynomial with constant coefficient $0$ (if $mj>n$) or $1$ (if $mj=n$), which lies in $\A(\Z a/m)$; so $y$ is integral
over $\A(\Z a/m)$ and $\mathsf z_n^j=Uy\in\mathsf I(\Z a/m)$.
\end{proof}

For $\mathsf z_{12}$ and $m=1,2,3,4,6,12$ the indices are $12,6,4,3,2,1$; index $1$ means that the residue has become $0$. Every refined workspace still
has nilpotents of unbounded index ($\mathsf z_n$ with $n$ large), so no single refinement removes all nilpotents; that each one is removed by some
refinement (\cref{osq:rm:thm:generalrefinement}) has the other order of quantifiers (23).

\paragraph{The residue criterion.} $\mathsf I$ is in general larger than $T\NN(\Z a)$: $\Pi(\Z a)$ contains arbitrary coefficients in $k$, which need not
lie in $\NN(\Z a)$. The following lemma accounts for them.

\begin{lemma}[Scaling \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:lem:scaling}
$T\mathscr B\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $b^d+p_{d-1}(T)b^{d-1}+\dots+p_0(T)=0$ with $p_j\in k[T]$, multiplying by $T^d$ gives
$(Tb)^d+Tp_{d-1}(T)(Tb)^{d-1}+\dots+T^dp_0(T)=0$, a monic equation with nonleading coefficients in $Tk[T]\subseteq\A(\Z a)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Residue criterion \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:residues}
Let $k(T)\subseteq L\subseteq K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ be finite and $f\in\mathscr B_L$. Then $f\in\NN(\Z a)$ if and only if $f\bmod\mathfrak q\in\ell_{\mathfrak q}$ is
integral over $D$ for every $\mathfrak q\mid T$. In particular $\sqrt{T\mathscr B_L}\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$ and $\mathsf J\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $f$ satisfies a monic equation over $\A(\Z a)$, reduce it modulo $\mathfrak q\mid T$: a coefficient $d+Tp(T)$ becomes $d\in D$. Conversely, for each of
the finitely many $\mathfrak q\mid T$ choose a monic $Q_{\mathfrak q}\in D[Y]$ killing $f\bmod\mathfrak q$, and let $Q$ be their product; then $Q(f)\in\mathfrak q$
for all $\mathfrak q\mid T$. With $T\mathscr B_L=\prod_{\mathfrak q\mid T}\mathfrak q^{e_{\mathfrak q}}$ and $r\ge\max e_{\mathfrak q}$, $Q(f)^r=Tb$ with
$b\in\mathscr B_L$. By \cref{osq:rm:lem:scaling} $Tb$ is integral over $\A(\Z a)$, $Y^r-Tb$ shows that $Q(f)$ is integral over $\A(\Z a)[Tb]$, and
$Q(Y)-Q(f)$ is monic over $\A(\Z a)[Q(f)]$ and kills $f$; transitivity gives $f\in\NN(\Z a)$. Elements of $\sqrt{T\mathscr B_L}$ have zero residues. An
element of $\mathsf J$ lies in some $\mathscr B_L$ with a power in $T\mathscr B$, hence in $T\mathscr B_L$ by \cref{osq:rm:lem:finite}.
\end{proof}

The proof holds for every coefficient field of characteristic $0$ and every unital $D$ in it; the real and complex hypotheses enter only in
\cref{osq:rm:thm:span}, through the small dimensions of the residue fields (23).

\begin{remark}[A finite certificate, not an oracle \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:rem:effective}
The sufficiency proof yields an explicit monic certificate once the normalization and the residues are known: if $b=Q(f)^r/T$ satisfies a monic
equation of degree $d$ over $k[T]$, \cref{osq:rm:lem:scaling} gives a monic $H$ of degree $d$ over $\A(\Z a)$ killing $Q(f)^r$, and $H(Q(Y)^r)$ kills $f$
and has degree $dr\deg Q$. This is a finite algebraic criterion for a represented algebraic Laurent element, not a decision procedure for arbitrary
real coefficients or arbitrary normal forms: an implementation must represent $L$, identify the chosen branch at infinity, normalize at the finite
places and decide integrality of the residue constants, and substituting $T=0$ in a possibly singular defining equation need not separate the
branches of its normalization (23).
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Coefficient span and the extended ideal \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:span}
$k\NN(\Z a)=\mathscr B$ (finite $k$-linear span) and $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$. Hence $\mathsf B(\Z a)=\NN(\Z a)/T\mathscr B\hookrightarrow\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$,
the two fibres have the same nilradical $\mathsf J/T\mathscr B$, and $\mathsf C(\Z a)=\NN(\Z a)/\mathsf J\hookrightarrow\mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Clearly $k\NN(\Z a)\subseteq\mathscr B$. Let $b\in\mathscr B_L$. By the Chinese remainder theorem $\mathscr B_L/\sqrt{T\mathscr B_L}\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q\mid T}\ell_{\mathfrak q}$,
a finite product of copies of $\C$ (if $k=\C$) or of $\R$ and $\C$ (if $k=\R$). The coordinate vectors, together for $k=\R$ with the vector equal to
$i$ in one complex factor and $0$ elsewhere, form a $k$-basis whose entries are integral over $D$. Lift them to $b_1,\dots,b_s\in\mathscr B_L$; they lie in
$\NN(\Z a)$ by \cref{osq:rm:thm:residues}. Choose $c_j\in k$ with $b-\sum_jc_jb_j\in\sqrt{T\mathscr B_L}\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$; so $b\in k\NN(\Z a)$. As $T\in\NN(\Z a)$,
$k[T]\NN(\Z a)=k\NN(\Z a)=\mathscr B$ and $\mathsf I=Tk[T]\NN(\Z a)=T\mathscr B$. The injection is immediate, $\mathsf J\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$ by
\cref{osq:rm:thm:residues}, and nilpotence modulo $T\mathscr B$ means the same in both rings; the radical of $\mathsf I$ in $\NN(\Z a)$ is $\mathsf J\cap\NN(\Z a)=\mathsf J$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Rational functions \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:rational}
$\NN(\Z a)\cap k(T)=\overline\Z_k+Tk[T]$ and $\mathsf I\cap k(T)=Tk[T]$, where $\overline\Z_k$ is $\overline\Z_\R$ for the real pair and $\overline\Z$ for the
Gaussian pair.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$k[T]$ is integrally closed in $k(T)$, and its only place over $T$ is $T=0$, so \cref{osq:rm:thm:residues} asks exactly that $f(0)$ be integral over $D$.
For the ideal use $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ and $\mathscr B\cap k(T)=k[T]$.
\end{proof}

For the real pair the first equality is 20's \cref{osq:bb:thm:rational}, credited by 23 and recovered as a check on the residue criterion. 20's second
equality concerns the full-class ideal, $\Pi\NN\cap\R(T)=T\R[T]$; by \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent} this is $\mathsf J\cap\R(T)$, and 23's $\mathsf I\cap\R(T)=T\R[T]$ is
the same set because $T\R[T]\subseteq\mathsf I\subseteq\mathsf J$. The Gaussian pair is new.

\paragraph{The ramification filtration and exact refinement.}

\begin{definition}[Minimum finite-place order \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:def:nu}
For $0\ne f\in\mathscr B$ choose a finite $L\ni f$ and put $\nu_T(f)=\min_{\mathfrak q\mid T}v_{\mathfrak q}(f)\in\Q_{\ge0}$; put $\nu_T(0)=+\infty$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Invariance and inequalities \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:lem:nu}
$\nu_T(f)$ does not depend on $L$. For $f,g\in\mathscr B$ and $r\ge1$, $\nu_T(f+g)\ge\min\{\nu_T(f),\nu_T(g)\}$, $\nu_T(fg)\ge\nu_T(f)+\nu_T(g)$ and
$\nu_T(f^r)=r\nu_T(f)$; and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:nuideal}
 f\in T^r\mathscr B\iff\nu_T(f)\ge r,\qquad f\in\mathsf J\iff\nu_T(f)>0 .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $L\subseteq L'$, every $\mathfrak q\mid T$ of $\mathscr B_L$ has a prime of $\mathscr B_{L'}$ above it, and with both valuations normalized at $T$ the larger
restricts to the smaller; so the set of values gains repetitions but no new values. Compare two choices in a compositum. The inequalities hold at each
prime of one finite field containing both elements. The ideal criterion is \eqref{osq:rm:eq:finitetest}; a positive minimum becomes at least $1$ after
multiplication by a large integer, a zero minimum never does.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The truncated order and its filtration \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:def:truncated}
For $\bar f\in\mathsf B(\Z a)$ put $\hat\nu_T(\bar f)=\min\{1,\nu_T(f)\}\in[0,1]\cap\Q$, and for rational $0\le r\le1$ put
$\operatorname{Fil}^r=\{x\in\mathsf B(\Z a):\hat\nu_T(x)\ge r\}$.
\end{definition}

Representatives differing by an element of $T\mathscr B$ have the same values below $1$, so $\hat\nu_T$ is well defined, and $\hat\nu_T(\bar f)=1$ exactly
when $\bar f=0$. Moreover $\hat\nu_T(x+y)\ge\min\{\hat\nu_T(x),\hat\nu_T(y)\}$ and $\hat\nu_T(xy)\ge\min\{1,\hat\nu_T(x)+\hat\nu_T(y)\}$; the $\operatorname{Fil}^r$ are
ideals with $\operatorname{Fil}^0=\mathsf B(\Z a)$, $\operatorname{Fil}^1=0$, $\operatorname{Fil}^r\operatorname{Fil}^s\subseteq\operatorname{Fil}^{\min(1,r+s)}$ and
$\operatorname{Nil}(\mathsf B(\Z a))=\bigcup_{0<r\le1}\operatorname{Fil}^r$. This is a rationally indexed filtration, not a valuation: the product inequality can
be strict because different branches realize the two minima, and nontrivial complementary idempotents (constructed below) have order $0$ while their
product has order $1$ (23).

\begin{corollary}[The index of any nilpotent \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:generalindex}
For $0\ne f\in\NN(\Z a)$ with $\nu_T(f)>0$ the residue of $f$ has nilpotency index $\lceil1/\nu_T(f)\rceil$; if $\nu_T(f)=0$ it is not nilpotent.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Its $r$th power vanishes exactly when $r\nu_T(f)\ge1$, by \cref{osq:rm:thm:span} and \eqref{osq:rm:eq:nuideal}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[General refinement law \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:generalrefinement}
For $m\ge1$ and $f\in\NN(\Z a)$, with $\nu_U$ normalized by $v(U)=1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:generalrefine}
 \nu_U(f)=m\,\nu_T(f),\qquad f\in\mathsf I(\Z a/m)\iff\nu_T(f)\ge\frac1m ;
\end{equation}
equivalently $\hat\nu_U(\bar f)=\min\{1,m\hat\nu_T(\bar f)\}$ under $\mathsf B(\Z a)\to\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$. Every nilpotent residue is killed by some refinement, and
a non-nilpotent residue by none.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $L\ni f$ be finite and $L'=L\,k(U)\subseteq K_{\Z a/m}$. The integral closures of $k[T]$ and of $k[U]$ in $L'$ coincide ($k[U]$ is integral over $k[T]$),
every prime of $\mathscr B_L$ above $T$ extends, and the extensions are exactly the primes above $U=0$. A valuation normalized by $v(U)=1$ sends $T$ to $m$,
so it is $m$ times the old normalization on $L$; every old prime occurs, so the minima scale by $m$. The second formula is \cref{osq:rm:thm:span} over
$\Z a/m$ with \eqref{osq:rm:eq:nuideal}. If $\nu_T(f)>0$ take $m\ge1/\nu_T(f)$.
\end{proof}

This is an exact finite certificate for the disappearance of a represented nilpotent: compute its positive minimum order at the finitely many branches
over zero and take a root refinement at least its reciprocal. The bound is a threshold for ideal membership, not a ramification index or a common
multiple of ramification indices; for $\mathsf z_n$ every branch has order $1/n$ (23).

\paragraph{The bounded-denominator Puiseux limit.} For $m\mid m'$ the inclusions $K_{\Z a/m}\subseteq K_{\Z a/m'}$ form a directed system. Put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:pui}
 \begin{gathered}
 K_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\bigcup_mK_{\Z a/m},\qquad \A_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\bigcup_m\A(\Z a/m),\qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\bigcup_m\Pi(\Z a/m),\\
 \NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\IC_{K_{\mathrm{Pui}}}(\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}),\qquad \mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Each element of $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ has exponents with a bounded common denominator, so $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is strictly smaller than the Hahn field $K_{\Q a}$:
$\sum_{n\ge1}T^{1/n}$ has reverse well-ordered support in $\Q a$ and no common denominator.

\begin{theorem}[Reduction by rational scales \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:pui}
$\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\bigcup_m\NN(\Z a/m)$, $\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\bigcup_m\mathsf I(\Z a/m)$ and $\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}/\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}\cong\operatorname{colim}_m\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$.
The ideal $\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is radical, and for each $m$ the kernel of $\mathsf B(\Z a/m)\to\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}/\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is exactly
$\operatorname{Nil}(\mathsf B(\Z a/m))$. Finitely many nilpotent residues are killed at one common later stage, and no finite stage is reduced.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An element of $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ and the finitely many coefficients of an integrality equation over $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ lie in a common stage; so do the finitely
many factors of an extended-ideal expression. This gives the two unions and the colimit. If $f^r\in\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$, move $f$ and the expression to a
common stage $m$; the residue of $f$ in $\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$ is nilpotent, so \cref{osq:rm:thm:generalrefinement} (over $\Z a/m$) kills it at a later stage and
$f\in\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$. A residue that dies in the colimit dies at a finite later stage, so its minimum order was positive by \eqref{osq:rm:eq:generalrefine}
and it was nilpotent. For finitely many residues take a common refinement above all thresholds. Each finite stage is a cyclic workspace and contains
the family of \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A set-sized positive case \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:rem:positivecase}
For $k=\R$, $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is real closed and $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]$ is the complex Puiseux field, algebraically closed by the Newton--Puiseux theorem
\cite{Nowak}; the real case also follows from the characterization of real closed fields by algebraic closedness after adjoining $i$. $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is
its truncation integer part. So radicality is restored in a set-sized real closed surreal subfield, without a proper class of scales. This concerns the
bounded-denominator support class only: it decides nothing for the Hahn field $K_{\Q a}$ (\cref{osq:rm:q:fullQ}), and it does not say that the colimit
fibre is isomorphic to a reduced finite-stage fibre; the kernel on each stage is known, but the image may grow (23).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[A second route through the finite-axiom theorem \merge]\label{osq:rm:rem:puiabstract}
For the real pair, the field $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$, the ring $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}=\Z+\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$, the retraction $\ct$ and its kernel $\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ (the
$F$, $A$, $c$ and $J$ of \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}) satisfy its hypotheses: $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is real closed and contains the real algebraic numbers;
(i) $\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is divisible by nonzero integers; (ii) if
$x_1,\dots,x_r\in\Pi(\Z a/n)$ and $m\ge1$, then $d=T^{1/(2mn)}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ and every $x_j/d^m$ has $T$-exponents at least $\frac1n-\frac1{2n}>0$ with
denominator dividing $2n$, so lies in $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}$; (iii) the powers $T^j$ are cofinal. So 19's theorem gives the radicality of
$\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ for the real pair again, and more: $\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}/\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is integrally closed in its rationalization and is the
Boolean power $\overline\Z[\Idem(\NN_{\mathrm{Pui}}/\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}})]$, and the fibre of the integral closure $\NN'$ of $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ in $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]$
is absolutely integrally closed and splits as the square of the real one (\cref{osq:nf:thm:saturation,osq:nf:thm:boolean,osq:nf:thm:doubling,osq:nf:cor:aic}).
The Gaussian pair is covered too: $\Z[i]+\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]=\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]$ is integral over $\A_{\mathrm{Pui}}$, so its integral closure in $K_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]$ is
$\NN'$, and its extended ideal $\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}[i]\NN'=\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}\NN'$ is the ideal of \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}. Its Boolean algebra is atomless of
cardinality $\mathfrak c$: an idempotent of the colimit is the residue of an idempotent of some $\mathsf B(\Z a/m)$, which \cref{osq:rm:thm:uniformsplit} (over
$\Z a/m$) splits into two nonzero idempotents; these are not nilpotent and so survive by \cref{osq:rm:thm:pui}, and likewise the independent family of
\cref{osq:rm:thm:cardinality} survives, while $|K_{\mathrm{Pui}}|=\mathfrak c$. This is an instance of the second clause of \cref{osq:nf:q:fibre}(b):
real-rooted lifting gives a Boolean-power fibre here, with the monomial divisibility (ii), although set-family divisibility fails ($T^{1/n}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$
for all $n$ and no $T^\delta$ divides all of them in $\Pi_{\mathrm{Pui}}$). The cyclic workspace itself
is outside \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}: $K_{\Z a}$ is not real closed and (ii) fails there.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Local structure and the nilradical.} The valuation facts used are standard \cite{StacksVal}.

\begin{theorem}[Local structure of the coefficient normalization \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:localtype}
$\mathscr B$ is a Pr\"ufer domain. For every maximal ideal $\mathfrak q\ni T$ of $\mathscr B$, the valuation domain $\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$ has value group $\Q$,
normalized by $v(T)=1$, and residue field isomorphic to $\C$, for both pairs; it has rank one and is not a discrete valuation ring.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $\mathscr B$ contracts to a maximal ideal of $k[T]$, as $\mathscr B$ is integral over $k[T]$, and with $\mathfrak q_L=\mathfrak q\cap\mathscr B_L$
one has $\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}=\bigcup_L(\mathscr B_L)_{\mathfrak q_L}$, a directed union of discrete valuation rings with common fraction field $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$: for
a nonzero element put numerator and denominator in one stage, where it or its inverse is regular. So $\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$ is a valuation domain. If
$T\in\mathfrak q$, its normalized value group is a union of groups $\frac1{e_L}\Z$, so lies in $\Q$, and $v(\mathsf z_n)=1/n$ for all $n\ge2$ by
\eqref{osq:rm:eq:zn}; so it is $\Q$, Archimedean and not discrete. The residue field is algebraic over $k$, the union of the finite residue fields; for
$k=\R$, 20's $\varrho_0=T(1-T^{-2})^{1/2}\in\mathscr B$ has $\varrho_0^2=T^2-1$, so its residue squares to $-1$ and the residue field is $\C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A real domain with a nonreal arithmetic fibre \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:rem:nonreal}
$\varrho_0$ is even integral over $\A(\Z a)$, since the constant coefficient of $T^2-1$ is $-1\in D$, and its residue in $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ squares to $-1$.
So the real arithmetic fibre is not formally real although $\NN(\Z a)$ lies in an ordered field; $\mathsf I$ is not order-convex, and the quotient is not a
standard-part construction. 23 notes that the full-class normalization shows the same phenomenon; its witness there is 19's $\upsilon_T$
(\cref{osq:nf:prop:unit}), which for $T=\omega^a$ also lies in $K_{\Z a}$ \merge, while $\varrho_0$ is a second witness inside the cyclic workspace.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The nilradical is idempotent \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:nilideal}
$\mathsf J^2=\mathsf J$, as an ideal of $\mathscr B$ and as an ideal of $\NN(\Z a)$. So the common nilradical $\mathsf J/T\mathscr B$ of $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ and
$\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ is nonzero and equal to its square, and it is neither nilpotent nor finitely generated.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At a maximal ideal not containing $T$ both $\mathsf J$ and $\mathsf J^2$ localize to the unit ideal. At $\mathfrak q\ni T$ the value group is $\Q$, so
$\sqrt{T\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}}=\mathfrak q\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$; for $0\ne b$ in it choose rational $0<\delta<v(b)$ and $u$ with $v(u)=\delta$, so that $b=u\cdot(b/u)$
is a product of two elements of the maximal ideal, which is therefore idempotent. Equality of ideals is local, so $\mathsf J^2=\mathsf J$ in $\mathscr B$.
As $\mathsf J\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$, a coefficient from $\mathscr B$ in a finite sum of products can be absorbed into one factor, which stays in $\mathsf J$; so the
same holds over $\NN(\Z a)$. The rest is \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:cor:unbounded}.
\end{proof}

This does not conflict with Nakayama's lemma, since the ideal is not finitely generated, and an idempotent ideal need not consist of idempotents:
here all its elements are nilpotent (23).

\begin{theorem}[The associated graded ring \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:graded}
For every $r\ge1$, $\mathsf I^r=T^r\mathscr B$ and $\mathsf I^r/\mathsf I^{r+1}\cong\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ as $\mathsf B(\Z a)$-modules, the action being through the
injection of \cref{osq:rm:thm:span}. Multiplication gives a graded isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:graded}
 \operatorname{gr}_{\mathsf I}(\NN(\Z a))\cong\mathsf B(\Z a)\oplus W\,\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)[W]=\{g\in\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)[W]:g(0)\in\mathsf B(\Z a)\},
\end{equation}
and in particular $\mathsf I/\mathsf I^2\cong\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)\ne0$ and $\Tor_1^{\NN(\Z a)}(\mathsf B(\Z a),\mathsf B(\Z a))\cong\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ gives $\mathsf I^r\subseteq T^r\mathscr B$, and $T^rb=(Tb)T\cdots T$ is a product of $r$ elements of $\mathsf I$. Multiplication by $T^r$
identifies $\mathscr B/T\mathscr B$ with $T^r\mathscr B/T^{r+1}\mathscr B$ ($\mathscr B$ is a domain), $\NN(\Z a)$ acts through its image in $\mathscr B/T\mathscr B$, and products of
these identifications multiply classes in $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$. Tensoring $0\to\mathsf I\to\NN(\Z a)\to\mathsf B(\Z a)\to0$ with $\mathsf B(\Z a)$, the map
$\mathsf I\otimes\mathsf B(\Z a)\cong\mathsf I/\mathsf I^2\to\mathsf B(\Z a)$ is zero, which gives the $\Tor_1$.
\end{proof}

The conormal module is a further reason not to transfer identities from the full-class ideal, which satisfies $\Pi\NN=(\Pi\NN)^2$
(\cref{osq:nf:prop:ideal}), to a cyclic workspace: $\mathsf I$ has a genuine descending sequence of powers, although the nilradical of its quotient is
idempotent (23).

\begin{corollary}[Adic completion as a pullback \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:completion}
With $\widehat{\mathscr B}=\varprojlim_r\mathscr B/T^r\mathscr B$ and $\widehat{\NN}=\varprojlim_r\NN(\Z a)/\mathsf I^r$,
$\widehat{\NN}\cong\widehat{\mathscr B}\times_{\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)}\mathsf B(\Z a)$, and $\mathscr B\to\widehat{\mathscr B}$ and $\NN(\Z a)\to\widehat{\NN}$ are injective.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Since $T\mathscr B\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$, the image of $\NN(\Z a)/\mathsf I^r$ in $\mathscr B/T^r\mathscr B$ is the inverse image of $\mathsf B(\Z a)\subseteq\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$;
pass to the limit. A nonzero element of $\mathscr B$ has finite $\nu_T$, so lies in only finitely many $T^r\mathscr B$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Boolean splitting without a new scale.} For a real $c>0$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:splitter}
 \varsigma_c=T(1+cT^{-2})^{1/2},\qquad \mathsf y_c=\frac{1+\varsigma_c/\sqrt c}2,\qquad \varsigma_c^2=T^2+c,\qquad \mathsf y_c^2-\mathsf y_c=\frac{T^2}{4c}.
\end{equation}
The last equation is monic over $\A(\Z a)$, so $\mathsf y_c\in\NN(\Z a)$ and $\bar{\mathsf y}_c$ is an idempotent of $\mathsf B(\Z a)$, for both pairs. Its
nontriviality and independence from given data are proved by choosing $c$ outside the finite branch locus of the data.

\begin{lemma}[A quadratic branch splitting every zero-place branch \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:lem:freshquad}
Let $k(T)\subseteq L\subseteq K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ be finite. For all but finitely many real $c>0$: (i) $T^2+c$ is not a square in $L$, and $[L(\varsigma_c):L]=2$;
(ii) every $\mathfrak q\mid T$ of $\mathscr B_L$ has extensions to $\mathscr B$ at which the residue of $\varsigma_c$ is $\sqrt c$, and extensions at which it is
$-\sqrt c$; (iii) at these, with $v(T)=1$, $(v(\mathsf y_c),v(1-\mathsf y_c))$ is $(0,2)$, respectively $(2,0)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Only finitely many primes of $k[T]$ ramify in $L$ (\cref{osq:rm:lem:branchlocus}); choose $c$ so that the prime factors of $T^2+c$ avoid them, which
excludes finitely many $c$ (for $k=\R$ the $T^2+c$ are distinct irreducible quadratics, for $k=\C$ their pairs of roots are disjoint). Then $T^2+c$ has
order $1$ at every prime of $\mathscr B_L$ above one of its factors, so it is not a square in $L$. Hence $\mathscr B_L[\varsigma_c]$ is free over $\mathscr B_L$ on $1,\varsigma_c$,
and modulo $\mathfrak q\mid T$ it is $\ell_{\mathfrak q}[Y]/(Y^2-c)\cong\ell_{\mathfrak q}\times\ell_{\mathfrak q}$, since $\sqrt c\in k$ and $2\sqrt c\ne0$. Both primes of this
algebra extend to $\mathscr B$ by lying over, in set-sized integral extensions. There $\mathsf y_c$ has residue $1$, respectively $0$, and
$\mathsf y_c(1-\mathsf y_c)=-T^2/(4c)$ fixes the other value as $2$.
\end{proof}

Irreducibility is forced at a previously unused finite place, while the two branches occur over zero, and the Laurent expansion at infinity is kept
throughout: a new Boolean coordinate with the exponent group still exactly $\Z a$ (23).

\begin{theorem}[Uniform relative splitting \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:uniformsplit}
Let $S$ be a unital subring of $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ with $|S|<\mathfrak c$. There is a real $c>0$ such that, for $e=\bar{\mathsf y}_c$, the ring homomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:uniformsplit}
 S\times S\to\mathsf B(\Z a),\qquad (s_0,s_1)\mapsto s_0(1-e)+s_1e,
\end{equation}
is injective. The same holds with $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ replaced by $\mathsf C(\Z a)$, $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ or $\mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a representative $f_s\in\NN(\Z a)$ of each $s\in S$. The finite subsets of representatives generate at most $\max(|S|,\aleph_0)<\mathfrak c$ finite
extensions of $k(T)$, each excluding finitely many $c$ in \cref{osq:rm:lem:freshquad}; choose $c>0$ outside their union. (No regularity of $\mathfrak c$ is
used.) The map is a ring homomorphism because $e$ is idempotent. Let $(s_0,s_1)\ne(0,0)$, say $s_j\ne0$, and put both representatives in one of the chosen
fields $L$. As $f_{s_j}\notin T\mathscr B$, some $\mathfrak q\mid T$ has $v_{\mathfrak q}(f_{s_j})<1$. At an extension of \cref{osq:rm:lem:freshquad} where the idempotent
multiplying $s_j$ has value $0$ and the other value $2$, the summand of $s_j$ has value below $1$ and the other at least $2$, so the sum is not in $T\mathscr B$.
For $\mathsf C(\Z a)$ a nonzero class has a branch of value exactly $0$, and the sum has value $0$, so it is not in $\mathsf J$. For the coefficient fibres take
representatives in $\mathscr B$, whose values are still nonnegative.
\end{proof}

If all representatives of a subring lie in one finite $L$, one finite exceptional set suffices, whatever the size of the subring; this is used for
countable coefficient fields in \cref{osq:rm:thm:countable} (23).

\begin{corollary}[Atomlessness \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:atomless}
The Boolean algebras $\Idem(\mathsf B(\Z a))$, $\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))$, $\Idem(\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a))$ and $\Idem(\mathsf C^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a))$
are atomless.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero idempotent $b$ generates a countable unital ring; \cref{osq:rm:thm:uniformsplit} gives $e$ with $be$ and $b(1-e)$ nonzero, disjoint and with sum $b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Independent idempotents and cardinal invariants \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:cardinality}
The family $(\bar{\mathsf y}_c)_{c\in\R_{>0}}$ is Boolean independent in each of the four fibres of \cref{osq:rm:cor:atomless}. Their Boolean algebras have
cardinality $\mathfrak c$ and order density $\mathfrak c$: no set of fewer than $\mathfrak c$ nonzero idempotents has a member below every nonzero idempotent.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For distinct $c_1,\dots,c_r>0$ the square classes of the $T^2+c_j$ in $k(T)$ are independent, since a nonempty product has odd order at a prime factor of
only one of them; by \cref{osq:bb:lem:multiquadratic} adjoining the $\varsigma_{c_j}$ gives degree $2^r$. So $k[T,\varsigma_{c_1},\dots,\varsigma_{c_r}]$ is free over
$k[T]$ on the square-root monomials (the monic relations span, the degree gives independence), and modulo $T$ it is the product of $2^r$ copies of $k$,
one for each assignment $\varsigma_{c_j}\mapsto\pm\sqrt{c_j}$. Every such prime extends to $\mathscr B$, and the corresponding Boolean word in the
$\mathsf y_{c_j}$ and $1-\mathsf y_{c_j}$ has residue $1$ there, so it is not in $\mathsf J$ and is nonzero in all four fibres. As $K^{\mathrm{alg}}$ is algebraic over
$k(T)$, $|K^{\mathrm{alg}}|\le|k(T)|\aleph_0=\mathfrak c$, which bounds the fibres. If $\mathcal D$ were order dense of size $<\mathfrak c$, the ring $S$ it generates
has $|S|<\mathfrak c$, and a splitter $e$ of $S$ is nonzero while $d(1-e)\ne0$ for every $0\ne d\in\mathcal D$, so no $d\le e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The number of zero-place branches \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:cor:manyplaces}
$\mathscr B$ has exactly $2^{\mathfrak c}$ maximal ideals containing $T$, hence at least $2^{\mathfrak c}$ distinct valuation domains as in
\cref{osq:rm:thm:localtype}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $\eta:\R_{>0}\to\{0,1\}$, the ideal generated by $T$ and the elements $\mathsf y_c-\eta(c)$ is proper, since every finite subset of these relations holds
at a prime of the proof of \cref{osq:rm:thm:cardinality}; a maximal ideal containing it determines $\eta$. There are at most $2^{|\mathscr B|}=2^{\mathfrak c}$ subsets
of $\mathscr B$, and distinct maximal ideals give distinct localizations.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What these invariants do not determine \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:rem:boolboundary}
An independent family of size $\mathfrak c$ does not make the algebra free on it; uniform splitting adds one independent coordinate over a prescribed
small subring and does not realize arbitrary infinite Boolean types; neither completeness nor infinite joins follow, and the isomorphism type for
$k=\R$ or $\C$ is open (\cref{osq:rm:q:boolean}). The nilradical does not obstruct comparison with the reduced fibre: in a commutative ring idempotents
lift uniquely across a nil ideal (if $b^2-b=t$ is nilpotent, $2b-1$ is a unit since $(2b-1)^2=1+4t$, and $b-t/(2b-1)$ squares the error up to a unit;
two idempotents differing by a nilpotent have nilpotent idempotent cross terms $e(1-f)$, $f(1-e)$, hence zero ones). This standard fact is not claimed
(23).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The Boolean-power form of the cyclic reduced fibre \merge]\label{osq:rm:rem:booleanform}
For the real pair \cref{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean} gives $\mathsf C(\Z a)\cong\overline\Z[\Idem(\mathsf C(\Z a))]$, and by
\cref{osq:rm:cor:atomless,osq:rm:thm:cardinality} the Boolean parameter is atomless of cardinality and order density $\mathfrak c$, with $2^{\mathfrak c}$
branches over zero. The same proof of \cref{osq:bb:prop:fixedboolean} applies verbatim over the coefficient field $k_0=\overline\Q\cap\R$ of
\cref{osq:rm:thm:countable}: it uses normality, divisibility of the ideal by nonzero integers, $\upsilon_T$ (whose Laurent coefficients are rational) and the
real algebraic integers, all present there. So the reduced fibre of the $k_0$-fragment is $\overline\Z[\mathfrak B]$ with $\mathfrak B$ the Cantor algebra, the
ring of locally constant functions from Cantor space $\{0,1\}^{\N}$ to the discrete ring $\overline\Z$. By \cref{osq:rm:rem:boolboundary} the idempotents of the
unreduced fibres are the same.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Exact zero divisors and periodic homology.}

\begin{theorem}[Exact annihilators in the coefficient fibre \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:annC}
Fix $n\ge2$ and let $\bar{\mathsf z}_n$ be the residue of $\mathsf z_n$ in $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$. For $1\le j<n$,
$\Ann_{\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)}(\bar{\mathsf z}_n^j)=\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The right side annihilates since $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^n=0$. If $y\in\mathscr B$ represents an annihilator, $y\mathsf z_n^j=Tb$ with $b\in\mathscr B$; multiplying by
$\mathsf z_n^{n-j}$ and cancelling $T$ in the domain $\mathscr B$ gives $y(1+T^{n-1})=b\mathsf z_n^{n-j}$, and $1+T^{n-1}\equiv1$ modulo $T\mathscr B$.
\end{proof}

Locally, in $\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}/T\mathscr B_{\mathfrak q}$, annihilation by $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^j$ means value at least $(n-j)/n$, which is the principal ideal of
$\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}$; the cancellation proof needs no local-to-global theorem (23).

\begin{theorem}[A periodic resolution \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:periodic}
With $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}=\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ and $\mathscr M_n=\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}/(\bar{\mathsf z}_n)$, the complex
\begin{equation}\label{osq:rm:eq:periodic}
 \cdots\xrightarrow{\ \bar{\mathsf z}_n\ }\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}\xrightarrow{\ \bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-1}\ }\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}\xrightarrow{\ \bar{\mathsf z}_n\ }\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}
 \longrightarrow\mathscr M_n\longrightarrow0,
\end{equation}
with the two maps alternating, is a free resolution, $\Tor_q^{\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}}(\mathscr M_n,\mathscr M_n)\cong\mathscr M_n\ne0$ for all $q\ge0$,
$\pd\mathscr M_n=\fd\mathscr M_n=\infty$, and $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ has infinite global and weak global dimension.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consecutive maps compose to multiplication by $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^n=0$, and \cref{osq:rm:thm:annC} (for $j=1$ and $j=n-1$) identifies every kernel with the preceding
image. Tensoring with $\mathscr M_n$ makes every differential zero, so the homology is $\mathscr M_n$ in every degree, and $\mathscr M_n\ne0$ because the
nilpotent $\bar{\mathsf z}_n$ is not a unit of the nonzero ring $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}$. Nonvanishing $\Tor$ in all degrees excludes every finite flat, hence every
finite projective, resolution.
\end{proof}

Periodicity from a pair of exact zero divisors is classical and related to matrix factorizations \cite{Eisenbud}; the content here is the explicit
pair in these non-Noetherian fibres, proved without a theorem that needs a regular Noetherian local ring (23).

\begin{proposition}[Arithmetic annihilators \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:prop:annR}
Under $\mathsf B(\Z a)\hookrightarrow\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$, for $1\le j<n$,
\[
 \Ann_{\mathsf B(\Z a)}(\bar{\mathsf z}_n^j)=\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)\subseteq\mathsf B(\Z a),\qquad
 \bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}\mathsf B(\Z a)\subsetneq\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a).
\]
So \eqref{osq:rm:eq:periodic} with $\mathsf B(\Z a)$ in place of $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ is not exact.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $b\in\mathscr B$ and $1\le r<n$ every value of $\mathsf z_n^rb$ over zero is at least $r/n>0$, so $\mathsf z_n^rb\in\mathsf J\subseteq\NN(\Z a)$ and
$\bar{\mathsf z}_n^r\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)\subseteq\mathsf B(\Z a)$; intersect \cref{osq:rm:thm:annC} with $\mathsf B(\Z a)$. If $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}/2=\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}u$ with
$u\in\mathsf B(\Z a)$, then $u-\frac12$ kills $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^{n-j}$ in $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$, so lies in $\bar{\mathsf z}_n^j\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$, and a representative of
$u$ has residue $\frac12$ at every place over zero; but $\frac12$ is integral over neither $\Z$ nor $\Z[i]$, contrary to \cref{osq:rm:thm:residues}.
\end{proof}

For $n=2$: the residue of $\mathsf z_2/2$ is killed by that of $\mathsf z_2$ but is not in the principal arithmetic ideal it generates; the missing
coefficient $\frac12$ is the obstruction. 23 computes the weak global dimension of $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$ and deliberately leaves that of
$\mathsf B(\Z a)$ open (\cref{osq:rm:q:arhomology}).

\paragraph{A countable fragment with a determined Boolean algebra.} Let $k_0=\overline\Q\cap\R$ (as in \cref{osq:nf:lem:coefficients}), a real closed
field, and $\overline\Q$. Repeat the definitions of $K_{\Z a}$, $\A(\Z a)$, $\NN(\Z a)$, $\mathscr B$, $\mathsf I$ and the four fibres with $k$ replaced by $k_0$
(and $D=\Z$), respectively by $\overline\Q$ (and $D=\Z[i]$). These are smaller coefficient fragments, not the workspaces above; their Laurent fields are
still uncountable, but the relative algebraic subfields are countable.

\begin{theorem}[Algebraic-coefficient fragments \src{23}]\label{osq:rm:thm:countable}
In either fragment: (i) $\NN(\Z a)$ and $\mathscr B$ are countable, $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$, and \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:thm:generalrefinement} hold;
(ii) every localization of $\mathscr B$ at a maximal ideal containing $T$ has value group $\Q$ and residue field $\overline\Q$; (iii) the Boolean algebras of
idempotents of the four fibres are each isomorphic to the algebra of clopen subsets of Cantor space $\{0,1\}^{\N}$, the countable atomless Boolean algebra.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are countably many polynomials over the countable field of rational functions, each with finitely many roots, so the relative algebraic closure
is countable, and it contains $\NN(\Z a)$ and $\mathscr B$. The normalization and residue arguments use characteristic $0$ and, for the coefficient span, that
finite residue extensions are the field itself or its extension by $i$ (real case) and the field itself (algebraically closed case); the basis vectors
with entries $0,1,i$ are integral over $D$. So $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ and the criterion hold. $\mathsf z_n$ and all refinement certificates have rational
coefficients; $\mathsf z_n$ supplies the values $1/n$ and $\varrho_0$ a square root of $-1$, giving the residue field $k_0(i)=\overline\Q$, respectively
$\overline\Q$. To split a nonzero idempotent put a representative in a finite $L$ and restrict the parameters of \cref{osq:rm:lem:freshquad} to positive rational
squares, of which only finitely many are excluded. So all four algebras are countable and atomless. Two countable atomless Boolean algebras are
isomorphic: an isomorphism of finite subalgebras extends to one more prescribed element, since atomlessness allows exactly the needed splits of atoms
on the other side, and alternating in both directions along enumerations gives an isomorphism. The finite unions of cylinder sets of $\{0,1\}^{\N}$ form
a countable atomless algebra, and by compactness they are all the clopen sets.
\end{proof}

The uniqueness of the countable atomless Boolean algebra is classical; the application is to these fibres, and the uncountable algebras of the
full-coefficient workspaces are not classified (\cref{osq:rm:q:boolean}). The fragment is a concrete countable model in which nilpotence, refinement
and Boolean splitting coexist and can be approached computationally (23).

\paragraph{Comparison with the full class.}

\begin{remark}[What larger scales kill \merge]\label{osq:rm:rem:fullclass}
By \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent} and \cref{osq:rm:thm:span}, $\Pi\NN\cap K_{\Z a}=\sqrt{\mathsf I}=\mathsf J$ for the real pair. So the natural map
$\mathsf B(\Z a)\to\mathsf B_\R$ has kernel exactly the nilradical $\mathsf J/T\mathscr B$, nonzero by \cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit}, and the radical in the second
equality of \eqref{osq:bb:eq:descent} cannot be removed for $G=\Z a$; the reduced fibre $\mathsf C(\Z a)$ embeds (\cref{osq:bb:cor:localinjection}). The
comparison of ideals is: $\Pi\NN$ is radical with $\Pi\NN=(\Pi\NN)^2$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:radical,osq:nf:prop:ideal}); $\mathsf I$ is not radical and
$\mathsf I/\mathsf I^2\ne0$ (\cref{osq:rm:thm:explicit,osq:rm:thm:graded}), while its radical $\mathsf J$ satisfies $\mathsf J^2=\mathsf J$ (\cref{osq:rm:thm:nilideal});
and $\mathsf I_{\mathrm{Pui}}$ is radical (\cref{osq:rm:thm:pui}). So the conclusion that \cref{osq:nf:thm:radical} proves for the full class fails in a fixed
workspace; it does not contradict \cref{osq:nf:thm:abstract}, whose hypotheses the cyclic workspace fails (\cref{osq:rm:rem:puiabstract}), and it says
nothing about real closed fixed workspaces such as $K_{\Q a}$ (\cref{osq:rm:q:fullQ}).
\end{remark}

23 records the resolution as follows: for every $G=\Z a$ the extended ideal is not radical and its fibre has nilpotents of every order, which is not
a classification for arbitrary ordered groups or support classes; the cyclic fibre is atomless with exact cardinality and order density $\mathfrak c$,
without its isomorphism type; the residue criterion is a finite-place test for algebraic Laurent elements, not an oracle for arbitrary coefficients or
Hahn input; in every cyclic workspace $\mathsf I\subsetneq\sqrt{\mathsf I}$, so removing the radical from \cref{osq:bb:thm:descent} would give a stronger,
false statement there, and that theorem is compared with, not used by, the cyclic proofs; the bounded-denominator Puiseux normalization has radical
extended ideal, and the full rational-exponent Hahn field is left open. Its dependencies are: finite normalization gives $\mathsf z_n$ and the exact
refinement; scaling and the residue criterion give $k\NN(\Z a)=\mathscr B$, hence $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$, hence the filtration and the general refinement law;
the finite ramification locus gives the fresh quadratic splitting and the Boolean results; and $\mathsf I=T\mathscr B$ gives the exact annihilators and the
periodic homology over $\mathsf B^{\mathrm{co}}(\Z a)$, with deliberately no arrow to $\mathsf B(\Z a)$, which \cref{osq:rm:prop:annR} disproves. All rings and modules
