in these proofs are sets; the surreal $a$ only names the exponent group; composita, primes, localizations and branches are taken in set-sized rings and
fields, with ordinary choice (the maximal-ideal theorem) and no class Zorn lemma, class module category or measurable cardinal. Neither the continuum
hypothesis nor regularity of $\mathfrak c$ is used. The Newton--Puiseux theorem is used only to identify the limit field as real closed or algebraically
closed; the reducedness of its fibre does not need it (23).

\subsection{Henselian branching at an omnific augmentation}\label{osq:hb:sub:henselian}

This subsection is manuscript~27's (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). It moves 20's splitters from the normalization fibre into \'etale neighbourhoods. For every
infinite cardinal $\kappa$ and every set $S_0\subseteq\No$ of at most $\kappa$ surreals, 27 builds a real closed field $\mathbb E\supseteq S_0$ of cardinality
$\kappa$ whose \emph{actual} omnific integer part $B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E\cap\Oz$ has an idempotent constant-term ideal, so that its local ring
$\mathfrak L$ at that ideal has residue field $\Q$, $\mathfrak n^2=\mathfrak n$ and completion $\Q$; yet the henselization $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ has
exactly $2^\kappa$ minimal primes, the most a ring of cardinality $\kappa$ can have, each with fraction field $\mathbb E[i]$, and its generic fibre is the
algebra $\LC(\mathsf X,\mathbb E[i])$ of locally constant functions on a Stone space with $|\mathsf X|=2^\kappa$ (\cref{osq:hb:thm:main}). The branches are
forced to be complex, the completion forgets all of them, strict henselization adds a factor $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q)$ and the Gaussian ring
doubles the generic fibre (\cref{osq:hb:thm:factors}); finite projectives, finite \'etale algebras and the centred Riemann--Zariski space are determined
(\cref{osq:hb:thm:projectives,osq:hb:prop:etale,osq:hb:cor:rz}). All rings, spectra and henselizations are sets. No numbered question of this report is
answered.

27 pins \texttt{fc27d87} (23 September 2026), whose text of this report is again blob \texttt{ef7aef1} (the sixth merge, without 23's \cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}
and without 24's to 26's subsections), and re-fetched there the file \texttt{20-boolean-branching-PROOF\_AUDIT.md} (blob \texttt{feea0ee}), from which it
reconstructs 20's splitter; it credits the constant-term retraction, monomial clearing, idempotence of the tail and the Boolean branching mechanism to the
repository. Printed once, under the existing labels, are: its two monomial operations (its Lemma~2.1: \cref{osq:lem:gap,osq:prop:common}), its omnific
floor (its Lemma~2.2: \cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}), its support projection and dominant scale (its Lemmas~2.3, 2.5: \cref{osq:bb:lem:projection,osq:bb:lem:laurent}),
its monic certificate (its Lemma~3.1: \cref{osq:bb:lem:certificate}), its nontriviality and integer-torsion lemma (its Lemma~3.2: \cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction}
with \cref{osq:nf:thm:radical}), its quadratic splitter (its Lemma~3.3: \cref{osq:bb:thm:split}, the same element $\mathsf w_t$ of \eqref{osq:bb:eq:splitter})
and its independent splitters (its Proposition~3.5: \cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal} for $\alpha<\kappa$, the same $t_\alpha=\omega^{\omega^\alpha}$); 27 is credited as an
independent re-derivation, and its proof of the splitter through the quadratic subalgebra alone, which it calls ``why one radical suffices'', is kept as a

\paragraph{Notation and renamings.} Throughout, $\kappa$ is an infinite cardinal and $S_0\subseteq\No$ a set with $|S_0|\le\kappa$. Exponents follow
\cref{osq:sub:orientation} (27's growth convention). The rings are
\begin{equation}\label{osq:hb:eq:rings}
 B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E\cap\Oz,\qquad \Pi_{\mathbb E}=\ker(\ct|_{B_{\mathbb E}})=B_{\mathbb E}\cap\Pi,\qquad \mathfrak L=(B_{\mathbb E})_{\Pi_{\mathbb E}},\qquad
 \mathfrak n=\Pi_{\mathbb E}\mathfrak L,\qquad \mathscr G=\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h},
\end{equation}
with $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ and $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}$ the henselization and strict henselization. 27's symbols are renamed as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its field $E$, seed $\mathcal S$, integer part $B$, ideal $J$, local ring $A$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, henselization $H$, field $C=E[i]$ and generic
fibre $G=E\otimes_AH$ are $\mathbb E$, $S_0$, $B_{\mathbb E}$ (a cofinal discretely ordered subring, as in \cref{osq:sa:sub:semialgebraic}), $\Pi_{\mathbb E}$,
$\mathfrak L$ with $\mathfrak n$, $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$, $\mathbb E[i]$ and $\mathscr G$ ($E$ is the ambient field and $\EE_a$ 07's field; $\mm$ is the
negative-support ideal; $H$ is a group or $H_a$; $G$ is a set-sized subgroup; $\mathsf C(G)$ a reduced fibre; $A$ a ring such as $\A_{D,k}$ or
$A^{08}_\kappa$; $J$ and $\mathsf J$ are other ideals). Its Stone space $X$ is $\mathsf X$ ($X^g$ are monomials), and its $\mathcal G_\Q$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline
\Q/\Q)$.
\item Its $F_\Gamma,O_\Gamma,\Pi_\Gamma,\pi_\Gamma$ are $K_G$, $\A(G)$, $\Pi(G)$ and $\operatorname{pr}_G$ of \cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}; its $\mathcal N$ is this report's $\NN$ (the same letter),
and its $\mathcal K=\sqrt{\Pi\NN}$ is $\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:nf:thm:radical}); its integral closures $N_B,N_A$ of $B,A$ in $E$ are $\IC_{\mathbb E}(B_{\mathbb E})$
and $\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)$.
\item Its polynomial $D(T)=(T^2-1)(T^2-4)$ is $\mathsf q(T)$ ($D$ is the constant ring), its $a(T)=(T^4-5T^2)/16$ and $w(T)$ are $\mathsf a(T)$ and $\mathsf w(T)$,
so $\mathsf w(t)=\mathsf w_t$ of \eqref{osq:bb:eq:splitter}; its $T_\alpha=\omega^{b_\alpha}$, $b_\alpha=\omega^\alpha$, are 20's $t_\alpha$ (here $T=\omega^a$
elsewhere), its $a_\alpha=\mathsf a(T_\alpha)$ are $\mathsf a_\alpha$ ($a_\alpha$ are the small scales of \eqref{osq:eq:scales}), and its $w_\alpha$ are
$\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}$.
\item Its roots $u_\alpha\in\mathfrak mH$, generic idempotents $e_\alpha$ and imaginary unit $j$ are $\tilde u_\alpha$, $\hat e_\alpha$ and $\jmath$ ($u_n$ and $e_\alpha$
are 21's and 20's elements, $e_\alpha=\mathsf e_{t_\alpha}$ being a residue in $\mathsf B_\R$); its pointed neighbourhoods $D_0$, $D=(D_0)_{\mathfrak n}$ are
$\mathfrak U_{F,0}$ and $\mathfrak U_F$ with residue-point ideal $\mathfrak u$; its minimal primes $P$ are $\mathfrak Q$; its $h$ with $h>1/4$ is written $h$.
\item In the hull, its clearing pairs $d_r,d_rr$ and factor pairs $e_x,x/e_x$ are $m_r,m_rr$ and $f_x,x/f_x$, and its $R_n$ are $\mathbb E_n$.
\end{itemize}
Four tempting readings are false. (1) $\mathfrak n$ is not the ideal of order-infinitesimals: it contains the positive infinite $\omega$, so the local topology
is not the valuation topology of $\mathbb E$, and henselian lifting need not respect the order. (2) $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is local and has no nontrivial
idempotents; the $2^\kappa$ branches live in $\mathscr G$, and $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is not a product of branches. (3) $\jmath^2=-1$ holds in $\mathscr G$;
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ contains no square root of $-1$, since its residue field is $\Q$. (4) The specializations $T\mapsto0$ act on finite algebras, not on
Laurent series, and projection is linear, not a ring map (\cref{osq:bb:rem:specialization,osq:bb:rem:notretraction}).

\begin{theorem}[Maximal branching at an omnific augmentation \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:thm:main}
There is a real closed field $\mathbb E\subseteq\No$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S_0\subseteq\mathbb E$; $|B_{\mathbb E}|=|\mathbb E|=|\mathfrak L|=|\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}|=\kappa$; $B_{\mathbb E}$ is an integer part of $\mathbb E$ with
$\Frac B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E$; $\Pi_{\mathbb E}$ and $\mathfrak n$ are nonzero and idempotent; $\mathfrak L$ is a local domain with residue field $\Q$.
\item $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is reduced, local and faithfully flat over $\mathfrak L$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ and residue field
$\Q$; $\widehat{\mathfrak L}_{\mathfrak n}=\Q=\widehat{\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}}$ and $\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2=0$.
\item $\mathscr G$ contains an $\mathbb E$-algebra copy of $\mathbb E[i]$, and for the copy of \cref{osq:hb:prop:complex} there is an $\mathbb E[i]$-algebra
isomorphism $\mathscr G\cong\LC(\mathsf X,\mathbb E[i])$ with $\mathsf X$ a Stone space, $|\mathsf X|=2^\kappa$, $\dim_{\mathbb E[i]}\mathscr G=\kappa$, where
$\LC$ means locally constant functions to the \emph{discrete} field (so of finite image); $\Idem(\mathscr G)$ contains a free Boolean algebra on $\kappa$
generators.
\item $|\operatorname{Min}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}|=2^\kappa$, $\Frac(\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}/\mathfrak Q)\cong_{\mathbb E}\mathbb E[i]$ for every minimal prime
$\mathfrak Q$, and there is no $\mathfrak L$-algebra map from $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ to $\mathbb E$ or to any ordered extension field of $\mathbb E$.
\end{enumerate}
No regularity of $\kappa$, cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis or large cardinal is used.
\end{theorem}

``Maximal'' is exact: a ring of cardinality $\kappa$ has at most $2^\kappa$ ideals; it does not mean that $\mathsf X$ is classified (27). The proof occupies the
rest of the subsection (\cref{osq:hb:prop:hull,osq:hb:cor:local,osq:hb:prop:complex,osq:hb:prop:exactsize,osq:hb:prop:minimal,osq:hb:prop:completion}).

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic and Gaussian factors \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:thm:factors}
Choose $\overline\Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb E[i]$. Then $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}\cong\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}\otimes_\Q\overline\Q$ and $\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}
\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}\cong\LC(\mathsf X\times\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q),\mathbb E[i])$, the Galois group acting on the second factor with fixed ring
$\mathscr G$. Also $\mathfrak L[i]$ is local with residue field $\Q(i)$, $(\mathfrak L[i])^{\mathrm h}\cong\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]$, and $\mathbb E[i]
\otimes_{\mathfrak L[i]}(\mathfrak L[i])^{\mathrm h}\cong\mathscr G\times\mathscr G$ as rings and $\mathbb E$-algebras, the two factors carrying conjugate
$\mathbb E[i]$-structures; the Gaussian generic spectrum is $\mathsf X\sqcup\mathsf X$.
\end{theorem}

This is \cref{osq:hb:prop:strict,osq:hb:thm:strict,osq:hb:prop:gaussloc,osq:hb:thm:gaussian} (27).

\paragraph{The splitter, a second route.}

\begin{remark}[One radical suffices \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:rem:oneradical}
Put $\mathsf q(T)=(T^2-1)(T^2-4)$, $\mathsf a(T)=(T^4-5T^2)/16$ and $\mathsf w(T)=\frac12-\frac14\sqrt{\mathsf q(T)}$ (positive root). Since $\mathsf q(t)=
4(t^2-1)(t^2/4-1)$, $\mathsf w(t)=\mathsf w_t$ of \eqref{osq:bb:eq:splitter}, and $\mathsf w(T)^2-\mathsf w(T)=\mathsf a(T)$. 27 proves \cref{osq:bb:thm:split}
with the quadratic subalgebra instead of 20's biquadratic one: $\mathsf q$ has the four simple zeros $\pm1,\pm2$, so it is not a square in $k(T)$ ($k=K_G$) and
$k[T,W]/(W^2-W-\mathsf a(T))\to k(\!(T^{-1})\!)$, $W\mapsto\mathsf w(T)$, is injective; the two $k$-algebra specializations $T\mapsto0$, $W\mapsto0$ and
$T\mapsto0$, $W\mapsto1$ exist because $\mathsf a(0)=0$. A monic certificate for $x\mathsf w\in\Pi\NN$, projected by \cref{osq:bb:lem:projection} and read in
this finite algebra through \cref{osq:bb:lem:laurent}, specializes under $W\mapsto1$ to a certificate for $x$; for $x(1-\mathsf w)$ use $W\mapsto0$. The
Laurent expansion is
\[
 \mathsf w(T)=-\tfrac{T^2}4+\tfrac98+\tfrac9{32}T^{-2}+\tfrac{45}{64}T^{-4}+\tfrac{981}{512}T^{-6}+\tfrac{5715}{1024}T^{-8}+O(T^{-10}),
\]
an expansion in $T^{-1}$, not a series for small $T$; its coefficient $\frac98$ shows that integral elements need not be omnific, and the specializations are
not evaluations of it (27). In the independent family of \cref{osq:bb:thm:ordinal}, for $\alpha<\kappa$ the support of $\mathsf w_{t_\beta}$ lies in
$\Z\omega^\beta$, $\omega^\alpha$ dominates the group generated by the earlier $\omega^\beta$, and applying the splitter in increasing order keeps every finite
atom $\prod_{\alpha\in F}\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}^{\epsilon_\alpha}(1-\mathsf w_{t_\alpha})^{1-\epsilon_\alpha}$ outside $\Pi\NN$; the family is defined by a formula,
with no class ultrafilter (27, as 20).
\end{remark}

\paragraph{The omnific hull.}

\begin{proposition}[A cardinal-preserving omnific hull \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:hull}
There are a real closed field $\mathbb E\subseteq\No$ and $B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E\cap\Oz$ with: $S_0\subseteq\mathbb E$; $|B_{\mathbb E}|=|\mathbb E|=\kappa$ and
$B_{\mathbb E}$ an integer part of $\mathbb E$ with $\Frac B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E$; every $t_\alpha$ and $\mathsf a_\alpha$ ($\alpha<\kappa$) in $B_{\mathbb E}$;
and every nonzero element of $\Pi_{\mathbb E}$ a product of two elements of $\Pi_{\mathbb E}$, so that $\Pi_{\mathbb E}^2=\Pi_{\mathbb E}\ne0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $0\ne s\in S_0$ choose a monomial $m_s\in\Pi$ with $m_ss\in\Pi$ (\cref{osq:lem:gap}). Let $B_0$ be the subring of $\Oz$ generated by $\Z$, all $t_\alpha,
\mathsf a_\alpha$ and all $m_s,m_ss$ ($\mathsf a_\alpha$ is purely infinite, so omnific despite the coefficient $\frac1{16}$); $|B_0|=\kappa$. Given $B_n$, let
$\mathbb E_n$ be the relative real algebraic closure of $\Frac B_n$ in $\No$, of cardinality $\kappa$, and adjoin to $B_n$: $\lfloor r\rfloor$ for every
$r\in\mathbb E_n$ (\cref{osq:nm:lem:intpart}); a clearing pair $m_r,m_rr\in\Pi$ for every $0\ne r\in\mathbb E_n$; and a factor pair $f_x,x/f_x\in\Pi$ for every
$0\ne x\in B_n\cap\Pi$ (\cref{osq:prop:common}). Put $B_{\mathbb E}=\bigcup_nB_n$ and $\mathbb E=\Frac B_{\mathbb E}=\bigcup_n\Frac B_n$. The clearing pairs give
$\mathbb E_n\subseteq\Frac B_{n+1}$, so $\mathbb E$ is real closed, and $S_0\subseteq\mathbb E$. Every $r\in\mathbb E$ has $\lfloor r\rfloor\in B_{\mathbb E}$, so
$B_{\mathbb E}$ is an integer part, and $r\in\Oz$ equals its floor, so $\mathbb E\cap\Oz\subseteq B_{\mathbb E}$. The factor pairs give
$\Pi_{\mathbb E}\subseteq\Pi_{\mathbb E}^2$, and $\omega=t_0\in\Pi_{\mathbb E}$. Countable unions keep the cardinal $\kappa$, even for singular $\kappa$.
\end{proof}

A convenient subring of $\Oz$ need not be the integer part of its fraction field; closure under the floor makes $B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E\cap\Oz$ an equality, and the
monomial operations are performed in $\No$, before the small hull is formed, because a fixed Hahn group need not admit fresh bounds (27). 08's integer part
$A^{08}_\kappa=F^{08}_\kappa\cap\Oz$ (\cref{osq:thm:model08}) is built in the same spirit, for truncation and support control, without a seed \merge.

\begin{corollary}[The local augmentation ring \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:cor:local}
$\Pi_{\mathbb E}$ is prime, $\mathfrak L\subseteq\mathbb E$, $\Frac\mathfrak L=\mathbb E$, $\mathfrak L/\mathfrak n=\Q$, $|\mathfrak L|=\kappa$ and
$\mathfrak n^2=\mathfrak n\ne0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
$\ct:B_{\mathbb E}\to\Z$ is onto with kernel $\Pi_{\mathbb E}$; localizing inverts the nonzero integers, giving $\Q$; localize $\Pi_{\mathbb E}^2=\Pi_{\mathbb E}$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{From normalization to henselian branches.} Put $\Sigma_0=B_{\mathbb E}\setminus\Pi_{\mathbb E}$. Then $\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)=
\Sigma_0^{-1}\IC_{\mathbb E}(B_{\mathbb E})$: an element integral over $\Sigma_0^{-1}B_{\mathbb E}$ times one common denominator of its monic equation is integral
over $B_{\mathbb E}$. Every $\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}$ lies in $\mathbb E$ (real closed and containing $t_\alpha$) and in $\IC_{\mathbb E}(B_{\mathbb E})$.

\begin{lemma}[Finite atoms survive local normalization \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:lem:atoms}
For finite $F\subseteq\kappa$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^F$, $p_\epsilon=\prod_{\alpha\in F}\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}^{\epsilon_\alpha}(1-\mathsf w_{t_\alpha})^{1-\epsilon_\alpha}$
is a nonzero idempotent in $\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)/\sqrt{\mathfrak n\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The quadratic equations make the $\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}$ idempotent modulo $\mathfrak n\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)$. If $p_\epsilon$ were in the radical, clearing
denominators gives $sp_\epsilon^q\in\Pi_{\mathbb E}\IC_{\mathbb E}(B_{\mathbb E})\subseteq\Pi\NN$ with $s\in\Sigma_0$; with $s=n+z$, $n=\ct(s)\ne0$, $z\in\Pi$, also
$zp_\epsilon^q\in\Pi\NN$, so $np_\epsilon^q\in\Pi\NN$ and $p_\epsilon\in\Pi\NN$ (\cref{osq:nf:lem:contraction,osq:nf:thm:radical}), against
\cref{osq:hb:rem:oneradical}.
\end{proof}

$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is henselian, local, faithfully flat and ind-\'etale over $\mathfrak L$ with the same residue field, without Noetherian hypotheses
\cite{StacksHensel,StacksPermanence}. For each $\alpha$ there is a unique $\tilde u_\alpha\in\mathfrak n\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ with
$\tilde u_\alpha^2-\tilde u_\alpha-\mathsf a_\alpha=0$ (simple root $0$ modulo $\mathfrak n$, derivative $-1$). For finite $F=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$ put
$\mathfrak U_{F,0}=\mathfrak L[U_1,\dots,U_n]/(U_j^2-U_j-\mathsf a_{\alpha_j})$, $\mathfrak u=(\mathfrak n,U_1,\dots,U_n)$ and $\mathfrak U_F=(\mathfrak U_{F,0})_{\mathfrak
u}$: essentially \'etale over $\mathfrak L$ (the Jacobian entries $2U_j-1$ are units at $\mathfrak u$), residue field $\Q$, and $\mathfrak U_F\to\mathfrak L^{\mathrm
h}$, $U_j\mapsto\tilde u_{\alpha_j}$, identifies $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ with $\mathfrak U_F^{\mathrm h}$, so it is faithfully flat \cite{StacksHensel,StacksPermanence}.

\begin{lemma}[Every finite generic branch survives localization \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:lem:allbranches}
$\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}\mathfrak U_F\cong\mathbb E^{\{0,1\}^F}$, and the map from this product into $\mathscr G$ is injective.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Before localizing, the Chinese remainder theorem gives $\mathbb E\otimes\mathfrak U_{F,0}\cong\prod_{\{0,1\}^F}\mathbb E$, each $U_j$ evaluated at
$\mathsf w_{t_{\alpha_j}}$ or $1-\mathsf w_{t_{\alpha_j}}$, distinct because $1-2\mathsf w=\sqrt{\mathsf q}/2\ne0$. Fix $v_j\in\{\mathsf w_{t_{\alpha_j}},
1-\mathsf w_{t_{\alpha_j}}\}$. By \cref{osq:hb:lem:atoms} the product $\prod_j(1-v_j)$ is nonzero in the set-sized ring
$R=\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)/\sqrt{\mathfrak n\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)}$, so some prime of $R$ omits it; in its residue domain the idempotents $1-v_j$ are $1$
and the $v_j$ are $0$. Lifting gives a prime $\mathfrak p\supseteq\mathfrak n\IC_{\mathbb E}(\mathfrak L)$ containing every $v_j$, contracting to $\mathfrak n$. A
representative of $g\in\mathfrak U_{F,0}\setminus\mathfrak u$ has nonzero residue $g(0,\dots,0)\in\Q$, and its value at $(v_j)$ reduces modulo $\mathfrak p$ to
the same residue, so it is nonzero in $\mathbb E$: every inverted element is nonzero on every factor, and localization keeps the product. Faithful flatness
survives base change, so the map to $\mathscr G$ is injective.
\end{proof}

A split generic polynomial need not keep every branch after localization at one residue point: a denominator outside the residue prime may vanish on a whole
generic component. The prime chosen above excludes this for every denominator and every finite branch pattern; this is 27's central new step, and the reason
the support certificates are needed (27).

\begin{proposition}[A free Boolean family in the generic fibre \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:boolean}
The elements
\begin{equation}\label{osq:hb:eq:idempotent}
 \hat e_\alpha=\frac{\tilde u_\alpha-\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}}{1-2\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}}\in\mathscr G\qquad(\alpha<\kappa)
\end{equation}
are idempotents freely generating a Boolean subalgebra of $\Idem(\mathscr G)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Over $\mathbb E$, $U^2-U-\mathsf a_\alpha=(U-\mathsf w_{t_\alpha})(U-1+\mathsf w_{t_\alpha})$, and the affine change \eqref{osq:hb:eq:idempotent} sends the roots to
$0,1$. By \cref{osq:hb:lem:allbranches} every finite root assignment is a factor of a product injecting into $\mathscr G$, and each Boolean atom is $1$ on one
factor.
\end{proof}

The $\mathsf w_{t_\alpha}$ are available only after passing to the generic fibre, and the $\hat e_\alpha$ are not idempotents of the local ring
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ (27). For $\alpha=0,1$, $t_0=\omega$, $t_1=\omega^\omega$, the four atoms $\mathsf w_\omega\mathsf w_{\omega^\omega},\dots,
(1-\mathsf w_\omega)(1-\mathsf w_{\omega^\omega})$ survive modulo $\Pi\NN$ (the support of $\mathsf w_\omega$ is in $\Z$ and $\omega$ dominates the integers), and the
four orthogonal idempotents $\hat e_0\hat e_1,\dots,(1-\hat e_0)(1-\hat e_1)$ of $\mathscr G$ sum to $1$ although the neighbourhood and the henselization are local; the
roots $\tilde u_0,\tilde u_1$ reducing to $0$ are not the real roots $\mathsf w_{t_0},\mathsf w_{t_1}$ (27).

\paragraph{Forced complexification and the Boolean power.}

\begin{proposition}[Forced complexification \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:complex}
Let $A$ be a local domain with real closed fraction field $\mathbb F$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_A$, and $h\in\mathfrak m_A$ with $h>\frac14$ in $\mathbb F$. Then
$\mathbb F\otimes_AA^{\mathrm h}$ contains an $\mathbb F$-algebra copy of $\mathbb F[i]$, and no $A$-algebra map takes $A^{\mathrm h}$ to an ordered extension field of
$\mathbb F$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$U^2-U+h$ reduces to $U(U-1)$, so henselization gives a root $u\in\mathfrak m_AA^{\mathrm h}$. With $c=\sqrt{4h-1}>0$ in $\mathbb F$ put $\jmath=(2u-1)/c$; then
$\jmath^2=(4u^2-4u+1)/(4h-1)=-1$. The generic fibre is nonzero by faithful flatness, so $\mathbb F[i]\to\mathbb F\otimes A^{\mathrm h}$, $i\mapsto\jmath$, is injective.
An $A$-algebra map to an ordered field extending $\mathbb F$ would send $u$ to a root of a quadratic with negative discriminant.
\end{proof}

Take $h=\omega$: algebraically small for $\mathfrak n$, order-theoretically large in $\mathbb E$. The root lands in the new algebra, not in $\mathbb E$, so this is no
failure of real closedness; and $\jmath$ lives in $\mathscr G$, where division by $c\in\mathbb E^\times$ is allowed, not in $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ (27). In
$\Oz$ itself $T^2-T-\omega$ has simple residue roots $0,1$ and no root (\nolinkurl{odg:ex:hensel}); here the henselization supplies them.

\begin{lemma}[Boolean powers from finite products \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:lem:booleanpower}
Let $\mathbb F$ be real closed, $\mathscr A$ a nonzero ind-\'etale $\mathbb F$-algebra with a chosen embedding $\mathbb F[i]\hookrightarrow\mathscr A$. Then $\mathscr A$ is
the directed union of finite $\mathbb F[i]$-subalgebras isomorphic to finite products of $\mathbb F[i]$; it is reduced and von Neumann regular, every prime is
maximal and minimal with residue field $\mathbb F[i]$; $\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr A$ is a Stone space $\mathsf X$; and residue evaluation is an isomorphism
$\mathscr A\cong\LC(\mathsf X,\mathbb F[i])$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An \'etale algebra over a field is a finite product of finite separable extensions \cite{StacksEtale}, over a real closed field $\mathbb F$ or $\mathbb F[i]$; finitely
many elements with the chosen $i$ lie in the image of one such algebra, a quotient of a finite product of fields, hence a finite product of fields, none equal to
$\mathbb F$ since it contains a root of $X^2+1$. In a finite product each $g$ has $y$ with $g=g^2y$ (reciprocal on nonzero coordinates), a relation that persists:
principal ideals are generated by idempotents, prime quotients are fields, nilpotents already vanish in a finite stage, and each residue field is the union of
images of $\mathbb F[i]$. Basic opens $D(e)$ of idempotents are clopen and separate primes, so with quasi-compactness $\mathsf X$ is compact, Hausdorff and
zero-dimensional. Each $g$ is constant on the parts of a finite clopen partition, so evaluation is locally constant, injective by reducedness, and onto because a
locally constant function has finite image with clopen fibres, each a finite union of basic clopens, hence given by an idempotent.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Size of the henselization \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:lem:size}
An infinite local ring of cardinality $\kappa$ with residue field $\Q$ has a henselization of cardinality $\kappa$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are at most $\kappa$ finite presentations of \'etale algebras, each of size at most $\kappa$, and each has finitely many points over the closed point with
residue field $\Q$; the pointed-neighbourhood colimit has at most $\kappa$ objects of size at most $\kappa$, and $A\to A^{\mathrm h}$ is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact generic size \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:exactsize}
With $\mathsf X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr G$, $|\mathsf X|=2^\kappa$, $|\mathscr G|=\kappa$ and $\dim_{\mathbb E[i]}\mathscr G=\kappa$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$\mathscr G$ is a localization of $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ containing $\mathbb E$, so $|\mathscr G|=\kappa$ (\cref{osq:hb:lem:size}) and $|\mathsf X|\le2^\kappa$. The map
$\mathsf X\to\{0,1\}^\kappa$, $\mathfrak p\mapsto(\hat e_\alpha\bmod\mathfrak p)$, is continuous and onto: finite parts of an assignment are realized because the atoms
are nonzero, and compactness realizes the whole. A relation $\sum_jc_j\hat e_{\alpha_j}=0$ with $c_j\in\mathbb E[i]$, multiplied by the atom with $\hat e_{\alpha_j}=1$
and the others $0$, gives $c_j=0$; so the $\hat e_\alpha$ are independent, and $|\mathscr G|$ bounds the dimension.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Henselian minimal primes \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:minimal}
Localization is a bijection $\operatorname{Min}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr G$, and for $\mathfrak Q\in\operatorname{Min}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ the
fraction field of $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}/\mathfrak Q$ is the corresponding residue field of $\mathscr G$, which is $\mathbb E[i]$ over $\mathbb E$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is reduced (reducedness passes to henselizations \cite{StacksPermanence}). Flat going down sends a minimal prime to a minimal prime of the domain
$\mathfrak L$, that is to $0$, so it survives in $\mathscr G$. A prime contracting to $0$ contains, and localizes to, a minimal one, and all primes of $\mathscr G$ are
minimal (\cref{osq:hb:lem:booleanpower}), so the two coincide. $(\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}/\mathfrak Q)\otimes\mathbb E$ is the corresponding prime quotient $\mathbb E[i]$
of $\mathscr G$, a localization of the domain $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}/\mathfrak Q$ that is already a field.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Completion sees only the residue.}

\begin{proposition}[Adic invisibility \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:completion}
$\mathfrak L/\mathfrak n^n=\Q=\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}/(\mathfrak n\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h})^n$ for every $n\ge1$; both completions are the discrete field $\Q$, with kernels
$\mathfrak n$ and $\mathfrak n\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$; neither completion map is flat; neither maximal ideal is finitely generated, and $\mathfrak L$, $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm
h}$ are not Noetherian.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$\mathfrak n^2=\mathfrak n$ makes both inverse systems constant. $h=\omega$ is a nonzerodivisor on $\mathfrak L$, and on the flat $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$, but acts by zero on
$\Q$. A finitely generated idempotent maximal ideal is zero by Nakayama's lemma, and both contain $h\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No nilpotent local deformation \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:cor:nilpotent}
For a local $\Q$-algebra $(R_0,\mathfrak r)$ with nilpotent maximal ideal and residue field $\Q$, every local $\Q$-algebra map from $\mathfrak L$ or $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ to
$R_0$ factors through the residue field; in particular the residue-preserving maps to $\Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^n)$ are unique.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $\mathfrak r^n=0$, the image of $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak n^n$ lies in $\mathfrak r^n=0$.
\end{proof}

This is the idempotent-ideal mechanism of \cref{osq:hd:prop:etale} (27 credits it to the repository). Both tangent spaces vanish, yet $\mathscr G$ has $2^\kappa$
points; $\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}\widehat{\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}}=0$ since $h$ is inverted on the left and kills $\Q$, while $\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}
\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}=\LC(\mathsf X,\mathbb E[i])\ne0$: completion destroys every generic branch at once. $\operatorname{Spec}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ is connected, all
minimal primes lying in one maximal ideal, and the clopen structure appears only after inverting $\mathfrak L\setminus\{0\}$; $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ must not be
replaced by a product of branches (27). No infinitesimal lifting criterion for smoothness applies, the rings being neither Noetherian nor of finite type (27).

\paragraph{Strict henselization and the Galois factor.}

\begin{proposition}[Strict henselization by constants \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:strict}
With $\overline\Q$ an algebraic closure of the residue field, $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}\cong\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}\otimes_\Q\overline\Q$ as local $\mathfrak L$-algebras;
its maximal ideal is generated by $\mathfrak n$, its residue field is $\overline\Q$ and its completion the discrete field $\overline\Q$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For finite $L/\Q$ inside $\overline\Q$, $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}\otimes_\Q L$ is finite \'etale over $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$, local with residue field $L$ (finite over a local
ring with a field as residue algebra), hence henselian \cite{StacksLocal}. The union is henselian, local, ind-\'etale over $\mathfrak L$ with residue field
$\overline\Q$, which identifies it with $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}$ \cite{StacksHensel}; the maximal ideal stays idempotent.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Splitting the arithmetic tensor product \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:lem:galois}
For an algebraically closed field $\mathbb F'$ of characteristic zero containing $\overline\Q$, $\mathbb F'\otimes_\Q\overline\Q\cong\LC(\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q),
\mathbb F')$ by $c\otimes a\mapsto(\sigma\mapsto c\sigma(a))$, the Galois group profinite and $\mathbb F'$ discrete.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For finite Galois $L/\Q$, $\mathbb F'\otimes_\Q L\cong\prod_{\operatorname{Gal}(L/\Q)}\mathbb F'$, compatibly with inflation; a locally constant function on the profinite
group has finite image and factors through a finite quotient.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The strict generic fibre \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:thm:strict}
With $\overline\Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb E[i]$ chosen, $\mathbb E\otimes_{\mathfrak L}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}\cong\LC(\mathsf X,\mathbb E[i])\otimes_\Q\overline\Q\cong
\LC(\mathsf X\times\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q),\mathbb E[i])$; $1\otimes\tau$ acts by $f(x,\sigma)\mapsto f(x,\sigma\tau)$ with fixed ring $\mathscr G$; and
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm{sh}}$ has cardinality $\kappa$ and exactly $2^\kappa$ minimal primes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first isomorphism is base change of \cref{osq:hb:prop:strict}; the second holds on each finite stage by \cref{osq:hb:lem:galois}, and a locally constant function
on the compact zero-dimensional product is given by finitely many clopen rectangles. Right translation is transitive, so invariants ignore the second coordinate.
$\overline\Q$ is countable; the generic spectrum $\mathsf X\times\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q)$ has cardinality $2^\kappa$, as $|\operatorname{Gal}(\overline\Q/\Q)|\le
2^{\aleph_0}\le2^\kappa$; and the minimal primes correspond to generic points as in \cref{osq:hb:prop:minimal}.
\end{proof}

The product depends on the chosen algebraic closure and embedding; it separates two sources of branching, $\mathsf X$ recording normalization and henselian
choices and the Galois group recording arithmetic embeddings of the residue closure (27).

\paragraph{Gaussian omnific integers.} Put $B_{\mathbb E}[i]\subseteq\mathbb E[i]$, with constant term in $\Z[i]$ and kernel $\Pi_{\mathbb E}+i\Pi_{\mathbb E}$.

\begin{proposition}[Gaussian localization \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:gaussloc}
The localization of $B_{\mathbb E}[i]$ at $\Pi_{\mathbb E}+i\Pi_{\mathbb E}$ is $\mathfrak L[i]$, a local domain with residue field $\Q(i)$ and fraction field $\mathbb E[i]$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $b+ci$ has nonzero Gaussian constant term, $(b+ci)^{-1}=(b-ci)/(b^2+c^2)$ with $\ct(b)^2+\ct(c)^2\ne0$, already inverted in $\mathfrak L$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Henselization and doubling \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:thm:gaussian}
$(\mathfrak L[i])^{\mathrm h}\cong\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]$, and $\mathbb E[i]\otimes_{\mathfrak L[i]}\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]\cong\mathbb E[i]\otimes_{\mathbb E}\mathscr G\cong
\mathscr G\times\mathscr G$ as rings and $\mathbb E$-algebras; its spectrum is $\mathsf X\sqcup\mathsf X$, it has $2^\kappa$ generic points, and the completion of
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]$ is $\Q(i)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]$ is finite \'etale over $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$, local with residue field $\Q(i)$, henselian and ind-\'etale over $\mathfrak L[i]$ with the
same residue field, which gives the first identification. In the generic fibre $Z^2+1=(Z-\jmath)(Z+\jmath)$ with $2\jmath$ a unit, so $a+bZ\mapsto(a+b\jmath,a-b\jmath)$
is an isomorphism $\mathscr G[Z]/(Z^2+1)\to\mathscr G\times\mathscr G$ with inverse $(r,s)\mapsto\frac{r+s}2+\frac{r-s}{2\jmath}Z$; the external $i$ acts as
$(\jmath,-\jmath)$, so the factors carry conjugate scalar structures.
\end{proof}

The doubling decomposes the generic fibre; $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}[i]$ itself is local, and $\mathsf X\not\cong\mathsf X\sqcup\mathsf X$ is not asserted (27).

\paragraph{Projective modules, \'etale algebras and valuations.}

\begin{theorem}[Finite projectives on the generic fibre \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:thm:projectives}
Isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $\mathscr G$-modules correspond to locally constant $r:\mathsf X\to\N$ (pointwise rank); $\operatorname{Pic}\mathscr G=0$,
$K_0(\mathscr G)\cong\LC(\mathsf X,\Z)$ as rings, and constant rank $d$ means free of rank $d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An idempotent matrix over $\mathscr G$ is constant on the parts of a finite clopen partition, where it is an idempotent matrix over $\mathbb E[i]$ with image of some rank;
the local free identifications assemble along the central idempotents, and every locally constant rank function is realized by free summands on clopen pieces.
Direct sum and tensor product are addition and multiplication of ranks.
\end{proof}

This is a general consequence of the Boolean-power description, not special to surreal coefficients (27).

\begin{proposition}[Finite \'etale algebras \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:prop:etale}
Reduction gives an equivalence $\operatorname{Fin\acute Et}(\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h})\simeq\operatorname{Fin\acute Et}(\Q)$, the lift of a number field $L$ being
$\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}\otimes_\Q L$, with generic fibre $\mathscr G\otimes_\Q L\cong\mathscr G^{[L:\Q]}$; finite \'etale $\mathscr G$-algebras are classified up to
isomorphism by locally constant ranks $\mathsf X\to\N$, and constant rank $d$ means $\mathscr G^d$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first is the henselian finite \'etale equivalence \cite{StacksLocal} with \cref{osq:hb:prop:strict}. A finite \'etale $\mathscr G$-algebra descends to a finite stage
$\mathbb E[i]^r$ \cite{StacksEtale}, where it is a product of copies of the algebraically closed field on each factor; ranks at residue points determine it.
$\mathbb E[i]\otimes_\Q L$ is $[L:\Q]$ copies of $\mathbb E[i]$.
\end{proof}

The rank classification is of isomorphism classes, not of morphisms, and the equivalence for $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ says nothing about $B_{\mathbb E}$ or $\Oz$ (27). Let
$\operatorname{RZ}(\mathfrak L)$ be the valuation rings of $\mathbb E$ dominating $\mathfrak L$, with the Zariski topology of finite-subset containment.

\begin{corollary}[Centred valuation components \src{27}]\label{osq:hb:cor:rz}
$\operatorname{RZ}(\mathfrak L)$ has exactly $2^\kappa$ connected components.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
De Felipe and Teissier prove, for local domains without Noetherian hypotheses, that these components correspond to the minimal primes of the henselization
\cite[Corollary~4.2]{DFT}; apply \cref{osq:hb:prop:minimal,osq:hb:prop:exactsize}.
\end{proof}

The external theorem is imported; the count is the application, and nothing is said about the components themselves (singletons, openness, a fixed valuation
space) or about the quotient topology compared with $\mathsf X$ (27).

\begin{remark}[Branch counts compared \merge]\label{osq:hb:rem:counts}
Three maximal branch counts now appear in the report, for different rings. 20's full-class fibre $\mathsf B_\R$ has a proper class of idempotents
(\cref{osq:bb:thm:atoms}). 23's cyclic coefficient fibre has exactly $2^{\mathfrak c}$ maximal ideals over $T=0$ for the ring $\mathscr B$ of cardinality
$\mathfrak c=|K_{\Z a}|$ (\cref{osq:rm:cor:manyplaces}), and its Boolean algebras have cardinality $\mathfrak c$. 27's $\mathfrak L^{\mathrm h}$ has $2^\kappa$
minimal primes for a ring of cardinality $\kappa$, every $\kappa$ allowed; for $\kappa=\aleph_0$ a countable ring has continuum many minimal primes, which is no
paradox, $\mathscr G$ containing only finite-image locally constant functions (27). In all three the new idempotents come from quadratic branches at a scale
unseen by the given data; 23 needs no fresh scale (ramification at unused finite places), while 20 and 27 use 20's splitter at dominant scales. 27's local ring
$\mathfrak L$ is not a cyclic workspace: its exponent group contains the $\omega^\alpha$, $\alpha<\kappa$, and its fraction field is real closed.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Seeds and dependencies (27).} The seed may consist of infinite scales, infinitesimals or earlier surreal values, all placed in $\mathbb E$ with their
floors in $B_{\mathbb E}$ without exceeding $\kappa$; for surcomplex values seed the real and imaginary parts, and the Gaussian statements apply. This is seed
containment, not preservation of the algebraic or analytic operations of a prior workspace without further closure. The dependencies are: normal forms and
monomial bounds; monic certificates and support projection; the dominant-scale splitter and finite Boolean atoms; the actual hull and survival in the local
normalization; survival of every finite generic branch under localization; free generic idempotents and forced complexification; the Boolean power, exact
cardinality and minimal primes. Completion is a separate consequence of the idempotent ideal; the strict and Gaussian results depend on the generic fibre, and
the valuation corollary also on de Felipe--Teissier. 27 lists ten failure points it addresses: a convenient subring need not be the integer part (the floor
closure proves $B_{\mathbb E}=\mathbb E\cap\Oz$); a fixed Hahn group need not admit fresh bounds (the splitters are built in $\No$ first); projection is not a ring map;
a Laurent series cannot be evaluated at zero; the displayed identity does not prove nontriviality (arbitrary radical witnesses are excluded by certificates and
projection); localization may delete generic factors (\cref{osq:hb:lem:allbranches}); a local ring has no nontrivial idempotents; the generic imaginary unit is
not a residue-field extension; Noetherian finiteness theorems for branches do not apply; and finite tests are not transfinite verification.

\section{Arithmetic of polynomial maps on the omnific lattices}\label{osq:sec:polynomial}

This section is manuscript~10's arithmetic of finite-degree polynomial and rational maps on
the real lattice $\Oz\subset\No$ and the Gaussian lattice $\GOz\subset\SC$, followed by manuscript~16's
fresh-scale results for $D+\Pi_k$ with any unital constant ring $D$
(\cref{osq:fs:sub:gaps,osq:fs:sub:tests}) and by manuscript~18's ordinary-output rigidity
(\cref{osq:or:sub:outputs}), with manuscript~22's single-scale certificates at the end (\cref{osq:ft:sub:tests}). It uses from the
core only the universal theorem \cref{osq:thm:universal}, the quotient list
\cref{osq:thm:quotients} with the identity \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}, the constant-term lemma
\cref{osq:lem:ct}, the clearing of supports \cref{osq:prop:fractions}(i) and the unit lists of \cref{osq:lem:units}.

\paragraph{Renamings.} Manuscript~10's symbols are renamed as follows. Its ideals
$\mathfrak P$ and $\mathfrak P_\C$ are $\Pi$ and $\Pi_\C$; its constant-term map $\pi$ is
$\ct$; its projection $\Pi$ on polynomial rings (the \emph{shadow}) is $\ct_*$, the
coefficientwise constant term; its Gaussian lattice is $\GOz$ inside $\SC$; its ring
$R(D,K)$ is $\A_{D,K}$; its binomial polynomials $B_k(X)$ are written $\binom Xk$; its
$L_k=\lcm(1,\dots,k)$ is written $\lcm_k$; and its rings $S_r$ and $I_r$ are written
$\Num_r(\Oz)$ and $\Int(\Z^r)$ (the letter $I_r$ would collide with ideals). The numbered
results keep 10's content.

\paragraph{Notation.} Throughout, $r\ge1$ is an ordinary integer,
$\mathbf X=(X_1,\dots,X_r)$, and bold letters denote $r$-tuples. For an ordinary $k\ge0$,
\[
 \binom Xk=\frac{X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)}{k!},\qquad \binom X0=1,
\]
and for a multi-index $\mathbf k=(k_1,\dots,k_r)$ we put
$\binom{\mathbf X}{\mathbf k}=\prod_{j=1}^r\binom{X_j}{k_j}$. We write $\Delta_jF(\mathbf
X)=F(\mathbf X+\mathbf e_j)-F(\mathbf X)$, and $\Delta=\Delta_1$ when $r=1$. Put
$\lcm_0=1$ and $\lcm_k=\lcm(1,\dots,k)$ for $k\ge1$. Recall
$\A_{\Q,\R}=\Q+\Pi$ and $\A_{\Q(i),\C}=\Q(i)+\Pi_\C$; by \cref{osq:lem:ct} the constant
term $\ct$ is a ring homomorphism on both, with kernels $\Pi$ and $\Pi_\C$, so
$\Pi$ is an ideal of $\Q+\Pi$ and $\Pi_\C$ is an ideal of $\Q(i)+\Pi_\C$. Its
coefficientwise extension
\[
 \ct_*:(\Q+\Pi)[\mathbf X]\to\Q[\mathbf X],\qquad
 \ct_*:(\Q(i)+\Pi_\C)[\mathbf X]\to\Q(i)[\mathbf X]
\]
is therefore a ring homomorphism with kernel $\Pi[\mathbf X]$, respectively
$\Pi_\C[\mathbf X]$. Define
\begin{align*}
 \Num_r(\Oz)&=\{F\in\No[\mathbf X]:F(\Oz^r)\subseteq\Oz\},&
 \Int(\Z^r)&=\{f\in\Q[\mathbf X]:f(\Z^r)\subseteq\Z\},\\
 \Num_r(\GOz)&=\{F\in\SC[\mathbf X]:F(\GOz^r)\subseteq\GOz\},&
 \Int(\Z[i]^r)&=\{f\in\Q(i)[\mathbf X]:f(\Z[i]^r)\subseteq\Z[i]\}.
\end{align*}
These are rings under pointwise operations. All degrees, finite sums and factorials are
ordinary.

\subsection{Lattice separation and an omitted congruence type}\label{osq:pm:sub:lattice}

\begin{lemma}[Lattice separation and cofinality \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:lem:lattice}
For $\Lambda=\Oz$ and for $\Lambda=\GOz$, every nonzero $x\in\Lambda$ satisfies
$|x|\ge1$. The finite elements of $\Oz$ are exactly the ordinary integers. The positive
elements of $\Oz$ are cofinal in $\No$. The units are $\Oz^\times=\{\pm1\}$ and
$\GOz^\times=\{\pm1,\pm i\}$ \textup{(}\cref{osq:lem:units}\textup{)}.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero real purely infinite series has a positive leading exponent, so its absolute
value exceeds every positive real. Hence $n+u$ with $n\in\Z$ and $0\ne u\in\Pi$ is
infinite, the finite elements of $\Oz$ are the ordinary integers, and every nonzero
element of $\Oz$ has absolute value at least $1$. In the Gaussian case write
$x=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\Oz$, not both zero; the surcomplex modulus dominates either
coordinate, $|x|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\ge\max(|a|,|b|)\ge1$.

Given $y\in\No$, choose an exponent $g>0$ larger than the leading exponent of $y$ (any
$g>0$ if $y=0$). Then $\omega^g\in\Oz$ is positive and exceeds $n|y|$ for every ordinary
$n$, in particular $\omega^g>|y|$. This proves cofinality. The unit lists are
\cref{osq:lem:units}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Modulus and standard part \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:rem:modulus}
The surcomplex modulus needs only real closedness of $\No$: $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ for
$a,b\in\No$, and it is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality. The
standard part of a finite surcomplex number is taken coordinatewise in $\C$; on the
finite rings $\OO_\R$ and $\OO_\C$ it is the map $\st$ of \cref{osq:lem:ct}.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[A finitely satisfiable countable congruence type \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:prop:type}
Fix an ordinary prime $p$ and $\alpha\in\Z_p\setminus\Z$. For $e\ge1$ let $a_e$ be the
representative of $\alpha\bmod p^e$ in $\{0,\dots,p^e-1\}$. The countable family of ring
formulas
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:type}
 \exists y\ (x-a_e=p^e y),\qquad e=1,2,\dots,
\end{equation}
is finitely satisfiable in $\Z\subset\Oz$ but has no realization in $\Oz$. An explicit
choice is
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:lacunary}
 \alpha=\sum_{j\ge0}p^{2^j}\in\Z_p .
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a finite subfamily let $E$ be its largest index and take $x=a_E$. Since the residues
are compatible, $a_E\equiv a_e\pmod{p^e}$ for $e\le E$, which gives witnesses $y\in\Z$ for
every formula of the subfamily. If $x\in\Oz$ realized all formulas, applying the ring
homomorphism $\ct$ would give an ordinary integer $\ct(x)$ with
$\ct(x)\equiv a_e\equiv\alpha\pmod{p^e}$ for every $e$ (by \eqref{osq:eq:nOz},
$x-a_e\in p^e\Oz$ means $\ct(x)-a_e\in p^e\Z$). In $\Z_p$ this forces
$\ct(x)=\alpha$, contradicting $\alpha\notin\Z$.

For \eqref{osq:pm:eq:lacunary}: the powers $p^{2^j}$ are distinct, so the base-$p$ digits
of $\alpha$ are $1$ at the positions $2^j$ and $0$ elsewhere. They are not eventually
zero, so $\alpha$ is not a nonnegative integer; and they are not eventually $p-1$ (for
$p=2$ the positions $2^j+1<2^{j+1}$ with $j\ge1$ carry the digit $0$), so $\alpha$ is not a
negative integer.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Ring types, not saturation \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:rem:saturation}
This elementary omitted type concerns the ring structure. It shows that the
order-theoretic richness of the full surreal class does not give a corresponding
realization property for countable ring types. No use of the term ``saturated model'' for
a proper-class structure is needed, and none is made.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Polynomials preserving the omnific lattices}\label{osq:pm:sub:numerical}

\begin{lemma}[Omnific binomial closure \src{10; 22}]\label{osq:pm:lem:binomial}
For every $x\in\Oz$ and every ordinary $k\ge0$, $\binom xk\in\Oz$. More generally, if
$f\in\Q[\mathbf X]$ and $f(\Z^r)\subseteq\Z$, then $f(\Oz^r)\subseteq\Oz$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $x_j=n_j+u_j$ with $n_j\in\Z$ and $u_j\in\Pi$. Expanding each monomial of $f$ shows
that $f(\mathbf n+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf n)$ is a finite sum of terms, each a rational
multiple of a product of ordinary integers and of powers of the $u_j$ containing at least
one factor $u_j$. Since $\Pi$ is an ideal of $\Q+\Pi$, every such term lies in $\Pi$; thus
\[
 f(\mathbf n+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf n)\in\Pi .
\]
As $f(\mathbf n)\in\Z$, we get $f(\mathbf x)\in\Z+\Pi=\Oz$. The binomial case is the
case $f=\binom Xk$, which takes integer values at all ordinary integers, including
negative ones: $\binom{-n}{k}=(-1)^k\binom{n+k-1}{k}$.
\end{proof}

Thus $\Oz$ is a binomial ring in the usual torsion-free sense: it is $\Z$-torsion free and
closed under $x\mapsto\binom xk$ \cite{ElliottBinomial}. The terminology is classical; the
support argument above explains its application here without importing an abstract
free-ring theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-grid test \src{10; 16; 22}]\label{osq:pm:thm:grid}
Let $F\in\No[\mathbf X]$ with $\deg_{X_j}F\le d_j$ for $j=1,\dots,r$. The following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $F(\Oz^r)\subseteq\Oz$;
 \item $F(n_1,\dots,n_r)\in\Oz$ for all ordinary integers $0\le n_j\le d_j$;
 \item in the unique expansion
 \begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:newton}
  F(\mathbf X)=\sum_{\mathbf k\le\mathbf d}c_{\mathbf k}\binom{\mathbf X}{\mathbf k}
 \end{equation}
 all coefficients $c_{\mathbf k}$ belong to $\Oz$.
\end{enumerate}
Explicitly,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef}
 c_{\mathbf k}=(\Delta_1^{k_1}\cdots\Delta_r^{k_r}F)(\mathbf 0)
 =\sum_{\boldsymbol\ell\le\mathbf k}
   (-1)^{\sum_j(k_j-\ell_j)}
   \Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^r\binom{k_j}{\ell_j}\Bigr)F(\boldsymbol\ell).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The polynomials $\binom X0,\dots,\binom Xd$ form a basis of the univariate polynomials of
degree at most $d$ over the field $\No$: their degrees are $0,\dots,d$ and their leading
coefficients are nonzero. Taking products, the $\binom{\mathbf X}{\mathbf k}$ with
$\mathbf k\le\mathbf d$ form a basis of the polynomials with $\deg_{X_j}\le d_j$, which
gives existence and uniqueness of \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newton}. Since
$\Delta\binom Xm=\binom X{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$ and $\Delta\binom X0=0$, one has
$\Delta_j^{k_j}\binom{X_j}{m_j}=\binom{X_j}{m_j-k_j}$ for $m_j\ge k_j$ and $0$ otherwise;
as $\binom 0m=0$ for $m>0$, applying $\Delta_1^{k_1}\cdots\Delta_r^{k_r}$ to
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:newton} and evaluating at $\mathbf 0$ leaves exactly $c_{\mathbf k}$.
Writing $\Delta_j=\tau_j-1$ with the shift $\tau_j$ and expanding by the binomial theorem
gives the last expression in \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef}.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is restriction to ordinary grid points. Under (ii), the last
expression in \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef} is an integral linear combination of grid values
in $\Oz$, which proves (iii). Under (iii), each factor $\binom{x_j}{k_j}$ with $x_j\in\Oz$
lies in $\Oz$ by \cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial}, and evaluating \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newton}
proves (i).
\end{proof}

The test is finite for a given finite-degree polynomial, although the preservation
property quantifies over the entire class $\Oz^r$. It is a mathematical test with exact
surreal input; no claim is made that arbitrary surreal coefficients have an effective
finite encoding.

\begin{theorem}[The real numerical-polynomial ring \src{10; 16; 18; 22}]\label{osq:pm:thm:numreal}
Every $F\in\Num_r(\Oz)$ has a unique decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:decomp}
 F=U+f,\qquad U\in\Pi[\mathbf X],\quad f\in\Int(\Z^r),
\end{equation}
so that $\Num_r(\Oz)=\Pi[\mathbf X]\oplus\Int(\Z^r)$ additively. The coefficientwise
constant term $\ct_*(F)=f$ is a surjective ring homomorphism
$\Num_r(\Oz)\to\Int(\Z^r)$ with kernel $\Pi[\mathbf X]$, split by the inclusion
$\Int(\Z^r)\subseteq\Num_r(\Oz)$. For $\mathbf x\in\Oz^r$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:evshadow}
 \ct\bigl(F(\mathbf x)\bigr)=\ct_*(F)\bigl(\ct(x_1),\dots,\ct(x_r)\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $F\in\Num_r(\Oz)$. By \cref{osq:pm:thm:grid} its Newton coefficients $c_{\mathbf k}$
lie in $\Oz$; write $c_{\mathbf k}=m_{\mathbf k}+u_{\mathbf k}$ with $m_{\mathbf k}\in\Z$
and $u_{\mathbf k}\in\Pi$, and put
\[
 U=\sum_{\mathbf k}u_{\mathbf k}\binom{\mathbf X}{\mathbf k},\qquad
 f=\sum_{\mathbf k}m_{\mathbf k}\binom{\mathbf X}{\mathbf k}.
\]
The binomials have rational coefficients and $\Pi$ is a $\Q$-vector space, so
$U\in\Pi[\mathbf X]$; products of binomials are integer valued on $\Z^r$, so
$f\in\Int(\Z^r)$. Conversely, a polynomial in $\Pi[\mathbf X]$ takes values in $\Pi$ on
$\Oz^r$, because $\Pi$ is an ideal of $\Q+\Pi\supseteq\Oz$, and $\Int(\Z^r)\subseteq
\Num_r(\Oz)$ by \cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial}; hence $\Pi[\mathbf X]+\Int(\Z^r)
\subseteq\Num_r(\Oz)$. The sum is direct because a coefficient that is both rational and
purely infinite is zero.

By \eqref{osq:pm:eq:decomp} all coefficients of $F$ lie in $\Q+\Pi$, so $\Num_r(\Oz)$ is a
subring of $(\Q+\Pi)[\mathbf X]$ and $\ct_*$ restricts to a ring homomorphism on it. It
sends $U$ to $0$ and fixes $f$, so its restriction is the projection onto the second
summand; its kernel is $\Pi[\mathbf X]$ and the inclusion of $\Int(\Z^r)$ is a ring
section. Finally write $x_j=n_j+u_j$ with $n_j=\ct(x_j)$. Then $U(\mathbf x)\in\Pi$ and
$f(\mathbf x)-f(\mathbf n)\in\Pi$ by the proof of \cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial}, while
$f(\mathbf n)\in\Z$. Hence $\ct(F(\mathbf x))=f(\mathbf n)$, which is
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:evshadow}.
\end{proof}

The decomposition is an additive direct sum whose first summand is an ideal; it is
\emph{not} a direct product of rings.

\begin{example}[\src{10}]\label{osq:pm:ex:numreal}
The polynomial
\[
 F(X)=3\binom X2+\omega^{\sqrt2}X^3+\Bigl(\sum_{m\ge1}\omega^{1/m}\Bigr)(X-1)
\]
is omnific-integer valued and has shadow $\ct_*(F)=3\binom X2$. By contrast
$\omega^{-1}X$ fails already at $X=1$. No negative-exponent coefficient can be hidden in a
finite-degree lattice-preserving polynomial: by \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal} every
coefficient of an element of $\Num_r(\Oz)$ lies in $\Q+\Pi$.
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian numerical polynomials \src{10; 16; 18; 22}]\label{osq:pm:thm:numgaussian}
For every ordinary $r\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:gaussiandecomp}
 \Num_r(\GOz)=\Pi_\C[\mathbf X]\oplus\Int(\Z[i]^r)
\end{equation}
additively. The coefficientwise constant term $\ct_*$ is a surjective ring homomorphism
$\Num_r(\GOz)\to\Int(\Z[i]^r)$ with kernel $\Pi_\C[\mathbf X]$, split by inclusion, and
for $\mathbf x\in\GOz^r$, with $\ct:\GOz\to\Z[i]$ the Gaussian constant term,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:evshadowC}
 \ct\bigl(F(\mathbf x)\bigr)=\ct_*(F)\bigl(\ct(x_1),\dots,\ct(x_r)\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $F\in\Num_r(\GOz)$ with $\deg_{X_j}F\le d_j$. The Newton expansion
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:newton} and formula \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef} hold over the field
$\SC$ by the same basis argument. The ordinary grid points lie in $\GOz^r$, so
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef} shows $c_{\mathbf k}\in\GOz=\Z[i]+\Pi_\C$. Expanding the
binomials, each monomial coefficient of $F$ is a $\Q$-linear combination of the
$c_{\mathbf k}$, hence lies in $\Q(i)+\Pi_\C$. Put $f=\ct_*(F)\in\Q(i)[\mathbf X]$ and
$U=F-f\in\Pi_\C[\mathbf X]$. For an ordinary Gaussian tuple $\mathbf z\in\Z[i]^r$ we have
$U(\mathbf z)\in\Pi_\C$, because $\Pi_\C$ is an ideal of $\Q(i)+\Pi_\C$, and
$F(\mathbf z)=w+v$ with $w\in\Z[i]$, $v\in\Pi_\C$. Then $f(\mathbf z)-w=v-U(\mathbf z)$
lies in $\Q(i)\cap\Pi_\C=0$, so $f(\mathbf z)=w\in\Z[i]$. Thus $f\in\Int(\Z[i]^r)$.

Conversely write a Gaussian omnific input as $\mathbf z+\mathbf u$ with
$\mathbf z\in\Z[i]^r$ and $u_j\in\Pi_\C$. For $f\in\Int(\Z[i]^r)$ the expansion argument
of \cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial} gives $f(\mathbf z+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf z)\in\Pi_\C$, so
$f(\mathbf z+\mathbf u)\in\Z[i]+\Pi_\C=\GOz$; and a polynomial in $\Pi_\C[\mathbf X]$
takes values in $\Pi_\C$ on $\GOz^r$. This proves \eqref{osq:pm:eq:gaussiandecomp};
the sum is direct since $\Q(i)\cap\Pi_\C=0$. As in \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal},
$\Num_r(\GOz)$ is a subring of $(\Q(i)+\Pi_\C)[\mathbf X]$, on which $\ct_*$ is a ring
homomorphism; this gives multiplicativity, the kernel and the section. The same
computation, $\ct(F(\mathbf z+\mathbf u))=f(\mathbf z)$, proves
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:evshadowC}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the real Newton test cannot simply be copied \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:rem:gaussnewton}
The ordinary binomial polynomials need not be Gaussian-integer valued:
\[
 \binom i2=\frac{i(i-1)}2=\frac{-1-i}{2}\notin\Z[i].
\]
Consequently values on an ordinary integer grid do not by themselves certify
preservation of $\GOz$ (the grid values are necessary, not sufficient). The Gaussian
theorem retains the ordinary ring $\Int(\Z[i]^r)$ rather than imposing a false binomial
basis on it; the arithmetic of $\Int(\Z[i]^r)$ is not replaced by the simpler real
Newton basis.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Small-target reflection for numerical polynomials \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:thm:numreflection}
Every class ring homomorphism $\varphi$ from $\Num_r(\Oz)$ to a set-sized ring $A$
factors uniquely through
\[
 \ct_*:\Num_r(\Oz)\longrightarrow\Int(\Z^r).
\]
The analogous assertion holds for $\Num_r(\GOz)$ with universal image $\Int(\Z[i]^r)$.
Therefore the set-sized quotient presentations of either numerical-polynomial ring are
precisely the quotient presentations of its ordinary shadow pulled back along $\ct_*$:
their kernels are the class ideals $\ct_*^{-1}(\mathfrak a)$ for ideals $\mathfrak a$ of
$\Int(\Z^r)$, respectively $\Int(\Z[i]^r)$, with quotients $\Int(\Z^r)/\mathfrak a$,
respectively $\Int(\Z[i]^r)/\mathfrak a$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The restriction of $\varphi$ to the ideal $\Pi$ of constant polynomials is a (possibly
nonunital) class ring homomorphism $\Pi\to A$, hence zero by \cref{osq:thm:universal}.
Every element of $\Pi[\mathbf X]$ is a finite sum of products $u\,\mathbf X^{\mathbf m}$
with $u\in\Pi$ and $\mathbf X^{\mathbf m}\in\Num_r(\Oz)$, so
$\varphi(u\mathbf X^{\mathbf m})=\varphi(u)\varphi(\mathbf X^{\mathbf m})=0$ and $\varphi$
kills $\Pi[\mathbf X]=\ker\ct_*$ (\cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal}). Hence
$\varphi=\psi\circ\ct_*$ with $\psi$ the restriction of $\varphi$ to the section
$\Int(\Z^r)$; $\psi$ is unique because $\ct_*$ is surjective. The Gaussian case is
identical, with $\Pi_\C$ and \cref{osq:pm:thm:numgaussian}.

If $\varphi$ is surjective onto a set-sized ring with kernel $J$, then $\psi$ is surjective
and $J=\ct_*^{-1}(\ker\psi)$. Conversely, for an ideal $\mathfrak a$ of the shadow ring,
the composite of $\ct_*$ with the quotient map onto the set $\Int(\Z^r)/\mathfrak a$ is a
set-sized quotient presentation with kernel $\ct_*^{-1}(\mathfrak a)$. This is the
kernel argument of \cref{osq:thm:quotients}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Congruences modulo every omnific integer}\label{osq:pm:sub:congruence}

\begin{definition}[\src{10}]\label{osq:pm:def:cp}
A function $F:\Oz\to\Oz$ is \emph{congruence preserving} if $a-b$ divides $F(a)-F(b)$ in
$\Oz$ for all $a,b\in\Oz$; equivalently, for every $m\in\Oz$, $a\equiv b\pmod{m\Oz}$
implies $F(a)\equiv F(b)\pmod{m\Oz}$. We write $\CP(\Oz)$ for the congruence-preserving
elements of $\Num_1(\Oz)$ and $\CP(\Z)$ for the elements $f\in\Int(\Z)$ such that $a-b$
divides $f(a)-f(b)$ in $\Z$ for all $a,b\in\Z$.
\end{definition}

The two formulations agree: the forward implication is transitivity of divisibility, and
the reverse one takes $m=a-b$. When $a=b$ the condition reads $0\mid0$, which holds.
Differences and finite sums of congruence-preserving functions are congruence preserving.

\begin{lemma}[Integral divided differences of weighted binomials \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:lem:divdiff}
For every ordinary $k\ge1$, the identity
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:divdiff}
 \frac{\binom{X+T}{k}-\binom Xk}{T}
   =\sum_{j=1}^k\binom X{k-j}\,\frac1j\binom{T-1}{j-1}
\end{equation}
holds in $\Q[X,T]$. In particular $\lcm_k\binom Xk$ is congruence preserving on $\Oz$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Vandermonde's identity gives $\binom{X+T}k=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom X{k-j}\binom Tj$. For
$j\ge1$ the falling-factorial formula gives $\binom Tj=\frac Tj\binom{T-1}{j-1}$.
Subtracting the term $j=0$ and cancelling the polynomial factor $T$ gives
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:divdiff}.

After multiplication by $\lcm_k$, every scalar $\lcm_k/j$ with $1\le j\le k$ is an
ordinary integer, so by \cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial} the right side evaluates into $\Oz$ for
all $X,T\in\Oz$. Taking $X=b$ and $T=a-b$ gives
$\lcm_k\binom ak-\lcm_k\binom bk=(a-b)w$ with $w\in\Oz$, including for nonzero infinite
$a-b$; the case $a=b$ is trivial.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All-modulus Newton criterion \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:thm:cp}
Let $F\in\Num_1(\Oz)$ have Newton expansion $F=\sum_{k=0}^dc_k\binom Xk$, $c_k\in\Oz$.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $F$ is congruence preserving on $\Oz$;
 \item $c_k\in\lcm_k\Oz$ for every $0\le k\le d$;
 \item $\ct(c_k)\in\lcm_k\Z$ for every $0\le k\le d$;
 \item the ordinary numerical polynomial $\ct_*(F)$ is congruence preserving on $\Z$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, within the respective numerical-polynomial rings,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:CPdecomp}
 \CP(\Oz)=\Pi[X]\oplus\CP(\Z).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i). Write $c_k=\lcm_kd_k$ with $d_k\in\Oz$. Each summand
$d_k\lcm_k\binom Xk$ is congruence preserving by \cref{osq:pm:lem:divdiff} (multiply the
divisibility by $d_k$), and a finite sum of congruence-preserving functions is congruence
preserving.

(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii). We show $c_k\in\lcm_k\Oz$ by induction on $k$. For $k=0$ it is
automatic since $\lcm_0=1$. Suppose it holds for all $j<k$. Then
$\sum_{j<k}c_j\binom Xj$ is congruence preserving by the previous paragraph, so
\[
 G(X)=F(X)-\sum_{j<k}c_j\binom Xj=\sum_{j\ge k}c_j\binom Xj
\]
is congruence preserving. Since $\binom nj=0$ for ordinary $0\le n<j$ and
$\binom kk=1$, we get $G(0)=\dots=G(k-1)=0$ and $G(k)=c_k$. For each $1\le m\le k$,
comparing the inputs $k$ and $k-m$ gives $m\mid G(k)-G(k-m)=c_k$ in $\Oz$. By
\eqref{osq:eq:nOz}, the ordinary integer $\ct(c_k)$ is divisible by every $m\le k$, hence
by $\lcm_k$, and again by \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}, $c_k\in\lcm_k\Oz$.

(ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii) is \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}. For (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv), note
that $\ct_*(F)=\sum_k\ct(c_k)\binom Xk$ is the Newton expansion of $\ct_*(F)$, since the
binomials have rational coefficients. The same two arguments over $\Z$ (the identity
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:divdiff} with $X,T\in\Z$, and the same induction with divisibility in
$\Z$) show that an $f\in\Int(\Z)$ with Newton coefficients $m_k\in\Z$ is congruence
preserving on $\Z$ if and only if $m_k\in\lcm_k\Z$ for all $k$. Applied to $m_k=\ct(c_k)$,
this is (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv).

For \eqref{osq:pm:eq:CPdecomp}, decompose $F=U+f$ by \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal}. The Newton
coefficients of $U\in\Pi[X]$ are integral combinations of values $U(\ell)\in\Pi$, and
$\Pi\subseteq\lcm_k\Oz$ by \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}; so $U\in\CP(\Oz)$ by (ii). An
$f\in\Int(\Z)$ lies in $\CP(\Oz)$ exactly when it lies in $\CP(\Z)$, by
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv) applied to $f=\ct_*(f)$. Since $\ct_*(F)=f$, the equivalence
(i)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv) for $F$ now gives $F\in\CP(\Oz)$ if and only if $f\in\CP(\Z)$.
\end{proof}

The divisibility condition in (i) includes infinite differences and therefore every
infinite omnific modulus; no extra coefficient condition appears at those moduli. The
ordinary least-common-multiple pattern is classical, and related finite-ring formulations
are proved in \cite{CGG}; Newton bases and integer-valued polynomials are treated in
\cite{CC}. The content specific to the present domain is that the pattern suffices for
differences at every surreal scale, not only for congruences modulo ordinary integers.

\begin{example}[Two kinds of denominators \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:ex:cp}
The polynomial $12\binom X4$ is congruence preserving ($\lcm_4=12$), although its leading
coefficient $1/2$ is not an ordinary integer. On the other hand
\[
 F(X)=\binom X2+\omega^{\sqrt2}X^3
\]
is integer valued on all of $\Oz$ but not congruence preserving:
$F(2)-F(0)=1+8\omega^{\sqrt2}$ has odd constant term and so is not divisible by $2$ in
$\Oz$, by \eqref{osq:eq:nOz}. The purely infinite term does not repair the odd constant
term.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What \cref{osq:pm:thm:cp} does not say \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:rem:cpnot}
The theorem does not say that reduction modulo an infinite omnific integer is an ordinary
finite congruence; such a quotient need not have any set-sized presentation (by
\cref{osq:thm:quotients} it has one only when it contains $\Pi$). It says that the
polynomial \emph{operation} respects those congruences, with an explicit quotient
supplied by \eqref{osq:pm:eq:divdiff}. It also does not classify all congruence-preserving
class functions $\Oz\to\Oz$: the finite Newton expansion is essential to the statement and
the proof, and no infinite interpolation formula or full-class summation is implicit.
\end{remark}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{$p$}{p}-adic characters and completions}\label{osq:pm:sub:padic}

In this subsection $p$ is an ordinary prime, $e\ge1$ and $r\ge1$ are ordinary integers,
and $C(\Z_p^r,M)$ denotes the continuous functions from $\Z_p^r$ with its $p$-adic
topology to $M$ ($M=\Z/p^e\Z$ or $\F_p$ discrete, or $M=\Z_p$). All $p$-adic fields,
rings and function spaces here are ordinary set-sized structures.

\begin{lemma}[Continuous extension \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:lem:padicext}
Every $f\in\Int(\Z^r)$ extends, by its rational-coefficient formula, to a continuous
function $\Z_p^r\to\Z_p$, and this continuous extension is unique.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A rational polynomial defines a continuous function $\Q_p^r\to\Q_p$. Ordinary integer
tuples are dense in $\Z_p^r$ and take values in $\Z\subseteq\Z_p$; since $\Z_p$ is closed
in $\Q_p$, all values on $\Z_p^r$ lie in $\Z_p$. Density also gives uniqueness.
\end{proof}

Reduction of values modulo $p^e$ is therefore a ring homomorphism
$\Int(\Z^r)\to C(\Z_p^r,\Z/p^e\Z)$. Its surjectivity needs an approximation argument; we
prove it explicitly by indicator polynomials rather than assume it, so no unproved
approximation assertion is used. For $0\le a<p^k$ write $a=a_0+a_1p+\dots+a_{k-1}p^{k-1}$
with digits $0\le a_j<p$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:indicator}
 E_{a,k}(X)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\Bigl[1-\Bigl(\binom X{p^j}-a_j\Bigr)^{p-1}\Bigr]
 \in\Int(\Z),
 \qquad
 I_{a,k,e}(X)=E_{a,k}(X)^{p^{e-1}}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Digit and indicator congruences \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:lem:indicator}
For every $x\in\Z_p$, with $\mathbf 1_{a,k}(x)=1$ if $x\equiv a\pmod{p^k}$ and
$\mathbf 1_{a,k}(x)=0$ otherwise,
\[
 E_{a,k}(x)\equiv\mathbf 1_{a,k}(x)\pmod p,
 \qquad
 I_{a,k,e}(x)\equiv\mathbf 1_{a,k}(x)\pmod{p^e}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First let $x$ be a nonnegative ordinary integer with base-$p$ digits $x_j$. In
$\F_p[T]$ the Frobenius identity gives
\[
 (1+T)^x=\prod_{j\ge0}(1+T)^{x_jp^j}=\prod_{j\ge0}\bigl(1+T^{p^j}\bigr)^{x_j}.
\]
The coefficient of $T^{p^j}$ on the right is $x_j$: the factors of index below $j$ have
combined degree at most $\sum_{i<j}(p-1)p^i=p^j-1$, and factors of index above $j$
contribute only exponents $0$ or at least $p^{j+1}$. Hence $\binom x{p^j}\equiv
x_j\pmod p$. Both sides are continuous functions $\Z_p\to\F_p$ of $x$
(\cref{osq:pm:lem:padicext}; the $j$th digit depends only on $x\bmod p^{j+1}$), and the
nonnegative integers are dense in $\Z_p$, so the congruence holds for all $x\in\Z_p$ with
$x_j$ the $j$th $p$-adic digit. By Fermat, $t^{p-1}=1$ for $0\ne t\in\F_p$, so the $j$th
factor of $E_{a,k}(x)$ is $\equiv1$ if $x_j=a_j$ and $\equiv0$ otherwise. The product is
the indicator of $x_j=a_j$ for all $j<k$, that is, of $x\equiv a\pmod{p^k}$.

For the lift, let $z\in\Z_p$. If $z\equiv0\pmod p$ then $z^{p^{e-1}}\equiv0\pmod{p^e}$,
because $p^{e-1}\ge e$. If $z=1+pw$, then $(1+pw)^{p^{e-1}}\equiv1\pmod{p^e}$ by
induction from $(1+p^sv)^p\equiv1\pmod{p^{s+1}}$ for $s\ge1$: in
$(1+p^sv)^p=1+p^{s+1}v+\sum_{i=2}^{p}\binom pi p^{si}v^i$ the middle binomial coefficients
are divisible by $p$ and $sp\ge s+1$; this is also valid for $p=2$. Applying these two
cases to $z=E_{a,k}(x)$ gives the second congruence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-level function rings \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:thm:finitelevel}
The coefficientwise constant term and $p$-adic evaluation induce natural ring
isomorphisms
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:finitelevel}
 \Num_r(\Oz)/p^e\Num_r(\Oz)\ \simeq\ \Int(\Z^r)/p^e\Int(\Z^r)
 \ \simeq\ C(\Z_p^r,\Z/p^e\Z).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal}, $\Num_r(\Oz)=\Pi[\mathbf X]\oplus\Int(\Z^r)$ additively,
and $p^e\Pi[\mathbf X]=\Pi[\mathbf X]$ because $\Pi$ is a $\Q$-vector space. Hence
$p^e\Num_r(\Oz)=\Pi[\mathbf X]\oplus p^e\Int(\Z^r)$, and the ring homomorphism $\ct_*$
induces the first isomorphism.

For the second, the map sends $f$ to $x\mapsto f(x)\bmod p^e$
(\cref{osq:pm:lem:padicext}). If $f=p^eg$ with $g\in\Int(\Z^r)$, its reduction is zero.
Conversely, if $f$ vanishes modulo $p^e$ at every $p$-adic tuple, its values at ordinary
integer tuples are divisible by $p^e$, so $f/p^e\in\Int(\Z^r)$. The kernel is exactly
$p^e\Int(\Z^r)$.

Let $g\in C(\Z_p^r,\Z/p^e\Z)$. The target is discrete, so every point has a residue box
$\mathbf y+p^{k}\Z_p^r$ on which $g$ is constant; by compactness of $\Z_p^r$ finitely many
of these boxes cover it. Let $k$ be the largest of their levels. Every level-$k$ box
$\mathbf y+p^k\Z_p^r$ lies in the covering box that contains $\mathbf y$, so $g$ is
constant on every residue box modulo $p^k$. For
$\mathbf a\in\{0,\dots,p^k-1\}^r$ choose an ordinary integer $c_{\mathbf a}$ lifting the
value of $g$ on the box of $\mathbf a$, and put
\[
 f(\mathbf X)=\sum_{\mathbf a}c_{\mathbf a}\prod_{j=1}^rI_{a_j,k,e}(X_j)\in\Int(\Z^r).
\]
By \cref{osq:pm:lem:indicator}, at $\mathbf x$ in the box of $\mathbf a$ the product
indexed by $\mathbf a$ is $\equiv1$ and all others are $\equiv0$ modulo $p^e$, so
$f(\mathbf x)\equiv g(\mathbf x)\pmod{p^e}$. This proves surjectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The $p$-adic completion \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:cor:completion}
There is a canonical isomorphism of topological rings
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:completion}
 \varprojlim_{e\ge1}\Num_r(\Oz)/p^e\Num_r(\Oz)\ \simeq\ C(\Z_p^r,\Z_p),
\end{equation}
where the left side carries the inverse-limit topology of the discrete quotients and the
right side the uniform $p$-adic topology. The canonical map
$\Num_r(\Oz)\to C(\Z_p^r,\Z_p)$ sends $F$ to the continuous extension of $\ct_*(F)$, has
dense image, and has kernel $\Pi[\mathbf X]$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The isomorphisms of \cref{osq:pm:thm:finitelevel} commute with reduction of values from
level $e+1$ to level $e$. A coherent sequence of functions $g_e:\Z_p^r\to\Z/p^e\Z$
determines a unique function $g:\Z_p^r\to\Z_p$ pointwise, and $g$ is continuous exactly
when every $g_e=g\bmod p^e$ is continuous, since the sets $y+p^e\Z_p$ form a base of the
topology of $\Z_p$. This identifies the inverse limit with $C(\Z_p^r,\Z_p)$ as rings.
The kernel of the projection to level $e$ corresponds to the functions that vanish modulo
$p^e$ everywhere, which are the basic neighbourhoods of $0$ in the uniform $p$-adic
topology; so the topologies agree. Surjectivity at every finite level gives density of
the image.

If the continuous extension of $f\in\Int(\Z^r)$ is zero, then $f$ vanishes on $\Z^r$, and
a rational polynomial vanishing on $\Z^r$ is zero (write it as a polynomial in $X_r$ with
coefficients in $\Q[X_1,\dots,X_{r-1}]$; for each ordinary tuple
$(n_1,\dots,n_{r-1})$ the resulting univariate polynomial has infinitely many roots, so
all coefficients vanish on $\Z^{r-1}$; induct on $r$). With \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal} the
kernel on $\Num_r(\Oz)$ is exactly $\Pi[\mathbf X]$. Equivalently
$\bigcap_ep^e\Int(\Z^r)=0$, because an ordinary integer divisible by every $p^e$ is
zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Not a profinite ring completion \src{10}]\label{osq:pm:rem:notprofinite}
For $r\ge1$ the characteristic functions of residue boxes at increasing depths are
infinitely many distinct elements of $C(\Z_p^r,\F_p)$. Therefore
$\Num_r(\Oz)/p\Num_r(\Oz)$ is infinite (and discrete in its quotient topology), as are all
the rings in \eqref{osq:pm:eq:finitelevel}. The completion \eqref{osq:pm:eq:completion} is
a $p$-adic completion, not an inverse limit of finite rings. This differs from the
genuine profinite completion of $\Oz$: its finite quotient presentations are the rings
$\Z/n\Z$ with kernels $n\Oz$ (\cref{osq:thm:quotients}), so
$\varprojlim_n\Oz/n\Oz\simeq\widehat\Z$.
\end{remark}

The ordinary polynomial-approximation content is part of the classical theory of
integer-valued polynomials \cite{CC}. The explicit proof above also identifies exactly
which omnific coefficients disappear, rather than only invoking density for the ordinary
subring. The compactness of $\Z_p^r$ used here is ordinary $p$-adic compactness, not
compactness of an omnific interval.

\begin{theorem}[$p$-adic classification of characters \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:thm:characters}
Every unital class ring homomorphism $\chi:\Num_r(\Oz)\to\F_p$ has the form
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:character}
 \chi_{\boldsymbol\alpha}(F)=\ct_*(F)(\boldsymbol\alpha)\bmod p
\end{equation}
for a unique $\boldsymbol\alpha\in\Z_p^r$, and every $\boldsymbol\alpha\in\Z_p^r$ defines
such a character. The prime ideals of $\Num_r(\Oz)$ containing $p\Num_r(\Oz)$ are exactly
the kernels $\ker\chi_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$, with distinct $\boldsymbol\alpha$ giving
distinct kernels; every such prime ideal is maximal with quotient $\F_p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The map $\chi_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ is a composite of ring homomorphisms
(\cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal,osq:pm:lem:padicext}), so it is a character. Conversely, a
unital $\chi$ kills $p\Num_r(\Oz)$, so by \cref{osq:pm:thm:finitelevel} with $e=1$ it is
$\psi\circ\rho$, where $\rho(F)=\ct_*(F)\bmod p$ and $\psi:C(\Z_p^r,\F_p)\to\F_p$ is a
unital ring homomorphism. At level $k$, the indicators of the $p^{kr}$ residue boxes modulo
$p^k$ are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with sum $1$. Their images are idempotents of
$\F_p$, hence $0$ or $1$, pairwise orthogonal with sum $1$, so exactly one box of level
$k$ is selected. A box indicator is the sum of the indicators of its children at level
$k+1$, and a child indicator $c$ satisfies $c=c\cdot b$ for its parent $b$; so the
selected boxes are nested. They are nonempty compact sets with diameters tending to $0$,
so by completeness of $\Z_p^r$ they have exactly one common point $\boldsymbol\alpha$.
Every $h\in C(\Z_p^r,\F_p)$ is constant on the residue boxes of some level $k$
(as in the proof of \cref{osq:pm:thm:finitelevel}), so $h$ is an $\F_p$-linear
combination of box indicators and $\psi(h)$ is the value of $h$ on the selected box, that
is, $h(\boldsymbol\alpha)$. Hence $\chi=\chi_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$. Distinct points are
separated by a residue-box indicator, which is $\rho(F)$ for some $F$ by surjectivity; so
$\boldsymbol\alpha$ is unique.

The prime ideals of $\Num_r(\Oz)$ containing $p\Num_r(\Oz)$ correspond, through the
explicit set-sized presentation $\rho$, to the prime ideals of $C(\Z_p^r,\F_p)$. Every
element $z$ of this ring satisfies $z^p=z$ pointwise. The quotient by a prime ideal is a
commutative domain in which every element is a root of $X^p-X$; such a domain has at most
$p$ elements, and it contains the $p$ distinct images of the constants, so it is $\F_p$.
Thus every such prime is maximal with quotient $\F_p$, and the quotient map is a character,
hence some $\chi_{\boldsymbol\alpha}$. A unital surjection onto $\F_p$ is determined by its
kernel, because $\F_p$ has only the identity automorphism; with the uniqueness of
$\boldsymbol\alpha$ this shows that distinct parameters give distinct kernels.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Most characters are not omnific evaluations \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:cor:nonevaluation}
A character $\Num_r(\Oz)\to\F_p$ obtained by evaluating at a tuple $\mathbf x\in\Oz^r$
and then applying a unital ring homomorphism $\Oz\to\F_p$ has parameter
$\boldsymbol\alpha=(\ct(x_1),\dots,\ct(x_r))\in\Z^r\subset\Z_p^r$. Conversely every
parameter in $\Z^r$ arises in this way. Parameters in $\Z_p^r\setminus\Z^r$ give
characters that are not evaluation at any omnific tuple.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:thm:universal} the unital homomorphism $\Oz\to\F_p$ is uniquely $\ct$
followed by reduction modulo $p$. By \eqref{osq:pm:eq:evshadow}, its composite with
evaluation at $\mathbf x$ is $F\mapsto\ct_*(F)(\ct(\mathbf x))\bmod p$, the character with
parameter $\ct(\mathbf x)$. An ordinary integer tuple is itself an allowed input, which
gives the converse. The last assertion follows from the uniqueness of the parameter in
\cref{osq:pm:thm:characters}.
\end{proof}

For $r=1$ the lacunary $p$-adic integer \eqref{osq:pm:eq:lacunary} of the omitted type in
\cref{osq:pm:prop:type} gives a concrete nonevaluation character. There are uncountably
many parameters and only countably many integer ones. The enormous class of omnific inputs
does not enlarge the evaluation parameters beyond the ordinary integers, because the
constant term of every omnific input is an ordinary integer.

\subsection{Rational self-maps and gaps at arbitrary surreal scales}
\label{osq:pm:sub:rigidity}

Throughout this subsection $(E,\Lambda)$ is one of the pairs $(\No,\Oz)$ or $(\SC,\GOz)$;
in the second the absolute value is the surreal-valued modulus. The input and output
lattices are the full classes, not a fixed set-sized truncation. We write $\Num_1(\Lambda)$
for $\Num_1(\Oz)$, respectively $\Num_1(\GOz)$, and $E(X)$ for the rational functions in
one variable over the class field $E$. We use repeatedly the following estimate, valid in
$E$ by the properties of the modulus: if $Q(X)=\sum_{j\le n}q_jX^j\in E[X]$ has
$q_n\ne0$ and $|y|\ge R_Q:=1+2\sum_{j<n}|q_j/q_n|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:polyest}
 \tfrac12|q_n||y|^n\le|Q(y)|\le\tfrac32|q_n||y|^n,
\end{equation}
because $|\sum_{j<n}q_jy^j|\le\sum_{j<n}|q_j||y|^{n-1}\le\frac12|q_n||y|^n$.

\begin{lemma}[Finite differences of a proper rational function \src{10}]
\label{osq:pm:lem:rationaldiff}
Let $r\in E(X)$ be nonzero and proper, and let $\Delta r(X)=r(X+1)-r(X)$. For every
ordinary $k\ge0$, $\Delta^kr$ is nonzero and proper. If the leading Laurent term of $r$ at
infinity is $cX^{-m}$ with $m\ge1$, then the leading term of $\Delta^kr$ is
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:rationalleading}
 (-1)^kc\,m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1)X^{-m-k},
\end{equation}
the empty product for $k=0$ being $1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Compute in the field of formal Laurent series in $X^{-1}$ over a set-sized subfield of $E$
containing the finitely many coefficients involved; the rational functions over that
subfield embed in it, a rational function is proper exactly when its expansion has only
negative exponents, and the shift $X\mapsto X+1$ becomes the substitution
$X^{-1}\mapsto X^{-1}(1+X^{-1})^{-1}$. The binomial series gives
\[
 (X+1)^{-n}-X^{-n}=X^{-n}\bigl((1+X^{-1})^{-n}-1\bigr)
 =-nX^{-n-1}+\text{terms of lower degree in }X .
\]
Since $r=cX^{-m}+(\text{terms }X^{-n},\ n>m)$, and $\Delta$ sends each such lower term to
terms of degree at most $-n-1<-m-1$, the leading term of $\Delta r$ is $-cmX^{-m-1}$.
Induction on $k$ gives \eqref{osq:pm:eq:rationalleading}. The coefficient is nonzero in
characteristic zero and the exponent is negative, which proves both assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomiality of rational lattice self-maps \src{10; 16; 18}]
\label{osq:pm:thm:rational}
Let $f\in E(X)$ satisfy $f(x)\in\Lambda$ for every $x\in\Lambda$ at which $f$ is defined.
Then $f\in E[X]$. In particular its reduced rational presentation has no finite poles
anywhere in $E$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Divide the numerator by the denominator to write $f=P+r$ with $P\in E[X]$ and $r$ proper,
and suppose $r\ne0$. Choose an ordinary $k\ge1$ larger than $\deg P$ (any $k\ge1$ if
$P=0$). Then $\Delta^kP=0$, so $g:=\Delta^kf=\Delta^kr$ is nonzero and proper by
\cref{osq:pm:lem:rationaldiff}. Write $f$ and $g$ in reduced form, $f=N_f/D_f$ and
$g=N_g/D_g$, with $\deg N_g<\deg D_g$.

We find $B\in\No$ such that for every $x\in\No$ with $x>B$ all of $f(x),\dots,f(x+k)$ are
defined, $g(x)$ is defined, and
\begin{equation}\label{osq:pm:eq:smallrational}
 0<|g(x)|<1 .
\end{equation}
By \eqref{osq:pm:eq:polyest}, $D_f(y)\ne0$ for $|y|\ge R_{D_f}$, $N_g(y)\ne0$ for
$|y|\ge R_{N_g}$, and for $|y|\ge\max(1,R_{N_g},R_{D_g})$,
\[
 |g(y)|\le\frac{\frac32|\ell(N_g)||y|^{\deg N_g}}{\frac12|\ell(D_g)||y|^{\deg D_g}}
 \le3\,\frac{|\ell(N_g)|}{|\ell(D_g)|}\,|y|^{-1},
\]
where $\ell(\cdot)$ is the leading coefficient. Take $B$ larger than $1$, than
$R_{D_f},R_{N_g},R_{D_g}$ and than $3|\ell(N_g)/\ell(D_g)|$; for real $x>B$ the points
$x,\dots,x+k$ are real and larger than $B$, so every requirement holds. These are finitely
many inequalities in the ordered field $\No$.

By \cref{osq:pm:lem:lattice} choose $x\in\Oz$ with $x>B$. Then $x+j\in\Oz\subseteq\Lambda$
for $0\le j\le k$, $f$ is defined at these points, and
\[
 g(x)=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{k-j}\binom kjf(x+j)\in\Lambda .
\]
This contradicts \eqref{osq:pm:eq:smallrational} and the lattice separation of
\cref{osq:pm:lem:lattice}. Therefore $r=0$ and $f=P$.
\end{proof}

The finite-difference argument is a general discrete-lattice method. It is included as a
supporting result, not asserted to be a new ordinary theorem about rational functions on
$\Z$. 16 proves the theorem for every unital constant ring with one fresh input
(\cref{osq:fs:thm:collapse}); the two routes are kept.

Recall that $y\in E$ is finite if $|y|$ is bounded by an ordinary integer and
infinitesimal if $|y|<1/n$ for every ordinary $n\ge1$; the standard part of a finite
