fresh monomial in every coordinate; 22's points use one fresh exponent, in one coordinate, with ordinary integers elsewhere, and a failed test comes with
an explicit specialization $\mathbf a$ at which the one-variable restriction has a negative block. Both are sizes of explicit certificates; neither is
claimed minimal.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Common tests for a set of functions \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:cor:common}
Every set-sized family of rational functions in $m$ variables over $\No$ has one countable set of points testing preservation of $\Oz$ for all its
members, and one finite set of the form $\mathsf{Test}_{m,d}(t)$ if the coordinate degrees of the reduced presentations are bounded by $d$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Put all coefficient supports of the family into one set-sized $G$ (\cref{osq:fs:lem:fresh}) and take $t=\omega^b$ with $b>G$. In the bounded case
apply \cref{osq:ft:thm:certificate}; in general the countable set
$\Z^m\cup\bigcup_{j=1}^m\Z^{j-1}\times\{t\}\times\Z^{m-j}$ contains every grid needed for every member.
\end{proof}

So \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall} is sharp with respect to the quantification over coefficients: every set of functions has common tests, and the class of
all functions has no set of common tests (22). For bounded degree over one workspace $K_G$ this is also the uniformity of
\cref{osq:fs:cor:certificates}.

\begin{remark}[A second witness for \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall} \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:rem:deceiver}
Let $S\subseteq\Lambda$ be a set, $G$ a set-sized group containing the supports of its elements, $b>G$ and $t=\omega^b$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:ft:eq:deceiver}
 \widetilde R_S(X)=\frac{\omega^{\omega b}}{X+t+\frac12}=\frac{2\omega^{\omega b}}{2X+2t+1},
\end{equation}
where $\omega b$ is a product in $\No$ and $\omega^{\omega b}$ a monomial. Numerator and denominator have coefficients in $\Oz$ and are coprime, and the
only pole $-t-\frac12$ has constant coefficient $-\frac12\notin D$, so it is not in $\Lambda$. For $s\in S$, $u=(s+\frac12)/t$ is infinitesimal (its
exponents are $g-b<0$), and $\widetilde R_S(s)=\omega^{\omega b}t^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}(-u)^n$ has its $n$th summand supported in $\omega b-(n+1)b+G$, whose
elements exceed $(\omega-n-2)b>0$; the blocks are ordered as in \cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding}, so $\widetilde R_S(s)\in\Pi_k$. For $a>0$ above the group
generated by $G$, $b$ and $\omega b$, and $x=\omega^a\in\Oz$, the value $\widetilde R_S(x)$ is nonzero with all exponents at most $\omega b-a<0$, so it
is not in $\Lambda$. For $S\subseteq\Lambda^m$ apply this to the first coordinates and let the function depend on $X_1$ only; so
\cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall} holds in every number of variables and for $\GOz$, still with numerator degree $0$, denominator degree $1$, coefficients in $\Oz$
and no pole on $\Lambda^m$. 16's $R_S=\omega^\beta/(X-\frac12)=2\omega^\beta/(2X-1)$ also has coefficients in $\Oz$; its pole is at $\frac12$, 22's at
the fresh scale. The failure of either witness is not caused by a high degree or by a pole at an untested input, but by coefficients at scales above the
prescribed inputs (22).
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Every ordinary integer passes \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:ex:integers}
$F(X)=\omega^\omega/(X+\omega+\frac12)=2\omega^\omega/(2X+2\omega+1)$ is defined on $\Oz$, and for $n\in\Z$,
$F(n)=\sum_{r\ge0}(-n-\frac12)^r\omega^{\omega-r-1}\in\Pi$; but $F(\omega^{\omega^2})$ has leading exponent $\omega-\omega^2<0$. The ordinary integers,
an exact test set for polynomials, miss this obstruction, and $\omega^{\omega^2}$ is the remote test for the group generated by $1$ and $\omega$. 16's
$\omega/(X-\frac12)$ (after \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall}) is an example of the same kind.
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[Removal of set-sized exceptions in several variables \src{22}; 16 for $m=1$]\label{osq:ft:thm:exceptions}
Let $F\in E(X_1,\dots,X_m)$ be defined and $\Lambda$-valued at every point of $\Lambda^m$ outside a set $S\subseteq\Lambda^m$. Then $F$ preserves
$\Lambda$. Equivalently, the class of points of $\Lambda^m$ at which $F$ is undefined or not $\Lambda$-valued is empty or a proper class.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $F=P/Q\ne0$ in lowest terms. If $Q$ is not constant, choose $j$ and ordinary integers $\mathbf a$ with $\mathsf h_j(\mathbf a)\ne0$
(\cref{osq:ft:lem:grid,osq:ft:lem:resultant}; only characteristic $0$ is used, so this works over $\SC$). Put the supports of the coefficients and of all
coordinates of all points of $S$ into one set-sized $G$ and take $b>G$, $t=\omega^b$. The point with $j$th coordinate $t$ and other coordinates
$\mathbf a$ is not in $S$, because the exponent $b$ lies outside $G$, and there $F$ is defined with a value outside $\A_{k,k}\supseteq\Lambda$
(\cref{osq:fs:thm:onepoint}), a contradiction. So $F$ is a polynomial. If $F(\mathbf a)\notin\Lambda$ for some $\mathbf a\in\Lambda^m$, write
$F(a_1+X,a_2,\dots,a_m)=F(\mathbf a)+\sum_{n=1}^ec_nX^n$ and enlarge $G$ by the supports of the coefficients of $F$, of $\mathbf a$ and of the points
of $S$. For fresh $t$ the value at $X=t$ differs from $F(\mathbf a)$ by an element of $\Pi_k$ (\cref{osq:fs:cor:blocktest}), which cannot move a
nonmember of the additive group $\Lambda$ into it, and $(a_1+t,a_2,\dots,a_m)\notin S$, since its first coordinate has the new leading exponent $b$.
\end{proof}

\Cref{osq:ft:thm:exceptions} and \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall} are compatible for the reason given after \cref{osq:fs:thm:cosmall}: one prescribes good
values on a set, the other assumes good values off a set. The two steps of the proof use different mechanisms (22). A denominator is detected by a
negative Laurent block at a new scale. A polynomial failure is propagated by adding a positive-support block, which cannot alter an old negative tail or
an old nonintegral constant coefficient; this step does not assume that the bad value is finite or that it has finitely many exponents.

\begin{remark}[Specialization and composition \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:rem:composition}
The coefficientwise constant term of \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal} respects composition: if $F\in\Num_m(\Oz)$ and $F_1,\dots,F_m\in\Num_n(\Oz)$, then
$F(F_1,\dots,F_m)\in\Num_n(\Oz)$ and $\ct_*\bigl(F(F_1,\dots,F_m)\bigr)=\ct_*(F)\bigl(\ct_*(F_1),\dots,\ct_*(F_m)\bigr)$, because all coefficients lie
in the ring $\Q+\Pi$, on which $\ct$ is a ring homomorphism, and substitution is built from finitely many sums and products; the same holds for $\GOz$.
The decomposition $F=\ct_*(F)+(F-\ct_*(F))$ is an arithmetic classification, not a statement that the purely infinite part is negligible: a coefficient
such as $\omega^\alpha$ dominates every ordinary coefficient, and preservation places no condition on it beyond positive support (22).
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Leading exponents are not enough \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:ex:leading}
If $0<b<c$, the coefficient of $(1+\omega^{-c})X$ has leading exponent $0$, but the value $\omega^b+\omega^{b-c}$ at $\omega^b$ has a negative
exponent. A scale chosen above leading exponents only does not give the conclusion of \cref{osq:fs:cor:blocktest} for polynomials; $G$ must contain the
complete supports, remote tails included (compare the remark after \cref{osq:fs:lem:fresh}).
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian coordinate-degree grid \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:thm:gausspoly}
Let $F\in\SC[Z_1,\dots,Z_m]$ with $\deg_{Z_j}F\le d_j$, and $C_{d_j+1}=\{a+bi:a,b\in\{0,\dots,d_j\}\}$. Then $F(\GOz^m)\subseteq\GOz$ if and only if
$F\bigl(\prod_jC_{d_j+1}\bigr)\subseteq\GOz$; for a uniform bound $d$ these are $(d+1)^{2m}$ tests.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$H(\mathbf U,\mathbf V)=F(\mathbf U+i\mathbf V)$ has degree at most $d_j$ in each of $U_j$ and $V_j$, and the tests are its values on the box
$\prod_j\{0,\dots,d_j\}^2$. By \eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef} its Newton coefficients lie in $\GOz$, and binomials of elements of $\Oz$ lie in $\Oz$
(\cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial}), so $H(\Oz^{2m})\subseteq\GOz$; every element of $\GOz$ is $x+iy$ with $x,y\in\Oz$. The converse is restriction.
\end{proof}

This is the coordinate-degree twin of 18's simplex test (\cref{osq:or:prop:gausstest}), which uses the total degree and the $\binom{2m+d}{2m}$ points
$\mathbf a+i\mathbf b$ with $|\mathbf a|+|\mathbf b|\le d$, a subset of $C_{d+1}^{\,m}$; for polynomials of total degree at most $d$ the simplex is the
smaller test, and neither is claimed minimal. The ordinary box is not enough over $\GOz$ (\cref{osq:pm:rem:gaussnewton}).

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian single-scale certificate \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:thm:gaussrational}
Let $F=P/Q\in\SC(Z_1,\dots,Z_m)$ be in lowest terms with all coordinate degrees of $P$ and $Q$ at most $d\ge1$, let $G$ contain the supports of the real
and imaginary parts of all coefficients, $b>G$ and $t=\omega^b$. Then $F$ preserves $\GOz$ if and only if it is defined and $\GOz$-valued on
$C_{d+1}^{\,m}\cup\mathsf R_{m,d}(t)$, a set of at most $(d+1)^{2m}+m(2d^2+2d+1)^{m-1}$ points. Every rational function preserving $\GOz$ is a
polynomial.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Run the proof of \cref{osq:ft:thm:certificate} over $K_G$ with $k=\C$: a nonconstant denominator gives a nonpolynomial one-variable restriction at
ordinary integer values of the other coordinates, whose value at $t$ has a negative block. So the remote tests force a constant denominator, and
\cref{osq:ft:thm:gausspoly} applies. The last assertion is also \cref{osq:fs:thm:probes}.
\end{proof}

The remote points need no Gaussian coordinates: ordinary integers already avoid a nonzero polynomial in characteristic $0$, and only the arithmetic
stage needs the Gaussian grid (22). \Cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall,osq:ft:thm:exceptions} hold for $\GOz$ as stated.

\begin{theorem}[Tensor base change \src{22}; the decomposition is 10's, 16's and 18's]\label{osq:ft:thm:basechange}
$\Num^{\mathrm{rat}}_m(\Lambda)=\Num_m(\Lambda)=\Int(D^m)\oplus\Pi_k[\mathbf X]$, and the multiplication map
\begin{equation}\label{osq:ft:eq:basechange}
 \Lambda\otimes_D\Int(D^m)\longrightarrow\Num_m(\Lambda),\qquad \lambda\otimes f\longmapsto\lambda f,
\end{equation}
is a ring isomorphism, the tensor product being read through finite sums of pure tensors, or in a containing universe in which $\Lambda$ is a set; it
does not assert that $\Lambda$ is a set in the original universe. The coefficientwise constant term is a split retraction onto $\Int(D^m)$, and
evaluation commutes with it.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first equality is the polynomiality of preserving rational functions (\cref{osq:fs:thm:probes}; 22's Corollary~5.3 and Theorem~7.2), and the
decomposition is \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal,osq:pm:thm:numgaussian,osq:fs:prop:transfer}; 22 proves it as 16 does, without a basis of $\Int(D^m)$: values
on a large ordinary box put the Newton coefficients, hence the monomial coefficients, in $F_0+\Pi_k$; constant terms at points of $D^m$ put the ordinary
part in $\Int(D^m)$; and $f(\mathbf z+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf z)\in\Pi_k$ for $\mathbf z\in D^m$, $\mathbf u\in\Pi_k^m$. Put $M=\Int(D^m)$. As $D$-modules
$\Lambda=D\oplus\Pi_k$, so $\Lambda\otimes_DM\cong M\oplus(\Pi_k\otimes_DM)$. Since $D[\mathbf X]\subseteq M\subseteq F_0[\mathbf X]$ and every polynomial
over $F_0$ has a common denominator in $D\setminus\{0\}$, localization gives $F_0\otimes_DM\cong F_0[\mathbf X]$ (injective because $M$ lies in the
torsion-free module $F_0[\mathbf X]$); $\Pi_k$ is an $F_0$-vector space, so
$\Pi_k\otimes_DM\cong\Pi_k\otimes_{F_0}(F_0\otimes_DM)\cong\Pi_k[\mathbf X]$. Under these identifications the multiplication map is the direct-sum map
of the decomposition. The assertions on the constant term follow from its multiplicativity on $F_0+\Pi_k$ (\cref{osq:lem:ct}).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[\src{22}]\label{osq:ft:def:universal}
For a coordinate degree bound $\mathbf d$, a finite set $S\subseteq D^m$ is \emph{universal} in that degree space if every $f\in F_0[\mathbf X]$ with
$\deg_{X_j}f\le d_j$ and $f(S)\subseteq D$ satisfies $f(D^m)\subseteq D$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Lifting constant test sets \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:thm:lifting}
A finite set $S\subseteq D^m$ is universal in a coordinate degree space if and only if every $F\in E[\mathbf X]$ in that degree space with
$F(S)\subseteq\Lambda$ satisfies $F(\Lambda^m)\subseteq\Lambda$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $S$ be universal. Its evaluation matrix on the monomials of the degree space has full column rank over $F_0$: otherwise a nonzero
$h\in F_0[\mathbf X]$ in the space vanishes on $S$, \cref{osq:ft:lem:grid} gives $\mathbf c\in\Z^m\subseteq D^m$ with $h(\mathbf c)\ne0$, and
$h/(2h(\mathbf c))$ is $D$-valued on $S$ but takes the value $\frac12\notin D$ at $\mathbf c$. Inverting a square invertible submatrix writes every
coefficient of $F$ as an $F_0$-linear combination of values in $\Lambda=D\oplus\Pi_k$, so $F=f+g$ with $f\in F_0[\mathbf X]$ and
$g\in\Pi_k[\mathbf X]$ in the same space. Constant terms at the points of $S$ give $f(S)\subseteq D$, so $f\in\Int(D^m)$, and $F$ preserves $\Lambda$ by
\cref{osq:ft:thm:basechange}. Conversely, if $S$ tests $\Lambda$ and $f\in F_0[\mathbf X]$ has $f(S)\subseteq D$, then $f(\Lambda^m)\subseteq\Lambda$
and $f(D^m)\subseteq\Lambda\cap F_0=D$.
\end{proof}

So among test points in the ordinary lattice $D^m$, minimal polynomial testing is the same problem before and after adjoining the purely infinite part
(22). This turns the last assertion of \cref{osq:or:prop:gausstest}, the forward direction for $D=\Z[i]$ in one variable (18), into an equivalence in
every number of variables, for $\Z$ and for $\Z[i]$. In one Gaussian variable the ordinary problem is the classical universal-set problem connected with
simultaneous $p$-orderings (Byszewski, Fr\k aczyk and Szumowicz \cite{BFS}, with the work of Volkov and Petrov \cite{VP} discussed there); 22 does not
determine the optimal sets, and supplies only the transfer and the grid of \cref{osq:ft:thm:gausspoly}. The theorem bears on \cref{osq:fs:q:fresh}(a),
not on \cref{osq:or:q:outputs}(c): its test points lie in $D^m$, and whether points of $\GOz$ outside $\Z[i]^m$ can do better is not addressed.

\begin{theorem}[Finite generators of image ideals \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:thm:ideals}
Let $F\in\Num_m(\Oz)$ have $\deg_{X_j}F\le d_j$ and Newton coefficients $c_{\mathbf k}$ (\cref{osq:pm:thm:grid}), and let $I_F$ be the ideal of $\Oz$
generated by $F(\Oz^m)$, the class of finite $\Oz$-linear combinations of values. Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:ft:eq:imageideal}
 I_F=(c_{\mathbf k}:\mathbf k\le\mathbf d)=\Bigl(F(\boldsymbol\mu):\boldsymbol\mu\in\prod_j\{0,\dots,d_j\}\Bigr).
\end{equation}
Hence for every ideal $I$ of $\Oz$, $F(\Oz^m)\subseteq I$ if and only if the finitely many box values lie in $I$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The Newton expansion writes each value $F(\mathbf x)$ as an $\Oz$-linear combination of the $c_{\mathbf k}$ (\cref{osq:pm:lem:binomial});
\eqref{osq:pm:eq:newtoncoef} writes each $c_{\mathbf k}$ as an integral combination of box values; and box values are values.
\end{proof}

A finite generating set avoids set-size questions about an ideal generated by a class, and no principal generator or greatest common divisor is
assumed or inferred (22). The Gaussian version, with the box $\prod_jC_{d_j+1}$, follows in the same way from the $2m$-variable polynomial $H$ in the
proof of \cref{osq:ft:thm:gausspoly}: the ideal of $\GOz$ generated by all values on $\GOz^m$ is generated by the finitely many box values.

\begin{corollary}[Arithmetic birational rigidity \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:cor:birational}
If $\Phi,\Psi:E^m\dashrightarrow E^m$ are rational maps inverse to each other as rational maps, and both are defined on $\Lambda^m$ with values in
$\Lambda^m$, then all coordinates of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are polynomials in $\Num_m(\Lambda)$, and $\Phi,\Psi$ are mutually inverse polynomial
automorphisms of $E^m$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Each coordinate preserves $\Lambda$, so it is a polynomial (\cref{osq:fs:thm:probes,osq:ft:thm:gaussrational}); the rational identities
$\Psi\circ\Phi=\id$ and $\Phi\circ\Psi=\id$ are then polynomial identities.
\end{proof}

The rational inverse is a hypothesis: nothing is asserted about a bijective polynomial map of $\Lambda^m$ without one, no Jacobian-conjecture claim is
made, and the coordinates need not have coefficients in $\Lambda$ (22).

\begin{example}[\src{22}]\label{osq:ft:ex:shear}
$\Phi(X,Y)=\bigl(X+\tfrac12Y(Y-1),Y\bigr)$ and $\Psi(X,Y)=\bigl(X-\tfrac12Y(Y-1),Y\bigr)$ are inverse polynomial maps that induce inverse bijections of
$\Oz^2$, with the coefficient $\frac12\notin\Oz$; the Gaussian analogue uses $Y(Y-1)/(1+i)$. So arithmetic polynomial maps form a larger class than maps
with coordinates in $\Oz[X,Y]$. 16's shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y^2,y)$ (after \cref{osq:fs:thm:surjective}) has coordinates in $\Oz[X,Y]$.
\end{example}

Three conditions on a polynomial are distinct (22): coefficients in $\Lambda$, values in $\Lambda$ on $\Lambda^m$, and values in $\Lambda$ at sampled
points. The first implies the second but not conversely ($\binom X2$); for bounded degree the tests above make the second and third equivalent, while
for rational functions no coefficient-independent set of samples does (\cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall}). Coefficients in $\Oz$ for numerator and
denominator do not make the denominator invertible at every omnific input (\cref{osq:ft:ex:integers}).

\begin{proposition}[Fresh scales in a fixed Hahn workspace \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:prop:relative}
Let $\Gamma$ be a set-sized ordered abelian group, $G\subseteq\Gamma$ a subgroup containing the coefficient supports, and
$\operatorname{cvx}_\Gamma(G)=\{x\in\Gamma:|x|\le g\text{ for some }g\in G\}$ the convex subgroup it generates. A positive $b\in\Gamma$ with $b>G$
exists if and only if $\operatorname{cvx}_\Gamma(G)\ne\Gamma$. When it exists, the Laurent blocks, the detector and the one-point test
(\cref{osq:fs:thm:embedding,osq:fs:cor:blocktest,osq:fs:thm:onepoint}) and the certificates of
\cref{osq:ft:thm:certificate,osq:ft:thm:gaussrational} hold in $\hahn k\Gamma$, for $\A_{D,k}(\Gamma)$ and coefficients supported in $G$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $b>G$, then $b\notin\operatorname{cvx}_\Gamma(G)$. Conversely a positive $b\notin\operatorname{cvx}_\Gamma(G)$ satisfies $b>|g|$ for all $g\in G$,
since $b\le|g|$ would put it in the convex subgroup. The remaining arguments use only supports, block separation, finite polynomial algebra and the
split ring $D\oplus\Pi_k(\Gamma)$; the exponents $jb+g$ stay in $\Gamma$, and the countable union of the blocks is a legitimate support.
\end{proof}

For an Archimedean $\Gamma$ every nonzero $G$ is cofinal, and no fresh exponent exists in $\Gamma$; this is a failure of the method's hypothesis, not a
theorem that every finite test fails there, and one may enlarge $\Gamma$ by a lexicographic factor or work in $\No$ (22). \Cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall}
cannot hold for a set-sized ring, which is itself a set of tests; its strength comes from the unbounded supply of surreal scales, and
\cref{osq:ft:cor:common} explains how set-sized computations coexist with it (22). Where no fresh exponent exists, rational collapse still holds by 18's
discrete-gap argument, which uses none (\cref{osq:or:thm:rational,osq:or:cor:workspace}); what 22's method loses there is the finite rational
certificate, and whether another finite certificate exists is open (\cref{osq:fs:q:fresh}(c)) \merge.

\begin{example}[One new coordinate exposes a denominator \src{22}]\label{osq:ft:ex:resultant}
For $F(X,Y)=(X+Y)/(XY+1)$ over $\Q$, the leading coefficients in $X$ are $1$ and $Y$ and $\operatorname{Res}_X(X+Y,XY+1)=1-Y^2$, so
$\mathsf h_X=Y(1-Y^2)$. At $Y=2$, $F(X,2)=(X+2)/(2X+1)=\frac12+\frac3{2(2X+1)}$, whose second term has a nonzero negative block at every fresh $t$. The
resultant excludes exactly the values of $Y$ at which the denominator loses degree or a cancellation occurs.
\end{example}

For every $u\in\Pi$, even of infinite support, $\binom X3-4\binom Y2+uX^2Y$ preserves $\Oz$ with specialization $\binom X3-4\binom Y2$, while
$\omega^{-1}X$ fails at $X=1$ and $\sqrt2+\omega\notin\Oz$: what matters is negative support or a nonintegral constant coefficient, not magnitude, and
adding positive support cannot repair a nonintegral constant coefficient, which is the invariance behind the polynomial step of
\cref{osq:ft:thm:exceptions} (22; compare \cref{osq:pm:ex:numreal}).

A construction of the certificate reduces $P/Q$ over the coefficient field, collects every exponent of every coefficient support, forms the group they
generate, chooses $b$ above it, and tests exact values on the box and the remote grids. An effective version needs an implementation contract for
equality, polynomial gcd, support bounds and membership in $\Lambda$, none of which can be presumed decidable for arbitrary notations of surreal numbers;
when the coefficients can be inspected exactly, checking that the reduced denominator is constant and then the Newton coefficients may be cheaper than
evaluating the grid. The theorem is an exact value certificate, not a complexity improvement over symbolic algebra. Once a nonzero resultant
specialization is found it is also a witness generator: it names a failing point without numerical approximation, since the first nonzero negative
Laurent coefficient contributes a whole block that cannot cancel (22).

\begin{remark}[Other constant rings \merge]\label{osq:ft:rem:otherD}
The conclusion of \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall} holds for $\A_{D,k}$ with every unital $D\subsetneq k$, in every number of variables. Take $c\in k\setminus D$.
The only pole of $\omega^\beta/(X_1-c)$ is $c\notin\A_{D,k}$; if $\beta>0$ exceeds the absolute values of all exponents in the supports of the
$(s_1-c)^{-1}$, $s\in S$ (a set), the values on $S$ lie in $\Pi_k$, while at a point with first coordinate $\omega^{2\beta}$ the value is the nonzero
infinitesimal $\omega^{-\beta}(1-c\,\omega^{-2\beta})^{-1}$. This is 16's proof with $\frac12$ replaced by $c$; for $D=k$ it does not apply.
\end{remark}

22 summarizes its dependencies as follows: the certificate uses the fresh scale, the resultant specialization and the ordinary binomial test; the
no-set-test theorem uses the fresh scale and a geometric inverse, not the resultant or the binomial machinery; the removal of exceptions combines
denominator detection with invariance under positive-support additions; and the Gaussian versions change the constant arithmetic and keep the support
mechanism. Its proofs need neither algebraic closedness of $\SC$, nor differentiation, nor a topology, and $\omega^\gamma$ is the normal-form monomial,
not an analytic exponential.

\subsection{Semialgebraic preservers: smooth rigidity and bounded-scale flexibility}\label{osq:sa:sub:semialgebraic}

This subsection is manuscript~25's (\cref{osq:sub:sources}). It answers the first clause of \cref{osq:ft:q:maps}(a) for globally smooth maps: over any
real closed field $E$ with a cofinal discretely ordered subring $B$, a globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic map $E^r\to E^{r'}$ maps $B^r$ into $B^{r'}$ if
and only if its coordinates are integer-valued polynomials in $\Num_r(B)$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany}), and for a scalar graph of degree at most
$\mathsf D$ global $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ regularity suffices in every dimension; for $\Oz$ and $\GOz$ this gives finite binomial expansions with omnific
coefficients (\cref{osq:sa:cor:explicit,osq:sa:thm:complexreal}). Without smoothness every semialgebraic preserver is still polynomial on each of its
two tails (\cref{osq:sa:thm:tails}), but on a bounded interval it can be far from polynomial: $\omega^b\sqrt x$ is omnific for every omnific $x\in[0,
\omega^a]$ exactly when $a\ll b$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:radical}), the same threshold as \cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}; for every ordinary $\mathsf k$ an explicit
$C^{\mathsf k}$ bump sends $\Oz$ into $\Pi$ and agrees with no finite family of polynomials on $\Oz$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:bumps}); and no set-sized sample
tests preservation, even for the globally $C^\infty$ branch of an irreducible quadratic graph (\cref{osq:sa:thm:nosettests}). So the answer to the first
clause of \cref{osq:ft:q:maps}(a) is complete for globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic maps in every dimension and negative, as far as polynomial or
finitely piecewise polynomial descriptions go, below that regularity; the certificate clause is answered negatively for samples chosen independently of
the coefficients, and coefficient-adapted certificates stay open.

\paragraph{Conventions and renamings.} $E$ is a real closed ordered field and $B\subseteq E$ a unital subring that is \emph{discretely ordered}, $1$
being its least positive element, as for 18's rings (\cref{osq:or:sub:outputs}), and \emph{cofinal}: every element of $E$ lies below some element of $B$.
Every integer part of a real closed field satisfies both conditions, and the proofs use no floor function; $\Z$ is not cofinal in a
non-Archimedean field. $\Oz$ is a cofinal discretely ordered subring of $\No$: a nonconstant omnific integer has a positive leading exponent and so
exceeds every ordinary real in absolute value, and a monomial above the leading scale of a given surreal is omnific (25). A function $E^r\to E$ is
\emph{semialgebraic} if its graph is defined by a finite ordered-field formula with finitely many parameters from $E$, which by quantifier elimination may
be taken quantifier-free; the predicate $x\in B$ (or $x\in\Oz$) is \emph{not} allowed in the formula, and preservation of $B$ is a separate hypothesis.
Differentiability is taken in the order topology of $E$, all positive elements of $E$ being tolerances; $C^{\mathsf k}$ means continuous partial
derivatives through order $\mathsf k$, and global $C^\infty$ means $C^{\mathsf k}$ for every ordinary $\mathsf k$. Exponents follow
\cref{osq:sub:orientation} (25's growth convention). For a divisible ordered subgroup or subclass $H\subseteq\No$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:KH}
 K_H=\{x\in\No:\supp x\subseteq H\},\qquad H^{\uparrow}=\{\gamma\in\No:\gamma>h\text{ for every }h\in H\};
\end{equation}
for a set $H$ this is 16's Hahn field $K_H$ with $k=\R$, and $K_{H_a}=\FF_a$. $T=\omega^a$ is the actual monomial, as in
\cref{osq:bb:sub:branching,osq:rm:sub:cyclic}, and $a\ll b$ is the relation of \eqref{osq:eq:Ha}. For an ordinary $\mathsf D\ge1$, a \emph{degree-$\mathsf
D$ graph description} of $f:E^r\to E$ is a quantifier-free Boolean formula defining the graph of $f$ whose polynomial atoms all have total degree at most
$\mathsf D$; the number of atoms is finite but not bounded, and the coefficients are arbitrary elements of $E$. 25's symbols are renamed as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its real closed field $F$ and cofinal discrete ring $R$ are $E$ (the ambient field, as in \cref{osq:or:sub:outputs,osq:ft:sub:tests}) and $B$ (18's
letter; $\B$ is the ring $D+\mm_k$); its input and output dimensions $n,m$ are $r,r'$, as in $\Num_r$; the order $m$ of its finite differences is $s$, as in
the proof of \cref{osq:or:thm:rational}.
\item Its graph degree $D$ is $\mathsf D$ and its smoothness order $k$ is $\mathsf k$ ($D$ is the constant ring and $k$ the coefficient field); so its
$C^{D^2}$, $C^k$ and $s(D)$ are $C^{\mathsf D^2}$, $C^{\mathsf k}$ and $\mathsf s(\mathsf D)$. $C^{\mathsf k}$ is a regularity class, not a fibre
$\mathsf C(G)$ or a set $C_j$.
\item Its convex subgroup $H_a=\{\gamma:|\gamma|\le na\text{ for some }n\}$ is $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, as in \cref{osq:cr:sub:residues}; it is the
\emph{opposite} of this report's $H_a$ of \eqref{osq:eq:Ha}, which collects the exponents infinitesimal relative to $a$. Its $K_H$ keeps its name,
extended to classes, and its $H^+$ is $H^{\uparrow}$ ($\kappa^+$ is a successor cardinal).
\item Its multiplier $L=\omega^b$ is written $\omega^b$ ($L(M)$ is 14's module and $L_h$ 03's field); its bumps $B_k$ are $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}$ ($\B$ is
the negative-support ring); its ring $\mathcal E_R$ of semialgebraic preservers and ideal $\mathcal B_R$ of bounded-region ones are $\operatorname{SA}(B)$
and $\operatorname{SA}_{\mathrm b}(B)$ ($\EE_a$ is 07's field and $\mathsf B_\R$ 19's fibre).
\item Its test function $G_b$ is $\mathsf r_b$ ($G$ is a group), its shears $S_k$ are $\operatorname{Sh}_{\mathsf k}$ ($S$ is a set of points), and in
proofs its polynomial $A(x,h)$, bound $M$ and Lagrange basis $\ell_j$ are $\mathsf u(x,h)$, $M_0$ and $\mathsf l_j$.
\end{itemize}
Five tempting readings are false. (1) 25's $H_a$ is $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)\supsetneq H_a$; its threshold ``$b>na$ for every $n$'' is $a\ll b$, not
$b\in H_a$. (2) Ordinary shifts are not cofinal: $\Z$ is not cofinal in a non-Archimedean $E$, so extrapolation must use a large step in $B$
(\eqref{osq:sa:eq:extrapolation}). (3) A finite difference below $1$ is an estimate; it becomes $0$ only at lattice points, by the discrete gap, and
semialgebraicity then spreads the zero set to a ray. (4) Rolle's theorem, the mean-value theorem and the identity principle are used only for
semialgebraic functions and finite derivative orders, never for arbitrary functions on $\No$ (\cref{osq:sa:rem:calculus}). (5) The multiplier acts on
supports: $|\omega^b\phi(x)|>1$ does not make $\omega^b\phi(x)$ omnific, since an infinite surreal may still have negative support.

\paragraph{Polynomial rigidity on the two tails.}

\begin{lemma}[Polynomial and reciprocal growth \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:growth}
If $g:(c_0,\infty)\to E$ is semialgebraic, there are an ordinary $d\ge0$ and $C>0$ in $E$ with $|g(x)|\le Cx^d$ for all sufficiently large $x$. If a
semialgebraic $h$ is nonzero on $(c,c+\delta)$, then, after shrinking $\delta$, $|h(c+t)|\ge Ct^N$ for $0<t<\delta$, some $C>0$ and an ordinary $N\ge0$;
similarly on the left of $c$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A graph has empty interior, so in a quantifier-free description at every graph point some nonzero defining polynomial vanishes (otherwise all signs are
locally constant and the formula contains an open box). There are finitely many of them, so after a finite semialgebraic partition, on a final interval
$Q(x,g(x))=0$ for a nonzero $Q\in E[X,Y]$ of positive degree in $Y$, whose leading coefficient in $Y$ is nonzero for large $x$. The root bound
$|y|\le1+\sum_{j<q}|a_j/a_q|$ for $a_qy^q+\cdots+a_0=0$ (compare the leading term with the others when $|y|>1$) bounds $g(x)$ by finitely many rational
functions of $x$, hence by $Cx^d$. For the second assertion apply the first to $u\mapsto1/|h(c+1/u)|$ on a final ray and substitute $u=1/t$. No
Archimedean assumption and no convergent real sequence is used.
\end{proof}

The same graph argument shows semialgebraic smoothness on small intervals: take a squarefree irreducible factor of $Q$ involving $Y$; its resultant with
its $Y$-derivative is a nonzero polynomial in $X$, away from whose finitely many zeros a branch is a simple algebraic root, differentiable to every finite
order by the semialgebraic implicit-function theorem; monotonicity follows after further finite partition (25). One-variable semialgebraic functions are
eventually monotone and eventually $C^{\mathsf k}$ for each fixed $\mathsf k$, their derivatives are semialgebraic, and Rolle's and the mean-value theorem
hold for them; these, quantifier elimination and a semialgebraic subset of the line being a finite union of points and intervals are the standard facts of
real algebraic geometry used \cite{BCR}.

\begin{remark}[What is not transferred \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:rem:calculus}
The mean-value theorem is not asserted for arbitrary functions on $\No$; it is used only for semialgebraic functions and a fixed finite derivative order,
where it holds over every real closed field by real-algebraic methods. This excludes the known pathologies of unconstrained surreal-valued calculus (25).
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[A derivative lowers the growth \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:derivative}
If $g$ is semialgebraic and eventually $C^1$ with $|g(x)|\le Cx^j$ eventually, $j\in\Z$, then $|g'(x)|\le C'x^{j-1}$ eventually for some $C'>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Eventually $|g'|$ is monotone. If it is nondecreasing, the mean-value theorem on $[x,2x]$ gives $|g'(x)|\le|g'(\xi)|=|g(2x)-g(x)|/x\le
C(2^j+1)x^{j-1}$; if it is nonincreasing, $[x/2,x]$ gives $|g'(x)|\le2C(1+2^{-j})x^{j-1}$. The constants lie in $E$; no real uniformity is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Small high differences \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:differences}
For a semialgebraic $f:E\to E$ there is an ordinary $s\ge1$ such that $\Delta^sf(x)=\sum_{j=0}^s(-1)^{s-j}\binom sjf(x+j)$ satisfies $|\Delta^sf(x)|<1$
for all sufficiently large $x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take $|f(x)|\le Cx^d$ (\cref{osq:sa:lem:growth}) and $s=d+1$. On a final ray $f$ is $C^s$, and \cref{osq:sa:lem:derivative} applied $s$ times gives
$|f^{(s)}(x)|\le C_s/x$. The interpolating polynomial of $f$ at $x,x+1,\dots,x+s$ has leading coefficient $\Delta^sf(x)/s!$, and repeated Rolle applied to
the difference gives $\Delta^sf(x)=f^{(s)}(\xi)$ with $x<\xi<x+s$; take $x>C_s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A semialgebraic difference kernel \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:kernel}
A semialgebraic function with $\Delta^sf=0$ on a final ray agrees on a final ray with a polynomial of degree at most $s-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A semialgebraic $g$ with $g(x+1)=g(x)$ on a final ray is constant there, being eventually constant or strictly monotone. Applied to
$\Delta^{s-1}f$ this gives a constant $c$, and since $\Delta\binom Xj=\binom X{j-1}$, $f-c\binom X{s-1}$ has vanishing $(s-1)$st difference on a
final ray; induce on $s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tail values determine membership \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:tailmembership}
Let $B\subseteq E$ be cofinal and $P\in E[X]$ of degree at most $d$. If $P(a)\in B$ for all sufficiently large $a\in B$, then $P(B)\subseteq B$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $a\in B$. By cofinality there is a positive $h\in B$ such that all $a+jh$, $1\le j\le d+1$, lie in the allowed tail, and the vanishing of the
$(d+1)$st difference with step $h$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:extrapolation}
 P(a)=\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}(-1)^{j+1}\binom{d+1}jP(a+jh)\in B .
\end{equation}
The step $h$ may be an infinite element of $B$; an ordinary integer step would not reach the tail in a non-Archimedean field.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-tail polynomiality \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:tails}
Let $B$ be a cofinal discretely ordered subring of the real closed field $E$. If $f:E\to E$ is semialgebraic and $f(B)\subseteq B$, there are unique
$P_-,P_+\in\Num_1(B)$ and $H>0$ with $f=P_-$ on $(-\infty,-H)$ and $f=P_+$ on $(H,\infty)$. For $P_+$ alone it suffices that $f(a)\in B$ for all
sufficiently large $a\in B$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:sa:lem:differences}, $|\Delta^sf|<1$ on a final ray. At lattice points $a$ far enough out, all $f(a+j)$ lie in $B$, so $\Delta^sf(a)\in B$
has modulus below $1$ and is $0$. The zero set of $\Delta^sf$ is semialgebraic and contains a cofinal subset of $E$, and a finite union of points and
intervals with that property contains a final ray. \Cref{osq:sa:lem:kernel} gives a polynomial $P_+$ on a final ray and \cref{osq:sa:lem:tailmembership}
puts it in $\Num_1(B)$; apply the same to $x\mapsto f(-x)$ for $P_-$. Two distinct polynomials do not agree on a ray.
\end{proof}

This isolates the mechanism: semialgebraicity turns infinitely many discrete zero values into an identity on a tail, and the lattice gap supplies those
zeros; it is a non-Archimedean adaptation of a classical finite-difference idea, not an asymptotic expansion (25). For rational functions over a
discretely ordered ring these are the \emph{Collapse} and \emph{Filling} steps of \cref{osq:or:thm:rational} (18).

Let $\operatorname{SA}(B)$ be the ring of semialgebraic functions $E\to E$ preserving $B$, and $\operatorname{SA}_{\mathrm b}(B)$ its ideal of those
vanishing outside a bounded interval.

\begin{corollary}[The two-end quotient \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:germs}
There is a split exact sequence of rings
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:germs}
 0\longrightarrow\operatorname{SA}_{\mathrm b}(B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{SA}(B)\xrightarrow{\ (P_-,P_+)\ }\Num_1(B)\times\Num_1(B)
 \longrightarrow0,
\end{equation}
so $\operatorname{SA}(B)/\operatorname{SA}_{\mathrm b}(B)\cong\Num_1(B)^2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Uniqueness of the tail polynomials makes the map a ring homomorphism, with kernel $\operatorname{SA}_{\mathrm b}(B)$; a splitting sends $(P,Q)$ to the
function equal to $P$ on $x<0$ and to $Q$ on $x\ge0$.
\end{proof}

``Bounded'' is order-theoretic; no compactness of $[-H,H]$ is asserted. For $E=\No$ the function rings are read through finite formula codes with
finite parameter tuples, statements about their operations pointwise; no set of arbitrary class functions is formed (25).

\paragraph{Global smoothness and a degree bound.}

\begin{lemma}[Smooth identity principle \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:identity}
Let $I\subseteq E$ be an interval and $h:I\to E$ semialgebraic and $C^\infty$. If $h$ vanishes on a nonempty open subinterval, it vanishes on $I$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Otherwise, since the zero set is a finite union of points and intervals, there is an interior point $c$ where a zero interval meets an adjacent interval
on which $h\ne0$; all derivatives of $h$ vanish at $c$, by continuity from the zero side. On the other side \cref{osq:sa:lem:growth} gives $|h(c+t)|\ge
C|t|^N$ for small $t\ne0$. If $N=0$ continuity is contradicted; if $N\ge1$, Taylor's formula with Rolle remainder, $h(c+t)=h^{(N)}(\xi_t)t^N/N!$ with
$h^{(N)}(\xi_t)\to0$, gives $h(c+t)=o(|t|^N)$ in the order topology, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

This is the elementary semialgebraic nonflatness argument, with classical and more general antecedents \cite{Miller,BCR}; 25 uses it to propagate an
arithmetic tail identity, not as a new identity theorem.

\begin{theorem}[One-variable smooth classification \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:smoothone}
A globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic $f:E\to E$ preserves $B$ if and only if $f$ is a polynomial in $\Num_1(B)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$f=P_+$ on a final ray (\cref{osq:sa:thm:tails}); apply \cref{osq:sa:lem:identity} to $f-P_+$. The converse is clear.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[One irreducible graph equation \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:irreducible}
If $f:E\to E$ is semialgebraic, preserves $B$ and satisfies $Q(x,f(x))=0$ for all $x$ for one irreducible nonconstant $Q\in E[X,Y]$, then $f\in\Num_1(B)$,
without any smoothness hypothesis.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
On a final ray $f=P$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:tails}), so $Q(X,P(X))$ has infinitely many roots and vanishes; division in $Y$ shows $Y-P(X)\mid Q$, and
irreducibility makes $Q$ a scalar multiple of $Y-P(X)$, so $f=P$ everywhere.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis is one global irreducible equation; an arbitrary semialgebraic graph may switch between components, as the bumps below do at the ends of
their support (25).

\begin{theorem}[An explicit smoothness threshold \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:degree}
Let $f:E\to E$ be semialgebraic with a degree-$\mathsf D$ graph description, and suppose $f$ agrees with a polynomial $P$ on a nonempty open interval. Put
$d=\max(0,\deg P)$ ($d=0$ also for $P=0$) and $N=\mathsf D\max(1,d)$. Then $d\le\mathsf D$, and if $f$ is globally $C^N$, then $f=P$ everywhere. In
particular a globally $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ semialgebraic preserver of $B$ with a degree-$\mathsf D$ graph description lies in $\Num_1(B)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At every graph point some nonzero atom vanishes. Factoring the atoms, on a subinterval of agreement one irreducible factor $Q$ vanishes along $(x,P(x))$,
so $Y-P(X)$ divides $Q$ and $\max(1,d)\le\mathsf D$. Suppose $h=f-P\ne0$. Its semialgebraic zero set contains an open interval, so it has a boundary point
$c$ with $h=0$ on one side and $h\ne0$ on an adjacent interval on the other, which we shrink so that one irreducible factor $Q$ of an atom vanishes along the
graph of $f$ there. $Q$ is not a scalar multiple of $Y-P(X)$, since $f\ne P$ there, so $q(X)=Q(X,P(X))\ne0$ with $\deg q\le\mathsf D\max(1,d)=N$, and
$q(c)=Q(c,f(c))=0$ by continuity. If $q$ vanishes to order $j_0$ at $c$, then $1\le j_0\le N$ and $|q(x)|\ge C|x-c|^{j_0}$ near $c$. On the other hand
$Q(x,P(x)+h(x))-Q(x,P(x))=h(x)\,\mathsf u(x,h(x))$ for a polynomial $\mathsf u$, and the first term is $0$; as $h$ is continuous with $h(c)=0$,
$|\mathsf u(x,h(x))|\le M_0$ near $c$, so $|h(x)|\ge(C/M_0)|x-c|^{j_0}$. All derivatives of $h$ through order $N$ vanish at $c$, and the Taylor argument
of \cref{osq:sa:lem:identity} through order $j_0\le N$ contradicts this bound. For preservers, \cref{osq:sa:thm:tails} supplies the initial agreement.
\end{proof}

The bound $\mathsf D^2$ is an elementary sufficient bound, not claimed optimal; it does not depend on the size of the surreal parameters, the number of
atoms or the ring $B$. Finite-differentiability-to-smoothness phenomena have classical antecedents \cite{Miller}; the arithmetic contact estimate is proved
here explicitly (25). The degree is that of a quantifier-free description; a degree bound for a formula with unresolved quantifiers is a different notion
and is not covered.

\paragraph{Several variables and the numerical polynomials.}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform degree of polynomial slices \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:slices}
Let $f:E^r\to E$ have a degree-$\mathsf D$ graph description. If fixing all but one coordinate gives a polynomial in the remaining one, its degree is at
most $\mathsf D$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Specialize the fixed coordinates and discard atoms that become zero. At every point of the specialized graph some remaining nonzero atom vanishes,
otherwise the formula would contain an open box; so one of them vanishes at infinitely many points $(t,P(t))$, hence vanishes after $Y=P(X)$ and is
divisible by $Y-P(X)$. Its degree is at most $\mathsf D$; a constant slice is included.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-dimensional smooth classification \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany}
Let $B$ be a cofinal discretely ordered subring of the real closed field $E$. If $f:E^r\to E$ is globally $C^\infty$, semialgebraic and maps $B^r$ into
$B$, then $f\in\Num_r(B)$. If its graph has a degree-$\mathsf D$ description, global $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ regularity suffices, independently of $r$, and
$f$ has total degree at most $\mathsf D$. Applied coordinatewise: a globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic map $E^r\to E^{r'}$ maps $B^r$ into $B^{r'}$ if and
only if its coordinates lie in $\Num_r(B)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
It suffices to assume global $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ regularity for a degree-$\mathsf D$ description. Fixing all but one coordinate at elements of $B$ gives a
semialgebraic $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ function preserving $B$ with a graph of degree at most $\mathsf D$, so by \cref{osq:sa:thm:tails,osq:sa:thm:degree} a
polynomial of degree at most $\mathsf D$. With the Lagrange basis $\mathsf l_j$ of the nodes $\{0,1,\dots,\mathsf D\}$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:tensor}
 P(\mathbf X)=\sum_{\mathbf j\in\{0,\dots,\mathsf D\}^r}f(\mathbf j)\prod_{i=1}^r\mathsf l_{j_i}(X_i);
\end{equation}
repeated one-variable interpolation gives $f=P$ on $B^r$. A lattice is not order-dense, so equality off the lattice needs an argument. Put $h=f-P$. For
fixed $x_2,\dots,x_r\in B$, $t\mapsto h(t,x_2,\dots,x_r)$ vanishes on $B$, so its zero set contains a final ray, and as the slice of $P$ has degree at most
$\mathsf D$, the propagation of \cref{osq:sa:thm:degree} makes it zero on $E$: $h=0$ on $E\times B^{r-1}$. Fixing the first coordinate in $E$ and the last
$r-2$ in $B$, the same argument in the second coordinate gives $h=0$ on $E^2\times B^{r-2}$, and so on; at each stage the slice of $f$ is $C^{\mathsf D^2}$
with graph degree at most $\mathsf D$ and the slice of $P$ has degree at most $\mathsf D$. So $f=P$, and its values on $B^r$ put $P\in\Num_r(B)$. For the
total degree, with the nonzero atoms $Q_j(\mathbf X,Y)$ of the description, $\prod_jQ_j(\mathbf X,P(\mathbf X))$ vanishes on $E^r$, so some
$Q_j(\mathbf X,P(\mathbf X))$ is identically zero, $Y-P(\mathbf X)$ divides $Q_j$, and $\deg P\le\mathsf D$.
\end{proof}

No analyticity, no ordinary-real coefficients and no density of lattice points is used; the uniform complexity bound supplies one tensor interpolant
instead of unrelated polynomials on different lines. For a map $E^r\to E^{r'}$ the bound $C^{\mathsf D^2}$ applies when each scalar coordinate graph has a
degree-$\mathsf D$ description; a degree bound for the full vector graph must first be converted into bounds for the coordinate graphs (25).

For $\Oz$, 25's Proposition~5.3 is \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal} with the Newton coefficients of \cref{osq:pm:thm:grid}: every $P\in\Num_r(\Oz)$ is a unique
finite sum $\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\binom{\mathbf X}{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ with $c_{\boldsymbol\alpha}=(\Delta_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots
\Delta_r^{\alpha_r}P)(\mathbf 0)\in\Oz$, and $\Num_r(\Oz)=\Int(\Z^r)\oplus\Pi[\mathbf X]$ additively. 25's proof is 10's (binomial closure, the ordinary
Newton expansion and the splitting $c=m+p$); it credits this report. $\binom X2$ is numerical although $\frac12\notin\Oz$, which is why ``polynomial''
alone would be an incomplete arithmetic answer (25).

\begin{corollary}[An explicit smooth omnific classification \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:explicit}
A globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic map $f:\No^r\to\No^{r'}$ preserves $\Oz^r$ if and only if each coordinate has a finite expansion
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:newton}
 f_j(\mathbf X)=\sum_{\boldsymbol\alpha}c_{j,\boldsymbol\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^r\binom{X_i}{\alpha_i},\qquad c_{j,\boldsymbol\alpha}\in\Oz .
\end{equation}
Its constant-term action at a lattice input is obtained by applying $\ct$ to every coefficient and every input.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine \cref{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany} with \cref{osq:pm:thm:numreal,osq:pm:thm:grid}; the last assertion is \eqref{osq:pm:eq:evshadow}, since $\ct$ is
multiplicative on nonnegative supports.
\end{proof}

The expansion is an exact algebraic description, not an algorithm on arbitrary symbolic descriptions of surreal numbers: equality, support membership and
exact coefficient operations are not assumed decidable (25).

\paragraph{Convex support fields and absorption.} Tail rigidity says nothing inside a bounded interval; there the relevant object is a convex portion of
the exponent group, not a set of values (25).

\begin{lemma}[Real closed support fields \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:KH}
For a divisible ordered subgroup or subclass $H\subseteq\No$, $K_H$ is a real closed subfield of $\No$, and a semialgebraic function defined over $K_H$
takes an argument in $K_H$ to a value in $K_H$ whenever it is defined.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Hahn operations keep supports in the group generated by the original supports, so $K_H$ is a field. For a polynomial over $K_H$ the union of the supports
of its coefficients is a set whose divisible hull $G\subseteq H$ is a set-sized divisible group; $K_G$ is real closed \cite{LM} and embeds in $\No$ by normal
forms, so positive elements have square roots and odd-degree polynomials have roots in $K_H$. An inclusion of real closed fields is elementary, so for
parameters and input in $K_H$ the unique output lies in $K_H$; for a class $H$ this is a pointwise argument inside a set-sized support field containing the
finitely many parameters and the input.
\end{proof}

This is \cref{osq:if:prop:closed} for $H=H_a$, and the same set-sized reduction.

\begin{theorem}[Exact support-field absorption \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:absorption}
For $c\in\No$ and a divisible $H\subseteq\No$,
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:absorption}
 cK_H\subseteq\Pi\iff\supp c\subseteq H^{\uparrow}.
\end{equation}
In particular $\omega^bK_H\subseteq\Pi$ whenever $b>h$ for every $h\in H$. If $H^{\uparrow}$ is empty, the only such multiplier is $c=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $cK_H\subseteq\Pi$, then for each $h\in H$ the monomial $\omega^{-h}\in K_H$ translates $\supp c$ without cancellation, so every $\gamma\in\supp c$ has
$\gamma-h>0$; hence $\gamma\in H^{\uparrow}$. Conversely, if $\supp c\subseteq H^{\uparrow}$ and $x\in K_H$, every exponent that can occur in $cx$ is
$\gamma+\eta$ with $\gamma\in\supp c$, $\eta\in H$, and $-\eta\in H$ gives $\gamma+\eta>0$; cancellation removes exponents but cannot create a nonpositive
one.
\end{proof}

The sufficiency half contains \cref{osq:lem:Ha}(ii) ($H=H_a$ and $c=X^{c'}$ with $2c'\ge a$, since $H_a<a/2$), 07's \cref{osq:if:lem:gf} ($H=H_a$ and
$\supp g>a$) and the freshness of \cref{osq:fs:lem:fresh} ($H$ a set group $G$ and $b>G$) \merge. The theorem is a direct support calculation, not a
union-of-supports argument over a proper class: $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$ contains every omnific input of a bounded box and every semialgebraic value
defined over it (25).

\begin{lemma}[A bounded omnific window lies in one support field \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:lem:window}
If $x\in\Oz$ and $|x|\le T=\omega^a$, then $\supp x\subseteq[0,a]\subseteq\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Omnific supports are nonnegative, and a leading exponent above $a$ would make $|x|>\omega^a$ whatever its nonzero real coefficient.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-window absorption \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:window}
Let $a\ll b$, $T=\omega^a$, and let $\phi:\No^r\to\No^{r'}$ be semialgebraic with parameters in $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:window}
 \Phi(\mathbf x)=\begin{cases}\omega^b\phi(\mathbf x),&|x_j|\le T\text{ for every }j,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
\end{equation}
is semialgebraic and $\Phi(\Oz^r)\subseteq\Pi^{r'}$. The same holds for a semialgebraic partial map, set to $0$ outside its domain and the box.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The defining conditions are semialgebraic. An omnific input in the box has coordinates in $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$ (\cref{osq:sa:lem:window}), so the
outputs of $\phi$ lie there (\cref{osq:sa:lem:KH}), and $a\ll b$ means $b>\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, so \cref{osq:sa:thm:absorption} moves them into $\Pi$.
\end{proof}

A multiplier always exists: $b=\omega a$, a product in $\No$, satisfies $a\ll b$, although $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$ need not be a set; here
$\omega^b$ is a normal-form monomial, not an analytic exponential (25). So no rule forces a semialgebraic lattice preserver to be locally polynomial
throughout an infinite bounded interval: a radical, an algebraic implicit
branch or any finite semialgebraic construction survives there after multiplication by a higher scale, and every ordinary constant-term output is $0$
although the underlying geometry is nontrivial. The theorem asserts no regularity at the boundary of the box (the bumps below prescribe finite
regularity), and it gives no holomorphic cutoff: the surcomplex reading is through real coordinates (25).

\paragraph{The square-root threshold.}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp square-root threshold \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:radical}
Let $a>0$, $b\in\No$ and $T=\omega^a$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\omega^b\sqrt x\in\Oz$ for every $x\in\Oz$ with $0\le x\le T$;
\item $\omega^b\sqrt{T-1}\in\Oz$;
\item $a\ll b$.
\end{enumerate}
Then all the values in (i) lie in $\Pi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) because $T-1$ is a positive omnific integer, and (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i), with values in $\Pi$, by
\cref{osq:sa:lem:window,osq:sa:lem:KH,osq:sa:thm:absorption}. For (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii) use the formal binomial expansion
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:radical}
 \omega^b\sqrt{T-1}=\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\binom{1/2}j\,\omega^{\,b+(1/2-j)a},
\end{equation}
a Hahn series, not a limit in the fine topology: its exponents strictly decrease, its square is $\omega^{2b}(T-1)$ by multiplying the formal power series,
and its leading coefficient is positive. Every coefficient is nonzero. If $b\le na$ for an ordinary $n$, then $b+(1/2-j)a<0$ for $j>n+1$, and that exponent
cannot cancel with another, so the value has negative support.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Other rational powers \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:powers}
If $r_0\in\Q\setminus\Z_{\ge0}$ and $x^{r_0}$ is taken in the positive real closed sense on $x>0$, then $\omega^bx^{r_0}\in\Oz$ for every $x\in\Oz$ with
$1\le x\le\omega^a$ if and only if $a\ll b$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Sufficiency is \cref{osq:sa:thm:absorption}, positive rational powers being algebraic and so in $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$. For necessity expand
$\omega^b(T-1)^{r_0}=\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\binom{r_0}j\omega^{b+(r_0-j)a}$; no binomial coefficient vanishes for $r_0\notin\Z_{\ge0}$, and without $a\ll b$ an
exponent becomes negative for large ordinary $j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[An ordinary power of the scale never suffices \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:ex:finite}
For $a=1$ no $\omega^M$ with ordinary $M$ makes $\omega^M\sqrt x$ omnific for all omnific $x\in[0,\omega]$: already $x=\omega-1$ leaves a nonzero negative
tail. $\omega^\omega$ works for every such $x$ at once.
\end{example}

The threshold is an Archimedean-rank statement about the \emph{exponent}: $\omega^b$ must have an exponent above every ordinary multiple of the exponent of
$T$, not merely be larger than $T$ or a few of its powers (25).

\begin{remark}[One threshold, three readings \merge]\label{osq:sa:rem:threshold}
For $a>0$ and $b\ge0$ the following are equivalent: $a\ll b$; $q_a(\omega^b)=0$ in the binomial quotient $\Qa_a$ (\cref{osq:cr:thm:cutoff}, 24);
$\omega^b\sqrt{\omega^a-1}\in\Oz$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:radical}, 25); $\omega^bK_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}\subseteq\Pi$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:absorption}); and
$\omega^b/(1+\omega^a)\in\Oz$. All rest on one computation, the positivity of every exponent $b-ja$ of a binomial expansion in $\omega^{-a}$; 24's ideal
$\Pi^{\gg a}$ (\eqref{osq:cr:eq:tails}) is the set of $c\in\Pi$ with $\supp c\subseteq\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)^{\uparrow}$, the multipliers absorbing
$K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$ into $\Pi$. The two sources state the threshold independently, 24 as $b\gg a$ and 25 as ``$b>na$ for every $n$''.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Counterexamples at every finite order of differentiability.}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-smoothness flexibility \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:bumps}
Let $a\ll b$ and $T=\omega^a$. For an ordinary $\mathsf k\ge0$ put
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:bump}
 \mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x)=\begin{cases}\omega^b\,[x(T-x)]^{\mathsf k}\sqrt{x(T-x)},&0\le x\le T,\\ 0,&x<0\text{ or }x>T.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}$ is semialgebraic, globally $C^{\mathsf k}$ and not $C^{\mathsf k+1}$;
\item $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(\Oz)\subseteq\Pi$;
\item no finite family $P_1,\dots,P_s\in\No[X]$ has $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x)\in\{P_1(x),\dots,P_s(x)\}$ for every $x\in\Oz$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On $(0,T)$ the function is a positive algebraic branch of
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:bumpeq}
 Y^2=\omega^{2b}[X(T-X)]^{2\mathsf k+1},\qquad Y>0,
\end{equation}
which with the zero branches outside $[0,T]$ is a finite semialgebraic description. Near $0$ on the right, $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x)=\omega^bx^{\mathsf
k+1/2}(T-x)^{\mathsf k+1/2}$, the second factor being smooth near $0$ with value $T^{\mathsf k+1/2}\ne0$; derivatives of order $j\le\mathsf k$ have smallest
power $x^{\mathsf k+1/2-j}$, which tends to $0$, and the same at $T$ with $T-x$, so all derivatives through order $\mathsf k$ match the zero branches (for
$\mathsf k=0$ this is continuity). The $\mathsf k$th derivative is $A_0x^{1/2}+o(x^{1/2})$ with $A_0=\omega^bT^{\mathsf k+1/2}(\mathsf k+\frac12)(\mathsf
k-\frac12)\cdots\frac32\ne0$ (the empty product being $1$ for $\mathsf k=0$), so its difference quotient at $0$ is unbounded as $x\downarrow0$ and
$\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}$ is not $C^{\mathsf k+1}$; these are order-topological statements, valid with infinite $T$ and $\omega^b$ since arbitrarily small
surreal radii may be chosen for a prescribed surreal tolerance. For omnific $x\in[0,T]$, $x$ and $T-x$ lie in $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$, and so do
their product, its square root and its powers; multiplication by $\omega^b$ moves the value into $\Pi$ (\cref{osq:sa:thm:absorption}), and outside $[0,T]$
the value is $0$. For (iii), $P(X)^2-\omega^{2b}[X(T-X)]^{2\mathsf k+1}\ne0$ for every $P\in\No[X]$, since the second term has odd multiplicity $2\mathsf
k+1$ at the distinct roots $0,T$ and a square has even multiplicities; so $P$ agrees with $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}$ at finitely many points of $(0,T)$, and
finitely many such sets cannot cover the ordinary positive integers, which all lie in $(0,T)$.
\end{proof}

With $a=1$ and $b=\omega$ this is 25's overview Theorem~1.2. Assertion (iii) is stronger than failing to be piecewise polynomial on a finite
semialgebraic partition: even with arbitrary pieces, finitely many polynomial formulas do not suffice. The family shows that no coefficient-independent finite regularity order forces global
polynomiality; it does not contradict \cref{osq:sa:thm:degree}, because the degree of \eqref{osq:sa:eq:bumpeq} grows with $\mathsf k$ (25).

\begin{corollary}[Bounds for the least regularity order \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:regularity}
Let $\mathsf s(\mathsf D)$ be the least $s_0\ge0$ such that every globally $C^{s_0}$ semialgebraic preserver $\No\to\No$ of $\Oz$ with a degree-$\mathsf D$ graph
description is a polynomial. Then $\mathsf s(1)=1$, and $1+\lfloor(\mathsf D-2)/4\rfloor\le\mathsf s(\mathsf D)\le\mathsf D^2$ for every $\mathsf D\ge2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The upper bound is \cref{osq:sa:thm:degree}. For $\mathsf D=1$, $|X|$ is a continuous nonpolynomial preserver with a degree-one description. For $\mathsf
D\ge2$ put $\mathsf k=\lfloor(\mathsf D-2)/4\rfloor$: the description of $\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}$ has total degree at most $4\mathsf k+2\le\mathsf D$, its
only high-degree atom being \eqref{osq:sa:eq:bumpeq} and its cutoff and sign conditions linear, so \cref{osq:sa:thm:bumps} gives $\mathsf s(\mathsf D)>\mathsf k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite-smoothness shears \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:shears}
For $\mathsf k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Sh}_{\mathsf k}(x,y)=(x,y+\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x))$ is a semialgebraic $C^{\mathsf k}$ diffeomorphism of $\No^2$ with
Jacobian determinant $1$ that restricts to a bijection of $\Oz^2$, and no finite family of polynomial maps represents it on $\Oz^2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y-\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x))$ has the same regularity and preserves $\Oz^2$; the Jacobian matrix is
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}'(x)&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. A finite polynomial representation, restricted to the line $y=0$ and
to the second coordinate, would contradict \cref{osq:sa:thm:bumps}(iii).
\end{proof}

These are maps of the lattice as a set, not ring automorphisms, and the Jacobian statement is a triangular calculation, not a claim about the Jacobian
conjecture. Under $z=x+iy$, $z\mapsto x+i(y+\mathfrak b_{\mathsf k}(x))$ is a real-semialgebraic bijection of $\GOz$ that is not holomorphic in general
(25). They are not polynomial automorphisms, so they do not bear on \cref{osq:ft:q:maps}(c), and 16's and 22's shears (\cref{osq:ft:ex:shear}) are
polynomial.

\paragraph{Surcomplex consequences.}

\begin{theorem}[Surcomplex smooth classification \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:complexreal}
Identify $\SC^r$ with $\No^{2r}$. A globally $C^\infty$ real-semialgebraic map $\SC^r\to\SC^{r'}$ preserves $\GOz^r$ if and only if every real and
imaginary coordinate lies in $\Num_{2r}(\Oz)$, that is, has a finite binomial expansion \eqref{osq:sa:eq:newton} with omnific coefficients in the $2r$ real
coordinates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\Cref{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany,osq:sa:cor:explicit} under $\GOz^r=\Oz^{2r}$.
\end{proof}

The statement concerns the actual surcomplex lattice but is deliberately real-algebraic: it presupposes no global surreal exponential, no global sine and
no topology in which all real analytic series converge (25).

\begin{corollary}[Holomorphic polynomial rigidity \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:holomorphic}
If such a map also satisfies the Cauchy--Riemann equations in every complex input coordinate, each coordinate is a polynomial in $z_1,\dots,z_r$ alone,
with coefficients in $\SC$, and is $\GOz$-valued on $\GOz^r$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{osq:sa:thm:complexreal} a coordinate is a polynomial in the $x_j,y_j$; the invertible linear substitution $x_j=(z_j+\bar z_j)/2$,
$y_j=(z_j-\bar z_j)/(2i)$ makes it a polynomial in the $z_j,\bar z_j$, whose formal $\bar z_j$-derivatives vanish by the Cauchy--Riemann equations; in
characteristic $0$ all positive powers of the $\bar z_j$ then have zero coefficients.
\end{proof}

In one variable the coefficient ring is \cref{osq:pm:thm:numgaussian} with $r=1$: the polynomials $P\in\SC[Z]$ with $P(\GOz)\subseteq\GOz$ are
$\Int(\Z[i])\oplus\Pi_\C[Z]$ additively. This is 25's Proposition~9.3, whose proof (interpolation at $0,\dots,d$ and coefficientwise constant terms) is
10's, and 25 credits it; it is not a Gaussian binomial-basis theorem, ordinary binomial polynomials need not be $\Z[i]$-valued on $\Z[i]$
(\cref{osq:pm:rem:gaussnewton}), and the smooth classification must be combined with this Gaussian coefficient condition (25).

\paragraph{Sampling and exceptional sets.} For polynomials of known degree finite interpolation gives exact tests; smooth algebraic branches of fixed
degree behave differently (25).

\begin{theorem}[No coefficient-independent set of quadratic tests \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:thm:nosettests}
For every set $S\subseteq\Oz$ there is $b>0$ such that the globally $C^\infty$ semialgebraic function
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:testfunction}
 \mathsf r_b(x)=\omega^b\sqrt{x^2+1}
\end{equation}
satisfies $\mathsf r_b(S)\subseteq\Pi$ but does not preserve $\Oz$. Its graph is one branch of an irreducible polynomial equation of total degree $2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The supports of the $\sqrt{s^2+1}$, $s\in S$, form a set; take $b>0$ with $b+\gamma>0$ for every exponent $\gamma$ in their union (\cref{osq:lem:gap}), so
$\mathsf r_b(S)\subseteq\Pi$. At the omnific monomial $x_b=\omega^{b+1}$ the formal binomial expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:sa:eq:testfailure}
 \mathsf r_b(x_b)=\omega^{2b+1}+\tfrac12\,\omega^{-1}-\tfrac18\,\omega^{-2b-3}+\cdots,
\end{equation}
with strictly decreasing exponents since $b>0$; the coefficient of $\omega^{-1}$ is $\frac12\ne0$ and cannot cancel, so $\mathsf r_b(x_b)\notin\Oz$. The
graph is the positive branch of $Y^2-\omega^{2b}(X^2+1)=0$, which is irreducible in $\No[X,Y]$: a factorization of this monic quadratic in $Y$ would make
$X^2+1$ a square in $\No(X)$, contrary to the simple roots $\pm i$ in $\SC$. Since $x^2+1>0$ everywhere, $\mathsf r_b$ is semialgebraic and $C^\infty$ on
$\No$.
\end{proof}

The adversary is severe: a globally smooth branch of an irreducible quadratic graph, whose degree stays $2$ while the scale of its coefficient changes with
the test set (25). There is no contradiction with \cref{osq:sa:cor:irreducible}, which assumes preservation at every lattice point, nor with
coefficient-adapted tests: once $b$ is known, \eqref{osq:sa:eq:testfailure} gives a bad point. 16's and 22's witnesses for \cref{osq:fs:thm:nosmall},
$\omega^\beta/(X-\frac12)$ and $\omega^{\omega b}/(X+t+\frac12)$ (\cref{osq:ft:rem:deceiver}), are rational functions of degree one with a pole in $\No$
(outside $\Lambda$); $\mathsf r_b$ has no pole, is globally smooth, and has graph degree $2$.

\begin{corollary}[Removal of set-sized exceptions \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:exceptions}
Let $f:\No\to\No$ be semialgebraic and globally $C^\infty$. If $\{x\in\Oz:f(x)\notin\Oz\}$ is a set, it is empty and $f\in\Num_1(\Oz)$; a globally smooth
semialgebraic function that fails to preserve $\Oz$ fails on a proper class of omnific inputs.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A set of surreals is bounded above, so the exceptions miss a final ray; the one-sided form of \cref{osq:sa:thm:tails} gives a numerical polynomial on a
positive tail, and \cref{osq:sa:lem:identity} extends the equality to $\No$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Removal of exceptions in several variables \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:cor:exceptionsmany}
Let $f:\No^r\to\No^{r'}$ be globally $C^\infty$ and semialgebraic. If the set of bad lattice inputs is a set, $f$ is a coordinatewise numerical polynomial
and has no bad lattice input.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The coordinate projections of the exceptional set are sets, hence bounded. On each coordinate line with the other coordinates fixed in $\Oz$, all
sufficiently large positive lattice inputs are good, and the one-sided tail theorem with the identity principle makes each output coordinate on that line a
numerical polynomial; evaluating at the chosen coordinate shows that every lattice point is good. Apply \cref{osq:sa:thm:smoothmany}.
\end{proof}

The two results are complementary: every fixed set of witnesses is fooled by a new coefficient scale, yet every nonpreserving smooth semialgebraic function
has more bad inputs than a set can hold. This is a proper-class quantifier phenomenon, not a statement about running time (25). For rational functions the
same alternative is \cref{osq:fs:thm:cosmall} (one variable, 16) and \cref{osq:ft:thm:exceptions} (several, 22).

\begin{remark}[Smoothness cannot be dropped \merge]\label{osq:sa:rem:exceptionsnecessary}
For every ordinary $\mathsf k\ge0$ the function $f(x)=\frac12(1-4x^2)^{\mathsf k+1}$ on $|x|\le\frac12$, and $0$ elsewhere, is semialgebraic and globally
$C^{\mathsf k}$ (its derivatives through order $\mathsf k$ vanish at $\pm\frac12$), and its set of bad omnific inputs is $\{0\}$, since $\Oz\cap
[-\frac12,\frac12]=\{0\}$. So \cref{osq:sa:cor:exceptions} fails for $C^{\mathsf k}$ in place of $C^\infty$, and nonempty set-sized exceptional sets occur.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Set-sized models and the role of rank.} The bounded-window construction is not an artifact of proper classes; the no-set-test theorem, by
contrast, uses scales beyond an arbitrary set (25).

\begin{proposition}[A set-sized realization \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:prop:setmodel}
Let $\Gamma=\Q\times\Q$ with the lexicographic order, $a=(0,1)$, $b=(1,0)$, $E=\hahn\R\Gamma$ with reverse well-ordered supports and $X^g$ written
$\omega^g$, and $B=\Z\oplus\{x\in E:\supp x\subseteq\Gamma_{>0}\}$. Then $E$ is real closed, $B$ is an integer part of $E$, and the functions
\eqref{osq:sa:eq:bump} with $T=\omega^a$ and multiplier $\omega^b$ satisfy (i)--(iii) of \cref{osq:sa:thm:bumps} with $E,B$ in place of $\No,\Oz$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$\Gamma$ is divisible, so $E$ is real closed; truncating positive support and flooring the constant coefficient, with the correction for a negative
infinitesimal remainder, gives an integer part. For every ordinary $n$, $b>na$, and the convex subgroup generated by $a$ is $\{0\}\times\Q$, which is
divisible; the absorption, the endpoint calculation and the square obstruction apply unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The rank-one obstruction to the multiplier mechanism \src{25}]\label{osq:sa:prop:rankone}
Let $\Gamma\ne0$ be an Archimedean divisible ordered group and $a\in\Gamma_{>0}$. In $\hahn\R\Gamma$ with its normal-form integer part, no monomial
$\omega^b$, $b\in\Gamma$, sends $\sqrt x$ into the integer part for every integer-part input $x\in[0,\omega^a]$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For every $b\in\Gamma$ some ordinary $n$ has $b\le na$, and the expansion \eqref{osq:sa:eq:radical} at $x=\omega^a-1$ has negative support.
\end{proof}

This limits the uniform monomial multiplier only; it does not classify the semialgebraic preservers in rank one, and nonmonomial multipliers or other
input domains need separate analysis (25). It is the analogue of the fixed-workspace remark after \cref{osq:ft:prop:relative}: in an Archimedean group the
hypothesis of the method fails, which is not a proof that nonpolynomial preservers do not exist. The rigidity half, \cref{osq:sa:thm:tails,osq:sa:thm:smoothmany},
holds in every such Hahn field, since it needs only a cofinal discretely ordered subring of a real closed field; this matches 18's observation that
discrete-gap arguments survive in fixed workspaces (\cref{osq:or:cor:workspace}).

For $\No$ itself every normal-form support and every formula used is set-sized; the possibly proper-class $K_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}$ is used only through
its individual elements, finitely many at a time, and real closedness is reduced to the set-sized divisible hull of a finite support union. The absorption
theorem is checked on individual Hahn products. No class Zorn lemma, no set of all class ideals and no class-indexed product is used. In
\cref{osq:sa:thm:nosettests} there is a set-indexed support union, so an exponent above it exists; in \cref{osq:sa:thm:window} the inputs form a proper class
in general, and their exponents are controlled by the explicitly bounded convex group $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$. Confusing the two arguments would leave a
foundational gap, which is one reason to state the absorption theorem separately (25).

\paragraph{Dependencies and tempting errors (25).} The argument has two largely independent halves. Rigidity (tails, smooth classification, the
$\mathsf D^2$ threshold) uses real closed semialgebraic calculus, cofinality and the discrete gap, and needs surreal normal forms only for the final
numerical-polynomial reading; it needs neither lattice density nor infinite Taylor series. Flexibility (window absorption, the $C^{\mathsf k}$ examples)
uses normal forms, real closedness of support fields and a larger Archimedean exponent scale, not the tail theorem and not a set of all window inputs; the
quadratic no-set theorem uses a set support union and one explicit negative term, no undecidability assumption. 25 lists six places where an incorrect
argument is tempting.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Ordinary shifts are not cofinal: \eqref{osq:sa:eq:extrapolation} uses a large element of $B$ as its step, and moving an infinite negative point into a
positive tail by an ordinary integer would fail.
\item Finite differences vanish only after the discrete-gap argument: an estimate tending to zero is not an identity; the difference lies in $B$ and has
modulus below $1$ at lattice points, and semialgebraicity then extends the zero set to a ray.
\item The smooth identity principle is not available for arbitrary functions; the reciprocal-growth argument is why a semialgebraic function cannot be
infinitely flat where it stops vanishing.
\item The multiplier acts on supports, not on numerical approximations: $\omega^bK_{\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)}\subseteq\Pi$ because every shifted exponent is
positive, not because $|\omega^b\phi(x)|>1$.
\item The radical tail is an exact Hahn object: the proof at $T-1$ uses an infinite binomial series with distinct exponents and nonzero coefficients;
checking many terms cannot prove the threshold.
\item Set-sized and class-sized families differ: a support union over a sample set is a set, over all inputs of a bounded window it need not be, and the
latter case is controlled by $\operatorname{cvx}(\Z a)$, not by a union over a proper class.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Natural ordinal arithmetic is not a quotient of the omnific integers}\label{osq:sec:ordinal}

This section is manuscript~11's. Let $\mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}$ be the Grothendieck ring of the
ordinals under Hessenberg's natural sum and natural product. Every ordinal has a finite Cantor normal
form $\sum_jn_j\omega^{\gamma_j}$, each $\gamma_j$ has its own finite Cantor normal form
$\sum_\alpha m_{j,\alpha}\omega^\alpha$, and under natural multiplication
$\omega^{\gamma_j}=\prod_\alpha(\omega^{\omega^\alpha})^{m_{j,\alpha}}$. Uniqueness of these forms gives
the free commutative semiring $\N[T_\alpha:\alpha\in\On]$, and adjoining additive inverses gives
\begin{equation}\label{osq:eq:ordinalring}
 \mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}\cong\Z[T_\alpha:\alpha\in\On],
\end{equation}
with $T_\alpha$ represented by $\omega^{\omega^\alpha}$ under the natural embedding in $\No$. Natural
operations, not the usual noncommutative ordinal operations, are essential. The description
\eqref{osq:eq:ordinalring} appears in the question \cite{MO188430}; the argument above fixes the operations.

\begin{theorem}[The ordinal quotient question \src{11, 13}]\label{osq:thm:ordinal}
Every unital ring map $h:\Oz\to\mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has image exactly the ordinary integral
constants. In particular $\mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}$ is not isomorphic to a quotient ring of $\Oz$.
More generally, no ring map $\Oz\to\Z[X]$ with $X\ne\varnothing$ is surjective.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{First proof.} $\Z[X]$ is residually set-sized by \cref{osq:thm:residual} (for any class $X$ of
indeterminates), so $h$ kills $\Pi$ and factors through $\ct$; its image is $\Z$, a proper subring
since $T_0\notin\Z$.

\emph{Second proof, specific to this target.} The additive group of $\Pi$ is divisible
($s/n\in\Pi$ for every ordinary $n\ge1$), while no nonzero element of $\Z[T_\alpha]$ is divisible by
every $n$ (each of its finitely many integral coefficients would be). So every additive map from $\Pi$
to $\Z[X]$ is zero, and a unital ring map from $\Oz=\Z+\Pi$ has image $\Z$.
\end{proof}

The question was posted by Jesse Elliott as the final addition to MathOverflow question~188430,
``Transcendence degree of the surreals over the subfield generated by the ordinals'' (30 November 2014)
\cite{MO188430}; the displayed answer, by Eric Wofsey, concerns the transcendence degree, a different
question. The answer to the quotient question is negative. 11 gives the short additive proof precisely so
that the answer is not mistaken for a difficult new factorization theorem: no claim is made that the
elementary obstruction was unknown to specialists or absent from every other source. The first proof
illustrates the general residual theorem, and the second isolates the weaker mechanism that suffices for
this target. The obstruction is not a cardinal comparison, since both rings may be proper classes; it is
their divisibility and representation properties (11).

\begin{remark}[An independent answer \src{13}]\label{osq:str:rem:elliott}
Manuscript~13, dated a day after 11 and pinned to a repository commit that precedes 11's placement, answers the same addendum negatively with
the same two proofs: its lemma that every unital map from $\Oz$ into a ring $B$ with $\bigcap_nnB=0$ factors through
$\ct$ is the second proof above, and its route through the maps
$q_F:\mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}\to\Z[T_\alpha:\alpha\in F]$ ($F$ finite) and the universal theorem is the first
(its corollary for rings ``separated by set-sized ring targets'' is \cref{osq:thm:residual}). 13 adds that the
inclusion $\mathcal G_{\mathrm{nat}}\subset\Oz$ has no unital ring retraction, which is immediate since every unital map
has image $\Z$, and derives \eqref{osq:eq:ordinalring} from Cantor normal forms in the same way. 13 records that the
question writes the ring as $K[\Omega]$, with $K$ a Grothendieck construction; that notation was not rechecked for
this merge. 13 does not claim to answer the original transcendence-degree question, and states that its priority as
a first answer is not established.
\end{remark}

\section{Boundaries, non-claims and open questions}\label{osq:sec:boundaries}

\subsection{What the results do not say}\label{osq:sub:notsay}
The universal theorem is a statement about homomorphisms into set-sized rings and about
set-sized modules. It is not an isomorphism $\Oz\cong\Z$; it does not classify class ideals,
class modules, automorphisms or factorizations of $\Oz$; it concerns multiplicative maps and
says nothing against additive or valuation-theoretic observations; and it fails verbatim for every
fixed set-sized exponent group, whose identity map is a set-sized target. Size alone does not prove
it (finite supports have proper-class many monomials and an augmentation), nor does divisibility
alone (only targets of positive characteristic are handled). The set-sized thresholds are exact
for the five constructions and the two fixed-group examples treated; no classification of exponent
groups or support restrictions is claimed, and generator counts follow no general law stated here.
The large-quotient results describe specified subalgebras of $\Oz/(1+\omega^a)$ and conditional
statements about primes; no existence theorem for nonarithmetic class primes is claimed. (Status (batch 34): the eighth-batch addition proves
one with global choice, \cref{osq:cr:thm:binomialmax}; without global choice, and for $\Oz$ specifically, the question of \cref{osq:cr:q:choice}
remains, and the nonarithmetic primes and maximal ideals are not classified.)
The later additions do not change this. The flat and projective dimensions of \cref{osq:hd:sec:cores} are those of
set-sized finite-support cores, of coefficient-lattice modules and of the rings of \cref{osq:sec:homological}; they
say nothing about the homological dimensions of the class ring $\Oz$, and a flat dimension computed for one subring of
$\Oz$ bounds nothing for another (\cref{osq:hd:rem:reconcile}). The finite-support cores are not invisible to set-sized
rings, only to finite ones (\cref{osq:hd:prop:finite}). The fresh-scale theorems concern polynomials and rational
functions with finitely many coefficients and use the whole surreal exponent class, or a fixed Hahn workspace in which the coefficient group
generates a proper convex subgroup (\cref{osq:ft:prop:relative}). Nor do the third-batch additions:
the relation counts and $\Tor$ groups of \cref{osq:rel:sub:relations} concern the lattice ideals $J_g(M)$ and constant
matrices at one common scale, not arbitrary finitely generated ideals; the ordinary-output dichotomy is a one-variable
statement; and the fibre theorem of \cref{osq:nf:sub:fibre} gives no membership test for $\NN$. The fourth-batch addition
determines of $\Idem(\NN/\Pi\NN)$ that it is nontrivial, atomless and a proper class with independent families of every set size,
not its isomorphism type, and its descent theorem is not a decision procedure; its fixed-workspace statements concern reduced
fibres and assert neither radicality of $\Pi(G)\NN(G)$ nor atomlessness of $\Idem(\mathsf C(G))$ (\cref{osq:bb:sub:branching}; status of batch 32:
for cyclic $G$ the seventh-batch addition decides both, the first negatively and the second positively, \cref{osq:rm:sub:cyclic}).
Nor does the fifth-batch addition: its exact projective dimensions are those of the set-sized cores $A_d$ and of specified modules over
them, not global or weak global dimensions and not those of $\Oz$; its $\Tor$ statements over the class ring are read in two universes;
and its reconstruction of an order needs the framed boundary data (\cref{osq:da:sub:derived}).
Nor does the sixth-batch addition: its certificates are relative to exact arithmetic, its rational bound and its Gaussian grid are not claimed
optimal, its birational corollary assumes a rational inverse, and its fixed-workspace criterion says when its method applies, not that finite
tests fail otherwise (\cref{osq:ft:sub:tests}).
Nor does the seventh-batch addition: it concerns one cyclic exponent group, its root refinements and their bounded-denominator union, not
arbitrary groups or support classes or the Hahn field over $\Q a$; its residue criterion is a criterion, not an algorithm; of the uncountable
Boolean algebras it determines atomlessness, cardinality and order density, not the isomorphism type; and its periodic resolution and infinite
